t: Marini's theory of super-exploitation and its contemporary value
st: Theoretical innovation grounded in the dilemma of dependent development in Latin America
zh: 马里尼的超级剥削理论及其当代价值——基于拉丁美洲依附发展困境的理论创新
paras: Why did economic growth in mid-twentieth-century Latin America bring deepening poverty rather than general prosperity? Liu Xi takes up this question through Ruy Mauro Marini's theory of super-exploitation, set out in Dialectics of Dependency. The article argues that the theory is an independent and still valuable contribution: dependent capitalism offsets value lost in unequal international exchange by pushing workers' wages below the value of labour-power.

The article has three parts. It first reconstructs Latin American debates over whether super-exploitation fits Marx's Capital, both on its nature and on whether it is general or exceptional. It then sets out Marini's main contributions: an independent category, a mechanism for peripheral accumulation, and an account of structural inequality in the capitalist system. Finally it assesses the theory's present-day value, drawing on Foster, Harvey and John Smith.

On the nature of super-exploitation, Liu contrasts Hugo Figueira Corrêa and Marcelo Dias Carcanholo, who treat it as pre-capitalist 'plunder' and a temporary deviation, with Jaime Osorio, who sees it as exploitation specific to dependency. Liu sides with the view that it combines the features of plunder with the substance of exploitation, and that it is the law of surplus value working under unequal conditions in the world market. Core countries keep labour relations relatively mild by shifting contradictions onto the periphery, while peripheral capital compensates by cutting labour-reproduction costs. Liu also presents Marini as extending Marx's remark in Capital, Volume III, on wages pushed below the value of labour-power as a counteracting factor to the falling rate of profit. In this reading Marini turned an incidental fluctuation into a standing feature and gave exploitation analysis a spatial dimension.

Liu concludes that super-exploitation explains twenty-first-century imperialism, including global value chains, financial expansion, platform and gig work, and value transfer without direct colonisation. The article also holds that it underpins solidarity among workers in the Global South, illustrating this with Brazil's 'economic miracle' of 1964–74. It calls on the global left to build an internationalist alliance against imperialism and neo-colonialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language survey of the Latin American dependency debate and of how Marini's concept is being applied to the contemporary world system.
quoteEn: Super-exploitation is the necessary outcome of the law of surplus value unfolding in space, and it cannot be treated as an exception outside capitalism's general law of valorisation.
quoteZh: 超级剥削成为剩余价值规律在空间上展开的必然结果，不能将其视为资本主义一般增殖规律之外的例外。

glossary.explanation: A term for developing and formerly colonised countries, widely used in Chinese official and academic discourse. Here it refers to the peripheral economies whose workers are said to bear super-exploitation.

t: Moving forward through reflection and critique, debate and reconstruction: developments in foreign Marxism in 2025
zh: 在反思与批判、争论与重构中不断前行——2025年国外马克思主义发展动态
paras: This is an annual survey of Marxist scholarship outside China in 2025, published in World Socialism Studies in 2026. Wang sets it against deepening global ecological crisis, accelerating technological revolution, sharper gender and racial problems in Western societies, and unusual intellectual ferment. The survey holds that foreign Marxism advanced through reflection and critique, debate and reconstruction, and that this is how the theory builds its explanatory, critical and practical force.

The review is organised around four fields: Frankfurt School critical theory, ecological Marxism, Marxist feminism, and research on digital capitalism. For each it reports new books, seminars and journal articles, naming scholars from Germany, Britain, the United States, Canada, Italy, Japan and elsewhere. A short conclusion draws out four general features of the year's work.

Wang reports the main debates in each field. On critical theory, scholars such as Lukas Meisner and Lauren Langman affirm its emancipatory value, while Lois McNay, Amy Allen and John Bellamy Foster criticise its normative turn and Western Marxism's "four retreats" (from class struggle, from anti-imperialism, from materialism and from reason). In ecological Marxism, Ian Angus and Foster defend Marx's ecological thought and the Anthropocene concept; Jason W. Moore rejects the latter, and Kohei Saito's degrowth communism is judged by Roulx and Fritsch to be original but ahistorical and strategically hesitant. On digital capitalism, Christian Fuchs's account of digital labour is set against the claims of Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean that capitalism has become technofeudal or neo-feudal. Nicholas Gane and Radhika Desai reject that claim, arguing that rent, monopoly and profit remain capitalist categories. In Marxist feminism, Wang covers renewed interest in the 1970s wages-for-housework movement and the turn towards intersectionality.

Wang's conclusion identifies four features: the established currents and their core issues still dominate; historical and contemporary studies coexist; reflective and critical work sets the tone and drives theoretical innovation; and the practical guidance of these theories remains weak. Examples given are the unclear measure and path of degrowth, the difficulty of uniting different gender groups, and the problem of organising digital workers to strike. Wang also evaluates individual positions, finding Foster's critique of Western Marxism apt and Fuchs's digital socialism somewhat utopian. Read the original if you want a map of the year's debates in foreign Marxism, with named scholars and titles, as seen from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
quoteEn: Some foreign Marxist scholars put forward fairly innovative theoretical views, but these are not very workable and clearly lack practical guiding force.
quoteZh: 一些国外马克思主义学者提出的理论观点比较有创新性，但其可操作性不强，实践指导力明显不足。

t: The history, present and future of the Danish communist movement
st: An interview with Lotte Rørtoft-Madsen, chair of the Communist Party (Denmark)
zh: 丹麦共产主义运动的历史、现状与未来——访共产党（丹麦）主席洛特·于特夫特·麦德森
paras: This is an interview, published in World Socialism Studies (2026, no. 1), in which two Chinese researchers question the chair of the Communist Party (Denmark), identified in the Chinese text as Lotte Yutefute Maideseng. They ask about the history of Danish communism, the party's current situation, Danish social movements and capitalist crisis, and the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The interviewee presents a movement that is divided and not yet in a position to lead, but that she sees as growing.

The first part runs from the founding of organised communism in 1919 to the present. It covers the interwar years, the wartime resistance against German occupation, the Cold War splits, the Sino-Soviet divide and the Maoist-oriented groups of the 1960s. It then turns to the crisis after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern European socialist regimes. The later parts take up the party's present tasks, the Nordic welfare state, the far right, and China's role in the world.

On history, the interviewee stresses that the Danish resistance succeeded through a broad popular front, which she attributes to communist initiative and links to the Comintern's 1935 strategy. She traces the later fragmentation into three parties and the 2006 merger that created the Communist Party (Denmark), and says the party aims to shift the balance of forces towards the working class through an anti-monopoly alliance. On welfare, she argues that the Nordic system was won by organised labour through class struggle, not granted by the bourgeoisie, and is not a bridge to socialism. She adds that it is being dismantled now that the pressure of European socialism has gone. She describes neo-fascism as fed by decades of neoliberalism, and holds that a full communist revival in Denmark would be premature to proclaim.

On China, she calls the 1949 revolution one of the twentieth century's most important events and describes China as upholding socialism while Europe's collapsed. She presents China as a counterweight to the transatlantic alliance and says her party opposes what she calls a new Cold War and interference in China's internal affairs. She says her party will counter rumours about China in the Danish left. Read the original if you want a Danish communist leader's account of her party's history, strategy and view of China, as presented to a Chinese academic audience.
quoteEn: The welfare system became possible because the working class, through unrelenting class struggle, changed the balance of power between labour and capital.
quoteZh: 福利制度之所以能够实现，是因为工人阶级通过不懈的阶级斗争改变了劳动与资本之间的力量平衡。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of building socialism since reform and opening up. It is used to describe China's political and economic system.

t: The implications of capital power in Foucault's theory of power: a reflection from Althusser's perspective
zh: 福柯权力理论中的资本权力意蕴——基于阿尔都塞视角的反思
paras: Dong Jianming asks how Michel Foucault's analyses of power, especially his biopolitics, can be related to Marx's critique of political economy without simply grafting one onto the other. The article argues that Louis Althusser's theory of repressive and ideological state apparatuses can serve as a theoretical bridge. Through it, Dong contends, the 'capital power' implicit in Foucault's account becomes visible, and the basis is laid for a theory of capital power consistent with Marx.

The article has three parts. The first presents Foucault's method (archaeology and genealogy), his rejection of both 'economism' and the 'economic functionality' of power, and his resulting 'non-economic' analysis of power. The second turns to Althusser's analysis of power in terms of the reproduction of the conditions of production, and the third reconstructs Foucault's themes through that lens. It addresses disciplinary power and biopolitics, the 'war' model of power, and liberal governmentality, and ends with remarks on digital capitalism and socialist governance.

Dong argues that by detaching power from economic analysis Foucault produced a 'descriptive theory' of power, in Althusser's sense of a first stage that has not yet become theory proper. Althusser, by contrast, insists that critique of oppression must not replace critique of exploitation. He shows how repressive and ideological state apparatuses reproduce labour-power and the relations of production. Read this way, Dong claims, Foucault's disciplinary and biopolitical techniques serve to reproduce capitalist conditions of production; his proposition that power is war expresses class struggle; and his 'naturalness' of society and population is an ideology produced by the bourgeoisie, so that his history of power is in fact the history of capitalism's self-reproduction.

Dong concludes that a sound theory of capital power must tie power mechanisms to exploitation and capital's logic and must retain class analysis, since Marx held that population without classes is an abstraction. It should also avoid confusing critique of capital with critique of digital technology, as in Byung-Chul Han's Heideggerian approach. Socialism, Dong adds, cannot simply adopt liberal governmentality; it must work towards a proletarian state apparatus beyond the bourgeois one, a point the author says matters for China's modernization. Read the original if you study Foucault–Marx relations, Althusser's state apparatus theory, or Chinese Marxist debates on power and governance.
quoteEn: What Foucault has formed is a descriptive theory of power, one that has not yet been raised from descriptive theory to theory proper.
quoteZh: 福柯所形成的是一种关于权力的描述性理论，还没有将描述性理论上升为理论本身。

glossary.explanation: A concept in recent Chinese Marxist scholarship for the power relations and mechanisms that serve capitalist exploitation and the self-expansion of capital. The article uses it to name the substance of power under capitalism.
Althusser's term for institutions such as schools, family, churches and media that function mainly through ideology and help reproduce the relations of production.

t: Quasi-cause of affect, or empty set of the state of the situation? A comparison of Deleuze's and Badiou's conceptions of the event
zh: 是情动的准原因，还是情势状态的空集?——德勒兹与巴迪欧事件观比较
paras: Sun Lin compares the conceptions of the event in Gilles Deleuze and Alain Badiou. The article starts from what it calls the "overflow" of presence, the problem both thinkers share with phenomenology, structuralism and post-structuralism after Hegel and Marx. Its thesis is that the two form a "paradoxical pair": both stand on a materialist ground, criticise Hegel's "One" and rebuild the Spinozist trinity, yet Deleuze moves toward a "relative nothing" and Badiou toward the "void" or empty set.

Sun notes that the comparison is well established abroad, citing Badiou and Žižek, but has barely begun in Chinese scholarship. The body has three parts: the rebirth of the subject (body, intuition, difference); the rifts in the object (repetition, multiplicity, exception); and the event's inner drive (immanence, power, cause). A final section sets out similarities, differences and implications, with references to Spinoza, Bergson, Husserl, Heidegger, Foucault, Althusser and Lacan.

In Sun's reading, Deleuze starts from the body and temporal intuition. Difference is infinitesimal and the event is a "quasi-cause", an immanent force (affect) that repeats creatively and moves toward a unified ideal event. Badiou rejects intuition and repetition. He works with set theory: the event site is a multiple on the edge of the void, "fidelity" and "generic forcing" proceed from there, and the event ruptures the "state of the situation" rather than flowing from it. Sun argues this makes Deleuze's epistemology closer to Foucault's, with a break that does not sever, and Badiou's closer to Althusser's structural rupture.

Sun finds four points of agreement with historical materialism. These are that history develops from within, that capitalist ideology and reification must be opposed, that the new subject rests on a community of individuals, and that creative collective action and mutual love drive world history. The differences are continuity versus rupture, "relative nothing" versus void, and how a rupture can be acted on. Sun adds that Badiou proclaims himself anti-humanist but in practice sides with Sartre. The article ends with a warning not to let historical materialism drift from the dialectic of productive forces and relations of production. Read the original if you work on Deleuze, Badiou or French post-war philosophy and want a Chinese Marxist reading that links their ontologies to Hegel, Spinoza and historical materialism.
quoteEn: Both Deleuze and Badiou hold a kind of \"new trinity\" thought, which in some way reconstructs Spinoza's trinity of substance, cause and power.
quoteZh: 德勒兹与巴迪欧都有某种“新三一体”思想，对斯宾诺莎的实体、原因、力的三一体存在某种重构性。

t: Communicative capitalism, neofeudalism and the latest developments in capitalism
st: An interview with the American Marxist political theorist Jodi Dean
zh: 交往资本主义、新封建主义与资本主义的最新动态——访美国马克思主义政治理论家乔蒂·迪恩教授
paras: This is an interview, published in World Socialism Studies (2025, no. 12), in which Wang Yin and Chang Yutong question Jodi Dean, a Marxist political theorist who teaches politics at Hobart and William Smith Colleges in the United States. Dean is known for the concepts of "communicative capitalism" and "neofeudalism". The interview asks her to explain them, to assess where capitalism is heading, and to comment on communism and on China.

The questions move from communicative capitalism and its link to Habermas, through artificial intelligence and the "attention economy" of her book Blog Theory, to neofeudalism as a tendency inside capitalism. They then turn to her new introduction to The Communist Manifesto, her reading of Marx on communism, and her book Comrade. The last two questions invite her impressions of socialism with Chinese characteristics and of Chinese modernization.

Dean says communicative capitalism arises from the fusion of democratic ideals and capitalist logic. Openness, inclusion and participation are realised materially through global networks, yet this produces tech billionaires, the far right, lost trust and isolation, not a more rational society. She reads Habermas materially, as the ideology of "technoculture". She sees AI as a bid by tech firms and the US government to restore growth and hegemony after 2008, with job losses, damage to education and heavy resource use. Neofeudalism, in her account, is an internal tendency of capitalism: growth slows, accumulation depends on rents, services and finance, and asset-holders use the state to redistribute wealth upwards. She tracks it across the state, class relations, space and subjectivity, citing Trump, Musk, Adani and Modi as examples.

Dean argues that the Manifesto is still relevant, perhaps more than in the nineteenth century. She holds that communism requires public ownership and planning, cannot be built in one country alone, and keeps the principle "from each according to ability, to each according to need". She presents "comrade" as a distinct political bond that helps build communist habits. On China, she says her expertise is not modernization theory and her view is intuitive. She credits the Communist Party's leadership and its use of markets within a planned, collective framework, and contrasts this with what she calls the anarchic and imperialist character of Western capitalist modernization. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist's own short statement of communicative capitalism and neofeudalism, or her views on China as put to a Chinese journal.
quoteEn: I theorise \"neofeudalism\" as a tendency within capitalism, a form generated by capitalism's internal contradictions.
quoteZh: 我将“新封建主义”理论化为资本主义内部的一种趋势，是资本主义内部矛盾所催生的一种形态。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism combining Party leadership, public ownership and market mechanisms. It has been used since the early 1980s.
The Party's official term for China's own path of modernization, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.

t: British Marxist historiography and the study of the popular radical tradition
zh: 英国马克思主义史学对大众激进传统的研究
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 9 January 2026
paras: This short commentary in a Chinese social-science newspaper asks how British Marxist historians came to study the popular radical tradition and what that work still offers. Chang and Liang argue that, from the 1960s, these historians recovered a strong and continuous tradition of popular radicalism. In doing so they renewed historical method and supplied intellectual resources for understanding present-day crises and paths of change.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical context and intellectual sources of the research in post-war British society. The second identifies five features of its approach. The third traces its spread and current uses since the 1990s. The authors draw on Edward Thompson, Eric Hobsbawm, Christopher Hill, Dorothy Thompson, Raymond Challinor, George Rudé, John Saville and others.

On origins, the authors say post-war changes in the working class and the rise of radical movements pushed historians from "high politics" towards social and economic processes and the everyday life of ordinary people. They also stress a direct debate: Perry Anderson and the second-generation New Left held that reformism had suppressed revolutionary Marxism, leaving the English working class without real revolutionary character. Hill and Thompson countered that a powerful radical tradition existed but had been hidden by reformist narratives. The five features are a focus on inequality and marginal groups, opposition to economic determinism, attention to how radical ideas spread, critical analysis of power relations, and an explicit socialist political engagement. The authors acknowledge that some scholars criticise this last feature as over-politicisation.

Chang and Liang conclude that radical social history has rebuilt the subjects and content of historical writing. They report its influence on Western scholarship, on Latin American and African studies, and on subaltern studies and post-colonial identity research, where it is used to challenge Eurocentrism. They add that it now draws on feminism, post-colonial theory and cultural studies. In their view, as globalisation, inequality and ecological crisis deepen, its questions and methods remain an irreplaceable resource. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of how British Marxist social history is presented to Chinese readers and where its legacy is placed.
quoteEn: They stressed that Britain's history contained a powerful and continuous popular radical tradition, which had merely been obscured by reformist narratives.
quoteZh: 他们强调英国历史上存在强大而持续的大众激进传统，只不过被改良主义叙事所遮蔽。

t: New conditions, new tactics and new developments in the US communist movement: an interview with Haz Al-Din, executive chairman of the American Communist Party (ACP)
zh: 美国共产主义运动的新形势、新策略和新发展——美国共产党(ACP)执行主席哈兹·阿尔丁访谈
paras: This is an interview, conducted by Feng Jiaxin, a doctoral student at Peking University's School of Marxism, with Haz Al-Din, first executive chairman of the American Communist Party (ACP). The ACP was formed in 2024 by members who left the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) around its 32nd National Convention. The interview asks how the new party understands its origins, strategy and place in the US left, and how it views China.

The questions fall into three parts: the background to the ACP's founding and its differences from the CPUSA; its theory and practice, covering elections, Trump's second term, labour and welfare policy, inequality, digital organising, anti-communism, other left groups, foreign contacts and five-year goals; and its views on China's achievements. Al-Din answers at length on each topic.

Al-Din says the CPUSA has become a dependent adjunct of the Democratic Party and, in his words, a revisionist body, whereas the ACP stresses practice, discipline and 'socialist patriotism'. He criticises the US left, including the Democratic Socialists of America, for sectarianism and for losing touch with working people. The ACP does not expect to win the presidency. It aims to build local authority and survive an anticipated constitutional crisis, through community service, labour support and cooperatives. Its programme includes debt cancellation, nationalised banking and key industries, and five-year-plan-style coordination. Al-Din argues that Trump is unintentionally accelerating the decline of US hegemony.

On China, Al-Din calls it the most advanced socialist country and a model the ACP cites to Americans. He praises Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and Chinese modernization as dialectical and long-term, in contrast with a Western modernization driven by private profit. For the next five years the ACP seeks financial self-sufficiency, local footholds and the public standing the DSA has today. Read the original if you want a first-hand account of a new US communist party's strategy and of how its leader reads China, shown in a Chinese journal.
quoteEn: We do not fantasise about seizing state power in the short term; as far as we know, this may be a process lasting as long as ten years.
quoteZh: 我们并不幻想在短期内夺取国家权力，据我们所知，这可能是一个长达十年之久的过程。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Chinese Communist Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
The official name for China's development path, which the Party presents as distinct from Western modernization.
The official name for China's system since the reform era, combining Party leadership, a socialist market economy and public ownership as the main body.

t: Foreign Marxists' critique of capitalist modernization
zh: 国外马克思主义者对资本主义现代化的批判
paras: Ma Xinying asks how Marxists outside China have criticised capitalist modernization in the twenty-first century, and what that critique shows. The article argues that, even in the digital age, capitalist modernization remains a troublemaker in world modernization because of capitalism's inherent contradictions. In Ma's account, foreign Marxists combine Marx's critical stance with new theoretical resources to produce a new critique.

The article has three parts. The first surveys six strands of critique: digital capitalism, biopolitics, the modern state (including new imperialism), ecological crisis, space, and modern society (alienation and social acceleration). Thinkers discussed include Dan Schiller, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Giorgio Agamben, Roberto Esposito, Bob Jessop, Edward Soja, Rahel Jaeggi and Hartmut Rosa. The second part identifies three trends distinguishing this work from twentieth-century critique, and the third assesses its significance.

Ma's central claim concerns the three shifts. Critique moves from diachronic to synchronic, borrowing Saussure's terms: it no longer traces modernization's historical origins but cuts across its present features and their internal connections. It moves from critiquing modernity to critiquing modernization itself, because, Ma says, postmodern discourse has dissolved the authority of metaphysical reason and modernity's harms are now accepted as given. And it moves from socio-cultural to political critique, with hegemony, power, justice and biopower as key concepts, reactivated by the 2008 financial crisis.

Ma concludes that this critique exposes new contradictions of contemporary capitalism, which the article calls international financial monopoly capitalism. It also shows that a fragile planet cannot bear capitalist modernization, and that capitalism's private appropriation is increasingly incompatible with globalization. Ma notes that foreign Marxists such as John Bellamy Foster and David Kotz are less pessimistic than before, because socialist modernization offers a new point of reference. The article presents Chinese modernization as embodying a more progressive path of civilisation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how Western and foreign Marxist theories of digital capitalism, biopolitics, space and alienation are classified and evaluated in Chinese academic discourse.
quoteEn: The contradiction between twenty-first-century 'globalization' and 'capitalization' is not merely one between 'form and content'; it also signals that capitalist modernization is by no means a bright road to human civilisation.
quoteZh: 21世纪的“全球化”与“资本化”的矛盾不仅仅是“形式与内容”的矛盾，更预示着资本主义现代化绝非通向人类文明的光明之路。

glossary.explanation: Official Party term for China's own path of modernization, developed prominently since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as socialist and as an alternative to Western models.
A broad Chinese academic category covering Marxist thought developed outside China, including Western Marxism, ecological Marxism and post-Marxism.
A term, associated with Dan Schiller, for capitalism's fusion with computer networks and digital technology, which critics link to exploitation of digital labour and platform monopoly.

glossary.zh: 国际金融垄断资本主义
glossary.explanation: A Chinese Marxist characterisation of the current stage of capitalism, marked by globalised financial monopoly capital, transnational corporate alliances and financial dominance.

t: The property-rights logic of technological colonialism and its critique
zh: 技术殖民主义的产权逻辑及其批判
source: Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育), 2025 no. 6
paras: Yu Genxiong takes up the "technology cold war" fought over intellectual property, patents and copyright, and argues that Western capitalist states are using their technological advantage to practise a new form of colonialism. The article's thesis is that this technological colonialism rests on a property-rights logic: a fusion of technology-as-property and capital power. Yu contends that exposing and criticising this logic can check hegemonic attempts to crush other countries and support equal, mutually beneficial cooperation on technology rights.

The article has three parts. The first traces colonialism from old military conquest through neo-colonialism to technological colonialism, which Yu says now appears as an independent form. The second reconstructs its logical structure from the concepts of technology property rights and capital power. The third criticises technology property and the conception of rights built on it, drawing mainly on Marx's Grundrisse, Capital and the 1844 manuscripts, with references to Lenin, Marcuse and Stirner.

Yu identifies three features of technological colonialism: it is deeply concealed behind "voluntary" agreements and consumerist technology fetishism; it exerts systemic control over whole societies; and it is extremely oligarchic, producing technological impoverishment elsewhere. In the logic of this system, technology property is treated as an ideal, knowledge-based form of personal property, while capital power controls its monopoly, global spread and distribution. Yu answers that technology property is both a result and a precondition of labour, is the product of social rather than purely private labour, and unites the material and the ideal. On this reading, the claimed right to own it rests on three illusions: that property is simply a relation between people and things, that property rights are purely private, and that they are the exclusive advantage of certain nations, an idea Yu links to Eurocentrism and the theory of civilizational superiority.

Yu concludes that technological colonialism damages colonised countries systemically, harms the capitalist countries themselves by deepening the opposition between technology and labour, and obstructs technological progress through monopoly, citing Lenin on monopoly prices. The article argues that the fruits of human civilization should be distributed on the basis of an equal and open conception of rights. Read the original if you want a Marxist property-theory critique of Western technology monopoly and the "technology cold war" from a Chinese academic perspective.
quoteEn: The mutual interpenetration of technology property and capital power, and their linkage on a world-historical scale, constitute the property-rights logic of contemporary Western technological colonialism.
quoteZh: 技术财产与资本权力的相互渗透及其在世界历史意义上的勾连，构成了当代西方技术殖民主义的产权逻辑。

t: How to view right-wing populism in the United States
zh: 怎么看美国右翼民粹主义
paras: Wang Dong, a professor at Peking University's School of International Studies, asks how American right-wing populism should be understood. Writing in Qiushi in 2025, Wang argues that it is no accident but the product of intertwined economic, political and cultural factors, deliberately stoked by right-wing politicians. Wang describes a current that has become systematised, ideological and programmatic, with the "Make America Great Again" (MAGA) movement as its core driver.

The commentary has three parts: the roots of this populism, its distinguishing features, and its practical effects at home and abroad. The roots are traced along economic, political and cultural lines. The features include an anti-elite narrative, extreme nationalism, social-media mobilisation and an economic-geographic split. The effects cover democratic institutions, trade, social cohesion and foreign policy.

On causes, Wang points to the losses of industrial workers under neoliberal globalisation, citing Federal Reserve data for 2025 that the richest 0.1% of households hold 13.8% of national wealth and the bottom 50% hold 2.5%. Wang also points to representative democracy's failure, with money-driven politics, party polarisation and "veto politics". Wang gives most weight to identity and culture: since 2016, dispersed grievances have been recast as a "white working class versus immigrants" opposition, making populism the latest form of the long "culture war". Wang contrasts it with left-wing populism, which the author describes as rooted in urban and low-income groups on the coasts and aimed at redistribution. Right-wing populism, in Wang's account, rests on middle-class and Rust Belt white blue-collar voters and is more xenophobic and culturally conservative.

Wang judges that, although populism partly responds to the failure of traditional governance, it poses a serious challenge to America's internal and external development and to the international order. Wang cites the 6 January Capitol attack, tariffs, social division and withdrawals from multilateral bodies and agreements as evidence. Wang concludes that while structural problems remain unresolved, populism will keep resurfacing, and that studying it helps in grasping US policy and the global situation amid "changes unseen in a century". Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-journal author frames US populism and its global consequences.
quoteEn: It can be said that right-wing populism is the latest form of America's long-running "culture war" and the concentrated eruption, at the political level, of contradictions in the sphere of values.
quoteZh: 可以说，右翼民粹主义是美国长期“文化战争”的最新表现形式，也是价值观领域矛盾在政治层面的集中爆发。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese Communist Party Central Committee's main theoretical journal, published twice a month. Articles in it are widely read as reflecting official lines of argument.
A phrase used in Chinese official discourse since about 2017 for a perceived deep shift in the global balance of power and international order.

t: An analysis of the event-centred view of history in foreign Marxist theory
zh: 国外马克思主义理论中的事件史观探析
paras: How should historical change be understood when revolutions do not coincide with the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production? Hu Yaohui takes up this problem by tracing a lineage of "event-centred" views of history within Marxism outside China. These thinkers give priority to discontinuity, contingency and human agency over continuity, teleology and evolutionism. Hu argues that the lineage recovers real strengths of historical materialism but exaggerates rupture until the event becomes mystified, and that Marx's own event analysis offers the corrective.

The article moves through four sections. It begins with Walter Benjamin's "now-time" (Jetztzeit) in the Theses on the Philosophy of History, then turns to Louis Althusser's theory of the conjuncture and overdetermination, and then to Alain Badiou's theory of the event, with Slavoj Žižek and Giorgio Agamben mentioned as related figures. The final section reads Marx's The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte as a model of event analysis and uses it to criticise the three thinkers. Hu treats the October Revolution as the practical backdrop, since it undermined linear evolutionary history.

Hu reads Benjamin as breaking with homogeneous, empty time and with Social Democratic faith in progress. Benjamin's "real state of exception" is the event, but his appeal to messianism sits uneasily with materialism. Althusser, in Hu's reading, is better seen as a theorist of the conjuncture than a structuralist: the conjuncture contains an empty place filled only by action, though he never settled "determination in the last instance" by the economy and ended in an aleatory materialism of the encounter. Badiou pushes contingency to the absolute, so that event and being are severed, and Hu says this leaves a Kantian split and a dialectic that discards Hegel "with the bathwater". Against these, Hu reads the Brumaire as linking three levels: the economic base (long duration), class perspective (conjuncture) and the event (short duration). On this reading Marx admits contingency, even of personal character, while keeping it within class structure and the contradiction of productive forces and relations of production.

Hu concludes that these thinkers each emerged when the international communist movement was blocked, and that they share a view of the world as unclosed and reject Hegelian totality. Two criticisms follow. They grasp only conjuncture and event, not the longer time span, and so confuse contingency with openness; Hu cites Badiou's treatment of May 1968 as isolated rather than part of a world-historical wave. They also dilute class, whereas the proletariat remains the fundamental subject and needs a strong party, or action falls into voluntarist decisionism or a messianic view of miracles. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese-Marxist assessment of Benjamin, Althusser and Badiou on contingency and revolution, set against Marx's Brumaire.
quoteEn: What we need to do is strip the event of its metaphysical colouring, return to Marx's analysis of events, and place people back in real circumstances, attending to how people make history within basic social structures and the totalizing truth of history, so as to understand dialectically the tension between contingency and necessity, and between subject and structure.
quoteZh: 我们要做的是，去除事件的形而上学色彩，回归马克思的事件分析，重新将人放到现实的环境中，在基本的社会结构与历史的总体性真理中关注人如何创造历史，从而辩证地理解历史中偶然与必然、主体与结构之间的张力。

t: The four dimensions of foreign left-wing scholars' spatial critique of twenty-first-century capitalism
zh: 国外左翼学者对21世纪资本主义空间批判的四重维度
paras: Li Shule asks how Western left-wing scholars have reworked the critique of capitalist space for the twenty-first century. The article argues that the field has moved from Henri Lefebvre's "production of space" to the "production of spatial scale", which David Harvey and Neil Smith treat as the key to understanding contemporary capitalism. Li reconstructs this turn as four interlocking dimensions of critique: the global city, the new state space, the new world system and bodily space.

The article draws on Lefebvre, Harvey, Smith, Edward Soja, Manuel Castells, Saskia Sassen, Doreen Massey, Neil Brenner, Bob Jessop, Etienne Balibar, Neil Davidson, Alex Callinicos, Ellen Meiksins Wood and Peter Sloterdijk, among others. Each dimension gets its own section with two sub-themes: global-city landscape and power-geography networks; geopolitical effects of state restructuring and the rescaling of state space; uneven geography and new imperialism; and the political-economic and ontological critiques of the body. A concluding section sets out the logical order of the four dimensions and assesses their limits.

Li argues that capitalism reorganises urban scale to create global cities, then reshapes state space to stabilise accumulation, then rebuilds global scale into an asymmetric world order. Finally, it exploits workers through hierarchies of bodily scale. In Li's account Harvey's "body-scale" system measures differences in the value of workers' bodies in order to exploit dispersed, varied subjects collectively. Smith's examples include the displacement of homeless people from public space, while Sloterdijk's "crystal palace" is read as capital's interior space, which excludes those outside it. Li also defends the capital-logic/territorial-logic analysis of the new imperialism against Davidson's objection that it offers no deeper internal relations.

Li concludes that the four dimensions form a closed logical whole, running from the global city as starting point to the body as the point at which exploitation lands. The scholars' contribution, in Li's view, is to reveal how capitalist spatial domination operates across macro and micro scales, and the left must respond at the level of scale to set its political demands. Li also names three weaknesses: a drift towards "scale-centrism", a weakened Marxist class analysis, and no effective link between spatial critique and revolutionary practice. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Harvey and the geography of capitalism, or want a Chinese scholar's systematic assessment of this literature.
quoteEn: The shift among foreign left-wing scholars from the \"production of space\" to the \"production of spatial scale\" does not negate the basic theoretical paradigm of Lefebvre and others, but reflects the new multi-scalar, co-existing spatial forms of twenty-first-century capitalism.
quoteZh: 国外左翼学者从“空间的生产”到“空间尺度的生产”的研究转向，并非要否定列斐伏尔等学者对资本主义空间批判的基本理论范式，而是要反映21世纪资本主义所呈现出的多尺度融通与空间共存的新形态特征。

t: Foreign Marxists' critique of capitalist modernization
zh: 国外马克思主义者对资本主义现代化的批判
paras: Ma Xinying asks how Marxists outside China have criticised capitalist modernization in the twenty-first century, and what distinguishes this critique from that of the twentieth century. The article argues that, in the era of digital technology, capitalist modernization remains a "troublemaker" in world modernization because of capitalism's inherent contradictions. In Ma's account, foreign Marxists have combined Marx's critical stance with new theoretical resources to produce a new critique, marked by three shifts and carrying three kinds of significance.

The article has three parts. The first surveys six new lines of critique: digital capitalism, biopolitics, the modern state (including new imperialism), ecological crisis, space, and modern society. It draws on Dan Schiller, Hardt and Negri, Agamben, Esposito, Bob Jessop, Edward Soja, Rahel Jaeggi and Hartmut Rosa. The second part identifies three trends. The third part sets out what the critique reveals about contemporary capitalism, about the stage reached by modernization, and about hopes for the future.

Ma's central claim is that the critique has moved from diachronic to synchronic analysis, from critique of modernity to critique of modernization itself, and from socio-cultural to political critique. Borrowing Saussure's terms, Ma argues that twentieth-century critics traced the historical origins of capitalist modernization, whereas present-day critics cut across the present and ask how it shapes people's lives. Ma also argues that, after the 2008 financial crisis, themes such as hegemony, power, justice and biopower became the core of the critique. Ma contends that this critique exposes new contradictions: between expanding productive capacity and insufficient world demand, between financial predation and the financial sovereignty of developing countries, and between technological acceleration and alienation. Globalisation, in this view, is increasingly at odds with capitalist private appropriation.

Ma concludes that capitalism is not the only path of modernization and that the world is too fragile to bear its unlimited mode of development. Unlike their twentieth-century predecessors, foreign Marxists are described as less pessimistic, because socialist modernization now offers a reference point. Ma cites John Bellamy Foster on ecosocialism, David Kotz and proposals for digital socialism, and presents Chinese modernization as embodying a progressive, people-centred and green alternative. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how recent Western Marxist theory is classified and used in debates about modernization.
quoteEn: The contradiction between twenty-first-century \"globalisation\" and \"capitalisation\" is not merely one between \"form and content\"; it also foreshadows that capitalist modernization is by no means a bright road to human civilisation.
quoteZh: 21世纪的“全球化”与“资本化”的矛盾不仅仅是“形式与内容”的矛盾，更预示着资本主义现代化绝非通向人类文明的光明之路。

glossary.explanation: Official term for China's path of modernization, presented by the Party as distinct from Western models. It has been prominent in Party discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
A field in Chinese academia covering Marxist thought developed outside China, broader than Western Marxism.

t: New trends in foreign Marxist critiques of capitalist modernization
zh: 国外马克思主义开展资本主义现代化批判的新趋势
source: Guangming Daily, 25 July 2025, p. 11; Theoretical Horizons, 2025 no. 5
paras: This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, asks how foreign Marxism has adapted its critique of capitalist modernization to the twenty-first century. Ma Xinying argues that, although digital technology has expanded capitalist productive forces, capitalism's inherent contradictions and the problems of global capital accumulation keep capitalist modernization a source of trouble in world modernization. In response, Ma identifies three trends in the new critique.

The piece sets twenty-first-century work against the twentieth-century tradition of critique. It treats each trend as a shift from one orientation to another: from diachronic to synchronic critique, from critique of modernity to critique of modernization itself, and from socio-cultural to political critique.

On the first shift, Ma says twentieth-century critics, working from Marx's world-historical outlook, traced capitalist modernization from feudal and pre-modern origins. Twenty-first-century critics instead take a cross-section of modernization as a single present context and concentrate on its current features and its effects on how people live. On the second, Ma argues that because most countries are now integrated into modernization, alienation and the crisis of industrial civilisation are treated as given. Critics therefore judge negative effects from subjects' own feelings, beliefs and actions, and examine modernization's structure, path, power control, new contradictions and global consequences. On the third, Ma contends that critical theory worked mainly in sociological, psychological and epistemological terms, whereas critique now turns on politics: new imperialism, neoliberalism, spatial and biopolitics, state governance, digital capitalism and ecological justice, with hegemony, power, equality and justice as key concepts.

Ma concludes that these three shifts characterise the current direction of foreign Marxist critique of capitalist modernization. Read the original if you want a brief overview of how a Chinese scholar maps recent changes in foreign Marxist thinking on modernization.
quoteEn: After entering the twenty-first century, political critique gradually became the core of the critique of capitalist modernization.
quoteZh: 进入21世纪后，政治批判逐渐成为资本主义现代化批判的核心。

t: The contemporary value of Aristotle's thought on friendship
zh: 亚里士多德友爱思想的当代价值
paras: This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks what Aristotle's account of friendship (philia) can offer a present marked by individualism, virtual and instrumental social ties. Wu argues that its core, friendship grounded in virtue and the common good, remains a valuable intellectual resource for ethics, governance and everyday life.

The article first sets out Aristotle's typology in the Nicomachean Ethics. It then draws three contemporary lessons: friendship's place in human happiness, its link with justice and happiness in global moral construction, and its role in community governance.

Wu reads Aristotle as dividing friendship into pleasant, useful and good friendship, with only the last being friendship in the highest sense. Virtuous friendship, Wu says, is the glue of the city-state and the greatest external good for happiness, though it grows out of the more common pleasant and useful kinds. Wu then claims that happiness, justice and friendship are dialectically interdependent: just order secures the conditions for happiness and friendship, and friendship adds emotional and social support. The author applies this to international relations, sustainable development and the harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature. Wu also applies it to governance of the digital economy and artificial intelligence, where states should adopt values of friendship and mutual help.

Wu concludes that Aristotle's thought goes beyond personal feeling and narrow interest and spans ethics, political philosophy and metaphysics. It is presented as a spiritual coordinate for easing instrumentalised relationships, building a harmonious and happy society and promoting people's all-round development. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese academic commentary draws on classical Greek ethics to address contemporary governance and global moral questions.
quoteEn: The questions of friendship, happiness and justice are fundamental problems that global moral construction today cannot avoid.
quoteZh: 友爱与幸福、公正的问题是当今全球道德建设无法回避的基本问题。

t: Surveillance capitalism: origins, history and impact
zh: 监控资本主义：起源、历史与影响
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2025 no. 2
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the historian Kenneth Lipartito on surveillance capitalism, the concept popularised by Shoshana Zuboff's 2019 book The Age of Surveillance Capitalism. Lipartito asks how surveillance became embedded in economic life and what it costs. The author argues that surveillance is best seen as a long-built infrastructure, and that its pursuit of certainty threatens the creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship that have driven capitalist growth.

The article moves from definition to history and then to theory. It sketches how firms extract and commodify personal data, traces surveillance back to nineteenth-century credit reporting and the FICO score, and compares the regulatory approaches of the EU and the United States. It then draws on Kenneth Arrow, Jens Beckert, Keynes, Hal Varian and Claude Shannon's information theory. A closing section considers generative AI and possible alternatives.

Lipartito makes three main moves. First, surveillance began in efforts to build trust among strangers in modern society and brought real benefits, such as wider access to credit. Algorithms built on historical data nonetheless risk 'automating inequality', and privacy laws that stress accuracy and consent may end up making surveillance more precise. Second, infrastructures gain momentum and become 'black boxes', and the open design of the internet allowed Google, around 2001, to discover the profit in user data. Third, drawing on Shannon, the author argues that information is the reduction of uncertainty. Varian's 'perfect contract' assumes information equality, whereas surveillance is strategic collection that deepens information asymmetry. Eliminating uncertainty replaces creative uncertainty with false certainty.

Lipartito concludes that total transparency and predictability reshape selfhood and agency, and that corporate algorithms, not centralised state planning, now threaten freedom. The author warns that generative AI could 'colonise' social life and degrade its own training data. Infrastructures are not unstoppable, however, and the author points to failed technologies such as the videophone and the One Laptop per Child programme. Coordinated political effort could build a different future around other values. Read the original if you want a historically grounded, information-theoretic critique of surveillance capitalism that stresses economic stagnation and innovation more than ethics.
quoteEn: Surveillance is a strategic act of information collection whose aim is to reinforce information asymmetry, not to eliminate it.
quoteZh: 监控是一种策略性的信息收集行为，其目的在于强化信息不对称，而非消除这种不对称。

t: Critique of capitalism amid deepening technological monopoly and global fracture: responses and reconstruction
st: A survey of foreign Marxist research in 2024
zh: 技术垄断深化与全球秩序裂变下的资本主义批判：应答与重构
paras: This is an annual review of Marxist scholarship outside China in 2024. Qiao Ruihua asks how foreign Marxists responded to what the article calls a structural crisis of capitalism, marked by technological monopoly, algorithmic exploitation, geopolitical conflict, ecological crisis and the rise of the Global South. Qiao's overall assessment is that the year's work kept the critical tradition alive and innovated in method, themes and practical paths.

The review has three parts. The first covers work on established currents: early Western Marxism (Lukács, Gramsci), the Frankfurt School (including the 101st-anniversary lectures by Axel Honneth and Nancy Fraser) and post-Marxism (Laclau and Mouffe's radical democracy, biopolitics). The second covers ecological, spatial and digital critiques of capitalism. The third tracks changes in contemporary capitalism through Lenin's theory of imperialism, critiques of new imperialism and critiques of neoliberalism.

Qiao reports each scholar's position and then adds a short evaluation. Post-Marxism is judged to have weakened class analysis and drifted into identity politics, so it should be assessed dialectically. Kohei Saito's "degrowth communism" is described as lacking textual basis in the late Marx, as vague in defining growth, and as utopian. In the digital section, Yanis Varoufakis, Slavoj Žižek and others argue that rent-driven "techno-feudalism" is replacing profit-driven capitalism. John Bellamy Foster is cited on the metabolic rift and on the continuing relevance of Lenin's imperialism theory. Qiao also reports Foster's rejection of the Western-left view that China and the United States are both imperialist powers.

Qiao concludes that 2024 foreign Marxist research deepened the understanding of capitalism's essence and offered theoretical resources for global crises, and that the Global South received growing attention. The review also names weaknesses: academic insularity, weak explanatory and practical force, fragmentation and shifting positions. Qiao calls for strengthening wholeness and practical orientation within the framework of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a quick map of the 2024 foreign Marxist literature on digital capitalism, ecology, imperialism and neoliberalism, together with a Chinese academic evaluation of it.
quoteEn: At the same time, it must be recognised that its theoretical innovation still needs to break through academic limitations and strengthen its explanatory power and practical guidance regarding contemporary global crises.
quoteZh: 同时，也要看到其理论创新仍需突破学院化局限，强化对当代全球危机的解释力与实践指导性。

glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Varoufakis, Durand and Dean. It holds that platform and cloud owners extract rents from users and firms, replacing profit-driven capitalism with a quasi-feudal order.
The Chinese academic label for Marxist thought and research outside China. It is broader than Western Marxism and includes ecological, post-Marxist and digital-capitalism strands.
Developing and formerly colonised countries, a term widely used in current Chinese official and academic discourse.
Marx's idea, developed by Foster, of a rupture in the metabolic exchange between human society and nature under capitalist production.

t: Critique of capitalism amid deepening technological monopoly and global fracture: responses and reconstruction
st: Developments in foreign Marxism in 2024
zh: 技术垄断深化与全球秩序裂变下的资本主义批判：应答与重构
zhSub: 2024年国外马克思主义发展动态
paras: This is an annual review of research in foreign Marxism (Marxism outside China) for 2024, published in World Socialism Studies in 2025. Qiao Ruihua asks how scholars outside China responded to what the article calls a structural crisis of capitalism, marked by technological monopoly, algorithmic exploitation, geopolitical conflict, ecological crisis and the rise of the Global South. The review concludes that foreign Marxism advanced in both theoretical critique and practical reconstruction, while remaining fragmented.

The survey has three parts. The first covers traditional schools: early Western Marxism (Lukács, Gramsci), the Frankfurt School and post-Marxism. The second covers problem-oriented work on ecological, spatial and digital capitalism. The third tracks changes in contemporary capitalism, including Lenin's theory of imperialism, new imperialism and neoliberalism. Each section summarises individual scholars' books, lectures and conferences from 2024.

Qiao highlights several positions. On the Frankfurt School, Axel Honneth called for a postcolonial rereading of critical theory, and Nancy Fraser argued that labour links gender, race and class. On post-Marxism, the review cites Clyde Barrow and others as showing a weakened focus on the working class, and Qiao judges that it drifts into identity politics. In ecological critique, John Bellamy Foster's metabolic-rift analysis is set against Kohei Saito's degrowth communism, which Qiao finds poorly grounded in Marx and utopian. In digital capitalism, Yanis Varoufakis's "technofeudalism" thesis, in which rent displaces profit, is presented alongside Žižek's similar diagnosis and warnings of a widening digital divide for the Global South. On imperialism, Foster's Monthly Review essay marking Lenin's centenary defends Lenin's theory and rejects Western-left claims that China and the US are equivalent imperial powers.

Qiao concludes that 2024 research deepened the understanding of capitalism and supplied theoretical resources for addressing global crises. The review also finds weaknesses: academic insularity, fragmentation, wavering political stances and limited explanatory and practical force. It calls for greater coherence within a historical-materialist framework and a stronger practical orientation. Read the original if you want a broad, China-based survey of 2024 Western and international Marxist scholarship, with named authors and titles, and a sense of how Chinese reviewers assess it.
quoteEn: In addition, the problems of theoretical fragmentation and wavering positions remain prominent, and there is an urgent need to strengthen coherence and practical orientation within the framework of historical materialism.
quoteZh: 此外，其理论的碎片化与立场摇摆问题依然突出，亟须在历史唯物主义框架下增强整体性与实践导向。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese academic field covering Marxist thought developed outside China, broader than the specific tradition of Western Marxism. Chinese institutions track and review it systematically.
A term for developing and formerly colonised countries, used in Chinese official discourse to describe China's international standing and solidarity.
A thesis associated with Yanis Varoufakis and others that digital platforms have shifted capitalism from profit-driven to rent-driven exploitation, with tech firms acting as "cloud lords".

t: The problem of the "real movement" in communist theory
st: A core issue in how the contemporary Western radical left interprets communism
zh: 共产主义理论中的“现实运动”问题
zhSub: 当代西方激进左翼阐释共产主义的核心议题
paras: Li Jian takes up Marx and Engels's definition of communism in The German Ideology as the "real movement which abolishes the present state of things" and asks what kind of communism deserves that name, and how it can take hold in actual history in the twenty-first century. The article examines influential Western radical-left thinkers to see how they have reconstructed communist theory around this problem. Li argues that these thinkers raise the right question and offer useful perspectives, but abandon historical materialism, so their accounts remain at the level of discourse.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the radical left's double approach to communism as both "idea" and "real movement", drawing on Alain Badiou, Slavoj Žižek, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. It then traces their shift from abolishing capitalism's existing conditions to "the production of subjectivity", through three themes: preconditions, main line of development and value goal. A third part gives Li's critical assessment from a historical-materialist standpoint. The last part draws lessons for developing a new form of human civilization.

In Li's account, the radical left rests the shift on changed class relations under digital capitalism, where immaterial labour is said to dominate. It sees the main line in the mutual reinforcement of heterogeneous subjects (Hardt and Negri's multitude, Jacques Rancière's "part of those without part") and community, and the goal in the recovery of human subjectivity and emancipation. Li's critique is that these thinkers do not tie the antagonism to abolishing private ownership, stress contingency and events over historical necessity, and leave the "real movement" in the realm of ideas. Their goal, Li says, is individual rather than class emancipation, and their subject concepts sit outside the proletariat.

Li concludes that this theory lacks a historical-materialist foundation and has little practical effect, yet it can be critically borrowed. He argues that it clarifies the relation between capitalist and communist civilization, links the historical and value dimensions of communism, and applies the principle that thought should tend toward reality. For the new form of human civilization, Li calls for institutional innovation guided by the direction of communism and for drawing out the historical initiative of the people. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Badiou, Žižek, Hardt, Negri and Rancière on communism, and of how such work is brought into debates on Chinese civilizational theory.
quoteEn: In answering what communism is, the communist theory of the Western radical left often seizes on the word "movement" while neglecting the importance of "real", so that it cannot truly grasp the historical preconditions for realising communism.
quoteZh: 西方激进左翼共产主义理论在回答共产主义是什么时，往往抓住了“运动”一词，而忽视了“现实”的重要性，导致其无法真正把握住共产主义实现的历史前提。

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A formulation in Chinese Party discourse, prominent since 2021, describing the civilization said to be created by socialism with Chinese characteristics as distinct from the Western capitalist model.
Marx and Engels's theory that material production and class relations drive historical change. The article uses it as the standard for judging the Western radical left.
Marx and Engels's phrase in The German Ideology for communism as an actual historical movement rather than an ideal. It is the central concept of the article.

t: Social spatial practice, representations of space and representational spaces
st: A reading of Lefebvre's The Production of Space
zh: 社会空间实践与空间表象和表征
zhSub: 列斐伏尔《空间的生产》解读
source: Journal of Wuhan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 3
paras: Zhang Yibing reads the core of Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space (1974): how social space is produced through the "triad" of spatial practice, representations of space and representational spaces. Zhang argues that Lefebvre's critique of everyday life moved from a time-based view of history to a logic of spatial production. Zhang calls this shift a "Lutheran revolution" in the understanding of space, and also identifies logical blind spots in Lefebvre's account.

The article is a close, concept-by-concept commentary on Lefebvre's French text. It moves through four sections: spatial practice as the reproduction of modes of production and social relations; the role of representations; the three-part dialectic itself; and the "micro-texture" of social space (the human subject, historicity and the primacy of practice). Zhang draws on Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology and Capital, and on Husserl and Heidegger. Zhang repeatedly uses Lefebvre's earlier works, Metaphilosophy and The Urban Revolution, as a comparison.

Zhang's central claim is that for Lefebvre social space is not a physical container but a field of relations that arises and vanishes in everyday practice. Buildings and roads serve only as tools that reactivate those relations. In capitalism Lefebvre identifies three levels of reproduction: of life, of labour-power and of the social relations of production. Representations of space (plans, knowledge, codes) and representational spaces (lived, imagined experience) can mask real relations, for instance by presenting market exchange as natural. Zhang's own critical addition is that Lefebvre overlooks how, in class societies, only rulers hold the power to conceive space, so the conceiving-doing distinction is historically specific rather than universal. Zhang ties this to Marx and Engels's account of the separation of self-activity from material production. Zhang also notes that Lefebvre holds practice to be primary while allowing mutual interaction among the three moments, and that Lefebvre rejects the primacy of ideas over practice as an illusion.

Zhang concludes that Lefebvre's spatial theory enriches historical materialism by showing in detail how ideas, symbols and lived experience take part in producing social relations. It keeps a materialist base in practice, and it locates people's own existence as the substance of social space. Zhang adds that its strengths are limited by Lefebvre's neglect of the development of productive forces and of class inequalities in who shapes space. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Western Marxism or spatial theory and want a Chinese Marxist critical reading, which uses Zhang's own interpretive vocabulary, of the three-part spatial dialectic.
quoteEn: Representations of space are not a universal component of the spatial dialectic, but a special phenomenon of spatial production under specific historical conditions of human society.
quoteZh: 空间表象不是一种普适性的空间辩证法构件，而只是人类社会空间生产特定历史条件下的特殊空间生产现象。

glossary.explanation: Zhang Yibing's recurring metaphor for a shift that moves the essence of a thing from external objects to human subjective activity, as Luther moved faith inward. Zhang applies it to both Marx's ontology and Lefebvre's view of space.
Lefebvre's term (pratique spatiale) for the everyday activities that produce and reproduce social relations within a given space. It is the first moment of his three-part spatial dialectic.
Lefebvre's conceived space: plans, knowledge, codes and blueprints that order social relations and are tied to those who design space.
Lefebvre's lived space: the imagined and bodily experience of space through symbols, art and everyday life.

t: A fluid-dynamics perspective on the relational field of social space
st: A reading of Lefebvre's The Production of Space
zh: 社会空间关系场境的流体动力学透视
zhSub: 列菲伏尔《空间的生产》解读
source: Journal of the Party School of the Fujian Provincial Committee of the CPC (Fujian Academy of Governance), 2025 no. 2
paras: Zhang Yibing reads Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space (1974) as the point where Lefebvre moves from a temporal to a spatial line of historical-materialist analysis. Lefebvre's critique of everyday life had already shifted alienation theory from macro political economy to micro social life. Zhang argues that the book's social space is not a container of objects but a field of relations produced by human activity, and that Lefebvre describes it through an analogy with fluid dynamics.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the complexity of social-spatial relations, the second the fluid-dynamics image and the market networks of the information age, and the third the principles Lefebvre proposes for studying social space. Zhang follows Lefebvre's text closely, quoting French terms, and adds contemporary illustrations such as Alipay, PayPal, online book purchases and the localisation of Coca-Cola and KFC products in China.

Zhang identifies three features of social space: its relations interpenetrate and overlap beyond the physical fabric of buildings and squares, they can conceal one another (capital's exploitation of wage labour is hidden behind commodity, money and financial forms), and they work at several levels, local, national and global, where the global does not abolish the local. Lefebvre's fluid-dynamics image is, in Zhang's reading, only a metaphor for non-substantial relations and flowing force relations, and Lefebvre himself warns against overusing it. Zhang then reports Lefebvre's principles: move from the old problematic of things to relations; focus on human practical activity; unmask the hidden production and reproduction of social relations, including class relations, so as to avoid 'space fetishism'; and expel the ideology that fragments space into passive containers. Zhang also notes that Lefebvre moves from industrialisation to urbanisation, and the author calls Lefebvre's line between broad and narrow historical materialism muddled.

Zhang concludes that Lefebvre's social-space research aims to see through the fetishised appearance of space to the hidden social relations, above all the contradiction between private ownership of the means of production and the socialisation of productive forces. Such research must be both retrospective and prospective, looking towards an 'other' space and time in a different society. Zhang presents this as a method derived from Marx's Capital. Read the original if you want a close, term-by-term guide to Lefebvre's spatial method, with the French originals, by a leading Chinese scholar of Western Marxism.
quoteEn: Social space is by no means an empty place plus things; it is a relational field constructed by human activity, except that in the bourgeois, economically thing-ified space these social relations are concealed once again.
quoteZh: 社会空间绝不是空场加物，而就是由人的活动建构起来的关系场境，只是在资产阶级的经济物相化空间中，这些社会关系被再一次遮蔽起来。

glossary.explanation: Treating space as a thing in itself, in analogy with Marx's commodity fetishism. It overlooks the social relations embedded in space.

t: Four dimensions of foreign left-wing scholars' critique of twenty-first-century capitalist space
zh: 国外左翼学者对21世纪资本主义空间批判的四重维度
paras: Li Shule asks how left-wing scholars outside China have updated the critique of capitalist space for the twenty-first century. The article argues that the field has moved from Henri Lefebvre's "production of space" to the "production of spatial scale", which Li presents as the key to understanding capitalism today. This shift is said to produce four linked dimensions of critique: the global city, new state space, the new world system and bodily space.

The article surveys Lefebvre, David Harvey, Neil Smith, Edward Soja, Doreen Massey, Saskia Sassen, Neil Brenner, Bob Jessop, Etienne Balibar, Neil Davidson, Alex Callinicos, Ellen Meiksins Wood, Peter Sloterdijk and others. Each of the four dimensions is divided into two sub-themes. For the global city these are urban landscape and the power-geographic network. For state space they are geopolitical critique and the scale of the new state space. For the world system they are uneven geography and new imperialism. For the body they are political-economic critique and ontological critique of life.

Li's central claim is that capitalism reorganises space at successive scales to sustain accumulation: the city, then the state, then the globe, and finally the body. Global cities are read as command points of unequal exchange, where gentrification and slums express capital's seizure of spatial rights. Brenner and Jessop treat the state as a re-scaled, path-dependent space rather than a fixed container. Harvey and Smith treat uneven geography, dispossession and "new imperialism" as the core of the new world system. Li defends the capital-logic/territorial-logic approach against Davidson's objection that it misses deeper relations. At the bodily scale, Harvey and Smith describe a "body-scale" system of value differentials that lets capital exploit dispersed workers in common, while Sloterdijk's "crystal palace" image shows how those outside capital's interior space are exposed to risk.

Li concludes that the four dimensions form a chain from logical starting point to extension, deepening and final target. The article credits this body of work with showing the unity of capitalist spatial domination across macro and micro scales, and says the left must answer these dilemmas at the level of scale. Li also names three limits: a tendency toward "scale-centrism", a weakened class analysis, and no effective link between spatial critique and revolutionary practice. Read the original if you want a systematic map of Anglophone and European spatial theory since Lefebvre, together with a Chinese Marxist assessment of its limits.
quoteEn: The four dimensions of the foreign left-wing scholars' critique of twenty-first-century capitalist space form an interlocking logical whole.
quoteZh: 国外左翼学者对21世纪资本主义空间批判的四重维度构成了一个环环相扣的逻辑整体

t: Analytical political economy: the revival of Analytical Marxism in economics
zh: 分析政治经济学：分析的马克思主义在经济学领域的复兴
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai Lilun Dongtai), 2024 no. 6
paras: Chen Weikai asks how Analytical Marxism, which declined after 1990, has re-emerged in economics as a community called Analytical Political Economy (APE), and what Chinese scholars can learn from it. The author argues that APE critically inherits the methodology of Analytical Marxism, avoids its narrowness, and has become one of the most active schools of Marxist economics outside China. Chen also holds that it has three shortcomings that need correcting.

The article has three parts. The first traces APE's development. It begins with the roots of Analytical Marxism in economics: Morishima Michio's mathematical Marxian economics, Sraffa's Production of Commodities by Means of Commodities, and John Roemer's reconstruction of Marxian theory. It then follows APE from the 1991 Notre Dame workshop to the 2007 revival at Queen Mary, London, and to the 2018 volume Analytical Political Economy. The second part sets out APE's methodological features and the third offers a critical assessment.

Chen's central distinction is between a broad and a narrow conception of the analytical method. The narrow one is Rational Choice Marxism, which insists on methodological individualism and reductionism and which, in Chen's view, caused the decline of Analytical Marxism's economics. The broad one, following Erik Olin Wright, stresses scientific norms, precise concepts and rigorous argument. APE adopts the broad conception and has three traits. It uses precision tools such as the axiomatic method. It seeks microfoundations while stressing the dialectical interaction of micro and macro, including structural constraints and the social formation of individuals. It is also pluralist about tools and paradigms, and Chen cites Roemer's class–exploitation correspondence principle as a valid result despite its neoclassical setting.

Chen identifies three weaknesses. APE lacks a distinctly Marxist research programme and should study the laws of motion of the contemporary mode of production, including platform-based forms of organisation. It also neglects dialectics, which Chen treats as complementary to analytical methods rather than a rival to them. And it concentrates on foundational problems such as the transformation problem and the falling rate of profit, so it should engage more with empirical questions. Those include monopoly power, digital labour relations, climate change, automation and AI, using tools like big data and causal inference. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of APE's origins, key figures and methodological debates, together with an assessment from the standpoint of Marxist political economy.
quoteEn: Analytical political economy should return to the core questions of Marxist economic theory and, in light of new changes in contemporary monopoly capital, further study the transformation, diffusion and effects of the new platform-based forms of production organisation brought about by digital information technology.
quoteZh: 分析政治经济学应当回归马克思主义经济理论的核心问题，结合当代垄断资本的新变化进一步研究数字信息技术引发的以平台为代表的新生产组织方式的变革、扩散及其影响。

glossary.explanation: A school that emerged in the late 1970s and 1980s. It combines analytic philosophy and modern social-science methods with Marxism, and its figures include G. A. Cohen, John Roemer and Jon Elster. Its 'September Group' formed in 1981.

An academic community of heterodox and Marxist economists who use formal, analytical methods. It began with a 1991 workshop at Notre Dame and revived after 2007. The article treats it as the economics-side revival of Analytical Marxism.

The view that all social phenomena can in principle be explained by the properties, goals, beliefs and actions of individuals. The article presents it as the narrow methodological stance that APE rejects as an exclusive requirement.

The strand of Analytical Marxism associated with Elster and Roemer that insists on rational-choice theory and methodological individualism. The article blames it for the decline of the school's economics.
The Marxist method of grasping things in their universal connection, change and development. Chen presents it as a guide to research that complements analytical tools.

t: New trends in the Philippine left-wing movement in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪菲律宾左翼运动的新态势
paras: Hei Ran asks how the Philippine left has developed since the early twentieth century and what shape it has taken in the twenty-first. The article argues that, although the left has gained theoretical and practical ground since 2000, it remains fragmented and politically weak, and its prospects are not optimistic.

The article is organised in four parts. It first traces the movement from the anti-colonial struggles and early labour unions, through the founding of the Communist Party of the Philippines in 1930 (PKP-1930), to the split of 1968 and the post-Marcos divisions. It then surveys the main parties of the present: the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) and the Revolutionary Workers' Party of Mindanao (RPM-M) on one side, and the Philippine Democratic Socialist Party and the Partido Lakas ng Masa (PLM) on the other. Hei goes on to identify three new features and ends with an assessment of prospects.

On theory, Hei reports that the parties sharpened their critique of capitalism after the 2008 financial crisis and sketched socialist futures, including the CPP's 2014 outline and the PLM's emphasis on communal solidarity ("Bayanihan") and ecological repair. On practice, the article describes party-building and wider international contacts. Its core argument is that the movement shows three features. Left politics is fragmented, because of ideological splits and the dominance of political dynasties. Tactics are flexible, with armed struggle combined with peace talks or electoral participation. Strategic aims are broader, extending from class struggle and land reform to labour rights, gender equality and the environment.

Hei concludes that the left's prospects depend on its adaptability. The author points to the CPP's leadership vacuum after the deaths of its founder Jose Maria Sison and other leaders, to doubts about the party's internal democracy, and to the weak electoral showing of the left in 2022. The article holds that only left unity could shift the position of the dynastic families and open a path towards socialism, while noting that the movement's future is still to be observed. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Philippine left parties, their doctrines and their divisions, from their origins to the mid-2020s.
