quoteEn: Since the start of the twenty-first century, the ideological and strategic differences among Philippine left-wing parties and organisations have kept widening, and with political dynasties dominating the party-political landscape, left politics and the party system have gradually shown a marked tendency towards fragmentation.
quoteZh: 进入21世纪以来，菲律宾左翼政党及组织在意识形态和战略路线上的分歧持续扩大，加之家族政治势力在菲律宾政党政治生态中占据主导地位，左翼政治和政党体系逐渐呈现出明显的碎片化倾向。

glossary.explanation: A current that seeks socialism through elections and parliamentary means. The article applies it to the Philippine Democratic Socialist Party and the PLM.

t: New trends in the Eurocentric Left's denial of the theory of imperialism
zh: 欧洲中心主义左翼否认帝国主义论的新动向
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2025 no. 1
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by John Bellamy Foster. It asks why large parts of the Western Left now deny or abandon the Marxist theory of imperialism, and what is at stake. Foster argues that the split between the Western Left and revolutionaries in the Global South is wider than at any time since the Second International collapsed in 1914. He traces it to the relative decline of US hegemony and the economic rise of former colonies and semi-colonies.

The article has three parts. The first re-reads Lenin's theory through all his writings on imperialism from 1916 to 1920, not only Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, together with early Comintern texts and Mao Zedong's class analysis. The second follows the theory after 1945 through Paul Baran, Samir Amin, Arghiri Emmanuel, world-systems theory and research on global value chains. The third surveys denials of imperialism, from Bill Warren and Giovanni Arrighi through Hardt and Negri and David Harvey to Vivek Chibber, William I. Robinson and Gilbert Achcar.

Foster's central claim is that critics wrongly present Lenin as a theorist only of rivalry among great powers. He contends that Lenin also made the exploitation of oppressed nations the economic root of imperialism, tied to monopoly capital and to a "labour aristocracy" in the core. Empirical work on labour-cost differences and global value chains is said to show that the Global South suffers super-exploitation. Foster reads the Eurocentric positions as a way of avoiding that evidence: Chibber's "Kautskyan world", Robinson's transnational capitalist class, Harvey's "accumulation by dispossession" and the labelling of China and Russia as imperialist or sub-imperialist. He describes China's foreign policy as non-interventionist, in contrast to US military interventions and bases.

Foster concludes that anti-imperialism does not mean abandoning class struggle in the core. He argues that revolution has for a century centred on the periphery, and that anti-racist traditions such as Du Bois's and the Black Alliance for Peace are central to it. In his view, Left thinkers who treat anti-imperialism as the enemy end up supporting imperialism amid ecological crisis and the risk of nuclear war. Read the original if you want a polemical, Marxist account of the Western Left's debates on imperialism, with a detailed bibliography and Foster's reading of Lenin, Baran and Amin.
quoteEn: This constitutes a purely national-political definition, detached both from proletarian internationalism and from any direct resistance to the laws of motion of capitalism in its monopoly stage.
quoteZh: 这构成了一个纯粹的民族政治定义，既脱离了无产阶级国际主义，也脱离了对处于垄断阶段的资本主义自身运动规律的任何直接反抗。

glossary.explanation: A term for the developing and formerly colonised countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America. In Chinese official discourse it is used for these states as a group, contrasted with the "Global North".
A concept from Engels and Lenin for a better-paid upper layer of workers in imperialist countries, said to be "bought off" by monopoly superprofits and so more conservative politically.
The claim that workers in the Global South are exploited above the global average, with wages pushed below the cost of subsistence. The idea comes from dependency theory.

t: Research progress among foreign left-wing scholars on the digital economy
zh: 国外左翼学者关于数字经济的研究进展
paras: This is a literature review, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2025, no. 1), of recent work by left-wing scholars outside China on the digital economy. Ma and Zhang trace the field back to 1970s contributions such as Dallas Smythe's "audience commodity", Maurizio Lazzarato's "immaterial labour", Tiziana Terranova's "digital labour" and Dan Schiller's Digital Capitalism. Their aim is to describe the trajectory of this research and offer leads for theoretical work on the digital economy.

The review is organised around four clusters of problems. These are algorithmic labour control and the upgrading of "manufacturing consent"; changes in workers' conditions, including the gig economy and prosumers; the varied forms of platform organisation and their monopolistic tendencies; and the critique of digital capitalism, with proposals for governing it and visions of digital socialism.

On labour control, Ma and Zhang report scholars describing algorithmic management as a digital "panopticon" (Rabih Jamil's "algopticon"), in which surveillance deepens information asymmetry between capital and labour. They present Michael Burawoy's "making out" game as extended into digital tournaments and gamified platforms, while workers resist through platform loopholes, social media organising and legal action. On the gig economy, some scholars see greater inclusion, but most stress precarity, and recent work attends to the heterogeneity of gig workers. The prosumer concept is contested: Christian Fuchs's "organic composition of labour" treats unpaid user activity as value-producing, whereas Nick Srnicek and Bartosz Mika deny that such activity is labour in the value-theoretic sense. On platforms, the review sets out Steven Vallas and Juliet Schor's five metaphors and explains monopoly by natural factors (scale, network effects, data) and by governance and financialisation, citing Cecilia Rikap on intellectual property rents.

On digital capitalism, the authors report the view that it remains governed by capitalist accumulation and exploitation, producing a "digital proletariat". Proposed responses include platform cooperativism, labour-law and antitrust reform, and data-privacy regulation such as the GDPR. Some thinkers, among them Evgeny Morozov and Kees van der Pijl, see big data as opening new possibilities for socialist planning, while others, such as Silvia Rief, warn that technology alone is no solution. Read the original if you want a map of Western left debates on algorithmic control, platform monopoly and digital socialism, with names and concepts to follow up.
quoteEn: First, the development of control technology and the upgrading of "manufacturing consent" show the evolution of the zones of struggle and the spaces of cooperation in the production process.
quoteZh: 首先，控制技术的发展及“制造同意”的升级展现了生产过程中斗争地带与合作空间的演变。

glossary.explanation: A journal of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau that reports on theoretical developments outside China, including foreign Marxism.

t: Techno-feudalism and the problem of the "general intellect" in the digital economy
zh: 技术封建主义与数字经济时代的“一般智力”问题
paras: Huang Dan takes up the concept of techno-feudalism, which foreign scholars have recently used to describe an economy dominated by digital oligarchs, and asks whether it explains the exploitation and power structures of the digital economy. The article's answer is double. The concept is flawed as a historical analogy and as an account of platforms, yet it points to a real phenomenon: the private enclosure of Marx's "general intellect".

The article first sets out the concept as developed by Cédric Durand and Yanis Varoufakis, who describe rent extraction by platforms, "cloud rent", cloud landlords, vassal capitalists and cloud serfs. It then criticises the concept on two counts, its reading of feudalism and its neglect of platforms' productive side. A third section turns to the preconditions of digital rent-seeking and then to the privatisation of the general intellect. It draws on Marx's "Fragment on Machines", Hardt and Negri, Žižek, Yann Moulier-Boutang and Carlo Vercellone. A short closing section discusses generative AI.

Huang argues that feudalism, as Ganshof, Bloch and Perry Anderson understand it, rests on extra-economic coercion and political-legal ties, not on the mere existence of rent. Digital rent is a purely economic, commercial form of capitalist rent. Platforms such as Amazon also produce and innovate, so their income combines profit and rent, and concepts like platform capitalism or cognitive capitalism fit better. Rent-seeking still depends on scarcity, and Huang argues that this scarcity is artificially created. Big data, open-source libraries and publicly funded patents are collectively produced but enclosed through intellectual property, algorithmic control and monopoly, which the article calls a "second enclosure". Following Moulier-Boutang and Vercellone, Huang holds that the capital logic of closure clashes with a cognitive-labour logic of open circulation and cooperation.

Huang concludes that this contradiction is both a deepening of exploitation and a source of emancipatory potential. Large language models trained on public data are cited as a new instance of the general intellect being absorbed by capital. The article calls for rediscovering its public character through institutions and technology, and points to platform cooperativism, democratic platforms and the redistribution and sharing of public data as early steps. Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of the techno-feudalism debate that turns it into a question about knowledge enclosure and the general intellect.
quoteEn: The concept of techno-feudalism reveals a new phenomenon: the widespread rent-seeking in the digital economy that rests on the "enclosure of knowledge".
quoteZh: 技术封建主义概念揭示了一个新现象，即数字经济中普遍存在着基于“知识圈地”的寻租行为。

t: Technofeudalism examined: a new form of monopoly capitalism
zh: 技术封建主义思潮辨析：垄断资本主义的新形态
paras: Zheng Han takes up the technofeudalism thesis advanced by Western left scholars, chiefly Cédric Durand and Yanis Varoufakis, who hold that digital capitalism has regressed into something resembling feudalism. The article grants that this current captures many features of the digital age. It argues, however, that its main concepts stay within Marx's own categories and that many of its judgements run against his analysis. Zheng's answer is that Big Tech is a new form of monopoly capitalism, not a feudal order.

The article first reconstructs technofeudalism through three claimed 'discoveries': profit has given way to 'cloud rent', class relations have turned into lord–serf dependence (Varoufakis's 'cloud proletarians' and 'cloud serfs'), and markets and profit are being eroded. It then tests these claims against Marxist theory in three steps: the circuit of capital, labour and users, and global monopoly. It closes with the question of emancipation, drawing on company data on cloud market shares, R&D spending, lobbying and staffing.

Zheng argues that the tech giants remain functioning capitalists. They pass through the full industrial-capital circuit, buy labour-power and appropriate surplus value, and also act as commercial capital by matching supply and demand. In the article's account they remain subject to competition and innovation, and they maintain infrastructure, unlike rentier landlords. Platform workers are wage-labourers under real subordination, and algorithmic management deepens that control. Users, by contrast, are said to take part in the reproduction of labour-power, so the claim that they perform unpaid 'serf' labour is judged a misreading of Marx's concept of labour. Finally, the concentration of cloud services, political lobbying and the 'revolving door' are presented as confirmation of Lenin's account of monopoly capitalism.

Zheng concludes that technofeudalism is a supra-historical philosophy that cannot grasp capitalism's developmental dynamic. The tech giants, the author says, redistribute power within the bourgeoisie but leave the capital–labour antagonism intact. Varoufakis's 'cloud uprising', which would include some vassal capitalists, is judged a bourgeois-style coalition that overestimates online mobilisation. The article calls for analysis in the Marxist tradition and for struggle strategies aimed at digital capitalism's weaknesses. Read the original if you want a Marxist rebuttal of Durand and Varoufakis, backed by detailed data on Big Tech's market power.
quoteEn: The power of the tech giants is capitalist in nature and by no means feudal.
quoteZh: 科技巨头的权力是资本主义性质而绝不是封建主义性质的。

t: Algorithmic hegemony and ideological manipulation: how Western states discipline intelligent algorithms
zh: 算法霸权与意识形态操控：西方国家规训智能算法的路径探赜
paras: Zhang Xuesen asks how Western states, drawing on their early lead in technology, have shaped intelligent algorithms into a system of "algorithmic hegemony" that serves their ideology, and how other countries can respond. The article argues that laws, industry standards and policy guidance in the West steer how algorithms are developed, used and supervised, so that algorithms become a hidden instrument for spreading Western ideology. It presents this as a global contest over algorithmic sovereignty and ideological security.

The article has four parts. The first describes mechanisms of control: algorithmic surveillance, recommendation systems and "data colonialism". The second treats the embedding of Western values in algorithm design, through bias, agenda-setting and information filtering. The third analyses monopoly in three forms, technological, data and capital. The fourth proposes strategies for breaking Western algorithmic dominance. Zhang draws on Foucault, Deleuze, Bauman, Zuboff, Sunstein, Couldry and Mejias, O'Neil, Pasquale, Harari and Samir Amin.

Zhang's central claim is that algorithms have moved society from Foucault's disciplinary society to a Deleuzian "society of control", in which a "post-panopticon" of fluid surveillance makes people's behaviour and emotions transparent. In the author's account, the PRISM programme and Meta's behavioural analysis illustrate this. Recommendation systems create "filter bubbles" and group polarisation, and Western media filter content about China. Cases such as Amazon's recruitment algorithm, a US criminal-risk tool and Meta's housing adverts illustrate algorithmic bias. Zhang then reads the whole system through Amin's centre–periphery model. Mathematical foundations, "black box" opacity, control of global data flows and a "global digital monopoly alliance" tie technology, data and capital together. In this reading, algorithms execute the logic of capital and entrench dependence in latecomer states.

Zhang calls for China and other developing countries to reduce dependence on Western algorithms. Proposals include special research funds, a "core algorithm" programme and closer links between universities, institutes and firms. Zhang also urges unified legislation and supervision, with algorithm registration, assessment and accountability, and training and recruitment of talent, including from overseas. Internationally, Zhang advocates joint standards, transparency and fairness assessments, and a fair, open and inclusive global algorithm order that reflects developing countries' interests. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship frames Western platform power as hegemony and what policy remedies it proposes.
quoteEn: Under the capitalist system, algorithms become executors of the logic of capital, and their design principles are oriented towards capital accumulation and efficiency gains.
quoteZh: 在资本主义体系下，算法成为资本逻辑的执行者，其设计原则以资本积累和效率提升为导向。

glossary.explanation: A term used by the author for the dominance that Western states and technology firms are said to hold over algorithmic technology, data and the information environment. It is used to criticise unequal power in the digital sphere.
The idea that a state should control the algorithms, data and rules that shape information within its borders and in global governance. It extends the concept of digital or cyber sovereignty.
A concept from Nick Couldry and Ulises Mejias, who compare large-scale data extraction by technology firms to historical colonial appropriation. Zhang applies it to Western tech giants' global reach.

t: Assessment of Japanese scholarship on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
zh: 日本学界习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想研究状况评析
paras: This is a review article on how Japanese academia has studied Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era since the 19th Party Congress (2017). Zhuo and Zhou argue that Japanese scholars' attention to the Thought has grown steadily. In their account, the Japanese view offers a useful "neighbour's perspective" for building an international system of interpretation and for strengthening China's international communication.

The article opens with library and database indicators of Japanese interest. It then surveys four main topics: Chinese modernization, common prosperity, the Belt and Road Initiative, and a community with a shared future for mankind. It closes with four features of the Japanese literature, concerning content, stance, researchers and institutions, and a short set of recommendations.

The authors first cite figures from CiNii, Japan's largest academic database. As of 2 November 2024 it listed 397 books and 2,651 papers under the keyword "Xi Jinping Thought", up from 249 books and 1,786 papers in April 2021. Under each topic they then group Japanese views. On Chinese modernization, scholars such as Muratada Tadayoshi, Nakagane Katsuji and Takahara Akio are reported to offer explanatory theories: large-country scale, external stimulus, political stability, late-development advantage and traditional inheritance. On common prosperity, scholars discuss expanding the middle-income group and the policy's relevance to Japan's own inequality. On the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind, they report praise from former prime ministers Fukuda Yasuo and Hatoyama Yukio, alongside analysis of effects on Japan's economy.

Zhuo and Zhou conclude that Japanese researchers focus on policy, economics and Sino-US and Sino-Japanese relations, and analyse the theoretical system itself less. They describe most scholars as objective and note that many are Japanese specialists with experience of China. They add that government and corporate think tanks also advise firms on trade with China. The authors call for tracking overseas research and for reforming international communication mechanisms, so as to "tell China's story well". Read the original if you want a Chinese-side overview of Japanese scholars, institutions and views on Xi Jinping Thought, or want to see how Chinese researchers present and use foreign reception of it.
quoteEn: Overall, analysis and interpretation of the theoretical system of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era itself is relatively weak.
quoteZh: 总体上对习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想理论体系本身的分析和解读相对较弱。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution at the 19th Party Congress in 2017. It brings together Xi Jinping's theories and policy positions.
Official term for China's path to modernization, described as socialist and distinct from Western models. It was elaborated after the 20th Party Congress in 2022.
A long-standing socialist goal that Xi Jinping has stressed in recent years. It refers to prosperity shared by all, with reduced gaps in income and development.
China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched by Xi Jinping in 2013.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign policy concept of interdependent states cooperating for mutual benefit. Chinese official texts present it as an alternative to zero-sum international relations.

t: The Communist Party of Argentina's exploration of the socialist road
st: Analysis of the current situation and outlook
zh: 阿根廷共产党对社会主义道路的探索
zhSub: 现状分析与趋势展望
source: Journal of Liaocheng University (Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 1
paras: The authors ask where the Communist Party of Argentina (PCA), founded in 1918, stands today and what its prospects are under the presidency of Javier Milei. They argue that the party's influence is limited by a hostile political climate and by weaknesses in its own organisation. They also contend that social crisis, working-class discontent and the resurgence of the Latin American left offer it new room for growth.

The article first traces the party's origins: the early spread of socialist ideas in Argentina, including Marx's 1872 envoy to the International Workingmen's Association, and the growth of an immigrant-fed working class. It then reviews the party's present theory and practice, covering its economic nationalism, its critique of capitalism, its defence of workers and students, its 28th National Congress (September 2024), its websites and journal, and its alliances at home and abroad. Two sections follow on current challenges and future trends.

In the authors' account, the PCA sees dependency on foreign capital and international financial institutions as the root of Argentina's problems. They cite the 2001 crisis and Monsanto's role in the soy sector as examples, and the party calls for state control of key industries and a socialist alternative. The authors then set out the party's difficulties. Milei's election and his alignment with Trump squeeze its space. Its reliance on larger left coalitions leaves it without seats in the legislature. It has about 130,000 members (2022) and an ageing leadership, and public sympathy for the left has fallen. Against this they set Milei's austerity, with a poverty rate of 52.9 per cent in the first half of 2024, the anger of workers and students, and the return of left governments across the region.

The authors conclude that the PCA, though constrained, still has potential to promote social justice and regional unity among progressive forces. They expect it to keep seeking a socialist model suited to Argentine and regional conditions while defending workers' rights and pushing for anti-capitalist change. The article also notes that the party's delegations have visited China to study its experience. Read the original if you want a China-based overview of a small Latin American communist party, its recent congress and the reasons Chinese scholars give for its weakness and prospects.
quoteEn: This trend will undoubtedly have a positive effect on the future development of the Communist Party of Argentina. Cooperation and exchange among the region's left-wing governments will build a broad international support network for the party, strengthen its external support and help raise its confidence in its future development.
quoteZh: 这一趋势无疑将对阿根廷共产党未来的发展产生积极影响，拉美地区左翼政权之间的联合与交流，将为阿根廷共产党构建广泛的国际支持网络，进一步增强其发展的外部支撑力，有助于提升阿根廷共产党未来发展的信心。

t: Habermas's revision of the consensus theory of truth and its contemporary implications
zh: 哈贝马斯对真理共识论的修正及其当代启示
source: Teaching and Research on Marxist Theory, 2025 no. 2
paras: Huang Meidi examines how Jürgen Habermas revised his consensus theory of truth in Truth and Justification (1999). The author argues that Habermas abandoned truth as an epistemological concept and recast it as a norm of action rooted in everyday practice. Huang holds that Chinese scholarship has mostly studied the earlier phases of his truth theory and neglected this third one. The article also asks how the revision can help meet the regression of intersubjective communicative action in the digital age.

The article has four sections. The first reconstructs the consensus theory and its self-negation, after Habermas's criticism of correspondence, coherence and pragmatist theories of truth. The second looks at the lifeworld, its 'non-thematized' and 'situational' sides, and at the dialogue (discourse) that clears doubts. The third presents the resulting 'truth of action'. The fourth applies the theory to information overload, algorithmic recommendation and false consensus.

Huang's core claim is that the early theory merged the performative attitude with the reflexive attitude, which made truth equivalent to justification and left the theory without a realist basis. Habermas's remedy was to treat the lifeworld as a quasi-transcendental background in which truth is unconditionally taken for granted. When doubts arise, participants step into discourse, adopt a reflexive attitude and test validity claims, then return to the lifeworld as actors. In Huang's reading, this 'actor–discussant–actor' shift reconciles the unconditionality of truth with the rational acceptability of justification. Huang also notes that Habermas's division of lifeworld situations is crude, because he borrows selectively from Husserl and Schütz.

Huang concludes that the 'truth of action' ties Habermas's epistemology to his critical social theory, discourse ethics and political philosophy. For the digital age, Huang argues that moving from the lifeworld into dialogue helps people assess false information. The reflexive attitude counters algorithmic filter bubbles, and an 'cognition–action' view means users can test platform-generated consensus through practice and cooperation. The author adds that Wellmer's criticism of the ideal speech situation shows why formally open platforms may still produce false consensus. Read the original if you want a close account of the Truth and Justification phase of Habermas, or a Chinese attempt to apply it to digital communication.
quoteEn: Habermas consistently held to the standpoint of truth and kept exploring the possibility of a social-action turn in philosophical epistemology, and this process is itself of special significance.
quoteZh: 哈贝马斯始终坚持真理立场，不断探索哲学认识论社会行动转向的可能性，这一过程本身就具有特殊的意义。

glossary.explanation: A concept from Husserl and Schütz taken up by Habermas. It is the taken-for-granted background of shared knowledge in which everyday communicative action takes place.
Habermas's term for social action coordinated through mutual understanding and the raising of validity claims, as opposed to strategic action.
Habermas's earlier view that a statement is true if all potential participants in discourse would agree to it under ideal conditions.
A counterfactual setting in which all participants have equal opportunity to speak and no coercion or manipulation intervenes.
A common Chinese term for the narrowing of users' exposure to like-minded content, typically through algorithmic recommendation.

t: The formation and main content of Lenin's thought on the Communist Party's long-term leadership of all undertakings of the workers' and peasants' state
zh: 列宁关于共产党长时期领导工农国家各项事业思想的形成及其重要内容
paras: Marx and Engels held that the proletarian state and the proletarian party would wither away once the transition period ended and the first stage of communist society began. Yu Min argues that Lenin, drawing on practice after the October Revolution, departed from this view. In Lenin's reading, both state and party must persist for a long time, through the transition period and the first stage of communist society, and the Communist Party must lead every undertaking of the workers' and peasants' state. The article presents this as having contemporary significance.

The article is in three parts. The first traces how Lenin arrived at the idea, from The State and Revolution (1917) through the civil war and the 1920 pamphlet "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder. The second sets out five areas of Party leadership that Lenin discussed: the state and its organs; economic work; culture and education, including ideology and the social sciences; diplomacy and foreign trade; and the Red Army. The third draws lessons for the present.

Yu argues that Lenin's experience of fierce class struggle, with armed rebellion, assassinations and foreign intervention, led him to see the dictatorship of the proletariat as a prolonged and desperate war. He also placed Russia only at the "initial stage" of the transition, which Yu reads as meaning that the transition itself has stages and is very long. On this basis Lenin rejected the German "Left" denial of the party as a leap to the highest stage of communism. Yu then reports Lenin's positions against the Trotskyist, Workers' Opposition and Democratic Centralist proposals on trade unions and economic management, where the Party was to lead as the vanguard. Yu cites Lenin's handling of the Brest-Litovsk peace, the Genoa Conference instructions, and the political commissar system as examples of Party leadership in practice.

Yu concludes that Lenin enriched Marx and Engels's thinking on the withering away of state and party. The article links this to the Chinese Communist Party's consolidation of its long-term governing position and to "upholding the Party's overall leadership", citing Xi Jinping's reports to the 19th and 20th Party Congresses. In Yu's account, Lenin lacked time to state the principle of comprehensive Party leadership explicitly, and the CCP has since summarised its own and Soviet experience and developed it. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Lenin's post-1917 practice is used to ground the doctrine of long-term Party leadership, with detailed citations of Lenin's texts.
quoteEn: Lenin's thought that the workers' and peasants' state must uphold Communist Party leadership over a long period enriched and developed the above ideas of Marx and Engels.
quoteZh: 列宁关于工农国家必须长时期坚持共产党领导的思想，丰富和发展了马克思恩格斯的上述思想。

glossary.literal: adhering to the Party's comprehensive leadership
glossary.explanation: A formula in Xi Jinping-era Party documents, holding that the Party leads all fields of state and social work. It is often summarised in the 19th Party Congress (2017) phrase that the Party leads everything.
In the Marxist tradition, the period between the capitalist revolution and the first stage of communist society, during which the dictatorship of the proletariat is maintained.

t: Anti-capitalism as a form of organisation: a psychoanalytic approach
zh: 作为组织形式的反资本主义：以精神分析为切入点
orig: Theory, Culture & Society (online, 29 June 2023)
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2024 no. 3
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by Nick Malherbe, first published in Theory, Culture & Society. It asks whether 'anti-capitalism' is too vague a term to guide left politics, since liberal reformists and fascist nationalists have also used it. Malherbe argues that the term is best read as a 'loose signifier' for a form of organisation: collectives assemble in whatever shape current struggles require, and psychoanalysis helps explain how this works for the people involved.

The article moves from the term's history, from the 1999 Seattle protests onward, to the psychoanalytic tradition's own political record. Malherbe cites Erik Olin Wright's typology of anti-capitalist strategies and Slavoj Žižek's warning that the word has lost its subversive edge. He then surveys psychoanalytic engagements with the left, from Freud and the Frankfurt School through Fanon, Deleuze and Guattari, Althusser, Mitchell, the Ljubljana school, the Essex School and Judith Butler to present-day scholars. The central sections discuss anti-capitalism's 'radical negativity' and then three dimensions of organisation: knowledge, action and being.

Malherbe's core move uses Lacan's notion of enjoyment (jouissance). When liberals and anti-capitalists share the word, it offers no enjoyment and the right wins over that enjoyment through racism and nationalism. Anti-capitalism, by contrast, can offer enjoyment in lack, because it refuses a fixed organisational form and is reshaped by whoever capitalism excludes. On knowledge, the author says organisations should accept contradiction and use fantasy strategically. On action, Malherbe favours many small, everyday acts of change, such as work refusal, union building and worker cooperatives, over reliance on single heroic acts, with Rosa Parks and the 2015 South African student protests as examples. On being, solidarity rests on a shared sense of otherness rather than identical identities, though groups such as the Black Panthers sometimes need to organise around subjective coherence.

Malherbe concludes that anti-capitalism, whether centralised or grassroots, local or international, depends on how people organised under a negative symbolic order understand their specific struggles. Naming it 'anti-capitalism' brings out its psychological and political value. The author calls for building organisational capacity in diverse forms to challenge capitalism's totality. Read the original if you work on psychoanalytic or Lacanian approaches to left organising, or want a survey of how psychoanalysis has been used in anti-capitalist theory.
quoteEn: The fundamental negativity of anti-capitalism allows a collective, under existing conditions, to adopt the most fitting organisational form for its most transformative action.
quoteZh: 反资本主义在根本上的否定性允许集体在现有的条件下采取最恰当的组织形式来组织最具变革性的行动。

t: Analytical political economy: the revival of Analytical Marxism in economics
zh: 分析政治经济学：分析的马克思主义在经济学领域的复兴
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 6
paras: Chen Weikai asks how Analytical Marxism, which declined after 1990, has revived in economics since the early 21st century, and what Chinese scholars can learn from it. The article argues that, especially after the 2008 financial crisis, a scholarly community called Analytical Political Economy has emerged. In Chen's account it critically inherits the methodology of Analytical Marxism and has become one of the most active schools of Marxist economics outside China, but it has weaknesses that need correcting.

The article has three parts. The first traces the school's development: the economic roots of Analytical Marxism in Japanese mathematical Marxian economics (Michio Morishima), Piero Sraffa's work and the September Group of 1981; its decline; and the Analytical Political Economy workshops from 1991, the 2007 relaunch in London, and the University of Massachusetts Amherst as a base. The second part sets out the school's methodological features. The third offers Chen's own critique.

Chen's central move is a distinction between a broad and a narrow conception of the analytical method. The broad version, drawing on Erik Olin Wright, stresses scientific norms, systematic concepts, careful argument and purposive individual action. The narrow version, 'rational choice Marxism', insists on methodological individualism and reductionism. Chen holds that this narrow approach exhausted Analytical Marxism's reconstruction of Marx's economics. Analytical Political Economy, by contrast, accepts the broad method and uses axiomatic approaches. It treats micro and macro levels as dialectically interacting, with structural constraints on individuals and the social formation of preferences. It is also pluralist about tools and paradigms, including neoclassical models, game theory and post-Keynesian economics.

Chen identifies three shortcomings. The school contains much non-Marxist work and lacks a Marxist research programme; Chen calls for returning to Marx's analysis of modes of production, including platform-based forms of organisation. It neglects materialist dialectics, which Chen sees as complementary to analytical methods. It is too focused on basic theory (value, the transformation problem, the falling rate of profit) and should address monopoly power, digital labour relations, climate change, automation and artificial intelligence, using big data and causal inference. Read the original if you want a Chinese economist's survey of Analytical Marxism's economic lineage and a critique of its methods from within a Marxist research programme.
quoteEn: Analytical political economy should return to the core questions of Marxist economic theory and, in light of new changes in contemporary monopoly capital, study further the transformation, diffusion and impact of the new, platform-based forms of production organisation brought about by digital information technology.
quoteZh: 分析政治经济学应当回归马克思主义经济理论的核心问题，结合当代垄断资本的新变化进一步研究数字信息技术引发的以平台为代表的新生产组织方式的变革、扩散及其影响。

glossary.explanation: A school emerging in the late 1970s that applies analytic philosophy and modern social-science methods to Marxist concepts. Its figures include G. A. Cohen, John Roemer and Jon Elster.
A community of mainly Marxist and heterodox economists, organised through workshops since 1991 and especially after 2007. It uses formal analytical tools in non-neoclassical economics.
A group of scholars, including Cohen, Roemer and Elster, who began meeting in 1981 and are regarded as the formal founding of Analytical Marxism.
The narrow strand of Analytical Marxism that insists on methodological individualism and rational choice theory. Chen treats it as the cause of the school's decline in economics.
The view that all social phenomena can in principle be explained through individuals and their goals, beliefs and actions.

t: The event-based view of history in foreign Marxist theory
zh: 国外马克思主义理论中的事件史观探析
paras: Hu Yaohui asks how historical materialism should understand revolutionary change when the moment of revolution does not coincide with the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. The article traces a lineage of 'event-based' views of history in Marxism outside China. These thinkers stress discontinuity, contingency and human agency, and reject teleology and evolutionism. Hu argues that this lineage recovers valuable elements of historical materialism but exaggerates rupture until the event becomes mystified, and that Marx's own analysis of events offers a corrective.

The article has four parts. It first examines Walter Benjamin's 'now-time' (Jetztzeit) and his Theses on the Philosophy of History. It then turns to Louis Althusser's theory of the conjuncture, overdetermination and late 'materialism of the encounter'. The third part covers Alain Badiou's event theory, with references to Žižek and Agamben. The last part returns to Marx's The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte as a model of event analysis. Hu links the rise of each view to periods when the international communist movement was blocked.

Hu reads Benjamin as breaking with linear progress: revolution can arise in any present, history is built from the standpoint of the oppressed, and a 'real state of exception' must be produced. Hu sees Althusser shifting to the conjuncture, where the 'empty place' is filled only by action, and Badiou pushing contingency to an absolute in which the event is a 'non-being' with no link to necessity. Hu argues that all three share an anti-Hegelian refusal of totality and negation of the negation, and that Benjamin's messianism, Althusser's 'determination in the last instance' and Badiou's Kantian split show the unresolved problem. Marx, by contrast, links three levels: the economic base (long duration), class analysis (the conjuncture) and the event (short duration). In this reading, contingency such as the February Revolution's unexpected turn is absorbed into class structure and the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production.

Hu offers two criticisms of the event theorists. They grasp only the conjuncture and the event, and so confuse contingency with openness; Badiou's treatment of May 1968 as an isolated event ignores its place in world history. They also blur the proletariat as the fundamental revolutionary subject, and without a strong party, resistance stays at 'single-point blasting' and falls into decisionism or a miracle-centred view of history. Hu calls for stripping the event of metaphysics and returning to Marx's analysis of how people make history within given structures. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese scholar assesses Benjamin, Althusser and Badiou against Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire.
quoteEn: The event-based view rightly sees this element in the occurrence of events, but it exaggerates the difference completely, treating it as pure contingency and rupture, and in the end mystifies the event itself and moves away from historical materialism.
quoteZh: 事件史观合理地看到了事件发生中的这一因素，但是又将这种不同彻底夸大，以至于将其视为纯粹的偶然和断裂，最终将事件本身神秘化，从而远离了历史唯物主义。

glossary.explanation: Marx's theory that history is shaped by the development of productive forces and relations of production. Chinese scholarship usually calls it 唯物史观 or 历史唯物主义.
The author's term for Althusser's focus on the conjuncture (conjoncture), the concrete convergence of forces from which events arise.
Althusser's idea that a social contradiction is determined by many interacting contradictions, not by the economy alone.

t: How foreign Marxist parties study and interpret Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
zh: 国外马克思主义政党对习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的研究阐释
paras: Zhuo Mingliang asks how Marxist and communist parties outside China have studied Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that these parties, of which the author says roughly 130 in over 100 countries still keep a communist name or Marxist character, are one of the main overseas forces interpreting the Thought. According to Zhuo, they have treated it as a systematic body of theory and have assessed its world significance.

The article first sets out the context: the shift of power from West to East amid "changes unseen in a century", and the growing international reach of the Thought, shown by the circulation of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China among politicians, scholars and ordinary readers. It then surveys the parties' work under four headings: the systematisation of the Thought, its core content, its worldview and methodology, and its value for world socialism and for humanity. It draws on statements by leaders of the Russian, Iraqi, Nepali, Italian, Brazilian, Czech and other parties, as well as by figures such as Hans Modrow. A closing section assesses the field.

Zhuo reports that these parties trace the Thought to Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. They see it as a product of the Two Integrations, and read its core content as the fourteen basic policies. They also discuss its worldview and methodology through the "six musts": putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking and a global perspective. On world value, they regard China's results as vindicating Marxism after the Soviet collapse and offering a method for adapting Marxism to national conditions. They also read the community with a shared future for mankind and the three global initiatives as contributions to humanity. Zhuo presents these views as evidence of the Thought's influence.

Zhuo distinguishes two strands of overseas research. One is practical and policy-oriented, done by foreign scholars, think tanks and journalists, who say little about the Thought itself. The other is theoretical, done mainly by Marxist parties and some left scholars, which is small in volume but valued by the author. Zhuo says these parties act as a main force in explaining the Party and rebutting Western criticism, and that their work rests on shared political identification. The author lists three shortcomings: too little work on specific fields, weak influence because many parties are small or stigmatised, and some views that need discussion or correction as misreadings. Read the original if you want a catalogue of foreign communist leaders' comments on Xi Jinping Thought, and the official Chinese academic framing of them, with sources in the notes.
quoteEn: Foreign Marxist parties' research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era rests on a natural sense of political identification and a real political closeness.
quoteZh: 国外马克思主义政党对习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的研究是基于天然的政治认同感与现实的政治亲近感。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Chinese Communist Party's guiding ideology, written into the Party Constitution in 2017 and the State Constitution in 2018. The Party presents it as the latest result of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions.
The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second "integration" was added in official discourse in 2021–2023.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since about 2012. It calls for shared development and security and for global governance based on cooperation.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: An official description of the current international situation, used by Xi Jinping since 2017–2018. It refers to a shifting global balance of power and rapid technological and geopolitical change.
A list of fourteen principles for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era, presented in the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017).

glossary.zh: 全球发展倡议、全球安全倡议、全球文明倡议
glossary.pinyin: quánqiú fāzhǎn chàngyì, quánqiú ānquán chàngyì, quánqiú wénmíng chàngyì
glossary.literal: Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative, Global Civilization Initiative
glossary.explanation: Three international proposals put forward by Xi Jinping in 2021–2023. They concern development cooperation, security and dialogue between civilisations.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Three ways contemporary Western scholars interpret the Marxist concept of productive forces
zh: 当代西方学者对马克思主义生产力概念的三种解读方式
source: Journal of Wuhan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2024 no. 6
paras: Yu Weidong and Wang Nan ask how contemporary Western scholars read the Marxist concept of productive forces, which Marx never defined in a final form. The article argues that the three most influential readings, technological determinism, nature conservation and wealth creation, each hold some rationality but all fall into the same error of seeing things and not people. The authors link this to the current Chinese strategy of developing new quality productive forces.

The article takes each reading in turn. Technological determinism is traced through William Shaw, Marvin Harris, James O'Connor, Slavoj Žižek and above all Jürgen Habermas. The nature-conservation reading is traced through Theodor Adorno, O'Connor, William Leiss and Alfred Schmidt. The wealth-creation reading is traced through Jean Baudrillard and Joseph Schumpeter, with roots in Petty, Quesnay, Smith and Ricardo. A fourth section assesses all three, and a conclusion draws out implications for new quality productive forces.

For each reading the authors identify two features and a Marxist counter-argument. They hold that technological determinism reduces Marx's three elements (labourers, means of labour, objects of labour) to technology alone and thereby defends capitalism by sidelining labour and surplus-value theory. In their account, the nature-conservation reading wrongly equates productive forces with the domination of nature and misses Marx's idea of the 'humanised nature' produced through labour, so that nature and human emancipation are not opposed. The wealth-creation reading, they say, repeats classical political economy and ignores the 'Copernican revolution' of Marx's analysis of relations of production. Against all three, Yu and Wang insist that productive forces are a generative resultant of real individuals' labour, with the human element primary, and are neither a purely scientific nor a purely economic category.

The authors conclude that the concept carries a value orientation toward human emancipation, and they draw three implications for new quality productive forces. First, development should combine the logic of capital with a people-centred logic. Second, ecological civilisation is inherent in productive-force development, citing Xi Jinping's remark that new quality productive forces are green productive forces. Third, socialist relations of production provide an institutional advantage, whereas the authors say Western scholars use distorted readings to defend capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical account of Habermas, Baudrillard, O'Connor and others on productive forces, and of how that critique is used to ground the policy concept of new quality productive forces.
quoteEn: There is no so-called objective nature, only 'humanised nature'.
quoteZh: 没有所谓客观自然，只有“人化自然”。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping from 2023 to describe advanced productive forces driven by technological innovation, high efficiency and green development. It is presented as the basis for high-quality development.
A concept drawn from Marx's early writings: nature as it is shaped by human labour and practice. Chinese Marxist writing uses it to argue there is no nature wholly independent of humanity.

t: An assessment of the impact of identity politics on contemporary Western left-wing movements
zh: 身份政治对当代西方左翼运动的影响评析
paras: Why have Western left movements lost ground to right-wing populism, even as identity politics has become a major force within them? Chen argues from a Marxist standpoint that identity politics, adopted in the post-industrial era as a way out of the left's predicament, has damaged the left's political ideals. In the article's account, it weakened the left itself and helped create a cultural and social structure favourable to the expansion of finance capital.

The article has three parts. The first sets out three features of identity politics in Western left movements: it replaces the working class with plural identities as the subject of struggle, it pursues cultural and everyday liberation instead of changing relations of production, and it favours decentralised individual action over parties and class organisation. Examples include Occupy Wall Street, the Global Climate Strikes, Black Lives Matter and Me Too. The second part sets out four practical dilemmas, and the third reflects on their causes.

Chen's core claim is that dropping the category of class turns the left into an "unconscious instrument" of capitalist rule. The four dilemmas are these: stressing cultural equality tacitly accepts capitalism's legitimacy, and the left ends up allied with financial and tech elites and the US Democratic Party; "victim politics" and the differentiation of identities fragment potential unity and put narrow group interests ahead of the common interest; and after the 2008 financial crisis, lower- and middle-class white people were pushed towards right-wing populism. Chen contends that identity politics misreads economic and class conflict as identity conflict, neglects material interests, and abandons the class unity and party organisation needed to confront finance capital.

Chen concedes that identity politics exposed new problems and mobilised marginal groups, giving it some historical significance. The article still concludes that it cannot change economic inequality, and that Western left theorists who criticise it without aiming to transform capitalist relations of production remain absorbed by capitalism. It ends by contrasting this with socialism with Chinese characteristics under the Communist Party, which Chen presents as the key force for reviving world socialism in the 21st century. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of identity politics, with its case examples from the United States and its account of the left's decline.
quoteEn: This shows that a political movement that denies class identity and ignores the people's material interests cannot gather the collective strength needed to transform the capitalist system, and so cannot escape failure.
quoteZh: 这表明，否定阶级同一性和忽视民众物质利益诉求的政治运动，并不能汇聚起变革资本主义制度的整体性力量，因而难逃失败命运。

glossary.explanation: Political mobilisation organised around group identities such as race, gender and sexual orientation rather than class. The article treats it as a strategy of the post-industrial Western left.
The period in advanced capitalist societies after industrial manufacturing declined, which the article links to the weakening of working-class revolutionary dynamism.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: Research on foreign Marxism from the perspective of China's independent knowledge system
zh: 中国自主知识体系视角下的国外马克思主义研究
source: Contemporary Chinese Marxist Studies (当代中国马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 2
paras: After more than forty years of rapid growth in foreign Marxism studies in China, Lan Jiang asks why Chinese scholars should study foreign Marxism, how they should do so, and what kind of research the country now needs. The author argues that translation and introduction alone no longer suffice, and that the field should be rebuilt within China's independent knowledge system on three footings: Chinese problems, Chinese discourse and China's future.

The article first traces the field's origins. It notes that in the 1950s and 1960s Lukács and Lefebvre were presented as revisionists or 'progressive writers' rather than as a distinct current, and that the field took shape in the 1980s with Perry Anderson's Considerations on Western Marxism and Xu Chongwen's work on 'Western Marxism'. It then sets out the three sections of its argument, which Lan labels ontology, methodology and teleology, and closes with a proposed coordinate system for the field.

Lan holds that the early generation of scholars, including Xu Chongwen and Chen Xueming, studied Western Marxism to understand contemporary capitalism at the start of reform and opening up, and that later work has often lost this problem-orientation. Methodologically, the author describes three stages: 'following' (translation), 'continuing' (genealogies such as Zhang Yibing's History of the Understanding of Capitalism) and 'speaking back' in Chinese discourse. As an example of the last, Lan criticises Kohei Saito's 'degrowth communism' as shaped by Western ideology and unsuited to China. On purpose, the author maintains that foreign Marxists' visions of the future remain partly utopian, and that their work should serve Chinese socialism: distribution and welfare at home, and the community with a shared future for mankind abroad.

Lan proposes a Cartesian-style coordinate system. Its vertical axis is the historical-materialist analysis of each thinker, school and country in its own era, and its horizontal axis is Chinese problems and Chinese discourse, such as ecology and carbon reduction. The conclusion borrows Lacan's triad: Chinese problems are the Real, Chinese discourse the Symbolic and the Chinese dream of the future the Imaginary. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism redefines the field's purpose, history and method, including a critical Chinese reading of Saito.
quoteEn: Taking Chinese problems as the orientation is the ontological foundation of China's research on foreign Marxism.
quoteZh: 以中国问题为导向，就是中国的国外马克思主义研究的本体论基础。

glossary.explanation: A slogan from Xi Jinping's speeches, calling for Chinese philosophy and social science to develop their own concepts and discourse rather than rely on Western frameworks.
The broad field of Marxist thought outside China, wider than 'Western Marxism' in the strict sense (Lukács, the Frankfurt School and others).
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world begun in China in 1978.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for China's vision of international relations and global governance.

t: The cultural programme of the Russian Narodniks and its historical echoes
zh: 俄国民粹派的文化纲领及其历史回响
paras: Zhou Laishun examines the cultural programme of the Russian Narodniks (populists), the movement that shaped Russian social thought and practice from the mid-nineteenth century to the early twentieth. The article argues that this programme, which rested on the people, the village commune and cultural enlightenment, supplied the theoretical core of the movement's practical goals. Zhou holds that it combined a real critique of autocracy and capitalism with romantic, class-limited illusions, and that Marxists such as Marx, Engels and Lenin criticised it for this.

The article has four parts. It first treats the "going to the people" movement as an awakening of consciousness, then the commune as the programme's foundation of belief, then its moral and political critique of tsarism and capital. It ends by tracing the programme's historical echoes in the Marxist reaction. Zhou draws on Narodnik writers such as Mikhailovsky, Lavrov, Tkachev, Zaichnevsky and Eliseev. He also draws on Silver Age philosophers and on Marx's reply to Vera Zasulich, Engels's postscript to "On Social Relations in Russia" and Lenin's polemics.

In Zhou's account, the Narodniks idealised peasants and the commune as a base for bypassing capitalism. Zhou describes this as a utopian, petty-bourgeois outlook close to Sismondi's romanticism, with a moral rather than economic basis, and as a heroic view of history. Zhou stresses that the commune was not uniquely Russian, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin. Marx treated it as a possible "fulcrum" of social regeneration only if a revolution protected it. The Narodniks attacked the tsar himself and Tkachev demanded immediate revolution, but Zhou argues that the movement failed. It lacked a vanguard party armed with advanced theory, swung between elite terror and one-way enlightenment, and was cut off from the masses.

Zhou concludes that the movement still had positive significance. It valued the masses' historical role, criticised the feudal nobility, and began organised revolutionary agitation. Its long polemic with Marxists in the 1890s, which Lenin completed, led Russian intellectuals to Marxism and turned it from theory into practice. Zhou presents this as opening a path to modernity different from the Western one. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Narodnik thought, drawn largely from Russian sources and from the classical Marxist critique of the movement.
quoteEn: The Narodniks' cultural programme held false expectations of the commune and of the people's character, never grasped the causes of the real predicament Russia faced, and its tactics of struggle were largely detached from the masses and from reality.
quoteZh: 民粹派的文化纲领存在对村社、人民性等的虚假期许，并未深入理解俄国所面临现实困境的成因，其斗争策略很大程度上与民众和现实相脱节。

t: An assessment of the impact of identity politics on the contemporary Western left
zh: 身份政治对当代西方左翼运动的影响评析
paras: Chen Yuntao asks why the Western left, once identified with critique and progress, has come to be seen by many ordinary people as a conservative obstacle to equality while right-wing populists such as Trump pose as anti-establishment. The article argues that identity politics, adopted in the post-industrial era to escape the exhaustion of working-class revolutionary energy, has undermined the left's own aims. In Chen's account, it has weakened the left and produced a cultural and social structure that suits financial capital.

The article has three parts. The first sets out three typical features of identity-led left movements: they replace the working class with plural identities as the subject of struggle; they pursue cultural and everyday-life liberation instead of changing relations of production; and they favour decentralised, individual action over party politics and unified class action. Examples include Occupy Wall Street, the Global Climate Strikes, Black Lives Matter and Me Too. The second part sets out four practical dilemmas, and the third reflects on why identity politics has become what Chen calls an "unconscious instrument" of capitalist rule.

Chen contends that identity politics tacitly accepts capitalist legitimacy by ignoring class inequality, and that the left has formed an alliance with Wall Street, Silicon Valley and Hollywood elites. In this reading, "victim politics" and differentiated identity mechanisms deepen divisions among ordinary people and replace the common goal of opposing injustice with narrow group interests. After the 2008 financial crisis, the article says, lower- and middle-class whites came to see the left as favouring minorities and were pushed towards right-wing populism. Chen's central Marxist claim is that identity conflicts derive from economic inequality, that material interests outweigh cultural identification, and that only a united class of labourers can confront financial capital. Identity politics, the author says, therefore misidentifies friends and enemies, and is "left in form, right in essence".

Chen concedes that identity politics exposed new contradictions and briefly advanced social equality. The article nonetheless concludes that it leads the Western left away from socialist ideals and working-class interests, and that Western left theorists who criticise it without aiming to transform capitalist relations of production remain co-opted. Chen contrasts this with socialism with Chinese characteristics under Communist Party leadership, which the author presents as the key force for reviving world socialism in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western identity politics, set within debates on the fate of the Western left and world socialism.
quoteEn: This is not only a loss of sight of the real enemy and the right direction but a betrayal of the highly combative working class, and on this point alone it confirms the "left in form, right in essence" nature of identity politics.
quoteZh: 这不仅是对真正敌人和正确方向的迷失，更是对极富斗争精神的工人阶级的背叛，仅此一点就做实了身份政治“形左实右的本质”。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. The article presents it as the leading force in reviving world socialism.
A term in Chinese scholarship for the global socialist movement and its historical trajectory. Chinese authors often discuss its decline and its twenty-first-century revival.

t: The new "networked" pattern of relations among communist parties abroad in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪国外共产党政党关系的“网络化”新态势
paras: Yu Weihai and Li Yuwei ask how relations among communist parties outside China should be characterised since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Existing Chinese studies, they say, are scattered and mostly describe either cooperation or splits. The authors argue that the dominant pattern in the twenty-first century is "networked" (wangluohua): parties of many types interact densely, link in varied ways, cooperate loosely and quarrel constantly. They frame the topic through Xi Jinping's 2017 call for a new type of inter-party relations.

The article first proposes the concept, then sets out five manifestations of networking. It then identifies four new structural features and ends with three reflections for the Communist Party of China. Evidence comes from party statements, the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties (IMCWP), regional forums such as the São Paulo Forum, the Party of the European Left and European Communist Action, and recent joint statements on the Middle East and Ukraine.

The authors' core claim is that the network combines opposed tendencies. The five manifestations are typified actors, intensive exchange, diversified linkage, loose internationalism and routine disputes. The authors count over 400 parties, classed by their guiding ideology (Marxism-Leninism, Marxism, Mao Zedong Thought, Trotskyism, Hoxhaism and others). These parties explore separate national paths yet share a consensus after the 2008 financial crisis. Their unity is "weak", because organisations such as the IMCWP have no leadership, programme or binding decisions. The IMCWP produced two conflicting resolutions in 2022, and the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties of Europe dissolved in 2023. The authors present the structure as flat and decentralised, replacing the Soviet-led centre–periphery model. Internationalism is set against a sectarianism that claims orthodoxy and seeks "one centre".

Yu and Li conclude that the international communist movement has not disappeared but has taken a new form. They also judge that networking reflects an immature stage of international unity. They argue that only "limited unity" is feasible now and that analysis must go beyond older frameworks. They call on the Communist Party of China to guide inter-party relations through the new type of party relations. They propose using the Dialogue with World Political Parties and the World Socialism Forum to build a Chinese discourse and to promote solidarity among communist parties. Read the original if you study contemporary communist parties abroad, or want to see how Chinese scholars frame them in relation to Party diplomacy.
quoteEn: To a certain extent it can be said that the "networking" of communist parties abroad today is in essence a sign of the immaturity of Marxist parties' exploration of international unity.
quoteZh: 一定程度上可以说，当今国外共产党“网络化”实质是马克思主义政党探索国际联合不成熟的表现。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping put forward in 2017. It calls for inter-party ties based on seeking common ground while shelving differences, mutual respect and mutual learning.

glossary.en: the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese term for the end of the Soviet bloc regimes in 1989–91. It is treated as a turning point for the international communist movement.

The worldwide network of communist parties and organisations, historically centred on the Comintern and later the Soviet party. Chinese scholars use it for both the history and the present state of these parties.

glossary.zh: 共产党和工人党国际会议
glossary.en: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
glossary.explanation: An annual multilateral forum of communist and workers' parties, running since 1998. It has no standing leadership or binding programme.

t: Engels studies abroad: latest developments and hot issues
zh: 国外恩格斯研究：最新进展与热点问题
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 5
paras: This review surveys recent scholarship on Friedrich Engels outside China. Weng notes that foreign Marxism has long carried an anti-Engels tendency, which blamed him for distorting Marx and for Marxism's crises. Weng argues that since the late twentieth century, foreign scholars have rethought this tradition, producing a revival of Engels studies that takes a 'one source, many streams' form and largely rehabilitates his standing as Marx's lifelong collaborator and co-founder of Marxism.

The article has four parts. The first traces the revival, covering new texts from the second Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe (MEGA2), the 'new reading' movement, interdisciplinary methods, key monographs, journals and conferences from 1995 to 2023. The second reviews reassessments of Engels's status. The third maps the multidimensional fields in which his thought is being reactivated. The fourth draws lessons for domestic research.

In the central section, Weng reports four lines of defence against older charges. Scholars such as Paul Blackledge and John Bellamy Foster reject the 'Marx–Engels opposition' thesis, including Norman Levine's 'Engelsism' and Kohei Saito's claim of an ecological divergence. Others rebut the portrait of Engels as positivist, mechanist or fatalist, and answer accusations of misreading or falsifying Capital. Here the Sendai group's catalogue of about 5,000 changes to the Capital Volume 2 manuscript is cited, and most changes are judged semantically minor. Weng then shows Engels being applied to digital capitalism, natural science and ecology, pandemics and women's conditions, war and the state, and geography and urbanisation.

Weng concludes that foreign work has re-evaluated and defended Engels and confirmed the present-day explanatory power of his thought. For Chinese research, Weng proposes a systematic Engels studies that combines detailed period-specific work with holistic study. It should be problem-oriented, address modernity problems in contemporary development, and join an ideological stance with academic standards. Foreign findings should be analysed and discriminated, not accepted wholesale, as Xi Jinping has urged. Read the original if you want a map of recent foreign Engels scholarship, with its authors, debates and conferences, and a view of how a Chinese scholar assesses it for domestic research.
quoteEn: Overall, we should build a systematic and holistic Engels studies for the twenty-first century, with both 'opening', meaning detailed studies of each period and field, and 'closing', meaning general, all-round studies of Engels as a whole.
quoteZh: 总体而言，应当面向21世纪构建体系化、整体性的恩格斯研究，既有“开”,即各时期、各领域的细化恩格斯研究，又有“合”,即整体性、全方位的一般化恩格斯研究。

t: A century after Lenin's death: new developments in Lenin studies abroad
zh: 列宁逝世百年：国外列宁研究新进展
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 5
paras: This review surveys how overseas scholars, left-wing parties and media marked the centenary of Lenin's death on 21 January 2024, and what the wave of commemoration shows about current Lenin studies abroad. Wang and Yang argue that the foreign literature confirms Lenin's standing as a political theorist and fuels calls to 'return to Lenin', but that Chinese readers must assess these views critically and take a firm position.

The article first lists the commemorative output: special issues and articles in Monthly Review, Jacobin, Platypus Review and similar outlets; conferences in London, Abuja, Berlin and online; a Cuban television programme; and new editions, biographies and studies. It then groups the scholarship into four themes: the philosophical sources of Lenin's thought, his theory of imperialism, his theory of socialist revolution and construction, and the contemporary meaning of Leninism. A concluding section gives the authors' own evaluation.

On philosophy, the review reports Kevin Anderson, Carlos Garrido, Michael Löwy and the Russian researcher Petr Kondrashov on Lenin's reading of Hegel, his Philosophical Notebooks and his development of dialectics. On imperialism, it cites Prakash Karat and Prabhat Patnaik on how Lenin extended Marxism into a theory of world revolution, and Sunanda Sen on contemporary financialised imperialism. On revolution and construction, it covers the worker–peasant alliance, the vanguard party and democratic centralism, national self-determination, socialism in one country, the transition after 1921, and strategic and tactical flexibility. Several authors, including Atilio Boron, Paul Le Blanc and Luca Cangemi, present Leninism as a resource for empowering the people, rebuilding mass socialist movements and linking anti-imperialism to the Global South.

In their closing section Wang and Yang draw three lessons. They call for a firm stance against Western scholars and politicians who, in their account, demonise Lenin under the influence of 'de-Sovietisation' and historical nihilism. They distinguish three groups behind the commemorations: Leninist communist parties, Trotskyist organisations, and independent left intellectuals. They also urge a scientific judgement of the many new theories of imperialism, using the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method. Read the original if you want a detailed map of the foreign authors, journals and events that shaped the 2024 Lenin centenary, together with a Chinese academic assessment of them.
quoteEn: One must hold a firm position on how the foreign academic community evaluates Lenin.
quoteZh: 对国外学界关涉列宁的评价问题要有坚定的立场。

glossary.explanation: A term for developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, widely used in Chinese official and academic discourse in contrast to the developed West.
In Chinese Party discourse, a label for views seen as denying or distorting the Party's and socialism's historical record, including that of the Soviet Union.
The organisational principle of Leninist parties combining discussion with binding, centralised decisions; it is also the Chinese Communist Party's formal principle.

glossary.literal: theory of victory in one country
glossary.explanation: The thesis that socialist revolution can first triumph in a single country. The article attributes it to Lenin and notes the later Soviet shift to the 'socialism in one country' line.

t: The "Global South" and its modernization in the view of foreign left-wing scholars
zh: 国外左翼学者视域中的“全球南方”及其现代化问题探析
paras: Zhou Miao asks how left-wing scholars outside China have explained the emergence of the "Global South" and the obstacles to its modernization. The article argues that these scholars trace the South's backwardness to the capitalist world system rather than to internal traditions. It presents their work as useful for understanding the roots of the North–South gap and for confirming China's place as a member of the Global South. The article opens by noting that many Global South states declined to condemn or sanction Russia after the Ukraine conflict began.

The article has three parts. The first traces how the Global South arose with the capitalist world system and compares related labels: "Third World", "developing countries" and "North/South". The second sets out four constraints on Southern modernization identified by Samir Amin, Andre Gunder Frank, Theotonio dos Santos, Immanuel-style dependency writers, Michael Hudson, Stavrianos and others. The third turns to remedies and to the role of socialism, including Chinese modernization.

Zhou reports that these scholars reject the term "developing countries" because it implies a linear path and hides the historical cause of underdevelopment. In Frank's and Stavrianos's reading, development and underdevelopment are two sides of one coin, and the "Third World" names a relationship of domination, not a group of states. The four constraints are monetary and financial hegemony (Hudson's account of the dollar-debt cycle), a neo-colonial system, an unequal international division of labour (dos Santos's "industrial-technological dependence"), and dependent accumulation. The remedy these scholars propose is autonomous, self-centred development. Zhou stresses that the "delinking" proposed by Amin and others means reforming unequal relations, not closing off, and notes that Cardoso and others revised dependency theory after the "East Asian miracle".

Zhou further argues that, on these scholars' accounts, socialism helped the South by inspiring independence movements, widening international room for manoeuvre and offering an alternative model. The article presents Chinese modernization as extending that alternative, citing loans without political conditions, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. It concludes that drawing on this scholarship can enrich China's proposals on global governance and help unite Southern countries. Read the original if you want a Chinese-published survey of dependency theory, world-systems and anti-imperialist writing on the Global South, or want to see how such work is used to support China's self-positioning.
quoteEn: To achieve genuine modernization, Global South countries must oppose the Euro-American-centred model of modernization and achieve sustained, autonomous, self-centred development.
quoteZh: 全球南方国家要实现真正的现代化发展，必须反对以欧美为中心的现代化模式，实现持续自主中心式的发展。

glossary.explanation: A term for countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, mostly former colonies, that are less industrialised than the North. Chinese official discourse presents China as a natural member.
The official Party-state formulation for China's own path of modernization, presented as distinct from the Western model.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s, setting out a vision of cooperative international relations.
A Chinese infrastructure and investment initiative launched in 2013, linking China with Asia, Africa and Europe.
A Cold War term for countries outside the capitalist and socialist blocs. Mao Zedong's 1974 'three worlds' formulation placed China among the Third World.

t: From climate ethics to climate justice: themes and trends in Western climate ethics research
zh: 从气候伦理到气候正义：西方气候伦理学研究的主题与趋势
paras: This review surveys Western scholarship on climate ethics from 1992 to the present. Yang and Gu argue that the field has moved from clarifying the ethical principles of the climate regime towards climate justice as its central theme, while steadily widening its scope. The text appeared in the journal Foreign Theoretical Trends (2024, no. 5).

The authors divide the literature into three stages tied to global climate governance: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change stage (1992–2003), the post-Kyoto Protocol stage (2004–2014) and the Paris Agreement stage (2015 onwards). They then examine four major themes: general theory of climate ethics, climate justice, the ethics of geoengineering, and the ethics of climate responsibility. A final section identifies three emerging directions: non-anthropocentric climate ethics, climate migrants and refugees, and population ethics.

Yang and Gu report that early scholars such as Dale Jamieson and Stephen Gardiner presented climate change as an ethical rather than purely scientific or economic problem, one that cost–benefit models cannot capture. On climate justice, the review sets out relational and non-relational foundations, the main distributive principles, and the dispute over historical responsibility, where supporters and sceptics offer competing grounds. On responsibility, it contrasts collectivists, who hold that individuals' main duty is to build just institutions because single emissions are inconsequential, with individualists, who reject the tragedy-of-the-commons model and defend personal duties to cut emissions. In geoengineering, the authors summarise doubts about moral hazard, the slippery slope and unequal procedures.

On the new directions, the article describes proposals for multi-species climate justice, debates over who should compensate climate migrants and how, and disputes over population policy, including Simon Caney's critique of restrictive proposals and the argument that developed countries should bear more responsibility for reducing birth rates. The authors conclude that climate ethics is increasingly interdisciplinary and tied to implementation of the Paris Agreement, and that designing population policy acceptable to many interest groups remains an open task.
