The article first reviews the Anthropocene narrative, from Eugene Stoermer and Paul Crutzen, and the disputes among its supporters over its starting date (1782, the rise of agriculture, or 1492), over whether the Earth is a mechanism or an organism, and over who is responsible. It then sets out the Capitalocene critique, noting alternatives such as the ecofeminist "Manthropocene". It goes on to examine capitalism's relation to science and technology, before tracing the Western conception of nature back to ancient Greece and Christianity.

The authors argue that the Anthropocene reproduces Cartesian dualism by separating humanity from nature, and that it blames an abstract "humanity" while ignoring class and the unequal responsibility of core and peripheral countries. The Capitalocene, in their account, answers this by locating the cause in capitalism's appropriation of cheap nature. The article then reverses the usual sequence: capitalism did not produce the idea of external, manipulable nature, since Bacon's science, Greek mechanics and rationalism, Plato and Aristotle, and Christian doctrine of dominion over the earth supplied it earlier. On this reading even contemporary geoengineering has Socratic and Greek roots, and the "technological power" of scientific elites is a continuation of that worldview.

The authors conclude that dating the Capitalocene to the sixteenth century hides the role of Greek technical rationalism and Christianity. In their formulation, capitalism is not "scientific" or "technological" but "Westernised", and Western science and technology were merely capitalised later. They hold that the shift to a new geological epoch is the culmination of Western history, so the Capitalocene is the Westernocene. Read the original if you want a critical-ecological account that pushes Moore's world-ecology approach back to ancient Greek and Christian ideas of nature, or if you follow debates on Anthropocene versus Capitalocene terminology.
quoteEn: Therefore, rather than saying the West is capitalist, it is better to say capitalism is Western; since capitalism is Eurocentric, the Capitalocene is naturally the Westernocene.
quoteZh: 因此，与其说西方是资本主义的，不如说资本主义是西方的，既然资本主义是西方中心主义的，那么资本世自然就是西方世。

glossary.explanation: A proposed geological epoch in which human activity is the dominant force changing the Earth system. The term was popularised by Paul Crutzen in the early 2000s.
Jason Moore's alternative to the Anthropocene, which holds that capitalism as a world-ecology, not humanity as a whole, drives ecological crisis.
The authors' proposed term, meaning that the roots of the climate crisis lie in a Western worldview of nature stretching back to ancient Greece and Christianity.

t: Living standards in the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s
st: Also on the economic factors in the Soviet collapse
zh: 20世纪七八十年代苏联人民生活水平探究
zhSub: 兼议苏联解体的经济因素
paras: A common view in the literature holds that low living standards, the result of a rigid planned economy, heavy-industry bias and arms-race spending, helped bring down the Soviet Union. Li Yinan argues that this claim has rarely been demonstrated. In the author's account, it rests either on projecting Stalin-era under-consumption onto the whole Soviet period, or on crude comparisons of nominal wages and Engel coefficients with Western countries. Li's thesis is that Soviet living standards rose without interruption until the late 1980s, and that their decline was a result of the collapse, not a cause.

The article has three parts. The first compares Soviet and major capitalist countries in the 1970s and 1980s on income, food, clothing, durable goods, culture, health, housing and education. The second examines how the Soviet commitment to rising welfare affected the political economy, and traces when living standards actually began to fall. The third assesses the link between living standards and the collapse. Li draws on Soviet and Western statistics, including CIA assessments, and on comparisons with Poland and the post-Soviet republics.

Li concedes that Soviet money wages were a fraction of Western ones, but argues that such comparisons mislead. Stable consumer prices, heavily subsidised necessities, free or nominal-cost housing, medicine and education, and taxes on luxuries gave a "hidden income" that nominal wages omit. Li also argues that more even income distribution made durable-goods ownership more equal than Western per-household averages suggest. The costs were heavy: grain and food imports, subsidies reaching 15–18 per cent of budget spending by the mid-1980s, and wages growing faster than productivity. Even so, Li maintains, the tension between slow growth and high consumption had not erupted before the collapse. Indicators such as life expectancy and food consumption turned down only from 1989, and Li attributes the shortages to disrupted circulation and distribution after Gorbachev's political reforms and rising national separatism.

Li concludes that the theory of low living standards causing popular discontent and collapse does not hold. The author calls the Soviet welfare system a landmark in the history of socialism, and notes that life expectancy in Russia, Ukraine and Belarus took more than two decades to regain Soviet peaks. The article closes with a 2007 remark by a former Soviet deputy foreign minister, who regretted that free medicine and stable prices had been taken for granted. Read the original if you want a data-rich revisionist argument on Soviet consumption and welfare, as it is presented in Chinese scholarship on world socialism.
quoteEn: The decline in living standards was a result of the Soviet collapse, not its cause.
quoteZh: 生活水平下降是苏联解体的结果，而非原因。

t: Ecological imperialism from a world-systems perspective
zh: 基于世界体系理论视角的生态帝国主义研究
orig: American Journal of Economics and Sociology, vol. 81, no. 3, 2022
source: Posted on marxism.cass.cn, 14 August 2024 (abridged Chinese translation)
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by the US economist Mariko L. Frame, drawn from her book on ecological imperialism, development and the capitalist world-system. Frame asks why global ecological crisis keeps worsening despite green growth and the Sustainable Development Goals. Her answer is that the consumption and growth of the Global North rest on ecological appropriation in the Global South, a relationship best understood through world-systems and dependency theory.

The article first reviews world-systems and dependency thinkers, including Samir Amin, Arghiri Emmanuel, Walter Rodney, Raúl Prebisch and Immanuel Wallerstein. It then sets out the concept of ecological unequal exchange, citing Alf Hornborg and Stephen Bunker. After that it defines five features of ecological imperialism and traces its dynamics in the core, semi-periphery and periphery. It closes with a three-stage history running from colonialism to neoliberalism.

Frame defines ecological imperialism by five features: capitalism's drive to expand and accumulate; unequal power within a hierarchical international division of labour; ecological debt and unequal exchange that money cannot compensate; its role as a reaction to protest movements; and continued accumulation in imperialist states. She dates its evolution in three stages: colonialism from 1492 to the 1960s, the economic nationalism and resource sovereignty of the 1940s to 1970s, and the neoliberal turn after the debt crisis. In the third stage she names three pillars: trade liberalisation, investor-friendly foreign-investment policy (including investor–state dispute settlement), and financial liberalisation. She illustrates these with cases such as mining firms in Africa and Vanguard's investments in deforestation-linked commodities. She argues that the rise of industrialised semi-peripheral states does not by itself show that they practise imperialism, since many act as suppliers to Northern firms.

Frame concludes that a world-systems view shows which political and economic arrangements sustain unsustainable Northern consumption and concentrate capital there. In her account, neoliberal globalisation and its development policies are the latest form of ecological imperialism, producing plunder, debt, corporate domination and worsening terms of trade in the periphery. Read the original if you want a Western world-systems account of ecological unequal exchange, with empirical examples, or if you follow foreign Marxist debates on imperialism and ecology.
quoteEn: The economic development and consumption levels of the Global North have to a large extent been, and will continue to be, built on the ecological exploitation of the Global South through the mechanisms of global economic integration.
quoteZh: 全球北方的经济发展和消费水平在很大程度上已经并将继续建立在全球经济一体化机制对全球南方的生态利用基础之上

glossary.explanation: A term for developing and formerly colonised countries, used in contrast to the industrialised Global North. In China it also appears in official discourse on South–South cooperation.

A concept developed from Emmanuel's unequal exchange. It holds that trade between core and periphery moves resources and environmental burdens asymmetrically, even when prices look fair in money terms.
In this article, a system in which dominant capitalist powers control the natural resources and ecological conditions of other regions to serve their own accumulation.

t: A penetrating analysis of the comprehensive crisis of contemporary capitalism and its harms
zh: 当代资本主义的全面危机及危害透析
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2023 no. 7
paras: Writing in 2023, Niu Xiafei takes up the question of whether the turmoil in Western societies since the 1970s is a temporary, local disturbance, as mainstream Western opinion holds, or something deeper. The article argues that capitalism, especially in the developed countries, is undergoing a comprehensive crisis spanning politics, culture, economics and the international order. In Niu's reading, this crisis is a marker of the 'great changes unseen in a century' and will shift the balance between capitalist and socialist forces in the world.

The article proceeds in four parts. It first examines polarisation and a new form of class conflict, then the rise of populism and polarised politics alongside the ossification of the separation-of-powers system. It goes on to discuss spiritual collapse and divided values after the collapse of 'post-class' narratives, and finally the return of extreme nationalism and intensifying geopolitical conflict, with the US, Europe and the Russia–Ukraine war as main cases. Niu draws on Marx and Engels and on Western scholars such as David Harvey and Earl Wysong.

Niu's central claim is that neoliberal globalisation and new technology have widened inequality and deepened class division. Niu attributes this to corporate restructuring, financialisation and crisis policies favouring finance capital, together with automation and 'digital exploitation'. The result, the article says, is a polarised 'double diamond' class structure and a left–right split within both bourgeoisie and working class. Niu reads populist revolts on both left and right as a common rebellion of the powerless against the moneyed, and argues that elections, party consensus and checks and balances have all degenerated. The article further holds that the myths of a 'post-class' and 'post-materialist' society have been exposed, leaving spiritual collapse and a tribalised liberalism. Abroad, it contends, 'free trade' and 'universal values' have been shown to serve US hegemony, citing the trade war with China and the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Niu concludes that in the long run capitalism's inherent contradictions point to its demise. In the medium term, however, digital and AI technology still raise productive forces, workers' class consciousness in developed countries is not fully awakened, and the bourgeoisie still holds firm control, so collapse is not imminent. The article adds that capitalism's crisis raises expectations of socialism in developing countries, and urges adherence to socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar assembles Western critical literature into an account of capitalist crisis and its implications for China's own path.
quoteEn: Viewed from the Marxist standpoint, left-wing and right-wing populist revolts against elite politics are in fact a common rebellion of the working class against the bourgeoisie, and of the powerless class against the moneyed class.
quoteZh: 站在马克思主义立场看待左翼和右翼民粹主义对精英政治的反叛，就能看出实际上是工人阶级对资产阶级的共同反叛，是无权阶级对金权阶级的共同反叛。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, combining Party leadership with market reforms since the late 1970s.
The official concept, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022), of a distinctively Chinese path to modernisation presented as an alternative to the Western model.

glossary.zh: 世界百年未有之大变局
glossary.pinyin: shìjiè bǎi nián wèiyǒu zhī dàbiànjú
glossary.en: great changes unseen in a century
glossary.literal: great changes in the world not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping since about 2017 to describe a shift in global power, including the relative decline of the West and the rise of emerging powers.

t: New trends in Western critical theories of the capitalist ecological crisis
zh: 西方资本主义生态危机批判理论的新动向
paras: Wang Xia and Wang Linxia ask how Western scholars now theorise the capitalist ecological crisis as a core of their critique of capitalist modernity, and what Chinese ecological-civilization theory can draw from this. They argue that Western work has moved along four lines: a "new alienation", a "new subject", a "new object" and a "new path". In their assessment, all four remain within Marx's theoretical horizon and none surpasses it.

The article is organised into four sections, one for each line. It draws on Hartmut Rosa, Nick Srnicek, Baudrillard, Deleuze, Benjamin Bratton and Byung-Chul Han on alienation; on Žižek, Badiou, Rancière and Negri on the subject; on the Australian ecologists Alan Gare and Andrew Brennan on community; and on Harvey, Agamben, Chomsky, Polanyi, Butler and Kohei Saito on neoliberalism and socialism.

On alienation, the authors report that Western scholars see crisis intensified by accelerationism, digital capitalism and a "control society", in which nature and people alike become data and raw material. On the subject, they describe Žižek's radicalised "new proletariat" of the excluded (slum-dwellers, refugees, migrants) as a community-minded agent of ecological governance. On the object, they present Gare's "community of communities" and Brennan's "holistic community" as ways of overcoming the human–nature split. Wang and Wang criticise Gare for staying at the level of cultural speculation, and Brennan for lapsing into eco-centric mysticism and offering no workable plan. They also note Gare's praise of China's ecological civilization. On the path, they report that left-wing writers see neoliberalism failing in the crisis and call for socialism or communism.

The authors conclude that these theories extend Marx's critique of alienation and his idea of reconciling humanity and nature. Because the Western thinkers remain enclosed in capitalist institutions and modernity, Wang and Wang judge their eco-socialism a speculative or cultural exploration that cannot reach Marx's vision of communism. They say the findings should encourage China to offer more Chinese wisdom and Chinese approaches to ecological-civilization building and to gain international discursive power. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of how Western left ecological thought on alienation, the proletariat, community and socialism is received and assessed in China.
quoteEn: These new theories present in concentrated form the new dynamics and new picture of the critique of the capitalist ecological crisis, and reveal the complicity of modernity in the development and transformation of that crisis.
quoteZh: 这些新理论集中呈现了资本主义生态危机批判的新动态与新图景，揭示了资本主义生态危机发展嬗变的现代性共谋

glossary.explanation: A Chinese official concept for a model of development that places environmental protection at the centre of economic and social life. It has been part of Party policy since the early 2000s and was written into the Party constitution in 2012.
A strand of left thought holding that the ecological crisis cannot be solved under capitalism and requires a socialist reorganisation of production. The article discusses Western versions of it.
A term in Chinese political writing for the ability to set agendas and have one's own concepts heard in international debate.

t: How neo-fascism arises from neoliberal capitalism
zh: 新法西斯主义如何从新自由资本主义中崛起
source: Teaching and Research on Marxist Theory (Marxist Theory Teaching and Research), 2023 no. 3
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the US political scientists Ronald W. Cox and Daniel Skidmore-Hess. They ask how the far right's rise relates to forty years of neoliberal capitalism, and argue that neo-fascism is a product of neoliberal capitalism's crisis. In their account, neoliberalism did not shrink the state but redirected its public functions towards corporate accumulation, eroding the legitimacy of liberal-democratic capitalist states.

The article first contrasts the fascism of the 1930s with contemporary neo-fascism, then sets out a five-part definition. It reviews the legitimacy crisis of capitalist states and the scholarly literature on the supply and demand sides of far-right growth. It then identifies the neo-fascist coalition: neoliberal think tanks, speculative finance, extractive sectors, small and local business, the petty bourgeoisie, a privileged segment of white workers, and far-right religious movements. Two case studies, Trump in the United States and Bolsonaro in Brazil, follow.

The authors argue that interwar fascism built strong authoritarian states with mass parties, whereas neo-fascism works in a globalised system and speeds the stripping of public and regulatory functions from already weakened states. Subsidies to finance after 2008 and during the pandemic, regressive taxation and the weakening of unions and social-democratic parties, they say, left a vacuum in working-class representation that far-right 'outsiders' filled with racial and anti-elite rhetoric. This shifts blame from capital to liberal-democratic institutions. They reject readings of the phenomenon as 'right-wing populism' opposed to neoliberalism, citing Trump's renaming of NAFTA as a reshaping of the order. They also dispute Perry Anderson's restriction of 'fascism' to interwar conditions, arguing that even mild social democracy, as in Brazil or in Sanders's campaign, can provoke pre-emptive authoritarian reaction.

The authors conclude that neo-fascism poses an existential threat and that the left must oppose it explicitly. They call for large civil-society organisations that demand wider democracy and public accountability and turn corporate welfare into social welfare. They also call for mobilising the working class for higher social wages and democratic representation, since otherwise corporate elites will keep control of the contest. Read the original if you want a Marxist account linking neoliberal state restructuring to the far right, with comparative material on the US and Brazil.
quoteEn: Only by promoting a working-class movement whose common mission is to defeat fascism and reverse neoliberal capitalism (and challenge capitalism itself) can neo-fascism be defeated and its direct link with capitalism weakened.
quoteZh: 只有通过推动以战胜法西斯主义和扭转新自由资本主义（以及挑战资本主义本身）为共同使命的工人阶级运动，才能既战胜新法西斯主义，又削弱新法西斯主义和资本主义之间的直接关系。

t: "Shortage economics" and the systemic crisis of global capitalism
zh: “短缺经济学”与全球资本主义的系统性危机
paras: Zhu Andong and Yang Shuaihong ask why capitalist economies, especially the developed West, experienced widespread shortages from 2020 to 2022. Many commentators treat these as temporary effects of external shocks such as the Covid-19 pandemic, extreme weather and the Russia–Ukraine conflict. The authors argue instead that the shortages express a deepening systemic crisis of global capitalism, rooted in neoliberal accumulation since the 1980s and in the long stagnation after 2008.

The article has three parts. It first documents shortages in shipping and supply chains (including semiconductors), in energy and food, and in labour, citing IMF, UN, US Labor Department and other figures. It then revisits János Kornai's Economics of Shortage and its relation to capitalism. Finally it examines the material, financial and world-system foundations of the shortages, ending with remarks on China.

The central theoretical move reinterprets Kornai. The authors define shortage through "serious intentions", meaning the input needs that producers' plans rest on, rather than through market-clearing prices. Kornai's two micro-conditions, soft budget constraints and a drive to overspend, are said to apply to capitalism too, through monopoly pricing, state bailouts, shareholder buybacks funded by credit, and capital inflows to emerging economies. The authors then trace the material base to the tendency of the profit rate to fall. In their account, neoliberal responses (just-in-time production, global production networks, union-busting, underinvestment in infrastructure) cut redundancy and shifted risk to society, as the 2023 Ohio train derailment illustrates. Finance-led accumulation worsens this, with costs falling mainly on workers and developing countries.

At the world-system level, the authors describe a four-tier division of labour centred on the United States and argue that US hegemony is declining. In their view, Washington's attempts at reindustrialisation by pressuring other countries leave it in a dilemma and make it a disruptor of the order. They conclude that shortages will persist, that more debt crises like those of Sri Lanka and Ghana may follow, and that conflict could fragment global production networks. They urge China, which they say resisted neoliberalism, to prepare for further disruption and for possible provocations by the United States. Read the original if you want a Marxist, world-systems reading of the post-pandemic shortages and a critique of Kornai's theory applied to capitalism.
quoteEn: The global shortages since the pandemic are another eruption of capitalism's systemic contradictions, and this eruption may not yet have reached its peak.
quoteZh: 疫情以来出现的全球普遍短缺是资本主义系统性矛盾的又一次爆发，而这次爆发可能尚未达到其顶点。

glossary.explanation: The 1980 book by Hungarian economist János Kornai, which attributes chronic shortage in socialist economies to soft budget constraints. The authors reread it as applicable to capitalism too.
Kornai's term for a situation where firms expect state rescue and so are not limited by their own solvency. The authors argue the tendency also appears in modern capitalism.
Kornai's term for the input needs that production plans rest on. The authors generalise it as expectations formed by experience and institutional constraints.
The market-oriented policy regime of deregulation, tax cuts and weakened unions since the 1980s. The authors treat it as capital's response to falling profit rates.

t: An assessment of Karel Kosík's Marxist view of reality
zh: 科西克马克思主义现实观评析
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2023 no. 11
paras: Yan Yan takes up a question that, in the author's view, remains underexamined in Marx scholarship: what Marx means by 'reality' and how it can be known and changed. Existing studies mostly trace Marx's view of reality to German classical philosophy. Yan turns instead to the Czech neo-Marxist Karel Kosík and his Dialectics of the Concrete, arguing that reality, not only 'concreteness' and 'totality', is the book's central concept. The article concludes that Kosík distinguishes fact from reality and phenomenon from essence with precision, but that his view is limited by subjectivism, utopianism and pessimism.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Kosík's concept of reality against Hegel, Lukács and Karl Popper. The second sets out six obstacles that, on Kosík's account, block the grasp of reality in capitalist society. The third gives Yan's own critique of the limits of Kosík's dialectics and of East European neo-Marxism more broadly.

In Yan's reading, Kosík treats reality as a 'concrete totality': a structured, self-forming whole that cannot be reduced to the sum of facts. Reality is human reality, produced by practice. Kosík's obstacles include the pseudo-concrete world of false autonomy, determinism and reductionism in epistemology, a world of manipulation, everyday life, the economic system and the 'economic man', and economic-factor determinism. Kosík defends instead a determination by economic structure that presupposes totality. Yan then criticises Kosík on three counts. His view remains a 'determinism of ideas' and a 'theory of consciousness revolution'. His humanist socialism merely negates capitalism and Soviet socialism and ignores the diversity of socialist paths. And he attacks the economic system without identifying the logic of capital behind it.

Yan concludes that Kosík's critique of capitalism is incisive and offers an alternative to dogmatic Soviet Marxism, but that his views on socialism and on human emancipation are flawed. Yan sets this against the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in which Chinese modernization is said to regulate and guide capital and so avoid 'manipulation of people by the system'. Read the original if you study East European neo-Marxism, Lukács's legacy, or Chinese scholarly assessments of foreign Marxism, and want a detailed account of Kosík's concept of reality.
quoteEn: Reality can be known and changed by dialectics because reality is constructed by human practical activity.
quoteZh: 现实之所以能够被辩证法认识和改变，是因为现实是由人的实践活动建构的。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, prominent in Party discourse since the 2020s. Here Yan invokes it as a practice said to regulate capital.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Party leadership with market mechanisms.

A concept in Chinese Marxist scholarship for capital's drive towards self-valorisation, to which individuals and society become means. Yan treats it as the hidden force behind the phenomena Kosík criticises.
Kosík's term for the familiar world of everyday appearances and manipulation, which hides the essence of things. Yan treats it as a key obstacle to grasping reality.
A humanist current of Marxism in Eastern Europe, including the Czech Kosík and the Yugoslav Praxis group, critical of both capitalism and Soviet-style socialism.

t: Ecosocialism for realists
zh: 现实主义者的生态社会主义
orig: Capitalism Nature Socialism, vol. 34, no. 1, 2023 ("Ecosocialism for Realists")
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2024 no. 2
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of Michael Albert's article "Ecosocialism for Realists". Albert asks why ecosocialism, now a major global alternative to "green capitalism", has said so little about how a transition would actually happen. The article argues that ecosocialists are held back by an "abstract utopian" habit of describing ideal futures without analysing the path, and by neglect of the trade-offs and dangers a ecosocialist regime would face. It proposes a "realist utopian" approach in their place.

Albert first sets out three shared principles of ecosocialism: use-value over exchange-value, collective ownership and planning that shape and constrain markets, and "contraction and convergence" in consumption between the Global North and Global South. The article then reviews the Green New Deal as a possible transition platform and examines the choice between degrowth and growth-oriented paths. It closes with the risks of emergency rule, negative-emission technologies, solar geoengineering and mineral extraction. Albert draws on Löwy, Foster, Richard Smith, Sam Gindin, Erik Olin Wright, Andreas Malm and others.

The central move is an analysis of why a growth-based Green New Deal may not stabilise capitalism. Albert gives three reasons: falling net energy as renewables with lower energy returns spread, over-promised "green jobs", and rising private and public debt without the growth needed to service it. On this reading the Green New Deal is a "temporary way station" before a fork: deeper socialisation with rationing and job guarantees, or a return to right-wing growth at any cost. Albert then argues that any ecosocialist government may be pushed towards institutionalised "state of emergency" measures such as carbon rationing, and would face resistance from the far right allied with capital. Two equilibria are sketched. One is degrowth emerging from Green New Deal crises around 2030–2050. The other is a slower transition around 2050–2080, dependent on negative-emission technology, geoengineering and intensified extractive conflict.

Albert concludes that ecosocialists and their allies should put more intellectual effort into strategy and into the limits of the best-case scenario, without abandoning utopian imagination. Facing these risks may strengthen rather than weaken belief in a new world, he suggests. He also calls for a stronger red-green alliance and a changed narrative of prosperity. Read the original if you study ecosocialism, degrowth or the Green New Deal and want a critical, strategy-focused account of the dilemmas of transition in core countries.
quoteEn: The author advocates a "realist utopian" approach, so as to attend more systematically to the problems of the ecosocialist forms that may emerge in future.
quoteZh: 笔者主张采取一种“现实主义乌托邦”（realist utopian）路径，借此更为系统地关注未来可能出现的生态社会主义形态的问题

glossary.explanation: A family of state-led investment programmes for green technology and green jobs, ranging from centrist to radical left versions. The article treats it as a possible but unstable transition platform.
A current of thought and movement that calls for reducing material and energy throughput in rich countries without lowering wellbeing. Albert distinguishes it from growth-oriented socialism.
An approach, associated in the article with Erik Olin Wright and Sam Gindin, that combines utopian imagination with rigorous analysis of constraints, trade-offs and paths of transition.
A political coalition of labour or socialist forces (red) and environmental movements (green). The article calls for a stronger and more coherent one.

Shorthand for wealthy, industrialised countries and poorer, formerly colonised or dependent countries. Ecosocialists in the article call for consumption contraction in the former and resource transfers to the latter.

t: Raymond Aron's reflections on the Marxist philosophy of history and their limits
zh: 雷蒙•阿隆对马克思主义历史哲学的思考及其局限
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2024 no. 2
paras: Raymond Aron, the French liberal thinker long overshadowed by Sartre and the left, described himself as a socialist but not a Marxist. Jia Xiangyun asks what Aron made of the Marxist philosophy of history and where his thinking fell short. The article argues that Aron's view of history overlaps with Marx's in important respects and that parts of his account of historical knowledge concretise and enrich historical materialism. It also holds that his "probabilistic determinism" slides into scepticism and that his stance remains that of an observer, not an actor.

The article has four parts. It begins with Aron's reading of Marx and his notion of "metascience". It then places the philosophy of history as a discipline, from Vico and Herder through Hegel and Ranke to Marx and Engels, and sets Aron's 1938 doctoral thesis, Introduction to the Philosophy of History, within that line. Next it sets out Aron's general problems of historical knowledge: history versus natural science, individual and totality, and objectivity. A conclusion weighs his contributions against his limits.

Jia reports that Aron distinguished Marx from Marxism and found two tendencies in Marx, an objectivising, law-governed one and a subjectivising one centred on class struggle. In Aron's view these could be reconciled only through some metascience, and the rival existentialist, structuralist and orthodox Marxist-Leninist schools each emphasise one side. Jia calls this attribution of the schools to Marx's own tendencies a misreading, because Marx's texts form a developing whole, and cites Lukács on the dialectic of subject and object. On historical knowledge, Aron held that history, unlike natural science, depends on understanding and narrative. He favoured William Dray's rational-explanation model over Carl Hempel's covering-law model. Jia argues that these views embody the disciplinary character and totalising method of historical materialism.

Jia concludes that Aron's account of the subject–object relation parallels Marx's claim that people make their own history, though not as they please. The article nonetheless finds two limits. Aron's pessimism about the historical subject yields historical nihilism and no account of history's meaning. His stance as an "engaged spectator" stays at analysis and enlightenment, whereas Jia presents Marx as a revolutionary actor committed to human emancipation and the free development of each individual. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Aron's debt to and distance from Marx, and of his place in debates on historical knowledge.
quoteEn: Aron's reflections on the Marxist philosophy of history undoubtedly have a certain rationality and value for reference, but they inevitably have many limitations.
quoteZh: 阿隆对马克思主义历史哲学的思考无疑具有一定的合理性和可借鉴性，但也不可避免地存在着诸多局限性。

glossary.explanation: Marx and Engels' theory that the development of society is driven by material production and the contradictions between productive forces and relations of production. Chinese scholarship uses it as the name for Marxism's theory of history.
In Chinese official and academic usage, a charge against views that deny or doubt the meaning, direction or objective laws of history, or the Marxist account of it.
Aron's term for the analysis of science itself, including whether a single model of science exists. He argued that the rival readings of Marx depend on the metascience each interpreter holds.
The label the article gives to Aron's view that historical conclusions reached through understanding and explanation remain uncertain and cannot be strictly necessary.

keywords: Introduction to the Philosophy of History

t: The threefold critique of contemporary capitalism and its new interpretation
zh: 当代资本主义的三重批判及其新阐释
paras: Kong asks how to understand contemporary financial capitalism, led by the United States, when it appears to have weathered the 2008 subprime crisis and the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank run and returned to apparent prosperity. The article draws mainly on Slavoj Žižek's psychoanalytic critique, supplemented by Alfred Sohn-Rethel's account of commodity fetishism. Kong argues that, beneath its legitimating surface, capitalism conceals contradictions in three areas: finance, political democracy and ecology.

The article has three main sections and a short conclusion. The first treats financial capital, digital capital and welfare capital. The second examines the form and paradoxes of capitalist democracy. The third covers the inevitability of ecological crisis and Žižek's rejection of what he calls the ecology of fear. Kong draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Habermas, Adorno and Dan Schiller, and sets Žižek's Lacanian readings beside them.

On finance, Kong reports Žižek's claim that speculators are paradoxical subjects, empty and desiring, driven by both greed and fear, in the way Lacan's object a works. Expansionary money creation after a crash only postpones crisis to the future. Digital capital, in Kong's reading with Sohn-Rethel, extends the abstract "oneness" of money into digital fetishism, and welfare capital, including billionaire philanthropy, merely delays collapse and strains public finances. On democracy, Žižek's "forced choice" (choosing between bad and worse, as in Sophie's Choice) and the lift "close door" button are used to argue that elections are formal and misrecognised, though Kong stresses that Marx credited bourgeois democracy with historic progress. On ecology, Žižek's claim that "nature does not exist" casts humanity as nature's wound. Kong reports that he therefore rejects both return to nature and fear-based ecology, and advocates a Bartleby-like refusal of capitalism.

Kong concludes that none of the three forms alters the capitalist system, and that only institutional opposition can end its alienation. Capitalism, in Kong's words, is neither about to perish nor immutable. Žižek's analysis is called incisive but also radical or extreme, and Kong calls for a fuller assessment grounded in Marx and in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist scholar's critical reception of Žižek's psychoanalytic account of finance, democracy and ecology.
quoteEn: Whether financial capital, digital capital or welfare capital, none has changed the capitalist system at its root; they have instead led to deeper social alienation.
quoteZh: 无论是金融资本、数字资本还是福利资本，都没有从根源上改变资本主义制度本身，反而导致了更深度的社会异化。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current path and system, formulated since the reform era. Chinese authors often use it as the framework for assessing foreign theories.
Marx's term for the way social relations appear as properties of things, such as commodities and money. Kong extends it to a "digital fetishism".
Kong's label for the post-war welfare policies of Western states, which he treats as a further variant of capital that postpones crisis.

t: A critique of capitalist political economy from the perspective of parallax dialectics
zh: 视差辩证法视域下的资本主义政治经济学批判
source: World Social Sciences (Shijie shehui kexue), 2024 no. 2
paras: Shi Fengge examines how Slavoj Žižek's "parallax dialectics" yields a critique of capitalist political economy. The article argues that, seen through this lens, the contemporary capitalist economy shows systemic antagonisms that differ from the path Marx took in Capital, namely the exploitation of surplus labour, but still expose the system's inner contradictions. Shi presents this as a new theoretical angle on global capital and a possible resource for the Left in rethinking emancipatory politics.

The article has five parts. It first reconstructs parallax dialectics: Žižek takes Kojin Karatani's "parallax" from Transcritique, reads it through Kant's antinomies and Lacan's Real, and grounds it in ontological difference and "minimal difference". Three sections then take up three parallax splits: the "Real" economy versus actual economy, the depoliticisation of the economy versus the primacy of politics, and material versus immaterial labour. A short conclusion assesses Žižek's approach.

In Shi's account, Žižek separates the "Real" economy, an absent quasi-cause that shapes society, from the actual economy, a symbolised sub-system. Class struggle mediates economy and politics, so the mainstream claim of a purely objective market economy is an ideological illusion. Shi reports Žižek's view that depoliticisation serves the unrestricted global movement of capital and produces semi-monopoly power in internet giants and gene-patenting firms. On labour, Shi follows Žižek's critique of Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt. They treat immaterial labour as dominant, capital as merely parasitic, and "exodus" as the route to liberation. Žižek replies that outsourcing separates knowledge workers from sweatshop workers, so capital still organises and unites global production. He holds that liberation requires collective ownership of the "commons" and of the management of things.

Shi concludes that Žižek offers the Left a distinctive way back to political economy critique. Shi also judges the approach "seemingly Marxist but not" (si "ma" fei "ma"): its philosophical deduction departs from Marx's historical-materialist analysis, which starts from the commodity, and risks sliding into idealist speculation. The author calls for drawing on Žižek's method while holding to Marxism's historical-materialist account of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading and assessment of Žižek's economic thought, including his debate with Negri and Hardt.
quoteEn: Žižek's theoretical reflection, characterised by the deduction of philosophical concepts, is in fact a line of thought that is seemingly Marxist but not, and it departs from Marx's historical-materialist account of capitalist economic development.
quoteZh: 齐泽克这种以哲学概念演绎为特征的理论反思实际上是一种似“马”非“马”的致思路径，偏离了马克思对资本主义经济发展的历史唯物主义阐释。

t: On the conservative elements in Lukács's History and Class Consciousness
zh: 论卢卡奇《历史与阶级意识》中的保守主义成分
paras: Lukács's History and Class Consciousness (1923) sought to rescue Marx's revolutionary dialectic by "returning to Hegel". Yan asks whether Lukács actually removed the conservative elements of Hegelianism, and whether he did the same with Max Weber's rationalisation theory, on which the book's concept of reification depends. The article argues that he did not fully succeed: Hegelian and Weberian conservatism survive in the book and leave it with unresolved paradoxes.

The article relies chiefly on the critique of Lukács by his pupil István Mészáros, developed over five chapters of Beyond Capital. It has four parts. The first argues that Hegel's philosophy is a form of "uncritical positivism". The second traces the negative influence of Hegelianism on History and Class Consciousness. The third examines the "Weber burden" in the book's treatment of rationality, calculability and bureaucracy. A short conclusion follows, drawing on Mészáros, Ferenc Fehér and Zhang Yibing.

On Hegel, Yan follows Mészáros in holding that his "political economy standpoint" takes the capital relation uncritically. His ethical state, his account of civil society and his teleological philosophy of history are read as indirect arguments for the eternity of capital and for its "virtue". Lukács's thesis that the proletariat is the identical subject–object of history is, in Yan's reading, a Hegelian remnant, as Lukács himself conceded. It also reflects an over-optimistic reading of the European revolutionary situation after 1917, an underestimation of capital and an overestimation of class consciousness. On Weber, Yan adds a criticism of Mészáros: Lukács condemns bureaucracy and reification at the level of values but accepts Weber's findings on efficiency and calculability. Yan holds that Lukács also confuses two senses of reification, the reification of production relations, which Marx criticised, and the objectification of the production process, which Marx affirmed. Weber's understanding thus prevails beneath Lukács's open opposition to him.

Yan concludes, with Mészáros, that Lukács treated the crisis of capitalism as a crisis of consciousness. This weakened the primacy of the material and economic, left him dependent on intellectuals bringing consciousness from outside, and led to his late turn to ethics and aesthetics. Yan stresses that Mészáros and the Budapest School still regard the book as a landmark. A closing note adds that Mészáros overlooks the positive influence of Marx's historical method, which Yan thinks kept critical and revolutionary elements alive. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, Lukács's reception of Hegel and Weber, or Mészáros's critique of him.
quoteEn: Although in History and Class Consciousness Lukács opposes instrumental reason, which clearly distinguishes him from Weber, his understanding of reification is built precisely on Weber's theory of reification, and so it can still be called a \"Weber burden\".
quoteZh: 卢卡奇虽然在《历史与阶级意识》中反对工具理性，这一点与韦伯明显不同，但他对物化的理解恰恰是建立在韦伯物化理论基础上的，因此仍可以被称为“韦伯包袱”。

t: Derrida and Marx: the "hauntology politics" guiding future justice
zh: 德里达与马克思：引导未来正义的“幽灵政治学”
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2024 no. 2
paras: Jia Liyan examines Jacques Derrida's "politics of spectres" (the "politics of ghosts" of Specters of Marx) and asks why a deconstructionist, often accused of apolitical textual play, declared himself an heir to Marx. The article argues that Derrida's project is a deconstructive reading of Marxism that keeps its critical spirit and its messianic promise of emancipation, and that its real aim is future justice.

The article is organised in three parts. The first places Derrida's book in the shock of the fall of the Berlin Wall and the "end of history" thesis of Francis Fukuyama. The second turns to the meaning of "spectres" and of Marx's "spirit" as an inheritance, drawing on Hamlet, the Communist Manifesto and the Western Marxist tradition of Lukács, Gramsci and Bloch. The third treats the "New International" and a "new politics", including Derrida's later work on law, hospitality and friendship.

Jia reads Specters of Marx as, in Derrida's own words, a book of resistance against the post-1989 consensus that Marx and communism were dead. Derrida lists ten "plagues" of the "new world order", such as unemployment, exclusion of migrants, economic wars and arms trading, and concludes that justice is still absent and history unfinished. In Jia's account the spectres are victims of violence, colonialism and oppression, and inheriting Marx means a duty to them and to the future; Derrida speaks of many "spirits" of Marx, not one, and inheritance requires deconstructing what is received. Jia reports that Derrida rejects historical determinism and party-based Marxism, imagines a "New International" that is neither a state body nor a party, redefines revolution as an ethical rupture, and holds that law can be deconstructed while justice, as a messianic promise, cannot.

Jia concludes that Derrida's "politics of spectres" is an ethicised extension of Marxist critique. It values the messianic call for justice but, as Jia points out, ignores Marxism as ontology, dialectical materialism and historical materialism. For Jia the case shows a longing for social solidarity and fairness in contemporary Western thought, and as long as real justice remains unrealised, many people are in some sense Marx's heirs. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese account of how Specters of Marx is read, from the Berlin Wall context through to Derrida's later politics of hospitality.
quoteEn: Evidently, future justice is the fundamental goal of Derrida's "politics of spectres".
quoteZh: 可见，未来正义才是德里达的“幽灵政治学”的根本目标之所在。

t: Resolving the puzzle of social "institution": a critical reading of Castoriadis
zh: 破解社会“建制”之困：卡斯托里亚迪斯的批判解读
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai Lilun Dongtai), 2024 no. 2
paras: The article asks how the Greek-French thinker Cornelius Castoriadis, whom Axel Honneth called "the last Western Marxist", understood social "institution", and argues that this concept organises his whole theoretical development. Qi and Zhao propose rendering the French/English "institution" as "建制" (jianzhi, rendered here as "institution" in the sense of an instituting process) rather than the usual "制度", because it stresses a dynamic, ongoing act of construction over a fixed, passively executed result. Their thesis is that for Castoriadis institutions are condensations of social imaginary significations, and that this reading keeps his thought tied to the practical aim of changing the world.

The article has four parts. It first traces the intellectual sources of the concept: Durkheim's sociology, Merleau-Ponty's late philosophy, and Marx's theory of alienation, together with Western Marxist figures such as Lukács, Gramsci, Adorno and Lefebvre. It then turns to signification, meaning and language, drawing on Heidegger's reading of logos and legein and on commentators including Olson, Adams, Arnason, Edgar and Sedgwick. A third part treats the essence of institution as social imaginary signification, and a fourth examines its "instituted" and "instituting" aspects.

The authors argue that Castoriadis replaces Durkheim's "social" qualifier with "imaginary", stressing that institutions are changeable creations, and that alienation arises when the imaginary element becomes autonomous and dominates society. Signification, which they describe as a "magma" without fixed elements or limits, is expressed through language but cannot be reduced to linguistics or structuralist frameworks. Institution is then presented as a creation "out of nothing", with the original imagination as its source, yet the authors insist this is materialist, extending materiality from production and need to the whole of society. Institutions tend to harden into the instituted, disguising themselves as permanent, but the authors hold that the instituting dimension is more fundamental.

Qi and Zhao conclude that the dialectic of the instituted and the instituting shows the necessity of change and affirms the revolutionary character of the social-historical. In their reading, where Marx indicates a direction of social development, Castoriadis stresses development itself, so that the legitimacy of the future is explained from revolution rather than the reverse. Read the original if you work on Western Marxism, post-Marxism or the Chinese reception of Castoriadis and want a detailed account of how the concept of institution links imagination, language and alienation.
quoteEn: Rather than using the necessity of the future to explain the legitimacy of revolution, it is better to start from revolution itself to explain the legitimacy of the future.
quoteZh: 与其以未来的必然性说明革命的合理性，不如从革命本身出发说明未来的合理性。

t: Deleuze's theory of affect and its critique of capitalism
zh: 德勒兹的情动理论及其资本主义批判
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 2
paras: Since the mid-1990s the "affective turn" has spread across the humanities, and Hu Yaohui takes up its most important theoretical source, Gilles Deleuze's theory of affect. The article asks how Deleuze builds, through Spinoza, a philosophy set against Hegel, and what that philosophy can say about contemporary capitalism. Hu argues that affect theory offers a new view of capitalism's current forms of control, but remains distant from genuine Marxism.

The article proceeds in three steps. It first places Deleuze's Spinoza in the French reaction of the 1960s against Hegelianism, a tradition shaped by Kojève's lectures and carried through Sartre and Merleau-Ponty, and contrasts him with Althusser's narrower critique of historicism. It then reads Deleuze's picture of the world through three concepts: power, affect and desire. Finally it turns to Anti-Oedipus and the "Postscript on the Societies of Control" to reconstruct his critique of capitalism.

Hu's central reasoning is that Deleuze answers Descartes's problem of the ground of the world with Spinoza's doctrine of expression, then answers Hegel's charge of "acosmism" with a theory of becoming. Things differ only in degrees of power, that is, in their capacity to be affected. Affect is the change of state when bodies meet, joyful or sorrowful, and desire is presented as productive rather than a lack, as in Freud and Lacan. On this basis Hu reports Deleuze's account of capitalism as a tension between two affects: cynicism, which decodes and levels all flows of desire, and piety, produced by the Oedipal family, which recaptures them. In the later control society, Hu adds, fear becomes the governing affect, and individuals become "dividuals" modulated through data.

Hu credits Deleuze with a creative reading of Marxism that points towards a materialist theory of desire and helps explain biopolitics and the consumer society. Yet Hu judges the critique too abstract: without touching ownership and wage-labour relations, no emancipation is possible, and radical change risks becoming aestheticism. Hu also questions how a society of differences, built on the "body without organs", could be organised or address intersubjectivity and social norms. Read the original if you want a compact, Marxist-oriented account of how Deleuze's Spinozism, affect and critique of capitalism fit together, together with a Chinese scholar's assessment of its limits.
quoteEn: Yet it must also be seen that Deleuze's critique of capitalism is clearly too abstract: without touching ownership and the relations of production based on wage labour, no emancipation is possible, and fundamental change would be reduced to an aestheticised pursuit of art and literature.
quoteZh: 但是，也应当看到，德勒兹的资本主义批判显然过于抽象，如果不触及所有制以及以雇佣劳动为基础的生产关系，一切解放都无从谈起，根本性的变革只会沦为对艺术和文学的美学化追求。

t: A review of overseas scholarship on China's comprehensively deepening reform
zh: 海外学者关于中国全面深化改革的研究述评
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 2
paras: This is a literature review of representative English-language scholarship on the policy of comprehensively deepening reform, which has been pursued since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang and Liu use outside views to understand the reform's achievements, historical significance and prospects. They also assess the theoretical contributions and limits of this literature, and they propose ways to improve the international narrative of China's reform.

The review has three parts. The first covers overseas scholars' general assessments: the overall reform goal, the decision-making system and reform methods, and comparative perspectives. The second surveys studies by field: economic, political, cultural, social, ecological-civilisation and Party-building reform. The third describes the literature's main features, and a conclusion follows. Among the scholars named are Barry Naughton, Dwight Perkins, Shang-Jin Wei, Fabrizio Zilibotti, Rana Mitter, Elizabeth Perry, Kerry Brown, David Shambaugh and Andrew Wedeman.

According to the review, many overseas authors judge the reform positively. They treat the modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity as an innovation, credit the central leading body with coordinating reform, and see top-level design combined with local experimentation. Some also argue that Chinese reform borrows selectively from the West without copying it. On the economy, they stress the market's decisive role, the need to raise total factor productivity, and a shift to innovation-driven growth. In environmental and Party-building studies, they examine vertical management, cadre training and the anti-corruption campaign. The authors identify four features of the literature: macro and micro topics together; area studies dominant but disciplinary theory growing; a wide range of scholars with more Chinese–foreign co-authorship; and support, sincere advice and ideological bias existing side by side.

Zhang and Liu conclude that this scholarship offers useful perspectives and some suggestions of reference value. They also say that some works misread the reform, show ideological bias, tie reform successes to the "China threat" thesis, or apply existing theories too mechanically. They propose four steps: understand the relation between institutional confidence and reform, use differentiated international communication, support Chinese scholars publishing abroad, and strengthen academic ties with overseas institutions and "China-friendly" experts. Read the original if you want a field-by-field guide to English-language studies of China's post-2012 reform, together with the Party School authors' view of how to respond to them.
quoteEn: The strength of area studies is that it presents the course and details of comprehensively deepening reform fairly fully; its limitation is that it over-stresses the uniqueness of China's reform and lacks a perspective that engages general reform theory.
quoteZh: 区域国别研究的优势是对中国全面深化改革的历程和细节展现较为充分，局限在于过于强调中国改革的独特性，缺乏与一般改革理论进行对话的视野。

glossary.explanation: The reform agenda adopted at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee in 2013. It covers the economic, political, cultural, social, ecological and Party-building fields.

glossary.zh: 国家治理体系和治理能力现代化
glossary.pinyin: guójiā zhìlǐ tǐxì hé zhìlǐ nénglì xiàndàihuà
glossary.en: modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity
glossary.explanation: The overall goal of comprehensively deepening reform, set out in 2013 together with improving socialism with Chinese characteristics. It refers to making institutions and their capacity to govern more effective.

t: Preface to "Updating Cuba's socialist model: a path of development towards prosperity, democracy and sustainability"
zh: 《古巴社会主义模式更新：面向繁荣、民主与可持续的发展道路》序言
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a preface by Carlos Miguel Pereira Hernández, Cuba's former ambassador to China, dated 18 May 2022. It was written for a 2024 book by He Qin of the Academy of Marxism, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, on the updating of Cuba's socialist model. Pereira presents the book as a panoramic account of Cuban socialism and argues that Cuban socialism is a home-grown model, forged in anti-imperialist struggle, whose viability has been proved over time.

After recalling his 2010 meeting with He Qin and the interview that followed, Pereira summarises the book's nine chapters. They cover the course of the Cuban Revolution, the thought of its leaders, the formation of Cuban views of socialism and the milestones of Cuba's development. He also notes the book's treatment of macroeconomic adjustment, strategic economic sectors, education and science, environmental protection, social governance and foreign strategy. He ends by outlining Cuba–China exchanges, including the China–Cuba Party theoretical seminars of 2014 and 2022.

Pereira's own argument runs from José Martí's four goals (independence, social justice, economic development, a Cuban democratic government) through the 1959 revolution and Fidel Castro's 1961 declaration of its socialist character. He argues that the US blockade, which he calls the longest and most unjust unilateral sanction in modern history, must be taken into account when judging Cuba's record, and that Cuba's problems should not be blamed on socialism. He names three features of Cuban socialism: people's democracy, social mission and national unity. He describes the update begun at the Sixth Party Congress (2011) as extending democracy, curbing bureaucracy and rigid hierarchy, retaining public ownership of the main means of production while recognising several forms of ownership, and renewing the economic structure.

Pereira concludes that Cuban socialism is the institutional guarantee of national independence and self-determination, and that Cuba faces blockade, crisis, pandemic and climate change with confidence. He credits the book with affirming the central role of Fidel Castro's thought, and stresses shared goals and a close strategic relationship between Cuba and China, including joint opposition to blockades and unilateral coercive measures. He congratulates the author on behalf of the Cuban Communist Party, government and people. Read the original if you want a Cuban official's view of the Cuban socialist model, its update since 2011 and Cuba–China ties, or want to judge whether to consult He Qin's book.
quoteEn: Socialism is the only thing that can explain why Cuba, the largest country in the Antilles, has survived and continued to develop under a cruel blockade.
quoteZh: 社会主义是唯一能够解释古巴这个安的列斯群岛的最大国家在残酷封锁中得以生存并不断发展的原因。

glossary.zh: 古巴社会主义模式更新
glossary.explanation: The reform process launched after the Sixth Congress of the Cuban Communist Party in 2011. It aims to improve Cuba's economic and social model while keeping socialism and the Party's leading role.

The April 2011 congress of the Cuban Communist Party, which adopted the Guidelines of the Economic and Social Policy of the Party and the Revolution. The preface treats it as the foundation of the model update.

t: "French Theory" and the philosophy of the future: constructing a new philosophical paradigm
zh: “法国理论”与未来哲学：一种新哲学范式的构建
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 2
paras: Why does contemporary French philosophy look so little like philosophy as traditionally understood? Ouyang Qian takes up the American-coined label "French Theory" and argues that it signals more than the "end of philosophy". In the author's reading, Foucault, Derrida, Deleuze, Lyotard, Baudrillard, Bourdieu and others are trying to end that "end" by building a new philosophical paradigm, which the article presents as a possible form of future philosophy.

The article is organised in three movements followed by a short conclusion. It traces the shift from a "system of critique" to a "critique of systems", then from "grand narrative" to "micro-perspective", and finally from "philosophy of consciousness" to "cultural studies". It draws on Habermas, Rorty, Gary Gutting, Badiou and the French thinkers' own texts, and sketches five research paradigms within French cultural critique.

Ouyang contends that traditional metaphysics, from Plato to Hegel, sought universal, eternal systems, and that French thinkers reject this as a totalising, identity-based mode of thought tied to power and reason's domination. Philosophy therefore turns to contingent events, to micro-analyses such as Foucault's archaeology and genealogy, and to Deleuze and Guattari's micropolitics of desire. The author describes this as replacing a telescope with a microscope. On the third move, Ouyang holds that, under the influence of structural linguistics and psychoanalysis, the subject is treated as produced by signs and culture. The five paradigms are Foucault's critique of reason, Derrida's deconstruction, Deleuze's analysis of desire, Baudrillard's critique of the political economy of the sign, and Bourdieu's "constructivist structuralism". The author notes that all of these maintain some link with Marxism, citing Derrida's praise of the Communist Manifesto.

Ouyang concludes that whether the future of philosophy will look like French Theory cannot yet be decided. Even so, the author argues, French Theory's interdisciplinary, present-oriented and practice-oriented character, together with its creation of concepts, holds the seed of a new philosophy. Two lessons are drawn: the world needs philosophy more than philosophy supposes, and philosophy can no longer be done in the old way. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's synthesis of French poststructuralism and postmodernism as a paradigm shift in philosophy, with many citations from the thinkers themselves.
quoteEn: French Theory seems non-philosophical, but in fact it is thinking philosophically in a more thoroughgoing way.
quoteZh: “法国理论”看似非哲学，实则却是在更加彻底地进行哲学思考。

t: Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England and the study of British modernization: a visual analysis
zh: 《英国工人阶级状况》关于英国现代化进程研究的可视化分析
source: Studies on Marxism (马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 3
paras: Liu Nana asks what Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England reveals about the process of British modernization, and what that account implies for Chinese modernization. The article argues that Engels read modernization through the interaction of industrialization and urbanization, and that he exposed the contradictions of capital-driven modernization. From this Liu concludes that Chinese modernization transcends the Western model.

The article is built in three parts. The first analyses the temporal and spatial features of British modernization as Engels observed them: the Industrial Revolution as starting point, urbanization as spatial carrier, and world history as the wider setting. It draws on figures and historical records, presented in charts, on population movement, transport (roads, canals, railways, steamships) and the growth of cities such as Manchester and Glasgow. The second part sets out three paradoxes, and the third draws theoretical lessons for China.

In Liu's reading, Engels shows that modernization brought no improvement for workers. The three paradoxes are these. First, workers become appendages of machines, damaged in body through child and female labour and long hours, and in spirit through the division of labour. Second, urban space develops unevenly: cramped and shoddy workers' housing, a city–countryside opposition, and the loss of common land and leisure space, which Liu connects to rising drinking that Engels traces to capitalist private ownership. Third, free trade, after protective tariffs had nurtured British industry, serves capital's freedom, intensifies competition among workers, lowers their purchasing power and enables the exploitation of poorer countries.

Liu draws three lessons. Chinese modernization is a modernization of people, set against the Western modernization of things, and rests on a people-centred approach and Marx's stages of human development. Socialist urban and rural space should be built through "people's cities" and rural revitalization, not capitalist city–country opposition. Finally, a new development pattern in which domestic and international circulations reinforce each other is said to widen the space for Chinese modernization, which Liu describes as both endogenous and open. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar uses Engels's early empirical study, with charts and data, to support claims about Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: That Western-style modernization is a modernization of things means that it sees \"things\" but not \"people\".
quoteZh: 西方式现代化是物的现代化意味着见“物”不见“人”

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of a modernization path with Chinese characteristics, presented as distinct from Western models. It has been elaborated especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.literal: taking the people as the centre
glossary.explanation: A guiding principle in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse that development should be for, reliant on and shared by the people.
A slogan on urban development, "people's cities are built by the people and for the people", used in Xi Jinping's remarks and the 20th Party Congress report.
A national strategy launched in 2017–2018 to develop the countryside and narrow the urban–rural gap.

keywords: The Condition of the Working Class in England

t: Seeking humanity's direction amid the deepening of great changes
st: New developments and changes in foreign communist parties in 2023
zh: 在大变局深度演进中探寻人类前进方向
zhSub: 2023年外国共产党的新发展与新变化
paras: This annual survey asks how communist parties outside China fared in 2023, a year the author describes as marked by shifting great-power relations, geopolitical rivalry and a post-pandemic world full of uncertainty. Yu argues that these parties kept to their stance and struggle goals and adjusted to new conditions. Their overall development showed continuity and stability, with the defining feature of advancing amid a low tide.

The article is organised in six sections. It covers anniversaries and commemorations, including Mao Zedong's 130th birthday and the deaths of several party leaders. It then reviews party congresses and Central Committee plenums, local and national election results, struggles against capitalism and for workers' rights, and the state of international solidarity. Cases range from ruling parties in Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and the DPRK to non-ruling parties in Germany, France, Britain, Pakistan, Venezuela, Ireland, Austria, Greece, Spain and Russia.

Two moves carry the argument. On elections, Yu reports breakthroughs at regional and local level, such as the Austrian communists' rise in Salzburg from 0.31% to 11.66% and the Greek party's reported rise above 10%. Yu also notes setbacks, for instance in India's Tripura state, and concludes that overall strength changed little. On unity, the author sees the Ukraine crisis deepening divisions: the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties in Europe dissolved, and the Greek party founded a new European Communist Action. Meanwhile, a Global Anti-imperialist Platform, whose programme blames Western imperialism for the crisis, took shape as a rival channel. Yu adds that parties split internally, as in Cyprus, and that some parties moved towards cooperation, notably the merger of two Danish communist parties and the 23rd International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties in İzmir, which issued a joint action plan despite differing views.

Yu concludes that, as great changes deepen, unity and coordinated action are of practical importance and would speed the revival of world socialism. The author names the main task for foreign communist parties in the coming period as widening consensus, bridging differences and achieving cooperation. Read the original if you want a detailed, party-by-party chronicle of the 2023 congresses, elections and international networks of non-Chinese communist parties, as seen from a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences researcher.
quoteEn: As great changes deepen, unity, cooperation and coordinated action are of outstanding practical importance, and will help speed up the historical pace of the revival of world socialism.
quoteZh: 在大变局深度演进中，团结合作、协调行动具有突出的现实意义，这将有利于加速世界社会主义复兴的历史步伐。

glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Chinese scholarship on world socialism for a hoped-for recovery of socialist movements after the setbacks of the early 1990s. The article presents communist-party cooperation as helping this process.

t: On the critical theory of "transitional capitalism"
st: Its problem logic and contemporary value, from the perspective of "Political Marxism"
zh: 论“转型资本主义” 批判理论的问题逻辑及其当代价值
zhSub: 基于 “政治马克思主义 ” 的视角
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2024 no. 6
paras: Feng Wangzhou asks how the Anglo-American school of "Political Marxism" analyses the development of capitalism and the prospects for moving beyond it. The article argues that the school, whose leading figures are Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood, has built a systematic critical theory that Feng labels "transitional capitalism". Feng holds that this theory has real value for developing twenty-first-century Marxism, for foreign Marxist critiques of capitalism, and for socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article first sets out the school's background: the collapse of the Soviet Union, the "end of history" thesis, and the retreat of many left intellectuals from criticising capitalism. It then traces three generations of scholars over some forty years, from Brenner, Wood and George Comninel to Benno Teschke and Hannes Lacher, and then to Xavier Lafrance and Eren Duzgun. The main section reconstructs the school's "problem domain" in six parts: the origins of capitalism, its stages of development, its ideology, the state and international relations, its general crisis, and ways of overcoming it.

Feng's core claim is that the school keeps to Marx's historical materialism and places social property relations, understood as class relations, at the centre. On this view capitalism arose contingently in English agriculture, through market dependence, and not through trade, population change or commercialisation. It then moved from agrarian to industrial capitalism, to colonial imperialism, and finally to capitalist imperialism. In Feng's account, the school treats "progress", democracy, "endless war" and liberalism as a chain of ideology that supports capitalist rule. It also sees class struggle, economic, ecological and social crises combining into a general crisis.

Feng reports that the school's way beyond capitalism has four elements: a renewed historical materialism, the working class as revolutionary subject, anti-capitalist struggle organised through the nation-state to achieve real democracy, and an international alliance of labour and new social movements. Feng concludes that the school continues earlier critiques of state capitalism, consumer society, late capitalism and global capitalism. Feng adds that it clarifies the revolutionary agency behind a revival of world socialism, and that it helps strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic overview of Brenner, Wood and their successors, and of how Chinese academics present this school's relevance to Chinese socialism.
quoteEn: "Political Marxism" starts from the reality of capitalist society, applies Marx's method of historical materialism, persists in a total critique of capitalism, and tries to find a path beyond it.
quoteZh: “政治马克思主义”立足于资本主义社会的现实,运用马克思的历史唯物主义方法,坚持对资本主义进行总体批判,试图探寻超越资本主义的道路。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party discourse, in its current form since 2016. It calls for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up. It combines Party leadership, public ownership and a market economy.
An Anglo-American current associated with Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood. It stresses social property relations and class struggle in explaining the origins and development of capitalism.

t: Engels and the English working class
zh: 恩格斯与英国工人阶级
orig: Paul Blackledge, Friedrich Engels and Modern Social and Political Theory (SUNY Press, 2019), chapter 2
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 2
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an excerpt from Paul Blackledge's book Friedrich Engels and Modern Social and Political Theory (2019). It takes up a paradox: critics who separate Engels's mature work from Marx's thought, the "Marx–Engels opposition" thesis, still praise The Condition of the Working Class in England. Blackledge argues that the book is continuous with the Marx–Engels worldview of The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto, so praising it while condemning Engels's later writings is incoherent.

The chapter first surveys admirers and detractors of the 1845 book, from Henderson and Chaloner to Hobsbawm, McLellan, Carver and Gilbert. It then traces Engels's earlier writings: the Letters from the Wuppertal, his articles on English domestic crises, the London letters and the critique of Carlyle in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher. Finally it works through the book's themes of industrialisation, humanism, gender, Malthusianism, Chartism and revolution, and closes with Marx's and Engels's later self-criticisms.

Blackledge reads the book as an internal strategic guide for the German left, not an academic study. In his account, Engels grounds socialism in the workers' own movement against existing conditions, not in an ideology brought from outside. He credits Engels with seeing trade unions and strikes as training grounds for revolution. He also credits Engels with treating the state as a capitalist structure and law as a whip prepared by the bourgeoisie. Blackledge notes that Engels traces the 'surplus population' to the capitalist trade cycle, not to nature as Malthus did, and sees drunkenness and crime as products of social conditions.

Blackledge concedes that the book is still marked by a youthful humanism and some fatalism. Its closing hope that communism might soften an otherwise bloody revolution, and its prediction of imminent revolution in England, reflect Engels's not yet fully Marxist outlook. Engels and Marx overcame these weaknesses in 1845 by breaking with socialist moralism, mechanical materialism and political fatalism. Blackledge concludes that the book is a foundation, not an aberration, of their shared view, which weakens attempts to draw a line between Marx and Engels. Read the original if you want a defence of Engels's early work against the Marx–Engels opposition thesis, or a guide to the scholarly debate over the book.
quoteEn: There is no doubt that Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England formed the foundation of this new worldview.
quoteZh: 毫无疑问，恩格斯的《英国工人阶级状况》构成了这一新世界观的基础。

glossary.explanation: A line of interpretation, common in Western scholarship, that separates Marx's own thought from Engels's later 'Marxism' and holds that the two men's worldviews diverged seriously.

keywords: The Condition of the Working Class in England

t: The origins, theoretical framework and critical assessment of "fossil capitalism"
zh: “化石资本主义”的概念源起、理论框架和理论评述
source: Journal of Nanjing Forestry University (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2024 no. 2
paras: Huang Yinlin takes up "fossil capitalism", a concept developed by Western left-wing scholars to criticise a capitalist mode of production dependent on fossil fuels, and notes that Chinese scholarship on it is still thin. The article sets out where the concept comes from, what its framework contains and where it falls short. Huang's overall view is that the theory offers a useful lens on contemporary capitalism and ecological crisis, but has real limits that call for a dialectical reading that takes "the essence and discards the dross".

The article draws mainly on Andreas Malm, Ian Angus, John Bellamy Foster, Naomi Klein and John Szabo. Part one traces the concept's historical origins in the industrial revolution's shift from water to steam power, its theoretical sources, and its practical logic. Part two reconstructs the framework: what fossil capitalism means, its main features, and how to overcome it. Part three assesses the theory's lessons and limitations.

In Huang's account, fossil capitalism has economic, political and natural dimensions. Economically, fossil fuels are the lifeline of capital's drive for endless growth; politically, the fossil-fuel industry is a powerful interest group that shapes state policy through lobbying and donations; and its exponential growth pushes the Earth system into the Anthropocene. Huang identifies four features: capital's anti-ecological logic, escalation into "fossil imperialism", a rift in the global metabolism, and war driven by oil. The theory's remedy, drawn from Angus and Foster, is an eco-socialist movement. It would draw in "Green-Left" forces, adapt to new science, hold to internationalism and anti-imperialism, and involve many groups in ecological practice. Huang says the theory draws on historical materialism, Marx's metabolic rift and the proletariat as the revolutionary subject.

Huang credits the theory with offering a dynamic view of contemporary capitalism and a critique of its destruction of nature. It also provides, in Huang's view, resources for China's socialist ecological civilisation and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Its limits, Huang argues, are a vague concept with utopian tendencies, a Western-centred viewpoint, a failure to uphold the basic principles of scientific socialism or to treat capitalism's basic contradiction as irreconcilable, and neglect of each citizen's responsibility. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Malm, Angus and Foster's eco-Marxist work on fossil fuels and climate.
quoteEn: The critical theory of "fossil capitalism" offers us a new perspective for discerning new changes in contemporary capitalism, new ideas for exploring a path beyond capitalism, and theoretical reference for advancing contemporary China's development.
quoteZh: “化石资本主义”批判理论为我们辨析当代资本主义新变化提供了新视角，为探索超越资本主义道路提供了新思路，为推进当代中国的发展提供了理论借鉴

glossary.explanation: A concept used by Western left-wing scholars, such as Andreas Malm and Ian Angus, for capitalism's dependence on fossil fuels. It links capital accumulation to climate change and ecological destruction.
