source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2023 no. 5
paras: Gao Ze asks how the Communist Party USA (CPUSA), founded in Chicago in 1919, has approached environmental questions since 2000, a subject the author says Chinese scholarship has neglected. The article argues that the CPUSA has built a distinctive Marxist environmental politics that joins theory to practical struggle. In the author's assessment, the party has little power over US policy but has an influence larger than its size and is an unavoidable part of the American left's environmental spectrum.

The article has three main parts: the CPUSA's theoretical critique of contemporary capitalist ecology, its policy positions, and its forms of action. It draws on CPUSA theorists and organisers such as John Bachtell, Mark Brodine and Anita Waters, on party congress reports and on the 2008 global warming report. It also covers the party's stance on the Green New Deal, its work with marginalised groups and its international cooperation. A short conclusion lists three features of the party's environmental politics.

On theory, Gao reports that CPUSA thinkers return to dialectical materialism and to Capital, using the metabolic rift framework and coining notions such as the "dialectics of climate change" and "ecological necessity". They hold capitalism responsible for the ecological crisis, say that only systemic change can resolve it, and treat the crisis as a "planetary emergency". They see the working class as the key agent and propose "working-class environmentalism". On policy, the slogan "people and planet before profit" guides the party's positions. The party gives the Green New Deal "reserved" support while demanding a larger role for workers and unions, and it presses for environmental rights for poor communities, immigrants and minorities. Its actions include joining the People's Climate Marches (2014 and 2017) and global climate strikes, publishing reports, running Marxist education, and backing technology transfer and ecological agriculture for developing countries.

Gao concludes that the party's theory serves its movement, that its populist propaganda shapes public opinion beyond its organisational weight, and that it combines American environmentalism with a global critique of capitalism. The author adds that the CPUSA praises China's ecological civilization, and calls for Marxist parties to cooperate on global ecological governance and on building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you study Western communist parties, the American left's environmental politics or how Chinese scholars present foreign Marxist parties.
quoteEn: Although the CPUSA does not yet have the strength to directly influence the planning and making of US environmental policy, it has a distinctive advantage in shaping the public's environmental awareness through public opinion.
quoteZh: 美共虽尚不具备直接影响美国环境政策规划与决策的实力，但它在通过舆论影响公众环境认知方面具有独特优势

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for shared responsibility and cooperation among states on global problems.
A Chinese official concept, prominent since the 2000s and written into Party documents in 2012, that puts environmental protection at the centre of development policy.
A US policy agenda of large-scale public investment in clean energy and a green economy, with attention to jobs and social justice. It is debated mainly in Congress and among left groups.
A concept the article attributes to the CPUSA. It means integrating environmental demands into the class struggle, with workers as the main agent of green change.

t: Leninism and "war and peace" in the twenty-first century
zh: 列宁主义与二十一世纪的“战争与和平”
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2024 no. 1
paras: Lü Xinyu asks why war has returned to Europe and the Middle East after the Cold War, and argues that the answer lies in the "de-communization" that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article contends that the Russia–Ukraine conflict, the Israel–Palestine war and the US "new Cold War" against China are extensions of twentieth-century Cold War logic. In Lü's view, lasting peace requires a return to Leninism.

The article has four parts. It first examines Cold War historiography and what Lü calls "reversal-of-verdict historiography" (翻案史学), including the "Lenin as German agent" rumour, and its echo in China. It then turns to civilizational discourse (Fukuyama, Huntington, Dugin) and the expansion of NATO. The third part reviews Cold War episodes from Churchill's Fulton speech to Mearsheimer's "offensive realism", and the fourth returns to Lenin's writings on the national question, the state and peace.

Lü argues that Western-dominated Cold War history, much of it reproduced in China, presents the Chinese and Russian revolutions as Soviet manipulation and so undermines their legitimacy. Balance-of-power theory, "civilizational conflict" and ethnic nationalism are described as the new guises of imperialism and as breeding grounds of war. Lü reads Russia's treatment after 1991, including what the article calls broken promises on NATO and the Minsk agreements, as a repeat of the Versailles settlement. The post-1917 contest between Leninism and Wilsonism is presented as the root dispute: Wilson's self-determination rests on ethnic nationalism, Lenin's on the liberation and eventual merging of oppressed nations.

Lü concludes that the Soviet failure does not show the failure of socialism and peace, and that suppressing socialism is what undermines peace. Lü calls for a fresh reckoning with the whole Cold War narrative and describes socialism with Chinese characteristics as the major historical result of Leninism. China's patriotism is distinguished from Western ethnic nationalism, and China is urged to help build a united front of the Global South and to treat the three global initiatives on development, security and civilization as a unity. Read the original if you want a long, polemical Chinese Marxist reading of the Cold War and the Ukraine war that ties them to Lenin's theory of nation and state.
quoteEn: Returning to Leninism is the only way forward.
quoteZh: 重返列宁主义是必由之路。

glossary.explanation: Lü's term for popular historical writing that revises established judgements on the Soviet Union, the Comintern and the Chinese revolution, which Lü treats as a form of historical nihilism.
The removal of communist symbols, institutions and legitimacy after the Soviet collapse. Lü uses it for a long process from the Cold War to the present.
A collective term for developing countries, increasingly used in Chinese foreign-policy discourse.
The official name for the Chinese Party-state's path since reform and opening up.

t: Western left-wing digital socialist theory: drivers, features and resistance
zh: 西方左翼数字社会主义理论：动力、特征与抗争
paras: Li Quan and Du Min examine the family of Western left-wing theories that tie socialism to digital technology. Since Kevin Kelly coined 'digital socialism' in 2009, the authors say, the concept has been debated and extended. They argue that, in a broad sense, cybercommunism, communicative socialism, platform socialism and Kelly's narrow 'digital socialism' share a common aim. All of them rest on reflection on socialist elements generated by digitalisation and on a critique of capitalism.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the historical types of digital socialism and the forces driving them. It then identifies the theory's features, covering its themes, its lines of development and its practical prospects. Next it discusses how these theories resist capitalism, through ideology, plunder and the logic of capital. It closes by assessing their value and limits. Thinkers discussed include Paul Cockshott, Christian Fuchs, Dimitris Boucas, James Muldoon, Evgeny Morozov and Dan Schiller.

Li and Du name three drivers: the revision of traditional socialism, the critique of contemporary capitalism, and the critique of digital exploitation. On the first, they trace cybercommunism to the old debate over whether central planning is computable, citing Soviet planning and Allende's Chile. They say theories of digital socialism rest on three kinds of judgement. The factual judgement is that networked communities already contain non-capitalist, shared relations; the authors consider Kelly's version a mere description that ignores private ownership. The value judgement is that digital work is 'free' and 'autonomous'; Fuchs's analysis of alienation is cited against this. The logical judgement concerns spontaneous versus conscious transformation, and the authors side with the conscious view of Morozov and others. They argue that these theories grow from capitalist cultural and platform soil and say little about political change.

The authors credit digital socialism with forward-looking thought and with critical value against ideological concealment, appropriation of digital labour and the privatisation of infrastructure. They nevertheless judge it historically limited. Citing Lenin on the dictatorship of the proletariat, they argue that the theories neglect class consciousness among digital workers and the movement needed to overthrow capitalism. In their view the revolutionary spirit stays confined to theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey and assessment of Western digital-socialist currents, from cybercommunism to platform socialism.
quoteEn: The rich revolutionary spirit inherent in digital socialism is, for the most part, confined within the narrow space of theory.
quoteZh: 数字社会主义内在丰富的革命精神更多地圈囿于理论的狭隘空间。

glossary.explanation: A term popularised by Kevin Kelly in 2009 for the sharing and collaborative features of the internet. The article also uses it broadly for all socialist currents based on digital technology.
A theory associated with Paul Cockshott and others, holding that modern computing makes rational, real-time planning of a socialist economy feasible.
A type of digital socialism developed by Christian Fuchs and Dimitris Boucas. It stresses solidarity-based, non-capitalist media and communication forms within digital capitalism.
James Muldoon's proposal to change the ownership of digital platforms from private to social or democratic control.

t: The Communist Party of Vietnam's indigenous exploration of modernization
zh: 越南共产党推进现代化建设的本土探索
source: Contemporary World Socialism Issues (Dangdai shijie shehuizhuyi wenti), 2023 no. 4
paras: Wang Chengjiu and Lai Huiting ask how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) has pursued socialist modernization, and what this shows against the idea that modernization means Westernization. Starting from the debate prompted by Chinese modernization, they present Vietnam as a second case. They argue that the CPV has broken with the Soviet model and kept industrialization and modernization 'socialist-oriented', and that this has produced notable results alongside serious problems.

The article has four parts. It first traces three stages: early exploration through industrialization (1954–1986), a turning point from 'industrialization' to 'industrialization and modernization' (1986–1996), and fast-track advance since 1996. It then lists five main measures, sets out achievements with statistics, and ends with current problems. The authors draw on CPV congress and plenum documents, including the 2022 Resolution 29 that extends the programme to 2030 and 2045.

In the authors' account, early policy followed the Soviet example by prioritising heavy industry at 'fast, vigorous, steady' speed, and this unbalanced the economy and led to crisis. After 1986 the CPV is said to have corrected course. It made agriculture the 'front of first importance', adopted a 'fast and sustainable' growth concept, and revised its phased targets. It also developed a socialist-oriented market economy, opened to the world while treating domestic resources as primary, and used the science and technology revolution, the knowledge economy and digital transformation as levers for leapfrogging. The authors cite GDP growth, structural change, urbanization, rural development, poverty reduction and rising life expectancy as results.

The authors also list problems: slowing growth, heavy reliance on foreign direct investment, low local content and a place at the bottom of value chains, weak state-owned and private enterprises, and shortages of skilled personnel. They conclude that Vietnam's path, like China's, goes beyond the Soviet model and refutes 'modernization equals Westernization', and that it adds to socialist countries' experience. They also see the recent China–Vietnam joint statement on a community with a shared future as a favourable opportunity. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Vietnam's modernization policy since 1954, with its statistics and Party documents, as seen from the Chinese debate on socialist modernization.
quoteEn: Vietnam's modernization has not only broken through the traditional Soviet model of modernization, but its principled requirement that industrialization and modernization be "socialist-oriented" has also broken the myth that "modernization equals Westernization."
quoteZh: 越南的现代化不仅实现了对苏联传统现代化模式的突破，而且对工业化、现代化必须“以社会主义为定向”的原则性要求也打破了“现代化=西方化”的迷思。

glossary.zh: 社会主义定向市场经济
glossary.explanation: The CPV's term for Vietnam's market economy under Party leadership, with the stated aim of advancing towards socialism. The article says it was set as the general model for the transition period at the 9th Congress.
The CPV's formula that industrialization and modernization must keep a socialist direction. The authors treat it as the principle separating Vietnam's path from Westernization.

t: Climate-political positions of Europe's radical left parties and the social-ecological transformation
zh: 欧洲激进左翼政党的气候政治立场与社会生态转型探析
paras: How have Europe's radical left parties responded to the climate and ecological crisis, and how do their positions differ from those of other party families? Wang argues that these parties blame capitalism for the crisis. They reject the EU's neoliberal "European Green Deal" and offer a "Left Green New Deal" built on social-ecological transformation, which stresses social justice more than the positions of the Greens and social democrats.

The article has four parts. It first surveys radical left responses at the organisational level (the "Now, The People" platform, the European Left Party, the GUE/NGL parliamentary group) and at the level of manifestos and policy reports. It then reconstructs the theory of social-ecological transformation, which draws on the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation and Ulrich Brand. Next, it compares climate and energy positions of Germany's and Sweden's parties across the left–right spectrum. A conclusion assesses the theory and the practice.

Wang identifies three strands in the radical left's transformation project. The first is a critique of the roots of the crisis: capitalist growth and profit-seeking, "green growth" as a corporate slogan, and climate injustice between rich and poor and between North and South. The second is a "red-green" vision with a new economic model under democratic planning, public ownership and control of energy, and a "just transition" with retraining and secure jobs. The third is a broad alliance of parties, unions and social movements, for example the European Forum of Left, Green and Progressive Forces. In the German and Swedish comparison, Wang finds the radical left and the Greens setting earlier carbon-neutrality targets than social democrats. Centre-right parties favour market and technological means, and the far right is divided: Germany's AfD is sceptical of climate policy, while the Sweden Democrats support national targets and nuclear power.

Wang concludes that the radical left's discourse offers an alternative to neoliberal "green capitalism" and helps explain its limits. Its response is shaped by ideology, history and internal factions as well as external conditions. In practice, Wang says, the parties' proposals are poorly integrated, their influence on mainstream policy is limited, and the programme still needs testing. Wang calls on them to sharpen their distinct "red-green" profile against social-democratic and Green eco-modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed survey of party documents and national cases on the European left's climate and energy policy.
quoteEn: European radical left parties generally regard the capitalist system as the root of the climate crisis.
quoteZh: 欧洲激进左翼政党普遍将资本主义制度看做气候危机的根源

t: The resurgence of anti-intellectualism in contemporary America
st: Rooted in the internal contradictions of meritocracy
zh: 当代美国反智主义的再兴起
zhSub: 源于优绩主义的内在矛盾
paras: Why has anti-intellectualism returned to American life, and why did earlier predictions of its decline fail? The authors argue that Richard Hofstadter's 1960s explanation, built around religion, McCarthyism and educational shortcomings, no longer accounts for the current wave. They propose that meritocracy, understood as both a distribution system and an ideology of 'equal opportunity' and 'rewards for the able', is the main driver of the new anti-intellectualism.

The article begins by reviewing the concept of anti-intellectualism (drawing on Hofstadter and Daniel Rigney) and the existing literature on its causes. It then analyses meritocracy's origins, its turn into a conservative ideology after the 1980s, and its defects. It goes on to trace how meritocracy feeds anti-intellectualism through education, elite–mass antagonism and the loss of work dignity and civic spirit. It ends with the features and consequences of the new wave.

The authors make three main moves. First, they hold that meritocracy masks substantive inequality: elites monopolise elite schooling through inherited cultural capital, so education becomes class-stratified and instrumental and no longer cultivates independent, reflective thought. Second, they argue that meritocratic morality casts the successful as deserving and the unsuccessful as lazy or stupid, while elite domination of public office breaks representation. As evidence they cite Congress, where no member of the 118th Congress was formerly an industrial worker, and the educational split in the 2016 vote. Third, they claim that the resulting resentment is directed less at knowledge itself than at elites, and that it expresses itself in more radical, populist forms, including refusal of masks and vaccines and the storming of the Capitol.

The authors conclude that the new wave makes social issues more conservative (climate change, abortion), erodes the legitimacy of American democracy, and weakens national cohesion and the country's international standing and hegemony. They add that the United States cannot simply abandon meritocracy for hereditary hierarchy, and that whether it can calm angry, anti-elite citizens remains an open question. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of American populism that links education, representation and distribution to anti-intellectualism, with the supporting data they cite.
quoteEn: Anti-intellectualism is only one consequence of the tyranny of meritocracy; the widening wealth gap, the decline of the middle class and the resulting political and social inequalities are also closely tied to meritocracy.
quoteZh: 反智主义仅仅是优绩主义暴政带来的后果之一，贫富差距增大、中产阶级衰落以及由此带来的政治、社会不平等与优绩主义也息息相关。

t: The development of Vietnam's theory of socialist democracy since Đổi Mới (reform and opening up)
zh: 革新开放以来越南社会主义民主理论发展研究
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2024 no. 1
paras: Ruan asks how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) has developed its theory of socialist democracy since the Đổi Mới policy of renovation and opening up began in 1986. The article argues that, guided by Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, the CPV has steadily revised its understanding of democracy and built a distinctive body of theory. In Ruan's account this theory treats democracy as both the goal and the driving force of socialist construction. It holds that the state should belong to the people, come from the people and serve the people.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the background: economic transition, political reform, and social change such as the rise of a middle class, which Ruan says made the older theory inadequate. The second traces how the CPV's understanding of democracy's essence, subject, status and content changed across its successive national congresses. The third presents the theory of democratic construction, which Ruan summarises as one overall model, two key relationships, three basic forms and five principles.

Ruan argues that the CPV moved from the earlier language of "collective mastery" and the working people to "the people" as a whole, including entrepreneurs and the private sector. Democracy was placed ahead of fairness in the 2011 platform and became the theme of the 12th Congress. The overall model is "the Party leads, the state manages, the people are masters", to which the 13th Congress (2021) added the Fatherland Front and other organisations. The two relationships are democracy with national unity, and democracy with law and social order; Ruan quotes CPV leaders rejecting multiparty politics and pluralism. The three forms are direct, representative and grassroots democracy. The five principles are popular sovereignty, Party leadership, democratic centralism, the rule of law, and checks and supervision over power. The author presents Vietnam's socialist democracy as a surpassing of Western "liberal democracy", as the CPV sees it.

Ruan concludes that, through renovation, the CPV has produced distinctive concepts and institutional arrangements that secure Vietnam's democratic construction. The author says these also offer theoretical understanding and practical experience for building socialist democratic theory in a period of great global change, and for developing democracy under a socialist market economy. Read the original if you study Vietnam's official political theory, the CPV's congress documents on democracy, or comparative work on socialist-oriented democratic discourse as presented from China.
quoteEn: The level and height of democratic theory determine the effectiveness and the horizon of democratic practice.
quoteZh: 民主理论的水平和高度决定民主实践的效度和境界。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of Vietnam's Đổi Mới policy, launched at the CPV's 6th Congress in 1986. It moved Vietnam from a planned, closed economy towards a market-oriented, open one.
A concept from the CPV's 4th Congress meaning that the organised working people collectively act as masters of society. The article says the 7th Congress (1991) stopped using it.

glossary.zh: 党领导、国家管理、人民当家作主
glossary.pinyin: dǎng lǐngdǎo, guójiā guǎnlǐ, rénmín dāngjiā zuòzhǔ
glossary.en: the Party leads, the state manages, the people are masters
glossary.explanation: The CPV's formula for the overall operating model of Vietnam's political system. The article says the 13th Congress added the Fatherland Front and other social organisations as pillars of popular mastery.
The Vietnam Fatherland Front is the CPV-led umbrella organisation of mass and social organisations. The article describes it as carrying out non-binding external supervision of state organs.

The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining discussion and election with unified discipline and subordination of lower to higher levels. The article says it applies to the CPV and to all state organs in Vietnam.

t: The content, social background and essence of the Biden administration's "middle-class" foreign policy
zh: 拜登政府“中产阶级”外交政策的基本内容、社会背景与实质
paras: Ma Feng examines the "foreign policy for the middle class" that the Biden administration adopted in place of Donald Trump's "America First". The article argues that the policy responds to domestic crisis and declining international standing, and that in essence it does not differ from "America First". In Ma's view both are devices by which US monopoly capital and the upper elite try to rescue themselves, and Biden, like Trump, is a political agent of that capital who cannot change the country's basic direction.

The article has three parts. The first traces how the policy took shape: a Carnegie Endowment report, Biden's 2020 Foreign Affairs essay, his February 2021 State Department speech, the accompanying memorandum, statements by Antony Blinken and Jake Sullivan, and the 2022 National Security Strategy. The second sets out the social background, namely the shrinking middle class, rising inequality and inflation. The third offers five claims about the policy's essence.

Ma first argues that "middle class" is a non-class "class" mixing proletarians, petty bourgeoisie and part of the bourgeoisie. The author cites figures on the shrinking middle class, the Gini coefficient, billionaire wealth and food insecurity to show that its position has not improved under Biden. Ma attributes inflation and polarisation to the contradiction between private ownership of the means of production and socialised large-scale production. The five claims are that the policy expresses economic nationalism and national egoism, for example through \"Build Back Better World\" and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework; that it exports domestic contradictions abroad; that it continues the tradition of putting US interests first; that it adjusts long-term foreign policy to preserve hegemony; and that it fosters bloc confrontation, as in the Ukraine crisis and policy towards China.

Ma concludes that whatever form or slogan it takes, the policy serves to maintain US unipolar hegemony and the domestic rule of the upper class. In the author's account, spending on war while cutting taxes for the rich deepens inequality, and the United States has lost its moral appeal. Ma contends that Washington should instead reform at home and compete with China on a basis of mutual respect. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Biden-era US foreign policy, with its class analysis and the sources it cites on inequality and inflation.
quoteEn: In essence this policy is still a product of putting American interests above all else: it is an "America First" policy without the "America First" label.
quoteZh: 这一政策实质上依然是美国利益至上的产物，是没有“美国优先”的美国优先政策。

glossary.explanation: The slogan of the Trump administration's foreign and trade policy, which prioritised US national interests, tariffs and withdrawal from international agreements.

t: Lenin's critique of non-Marxist currents in Russia and its lessons for contemporary China
zh: 列宁对俄国非马克思主义思潮的批判及其对当代中国的启示
paras: Jia Shupin asks what Lenin's polemics against non-Marxist currents in Russia around the turn of the twentieth century can teach China today. The article argues that such currents typically wear Marxist dress and claim to renew Marxism, which makes them deceptive. Jia holds that mastering Marxist fundamentals through Lenin's critiques helps identify and resist comparable currents in present-day ideological struggle.

The article has three parts. The first describes four currents the author treats as Russian variants of Bernsteinism: Menshevism, Economism, Narodism (populism) and Machism. The second sets out Lenin's criticism of each. The third draws lessons for contemporary China, with particular attention to ideological leadership and theoretical education.

In Jia's account, Lenin answered the Mensheviks' loose, self-governing party model by defending centralism and the vanguard party, while also insisting on close ties between the party and the masses. Against the Economists he argued that socialist consciousness must be brought to workers from outside, since workers alone develop only trade-union consciousness. Against the Narodniks he argued that capitalism in Russia was historically progressive and arose from existing conditions. Against Machism he defended philosophical materialism and the Party principle in philosophy, claiming that its claim of neutrality masked idealism.

Jia draws three lessons. China should uphold Marxism's guiding position and the Party's leadership over ideology, and Jia names historical nihilism, neoliberalism and the 'end of ideology' thesis as current erroneous currents. It should recognise that ideological work is complex and long-term, strengthen the ability to discern harmful currents, and take a firm stand against Western capitalist ideological infiltration. It should also deepen theoretical education, including the study of Party history and the promotion of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a Party-theory reading of Lenin's polemics and how Chinese scholars apply them to current ideological work.
quoteEn: Only by arming its mind with Marxism and building a firm ideological safeguard can a proletarian party fundamentally eliminate the harmful influence of bourgeois ideas and be a good ideological leader.
quoteZh: 无产阶级政党只有用马克思主义武装头脑，筑牢思想保障体系，才能从根本上破除资产阶级思想观念的不良影响，做好思想领导者

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Communist Party of China's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions after the 19th Party Congress (2017).
In official Chinese usage, a label for views that question or negate the Party's revolutionary history and socialist path. The author treats it as an erroneous current.

The Party's claim to lead and control ideological and cultural work, including education, media and publishing. It draws on Lenin's Party principle and is often discussed in Gramscian terms of hegemony.

t: Lenin's critique of the liberal Narodniks on Russia's path of development, and its lessons
zh: 列宁在俄国发展道路问题上对自由主义民粹派的批判及其启示
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2024 no. 1
paras: Wang and Du examine how Lenin criticised the liberal Narodniks (populists) such as Mikhailovsky, Vorontsov, Yushakov and Danielson in the debate over "where Russia is going" at the turn of the twentieth century. The authors argue that the liberal Narodniks offered a reformist, petty-bourgeois programme that denied capitalism's necessity in Russia, and that Lenin's rebuttal remains instructive for socialist construction today.

The article reconstructs Lenin's critique in three parts: the "non-capitalist path", the question of which social force should lead, and the Narodniks' claim to speak for "the people". A fourth part draws three lessons for contemporary China, citing Xi Jinping's statements on each. The authors rely on Lenin's writings, including The Development of Capitalism in Russia.

In the authors' account, Lenin first refuted the claims that capitalism was unworkable and destructive in Russia. He argued that the social division of labour, commodity production and the ruin of small producers were already enlarging the home market, and that Danielson and others misunderstood the realisation of products. Capitalism, Lenin held, was therefore both inevitable and progressive, because it socialised labour and created the material basis and class forces for socialism. Second, he analysed the peasantry as dual and vacillating, the intelligentsia as dependent on the bourgeoisie, and the proletariat as the "only fighter" for emancipation, so that a proletarian party must lead through research, propaganda and organisation. Third, he exposed the Narodniks' "revival of the people's economy" as patching up capitalism and treating the masses as a mob, and insisted that the path must start from the interests of working people and rely on them as makers of history.

The authors draw three lessons. Socialism must learn from the beneficial achievements of capitalist civilisation, while staying alert to its contradictions and rejecting the equation of modernization with Westernization, since Chinese modernization is socialist modernization. Adherence to the leadership of the Communist Party of China must be unwavering. The authors cite the Soviet collapse as a warning, attributing it to ideological and political pluralism under Gorbachev and to a Party that became a privileged bureaucratic group cut off from the people. The Party must also represent the people's interests and rely on them, developing whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist scholars use Lenin's polemic with the Narodniks to support current Party-leadership and development arguments.
quoteEn: Beyond doubt, what Lenin stresses here is that Russia's "activity aimed at socialism" can succeed only if it strives to draw in the broad working masses and gives full play to their initiative and creativity as the main force.
quoteZh: 毫无疑问，列宁这里强调的是，俄国“以社会主义为目标的活动”只有努力吸引广大劳动群众参加，充分发挥他们作为主体力量的主动性和创造性，才能取得成功。

glossary.explanation: An official concept promoted since the early 2020s, presented as a socialist path of modernization distinct from Western models.
An official term introduced by Xi Jinping around 2019 to describe China's political system as democratic at every stage, from elections to decision-making and oversight.

t: A critique of US digital hegemony from the perspective of digital imperialism
zh: 数字帝国主义视阈下美国的数字霸权批判
paras: Hu Ying asks what US digital hegemony consists of and what it is in essence. The article argues that digital imperialism is the latest form of imperialism and that US digital hegemony is its main expression. In Hu's account, the classical Marxist theory of imperialism has not become outdated: it remains the tool for seeing that the new technical forms conceal the same plunder of global surplus value.

The article is built in five parts. It first treats digital capital and digital oligarchs as the basis of US hegemony, drawing on figures on platform concentration and the Wintel alliance. It then describes how the US controls other countries' data and digital space, and how it uses digital advantages to consolidate cultural and political hegemony. A fourth part addresses the essence of this hegemony through Marx, Lenin, Luxemburg and world-systems writers such as Wallerstein and Frank, and a short conclusion turns to policy.

Hu identifies three means of control: the digitalisation of unequal exchange, in which raw data from peripheral countries is processed and sold back as software or advice; control of the access routes to digital space, such as operating systems, cloud infrastructure and network equipment; and digital colonisation through "digital technology assistance", illustrated with Africa. Using Lenin's view that monopoly is the essence of imperialism, the article treats digital monopoly capital as the logical starting point. It names four accumulation mechanisms: data extraction, digital enclosure, the fusion of digital capital with industrial and financial capital, and digital export. Hu also claims that platforms exploit unpaid "prosumer" labour and spread US values through search engines and social media.

Hu concludes that digital hegemony changes the form of imperial power but not its predatory purpose, and that digital imperialism is only a "new solution" that cannot resolve capitalism's basic contradiction. The article calls for a community with a shared future for mankind in digital space. It cites Xi Jinping's remarks on cybersecurity and China's 2020 Global Initiative on Data Security, and rejects data monopoly, digital colonisation and double standards. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical Chinese account of US digital power that combines classical imperialism theory with detailed company and market data.
quoteEn: Whatever changes occur in the concrete forms of imperialism, its constant aim is the predatory appropriation of global surplus value, while technological progress supplies ever newer instruments for that aim.
quoteZh: 无论帝国主义的具体表现形式出现了怎样的变化，实现对全球剩余价值的掠夺性占有始终是其不变的目的，而技术进步为这一目的的实现提供不断更新的先进工具。

glossary.explanation: A term for imperialism carried out through control of data, platforms and digital infrastructure. The article treats it as the newest form of imperialism.
An analogy with the historical enclosure of common land. It refers to tech giants building ecosystems of software, hardware and network connections to appropriate data.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept associated with Xi Jinping, stressing shared interests and cooperation among states. The article applies it to digital space.
A proposal issued by China in September 2020 setting out principles for global data security governance. The article cites it as China's alternative to data monopoly and mass surveillance.

t: The essence, crisis and alternative of neoliberal globalization
st: A commentary on David Lane's latest lectures
zh: 新自由主义全球化的实质、危机和替代
zhSub: 大卫·莱恩最新演讲评析
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 6
paras: This commentary reports and assesses three lectures given at Peking University on 24–26 May 2023 by David Lane, emeritus professor of sociology at Cambridge and author of Global Neoliberal Capitalism and the Alternatives: From Social Democracy to State Capitalisms (2023). The authors present Lane's thesis that neoliberal globalization is the ideology and framework of a transnational capitalist class, and that it is in crisis. They add that the rise of China as a "semi-core" power points to an alternative, which Lane calls socialist globalization.

The article has four parts: the essence of neoliberal globalization, its defects and crisis, the alternative, and a short conclusion. It begins with Lane's account of postwar capitalism, which moved from internationalism to globalization. Competitive market, coordinated market and social-democratic welfare models existed side by side before the 1970s. The authors then set out his critique of Wallerstein's world-system model and add their own reservations at the end of the third part.

On Lane's account, from the late 1970s Thatcher and Reagan pushed a neoliberal ideology that dissolved national borders and let multinational firms and a transnational capitalist class rule. Lane describes this class as including corporate owners, officials, the managers of the IMF, World Bank and WTO, think-tank members, and businesspeople and media. He sees three failures: it cannot avoid crises, as the 2007–2008 financial crisis showed. It weakens state sovereignty and welfare provision. It also fuels new populism such as Brexit, which Lane regards as a continuation of neoliberalism rather than a challenge to it. Lane holds that the crisis cannot be solved inside the capitalist world system, so a different globalization is needed. He credits China with a mixed-ownership market economy under socialist regulation and with a strong public-power state. He also credits it with building regional organizations and promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. Lane traces three stages since reform and opening up: peripheral dependence, competitive symbiosis and a new equilibrium. He proposes replacing Wallerstein's "semi-periphery" with "semi-core".

The authors conclude that China's constructive proposals on globalization offer a positive alternative to neoliberal globalization. They also criticise Lane's structural analysis as inaccurate. In their view, labelling China "semi-core" assumes that it belongs to a single capitalist world system. The label also stresses competition and confrontation while overlooking cooperation and exchange between socialism and transnational capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of a Western sociologist's view of neoliberalism, world-system theory and China's role in globalization.
quoteEn: Neoliberalism is the ideology and policy system that corresponds to the global rule of multinational corporations and the transnational capitalist class behind them.
quoteZh: 新自由主义是与跨国公司及其背后的跨国资本家阶级的全球统治相适应的意识形态和政策体系。

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping. It calls for shared development and sovereign equality among states.

t: Class, assets and work in rentier capitalism
zh: 食利资本主义中的阶级、资产和工作
orig: Historical Materialism, 2021, no. 2
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2023 no. 6
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the economic geographer Brett Christophers (Uppsala University), first published in Historical Materialism in 2021. It asks how class and inequality should be understood in what the author calls an age of rentier capitalism. Christophers argues that recent work on assets and inequality overlooks the fact that most rent-generating assets belong to corporations, not households. In his account, class position increasingly depends on how an employee's work relates to the assets the employer owns.

The article has three parts. The first reviews Thomas Piketty, Guy Standing and Lisa Adkins, Melinda Cooper and Martijn Konings, who bring asset ownership into class analysis, and sets them against Erik Olin Wright's employment-based schema. The second examines corporate ownership of seven asset types: property, financial assets, intellectual property, natural resources, digital platforms, long-term service contracts and infrastructure. The third asks what this means for Marx's categories. Christophers defines rent broadly as income from owning or controlling scarce assets under limited competition, which extends Marx's concept of ground rent beyond land.

Christophers argues that employees in rentier firms stand in four privileged relations to corporate assets: creating them, demonstrating their value (accountants), protecting them (lawyers, for example through patent 'evergreening') and maximising rent (lobbyists, tax lawyers and accountants). Most staff, by contrast, simply 'sweat' the assets, and the pay and class gap between the two groups is wide. He presents these roles as speculative hypotheses needing empirical testing. Applying Marx's distinction, he notes that labour exchanged against rent is unproductive, since it creates no surplus value. This poses two problems: whether Marx's concepts fit an economy centred on rent, and what class position these workers hold. Citing Ian Gough, he says Marx's argument that commercial workers are exploited does not extend to workers paid out of rent, so they challenge Marx's class theory more sharply than commercial workers do.

Christophers concludes that more empirical and theoretical work is needed. He proposes that class be understood through two questions: whether people own housing or other valuable assets, and what labour relation they have to employer-owned rent-yielding assets, whether sweating, creating or protecting them. As capital changes form, he says, the concepts used to understand it must change as well. Read the original if you work on Marxist class theory, rentier capitalism or the productive/unproductive labour debate and want an argument that tests Marx's categories against corporate asset ownership.
quoteEn: The only difference is that in rentier capitalism the division of labour among workers increasingly depends on their respective relations to income-generating assets, rather than to the means of production.
quoteZh: 不同之处只是在于，在食利资本主义中，工人之间的劳动分工日益取决于他们各自与创收资产的关系，而非与生产资料的关系。

t: Foreign left-wing scholars' critique of biocapitalism in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪国外左翼学者对生物资本主义的批判
source: Frontiers of Foreign Social Sciences (国外社会科学前沿), 2023 no. 10
paras: This review surveys how Western left-wing scholars since 2006 have analysed biocapitalism, the form of capitalism that extracts profit and accumulates capital through the life sciences and biotechnology. It starts from Kaushik Sunder Rajan's Biocapital: The Constitution of Postgenomic Life, which combines Marxist political economy with Foucauldian biopolitics. Liu and Gu argue that these scholars, though illuminating, remain at the level of phenomena and need a fuller Marxist political-economy critique.

The article draws on Rajan, Nikolas Rose, Clayton Pierce, Melinda Cooper, Joseph Dumit and others. It has three main sections: biocapitalism as the latest form of capitalist domination; its instrumental and "redemptive" character under the joint operation of capital logic and power logic; and its expression as neoliberalism and new imperialism in biological form. A short concluding section assesses the literature and raises questions for China.

In the authors' account, the foreign scholars hold that biocapitalism continues capitalism rather than breaking with it: private ownership, class exploitation of "bio-labourers" and profit-driven monopoly persist. What changes is the route of exploitation, which shifts from people as bearers of labour-power to people as biological organisms. Value is drawn from speculative "future products" and expectations, and extraction extends from working time to the whole of life, blurring work and leisure. The review adds that state funding, patent monopolies and a "pseudo-religious" ideology of national salvation legitimate this process. It also cites the deCODE genetics database in Iceland, the Human Genome Project's treatment of the Guaymi, and transnational organ trafficking as cases of what the scholars call bio-imperialism and biocolonialism.

Liu and Gu conclude that biocapitalism results from capital's rent-seeking in biotechnology and that its problems come from capital logic and the power logic it manipulates. They judge that most foreign left scholars stop at description and offer "reformist" or "utopian" remedies, and they call for a Marxist critique of political economy as the proper tool. They add that biotechnology has become a field of great-power rivalry, making biosecurity urgent for China, and they leave open whether biocapitalism might move towards "biosocialism". Read the original if you want a Chinese-language overview of Western left debates on biocapital and the way a Chinese Marxist assessment frames them.
quoteEn: Only by truly making good use of the sharp "scalpel" of the Marxist critique of political economy can one reach the inner core of biocapitalism and, on that basis, form scientific solutions and response strategies.
quoteZh: 唯有真正用好马克思主义政治经济学批判这把锐利的“手术刀”，方能触及生物资本主义的内里，并在此基础上形成科学的解决方案和应对策略。

glossary.explanation: A term for capitalism that accumulates capital through life sciences and biotechnology, developed from Kaushik Sunder Rajan's concept of biocapital. The article treats it as the latest form of capitalism rather than a new epoch.
A common term in Chinese Marxist writing for the inner drive of capital to expand and accumulate. Here it is paired with the logic of political power.
A term for rivalry between states over biological resources and biotechnology, with plunder of the bodies and resources of weaker populations. The article treats it as related to biocolonialism.
The article's term for both biotechnology workers and "volunteers" who supply tissue, services or trial participation to biotech firms.

t: The causes of "anti-globalization" and how to respond
zh: “逆全球化”的成因与应对
paras: Dan Qing's short commentary asks why the United States and other Western countries, once champions of globalization, have turned to "anti-globalization" measures such as "de-risking", trade "decoupling" and the chips act. The author argues that these moves serve Western hegemony and domestic interests, and that China and other countries should answer by promoting an open, inclusive and mutually beneficial globalization.

The piece has three parts: the main forms of anti-globalization, its root causes, and the proposed responses. It draws on examples such as the 2023 Munich Security Conference, the growth of the US "Entity List", and US withdrawals from agreements and organisations.

Dan describes the US as using political bloc-building, economic sanctions and diplomatic withdrawal to slow the rise of emerging countries. The causes are said to be the outward projection of domestic contradictions (financial crises, industrial hollowing-out, widening inequality), a negative-sum strategy of containing rivals even at a cost to itself, and global governance that lags behind the declining Western share of the world economy. In the author's reading, Western countries choose globalization or its reverse purely according to their interests.

Dan concludes that China should keep expanding opening up, help build a "new type of globalization" with more voice for developing countries, and work for a community with a shared future for mankind. The author cites the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative and Global Civilization Initiative as the means. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-journal commentary presents the Chinese official view of Western decoupling policies.
quoteEn: For the United States and the West, there is no permanent globalization or "anti-globalization", only permanent interests; whether they adopt globalization or anti-globalization depends entirely on what their own interests and hegemony require.
quoteZh: 对美西方国家来说，没有永远的全球化或者“逆全球化”，只有永远的利益，采用全球化还是“逆全球化”策略，完全视其维护自身利益和霸权的需要而定。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s. It calls for countries to treat their interests as interconnected and to pursue shared development and security.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013.
China's policy since 1978 of economic reform and engagement with the world economy. Here the commentary uses it for continued expansion of China's openness.

t: The reproduction of labour subjectivity under the logic of capital
st: A contemporary dimension of Western Marxist critical theories of capital
zh: 资本逻辑下劳动主体性的再生产——西方马克思主义资本批判理论的一个当代面向
paras: Niu asks why the strengthening of workers' subjectivity under contemporary capitalism has not liberated labour but has coincided with worse conditions. The article challenges the "subject-object inversion" paradigm, inherited from Lukács and influential in Chinese Marxist philosophy, which treats capital as usurping workers' subjectivity and liberation as its restoration. Niu argues that Western Marxists since the 1960s recognised a hidden complicity between labour subjectivity and capital's power, and developed theories of how capital reproduces labour subjects.

The article has three parts. It first criticises what Merleau-Ponty called "Weberian Marxism" (Lukács, Adorno, Marcuse). It then traces a line of thought on the production of subjects through Kojève, Lacan, Althusser and Foucault. Finally it examines Deleuze's theory of desire-production and its later development by Byung-Chul Han, followed by a critique of Negri's autonomism and the cognitive capitalism school of Yann Moulier-Boutang.

Niu contends that Lukács reached the rationalised labour process through Weber's rationalisation theory rather than through Marx's theories of valorisation and relative surplus value. The critique therefore fitted Fordist industrial capitalism, not the essential law of capital. Because capital's valorisation principle is non-identity, a ceaseless drive for "more", liberating differentiated subjectivity served capital. Niu says this fed neoliberalism and the post-1968 movements, and also hit bureaucratic unions, welfare states and socialist states. Althusser's ideological state apparatuses and Foucault's biopolitics treat power as productive. Deleuze defines surplus labour as a qualitative form internal to the worker's desire, so that workers "desire capital's desire". Niu adds that Deleuze's call to extend deterritorialisation still suits capital. Negri and the cognitive capitalism school repeat the Weberian error by treating more flexible, cognitive labour as emancipatory.

Niu concludes that under neoliberalism domination takes the form of liberation, and that the wage-labour subject is not automatically a political subject. Following Althusser's distinction, Niu calls for specific political procedures to turn capitalism's "labour subjects" into "political subjects", without which revolutionary action would fail. Niu says this also invites reflection on the existing paradigm in Chinese Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you want a critical account of how Western Marxist theories of the subject, from Lukács to Deleuze and Han, relate to capital accumulation and neoliberalism.
quoteEn: The labour subjects constructed by capitalism itself can hardly serve directly as political subjects resisting capitalism.
quoteZh: 资本主义本身所构造的劳动主体难以直接充当反抗资本主义的政治主体

t: The evolution of Kishida's "new capitalism" policy: theory and practice
zh: 岸田“新资本主义”政策的演进：理论与实践
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai Lilun Dongtai), 2023 no. 6
paras: Liu Rui examines the "new capitalism" programme that Fumio Kishida first put forward in September 2021 as Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party chose its leader. The article asks how the policy has developed, what lies behind it, what theory it draws on and how far it has worked. Liu's answer is that the policy corrects neoliberalism only in part: in practice it continues the main methods of "Abenomics", stays within Japan's traditional neoliberal framework and addresses short-term problems rather than long-term ones.

The article has four parts. It first traces the policy from the October 2021 framework and the new headquarters chaired by the prime minister through the 2022 and 2023 basic policy documents. It then sets out the background: long economic stagnation, a "disparity society", weak corporate innovation, feeble consumption and investment, and a changed international environment. The third part reviews the theoretical foundations, and the fourth assesses results and obstacles.

In Liu's account, the policy has three features: it stresses distribution, but this fades as it is folded into the growth strategy ("investment in people", structural wage rises); it takes on extra functions, notably economic security, which Liu says follows the United States in restraining China and works against the growth goal; and it widens government–private cooperation. Liu locates its theory in criticism of neoliberalism, stakeholder capitalism and the "public-interest capitalism" of Hara Joji, which draws on Japanese business traditions. Liu concludes that "new" means a correction of neoliberalism, not a rejection of capitalism. On results, Liu argues that the 2023 wage rises mainly reflect rising prices, so real wages kept falling. Growth was driven by external demand and a weak yen, while domestic demand declined and corporate retained earnings reached record highs.

Liu identifies three obstacles: a severe fiscal position and a fiscal-reconstruction target that is hard to meet; large funding gaps for defence, measures against the falling birth rate and green transformation; and an excessive emphasis on economic security that could hinder growth. Liu closes by asking how the government can strengthen growth, raise real wages and potential growth, and reform social security, and says these questions test the Kishida government. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's detailed, data-heavy assessment of Kishida's economic programme and its intellectual sources.
quoteEn: In practical effect, however, Kishida's "new capitalism" policy still continues the main practices of "Abenomics", remains confined within Japan's traditional neoliberal policy framework, concentrates on short-term practical problems, and has not truly tackled medium- and long-term ones.
quoteZh: 但从实际效果来看，岸田的“新资本主义”政策仍延续了“安倍经济学”的主要做法，局限在日本传统的新自由主义政策框架内，将重点置于应对短期现实问题，未能真正深入解决中长期问题。

t: New developments in the Middle East amid great changes: features, challenges and prospects
zh: 大变局下中东地区新发展：特征、挑战及前景
paras: Wang Lincong asks how the Middle East is changing as the international order shifts, and what obstacles and prospects follow. The article argues that the region has reached a historic turning point: states prioritise development, reconcile with one another and act with greater strategic autonomy, becoming an important force in the Global South. It holds that China's global initiatives can help the region leave its security and development predicaments and shape a "new Middle East".

The article has three parts: new features of regional development, the challenges it faces, and its prospects. The features are examined at three levels: national, regional and global. Wang draws on opinion surveys (Arab Opinion Index 2022, Arab Barometer), national vision plans such as Saudi Vision 2030, and events from 2019 to 2023, including the Saudi–Iranian rapprochement, the Ukraine crisis and BRICS enlargement.

Wang argues that the Arab upheavals deepened rather than resolved the region's development, security and governance deficits. Citizens now care more about economic livelihood than abstract democracy, and elites want to catch the fourth industrial revolution. The "wave of reconciliation" is presented as a rational choice based on security and economic costs, helped by US strategic contraction and Chinese mediation. Wang also stresses persistent obstacles: structural economic problems, debt crises and slow diversification in oil-rich states; continuing US pressure, which Wang describes as sanctions, proxy conflicts and exclusive "mini-multilateral" schemes such as I2U2 and IMEC; and layered security risks, including Gaza, Sudan, the Turkey–Syria earthquake and Libya's floods.

Wang concludes that the region's progress will be difficult and uneven, since strategic trust and security institutions are lacking. China is credited with a constructive role, shown in trade figures, the 2022 China–Arab summits, naval escorts in the Gulf of Aden and the brokering of the Saudi–Iranian deal. Wang proposes cooperation under the global development, global security and global civilization initiatives, together with the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Middle East realignment and China's role are framed, with figures and examples from 2019–2023.
quoteEn: The strengthening of Middle Eastern states' strategic autonomy is manifested mainly in two respects.
quoteZh: 中东国家的战略自主增强，主要表现在两个方面。

glossary.explanation: A term for developing and emerging countries, used in Chinese official discourse to frame them as a collective force in international affairs.
A Chinese proposal made in 2023 promoting respect for the diversity of civilizations and exchange between them.
China's infrastructure and economic cooperation programme, launched in 2013, linking China with Asia, Africa and Europe.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping that serves as the guiding idea of China's foreign policy.

t: The paradigm shift in research on foreign Marxism
zh: 国外马克思主义研究的范式转向
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2023 no. 8
paras: Sun Ying asks how Chinese research on foreign Marxism (Marxism outside China) has changed since the start of the new era, and where it should go next. The article argues that the field is already in a period of paradigm transition. It moves from object-oriented translation and exposition towards what Sun calls subject-centred, dialogical research that serves the development of contemporary Chinese Marxism.

Sun first summarises five scholarly positions on the shift: the contemporary-significance, problem-orientation, change-of-centre, change-of-role and breaking-disciplinary-walls views. The article then organises the change along three axes: content (from translation and introduction to genealogical research), method (from text commentary to theoretical system-building), and value orientation (from drawing direct lessons to returning to the Marxist classics and stressing China's significance). Examples include biopolitics, urban space, financial capitalism and ecological Marxism.

Sun argues that translation remains the foundation, but it mainly transports knowledge and cannot sort out tendencies in foreign thought that depart from Marxist fundamentals, such as instrumentalization, fragmentation and deconstruction. Genealogical research therefore compares thinkers such as Foucault, Agamben, Hardt and Negri and works across disciplines. Under a principle of wholeness, scholars compare Chinese and Western approaches, for instance Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization against Western ecological Marxism, which Sun describes as theoretically stagnant and ineffective in practice. They also place Western Marxism in the history of thought and build their own analytical paradigms. The third move is a new "return to the classics", after the "return to Marx" of the turn of the century. It draws on the Capital revival after the 2008 crisis and on MEGA2, and on studying texts of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, in dialogue with foreign studies of China.

Sun concludes that the core issue is the critique of capitalist modernity, with Marxism as guide, sinicized Marxism as centre and foreign Marxism as resource. Guided by the Two Integrations, the author expects future work to focus on capitalist modernity, paths of human emancipation and forms of civilization. It should also stress grand historical narrative and strengthen the construction and international spread of Chinese discourse. Read the original if you want to understand how a Chinese scholar maps the field's methodological self-reassessment and its stated aims.
quoteEn: Research on foreign Marxism has now fully entered a period of paradigm transformation.
quoteZh: 国外马克思主义研究在当下已全面进入范式转型期

glossary.explanation: The broad field of Marxist currents outside China, including Western Marxism, which Chinese scholars study as a discipline.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for combining Marxism with China's realities and contemporary conditions. It is used to describe Party theory since Mao Zedong.
Xi Jinping's formula of integrating Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
A research trend in Chinese Marxist philosophy around the turn of the century, calling for rereading Marx's original texts rather than later interpretations.

t: The theoretical value and practical significance of Lenin's intellectual legacy for the world revolution and the Vietnamese revolution
zh: 列宁思想遗产对世界革命和越南革命的理论价值与实践意义
paras: Written to mark the 150th anniversary of Lenin's birth (2020) and published in 2024, this article asks what Lenin's legacy means for world revolution and for Vietnam. The authors, a senior Vietnamese Party leader with two Chinese scholars, argue that Lenin defended and creatively developed Marxism, and that his thought gave Ho Chi Minh and the Communist Party of Vietnam the basis for combining national independence with socialism.

The article moves through seven sections. The first four deal with Lenin: his theory that revolution could succeed in the imperialist era and the October Revolution, his ideas on socialist construction and the New Economic Policy, his struggle against opportunism, and his theory of the national and colonial question. The fifth and sixth sections turn to Vietnam, covering Ho Chi Minh's conversion to Leninism and the Party's current line of renewal (đổi mới). A short conclusion restates the commitment to Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought.

The authors argue that Lenin built on Marx's expectation of simultaneous revolution in advanced countries. From the law of uneven development, they say, he concluded that socialism could win first in a single country, and that Russia was the weakest link in the imperialist chain. They present the October Revolution as an objectively necessary outcome, not an accident. They read the shift from war communism to the New Economic Policy as a model for reforming existing socialism, which includes a multi-sector economy and learning from capitalism. In their account, the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was the failure of a flawed model, not of socialism or Marxism-Leninism. The authors also stress Lenin's extension of the slogan to 'workers of all countries and oppressed nations, unite'. They hold that Ho Chi Minh's thesis that colonial revolutions may precede metropolitan ones, and that independence must be tied to socialism, enriched Marxism-Leninism.

The authors conclude that the Communist Party of Vietnam, guided by Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, has produced historic achievements through renewal. They cite a socialist-oriented market economy, stronger Party building and an anti-corruption campaign since the 12th Party Congress. They call for firmness in the goals of national independence and socialism and for Vietnam to become a developed, socialist-oriented country. Read the original if you want an official Vietnamese Party-theoretical account of how Lenin's legacy is used to legitimise renewal and the Party's leadership.
quoteEn: This was only the collapse of a model of actually existing socialism with many flaws.
quoteZh: 这只是一种带有很多缺陷的现实社会主义模式的垮台

glossary.explanation: The policy adopted in Soviet Russia in 1921 that replaced grain requisitioning with a tax in kind and allowed private trade and a mixed economy. The article treats it as Lenin's model for reforming socialism.
The emergency economic measures of 1918–1921 during the Russian Civil War, including compulsory grain requisitioning. The article says it became an obstacle once peace came.
The reform programme of the Communist Party of Vietnam, launched in 1986, that moved from a centralised planned economy to a socialist-oriented market economy.

glossary.zh: 社会主义定向的市场经济
glossary.pinyin: shèhuì zhǔyì dìngxiàng de shìchǎng jīngjì
glossary.explanation: The official name for Vietnam's economic system since renewal. It is a market economy under Party leadership with socialism as its declared aim.

The official ideological system of the Communist Party of Vietnam. It draws on Ho Chi Minh's adaptation of Marxism-Leninism to Vietnamese conditions and is placed alongside Marxism-Leninism as a guide to action.

t: New trends in British Marxist historiography since the 1990s
zh: 20世纪90年代以来英国马克思主义史学新趋向
source: Journal of Historical Theory Studies (Shixue lilun yanjiu), 2024 no. 1
paras: How has British Marxist historiography developed since the 1990s, after the generation of Hobsbawm and E. P. Thompson? Liang argues that the school has lost momentum and no longer produces figures of equal stature. Even so, its themes, core concerns and historical outlook remain a reference point for international historiography, and a second generation and later followers have extended its legacy in two areas: the new labour history and Marxist feminist history.

The article has three parts. The first describes the new setting after the end of the Cold War: British works defending or applying Marxist method, non-Marxist studies of Hobsbawm and Thompson, new histories of the Communist Party of Great Britain, and institutions and journals such as the Socialist History Society (1992), the Marx Memorial Library and Workers' School (1993), and periodicals like Past and Present, History Workshop Journal and New Left Review. The second part treats the new labour history under the "cultural turn". The third treats Marxist feminist history.

Liang's central claim is that Thompson's "culturalist" paradigm, which approached class consciousness through experience and a history "from below", is the theoretical base of the new labour history. Later historians turned it towards global labour history, partly in response to criticism that stress on experience and language fragmented the field. In feminist history, Sheila Rowbotham, Catherine Hall, Sally Alexander and Barbara Taylor are presented as building on Thompson while criticising his marginalising of women. Their move from women's history to gender history, joined with class analysis, widened the field in three ways: geographically (Scotland, Ireland, Australia), in historical context (second- and third-wave feminism, imperial and global history), and in theory (a call to return to class analysis and a critique of patriarchy).

Liang concludes that, over the past three decades, later British Marxist historians have mostly worked on the writings and thought of the first two generations, especially Thompson's culturalist model. In the article's account, British Marxist historiography still shapes British historical scholarship and receives international attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly survey of post-1990 British Marxist history, with many names and titles on the Communist Party's historiography, labour history and feminist history.
quoteEn: The new British labour history stresses the theory of history \"from below\" and the Marxist method of class analysis, examining the social life and the intellectual history of labour in a holistic and dynamic way.
quoteZh: 英国新劳工史学强调“自下而上”历史理论和马克思主义阶级分析方法，从整体性和动态性角度考察劳工社会生活与观念历史

t: Ownership in the digital age: from digital capitalism to digital socialism
zh: 数字时代的所有制议题：从数字资本主义到数字社会主义
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 6
paras: Hao Zhichang asks how ownership should be understood in the digital age and whether it points towards digital capitalism or digital socialism. The article argues that ownership, as the foundation of the relations of production, is the underlying logic of any digital civilisation, and that debates on data rights or privacy law stay superficial if they ignore it. Hao holds that the digital form of ownership is at a crossroads: under capitalism it yields new hidden forms of exploitation, while a socialist form of ownership can open a new digital civilisation.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's concept of ownership: its elements (objects of labour, means of labour, labourers, non-labourers and purposive activity), the attribution of the means of production, and the specific way labourers and means of production are combined. It then maps these elements onto digital forms. The second part analyses digital capitalist ownership, drawing on Nick Srnicek, Christian Fuchs, Kevin Kelly, Byung-Chul Han and others. The third sets out digital socialist ownership and relates it to China's basic economic system.

Hao's central move is to treat user data as the digital counterpart of Marx's 'filtered' raw material, and algorithms, cloud computing and AI as digital means of labour. Under digital capitalism, these digital means of production belong to platform owners, not to users. Users are combined with them through a 'non-standard' digital wage-labour system, in which 'free services' function as wages. The 'public use' model replaces exclusive private use and turns exploitation into self-exploitation. Hao disputes Han's claim that users own their means of production: in Hao's view they only use them, and are newly recruited wage-labourers. Against this, digital socialist ownership requires common or social ownership of data and platforms. It also requires a higher-level direct combination of labourers with the means of production, which Hao reads as the digital form of Marx's 're-establishing individual ownership'.

Hao concludes that 'public use' without public ownership is a new deception, and that open, shared digital means of production resist privatisation. The article presents the 'Digital China' project and China's basic economic system, with public ownership as the mainstay, as providing institutional guarantees for this path. It describes a Chinese model of digital socialism with global significance. Read the original if you want a Marxist, ownership-centred critique of platform capitalism that ends in an argument for digital socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteEn: Digital capitalist ownership not only extracts digital surplus value in new ways, but also creates the material potential, or digital singularity, that will overturn it.
quoteZh: 数字资本主义所有制不仅以新的方式攫取数字剩余价值，同时也制造出了颠覆自身的物质势能或数字奇点

glossary.explanation: In Chinese Marxist usage, the social form in which the means of production are held and controlled, as distinct from legal property rights. It is treated as the basis of the relations of production and of a society's character.
A national strategy for building digital infrastructure and a digital economy, society and governance. The 20th Party Congress report (2022) called for advancing its construction.
The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up. It combines Party leadership, public ownership as the mainstay, and a socialist market economy.

t: Revisiting the Lenin–Kautsky debate on the October Revolution from the perspective of revolutionary will
zh: 革命意志视角下列宁和考茨基关于十月革命理论论争的再探讨
source: Problems of Contemporary World Socialism, 2023 no. 4
paras: Ding Guanghao and Sun Daiyao ask why Lenin and Kautsky, after the 1917 October Revolution, reached such opposed judgements of it. They argue that the root of the dispute lies in how each understood 'revolutionary will'. Lenin held a logic of 'manufacturing' will under special revolutionary conditions, while Kautsky held a logic of 'generation', in which will arises naturally on a mature economic base.

The article opens with a review of earlier scholarship. It notes early Western Marxists' critique of Second International economic determinism, Cold War 'Leninology' that treated Kautskyism as Leninism's source, and Chinese studies of democracy and dictatorship, imperialism and revolutionary strategy. It then compares the two thinkers on three questions: the objective conditions for progressive will in backward Russia, how will is shaped through Soviet democracy, and whether wartime will can be carried into socialist construction. A final section traces the differences back to their understandings of historical materialism.

On conditions, the authors report that Lenin saw Russia's backwardness and crisis as an advantage for starting the revolution, though not for completing it. Kautsky, in The Dictatorship of the Proletariat, judged that will born of backwardness was blind mass psychology and not socialist. On shaping, Lenin favoured centralised leadership and training through struggle and practical work; Kautsky held that 'pure democracy' and free will were prerequisites, and that Soviet rule produced only 'unified opinion'. On the limits of will, Kautsky warned of 'barracks socialism', which Ding and Sun call a salutary warning that overlooked the survival logic of War Communism. Behind these differences, the authors argue, Kautsky's naturalist, scientistic reading led to 'economic fatalism' and a rigid use of general laws. Lenin's historical dialectic stressed the interplay of base and superstructure, the particular within the general, and the unity of Marxism's scientific and revolutionary character.

The authors conclude that the debate epitomised the clash between Russian Marxism and Second International 'orthodoxy'. After October, they say, revolution in relatively backward countries became the 'general' case. They cite Mao Zedong's view that seizing power precedes developing productive forces, and Xi Jinping's call for fighting spirit and will in building socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. They argue that a Marxist governing party must keep its revolutionary spirit. Read the original if you study the Lenin–Kautsky controversy, debates on 'skipping stages', or how Chinese scholars link Lenin's theory to contemporary Party discourse.
quoteEn: In the Lenin–Kautsky debate, Lenin held to the 'manufacturing' logic of revolutionary will, stressing that under special revolutionary conditions a powerful revolutionary will can be 'manufactured' in line with the historical situation.
quoteZh: 在列宁和考茨基的争论中，列宁坚持革命意志的“制造”逻辑，即强调在特殊的革命条件下，可以根据历史的形势“制造”出强大的革命意志的力量

glossary.explanation: The authors define it as a spiritual quality of the party and masses in a revolution: firm confidence in the revolutionary cause that can become a driving force. It is narrower than class consciousness because it concerns the process of overthrowing the old society and building a new one.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up. In the article it appears in the call to uphold and develop it in the new era.

Soviet Russia's emergency economic policies of 1918–21 during the civil war, including requisitioning and state control of production. The article debates whether they were a shortcut to socialism or a means of survival.
The authors' label for a reading of historical materialism that treats social development as dictated by economic conditions, leaving little room for human agency. They attribute it to Kautsky.

t: Financial hegemony and its effects in the light of Lenin's theory of imperialism
zh: 列宁帝国主义论视野下的金融霸权及其影响
paras: Prompted by the US Federal Reserve's rate rises and Western sanctions on Russia since 2022, which Xing Wenzeng says have caused currency collapses and debt crises in many developing countries, the article asks how financial hegemony became a tool for plundering global wealth and what deeper effects it has. Xing argues that its roots lie in Lenin's theory of imperialism, above all in the rule of finance capital and the financial oligarchy.

The article has four sections. It first sets out the institutional, military and technological foundations of present-day US financial hegemony. It then examines how the United States and its Western allies use it as a weapon of control and plunder, through financial sanctions, dollar hegemony and the engineering of crises abroad. The third section discusses how it sharpens capitalism's deeper contradictions, among developed countries and between the hegemon and developing ones. The last section turns to de-dollarisation and the case for a fairer international order. Evidence includes Russia, Sri Lanka, Egypt, Vietnam, South Korea and Latin America.

Xing's central move is to read Lenin's finance capital as the basis of hegemony. Banking and industrial capital merge, finance capital dominates, and a few states hold a special position over the rest. Since 1945, Xing says, this has been reinforced by financial monopoly, about 750 US military bases and technological control. The author cites the rising share of finance in US corporate profits and US stakes in major semiconductor firms. The second move applies Lenin's law of uneven development and his picture of a world split into a few usurer states and many debtor states. In Xing's account, the Fed alternates between easing and tightening to shift costs onto others, as with the Plaza Accord and Japan, pressure on the euro, and Asian and Latin American debt crises.
