Its open questions include the socialist direction of the 1970s revolutions, the form of African socialist democracy, the continent's political and economic unity, and the coming South African revolution. Read the original if you study African Marxism, Fanon and Cabral, or comparisons between Western Marxism and Third World revolutionary theory.
quoteEn: Classical African Marxism is not only a product of the African revolution; at the level of theorisation it is also an embodiment of the unity of theory and practice.
quoteZh: 经典非洲马克思主义不仅是非洲革命的产物，在理论化环节也是理论与实践统一的体现。

t: New developments in foreign eco-socialist research since the 2008 financial crisis
zh: 2008年金融危机以来国外生态社会主义研究新进展
paras: This is a literature review of foreign eco-socialist research over the decade and more since the 2008 financial crisis, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2023, no. 1). Gao and Huan argue that the crisis and the limited results of 'green capitalism' opened new room for eco-socialist theory. In their account, the field has since renewed its textual base, widened its theoretical schools and turned to concrete environmental problems. They present the survey as a first step to draw the attention of Chinese Marxist ecologists.

The review has three main sections. The first covers new readings of Marx and Engels, centred on Kohei Saito, Camilla Royle, Paul Blackledge and John Bellamy Foster. The second covers five schools that critique capitalism ecologically and propose alternatives: world-systems Marxism, radical socio-ecological transformation, post-development theory, democratic eco-socialism and Gramscian political ecology. The third covers 'red-green' analysis of labour-environmental movements, climate change, food security, biodiversity and the Anthropocene.

Gao and Huan describe Saito as using the MEGA2 edition and Marx's natural-science notebooks to reject the view of Marx as a 'Promethean' and to place the 'metabolic rift' at the centre of a late Marx's ecological critique. Among the schools, they single out Jason Moore's world-ecology, Ulrich Brand's critical political ecology, Latin American post-development thought, and the democratic eco-socialism of Michael Löwy and Hans Baer. The last of these rests on common ownership of the means of production and participatory democracy, and is partly a response to the shortcomings of Soviet-style socialism. They also report work on 'climate capitalism', on Vandana Shiva's defence of local agriculture against commodification, and on the Anthropocene and related terms such as the Capitalocene.

The authors conclude that the field has entered a new stage, marked by continuity with the textual work of Foster and Burkett and by a markedly wider scope. They hold that a global, cross-disciplinary eco-socialist movement is needed and that China should stay open to experience from elsewhere while continuing to build a modern socialist country in which humanity and nature coexist in harmony, and to build ecological civilization with Chinese characteristics. They also warn that many foreign 'green left' scholars lack a Marxist theoretical and methodological basis and are limited by their own social systems, so their views should be treated with caution. Read the original if you want a map of recent Western and Latin American eco-Marxist and eco-socialist authors and schools, seen through a Chinese Marxist lens.
quoteEn: Any theoretical expression that clings to simplistic slogans or to purely local experience will not help advance a 'red-green' transformative change whose common goal is to replace the capitalist system.
quoteZh: 任何偏执于简单化的口号结论或地域性经验的理论表达都无助于现实推进一场以资本主义制度替代为共同目标的“红绿”重塑性变革。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese official concept, promoted since the 2000s and written into Party and state documents, that makes environmental protection part of the country's overall development goals.
A concept drawn from Marx's remarks on the disruption of the metabolism between humans and nature under capitalism. Foster and Saito use it as a core idea of eco-Marxism.
The strategy of addressing environmental crises through markets, technology and corporate action within capitalism. Eco-socialists criticise it as inadequate.

t: New changes and characteristics of contemporary capitalism
zh: 当代资本主义的新变化及特点
source: People's Forum (Renmin Luntan), January 2023 (first issue), no. 752
paras: Tan Youzhi asks how contemporary capitalism has changed since the Second World War, and especially in the twenty-first century, and what those changes mean for its long-term fate. Citing Xi Jinping's call to study contemporary capitalism, the article argues that capitalism has gained new vitality from technological revolution while facing a rising tide of anti-globalisation. In Tan's reading, neither development alters its historical destiny of being replaced by socialism, though that replacement will be long and arduous.

The article has two parts. The first, on 'new changes', takes technological revolution and the course of globalisation as the two main forces shaping contemporary capitalism. It reviews the first three technological revolutions, from steam to electricity to atomic energy and computing, and links each to a stage of capitalist development. It then turns to the fourth, digital and intelligent, revolution. The second part, on 'characteristics', discusses the limits of capitalism's adaptive capacity and the slow pace of its replacement.

Tan argues that new technology has revived capitalism after the 2008 financial crisis by raising productivity and temporarily easing class conflict, citing Dan Schiller's notion of 'digital capitalism'. Globalisation, by contrast, has produced uneven gains, global problems and a backlash of unilateralism, populism and protectionism, which Tan says exposes the flaws of Western democracy. Drawing on Marx's 1859 Preface, Tan presents the 'two inevitables' (capitalism's demise and socialism's victory) as consistent with the 'two never wills' (no social formation perishes before its productive forces are exhausted). Capitalism still retains 'room for expansion'. But welfare and state intervention leave wage labour untouched, widen inequality, and sow new crises, and Tan describes capitalism as a 'dual' society, citing Michel Albert.

Tan concludes that capitalism is in transition towards socialism and is accumulating its material basis, yet will not collapse suddenly. Analysts should combine the 'inevitability' of its demise with the 'long-term' nature of the process, and avoid blind optimism. Tan also says the West still holds the upper hand overall but that 'the West declines, the East rises', and that capitalist powers, above all the United States, shift crises onto others and warrant vigilance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese international-relations scholar uses Marx's 'two inevitables' and 'two never wills' to frame contemporary capitalism and its prospects.
quoteEn: Contemporary capitalism, a tree that had withered, has been able to bud again in spring precisely because it has enjoyed, one after another, the dividends of a new round of technological revolution.
quoteZh: 当代资本主义这棵已枯之木，正是连续吃到了新一轮科技革命的时代红利，才得又逢春再萌新生。

glossary.explanation: Shorthand in Chinese Marxism for the Communist Manifesto thesis that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable.

Shorthand for Marx's 1859 Preface claims that no social formation perishes before its productive forces are exhausted, and no higher relations of production appear before their material conditions mature.
Term used in Chinese commentary for trends such as protectionism, decoupling and withdrawal from international bodies. It is not the same as the left-wing 'anti-globalisation movement'.

glossary.en: the West declines, the East rises
glossary.explanation: A slogan in Chinese official discourse describing a perceived shift of global economic and political weight from the West towards Asia, especially China.

t: The origins and evolution of Egyptian Marxist historiography in the twentieth century
zh: 20世纪埃及马克思主义史学的缘起与流变
paras: Zhao Yueqing takes up a field that, in the author's account, has received almost no attention in Chinese scholarship: Egyptian Marxist historiography. Chinese work has focused on Western and socialist-bloc cases or on the history of Egyptian communism, while foreign studies are said to lack systematic treatment and to show ideological bias. Drawing on Arabic sources and a historical-materialist method, Zhao argues that Egyptian Marxist historiography grew from Western socialist thought, classical Marxism and the Sinicization of Marxism. It developed distinctive theories, notably "dependency theory" and the "pseudo-Islam" thesis, that influenced global Marxist historiography.

The article traces the subject from the nineteenth century to the end of the twentieth. It first covers theoretical sources: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi and Saint-Simonian ideas, Salama Musa and Fabian socialism, the translation of classics by Henri Curiel's movement, Rifaat al-Said, and the reception of Mao Zedong's writings and of Samir Amin. It then follows three periods: the early stage from the October Revolution to the 1952 revolution; the Nasser era; and the post-Nasser period of infitah (economic opening) under Sadat and Mubarak. A final section assesses the value of this historiography and its limits.

Zhao's central claim is that each period shaped a different emphasis. Early historians used the left-wing press as their base and applied political economy to colonialism, with Fu'ad Mursi's 1949 study of capitalism and class struggle as the main example. Under Nasser, Zhao argues, historians merged Marxism with nationalism, adopted structural analysis, and professionalised through archives and institutions. After the 1970s, Amin's dependency theory enriched Marxist political economy, and Rifaat al-Said's "pseudo-Islam" thesis turned criticism towards religious extremism. Women historians such as Amina Shafiq also extended class analysis to gender. Zhao credits the tradition with building a Marxist vocabulary, a "history from below" focused on peasants and workers, and a broader range of fields.

Zhao also identifies limits. Party competition after the return of multi-party politics, the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood and the tension between religion and atheism constrained the tradition. Some historians, Zhao says, overstated economic determinism and neglected non-class factors. Zhao concludes that Egyptian Marxist historiography reflected its cultural and social setting, and that examining its gains and lessons can help the study of Middle Eastern historiography. Read the original if you work on Marxist historiography, Middle East intellectual history or Chinese scholarly views of Marxism in the Arab world, and want a detailed survey of Egyptian thinkers and their Arabic-language works.
quoteEn: Guided by a "history from below" outlook, Egyptian Marxist historians studied the lived experience of the lower strata while also attending to the historical development of the upper strata.
quoteZh: 埃及马克思主义史学家以一种“自下而上”的历史观念为指导，既研究社会下层的生活经历，也关注上层的历史发展。

glossary.explanation: The official idea that Marxism is adapted to Chinese conditions and developed through Chinese practice. Here the author treats it as an influence on Egyptian historians, who saw an alternative to Soviet and Western models.

A theory holding that peripheral countries' development is shaped by their subordinate position in the world capitalist economy. The author credits Samir Amin's 1974 book Unequal Development with a Marxist version of it.
Rifaat al-Said's 1996 thesis (al-Ta'aslim), which the author describes as rejecting the legitimacy of political Islam and as targeting the Muslim Brotherhood and religious extremism.
The 1952 coup by the Free Officers that ended the Egyptian monarchy. The author treats it as the dividing point between the early phase and the Nasser era.

t: Beyond "labelling": re-examining Europe's new radical parties
zh: 超越“标签化”——重新审视欧洲新激进主义政党
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2023 no. 5
paras: Xiang Zuotao and Gu Feng ask why European parties that traditional parties, mainstream media and many scholars brand "extreme", "xenophobic" or "populist" have won growing support since the 2008 financial crisis. Their thesis is that these labels reflect the bias of established forces. In the authors' account, the rise of the "new radical parties" results from the under-representation of lower- and middle-income groups in Western representative democracy.

The article covers a broad set of parties, including Fidesz in Hungary, the National Rally and La France Insoumise in France, Brothers of Italy, the Sweden Democrats, Podemos, Syriza, ANO 2011 and Alternative for Germany. It has four parts: the labels applied by traditional parties, media and Western academics; the parties' platforms on domestic politics, economy, society and foreign relations, along with their records in office; the social and geographical profile of their voters; and a short conclusion. It draws on 2022 election results and polling from France, Italy, Sweden, the Czech Republic and Hungary.

The authors argue first that the parties are an ideologically heterogeneous group. Their platforms are pragmatic: direct democracy and anti-corruption pledges, stronger state intervention in industry, agriculture and prices, welfare reform, restrictive positions on migration (with exceptions), and Euroscepticism of varying degrees. Their results in office are mixed. Hungary's Fidesz is presented as relatively successful, while Syriza and Italy's Five Star–League coalition are described as having been constrained. Second, they argue that the parties' supporters share a socio-economic position rather than a class ideology. These are blue-collar workers, farmers, the self-employed and the less educated, concentrated in economically declining regions and hurt by globalisation, austerity and the weakening of the nation-state. Their grievances are insecurity, with migrants seen as competitors, and the neglect of their material concerns by traditional parties.

The authors conclude that the parties largely follow existing electoral rules and do not aim at fundamental institutional replacement, so the "extreme" label is misplaced. They also say Western critics fail to link these parties to the inherent contradictions of capitalism. While noting that some proposals are utopian or treat only symptoms, they present the parties as an alternative response for the "disappointed" middle and lower strata. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic reading of European radical-right and radical-left parties, with country-level voter data, that challenges Western framings of populism.
quoteEn: The rise of the new radical parties reflects the insufficient representativeness of Western representative democracy.
quoteZh: 新激进主义政党的兴起反映了西方代议制民主的代表性不足。

t: Rebuilding the state's political system from society
st: The 1871 Paris Commune in the eyes of the communards
zh: 从社会出发重构国家政制
zhSub: 社员眼中的1871年巴黎公社
paras: Was the Paris Commune a new kind of state, or only a municipal revolt, a local self-government experiment or an anarchist negation of the state? Shan Chengxiu notes that Marx and his followers read the Commune as the embryo of a proletarian state, while Versailles, moderate republicans and Bakuninists portrayed it as "non-state". To settle the dispute, the article reconstructs how the communards themselves understood their project. It argues that they were concerned with the state throughout and tried to rebuild its political system starting from society.

The source base is the Commune's official gazette and the minutes of its sessions, supplemented by communards' later memoirs. The article first shows how the "commune" and the "republic" were equated in the Commune's own language. It then follows the changing powers of the Executive Commission up to the creation of the Committee of Public Safety, and the split of the Commune into majority and minority. It examines the Neo-Jacobin and Blanquist majority, and the Proudhonist minority, before a closing assessment.

Shan contends that the communards sought a "social republic" rather than municipal autonomy. Its social dimension appears in secularising decrees, anti-despotic democracy (universal suffrage, recall, capped officials' pay, mass associations) and measures restraining capital. The vote of late April 1871 on a Committee of Public Safety exposed two conceptions: for the majority, dictatorship was a transitional means to promote democracy, whether in the Jacobin tradition or Blanqui's "Parisian dictatorship". For the Proudhonist minority, communal sovereignty could not be surrendered, and the state could only be a bottom-up federation resting on mutual associations. Because the Commune lasted only 72 days, Shan says neither programme went beyond Paris and the Commune showed only a potential for a new state form.

In the conclusion, Shan holds that the communards' view contradicts both the municipalist reading and the anarchist reading. After defeat, survivors divided among radical republicans, Bakuninists, Blanquists and a small group turning to Marxism, while in the 1880s the labour movement stressed the Commune's socialist character. Shan sees in Commune democracy an early exploration of people's democracy: a composite democracy combining elections with consultation, whose dilemma over centralisation holds lessons for democratic centralism, and whose debate on dictatorship bears on the dictatorship of the proletariat. Read the original if you want a source-based study of the Commune's internal debates, with Chinese Marxist theory in view, on democracy, dictatorship and federalism.
quoteEn: The communards of 1871 were generally concerned with questions of the state, and, standing in the middle and lower strata, they sought to rebuild the state's political system starting from society.
quoteZh: 1871年的公社社员普遍关注国家议题，身处中下层的他们试图从社会出发重构国家政制。

glossary.explanation: The organisational principle of Leninist parties and of the Chinese state, combining democratic discussion and election with binding central decisions. The article treats the Commune's centralisation dilemma as relevant to it.

A Marxist term for working-class political rule in the transition to communism. Engels described the Commune as an example of it, and the article links it to the debate over dictatorship among the communards.
The term used in Chinese Communist discourse for a democracy of the working people, set against bourgeois representative democracy. The author uses it to characterise the Commune's early experiments.

t: The neo-fascist turn of neoliberal capitalism: roots and ways out
zh: 新自由资本主义的新法西斯主义转向：根源与出路
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 5
paras: Lu asks why neoliberal capitalism has turned towards neo-fascism and what could stop it. Drawing on Western left scholarship, the article argues that the root lies in neoliberalism's absolutisation of market and money power. Lu holds that Western left remedies resting on morality or ethics cannot answer this, and that an answer requires a return to, and going beyond, Hegel through historical materialism.

The article has three parts. The first describes the crisis of neoliberal capitalism through Foucault, Giroux, Jodi Dean, Byung-Chul Han, Wolin, Galbraith and others, and surveys scholars who link it to neo-fascism, including Cox, Foster, Robinson, Patnaik and Chomsky. The second reviews left proposals for alternatives: confrontation (Chomsky, Chibber), a renewed internationalism (Traverso, Alkin), a minimum programme (Foster), Hardt and Negri's commons, and moral or cultural renewal (Sweezy, Mason, Brown, Snyder). The third turns to Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Marx's critique of it, and the Chinese context.

Lu reports that, in these accounts, neoliberalism hollows out social bonds and democracy, subordinates the state to finance, and leaves unemployed people to channel resentment into identity politics. Lu argues that most left alternatives share neoliberalism's premise that state intervention is inherently authoritarian, and that moral appeals therefore remain utopian. In Lu's reading, Hegel already saw that civil society generates poverty and a resentful rabble, which Allen Wood treats as the mechanism behind fascism. Hegel's reliance on desire and private property also seeded the problem. Lu holds that Marx's notions of the positive essence and positive existence of the human being, together with free time, point beyond this.

Lu concludes that neo-fascism can be avoided only under the leadership of a Party and state that grasp historical necessity and draw on cultural resources that move people from their positive essence to their positive existence. Lu says this gives great significance to studying the spirit of Chinese civilisation, with its benevolence, people-centredness, good faith, justice, harmony and aspiration to great unity. Lu adds that Western left ethical proposals could be worth drawing on once a socialist revolution and communist party have prevailed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western left responses to neoliberalism and the far right, built around Hegel's theory of civil society.
quoteEn: Only under the leadership of a Party and state that understand historical necessity and the trend of social development, and that inherit and draw on all cultural and intellectual resources capable of guiding the human being's positive essence towards positive existence, is it possible to avoid the crises neoliberal capitalism provokes and its turn to neo-fascism.
quoteZh: 唯有在了解历史必然性和社会发展趋势的政党和国家的主导下，继承和借鉴一切可以引导人的积极本质向人的积极存在转换的文化和思想资源，才有避免新自由资本主义引发危机和向新法西斯主义转向的可能性。

glossary.zh: 人的积极本质与积极存在
glossary.pinyin: rén de jījí běnzhì yǔ jījí cúnzài
glossary.explanation: Categories the author draws from Marx's reading of Hegel. Positive essence refers to human material desire; positive existence refers to the free and all-round development of the person.
Marx's idea of time freed from compulsory labour and used for human development. The author treats it as the basis for overcoming domination by money and labour time.

t: The psychoanalytic critique of capitalism and its elements
zh: 资本主义的精神分析批判及其要素
orig: Psychotherapy and Politics International, vol. 20, nos. 1–2, 2022
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2023 no. 5
paras: This is a Chinese translation (abridged) of an article by Julien-François Gerber, a scholar at the International Institute of Social Studies in The Hague. Gerber notes that psychoanalysis has rarely been applied systematically to economic questions. The article seeks to organise scattered psychoanalytic work on capitalism into a single field of critique and to encourage dialogue across schools. It asks what the psychic foundations of capitalism are, why it holds so many people, and how people unconsciously shape and sustain the economy.

The article first sketches the history of the field. It starts with Freud's analogies between libido and money and the early analysts' studies of money and the 'anal character'. It then covers Edward Bernays and Ernest Dichter on the right, Otto Gross and Wilhelm Reich on the radical left, and the post-war work of the Frankfurt School, the Tavistock Institute and French post-structuralism. Finally it covers Lacanian and Jungian critiques since the 1980s. The main part offers a typology of four currents, each symbolised by a mythic figure.

Gerber's core move is this typology. Eros stands for repressed libido and resulting alienation (Reich, Marcuse, Deleuze and Guattari, Dejours, Rosa). Thanatos stands for compulsive repetition and the endless movement of desire. In the Lacanian account, capitalism exploits primordial loss and its superego now commands people to 'enjoy'. Ahriman stands for hedonistic will to power, centred on money and technology (Dufour, Harsch, Lietaer). Lucifer stands for narcissistic, rationalising arrogance, seen in Weisskopf's study of neoclassical economics and Fromm's 'monocerebral man'. Gerber adds that individuals both introject and project economic norms, which reinforces unjust systems.

Gerber suggests that each current fits a different social group: workers, consumers, the wealthy, and managers and economists. He identifies tensions among them over whether the superego represses or commands enjoyment, over whether alienation is universal or historical, and over whether desire should be released or restrained. He holds that the schools are not irreconcilable and calls for more dialogue, for attention to class, gender, race and non-Western contexts (Fanon, Nandy), and for use of under-exploited thinkers such as Klein and Winnicott. He argues that psychoanalysis can inform post-capitalist politics only alongside wider political, economic and ecological change. Read the original if you work on psychoanalysis and Marxism, Freudo-Marxism or Lacanian critiques of capitalism and want a mapped overview of the literature.
quoteEn: This article seeks to show that, in the study of capitalism, there are no insurmountable differences between the different schools of psychoanalytic thought.
quoteZh: 本文试图表明，在资本主义研究中，不同的精神分析思想流派之间并没有不可逾越的差异。

t: Basic experiences, main lessons and contemporary implications of a century of the communist movement in the United States
zh: 百年来美国共产主义运动的基本经验、主要教训及其当代启示
source: Journal of Liaocheng University (Social Sciences Edition), 2022 no. 6
paras: Li Dongming asks what a century of the communist movement in the United States, centred on the Communist Party USA (CPUSA, founded in 1919), can teach the present-day world socialist movement. The article argues that the movement's survival inside the heartland of capitalism rests on a few durable experiences, while its stagnation stems from identifiable errors, and that both yield lessons for communist parties in capitalist and socialist countries alike.

The article has three parts. It first sets out four basic experiences, then five main lessons, and finally two contemporary implications. Li's evidence is drawn mainly from the party's internal history: the two liquidation crises (under Earl Browder in the 1940s and after 1956 under the Gates group), factional struggles involving William Z. Foster, Jay Lovestone, Gus Hall and others, and the party's constitutions through to the 2014 revision.

On experience, Li credits the party with upholding Party leadership, holding firm to socialist and communist conviction, defending Marxism-Leninism against revisionism, and standing up to fight at critical moments. On lessons, Li identifies "Left" sectarianism, dogmatism and dependence on Moscow; overestimating the radicalism of the American working class; recurrent factional splits that weakened the organisation; a failure to understand American capitalism's capacity for self-adjustment and its cultural achievements; and a mishandled balance between democracy and centralism, including Hall's long tenure, an ageing membership and loose discipline in the 2014 constitution.

Li draws two implications. First, communists must distinguish the historical trend (the "two inevitables" of capitalism's replacement) from the actual situation, bearing in mind Marx's "two never" qualifications, and so avoid rash strategies. Second, Marxism must be applied creatively to national conditions without dogmatism and without diluting it in the name of localisation or American "exceptionalism". Li also cites Xi Jinping to argue that parties must not copy others' experience and must follow their own independent path. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of CPUSA history and the lessons it draws for the world socialist movement.
quoteEn: Whether a party can explore the socialist road independently, starting from its own country's concrete conditions rather than from the experience and conclusions of other countries' parties, is a problem every communist party must solve in practice.
quoteZh: 能否独立自主从本国具体国情出发而不是从别国党的经验和结论出发探索社会主义道路，是各国共产党在实践中必须要解决好的问题。

glossary.explanation: The claim that the United States is exempt from the general laws of capitalist development, so that socialism does not fit it. The article rejects the bourgeois version but also warns against over-emphasising national particularity.
The Marxist claim that capitalism will inevitably perish and socialism inevitably triumph. Chinese texts pair it with the "two never" (两个决不会) from Marx's 1859 Preface.

In Chinese Party vocabulary, an ultra-radical line that overestimates revolutionary conditions and refuses alliances with other forces. The article applies it to the CPUSA's early united-front policy.

t: The fascist culture of violence of neoliberalism and the way out
zh: 新自由主义的法西斯主义暴力文化和未来出路
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 5
paras: This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Canadian-American critical theorist Henry Giroux. It asks why cruelty and violence have become so visible and normalised in the contemporary United States. Giroux answers that the country has entered what he calls "neoliberal fascism": a new historical conjuncture in which neoliberalism, having lost its legitimacy, fuses with white supremacy, ultranationalism and a politics of disposability.

The article moves through five parts: cruelty as a core feature of fascist politics and its long history in the US; the return of fascism's spectre and the absence of any systemic analysis; neoliberalism as a stage of "gangster capitalism"; the near-complete militarization of American society; and a conclusion on resistance. Giroux draws on Etienne Balibar, Stuart Hall, Karl Polanyi, Hayek, Friedman, Paul Mason, David Harvey and others. His examples include mass shootings, attacks on transgender children, cuts to social safety nets, the military budget and right-wing extremist killings.

Giroux's central move is to read neoliberalism not as a break from fascism's heritage but as its enabling ground. In his account, a market ideology that treats society as nonexistent and freedom as market freedom strips away social responsibility and solidarity. Once it can no longer justify poverty and inequality, it turns to open racism and the dehumanization of people deemed surplus. He argues that the aestheticization of violence in media and entertainment normalises it and diverts attention from its systemic causes. Fragmented, issue-by-issue analysis by intellectuals and media, in his view, prevents people from seeing these connections.

Giroux concludes that voting alone is insufficient. He calls for mass collective resistance and sustained uprisings, and for a broad anti-capitalist movement guided by socialist democratic principles. In his view, capitalism is the "laboratory of fascism", so resistance must begin from abolition rather than reform, and he rejects ideas of compassionate capitalism. He also urges rebuilding critical mass consciousness, a multiracial progressive movement and radical political education. Read the original if you want a Western critical-left account of American politics as neoliberal fascism, as selected for a Chinese foreign-Marxism audience.
quoteEn: Capitalism is the laboratory of fascism, and any viable model of resistance must begin by calling for its abolition rather than its reform.
quoteZh: 资本主义是法西斯主义的实验室，任何可行的抵抗模式都必须从呼吁消除而非改革开始。

t: Lenin's critique of erroneous currents of thought on Russia's path of development
zh: 列宁在俄国发展道路问题上对错误思潮的批判
paras: Between the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the question "where is Russia heading?" divided Russian intellectuals. Wang Jinfen argues that its core was whether economically and culturally backward Russia should take the capitalist or the socialist road, and how socialism and capitalism should be related. The article contends that Lenin met a series of mistaken currents with systematic criticism, and that his arguments still matter under new historical conditions.

The article is organised chronologically around four targets. Before 1917 these were Narodnik (populist) "non-capitalist road" theory and the "legal Marxism" of Struve, which treated capitalism as eternal. After the October Revolution came the "historical catastrophe", "premature birth" and "economic determinism" charges of Plekhanov, Kautsky and Sukhanov. Last came the "petty-bourgeois reformism" and "petty-bourgeois revolutionism" aroused by the New Economic Policy (NEP).

Wang's first move is that Lenin rejected both utopian bypassing of capitalism and its glorification. Narodnism, in Lenin's view, expressed small producers' interests and ignored that socialism presupposes developed productive forces and a proletariat. Legal Marxism concealed capitalism's contradictions, which Lenin said prove its historical transience. Hence Russia must both use capitalism and move beyond it. Second, against Plekhanov and others, Lenin accepted that Russia lacked the economic preconditions but denied this barred revolution. Wang reads this as "revolutionary dialectics": a country can seize power first and then create the cultural and material conditions for socialism, an approach different from Western modernization. Third, on the NEP, Lenin opposed those who abstractly set capitalism against socialism, arguing that in a small-peasant country state capitalism is an intermediate link. He also warned against the Change-of-Landmarks group, who expected the NEP to restore capitalism.

Wang concludes that Lenin's central lesson is how a backward country that has chosen socialism treats capitalism. It must make use of capitalism while the Party keeps socialist direction. In Wang's reading, this depends on Communists learning to harness capital and delivering results that persuade the people the new order is better than the old. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Lenin's polemics on Russia's development path, along with the Chinese scholarly framing of their contemporary relevance.
quoteEn: The disagreement between Lenin and Plekhanov and others lay not in whether economically and culturally backward Russia possessed the civilisational preconditions for socialism, but in whether such a Russia could carry out a socialist revolution and build socialism.
quoteZh: 列宁和普列汉诺夫等人的分歧，并不在于经济文化落后的俄国是否具备实现社会主义所需要的文明前提，而在于这样的俄国能不能进行社会主义革命和建设社会主义？

glossary.explanation: The policy adopted by the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1921, replacing grain requisitioning with a tax in kind and permitting limited market relations and private trade.
Lenin's label for Struve and others who used Marxist arguments in tsarist-approved publications to defend capitalism's necessity and permanence.
The Russian movement (Herzen, Chernyshevsky, Danielson) that hoped to reach socialism through the peasant village commune without passing through capitalism.
Émigré and domestic intellectuals who backed Soviet power in the 1920s because they believed the NEP would lead Russia back to an ordinary bourgeois state.
In Lenin's NEP-era usage, capitalism operating under proletarian state control, seen as an intermediate link between small production and socialism.

t: Why the Australian Labor Party won the 2022 election: causes and assessment
zh: 2022年澳大利亚工党胜选的原因及评析
paras: Dong Muxi asks why the Australian Labor Party (ALP), a centre-left force within the capitalist framework, returned to government in the May 2022 federal election after nine years in opposition, defeating the Liberal–National Coalition and installing Anthony Albanese as prime minister. The article argues that the win rested on changed external conditions and on internal adjustments by the party, but was a limited return that leaves Labor facing serious difficulties.

The article has three parts. The first treats external factors since the 2008 financial crisis: widening inequality, a revival of class consciousness among wage earners, and the relative decline of the Coalition. The second covers internal factors: a leftward shift in policy, a drive to recruit members and widen intra-party democracy, and the reshaping of the leader's image. The third assesses the victory, setting out its limits and the party's future challenges, and a short conclusion places the result in the wider Western context.

Dong contends that the crisis dissolved middle-class illusions among white-collar workers, moving the class structure from an 'olive' towards a 'dumbbell' shape and pushing voters leftward. Under Bill Shorten and Albanese, Labor moved away from the neoliberal 'Third Way' towards opposing economic inequality, a more inclusive Indigenous and multicultural policy, and stronger climate commitments. Dong then argues that the return is limited in three ways: Labor's primary vote (32.58%) was a record low and the win depended on preferential voting; its leftward turn is a pragmatic, limited adjustment that mainly criticises neoliberalism without a new social-democratic discourse; and its 77 of 151 seats leave it constrained by crossbenchers.

Dong concludes that Labor's future depends on defining its position between class loyalty and a broader coalition, overcoming a theoretical bottleneck, and escaping policy constraints under a continuing capitalist structural crisis, with high public debt already forcing compromises such as retaining tax cuts for high earners. As a reformist party, Labor's capacity to break through remains, in Dong's view, highly uncertain, and the wider decline of Western social democracy has not been reversed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-oriented assessment of contemporary Australian social democracy, with figures on votes, seats and policy pledges.
quoteEn: Its leftward turn in ideology is a limited adjustment with a distinctly pragmatic character.
quoteZh: 其在意识形态上的左转是具有鲜明实用主义色彩的有限调整。

glossary.explanation: A centre-left political approach of the 1990s, associated with Tony Blair's Labour Party, that accepted market-oriented policies while claiming to go beyond both old social democracy and neoliberalism. The article treats Australian Labor's adoption of it as a compromise with neoliberalism.
Australia's system in which voters rank candidates and lower preferences are transferred, which the article says favours the two traditional major parties.

t: Returning to the economic context: how East European neo-Marxism supplements humanist readings of Marx
zh: 回归经济学语境：东欧新马克思主义对马克思人道主义解读视角的补充
paras: Du Hongyan asks how East European neo-Marxism read Marx's humanism from within his economic writings rather than from philosophy alone. The article argues that these thinkers supplemented the humanist interpretations of Western Marxism by returning to the context of political economy. Doing so, in Du's account, countered both the economic determinism of Soviet Marxism and the abstract humanism of Western humanist currents.

The article has four parts. It first sets out why a return to economics is needed. It then examines the "super-economic" character the East European thinkers found in Marx's economic work. Next it shows how they developed Marx's critique of "economic man" against economism in East European socialism. A final section assesses their contribution. Du draws mainly on Petrović, Kosík, Adam Schaff, Márkus and Marković, and on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Grundrisse and Capital.

Du's central claim is that Marx completed his study of the "real human being" in economics, by analysing the alienated relation between people and production. In Marx's formula, in antiquity "man appears as the purpose of production", whereas under capitalism production and wealth become the end. Schaff criticises existentialism for an asocial, ahistorical individual, and criticises ethical-humanist readings of the early Marx for discarding scientific socialism. Petrović reads Marx's economics as a critique, whose point is that humans are free, creative practical beings and not "economic animals". Marković and Kosík extend the critique of "economic man" to economism in East European socialism and to the world of pseudo-concreteness. Du adds that Schaff took the Grundrisse as evidence against Althusser's thesis of a break in Marx's thought.

Du concludes that the East European approach offers a case for the continuity of Marx's thought. It also moves beyond economic determinism, since Marx's historical determinism leaves room for human choice among real possibilities. The thinkers applied this to argue that East European socialism had not overcome the condition in which production is the human end, and they called for its humanisation. Du presents rereading Marx to analyse existing society as an important paradigm of Marxism outside China. Read the original if you study Marxism outside China, the debates over the young and mature Marx, or the Yugoslav Praxis school and its Polish and Czech counterparts.
quoteEn: By returning to the economic context, East European neo-Marxism confirmed that Marx did not deny human subjectivity in social development, and thoroughly refuted the economic-determinist reading of Marx.
quoteZh: 东欧新马克思主义回到经济学语境中确证了马克思并不否定人在社会发展中的主体性，彻底驳斥了对马克思经济决定论理解。

glossary.explanation: A label for the humanist, critical Marxist currents in Yugoslavia, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary in the mid-twentieth century, including the Praxis school. They criticised Stalinist orthodoxy from within Marxism.
The tradition associated with Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School, which stresses philosophy, culture and the human subject.
The article's term for the claim that Marx's economic works are critiques of economics whose real concern is the human being. They are not treated as pure economic science.
The classical political economy assumption of a rational individual maximising self-interest. Marx criticised it as an abstraction from capitalist relations.
Marx's term for historically situated people engaged in material production, set against abstract conceptions of the human.

t: The environmental politics of the Communist Party USA since the 21st century: theory, policy and action
zh: 21世纪以来美国共产党的环境政治：理论、政策与行动
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2023 no. 5
paras: Gao Ze asks how the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) has approached environmental questions since the turn of the century, a topic the author says Chinese scholarship has neglected. The article argues that the party has built a distinctive radical-left environmental politics that joins Marxist theory to practical campaigning. In Gao's reading, this has given the CPUSA a visibility in the American left that exceeds its small size.

The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. The first reconstructs the party's theoretical work, the second sets out its policy positions, and the third describes its forms of action. Gao draws on figures such as John Bachtel, Mark Brodine, Anita Waters and Donald Donato, on the party's 31st National Convention report, and on its 2008 global warming report.

On theory, Gao says CPUSA writers return to Marx and Engels, especially dialectical materialism and the idea of a metabolic rift. They treat capitalism as the root of ecological crisis, so that only systemic change, not reform, can resolve it. They frame the crisis as a 'planetary emergency' and propose the notion of 'working-class environmentalism', which keeps the working class as the key agent of change. On policy, the slogan 'people and planet before profit' leads the party to give qualified support to the Green New Deal, while pressing for workers' voice in it. It also defends marginalised communities against environmental racism and calls for green technology transfer to developing countries. In action, the party joins climate marches and strikes, publishes reports, runs Marxist education, and backs international cooperation.

Gao concludes that the party's theory serves its movement work, that it influences public opinion more than policy, and that it combines American environmentalist currents with a global critique of capitalism. The article also notes the party's praise for China's ecological civilization, and Bachtel's view of the Communist Party of China as a model. Gao calls for closer cooperation among Marxist parties worldwide on global ecological governance and on building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how a Western communist party frames climate politics, and how that account links to Chinese ecological discourse.
quoteEn: Although the CPUSA does not yet have the strength to directly influence the planning and decision-making of American environmental policy, it has a distinctive advantage in shaping the public's environmental awareness through public opinion.
quoteZh: 美共虽尚不具备直接影响美国环境政策规划与决策的实力，但它在通过舆论影响公众环境认知方面具有独特优势

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global governance concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13. It calls for shared responsibility among states on development, security and the environment.
A Chinese official goal, written into Party and state documents, of integrating environmental protection into economic and social development.

t: The Party of Labour of Austria's exploration of the road of socialist revolution
zh: 奥地利劳动党对社会主义革命道路的探索
paras: Wang Ximan and Xue Lijun examine the theory and practice of socialist revolution developed by the Party of Labour of Austria (PdA), the country's only party guided by Marxism-Leninism, in its first decade. The party was founded in 2013 out of a split from the Communist Party of Austria, whose turn to democratic socialism and entry into the European Left Party some members rejected. The authors argue that the PdA has built a distinctive revolutionary theory and made modest gains, but that its youth, weakness and limited grasp of national conditions leave theory and practice poorly connected.

The article has four parts. It first traces the theory through the party's five congresses (2013–2022) and the conditions behind it: the contemporary era and changes in capitalism, Austria's economic and political situation, and a revolutionary tradition running from the Austromarxists to the 1980s slogan of 'socialism in Austrian colours'. It then sets out seven strands of the theory, describes party-building, parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle and international work, and closes with an assessment.

In the authors' account, the PdA holds that the present era remains one of transition from capitalism to socialism and that contemporary capitalism is imperialism, bringing destruction and war. Austria is described as a subordinate member of the imperialist pyramid with a weakened bourgeois ruling system. The party rejects democratic socialism and reformism, and takes the core of revolution to be the political power of the organised working class and socialisation of the means of production. Its programme has three planks: nationalised production, democratised decision-making and class solidarity. It also calls for an anti-monopoly alliance, combines parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, and envisages a planned economy in a future society.

In practice, the authors report, the PdA has set up regional organisations, a youth front and its own press, won a seat on a municipal council in Lower Austria in 2020, and built ties with communist parties abroad. They judge its progress to be real: it continues the revolutionary tradition, adapts Marxism to Austria and opposes imperialism and monopoly. They also list its problems: fewer than a thousand members, scarce funds, harsh criticism of other left parties, and positions against the EU and the market economy that have little appeal. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-scholarly account of a small European communist party's programme and organisation, with the authors' evaluation of it.
quoteEn: The Party of Labour of Austria is young, weak in strength and lacking in experience of struggle.
quoteZh: 奥地利劳动党年轻、力量薄弱且斗争经验不足。

glossary.explanation: The reformist social-democratic current that seeks socialism through parliamentary and gradual means. In this article it is treated as a reformist path that the PdA rejects.

glossary.zh: 奥地利色彩的社会主义
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Communist Party of Austria in the 1980s calling for a socialism fitted to Austrian conditions. The authors see the PdA's theory as its creative continuation.

t: Basic practices of the Communist Party of Vietnam in Party political building since Đổi Mới
zh: 革新以来越南共产党党的政治建设的基本做法
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2023 no. 5
paras: Yan Jiehua and Zhang Shengjie ask how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) has carried out Party political building since the start of reform (Đổi Mới, 'renovation') 37 years ago. They argue that the CPV has gradually placed political building first among its Party-building tasks, using it to lead ideological, moral, organisational and cadre building, and that this has raised its leadership and governing capacity. They present the experience as a reference for Marxist ruling parties.

The article is organised around five areas of practice, followed by a conclusion on remaining problems. These are: setting the political direction and keeping the Party's working-class character; holding a 'people-based' political stance; anticipating political risks and strengthening political resolve; raising cadres' political capacity; and reshaping the political ecology. The authors draw on CPV congress documents (from the Sixth in 1986 to the Thirteenth in 2021), plenum resolutions and regulations, and statistics on training and discipline.

On direction, the authors report that the CPV drew from the Soviet and East European collapse the lesson that the failure was of a dogmatic model, not of socialism. It set out 'five basic principles' in 1989 and 'five adherences' in 2021. On the people, the authors describe the formula 'people as centre and subject' and the aim of unifying the 'Party's will' with 'the people's hearts', including public consultation on congress drafts and stronger grassroots organisations. On risks and cadres, they describe policy research bodies, lists of manifestations of 'self-evolution' and 'self-transformation', a four-tier Party school system, quantified cadre evaluation, rotation of posts, and protection for 'six-dare' cadres. On discipline, they cite 2012–2022 figures, including some 168,000 disciplined members, and anti-corruption law revisions.

The authors conclude that political building has unified Party thinking, curbed unhealthy tendencies, strengthened ties with the people and consolidated the CPV's ruling position. They identify four continuing problems: weak translation of Party decisions into policy ('hot above, cold below'); persistent 'self-evolution' and formalism; the long task of developing 'six-dare' cadres; and an incomplete system of hard rules lacking 'soft' cultural constraints. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based Chinese account of Vietnamese Party-building policies, with figures and regulation numbers, for comparison with Chinese Party-building discourse.
quoteEn: The CPV has always been a party of the working class, and this is integral to upholding the correct socialist direction in Vietnam.
quoteZh: 越共始终是工人阶级的政党，这是坚持越南社会主义正确方向的应有之义。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Party-building discourse covering political direction, stance, discipline and capacity. Chinese authors apply it to the CPV, which has used similar wording.
The reform policy launched by the CPV at its Sixth Congress in 1986, introducing a market economy under Party leadership.
CPV terms for officials' internal political and ideological degeneration, paired with the 'peaceful evolution' it attributes to Western pressure.

glossary.literal: cadres who dare in six ways
glossary.explanation: A CPV ideal of officials who dare to think, speak, act, take responsibility, innovate and face difficulty for the public good.

t: Reflections on Xi Jinping's important speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development
zh: 对习近平在文化传承发展座谈会上重要讲话的若干思考
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by Marco Rizzo and Alberto Lombardo of the Communist Party (Italy), responding to Xi Jinping's remarks of 2 June 2023 at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Xi called for building a modern Chinese civilization and a cultural powerhouse. The authors read this as a prompt for Western communists to reflect on the state of capitalist civilization and on Italy's position. They argue that Chinese modernization, which balances material and spiritual civilization, stands in sharp contrast to a degenerating West.

The commentary has five sections. It contrasts the coordinated development of modern Chinese civilization with Western decline, and China's intellectual independence with the subordination of Italy and Europe. It then compares China's openness with Western narrowness, presents multipolarity as the direction shown by Chinese civilization, and ends with China's stress on harmony and peace in the face of US policy. Italian history, NATO, the Belt and Road Initiative and Africa serve as the main cases.

The authors take Xi's five features of Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) and read them as the basic principles of a multipolar order. They set this against a US-led unipolarity that they describe as imperialist, marked by double standards, war, financialization and cultural homogenization. In their account, bourgeois nationalism and cosmopolitanism are two complementary faces of class rule, opposed by internationalism and patriotism of the oppressed. They argue that Italy has lacked independent choice since the Cold War, citing US bases and Washington's pressure over its Belt and Road memorandum and trade with Russia. They hold that China's self-reliant path, lifting about 800 million people out of absolute poverty, shows what independence makes possible.

The authors conclude that modern Chinese civilization, under Communist Party leadership and Marxist guidance, can contribute more to a world in which countries are guided rather than dominated. They call China the strongest bulwark against Western imperialist aggression and hope that Italians and Europeans will take up Xi's call for spiritual independence. The text is openly polemical and partisan in its characterisation of the United States and Europe. Read the original if you want to see how a European communist party leadership interprets Xi Jinping's cultural policy and China's international role.
quoteEn: Multipolarism shows the world a direction; it does not control or rule the world.
quoteZh: 多极主义是给世界指明方向，而不是掌控或统治这个世界。

glossary.explanation: Official Party concept of a distinct path of modernization led by the Communist Party, which stresses the coordination of material and cultural-ethical progress. It was elaborated especially after the 20th Party Congress (2022).
China's international infrastructure and trade initiative, launched by Xi Jinping in 2013. Italy signed a memorandum of understanding on it in 2019.

t: A century of British communist parties: historical evolution and the causes of decline
zh: 百年英国共产主义政党历史演变与衰败的原因分析
paras: Why have British communist parties remained split and marginal for a century? Song Xiongwei takes up this question, arguing that existing Chinese-language studies stress external shocks (the dissolution of the Comintern, Soviet actions, the Khrushchev "secret speech", the Sino-Soviet split) and neglect internal causes. The article contends that decline stemmed chiefly from ideological wavering, lack of independence from Moscow and organisational slackness.

The article first reconstructs the lineage of British communist organisations, which existing studies often conflate. It follows the Communist Party of Great Britain (CPGB) from its founding in 1920, through its wartime peak of over 56,000 members, to the 1956 exodus, the Maoist, Trotskyist and Eurocommunist splits, the 1988 founding of the Communist Party of Britain, and the CPGB's 1991 reorganisation as Democratic Left. It then offers six internal explanations and ends with lessons for the Chinese Communist Party.

Song's core claim is that the CPGB was formed in 1920 largely under Soviet pressure, without resolving deep ideological disagreement, notably over parliamentary participation. Song then argues that the party repeatedly negated its own line: documents of 1944 and 1951 pursued socialism by parliamentary means, Eurocommunism undermined the dictatorship of the proletariat and democratic centralism, and in 1990–91 the party abandoned Marxism-Leninism. Song adds that pro-Soviet factions dependent on Soviet funding hardened, that sectarian expulsions bred rival groups (over 70 Trotskyist bodies), that its programme resembled the Labour Party's, and that lax discipline and loose membership left weak branches.

Song concludes that wavering in the ideological sphere, absence of independence and a disorganised structure cost these parties public support. Drawing on this history, Song calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position in ideology, strengthening the Chinese Communist Party's overall leadership and the authority of the Central Committee, unifying thinking through the Party's innovative theory, tightening organisation and building a high-calibre cadre corps. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school account of the fragmentation of British communist organisations and how Chinese scholars draw governing-party lessons from it.
quoteEn: British communist parties long accepted Soviet funding and obeyed Soviet instructions, which hardened the pro-Soviet factions within the parties into a stable vested-interest group.
quoteZh: 英国共产主义政党长期接受苏联的资助，服从苏联的指示，使得党内的亲苏派系高度固化，形成了稳定的既得利益集团。

glossary.explanation: The Leninist organisational principle, also used by the Chinese Communist Party, combining discussion with binding discipline and subordination of lower bodies to higher ones. The article treats its abandonment as a mark of the CPGB's decline.

A current in Western European communist parties from the 1970s that sought paths to socialism independent of the Soviet model. The article says it weakened the dictatorship of the proletariat and democratic centralism in the CPGB.
A Marxist-Leninist concept for working-class political rule in the transition from capitalism. The article presents its abandonment as revisionism.

t: The "war without end" of contemporary imperialism and its inner logic
zh: 当代帝国主义的无限战争及其内在逻辑
source: Journal of Hubei University (Philosophy and Social Science Edition), 2023 no. 5
paras: Kong Ming'an and Chen Yu ask why the dominant war form of contemporary imperialism has shifted from territorial colonial war to what Ellen Meiksins Wood called "war without end", and what drives it. Drawing on Wood and Slavoj Žižek, they argue that this war mode is a ghost-like, open-ended form of objective violence that remains bound to the logic of capital. Published in the Journal of Hubei University in 2023, the article is a work of foreign Marxism studies.

The article has five parts. It first sets out four dimensions in which war without end is "unlimited": duration, military purpose, means and spatial reach. It then reads the concept through Žižek's idea of the ghost, and classifies its violence using Žižek's typology of subjective, objective and symbolic violence. The fourth part ties it to capital logic by way of Lacan's object a, and a short conclusion follows. The authors use the post-1945 United States as their main case, with the Iraq and Afghanistan wars as examples.

The authors contend that, once the costs of holding colonies became prohibitive, imperialism detached war from specific military goals while keeping a clear political aim, namely global hegemony. In their account the resulting war is ghostly: it persists, shifts shape, threatens unlimited destruction and is presented as justice while serving capital's interests. Its violence is objective, systemic and anonymous, in the sense of Žižek, and of Hardt and Negri's "Empire", rather than the act of individual rulers. The authors then argue, with Žižek, that capital now works like Lacan's object a, becoming invisible through finance and digital money. They cite figures on US military spending to show that war and capital reinforce each other, and they say this fits Marx's political economy and Lenin's view of imperialism as moribund capitalism.

The authors conclude that war without end is driven and served by imperial capital, so it can be eliminated only by overthrowing the capitalist system, as Lenin held. They add that opposing imperialist hegemonic logic, in order to safeguard world peace and build a community with a shared future for mankind, is a new task of the age. Read the original if you study Marxist theories of imperialism, Žižek or Wood, or want to see how Chinese scholars combine psychoanalytic concepts with Leninist analysis of contemporary war.
quoteEn: War without end essentially belongs to the category of objective violence in Žižek's sense, and its persistence and operation are by no means the result of the momentary evil intent of a few individuals.
quoteZh: 无限战争本质上从属于齐泽克意义上客观暴力的范畴，其存续和运作绝不仅仅是少数个体的一时歹念所致

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since about 2013, calling for shared security, development and governance among nations.

t: The "anti-ecological" nature of eco-capitalism: a critique from Marxist political economy
zh: 生态资本主义的“反生态性”——基于马克思主义政治经济学批判视角
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2023 no. 4
paras: Li Weiran asks whether eco-capitalism, the mainstream Western approach to environmental problems in developed capitalist countries, can solve those problems. Li argues from a Marxist standpoint that it cannot. In Li's account it overlooks the real source of ecological problems, which is the mode of production and the social system tied to it, and the capitalist system's logic is by nature "anti-ecological".

The article has three parts. The first sets out the two schools of eco-capitalism: eco-market-ism, which relies on free markets and price mechanisms, and eco-Keynesianism, which relies on state planning and macro-regulation. The second offers a political-economy critique of the "anti-ecological" character of capitalism. The third turns to public ownership as the basis for solving ecological problems and to the Chinese case.

In Li's reading, eco-market-ism turns ecological resources into commodities through eco-tax reform and tradable pollution permits. Eco-Keynesianism criticises this as a "fallacy of composition" and calls for state-led ecological investment and eco-friendly technology. Li treats both as reformist strategies within capitalism. Drawing on Marx, Michael Löwy and John Bellamy Foster, Li locates the anti-ecological character in three features of capitalist logic: expansion ("grow or die"), profit-seeking (production for exchange-value and money) and short-sightedness. Private ownership of the means of production, Li adds, splits humanity from nature and pushes environmental costs onto developing countries. Eco-capitalism therefore only gives capitalism a "green coat" and can at most ease problems, not cure them.

Li concludes that socialism has advantages in value orientation ("people-centred" rather than value-expansion), institutional basis (public ownership) and economic system (a socialist market economy in which government plans and regulates). On China's own environmental problems, Li attributes them to extensive growth, to exploring a market economy without precedent, and to pollution transfer from developed countries, not to public ownership. Li notes that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and so calls for guiding capital, helping it shift from industrial to ecological capital, on a path of socialist ecological civilisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar classifies and criticises Western eco-capitalist theories and links the critique to China's ecological civilisation policy.
quoteEn: The growth of ecological problems and the expansion of capital's self-valorisation are two sides of one coin and go hand in hand; wherever capital expands across the globe, it inevitably gives rise to ecological problems.
quoteZh: 生态问题的增加与资本增殖的扩张是一体两面、相伴相生的；只要资本在全球进行扩张，所到之处必然会引发生态问题。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy concept for a model of development that integrates environmental protection into economic, political and social life. It has been part of Party documents since the 2000s and was elevated under Xi Jinping.
The official judgement that China is still at an early, long-lasting stage of socialism with underdeveloped productive forces. It justifies a market economy and a role for non-public ownership.
The official name for China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market allocation of resources with public ownership as the mainstay and state macro-regulation.

glossary.literal: taking the people as the centre
glossary.explanation: A guiding principle of Party discourse, particularly under Xi Jinping, holding that development should serve the people's interests and wellbeing.

t: The Communist Party of Argentina's exploration of the road to socialism and an assessment of it
zh: 阿根廷共产党对社会主义道路的探索及对其评析
paras: Li and Ding examine a century of the Communist Party of Argentina (the first communist organisation in Latin America) and its search for a road to socialism. They argue that the party's exploration has not succeeded. In their view this is a common fate of non-governing communist parties in developing countries, whose root cause is that the subjective and objective conditions for socialism are not yet in place.

The article divides the party's history into three stages: the revolutionary struggle period (1918–1945), the stage of peaceful struggle (1945–1990), and the period of transition and adjustment from 1990 to the present. It then identifies five features of the party's approach: peaceful transition through parliament, the pursuit of democracy and anti-dependence politics, united fronts, economic struggles for workers' basic rights, and ties with left forces in the region. A final section offers an assessment and outlook.

In the authors' account, the early party relied on class struggle, strikes and trade unions, but was repeatedly repressed and spent long periods as an illegal organisation. After 1945 it turned to parliamentary and legal means, and since the 1990s it has run in electoral coalitions led by the Justicialist (Peronist) Party. It won only a handful of seats and, the authors say, remains a marginal participant rather than a leader of fronts. Li and Ding give four reasons for its limited results: harsh conditions of survival; dependence on the Justicialist Party, which in their view merely uses the communists against the right; strong influence from outside socialist movements, which produced shifts and reversals; and internal weaknesses, including four major splits in the second half of the twentieth century and a membership that fell from nearly 200,000 in the early 1980s to 170,000 in 2021.

The authors expect the party to remain a political force in Argentina and a member of the Latin American left, but to stay a small party for a long time. They conclude that its search for a socialist road is still unfinished, with a long road ahead. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of Latin American communist parties and of the limits facing non-governing communist parties in developing countries.
quoteEn: On the whole, the Argentine Communist Party's exploration of socialism has not succeeded. This is a common phenomenon among non-governing communist parties in developing countries, and the fundamental reason is that the subjective and objective conditions for achieving socialism in those countries are not yet in place.
quoteZh: 总体说来，阿共对社会主义的探索并未取得成功，这是发展中国家非执政的共产党面临的普遍现象，根本原因在于在这些国家实现社会主义的主客观条件尚不具备。

t: The development of the Communist Party USA since its 30th National Convention and its prospects
zh: 美国共产党三十大以来的发展图景与前景探析
source: Journal of Liaocheng University (Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 2
paras: Li Haiyu and Feng Xiaoxu ask how the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) has developed since its 30th National Convention in June 2014 and what lies ahead for it. They treat that convention as a turning point. It replaced the leadership of Sam Webb, who had urged abandoning Leninism, democratic centralism and the vanguard party and changing the party's name. The authors argue that the new leadership corrected this rightward line and that the party has since grown, though favourable conditions are offset by serious weaknesses.

The article has three parts. The first surveys CPUSA's development in five areas: party building, revised ideas about capitalism and socialism, opposition to the far right, assessment of the Biden administration, and involvement in strikes and anti-racist movements. The second sets out opportunities, namely continuing systemic crisis in the United States, a revival of socialist sentiment, and the revitalisation of world socialism. The third sets out challenges, both internal and external.

On party building, the authors report that the party kept its name, reaffirmed Leninism and democratic centralism, expanded Marxist education and local clubs, and grew from about 5,000 members in 2018 to roughly 11,000. They describe the opportunities through inequality figures, political polarisation, racial injustice and the pandemic, and through polling and election results showing wider interest in socialism, including the growth of the Democratic Socialists of America. The challenges include a small membership, financial strain, loosened admission rules, and disputes before the 31st Convention (2019) over Black self-determination and a revived Communist International. The authors also cite persistent anti-communist prejudice, a far right that remains strong, and weak class consciousness among American workers.

The authors conclude that CPUSA's influence among young people, who lack Cold War memories, will probably grow, and that its marginal position may ease somewhat. Its challenges, however, mean no fundamental change or breakthrough in the short term, and its effect on mainstream politics should be rationally assessed. They call for further localisation of Marxism, steady accumulation of strength, spreading of ideas, worker mobilisation and patience. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-academic account of CPUSA's post-2014 organisation, strategy and membership data, including its internal disputes.
quoteEn: The real challenges CPUSA faces mean that in the short term it can hardly change its own situation fundamentally, its struggles are unlikely to achieve breakthroughs, and its influence on mainstream American politics must be rationally assessed.
quoteZh: 美共所面临的现实挑战决定了它在短期内难以从根本上改变自身的状况，所开展的斗争难以取得突破性进展，对美国主流政治的影响也须被理性期待。

t: "The scar of democracy": critical theory's critical response to the New Right
zh: “民主的伤疤”：批判理论对新右翼的批判性回应
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2023 no. 4
paras: Li Li and Zhou Aimin start from Ralf Dahrendorf's 1997 forecast that the twenty-first century might be an authoritarian one. They ask where the contemporary New Right comes from, what drives it and why it attracts support. Their thesis is that the Frankfurt School's critical theory, early and contemporary, offers important intellectual resources for answering these questions.

The article has three main parts. The first traces the New Right in the United States, from Barry Goldwater in 1964 through Nixon, Reagan, the post-Cold War break-up of "fusionism" and Trump. It then traces the European New Right, from Alain de Benoist's 1968 research group to the electoral successes of parties such as Fidesz, the AfD, Vox and the Sweden Democrats. The second part examines early critical theory (Horkheimer, Adorno, Löwenthal, Fromm and others), and the third examines Habermas and his successors.

Drawing on early critical theory, the authors identify three levels of explanation. At the level of society, fascism and the far right are products of conditions that advanced capitalism generates, such as capital concentration, the "declassing" of the bourgeoisie and the threat of technological unemployment. At the level of the individual, studies such as Studies on Authority and the Family and The Authoritarian Personality treat authoritarian character as a product of social structure, not of nature. At the level of propaganda, agitation works on unconscious mechanisms through stereotyping, personalisation and ritual. The authors then turn to Habermas's legitimation-crisis theory. In this reading the New Right is a defensive reaction to the political system's loss of capacity under financialised globalisation, and Habermas treats its prejudices as symptoms and not as the underlying disease. He therefore urges "de-thematisation" of the right's agenda and supranational, EU-level cooperation to politically shape economic globalisation.

The authors conclude that, in the critical-theory tradition, the danger of the New Right lies in the fact that it grows out of Western democracy itself. In Adorno's phrase it is a "scar of democracy". Opposing it therefore requires examining the inner contradictions of Western democratic politics, including inequality, exploitation and mechanisms that exclude minorities and migrants. They call for critical absorption and transformation of these ideas in order to respond to the changes in international politics that the New Right's rise has caused. Read the original if you want a compact survey of how Frankfurt School thinkers from Adorno to Habermas are being mobilised to explain the contemporary Western far right, as seen from Chinese academic debate.
quoteEn: Critical theory stresses that the danger of the New Right lies not merely in its direct opposition to Western democracy, but in the fact that it always grows out of Western democratic institutions.
quoteZh: 批判理论强调，新右翼的危险并非仅在于其与西方民主的直接对立，而在于它总是滋生于西方民主制度之中。

t: Lefebvre as founder of the urban philosophy of Western Marxism
zh: 列斐伏尔为西方马克思主义城市哲学奠基
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (China Social Sciences Net), 2023
paras: This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2023, asks how Henri Lefebvre turned the scattered reflections on cities in Marx and Engels into a theoretical resource for a Marxist urban philosophy. Guan Wei argues that Lefebvre's systematic study of these texts, and his thinking about a path to human liberation through the city, make him the founder of Western Marxist urban philosophy.

The article follows Lefebvre's reading in sequence. It begins with his claim that Marx and Engels lived through the rise of the industrial capitalist city but never treated it systematically. It then turns to his separate treatments of Engels and of Marx, and to his account of the city as a subject and a historical category. It ends with his handling of the reproduction of the relations of production.

Guan reports that Lefebvre gathered Marx's and Engels's "fragments" into an approach grounded in historical materialism and the critique of political economy. In this reading Engels described the concrete life of the working class in the capitalist city, where civilisation and barbarism sit side by side as two faces of one coin. Marx, by contrast, worked from abstract principles that are intelligible only in an urban setting. For Lefebvre, the transition from feudalism to capitalism is a contradictory movement between town and country, and the city is itself a subject and a work, whose participants hold a "right to the city". That right may be marginalised, but it signals the possibility of change and points toward the "complete urbanisation of society". Guan adds that Lefebvre treats reproduction as the key to everyday alienation, space and the survival of capitalism. In his account capitalism creates new sectors of exploitation, including leisure, everyday life, knowledge, art and urbanisation, and it produces space as capital and capital as space.

Guan concludes that Lefebvre's work is more than a gathering of fragments. It brings the urban question into the field of historical materialism and lays epistemological and methodological foundations for urban studies. It also exposes the contradictions and alienation of the capitalist city. Lefebvre hopes for a new urban philosophy that holds out human liberation and a new urban form, order and set of relations. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how Lefebvre read Marx and Engels on the city and of the roots of his notions of the right to the city and complete urbanisation.
quoteEn: Lefebvre regarded the city and the evolution of urban–rural relations as a key to understanding the problems above.
quoteZh: 列斐伏尔将城市、城乡关系的演变视为理解上述问题的一把钥匙。

t: Lenin's critique of "freedom of criticism" and its lessons
zh: 列宁对“批评自由”的批判与启示
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2023 no. 5
paras: Fang and Du examine how Lenin answered the slogan of "freedom of criticism", which Eduard Bernstein put forward to "revise" Marxism from a bourgeois standpoint and which spread into the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party. The article argues that Lenin, in What Is to Be Done? and other works, exposed the slogan as a vehicle for bourgeois ideology and gave a scientific restatement of Marxism. It holds that this critique still offers guidance for ideological work today.

The article first traces the origins of the slogan: the late nineteenth-century changes in capitalism, the Second International's revisionist turn, and Bernstein's demand at the 1901 Lübeck congress. It then follows its Russian variants through four periods: "legal Marxism" and economism, Menshevism after 1903, liquationism after 1908, and social chauvinism in the First World War. Four sections then set out Lenin's critique from the standpoint of Marxism's view of the people, its holistic view, its view of practice and its view of development. A final section draws lessons for China.

The authors argue that Lenin treated the slogan as a cover for political aims: turning the workers' movement into a liberal "tail" and the revolutionary party into a reformist one. Against it, Lenin upheld the people's standpoint, mass initiative and the Party's ties to workers and peasants. He also defended Marxism as an integral worldview, "cast from a single piece of steel", whose parts cannot be separated. On practice and development, the authors report that Lenin demanded that theory rest on the full body of facts and be tested in revolutionary action. He also held that theory must advance with history, with proletarian struggle and with the best of human thought.

The authors draw five lessons. They call for vigilance toward currents that present themselves as Marxist, for a firm people's standpoint, and for a complete and clear worldview. They also stress starting from reality and carrying theory into practice, and continuing theoretical innovation.
