They quote Xi Jinping on ideology as the point where hostile forces first breach a society, and link these tasks to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school style reading of Lenin's polemic against revisionism is turned into current ideological guidance.
quoteEn: The point is not only to interpret the world but, above all, to change it through revolutionary practice.
quoteZh: 问题不仅在于解释世界，更在于通过革命实践活动改变世界

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept for China's path to modernization, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A slogan Bernstein used to demand the right to criticise and revise Marxism. Lenin attacked it in What Is to Be Done? as a pretext for introducing bourgeois ideas into the workers' movement.
A current among Russian intellectuals in the 1890s who adopted parts of Marxism while publishing legally under tsarist censorship. Lenin criticised it as a bourgeois adaptation of Marxism.
A trend in Russian Social-Democracy around 1900 that limited the workers' movement to economic struggles and downplayed political and theoretical work. Lenin criticised it.

t: The ideological character of Western party-system theory
zh: 西方政党制度理论的意识形态特性研究
paras: Zhang Fei'an asks why Western party-system theory, which presents itself as neutral science, cannot accommodate the party system led by the Communist Party of China. Taking up Xi Jinping's 2018 description of the multiparty cooperation and political consultation system as a "new type of party system", the article asks what makes the Western system "old" and why it must be transcended. Zhang's thesis is that this theory is an ideology defending the legitimacy of Western capitalist political institutions, and that Chinese scholars need to see through its "scientific illusion" before building their own party theory.

The article has four parts. It first traces the rise of the theory to Cold War social science in the United States after the 1950s. It then links the theory to the hegemony of liberal-democratic discourse. The third part examines the "competitiveness" norm in the theory's branches: definition, typology and causes (and, more briefly, transition). A short conclusion draws out the implications for China. Zhang draws on Duverger, Sartori, Schattschneider, Schumpeter, Dahl, Rokkan, Lipset, Mair and others.

Zhang's core argument is that party-system research was marginal until the Cold War, when the contest between the United States and the Soviet Union turned on who could claim "democracy". In Zhang's account, Schumpeter's procedural definition of democracy as competition for votes, together with Schattschneider's claim that democracy is a by-product of party competition, let liberalism annex democracy, tie it to multiparty elections and brand one-party socialism anti-democratic. Zhang says competition then became the "meta-standard" of the field. Definitions deny that non-competitive systems are party systems, typologies by party number (Duverger, Sartori) count only parties that compete for seats, and explanations of origin, whether Duverger's electoral-law approach or Lipset and Rokkan's social cleavages, never study non-Western systems. Zhang reads this through the Marx–Engels account of ideology as the ruling class presenting its interests as universal.

Zhang concludes that Western theory cannot grasp the functions, rationality or advantages of China's system, because that theory rests on social division and competition and aims to prevent a party representing the people's overall interest from taking power. Understanding the Western system's "oldness" through historical materialism, Zhang argues, will strengthen Chinese scholars' theoretical self-awareness and discourse power in building a Chinese party theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Cold War political science and its party typologies, or want to see how the "new type of party system" is theoretically contrasted with Western models.
quoteEn: Western party-system theory is an \"old\" theory that serves bourgeois interests and takes competition as its premise; it is built on social division and uses competitiveness to dissolve integration.
quoteZh: 西方政党制度理论是一种服务于资产阶级利益的、以竞争为前提的“旧”理论，它建立于社会分化的基础之上，用竞争性去瓦解整合性

glossary.explanation: Official term for China's system of multiparty cooperation and political consultation under Communist Party leadership. Xi Jinping used it in 2018 to contrast the system with Western competitive party systems.

glossary.zh: 中国共产党领导的多党合作和政治协商制度
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó Gòngchǎndǎng lǐngdǎo de duōdǎng hézuò hé zhèngzhì xiéshāng zhìdù
glossary.en: multiparty cooperation and political consultation system
glossary.literal: multiparty cooperation and political consultation system led by the CPC
glossary.explanation: The system in which China's eight non-Communist "democratic parties" cooperate with, and accept the leadership of, the CPC, including through the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference.
Used here in the Marxist sense of the ideas of the superstructure that serve the ruling class's interests, drawn from The German Ideology.

t: From critique to reaction: the New Right, critical theory and international relations
zh: 从批判到反动：新右翼、批判理论与国际关系
orig: Journal of International Political Theory, vol. 18 no. 1, 2022
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 4
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by Jean-François Drolet and Michael C. Williams, first published in the Journal of International Political Theory (2022). It asks why radical conservatism has been so effective on the world stage and argues that the answer lies partly in the New Right's appropriation of themes from critical theory. The authors contend that Gramsci's hegemony, the Frankfurt School's analysis of capitalist mass society, and postmodernism have been turned to reactionary ends, which challenges the assumption that critical theory is inherently tied to progressive politics.

The article defines the New Right as the intellectual vanguard of the radical right's revival since the end of the Cold War. It traces its origins to the French Nouvelle Droite of 1968 (Alain de Benoist and others) and its counterparts in Italy, Germany and the United States, including the paleoconservatism of Paul Gottfried and Sam Francis and today's white-nationalist "alternative right". It is organised in three main sections, on Gramsci, on the "New Class" and the Frankfurt School, and on postmodernism, followed by a conclusion.

First, the authors argue that the New Right adopted a "right-wing Gramscianism": a long-term "metapolitics" of cultural struggle, on the premise that political power rests on cultural hegemony that the left now holds. Second, it draws on Frankfurt School critiques of consumerism and the culture industry, together with James Burnham's idea of a managerial "New Class", to portray liberal managerialism, identity politics and Habermasian deliberative democracy as instruments of elite control. It also accuses critical intellectuals of being co-opted. Third, it reworks postmodern distrust of Enlightenment universalism into "identitarianism" and "differentialism", in which culture and ethnicity are defended against mixing, and into Faye's "archeofuturism". The authors add that the New Right seeks to create self-conscious social agents among those "left behind" by globalisation, the very agent that critical theory has failed to find.

The authors conclude that the New Right is not simply anti-intellectual or a continuation of historical fascism, though its rhetoric can foster violent, conspiratorial politics. They say it aims to take control of globalisation and build an alternative order in which capitalism thrives within a myth of shared civilisational heritage and the West is defined against "Global Islam" and the Global South. They contrast this confidence with a critical international theory paralysed by self-doubt and losing momentum. They offer no solution, but say critical scholars can no longer avoid these questions. Read the original if you study the intellectual genealogy of the contemporary radical right or the political uses and limits of Gramscian and Frankfurt School ideas in international relations theory.
quoteEn: The New Right actively draws on the themes of critical theory for reactionary ends, which directly challenges the view that critical theory is inherently bound up with progressive political aims.
quoteZh: 新右翼积极地调用批判理论的主题来达到反动的目的，这对认为批判理论与进步主义的政治目的有着固有联系的观点提出了直接挑战。

glossary.explanation: A term for developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, widely used in Chinese official discourse. Here the authors report the New Right as presenting it, with "Global Islam", as a cultural and demographic "threat" to the West.

t: The time of our lives: reflections on work and capitalist temporality
zh: 我们生命中的时间：对工作和资本主义时间性的反思
orig: Socialist Register, vol. 57, 2021
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 4
paras: This text is a Chinese translation (abridged) of an essay by the Canadian historian Bryan D. Palmer, first published in Socialist Register. Written in 2020 as Covid-19 dissolved the boundaries between work and home, it asks how capital controls time and why time must again become a central socialist question. Palmer argues that the struggle over time is a class struggle that cannot be resolved by shorter hours or the slogan of 'a fair day's wage for a fair day's work', and that only abolishing the wage system would free time.

The essay moves through a historical sequence. It starts with Marx's analysis of the working day and the nineteenth-century struggles for shorter hours. It then turns to the early twentieth century: the 1913 Paterson strike, the October Revolution, Taylorism and the stopwatch. It next examines the 1960s debates on leisure and alienation, centred on E. P. Thompson's 'Time, Work-Discipline and Industrial Capitalism'. It ends with the post-1973 period, the gig economy, and a critique of André Gorz.

Palmer's central move draws on Marx's picture of capital as a vampire that turns the many's free time into surplus labour. The working day is therefore a variable, and capital answers legal limits by intensifying work. He credits Thompson with showing how time discipline was internalised under early industrial capitalism. He faults Thompson, however, for romanticising task-oriented pre-capitalist work and for underrating women's oppression and the incomplete reach of capitalist time among colonised and marginalised groups. Palmer reads the gig economy as both new and old, a return to the 'putting out' system with round-the-clock surveillance, and cites figures on rising working hours and automation-driven job losses.

Palmer rejects Gorz's call for 'abolishing work' and a leisure society within reformed capitalism, and calls his argument a false utopianism. In Palmer's reading, Gorz misread Marx's dialectic of necessity and freedom, ignored imperialism, and treated time as a problem only of the wealthy countries. Palmer concludes that the eight-hour day no longer suffices and that a new commitment to abolishing the wage system is needed, closing with the 1968 graffiti 'beneath the paving stones, the beach'. Read the original if you want a Marxist history of working time that links Marx, Thompson and the present-day platform economy, together with a polemic against Gorz.
quoteEn: Our age needs a new kind of dedication: the abolition of the wage system.
quoteZh: 我们的时代需要一种新的奉献精神：废除工资制度。

t: Plekhanov and Lenin on the October Revolution: the political disagreement and its theoretical roots
zh: 普列汉诺夫与列宁关于十月革命的政治分歧及其理论根源
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2023 no. 4
paras: Why did Georgi Plekhanov, the "father of Russian Marxism", reject the October Revolution that Lenin led? Wang argues that the break between the two men, which ran from 1903 to Plekhanov's death in 1918, was not a matter of loyalty to Marx. It came from different abilities to apply theory to practice: Plekhanov is cast as a theorist and propagandist, Lenin as a theorist who also seized the pulse of society to advance revolution.

The article has four parts. It first sets out Plekhanov's rejection of the democratic dictatorship of workers and peasants and of the October Revolution, drawing on his response to Lenin's April Theses and his open letter to the Petrograd workers. It then examines his case for class cooperation during the First World War, and Lenin's philosophical defence of October in "Our Revolution" and related late writings. The last part traces the methodological roots of Plekhanov's error.

Wang contends that Plekhanov treated the level of the productive forces as an absolute precondition for socialism. He quoted Marx and Engels selectively, for example on the "premature seizure of power" in Engels's Peasant War in Germany, in ways that Wang says cut across Engels's own purpose. Against this, Wang presents Lenin's "revolutionary dialectic": the general laws of history presuppose particular forms and sequences of development. Wang notes that Lenin, citing Marx's remark on a peasant war supporting a proletarian revolution, argued that a revolutionary seizure of power could create the preconditions for cultural and economic advance.

Wang finds Plekhanov's dialectics confined to the conceptual level. They stressed the objective, economic side of revolution and ignored the subjective side. Plekhanov denounced dogmatism while turning some Marxist propositions into absolute dogma, and he fell into self-contradiction. Wang draws a parallel with Hegel and quotes Bukharin's verdict of a "bookish dialectician". The lesson Wang draws for Communists is to combine theory with practice and to use dialectical and historical materialism creatively. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Lenin's critics on the Marxist side are assessed, with extended quotations from Plekhanov's 1917 writings.
quoteEn: A dialectic that stays at the conceptual level, and is not joined to complex real life and historical conditions, that is, to the dialectic of practice, naturally cannot serve as a guide to action and an ideological weapon for revolution.
quoteZh: 停留在概念层面的辩证法，不与复杂的现实生活与历史条件或者说实践辩证法相结合，当然难以发挥革命的行动指南与思想武器作用。

t: Lenin's thought on Party leadership in "The Tax in Kind"
zh: 列宁《论粮食税》中党的领导思想解析
source: China Leadership Science (Zhongguo lingdao kexue), 2023 no. 5
paras: Zhu Lixia and Jin Doudou ask what Lenin's 1921 pamphlet "The Tax in Kind" (Lenin's Chinese title: Lun liangshi shui) contributes to the theory of Party leadership. They argue that, beneath its surface role of explaining the New Economic Policy, the text is about how a Marxist party can strengthen its leadership in a country dominated by small peasant farming. They hold that its ideas remain relevant a century later for the Communist Party of China's effort to strengthen Party leadership. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statement at the 20th Party Congress (2022) that Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article first sets out the background: war communism, the surplus-requisition system, the fuel and grain crises of early 1921, strikes and peasant uprisings, and the "Left" communists' attacks on the new policy. It then draws out three elements of Lenin's thinking on leadership. These are replacing requisition with a tax in kind, using capitalism to develop socialism, and opposing bureaucracy. A final section derives three lessons for the Party in the new era.

On the first element, the authors argue that the tax in kind eased tension between the ruling party and workers and peasants. They say it left peasants free to dispose of their surplus, strengthened the worker-peasant alliance, and thereby reinforced centralised and unified Party leadership. On the second, they present Lenin's use of state capitalism as an intermediate link between small production and socialism, under proletarian state limits. In their account this was progress, not retreat, and it improved the Party's own building. On the third, they follow Lenin in tracing bureaucracy to feudal remnants and to the scattered small-producer base. They say it was worsened by old-regime officials entering state organs, and that Lenin proposed promoting workers from below and sending officials to investigate at grassroots level.

The authors conclude that the Party today should safeguard the people's fundamental interests, uphold Party leadership over all work, and combat bureaucracy and formalism. On the last point they mention removing falsified performance indicators and using 5G, cloud computing and big data for real-time supervision in rural areas. They link China's reform and opening up to Lenin's use of capitalism to develop socialism. They also claim the Party's leadership explains China's rapid economic growth. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-building scholarship draws on Lenin's New Economic Policy writings for present-day arguments on leadership.
quoteEn: Lenin creatively answered the question of how to build socialism in Soviet Russia, where small peasants made up the great majority of the population.
quoteZh: 列宁创造性地回答了在小农占绝大多数人口的苏维埃俄国怎样建设社会主义的问题。

glossary.explanation: The policy Soviet Russia adopted in 1921, replacing war communism. It allowed limited private trade and a tax in kind on peasants.
The wartime Soviet practice of taking peasants' surplus grain, and part of their basic ration, for the state. It was replaced by the tax in kind in 1921.
The economic policy of Soviet Russia during the civil war and foreign intervention. It centred on grain requisition and bans on private trade.
In Lenin's usage, capitalism limited and supervised by the proletarian state. He saw it as a stepping stone between small production and socialism.
The 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in October 2022. It reaffirmed Party leadership as central to socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The policy begun in 1978 of economic reform and opening to the outside world. It introduced market mechanisms into China's socialist economy.

t: A century of exploration by Latin American communist parties and their present state
zh: 拉美共产党的百年探索与发展现状
source: Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2021–2022), Social Sciences Academic Press, 2023, pp. 235–253
paras: Xu Shicheng, a Latin Americanist, surveys more than a century of communist organisation in Latin America and the Caribbean and asks where the parties stand today. The article argues that these parties have survived repeated setbacks and remain an important left-wing force, but that they have never become the mainstream. Apart from the Communist Party of Cuba, none has governed alone.

The text opens with a historical sketch. It covers the founding of parties after the Russian Revolution, the splits of the 1950s–70s under the influence of the Sino-Soviet dispute, guerrilla warfare, the Chilean parliamentary road under Allende, the military dictatorships, and the shock of the Soviet collapse. It then profiles individual parties in three groups: those that take part in government (Brazil, Chile, Uruguay), legal opposition parties (Venezuela, Argentina, Colombia), and parties without legal registration (the two Peruvian parties and Bolivia). Each profile gives founding dates, membership, seats, leaders and guiding ideology.

The central section identifies shared theoretical shifts since the 21st century. Xu reports that the parties have moved from dogmatic Marxism-Leninism to its "localisation", for instance by pairing it with Mariátegui's thought in Peru or with Bolívar's in Venezuela. Several have redefined themselves from a vanguard of the proletariat to a party of working people or a "mass" party. Most have abandoned armed struggle for legal and electoral struggle, and they reject neoliberalism while seeking a path to socialism. In practice, Xu lists electoral participation, influence on government decisions, leadership of trade unions, use of party media and social networks, and regional coordination through the São Paulo Forum and party conferences. He also lists pandemic relief measures and solidarity with Cuba and Venezuela against US sanctions.

Xu also traces relations with the Communist Party of China. In his account, ties were broken in the 1960s and 70s and then restored, and many Latin American parties now praise the Chinese path. His conclusion is that the leftward turns in regional politics offer openings. To avoid marginalisation, the parties must integrate Marxism-Leninism with national conditions, innovate in theory and propose policies suited to their countries. Read the original if you want a party-by-party reference on Latin American communist parties, including membership and parliamentary strength, together with a Chinese academic view of their orientation.
quoteEn: Latin American communist parties need to proceed from their own national realities, combine Marxism-Leninism with their country's revolutionary practice, keep innovating in theory and put forward policies suited to national conditions and popular demands, if they are to escape the danger of marginalisation.
quoteZh: 拉美共产党需要从本国实际出发，将马列主义与本国革命实际相结合，不断进行理论上的创新，提出适合本国国情和民众要求的政策主张，才能摆脱被边缘化的危险

t: Left and right: on the Labour Party's economic policy and party positioning
st: Original title: "Labour, Left and Right: On Party Positioning and Policy Reasoning"
zh: 左与右：论英国工党的经济政策和政党定位
orig: The British Journal of Politics and International Relations, online 20 June 2022
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 4
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of a 2022 article by Michael Jacob and Andrew Hindmoor, both of the University of Sheffield. It asks why the British Labour Party has swung between left and right since 1945. Many commentators expected Keir Starmer to move Labour towards the centre after the 2019 defeat. The authors call this the "electoral–ideological" explanation: Labour must choose between ideology and winning votes. They propose a "political economy–policy" alternative. Labour moves right and favours redistribution when the economy performs well, and moves left towards structural reform when it is seen to perform badly.

The article first sets out two economic programmes. The "redistributive" programme, associated with the right, relies on growth to fund public services and welfare. The "structural reform" programme, associated with the left, stresses planning, public ownership and regulation of finance and labour. The authors use the Manifesto Project's left–right scores for Labour's election manifestos from 1945 to 2019. They test both explanations against Attlee, Gaitskell, Wilson, Kinnock, Blair and Brown, Ed Miliband and Corbyn. They give most attention to the Wilson years (1960–75), and they end with Starmer's Labour.

The authors tie each leftward turn to a perceived economic problem: postwar reconstruction, the stagflation and IMF loan of the 1970s with the 1983 "Alternative Economic Strategy", and the post-2008 crisis and austerity. They tie rightward turns to sustained growth in the 1950s, the 1980s recovery and the 1992–2008 boom. Wilson's radical 1964 and 1966 economic plans, they argue, do not fit the claim that moving right wins elections. Jacob and Hindmoor add that parties and voters shape preferences as well as follow them, so the "centre" is constructed. Drawing on the Rawlsian-style critique of Anthony Downs's rational-choice model, they stress policy reasoning ("policy deliberation"): internal debates in which actors change their minds as conditions change. Examples are Stuart Holland's influence in 1973, the New Labour revisionists in the 1990s, and Peter Mandelson's revival of industrial strategy in 2008–10.

The authors conclude that the economic conditions behind Labour's turn left after 2010 persist. They cite low investment, insecure work, regional inequality, an unreformed banking system and a cost-of-living crisis. They expect Labour's next manifesto to move towards the centre of the 2019 one but not necessarily back to Blair, since public opinion on economic policy remains fairly left-leaning. They also note that Rachel Reeves has proposed structural reforms. Read the original if you study the Labour Party, party-positioning theory or the debate between rational-choice and policy-reasoning accounts of party change.
quoteEn: Labour's policy positioning shifts with changes in the external economic environment: when the economy performs well, Labour moves right and adopts a redistributive economic strategy (stressing more spending on public services and welfare).
quoteZh: 工党的政策定位因外部经济环境的变化而改变：当经济表现良好时，工党右转并采取再分配的经济战略（强调增加公共服务和福利开支）。

t: The world and the left
zh: 世界与左翼
orig: New Left Review, no. 137 (September/October 2022)
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 4
paras: This is a Chinese translation, abridged, of an essay by the Swedish sociologist Göran Therborn that first appeared in New Left Review in 2022. Therborn asks where the global left stands at the end of the first quarter of the twenty-first century. He argues that the twentieth-century left was shaped by two systemic dialectics, industrial capitalism and colonialism, which had stalled by century's end. The new left of the twenty-first century, in his account, is a creative response to neoliberal globalization rather than a continuation of the old left.

The essay moves through six parts. It first reviews the twentieth century's achievements and exhaustion, then the rise and current decline of neoliberal hegemony. It then profiles the new left through the alter-globalization protests, climate mobilisation and the socialist turn in Latin America and the United States. A comparison of old and new left practice follows, across social base, organisational tools, democracy, strategy and protest. The essay ends by assessing gains and losses and naming the challenges ahead.

Therborn contends that digital financial capitalism no longer produces its own opponents as industrial capitalism did. Protesters are therefore mostly outsiders damaged by neoliberalism, not its key economic agents. The new left appeals to \"the people\" and radical democracy, favours movements over parties, and works through protests and uprisings. It lacks a programme or a strategy for winning power, which Therborn sees as its main difference from the twentieth-century left. He lists four tasks: the climate crisis, the risk of war under a new imperial geopolitics (which he ties to US-led sanctions and the rise of Asia), and class struggle against extreme inequality. He credits the new left with putting inequality and climate action onto mainstream agendas and with reducing inequality in Latin America. He faults it for scant institutional results beyond China, Vietnam and Cuba, which he credits to the twentieth century.

Therborn concludes with cautious optimism, based on the left's creativity and mass mobilisation. He says the twentieth century left no recipe, only a heritage of experience. He calls for a left with a global outlook that opposes US hegemony and works to prevent a new world war. He also argues that the loss of a socialist vision is serious and that a long march needs a direction. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist sociologist's periodisation of the twentieth- and twenty-first-century left, including his views on geopolitics and Asia's rise.
quoteEn: In every case, the left's great deficiency is the lack of a vision of transformative power or a strategy for winning it, which is perhaps the most important difference from the twentieth-century left.
quoteZh: 在每一个事例中，左翼的巨大缺陷都是缺乏变革权力的愿景或赢得变革权力的战略，这也许是与20世纪左翼最重要的区别。

t: The problem of gender identity in contemporary Western feminist research
zh: 当代西方女性主义研究中的性别身份问题
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 4
paras: He Cuixiang asks what a woman is and how gender identity should be understood, a question the author treats as central to contemporary feminist research. The article argues that neither biological essentialism nor pure social constructivism gives an adequate answer. Gender identity, in the author's view, should rest on the mutual fit of biological, sociocultural and psychoanalytic factors.

The article moves through three ways of defining woman. It begins with biological definitions, from traditional patriarchal norms (the Chinese 'three obediences and four virtues') to radical feminism and Shulamith Firestone's The Dialectic of Sex. It then turns to social constructionism, from Simone de Beauvoir to Judith Butler's theory of performativity, and to Lacanian psychoanalysis and its account of feminine jouissance. A fourth section reviews current disputes in identity politics.

He sets out three debates. The first concerns the relation between sex and gender: Butler treats even the body as constructed, while critics such as Somer Brodribb hold that ignoring biological difference denies the female body. The author adds that gender must also be read through class, race, colonialism and capitalism. The second concerns whether a unified category of 'woman' is needed. Butler rejects it as exclusionary, but Iris Marion Young, Seyla Benhabib, Nancy Fraser and Martha Nussbaum reply that the concept is necessary for criticising patriarchy. The third concerns the goal of liberation. He argues that identity politics in the third wave produces a 'difference dilemma' that fragments feminism and undermines universal rights, and cites US debates over gender policy and political correctness. Nussbaum's capabilities approach is offered as a way beyond it.

He rejects radical feminism's proposal to abolish women's reproductive role through technology. The author accepts cultural tolerance of gender plurality but urges caution in social construction and in law and policy. Feminism, the article says, should move beyond identity politics towards social emancipation and the cultivation of basic human capabilities, with attention to poor working women. The author adds that standards for a good life for women vary across societies, and that China's family-centred culture differs from Western individualism. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese overview of Western debates on sex, gender and identity from Beauvoir to Butler, Lacan and Nussbaum.
quoteEn: Feminism should go beyond the horizon of gender identity politics and, proceeding from the idea of social emancipation or the cultivation of basic human capabilities, attend to the condition of poor working women who are deeply exploited and oppressed.
quoteZh: 女性主义应该超越性别身份政治的视野，从社会解放或培育人类基本能力的观念出发，关注那些深受剥削和压迫的贫穷劳动妇女的状况。

t: Towards a culturally conservative critique of modernity
st: Kołakowski's twofold critique of utopianism and liberalism as a vantage point
zh: 走向一种文化保守主义的现代性批判
zhSub: 以科拉科夫斯基对乌托邦主义和自由主义的双重批判为观察点
paras: Utopianism and liberalism are usually treated as sworn enemies in Western political thought, and Marxism is often wrongly labelled a utopianism. Yan Yan examines how the Polish neo-Marxist Leszek Kołakowski, writing from a position of cultural conservatism, criticised both. In Yan's account, Kołakowski held that both can lead to totalitarianism and that the right course is to resist the temptation of uniformity and seek balance among competing values. Yan defends Marxism's scientific character while treating Kołakowski's ideas as partly instructive.

The article has three parts. The first covers Kołakowski's critique of utopian 'future society', including his types of utopia (epistemological, political, revolutionary) and his 'three motifs' reading of Marx. The second covers his critique of the liberal 'open society' in dialogue with Karl Popper, Karl Polanyi and Friedrich Hayek. A closing section places his thought in its Central and East European context and compares his idea of inconsistency with Aristotle's mean.

Yan argues that Kołakowski attacks a specific, levelling kind of utopia that promises final reconciliation and the end of evil, then wrongly attributes it to Marx. Drawing on Ernst Bloch and Agnes Heller, Yan distinguishes a 'good' utopia, a value-rational orientation towards a goal, from a 'bad', ahistorical one, and cites Marx and Engels in The German Ideology to show that communism is a real movement and not an ideal. Against liberalism, Kołakowski holds that the open society's values (market, democracy, individual freedom) conflict with one another. Pursuing them uniformly would threaten that society, and a measure of tradition and 'irrational' taboo is indispensable. Yan finds his critique of liberal equality of opportunity pertinent, since it would require abolishing the family and imposing collective education, though Yan sets aside his turn to Christian theology as religious mysticism.

Yan concludes that Kołakowski rejects uniformity without defending difference unconditionally: he seeks a dynamic balance between universality and particularity, and says one can be a 'conservative-liberal-socialist'. For him history has no happy endpoint, and every improvement carries a cost. Yan reads this against the Central and East European experience of the twentieth century. Yan warns against his misreading of Marxism but finds philosophical wisdom in his stress on human finitude and the universal–particular relation. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese Marxist assessment of Kołakowski, or of the debate over whether Marxism is utopian.
quoteEn: Kołakowski's opposition to 'consistency' is not an unprincipled defence of particularity and difference, but a search for a dynamic balance between universality and particularity, and between consistency and difference.
quoteZh: 科拉科夫斯基反对“一致性”，并不是要无原则地捍卫特殊性和差异性，而是要在普遍性与特殊性、一致性与差异性之间谋求动态平衡

t: Laos: the 11th Party Congress and new progress in socialist renovation
zh: 老挝：召开党的十一大，社会主义革新事业取得新进展
source: Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2021–2022), Social Sciences Academic Press, 2023, pp. 200–215
paras: This year-in-review chapter, from a 2021–2022 report on the international communist movement, examines how the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP) advanced what it calls socialist renovation in 2021. Fang and Hai argue that the Party's 11th Congress, followed by the second and third plenums of the 11th Central Committee, set a five-year course. In their account, the Party's centralised leadership, applied during the pandemic, produced progress at home and in foreign relations, above all with China.

The chapter has four parts. It first reviews the 11th Congress (January 2021): the achievements of the previous five years, four lessons of renovation, and the targets of the Ninth Five-Year Plan for 2021–2025. It then covers domestic developments in 2021: the two plenums, laws on budget losses, drug control and the environment, the 30th anniversary of the 1991 constitution, and the pandemic response. A third part treats diplomacy with China, Vietnam and other states. A short conclusion looks ahead to 2022.

The authors report Secretary-General Thongloun Sisoulith's findings: average GDP growth of 5.8% over five years despite Covid-19, 3.5% growth in 2021, and social security coverage of 94%. The four lessons are strengthening Party-building, developing distinctive industries, developing human resources, and strictly carrying out Party decisions. The plan aims at average growth of over 4% and per capita income of 2,887 US dollars by 2025, within a socialist-oriented market economy. The chapter gives particular weight to the China–Laos Railway, opened in December 2021. In the authors' reading it is a flagship of the Belt and Road Initiative, linking it to Laos's shift from a 'land-locked' to a 'land-linked' country, and a model of cooperation between socialist states. They also describe Chinese vaccine and medical aid, and the building of a China–Laos community with a shared future.

For 2022 the authors list five tasks. They are to localise Marxism-Leninism in Laos and apply Kaysone Phomvihane Thought, to strengthen Party-building, to keep the line of principled comprehensive renovation, to build a socialist rule-of-law state and modernise governance, and to integrate into regional and international processes. They present resistance to 'peaceful evolution' by hostile forces, and to 'self-evolution' within, as part of the ideological task. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned Chinese account of Lao policy documents, statistics and China–Laos–Vietnam relations in 2021.
quoteEn: Closer cooperation between Marxist parties and between socialist states is the general trend of the world; the China–Laos Railway links the peoples of two socialist countries and strengthens their solidarity, and can be called a masterpiece of cooperation between the two parties.
quoteZh: 马克思主义政党间加强合作、社会主义国家间加强合作是世界大势所趋，中老铁路连接两个社会主义国家的人民，加强和巩固社会主义国家之间的团结，堪称中老两党合作的杰作。

glossary.explanation: China's infrastructure and economic cooperation programme, launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, covering many countries in Asia, Africa and Europe.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future
glossary.explanation: A Chinese foreign-policy concept associated with Xi Jinping. Here it is applied bilaterally as the 'China–Laos community with a shared future'.
The LPRP's term for its reform line, launched in 1986 and combining market-oriented reform with continued one-party rule. It is comparable to Vietnam's Đổi Mới and to China's reform and opening up.

glossary.zh: 社会主义定向市场经济
glossary.explanation: The official description of the Lao economic system: a market economy guided by the Party towards socialist goals. Vietnam uses a similar formula.
The ideas of Kaysone Phomvihane, the LPRP's founding leader and first head of state of the Lao People's Democratic Republic. The Party treats them as a guide alongside Marxism-Leninism.
A term used in socialist-state discourse for the alleged strategy of hostile Western forces to undermine socialist systems by non-military means, such as ideological and cultural influence.

t: Primitive accumulation and the contemporary critique of capitalist patriarchy
st: An autonomist feminist perspective based on Federici
zh: 原始积累与资本主义父权制的当代批判
zhSub: 基于费德里西的自治主义的女性主义视角
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2023 no. 4
paras: Dai and Wu take up the work of Silvia Federici, the Italian autonomist Marxist and feminist theorist, whom they say Chinese scholarship has neglected. Chinese research on autonomism, they note, has concentrated on Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt and overlooked autonomist feminism, the school's most important branch. The article argues that Federici extended Marx's analysis of primitive accumulation to women's social position and the reproduction of labour-power. On this reading, the 16th–17th century witch hunt was a foundation of capitalism and wage labour, and a source of capitalist patriarchy.

The article has four parts. It first outlines Italian autonomist Marxism and its feminist wing (Dalla Costa, James, Fortunati and Federici) and the Wages for Housework campaign. It then presents Federici's mature theory, developed from the 1980s and above all in Caliban and the Witch (2004). A third part follows her argument into the era of neoliberal globalisation, drawing on her experience teaching in Nigeria in the 1980s. A conclusion assesses her influence on feminist Marxism, Negri and Hardt, Christian Fuchs's theory of digital labour, and social reproduction theory in the United States.

The authors argue that, for Federici, primitive accumulation separated producers from the means of production and also separated production from reproduction. The witch hunt, in this account, pushed women out of waged work and made their bodies a machine for producing workers. This created what she calls the patriarchy of the wage: men gain power through wages, while women are controlled through unpaid reproductive labour. In the second move, Dai and Wu say Federici treats primitive accumulation as a permanent mechanism within capitalism, not a one-off prehistory. She combines Luxemburg's and Harvey's ideas of an "outside" that capital must keep appropriating, and counts women's domestic labour as such an outside. Contemporary violence against women, including enclosure of their bodies and repression of their resistance to land privatisation, is read as class conflict and not merely gender conflict.

The authors conclude that Federici developed Marxist-feminist gender theory and, in their words, achieved a real union of Marxism and feminism. They credit her with showing patriarchy to be intrinsic to capitalism and with opening a new field of critique around non-productive or dispossessive accumulation. They hold that she deserves more attention and deeper discussion. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of autonomist feminism and Federici's theory of primitive accumulation, or want to see how Chinese Foreign Marxism studies receives Western feminist Marxism.
quoteEn: Primitive accumulation does not precede capital accumulation; it is a foundational mechanism internal to the structure of capital accumulation, and capital accumulation is always accompanied by the violence of primitive accumulation.
quoteZh: 原始积累并不是先于资本积累，而是内在于资本积累结构之中的基础性机制,资本积累始终伴随着原始积累的暴力。

glossary.explanation: The Italian current (operaismo and its successors) emerging in the 1960s–70s that stresses working-class subjectivity and autonomy from parties and unions. Negri, Hardt and Federici are associated with it.
A feminist campaign launched in the 1970s in Italy, Britain and North America demanding payment for unpaid domestic labour, as a way to expose its role in capital accumulation.
Federici's term for the system in which men's waged labour gives them power over women, whose unpaid reproductive work is made dependent and invisible.
Marx's term for the violent historical separation of producers from the means of production that preceded capitalism. Federici treats it as an ongoing mechanism.
The processes, including household work, childbearing and consumption of means of subsistence, by which the working population is renewed from day to day and across generations.

t: The radical feminist theory of social reproduction
st: Informal labour, the majority world and the need for inclusive theory and politics
zh: 激进女性主义的社会再生产理论
zhSub: 非正规劳动、多数世界以及对包容性理论和政治的需求
orig: Radical Philosophy, 2019 (originally titled "On the Value of Social Reproduction: Informal Labour, the Majority World and the Need for Inclusive Theories and Politics")
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 4
paras: This text is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by Alessandra Mezzadri of SOAS, University of London, first published in Radical Philosophy. It asks whether social reproduction, meaning the daily and generational reproduction of workers and labour-power, creates value in the Marxist sense. Mezzadri answers yes. She argues that this is especially clear once attention moves from the West to the "majority world", where most people work informally.

The article first reviews recent Social Reproduction Theory (SRT), notably the collection edited by Tithi Bhattacharya, with Nancy Fraser, Susan Ferguson and David McNally among its contributors. It then returns to earlier radical feminist work by Selma James, Maria Rosa Dalla Costa, Leopoldina Fortunati, Silvia Federici, Maria Mies, Rhoda Reddock, Angela Davis and Antonella Picchio. A further section contrasts the Western focus of SRT with the geography of informal labour, citing International Labour Organization figures. The article ends by discussing the politics that follows from this.

Mezzadri contends that SRT tends to attend to care institutions in Europe and North America, and that it sometimes treats use-value activities as non-value-producing. She calls this reasoning circular, because it assumes what it needs to prove. Drawing on the cases of India and China, she argues that in contexts of informal and informalised labour, a strict line between productive and reproductive spheres is misleading. She says reproductive spheres add to value generation in three ways. They tighten control over labour beyond working hours, as in factory dormitories. They externalise the costs of reproduction onto households and communities, which amounts to a de facto subsidy to capital. And they sustain the formal subsumption of labour under capital, as in home-based work within fragmented global production.

Mezzadri concludes that theoretical divisions are political. Excluding unpaid work from value creation, she argues, implicitly ranks forms of exploitation and gives paid labour a priority that undermines solidarity. She calls for inclusive theory and politics that link struggles over production and reproduction. She also warns against a capitalist "monism" that rests on Western experience and creates new dualisms of its own. Read the original if you study Marxist-feminist value theory, informal labour in the Global South, or the debate between early domestic-labour analysis and Social Reproduction Theory.
quoteEn: In short, from the standpoint of the lives of most of the world's people, social reproduction does create value, and does so in the Marxist sense.
quoteZh: 简而言之，从世界上大多数人的生活角度来看，社会再生产确实创造了价值，而且是在马克思主义的意义上创造了价值。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-feminist current, associated with Tithi Bhattacharya and others, that analyses how labour-power is reproduced through households and public institutions under capitalism.
A term for the developing regions where most of the world's population lives and works, used as an alternative to "Global South" or "developing countries".
Marx's term for capital's control of labour that has not yet been reorganised through machinery or a distinctly capitalist labour process.

t: Lenin's view of the essence of socialism: economic and political perspectives
zh: 列宁的社会主义本质观：经济与政治的视角
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2023 no. 4
paras: How did Lenin understand what socialism fundamentally is? Wang Zhongru argues that Lenin kept to the basic position of Marx and Engels, but, by contrasting socialism with capitalism and by working through the difficulties of building it in Russia, reached conclusions of both theoretical and practical value. In Wang's reading, Lenin's view can be reconstructed along two dimensions, the economic and the political.

The article has four main parts. It first looks at Lenin's limited direct treatment of human liberation and development, drawing mainly on the Party programmes of 1902 to 1919 and on his definition of class. It then turns to his understanding of the essence of capitalism, before setting out the economic essence and the political essence of socialism. A short conclusion links the findings to contemporary Chinese practice.

Wang holds that the Party programmes treat public ownership of the means of production as a means, while the welfare and all-round development of all members of society is the end and the essence of socialism. Lenin defined capitalism by commodity production and the commodity status of labour-power. Wang finds a logical gap here, since this excludes commodity production under any later social formation. Wang argues that the programme's stress on capitalist relations of production, above all ownership, gives a more accurate account than the market mechanism, citing later practice, especially socialism with Chinese characteristics. For Lenin's socialism, Wang distinguishes a theoretical socialism (the "ought") from a practical one (the "is"). Its economic essence is large-scale industry, public ownership, and organising labour and distribution through the state or society rather than the market, ending anarchy in production. Its political essence is the dictatorship of the proletariat, understood as one class holding power and exercising political leadership, with the Soviets as one form and not a universal model.

Wang concludes that Lenin located the essence of socialism in the welfare and all-round development of all members of society. This is realised economically through a mode of organising production and distribution different from capitalism, and politically through proletarian leadership of society via its vanguard. Wang says that drawing on Lenin's findings is part of the Chinese Communist Party's drive to build a modern socialist country and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The Party's own understanding of the question is left for separate study. Read the original if you are interested in a Chinese Party-school reading of Lenin's concepts of capitalism, socialism and the dictatorship of the proletariat, including its critical remarks on his stress on non-market planning.
quoteEn: Understanding the economic essence of the capitalist system through relations of production, especially ownership of the means of production, is more accurate and more scientific than understanding it through commodity production, that is, the mechanism of economic operation.
quoteZh: 从生产关系特别是生产资料所有制维度认识资本主义制度的经济本质，较之从商品生产即经济运行机制维度认识，更准确、更科学。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist term for rule by the working class during the transition from capitalism to communism. In the article it means one class holding state power and leading society politically, not only the use of coercion.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: An official Chinese Communist Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely associated with Xi Jinping's leadership.
The official name for China's current political and economic system, adopted since the reform era. It combines Party leadership and public ownership with market mechanisms.

t: German scholarship on Marx's London Notebooks: a review
zh: 德国学界关于马克思《伦敦笔记》的研究综述
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2023 no. 4
paras: This literature review surveys German research on Marx's London Notebooks of 1850–1853, concentrated in the 1970s to 1990s. Wu Ting notes that this work appeared when 'bourgeois Marxology' was fashionable in the West. German scholars therefore stressed that the Notebooks are an internal link in Marx's intellectual development and an important foundation of Capital and its manuscripts.

The review has three parts. The first covers the Halle research group on Marx and Engels, led by Wolfgang Jahn, which edited Notebooks I–XIV for the second Marx-Engels Complete Works (MEGA2) before its dissolution in 1991. The second covers overall readings of the Notebooks, centred on Jahn and Dieter Noske's 1979 study, together with specialist work on money, credit, banking and the major texts. The third covers studies of pre-capitalist modes of production and Asiatic landownership in the later, still unpublished notebooks.

Wu reports that Jahn read the Notebooks as the prehistory of Marx's 1858 'six-book plan' for his critique of political economy. Jahn and Noske, in this account, reject the Marxological split between Marx's research method and his mode of presentation and between a 'young' and a 'late' Marx. They hold that the 1848–49 revolutions led Marx to crisis theory and that the Notebooks prepared the discovery of surplus-value theory. Other scholars (Vasina, Müller, Schellhardt, Arnhold) trace the monetary and credit analyses, and Jahn treats the 'Reflections' of 1851 as a high point. The review then turns to Schellhardt's reading of Marx's extracts from Karl Hüllmann on medieval towns and finance, and to Winkelmann's work on Prescott's histories of Mexico and Peru. It ends with Wolfgang Rein's study of the Asiatic landownership extracts, which Rein links to Marx's later account of primitive accumulation and the subordination of pre-capitalist structures to capital.

Wu concludes that the Halle group made major contributions through its collection and editing of sources and its reconstruction of the historical thread of Marx's economic research. The review adds that the pre-capitalist and Asiatic material is little known among Chinese scholars because it lies in notebooks not yet fully published. Wu presents the German work as offering a way to examine the inner logic of Marx's thought. Read the original if you want a guide to German-language scholarship, names and sources on the London Notebooks, especially the Halle group and the unpublished later notebooks.
quoteEn: Marx's study in the London Notebooks of pre-capitalist modes of production, Asiatic landownership and related questions was extremely important for the scientific understanding of capitalist social formation and its laws of development that he finally reached.
quoteZh: 马克思在《伦敦笔记》中对前资本主义生产方式、亚细亚土地所有制等问题的研究，对他最后形成关于资本主义社会形态和发展规律的科学认识极为重要。

glossary.explanation: Marx's 24 notebooks of extracts and notes on economics, history and colonialism, made in London in 1850–1853. They are published in MEGA2 Division IV, volumes 7–9, and the later notebooks remain incomplete.
Marx's 1858 outline for his critique of political economy in six books: capital, landed property, wage labour, the state, foreign trade and the world market. Scholars debate whether he abandoned it.
A label used by Marxist scholars for Western academic Marx studies that, in their view, separate Marx's thought into disconnected parts. It is used critically here.

Marx's term for forms of landownership in Asian societies, in which the despot or state is the supreme owner and village communities hold land. It is linked to his idea of an Asiatic mode of production.

t: The new industrial revolution and the development of socialism in the twenty-first century
zh: 新产业革命与21世纪社会主义发展
paras: Li Caiyan asks how the new industrial revolution, also called the fourth industrial revolution and driven by artificial intelligence, big data, cloud computing and digital networks, changes the conditions for socialism in the twenty-first century. The article argues that, as with the three earlier industrial revolutions, this one brings socialism both new challenges and new opportunities. Li holds that Marx's analysis of class relations remains valid and that socialism can use its institutional advantages to overcome the negative effects of the new technologies.

The article places twenty-first-century socialism on the footing of the new industrial revolution and examines four areas: the growth of productive forces and global polarisation, the subjectivity of the working class, the unity of the proletariat, and the free and all-round development of the human being. It draws on Chinese digital-economy statistics, PwC forecasts, Western left-wing scholars such as Judith Butler, Guy Standing and Kees van der Pijl, and protest movements in the United States, France and India. Li closes with a section on how socialism can respond.

Li's central move concerns class. Against Western and Russian scholars who propose plural agents of change or a 'new middle class', Li argues that gig workers and the 'precariat' remain workers, because Marx and Engels defined the proletariat by non-ownership of the means of production, not by the form of labour. Digital labour, in Li's account, still yields surplus value, only in a more concealed way. Automation, the 'double diamond' class structure and the 'digital divide' are said to sharpen class contradictions and revive class consciousness, as shown by Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests. Li then weighs digital media, which aid organisation, against fragmented workplaces, individualisation and competition between workers in developed and developing countries, which hinder unity. AI is described as both freeing people from drudgery and producing a 'new alienation'.

Li concludes that big data and the Internet of Things can make planning more scientific and supplement market allocation under the socialist market economy. Socialist relations of production, the author argues, can narrow the digital divide in pursuit of common prosperity, and the shared character of information technology fits socialist values. Citing Mao Zedong, Li warns against blind optimism and calls for careful institutional responses. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar uses Marxist class theory to interpret digital capitalism, platform labour and AI.
quoteEn: Science and technology in themselves have no value stance; the key lies in how people apply them.
quoteZh: 科学技术本身不具有价值立场，关键在人们如何应用它。

glossary.explanation: A goal of socialism in official Chinese discourse, meaning prosperity shared by all rather than by a few. It has been stressed especially since the early 2020s.
The official description of China's economic system since the 1990s, which combines market allocation of resources with public ownership and state guidance.
The gap in access to, use of and capacity to innovate with information technology between countries, regions and groups. Li treats it as a driver of wealth polarisation.

t: New features of capital movement in Western developed countries since the 21st century
zh: 21世纪以来西方发达国家资本运动的新特点
source: World Social Sciences (Shijie shehui kexue), 2023 no. 2
paras: Responding to Xi Jinping's call to understand correctly the characteristics and behavioural laws of capital, Hu Leming and Li Lianbo ask how capital has moved in the developed capitalist countries since 2000. The authors argue that capital accumulation always follows three logics of scale, space and power. In their account, these logics have unfolded fully since the 2008 financial crisis: capital achieves unprecedented accumulation, opens new spaces for valorisation and becomes a power that dominates everything. They say studying Western theories of capital helps to deepen understanding of capital's laws and to regulate capital's behaviour in China.

The article surveys mainly Western Marxist and critical scholarship, including Dan Schiller, Christian Fuchs, John Bellamy Foster, David Harvey, Brett Christophers, Jodi Dean and Cecilia Rikap-style work on rents and platforms. It is organised in five parts. After an introduction, it covers three new capital forms (digital, natural and financial capital), changes in how surplus is extracted (rentierism, economic rent, a new enclosure movement), and the spread of capital's logic from daily life to ideology. It closes with four lessons for China.

The authors argue that the three forms are all, in Marx's terms, circulating capital detached from material production. Digital capital is chiefly commercial capital, green capital is fictitious capital, and financial capital is a pure means of appropriating income. The three increasingly interlock, for example in the financialisation of platforms and in green finance. In the authors' reading, surplus is now extracted less through value creation than through rents, patents, digital 'enclosure' of the internet and what some scholars call neo-feudalism, so that contemporary capitalism shifts from producing value to distributing it. Capital also builds ideologies of its own: the claims that digital technology brings equality and that markets are the best route to environmental protection. It further reshapes everyday life through household debt and the digitalisation of leisure into labour.

The authors draw four lessons. Capital should be seen neither as a monster nor as a cure-all: as a production factor it can advance productive forces, but as a social relation it is exploitative. Markets and government regulation must both be improved to curb disorderly expansion. Social value norms, including the core socialist values, are needed as a third barrier where markets and government both fail. Finally, they contend that only the socialist market economy, based on public ownership with public capital as the leading form, can successfully harness capital. Read the original if you want a dense survey of Western critical theories of digital, green and financial capital, read from the standpoint of Chinese debates on regulating capital.
quoteEn: The rise of these three forms of capital shows that contemporary capitalism is increasingly shifting from emphasising the production of value to emphasising its distribution.
quoteZh: 这三种资本形态的兴起表明，当代资本主义日益从强调价值的生产转向强调价值的分配。

glossary.explanation: China's official economic system, adopted in the early 1990s, which combines market mechanisms with a leading role for public ownership and state guidance.
Capital owned by the state or collectives under public ownership. The authors treat it as the leading capital form in a socialist market economy.
A set of twenty-four characters of official values promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering the national, social and individual levels.

t: Foreign left-wing rethinking of the global climate crisis in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪国外左翼对全球气候危机的再思考
paras: This survey, published in World Socialism Studies in 2023, reviews how communist and workers' parties and left-wing scholars outside China have analysed the global climate crisis. Chen Feng reports that these actors link the crisis to capitalism, building on Marx's idea of a rift in the metabolism between humanity and nature. The article's main finding is that the foreign left treats socialism as the fundamental way out, while also proposing supplementary measures.

The review covers a wide range of sources: European and North American communist parties, the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties, the European Left Party and the Party for Socialism and Liberation. It also draws on scholars such as John Bellamy Foster, Andreas Malm, Michael Löwy, Martin Empson and Alex Callinicos. It is organised in four parts: the flaws of capitalist green policies, capitalism as the root of the crisis, socialism as the fundamental solution, and other practical routes.

According to Chen's account, the left argues that carbon taxes, carbon trading and "green growth" serve monopoly capital. In this reading they widen inequality, burden low-income groups, fuel what the article calls environmental racism, and reinforce an unjust international order. The surveyed authors hold that capitalism is in essence a fossil-fuel system driven by profit, short-termism and accumulation, so that green capitalism and technological innovation cannot resolve the contradiction. Against this, they present socialism as offering planning, public ownership of energy and finance, and democratic ecological planning. Several argue that the survival crisis will push people towards it.

Chen also reports the left's complementary proposals: curbing consumerism, fair carbon taxation, new jobs and retraining for workers leaving fossil-fuel sectors, left unity, and alliances between labour, environmental and other progressive movements. The conclusion is that the foreign left has deepened its critique of capitalism but still needs further theoretical and practical exploration. Read the original if you want a catalogue of the positions of Western communist parties and left scholars on climate, as presented from a Chinese academic standpoint.
quoteEn: The capitalist modes of production and distribution are the fundamental cause of the global climate crisis, so establishing a socialist system is the only correct choice for resolving it.
quoteZh: 资本主义的生产方式和分配方式是导致全球气候危机的根本原因，因而建立社会主义制度是解决气候危机的唯一正确选择。

t: The absolute limits of capital and their rational transcendence
st: With a commentary on Mészáros's "theory of going beyond capital"
zh: 资本的绝对界限及其合理超越
zhSub: 兼评梅扎罗斯的“超越资本论”
paras: Writing in 2023, Yan Yan asks how Marxists should assess István Mészáros's claim, in Beyond Capital, that capital runs into "absolute limits" and must therefore be superseded. The author sets this against a practical problem: Marx and Engels did not foresee a market economy under socialism, so they did not analyse how a socialist society should treat capital. Yan argues that Mészáros's analysis of the limits follows Marx's line of thought and develops Marxist critique of capital, but that his demand to supersede capital rests on a metaphysical, one-sided view that does not fit China's conditions.

The article first sets out Mészáros's position, presenting him as a Hegelian Marxist, a student of Lukács, who nonetheless rejects Hegel's "uncritical positivism". It then goes through four limits in turn: the conflict between transnational capital and nation-states; the destruction of the natural conditions of social metabolic reproduction; women's emancipation and substantive equality; and chronic unemployment and the population crisis. Each is discussed against opposing thinkers, including Kant, Hegel, Smith, the Club of Rome, Sombart, Weber, Hayek and Malthus. A final section evaluates Mészáros's overall theory.

In Yan's account, Mészáros holds that the "no alternative" ideology of bourgeois thinkers is mistaken. He argues that capital's drive to expand cannot be contained by the state, by scale economies, by technology or by redefining needs, and that each attempt to manage contradictions reproduces them on a larger scale. In the critical section Yan accepts the distinction Mészáros draws between capital and capitalism. Yan objects, however, that for Marx the target is mainly capital in its social attribute, capital under capitalist relations of production, not capital in general. On Yan's reading Mészáros therefore wrongly presents the choice as binary: either capital controls you or you destroy it. Because of this, Yan says, he declares market socialism absurd and overlooks the diversity of socialist models and the way a socialist market economy can bring out "the civilising side of capital" while curbing its negative side. Yan also argues that the Soviet problem lay in failing to use capital effectively, not in retaining it.

Yan concludes that "going beyond" Marx is legitimate only if it supplements and develops Marxism in light of capitalism's new changes, given the unfinished and open character of Capital. It is not legitimate if it aims to overturn Marxism's basic views and method. For China in the new era, Yan says, the task is not to supersede capital but to regulate and guide its healthy development, while recognising that capital promotes productive forces. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Mészáros's Beyond Capital and of how capital should be treated under socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteEn: What should be superseded is not capital in general (the natural attribute of capital) but capital in particular (the social attribute of capital).
quoteZh: 应该超越的不是资本一般（资本的自然属性），而是资本特殊（资本的社会属性）。

glossary.explanation: The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market mechanisms with public ownership and Party leadership.
The official name for China's path and system of socialism since the reform era, presented as adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions.
Mészáros's term for the way a society organises production, exchange and control; he treats capital as a total mode of such control.
In Mészáros's account, the inner limits of capital that cannot be overcome within the capital system and that ultimately require going beyond it.

t: Totality, totalization and negative dialectics
st: The idea of totality in foreign Marxism in the mid-twentieth century
zh: 总体性、总体化与否定的辩证法
zhSub: 20世纪中叶国外马克思主义的总体性思想
source: Journal of Beijing Normal University (Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 3
paras: How did the Marxist concept of totality change after Lukács revived it, and what stayed constant? Yang Haifeng argues that between the 1930s and the post-1970s period, totality shifted from a critical method and a utopian ideal to an object of suspicion, then to a reconstructed open totality. Through these shifts, Yang holds, the constant theme was critical reflection on capitalist society and the search for a better one.

The article proceeds in five stages. It examines the Frankfurt School's critical theory and Marcuse's negation; the humanist rereading of the 1844 Manuscripts by Marcuse, Henri Lefebvre and Erich Fromm; Jean-Paul Sartre's move from totality to totalization; Adorno's critique in Negative Dialectics; and post-Marxism (Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Derrida). Althusser appears briefly as someone who replaced the humanist basis of totality with an objective structural one.

Yang's central distinction is between totality as a fixed structure and totality as an open, unfinished process or a differently conceived whole. Horkheimer and Marcuse treat the organized, monopoly-capitalist whole as a reified pseudo-totality, which leads to total critique and Marcuse's Great Refusal. For Lefebvre and Fromm the 'total human being' is the aim of liberation. Sartre treats structure as congealed and dialectic as movement, using the progressive–regressive method. Adorno reads Hegel's world spirit as the mirror of commodity exchange and identity-thinking. He answers with non-identity and the 'constellation'. Laclau and Mouffe, and Derrida, dissolve essentialist totality in favour of open articulation and difference.

Yang credits post-Marxist deconstruction with questioning the post-Cold War 'end of history' and the power structures behind it. The article contends, however, that a loose totality with no dominant element cannot reveal the structure of society. Overstressing difference in a globalized world, Yang argues, risks erasing the ruling logic of capital. Yang concludes that drawing on modern philosophy while preserving Marxism's critical force still needs exploration. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-language genealogy of the totality concept from Lukács to post-Marxism, with close readings of Marcuse, Sartre and Adorno.
quoteEn: Compared with totality, totalization better displays the dialectic of Marx's philosophy.
quoteZh: 相比于总体性而言，总体化更能展现马克思哲学的辩证法。

t: Critique and transcendence of justice
st: On Agnes Heller's interpretation of Marx's theory of justice
zh: 正义的批判与超越
zhSub: 评赫勒对马克思正义理论的解读
paras: Does capitalism contain distributive justice, and does communist society transcend justice? Yan Yan takes up these questions through the Hungarian Marxist Agnes Heller, in particular her Beyond Justice and her writings on Marx's idea of justice. Yan argues that Heller mixes misreadings of Marx with useful ideas. Sorting the two, Yan holds, helps in building a Marxist theory of justice suited to China, where capital remains a production factor in the socialist market economy and the primary stage of socialism sets the context.

The article is organised in five parts. Four sections follow Heller on capitalist distributive justice, whether distribution according to labour can transcend justice, the alleged contradictions in Marx's principle of distribution according to need, and whether freedom or justice is more fundamental. A short closing assessment weighs the strengths and weaknesses of her position. Yan compares her with Marx, Adam Smith, Kant, István Mészáros, John Rawls, Jürgen Habermas and critics such as Jean Cohen and Michael Walzer.

Yan's central move is to separate Heller's "formal justice" from Marx's view that the mode of production determines distribution. Heller holds that market rules applied to everyone make capitalist distribution just. Yan replies that Marx does not deny this formal side but regards it as an empty appearance resting on an unjust mode of production. On distribution according to need, Yan rejects Heller's claim of a clash between unlimited needs and finite lives. Following Mészáros, Yan says unlimited needs are shaped by capital's logic, so Heller's ethical-value solution is a subjectivist utopia. Yan also traces her reading of communism as a merely regulative ideal to Kant. On freedom and justice, Yan sees her priority of freedom as shaped by hostility to Soviet-bloc socialism and by Eastern European dissident experience. Yan adds that whether communism transcends justice resembles the question of whether it abolishes the state: it can be called both a transcendence of justice and a new type of justice.

Yan concludes that Heller's theory is liberal and utopian in tendency and fails to grasp the unity of the empirical and transcendent dimensions of Marxism, or the coercive force of capital. Yan still credits her analysis of dynamic justice, plural needs and the opposition to fixed norms, and her question of how plural cultures can be bound together. Yan says her alternative to Rawls offers a useful reference for realising fairness and justice under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese-Marxist assessment of Heller on justice, with links to current debates on capital and the socialist market economy.
quoteEn: Although Heller has not fundamentally ended the dispute over justice, she has put forward a scheme different from Rawls's and prompted our thinking.
quoteZh: 赫勒虽然没有从根本上终结关于正义的论争，但却提出了不同于罗尔斯的方案，启发了我们的思考

glossary.explanation: An official thesis that China is still in an early phase of socialism, which justifies a market economy and a mix of ownership forms. It is regularly cited as China's most basic national condition.
The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up. It combines Party leadership, a socialist market economy and public ownership as the main body of the economy.

Marx's principle for the first stage of communism, from the Critique of the Gotha Programme, in which workers receive rewards in proportion to their labour. It is the principle China officially names as the main form of distribution under socialism.
Marx's principle for the higher stage of communist society, summed up as "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs".

t: Innovating the research paradigm of foreign Marxism
zh: 创新国外马克思主义研究范式
paras: Writing in September 2023, Lan Jiang argues that research on foreign Marxism in China, productive since the 1980s, has reached a turning point. With socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era, the author holds that the field must move beyond translating and analysing foreign Marxist thinkers. It should reinterpret them in Chinese discourse, take a problem-oriented approach, and contribute to building China's own independent system of knowledge.

The commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, has three parts. It first sets out the historical mission of introducing foreign Marxism after reform and opening up, then names problems in the field after three decades of growth, and finally proposes a new research framework. Lan describes the framework as a coordinate system with a vertical and a horizontal axis. Examples range from Lukács, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School to Baudrillard, John Bellamy Foster and debates on the digital economy.

Lan says early introduction of foreign Marxism supplied a critique of capitalism from inside its own mode of production, a perspective that socialist countries outside the West lacked. In Lan's view it also helped Chinese readers face Western capitalist elements while avoiding wholesale Westernisation. Two problems follow. Early work stressed texts over their historical setting, although thinkers such as Marcuse, Baudrillard and Foster answered concrete stages of capitalism. Foreign Marxists also read Marx through Western ideological discourse, as Erich Fromm did when he set a humanist young Marx against the later author of Capital. The vertical axis, Lan says, is the existing work by period, country and school, which risks cutting links across regions. The proposed horizontal axis would reframe the field with Chinese questions, concepts and discourse.

Lan calls for foreign Marxism to be read against the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and with resources from fine traditional Chinese culture. On the digital economy, Chinese scholars should not simply echo Marcuse, Stiegler or David Harvey. They should ask how to prevent new inequality from capital monopoly and let the digital economy benefit all. Lan sees this as a way to enrich philosophy, sociology, politics and communication studies, to show academic confidence, and to lay a creative basis for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism sees the field's methodological shift towards an autonomous Chinese knowledge system.
quoteEn: If, in introducing foreign Marxism, we ignore its specific historical background and merely analyse it literally from text to text, that may amount to nothing more than buying the casket and returning the pearl.
quoteZh: 如果我们在引介这些国外马克思主义的时候，忽略了其特定的历史背景，仅从文本到文本做字面上的解析，那可能只是一种买椟还珠式的行为。

glossary.en: China's own independent system of knowledge
glossary.explanation: A slogan in Chinese official and academic discourse, stressed in the 2020s, calling for social science built on Chinese concepts, questions and experience rather than Western frameworks.
The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist system and market mechanisms.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping since 2012–13, presented as China's vision for international relations and global governance.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
A Chinese academic field covering Marxist currents outside China and the Soviet tradition, including Western Marxism, French and Italian Marxism, analytical Marxism and ecological Marxism.

t: Monopoly capitalism over the past 40 years
zh: 过去40年的垄断资本主义
orig: Cambridge Journal of Economics, vol. 46, no. 6, 2022
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2023 no. 3
paras: This is a Chinese translation, abridged, of an article by the British economist Malcolm Sawyer (Leeds University Business School), first published in the Cambridge Journal of Economics in 2022. Sawyer asks how neoliberalism, globalisation and financialisation since about 1980 relate to the theory of monopoly capitalism. His thesis is that "actually existing neoliberalism" has in practice been monopoly capitalism, now transnational and financialised, and that it has produced slower growth and rising inequality.

The article opens with the analytical basis of monopoly-capitalism theory: industrial economics (structure–conduct–performance), Kalecki's "degree of monopoly" and the work of Keith Cowling. It then takes in turn neoliberalism, globalisation and financialisation. It follows with empirical evidence on industrial concentration, markups and "Big Tech", and a section on secular stagnation that draws on Steindl, Kalecki and Hansen. Most of the evidence is drawn from the United States and Britain.

Sawyer argues that neoliberal doctrine promises competitive markets, yet the era saw rising concentration, merger-driven consolidation and weak antitrust enforcement. Cowling and Sugden are cited for the view that multinationals strengthen monopoly power, not weaken it, as intra-firm trade and foreign direct investment grow. On financialisation, Sawyer holds that the pursuit of shareholder value and financial payments shifts income from wages to profits and weakens investment and innovation. Studies he cites report rising markups and concentration, with a large role for intangible assets and knowledge monopolies held by technology firms.
