quoteEn: Lenin, by contrast, proceeded from the practice of production and construction in Soviet Russia, exploring the path of construction while expounding the spirit of uniting firmness of principle and belief with flexibility of struggle tactics.
quoteZh: 列宁则是立足于苏俄生产建设的实践，一边进行生产建设并探索建设的路径，一边阐述把原则和信仰的坚定性与斗争策略的灵活性统一起来的精神。

glossary.explanation: A phrase Lenin used in 1918 and which Chinese leaders also use to stress independent development paths. Yu says that Lenin meant steadfastness and acting from actual conditions.
In Lenin's 1918 usage, capitalist enterprises linked to and supervised by the Soviet state, as an intermediate link towards socialism in a country dominated by small producers.
The scientific-management method of F. W. Taylor, based on time-and-motion study and standardised work. Lenin urged learning from it while reforming it.

keywords: Immediate Tasks of the Soviet Government

t: Theoretical programme and policy adjustments of the Socialist International since its split
st: An assessment
zh: 社会党国际分裂以来理论纲领与政策主张调整评析
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2023 no. 2
paras: Wang Zhao asks how the Socialist International has reshaped its theory and policy in the decade since the founding of the Progressive Alliance in 2013 split the social-democratic movement into two parallel international organisations. The article argues that the adjustments are an attempt to revive social democracy by turning left under the banner of "progressive politics". In Wang's assessment this turn has some progressive value, but it lacks theoretical innovation and, judged from scientific socialism, remains structurally limited.

The article has four parts. It first describes three predicaments since the split: organisational (member parties falling to 132 against 140 in the Progressive Alliance, weaker cohesion and fewer meetings), ideological, and financial (large Western European parties cutting or stopping their dues). It then examines changes to the theoretical programme and to policy in organisation, democracy, the economy, migrants and refugees, and climate. A closing assessment treats the features, effects and essence of these changes.

Wang reports that the Socialist International now presents "progressive politics" as its goal. It rejects neoliberalism's idea of freedom in favour of responsibility, treats equality as an organising principle, and gives new weight to solidarity, democracy and peace. Policy follows from this: dues are tied to voting rights, competitive leadership elections and a one-third minimum of women in the presidium, opposition to austerity, and a climate policy built on common but differentiated responsibilities. Wang characterises the changes as value-centred, pragmatic, eclectic and reformist, increasingly global in outlook, and positioned to the left of the Progressive Alliance, which the author places centre-right.

Wang concludes that the changes aim to adapt social-democratic values to a changed era and to redefine the movement's relationship with liberalism and neoliberalism. The article credits them with limiting further fragmentation and speaking for developing countries and the vulnerable. It faults them for a gap between theory and practice, tension between internationalism and national interests, and no systematic vision of progressive politics. From the standpoint of scientific socialism, Wang argues, the programme ignores class conflict and the class nature of the state and stays within capitalism, so its structural predicament will persist. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese academic account of the post-2013 Socialist International and how Chinese scholars assess social democracy.
quoteEn: The Socialist International's theory and policy carry a utopian colouring, and many of the measures it proposes remain confined to the level of theoretical propaganda.
quoteZh: 社会党国际的理论与政策带有乌托邦色彩，其提出的诸多措施仍然局限于理论宣传层面。

glossary.explanation: The worldwide association of social-democratic, socialist and labour parties, re-founded in 1951 at Frankfurt. Since the 2013 split its membership has been dominated by parties from developing countries.

A network of centre-left parties founded on 22 May 2013, led by Western European social-democratic parties, including Germany's SPD. Many of them left or downgraded their membership of the Socialist International.
The Marxist tradition that bases socialism on class struggle and the historical laws of capitalism. The author uses it as the yardstick for judging social democracy.

t: Between nationalism and internationalism: the evolution and political participation of the Communist Party of Israel
zh: 在民族主义与国际主义之间：以色列共产党的发展演变与政治参与
paras: Ge Shuzhen asks how the Communist Party of Israel has fared since its origins in Mandate Palestine, caught between Jewish and Arab national feeling and the proletarian internationalism it professed. The article argues that the party was never able to reconcile the two. Ge treats this tension as the root of its internal splits, its marginal place in Israeli politics and its limited influence.

The article is a historical survey in five parts. It begins with the Palestine Communist Party under the Mandate, from the Socialist Workers Party of 1919 and its admission to the Comintern in 1924. It then covers the reorganised party's activity after 1948, the 1965 split into Maki and Rakah, and the party's theoretical positions after the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union around 1989–91. A short conclusion assesses the party's difficulties.

Ge's central claim is that the party's early Jewish nationalist stance clashed with Comintern internationalism. Under Comintern and Soviet pressure the party moved from a Jewish to an Arab line in the 1930s, a shift Ge says wounded Jewish members and led to a wartime division. After 1948 the party defended Arab citizens' equality, workers' interests and opposed US and German aid, which Ge says kept it on the margins of a mostly Jewish society. Disputes over the Arab–Israeli conflict, Zionism, Arab nationalism and Soviet policy then split it in 1965. Ge reports that the Jewish-led Maki lost its seats and dissolved in 1975, while Rakah continued as the Communist Party of Israel, increasingly dependent on Arab votes.

Ge notes that since the 2000s the party has criticised contemporary capitalism, described socialism as a continually renewed path, and put forward a peace programme for Israel and Palestine. It has also kept democratic centralism and a Jewish–Arab democratic front. Even so, Ge argues, Arab nationalist parties have drawn away its Arab support, its parliamentary seats have not exceeded four since the 1990s, and its weak capacity for self-renewal and the low tide of world socialism limit its prospects. Ge says it must strengthen itself, widen its public influence and deepen cooperation with left forces abroad. Read the original if you study communist parties in the Middle East, the national question within Marxist parties, or the history of Arab–Jewish politics in Israel.
quoteEn: The essence of the split was that nationalism and internationalism do not naturally blend, which showed itself in serious political disagreement between the party's two wings.
quoteZh: 分裂的实质是民族主义与国际主义天然不易相融，表现则为党内两派政见严重不合。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist principle that workers and communist parties of all nations should act in solidarity across national lines. The Comintern used it to demand that national parties follow a common line.
The Soviet-led international organisation of communist parties, founded in 1919 and dissolved in 1943. It directed its member parties' policies.
A Leninist organisational principle combining internal discussion with binding obedience to majority decisions once taken.

t: "Geyi" and "reverse geyi": Western Marxism studies in China in the 1980s
st: Chinese research on Western Marxism around the 1980s
zh: “格义”与“反向格义”
zhSub: 20世纪80年代中国的西方马克思主义研究
paras: How did Chinese theorists understand Western Marxism when it entered China around the 1980s, in the era of reform and opening up and "thought liberation"? Chen Xiangqin argues that every study of a Western Marxist school, general or specific, was subordinate to a prior judgement about the nature of Western Marxism and its relation to Marxism. This produced a "geyi" and "reverse geyi" between Marxism modelled on the Soviet textbook system and Western Marxism, which in Chen's view enriched Chinese Marxist research and opened new theories and scholarship.

The article first traces the origins of Western Marxism's introduction, from translations of Lukács, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty in the 1960s–70s and the pioneering work of Xu Chongwen, to the research boom after the 1978 truth-criterion debate. It then divides the period into four stages: 1978–82, 1982–87, 1987–89 and 1989–91. Next it surveys debates on philosophical questions (practice, dialectics, materialism) and political ones (the critique of capitalism, of Soviet socialism, and theories of revolution and utopia). It ends with the 1988 Xu Chongwen–Du Zhangzhi controversy.

Chen's central distinction concerns direction. Initially the Soviet textbook was used to judge, or "geyi", Western Marxism as a bourgeois, revisionist current. In 1987–89 some scholars reversed the process, treating Western Marxism as part of Marxism's history and using ideas such as practical ontology, totality and subjectivity to question the textbook's "objective" dialectics and material monism. Most Chinese critics, Chen reports, rejected practice-ontology as idealism and held that Western Marxism shifted from political economy to philosophical and cultural critique, leaving only utopian longing. The 1988 debate turned on whether the concept exists, how to classify Western Marxism, and whether Marxism is "one" or "many". Chen notes that the disputants' criteria for what counts as Marxism differed.

Chen concludes that Western Marxism was the only Western current to become deeply entangled with Marxism in 1980s China, taking part in debates on humanism and alienation, subjectivity and enlightenment, and the form of Marxist philosophy. Chen holds that it advanced thought liberation by supplying resources for understanding contemporary capitalism and for reflecting on the Soviet model, freeing Chinese theory from dogmas of both Soviet and Western systems. The article presents the post-1989 outcome as a move towards "two-way geyi", studying Western Marxism under the guidance of Marxism. Read the original if you want a detailed periodisation of Chinese reception of Western Marxism and the Xu–Du debate, as told by a Chinese scholar.
quoteEn: It was precisely this forward or reverse "geyi" that made Chinese Marxist research flourish and develop, and opened up new Marxist theories, ideas and scholarship.
quoteZh: 正是这种正向或反向的“格义”,繁荣和发展了中国的马克思主义研究，开创了马克思主义的新理论、新思想和新学术。

glossary.explanation: A term from the early Chinese reception of Buddhism, when Buddhist ideas were explained through native Daoist and Confucian concepts. Chen uses it for interpreting and judging one body of Marxism through the categories of another.
Chen's term for the process, in 1987–89, of using Western Marxism to re-examine and criticise Soviet-textbook Marxism.
A slogan of the late 1970s and 1980s associated with the break from rigid, ideologically dogmatic thinking and the start of reform and opening up.
The policy launched in 1978 of economic reform and opening to the outside world.
The tradition of Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and others. Chinese debates in the 1980s disputed whether it counted as Marxism at all.
The codified, orthodox presentation of Marxist philosophy and political economy of Soviet manuals, which dominated Chinese Marxist research before 1978.

t: The Yucatán socialist movement in Mexico and its causes, 1917–1924
zh: 墨西哥尤卡坦社会主义运动始末及其成因（1917—1924）
source: Journal of Shanghai Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 3
paras: Between 1917 and 1924 a socialist movement in Mexico's Yucatán state produced a government proclaimed to be the 'first socialist regime in the Americas', led by Felipe Carrillo Puerto. The authors note that Chinese studies of Latin American history have said little about it and that no specialist article had appeared. They narrate the movement and then ask why it arose in Yucatán. Their answer is a combination of six factors, from the spread of socialist ideas to Carrillo's own leadership. The movement ultimately failed but left a lasting legacy.

The article has three parts. The first narrates the movement in two stages: a preparatory phase (1917–1922), from Carrillo's election as head of the Socialist Party to his governorship, and his period as governor (February 1922 until his murder on 3 January 1924). It lists his reforms in land, rationalist education, women's rights, Maya cultural revival and law. The second part analyses causes, and the conclusion assesses the failure and the movement's afterlife.

On causes, the authors argue that socialist ideas had circulated in Mexico since the nineteenth century, including through Ricardo Flores Magón and Zapata's movement, where Carrillo worked. Maya communal traditions, in their reading, offered a cultural basis for socialism. A sisal monoculture tied to US capital, with debt peonage, created a polarised society. They also argue that Salvador Alvarado's earlier top-down reforms mobilised the population, though he was no Marxist and favoured class conciliation. They credit the party and its 'resistance leagues', a fusion of party and government with democratic-centralist features, and Carrillo's organising ability and alliance with President Obregón. The authors also note that his reliance on local caciques later fed corruption.

The authors attribute the defeat to several factors. Carrillo lacked military backing, and sisal prices fell, which cut revenue. His use of caciques bred corruption, and his radical land decrees alarmed planters and foreign capital. His goals also ran against the federal government's direction, and Obregón could not protect him during de la Huerta's 1923 rebellion. They nonetheless trace his influence on Cárdenas's collectivisation and socialist education, on Mexican cultural nationalism and on later Latin American memory, citing Armando Bartra's link to Bolivia's communitarian socialism. Read the original if you study Latin American socialism, the Mexican Revolution or Chinese scholarship on foreign socialist experiments and want a detailed account of the Yucatán case.
quoteEn: Maya village communities were the cultural basis for the choice of socialism.
quoteZh: 玛雅村社是社会主义选择的文化基础。

t: Western Marxism's changing evaluations of Engels's philosophy and its "theoretical bombast"
zh: 西方马克思主义对恩格斯哲学评价的历史演变及“理论浮夸”
source: People's Forum · Academic Frontiers, November 2022 (first half)
paras: How have Western Marxists judged Engels's philosophy since 1923, and why? Yi Xianfei argues that their assessments passed through two turns, tracking changes in Western capitalism and divisions within Western Marxism. The article concludes that the critics' attacks on Engels amount to what Marx called theoretical bombast, produced by a lack of revolutionary practice.

The article reviews three currents in turn. These are early Western Marxism (Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci), the humanist Marxism of the mid-twentieth century (Merleau-Ponty, Sartre), and the scientistic current of the 1960s (Althusser, Colletti). For each, Yi sets out the criticisms of Engels under dialectics, ontology and epistemology, then lists the current's main features and explains its stance by political context, philosophical background and attitude to Marxism.

Yi argues that early Western Marxists rejected Engels's extension of dialectics to nature and found his concept of practice too narrow. Even so, they did not reject him wholesale, and they judged him from Marx's standpoint. Humanist Marxists, shaped by the Second World War and the rediscovery of Marx's 1844 Manuscripts, moved to a general rejection. They treated Engels as having no philosophy, took him as a separate individual, and judged him from existentialist or other standpoints. The scientistic current, led by Althusser, partly returned to Engels, praised his genius, and criticised him for inheriting Hegel's flawed dialectic and so making Marxism metaphysical. Yi also notes the principle of 'abandoning Engels to protect Marx', in which the periphery of a theory is revised to save its core.

Yi contends that these critiques mostly serve to set off each school's own theory by casting Engels as its opposite. In Yi's account Marx and Engels agreed on the dialectics of nature, and Western Marxist critiques of contemporary capitalism fit Engels's view of nature and society. Yi holds that the critics, cut off from proletarian revolutionary practice and tied to bourgeois or petty-bourgeois outlooks, produce inflated theory and will end as dust of history. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how Western Marxism has judged Engels, and of how that debate is framed within Chinese scholarship.
quoteEn: It can be said that Western Marxism's critique of Engels mostly serves to consolidate its own "distinctive" theory: it presupposes that Engels's thought is the opposite of its own and affirms itself by negating him.
quoteZh: 可以说，西方马克思主义对于恩格斯的批判更多的是为了巩固自己“异彩”的理论，即预设恩格斯的思想是自己理论的对立面，通过否定对方的方式来肯定自己。

glossary.explanation: The tradition of Marxist thought that began with Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s. It emphasises philosophy, culture and subjectivity, and is often contrasted with Soviet orthodoxy.
Engels's view that dialectical laws operate in nature as well as in history. Many Western Marxists reject it, holding that dialectics concerns only the relation between human subject and object.
A label used in Chinese scholarship for the move of dropping Engels's philosophy in order to keep Marx's thought intact. The article attributes it to the scientistic current.
The mid-twentieth-century current that read Marx through the early, humanist writings, such as the 1844 Manuscripts. In this article Sartre and Merleau-Ponty are its leading figures.

t: Rhythmanalysis: a new perspective in foreign Marxist critical theories of time
zh: 节奏分析：国外马克思主义时间批判理论的新视域
source: Frontiers of Foreign Social Sciences (国外社会科学前沿), 2022 no. 6
paras: Why do people feel short of time and anxious about falling behind, and what can Marxism say about it? Lu Bao takes up Henri Lefebvre's late concept of "rhythmanalysis", which the author says has received too little attention in Chinese scholarship. Lu argues that it extends Marxist social critique to the abstraction and politicisation of time, and can explain the present acceleration of social life.

The article has four sections. The first traces the genealogy of rhythmanalysis through Gurvitch, Bachelard, Nietzsche, Lukács, the Frankfurt School and Debord, and shows how Lefebvre set it against Freudian psychoanalysis. The second covers the shift from pre-modern cyclical time to capitalist accumulation time, drawing on Le Goff, Marx, Postone, E. P. Thompson and Foucault. The third turns to "hypermodernity" and social acceleration, citing Virilio, Rosa, Lipovetsky, Nowotny and Jonathan Crary. The fourth sets out a way out.

Lu's central claim is that capital splits time into labour time and life time, and then extends linear, homogeneous, abstract time from the factory into all of everyday life. In Lu's account, this is a "colonisation" of the everyday that reproduces capitalist relations through control of bodily rhythm. Lu then argues that in hypermodern society acceleration forms a closed, self-driving loop of technological, social and everyday acceleration. Its costs, as Lu lists them, are exhaustion, anxiety, depression, the commodification of life itself, the erosion of sleep, lost local identity and "systematic stupidity". Lu criticises accelerationism as a new technological determinism that ignores the need to change the relations of production.

Lu concludes that the answer is deceleration, not a return to pre-modern life: a relative, harmonised slowing in which technology, institutions and daily rhythm are brought into step, and natural cycles and linear time coexist. Lu finds an echo of this in the Book of Changes. Lu then turns to Marx's view that the measure of wealth will become disposable free time once capitalist private ownership is overthrown, which opens the way to a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Western Marxist theories of time, or critiques of social acceleration and want a Chinese reading that links them to Marx's labour-time analysis.
quoteEn: Rhythmanalysis is a means of understanding time and, through time, resisting time itself.
quoteZh: 节奏分析是理解时间并通过时间反抗时间本身的一种中介手段。

glossary.explanation: Henri Lefebvre's late method for studying how cyclical and linear rhythms of body, nature and society interact in everyday life. It treats the control of time as a mechanism of capitalist domination.

A term associated with Gilles Lipovetsky for a stage in which modernity is pushed to excess rather than replaced by postmodernity. The article uses it for the age of accelerated, urgent abstract time.
A current of thought holding that capitalism can be overcome by speeding up technological and productive development. The article criticises it as a variant of technological determinism.

t: Totality, totalization and negative dialectics
st: The idea of totality in mid-twentieth-century foreign Marxism
zh: 总体性、总体化与否定的辩证法
zhSub: 20世纪中叶国外马克思主义的总体性思想
source: Journal of Beijing Normal University (Social Sciences), 2023 no. 3
paras: Yang Haifeng asks how the concept of totality, revived by Lukács, changed in foreign Marxism from the 1930s to the post-1970s period. The article argues that totality shifted in both definition and orientation. It began as a critical method and a utopian ideal of the "total human being", became a target of critique once capitalist society was seen as a reified totality, and was then deconstructed and reconstructed by post-Marxism. Yang holds that one theme stays constant: reflection on and critique of capitalism, and the search for a better society.

The study moves through five stages. It starts with the Frankfurt School's critical theory (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse). It then covers readings of the 1844 Manuscripts by Marcuse, Lefebvre and Fromm. Next come Sartre's distinction between totality and totalization, and Adorno's critique of totality in Negative Dialectics. The last section treats postmodernism and post-Marxism (Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Derrida). Yang mentions Althusser's structural totality along the way.

Yang's first move is that the Frankfurt School saw the organised, monopoly capitalism that followed the First World War as a "pseudo-totality" built on reification and private ownership. Critical theory therefore opposes it with interdisciplinary, totalising critique, which in Marcuse becomes the "Great Refusal". The second move is Sartre's: he treats totality as a congealed, reified structure and totalization as an open, ongoing process, which in Yang's reading restores the movement of Marxist dialectics. The third is Adorno's. He reads Hegel's world spirit as the philosophical image of commodity exchange and its identity principle, a source of domination, and answers with non-identity and the "constellation".

Yang reads Laclau, Mouffe and Derrida as deconstructing closed, essentialist totality in order to build an open, non-dominating one. Yang sees positive value in this as a response to post-Soviet claims about the "end of history". Yang also argues that stressing difference and looseness makes it hard to reveal the structure of society and risks obscuring the dominance of the logic of capital under globalisation. In Yang's view, how to draw on modern philosophy while keeping Marxism's critical force still needs exploration. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, the Frankfurt School or Sartre and post-Marxism and want a long, text-based account of how totality evolved as a concept.
quoteEn: Compared with totality, totalization better shows the dialectics of Marx's philosophy.
quoteZh: 相比于总体性而言，总体化更能展现马克思哲学的辩证法。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese academic field covering Marxist currents outside China, including Western Marxism, the Frankfurt School and post-Marxism.
A concept from Hegel and Marx, revived by Lukács, of society as an interconnected whole that must be grasped as such rather than in fragments.
Sartre's term for the dynamic, never-completed process of unifying society and knowledge, as opposed to a fixed totality.
Marcuse's term for a radical rejection of the established one-dimensional society.
A current associated with Laclau and Mouffe, shaped by postmodernism, that rejects essentialism and economic determinism in Marxism.

t: The political narrative of the rise and decline of "labour socialism" in Brazil's Workers' Party
zh: 巴西劳工党“劳工社会主义”兴衰逻辑的政治叙事
paras: Why did Brazil's Workers' Party (PT), which governed from 2003 to 2016 under the banner of "labour socialism", rise and then fall? Wang Shaoyuan argues that this doctrine could achieve only limited results. In the short run its effects depended on whether the international market environment favoured Brazil. In the long run, Wang contends, it was not a scientific governing philosophy, because it left untouched the domestic factors that constrain Brazilian growth.

The article first sets out the party's "labour socialism", adopted as its guiding ideology in 1990, and its policy approach of change through peaceful, gradual means and of winning the interests of the "C class", the so-called new middle class. It then divides the PT's time in office into a prosperous phase (2003–2010, under Lula) and a declining phase (2011–2016, under Rousseff). It uses figures on GDP growth, exports, minimum wages, credit, poverty and the Gini coefficient. A final section reflects on why the party lost power.

Wang's core claim is that the PT's success came from resisting neoliberalism, while its decline came from never abandoning capitalism. Lula kept parts of Cardoso's neoliberal framework, including fiscal and monetary austerity, a floating exchange rate and inflation targeting, and appointed orthodox figures to economic posts. Growth rested on commodity exports, rising minimum wages and consumer credit. When external conditions turned, the article reports structural supply problems, inflation, a deteriorating current account and persistent income polarisation. It also describes a party split over identity, with critics seeing a "left government without a left agenda". Wang names three failings. Labour socialism is not scientific socialism. The party lost ideological leadership by lurching between developmentalism and neoliberalism. It also lacked the people as a real subject, covering the gap with "radical democracy" and broad alliances.

Wang concludes that the PT must keep its original socialist aims while adjusting to history's laws and to national and world conditions, and must stand firmly with the people. The article notes Lula's 2022 candidacy and Bolsonaro's weak record as signs that the left may return. It also says the Brazilian case matters for China in guarding against neoliberal erosion and building socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Latin American left governments, with the economic data and a critique based on scientific socialism.
quoteEn: The "rise" came from resistance to neoliberalism; the "decline" came from not fully abandoning capitalism, and from trying through reform to overcome the peripheral and dependent position of Third World countries in the world capitalist system.
quoteZh: “兴盛”是由于对新自由主义的反抗，“衰落”是由于对资本主义没有彻底抛弃，而是用改良的办法企图克服第三世界国家在世界资本主义体系中的边缘和依附地位。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current path and system, associated with reform and opening up from the late 1970s. The article invokes it as the setting in which Brazil's experience is relevant for China.
The guiding ideology the Brazilian Workers' Party adopted in 1990. The article presents it as a moderate, pluralist left outlook that opposes capitalist exploitation but seeks gradual reform.
The Marxist term for socialism grounded in historical materialism and the analysis of capitalism's contradictions. The article uses it as the standard against which labour socialism is judged.

t: The predicaments facing the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre) and how to overcome them
zh: 尼共（毛主义中心）面临的困境与克服
paras: Tang Xin examines the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre), described as one of Nepal's two largest communist parties and its third-largest party overall. The article argues that, since the republic was founded in 2008, the party has lost its earlier edge and faces long-standing difficulties. Whether it overcomes them, Tang contends, will shape the direction of the whole Nepali communist movement.

The article first sets out four predicaments: identity, organisation, mass base and external pressure. It then reviews the party's own diagnosis and response in the political report of its Eighth Congress (26 December 2021 to 2 January 2022). A final section assesses early results and prospects in the run-up to the 2022 general elections, drawing on the party's performance in the 2017 elections and the May 2022 local elections.

On identity, Tang argues that the party has become an electoral, within-the-system party. It dropped armed struggle and the language of "protracted people's war" and new democratic revolution, and its patriotism is questioned over its stance on the US Millennium Challenge Corporation compact. On organisation, Tang points to the 2012 split, Baburam Bhattarai's 2015 exit, the failed 2018 merger into the Nepal Communist Party and weak democratic centralism. The mass base has shrunk, Tang says, as vote totals fell and corruption and opportunism spread. The party is also squeezed between the Nepali Congress and the CPN (UML). The Eighth Congress report, in Tang's account, declares Nepal to be in a socialist-revolution stage and calls for a united front, party discipline and self-criticism.

Tang concludes that the party's first task is to keep its political influence, which it did for now through its coalition with the Nepali Congress. Its way out of the identity crisis, Tang says, is theoretical innovation, because the Congress report does not clearly distinguish its line from the UML's "people's multiparty democracy". Tang also calls for broad communist unity, with theoretical dialogue and management of factionalism. The article further urges firmer defence of national sovereignty, proletarian internationalism and closer ties with the Communist Party of China and the People's Republic of China. Read the original if you follow Nepali communist politics, or want a Chinese academic assessment of a Maoist party's move into parliamentary politics.
quoteEn: The question of guiding ideology and fundamental line is the basic way out of crisis and predicament for the CPN (Maoist Centre), and also the foundational issue that the continued development of the Nepali communist movement must face.
quoteZh: 指导思想和根本路线问题是尼共（毛主义中心）摆脱危机和困境的根本出路，同时也是尼泊尔共产主义运动继续发展必须面对的基础问题。

glossary.explanation: The Leninist organisational principle by which a party debates freely but acts in unity under decisions of higher bodies. Tang uses it as the standard against which the Nepali party's internal practice is judged.

A strategy of allying with other classes, organisations and parties around shared goals while keeping the party's leading role. The article presents it as the Maoist Centre's proposed route to broader unity.
The Maoist strategy of protracted armed struggle based on mass mobilisation. The Nepali Maoists waged one from 1996 until the 2006 peace agreement.
Mao Zedong's concept of a revolution led by the proletariat against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism, as a stage before socialism. Hardline Nepali Maoists kept it as their goal.
The principle that communist parties and workers of all countries should act in solidarity. Tang urges the Nepali party to keep it and to strengthen ties with China.

t: Principles and methods for building an autonomous knowledge system in the study of foreign Marxism
zh: 国外马克思主义研究自主知识体系建构的原则与方法
source: Marxist Theory Discipline Studies (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2023 no. 5
paras: Han Qiuhong asks how the study of foreign Marxism, a second-level discipline within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory, can build its own autonomous knowledge system in line with the call to accelerate a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that the system must rest on Marxism and the results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that the field has already moved from following its object to a more independent, dialogical research model.

The article has three parts. The first presents the basic framework of the discipline as "one theory, two histories": an introduction to foreign Marxism, the history of Marxism's worldwide spread and theoretical development, and the history of foreign Marxism research in China. The second sets out a methodological stance called "one body, two faces". The third proposes a practical route, "one core, three dimensions", covering the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems.

Han divides Chinese research since Xu Youyu's 1982 book into three paradigms: a "nature" debate over whether Western and foreign Marxism is Marxism at all, an intellectual-history paradigm of translation and textual study, and a problem-oriented paradigm engaging Western scholars on digital capitalism, biopolitics, ecological crisis and artificial intelligence. The "one body" is Marxism as guide. The "two faces" are facing China and the world, and facing reality (critiques of capitalism and modernity) and the future (scientific socialism and the international communist movement). Han treats foreign Marxism as a source of critical concepts and academic targets but warns against copying it. The article lists, as deviations to be criticised, replacing proletarian revolution with the "multitude", ecological crisis replacing economic crisis, and "green parties" replacing proletarian parties.

Han concludes that the discipline should define its place within Marxist theory and train scholars versed in both Chinese and Western thought. It should renew its academic paradigms by returning to Marx and the classics, and build original discourse that draws on the conceptual vocabulary of foreign Marxism without adopting its methods wholesale. The guiding principles are a Chinese standpoint, Chinese problems and the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese specialist in foreign Marxism frames the field's history, its guiding principles and its purpose for Chinese Marxist theory.
quoteEn: The history of foreign Marxism research is the scholarly course through which we, as the research subject, have studied foreign Marxist theory.
quoteZh: 国外马克思主义研究史是我们作为研究主体对国外马克思主义理论进行研究的学术历程

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party theory: combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture.

glossary.zh: 中国特色哲学社会科学
glossary.en: philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The official aim of building Chinese philosophy and social sciences with their own disciplinary, academic and discourse systems under Marxist guidance. It is often linked to Xi Jinping's 2016 and later speeches.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formulation for developing Marxism by tying it to China's conditions and to contemporary conditions.

A concept in current Party discourse for a body of knowledge produced from Chinese standpoints and problems rather than borrowed from the West. It is said to underpin the discipline, academic and discourse systems.
The author's shorthand for the basic knowledge framework of a discipline: general principles, the world history of the field's theory, and its history in China.
The broad Chinese term for Marxist currents outside China. It includes, but is wider than, Western Marxism.

t: Lenin's conception of cultural anti-poverty work in a socialist state and its implications
zh: 列宁关于社会主义国家文化反贫困的构想及其启示
paras: Lin Ke asks how Lenin, during the New Economic Policy (NEP) period in Soviet Russia, conceived of lifting the masses out of "cultural poverty" and what this offers present-day China. The article argues that Lenin's approach joined the leadership of the Marxist party with the principal role of the people, and that its methodological lessons can inform a Chinese anti-poverty discourse. Lin notes that existing scholarship has dwelt on Lenin's basic principles or their sinicisation, leaving this practical side less studied.

The article has five sections. The first treats the socialist system as the basic guarantee for eliminating cultural poverty; the second, the vanguard party's guiding role in changing social attitudes; the third, embedding propaganda and education in everyday life. The fourth examines the parallel pursuit of enlightenment and political mobilisation, and the fifth draws lessons for China. Lin draws on Lenin's speeches and drafts, Soviet literacy and education measures, and the system of worker and peasant correspondents.

Lin's central claim is that cultural anti-poverty work needs a socialist institutional base, such as the People's Commissariat for Education and the literacy campaign. It also needs a vanguard that moves the masses from intuitive, emotional grievance to rational understanding of a complicated revolution, including the use of state-regulated capitalism under the NEP. Propaganda must be tied to practical livelihood questions, with newspapers presenting concrete local experience instead of abstract slogans. Lin singles out the worker and peasant correspondents, who wrote for the press and fed material to the Workers' and Peasants' Inspectorate on bureaucracy and corruption. In Lin's reading, this turned readers from an audience into agents of revolutionary consciousness and of supervision.

Lin draws three lessons for China. The Party's vanguard role should guide changes in social attitudes, tying Chinese modernization to material conditions and advanced socialist culture. Varied forms of participation should turn popular aspirations into conscious action against poverty, supporting whole-process people's democracy. Cultural work should follow the principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability, avoiding impatience and rashness. Read the original if you want a close account of how Lenin's cultural and propaganda thinking is linked to China's current anti-poverty and governance discourse.
quoteEn: When a socialist state carries out cultural anti-poverty work, it should follow the general tone of seeking progress while maintaining stability and foster a public consciousness of seeking truth from facts, which helps it keep the initiative in overcoming all kinds of risks and challenges on the path of Chinese modernization.
quoteZh: 社会主义国家开展文化反贫困，应贯彻稳中求进工作总基调，在公众中推动形成坚持实事求是的社会意识，有助于在中国式现代化道路中把握战胜各类风险挑战的主动权。

glossary.explanation: The idea that poverty has a cultural and ideological dimension, such as illiteracy and backward attitudes, to be tackled alongside material poverty. Here the author applies it to Lenin's educational and propaganda policies.
The policy Soviet Russia adopted from 1921, allowing limited private trade and state-regulated capitalism after War Communism.
The official term for China's path of modernization as set out by the Party, especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
An official concept, promoted by Xi Jinping, describing Chinese democracy as covering all stages of governance, not only elections.
The Party's general guiding tone for economic and other work, favouring steady, gradual advance over abrupt change.

t: Foreign Marxist scholarship on digital capitalism
zh: 国外马克思主义学者关于数字资本主义的研究
paras: This review surveys how Marxist scholars outside China have studied digital capitalism, which the authors define as the digital economy under capitalist relations of production. The authors find that this scholarship is strong on critique but weak on forward-looking proposals. They add that it suffers from four tendencies, which they set out in an assessment at the end.

The review follows the historical course of digital capitalism in three stages. The first, from the post-war US information industry to the dot-com crash of 2001, is the stage of germination. The second, from 2001 to the financial crisis of 2008, is expansion and crisis. The third, from 2008 onwards, is decline followed by a recovery from about 2014 with mobile internet. It draws on Dan Schiller, Herbert Schiller, Christian Fuchs, Nick Dyer-Witheford, Hardt and Negri, Bernard Stiegler, Nick Srnicek, Fredric Jameson and others, on themes such as digital labour, immaterial labour, the culture industry, the digital divide and surveillance.

In the authors' account, foreign Marxists generally keep to historical materialism and stress that state power and commercial interests shaped digital technology. In their assessment, however, recent work leans towards cultural and ideological topics such as digital fetishism and cultural hegemony. It therefore drifts from material production and offers little on building a new economic base. The authors also say the literature stretches the category of labour to cover everyday activity and dissolves the proletariat into the "multitude", which they call a retreat from class analysis. Many works treat digital capitalism as a new historical formation, whereas the authors hold that it remains within large-scale machine industry and Marx's second social formation. In their view data has value only because of labour and capital invested in it. They also charge that the literature neglects the theory and practice of twentieth-century socialist countries.

The authors conclude that digital capitalism has not escaped capitalism's crisis tendencies. They point to platform cooperativism and online occupation movements as signs that digital tools can serve proletarian struggle. They suggest that "digital socialism" may emerge in developing countries, citing China's policy limits on capital in the digital economy and the early results of the sharing economy and digital commons. They propose public ownership of data and the use of digital technology for centralised, dynamically adjusted planning. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western digital-capitalism theory, with a broad bibliography of the field.
quoteEn: Foreign Marxist scholars' research on digital capitalism still follows a narrative logic dominated by Western-centrism.
quoteZh: 国外马克思主义学者关于数字资本主义的研究仍然遵循西方中心主义主导的叙事逻辑

glossary.explanation: A prospective socialist form of the digital economy that the authors associate with practice in developing countries. They link it to public ownership of data and planning supported by digital technology.
The broad field of Marxist thought outside China, wider than the specific tradition called Western Marxism.

The Marxist view that the interaction of productive forces and relations of production, and of economic base and superstructure, drives history. The authors use it as their standard for assessing the literature.
Hardt and Negri's term for the new form of the proletariat under immaterial labour. The authors criticise its use as a replacement for the proletariat.

t: On the theoretical preconditions of research on foreign Marxism
zh: 论国外马克思主义研究的理论前提
paras: Juan Hongfei asks what foundations Chinese research on foreign Marxism must rest on, given the field's growth and, in the author's view, its fragmentation. The article argues that the field has paid too little attention to its own theoretical preconditions, which has seriously hampered its development. It names three: the study of Marx's thought, the history of ideas, and the real history of the twentieth century.

The article is organised in three sections, one for each precondition, and ends with a short summary. It takes in the Western Marxism of Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci, humanist and scientistic Marxism, and the pluralised currents after 1968, including feminist, ecological and digital-capitalism critiques. It also covers the neo-Marxism of Eastern Europe and the changing attitude of Chinese scholarship since reform and opening up.

First, Juan holds that foreign Marxism should be judged by its stance and method, not by whether it uses Marx's concepts. Grasping Marx's thought as a whole is therefore the base for judging these currents. Humanist and scientistic Marxism, in this reading, each take only one of two logics that are unified in Marx: human emancipation and the critical analysis of capitalism in Capital. Second, the history of ideas supplies the wider view. It lets researchers place new thinkers and concepts, avoid chasing novelty, link thinkers across schools, and see how Chinese attitudes moved from negative criticism to positive borrowing and from indirect appropriation to direct dialogue. Third, each major turn in foreign Marxism is tied to a real historical problem. These include the contrast between the October Revolution and the failed European revolutions, the May 1968 upheaval, the 2008 financial crisis, and the Eastern European experience of socialist reform.

Juan concludes that foreign Marxism can be correctly located, and used as a resource for building Marxist theory in China, only when these three foundations are combined. The article criticises the long-dominant 'introduce and review materials' paradigm for detaching theorists from their social and intellectual contexts. It also calls for dialogue between Chinese and foreign Marxism in light of the 'great changes unseen in a century', while maintaining the leading position of Marxism. Read the original if you want to understand how a Chinese scholar sets out the methodological premises and aims of the foreign Marxism field in China.
quoteEn: The study of Marx's thought is of foundational significance for research on foreign Marxism.
quoteZh: 马克思思想研究对于研究国外马克思主义来说具有根基性意义。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese academic field and sub-discipline covering Marxist thought and socialist practice outside China. It includes Western Marxism, foreign Communist Parties' theory and Western left critiques of capitalism.
The tradition begun by Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci after the October Revolution and the failure of revolutions in Europe. It is a narrower category than foreign Marxism.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.en: great changes unseen in a century
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Chinese official discourse, notably by Xi Jinping, for the current shifts in the global political and economic order.

t: The poverty of Popper's critique of communism
st: With a discussion of historical laws and the necessity of communism
zh: 波普尔共产主义批判的贫困
zhSub: 兼论历史规律和共产主义的必然性
paras: Karl Popper's doubts about communism, set out in The Poverty of Historicism and The Open Society and Its Enemies, have been influential. Wei Xu argues that his critique is itself "impoverished": it treats communism as a form of historicism, rests on his theory of knowledge growth, and contains an "Achilles' heel" in the relation between knowledge growth and the course of history. The author contends that Marx's argument for communism strikes exactly this weak point.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Popper's chain of five theses against historicism, his falsifiability criterion and his alternative of "piecemeal engineering". The second exposes the ambiguities and conservative standpoint behind this reconstruction and shows how Popper misreads Marx. The third sets out Marx's grounds for historical laws and for communism, drawing on Engels, Lenin and Lukács, and closes with a note on China's experience.

Wei argues that Popper concedes too much: he allows testable social-scientific predictions, partial regularities, holistic "Gestalt" study and trends, yet still denies any prediction of history. His demarcation criterion, in Wei's view, only fixes what counts as "science" and does not settle whether historical claims are true. The fact that knowledge shapes history does not rule out laws or trends that knowledge growth cannot divert. Against this, Wei presents the laws of historical materialism as abstracted from the structure of society as a whole. They do not require omniscience about history, and they are conditional, resting on the movement of the productive forces. Communism is then derived in two steps: productive forces advance cumulatively because production is continuous, creative and irreversible, and capitalist private property negates itself through the contradiction between socialised division of labour and private ownership, the "negation of the negation" described in Capital.

Wei concludes that communism is a natural-historical process, grounded in laws and reliable trends, and compatible with an open future. Wei adds that historical materialism meets Popper's own criterion of falsifiability, while progress toward public ownership is better called a "trend" that needs dialectical thinking. The article closes by presenting the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization as further empirical evidence for the necessity of communism. Read the original if you want a Marxist reply to Popper's anti-historicism that engages his epistemology in detail and sets out the logic of Marx's case for communism.
quoteEn: Popper's critique of communism has an \"Achilles' heel\": it arises from his using his study of the growth of human knowledge as the thesis for his anti-historicism, which exposes the poverty of his theory.
quoteZh: 波普尔对共产主义的批判存在“阿喀琉斯之踵”，这源于他将对人类知识增长问题的研究用作反历史主义的论纲，暴露出了理论的贫困。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up. It combines public ownership with a socialist market economy under Party leadership.
An official concept, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022), describing China's own path to modernization as distinct from Western models.
The Marxist theory that the development of productive forces and relations of production shapes society's economic base and superstructure. The article treats its laws as scientific.
Popper's term for cautious, partial and revisable social reform, which he contrasts with holistic social planning.

t: The historical evolution and development trends of the socialist movement in West Asia and North Africa
zh: 西亚北非地区社会主义运动的历史演进与发展趋势
source: Journal of China Executive Leadership Academy Pudong, 2023, vol. 17, no. 1
paras: Chai and Lian ask how socialism has developed in the Arab region of West Asia and North Africa, and where it is heading. They argue that, as nationalist and political-Islamist forces weaken, Arab left-wing parties and communist parties in Turkey, Iraq, Egypt and elsewhere are becoming more active. In their view the movement is still growing, but it remains weak and of limited political influence.

The article moves from ideas to organisations to the present day. It first examines Arab socialism, from Michel Aflaq's 1940s formulation to the state-led socialisms of Nasser's Egypt, Algeria, Syria, Iraq and Libya. It then sorts the region's left-wing parties into Marxist, socialist and nationalist types. Next it surveys the period since the "Arab Spring" country by country, covering Egypt, Tunisia, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Turkey, and ends with the movement's features and trends.

The authors identify three shared traits of Arab socialism. It aims at national liberation and unity, with the Palestine question as its test. It is strongly nationalist, treating socialism as a means to national revival. It is rooted in Islam, which the authors say left parties see as containing egalitarian elements, while opposing Islamist fundamentalism. They argue that communist parties were hampered by dogmatism, dependence on the Soviet Union, poor understanding of national conditions and wavering positions on the national question. The authors also say many regimes used a socialist label to cover ethnic, nationalist or religious aims.

Chai and Lian describe the present movement as engaged in national politics, focused on left unity (for example the Arab Left Forum), and keen on ties with the Communist Party of China. They expect parties to adjust theory and policy flexibly, to sharpen their socialist profile after the pandemic, and to need considerable time before rising as a whole. They give the main obstacle as the dominance of political Islam and populism, and the left's lack of agreement on how to respond. Read the original if you want a party-by-party survey of Arab and Turkish left organisations, written from a Chinese perspective that stresses their friendly relations with the Chinese Communist Party.
quoteEn: Arab socialism comes in all varieties; it is a miscellany.
quoteZh: 阿拉伯社会主义各式各样，是个大杂烩。

glossary.explanation: A range of nationalist, Islam-influenced socialist doctrines and state policies, dating from the 1940s and associated with Aflaq, Nasser and the Ba'ath parties. It treats national liberation and Arab unity as the first task and socialism as a third path between capitalism and communism.

The wave of protests and regime changes that began in Tunisia in late 2010 and spread across the Arab world. The article puts the term in quotation marks and treats it as an opening for left parties as well as for Islamist forces.
Movements and parties that seek to base political authority and policy on Islam. The article treats them as the main rival that squeezes the space of the Arab left.

t: How to kill the greedy capitalist glutton: reading Nancy Fraser's Cannibal Capitalism
zh: 如何干掉贪婪的资本饕餮——解读南希·弗雷泽的《食人资本主义》
source: China Book Review (Zhongguo tushu pinglun), 2023 no. 3
paras: This is a review essay on Nancy Fraser's Cannibal Capitalism (Verso, 2022). Lan asks why Fraser calls contemporary capitalism, especially after the Covid-19 pandemic, 'cannibal', and how it 'eats' people. Lan's answer is that the book marks Fraser's break with the feminist identity politics and redistributive reformism of her early career, and her return to a thoroughgoing critique of the capitalist system itself.

The review first traces Fraser's intellectual path: her feminist and Frankfurt School background, her debate with Axel Honneth over recognition and redistribution, and the later influence of Rahel Jaeggi. It then turns to the two resources Fraser draws on, Marx's critique of political economy and Karl Polanyi's The Great Transformation. It closes with the book's periodisation of capitalism, its account of the financial stage, and its reading of the pandemic.

Lan argues that Fraser first treated redistribution as a supplement to Honneth's recognition theory, but that this already implied capitalism cannot solve inequality from within. A 2016 conversation with Jaeggi, later published as Capitalism: A Conversation in Critical Theory (2018), pushed her to see capital as a self-propelling subject that feeds on humans. Fraser then extends Marx: exploitation of workers rests on the 'expropriation' of colonies, racialised groups, women's care work and nature. Following Polanyi, she separates the economic system from the social and natural conditions that make it possible. In Fraser's periodisation, merchant, liberal-colonial, state-managed and now financialised capitalism each consume these foundations in new ways. The ouroboros on the cover expresses a system that devours its own base. Lan's example is the care work that financialised firms commodify, such as paying for surrogacy and egg freezing for female employees.

Lan concludes that Fraser regards the pandemic as the point where the contradictions of cannibal capitalism converge, and as proof that the system must be abolished. Lan reads the book as showing that equality can only be reached by discarding the capitalist order, and ends with Fraser's call to 'starve the beast'. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Fraser's shift from recognition politics to anti-capitalist critique, or a concise map of her debts to Honneth, Jaeggi, Marx and Polanyi.
quoteEn: So the way to resolve the exploitation and oppression of the lower strata by capitalism is not identity politics, nor a politically correct cultural politics, but Marx's critique of political economy.
quoteZh: 所以，解决底层被资本主义剥削和压迫的问题，不是身份政治，不是讲究政治正确的文化政治学，而是马克思的政治经济学批判。

t: The genesis, theoretical construction and contemporary value of Lenin's organisational building
st: A re-examination from the perspective of democratic centralism
zh: 列宁加强组织建设的生成逻辑、理论建构与时代价值
zhSub: 基于“民主集中制”视域下的再考察
paras: Liu Jinxu and Li Genshou ask how Lenin's thinking on Party organisation, and above all his doctrine of democratic centralism, arose, what it consisted of, and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. They argue that Lenin inherited Marx and Engels's Party-building theory and shaped it through the practical problems of the Russian revolution. In their view it remains a classic body of theory with direct lessons for the Party's governance.

The article, published in Tangdu Journal in 2023, has three parts. The first traces the origins of Lenin's thinking in Marx and Engels's Party theory and in Russian revolutionary practice, from the 1890s to the formal adoption of democratic centralism at the Fourth Congress of the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party in 1906. The second reconstructs the theory itself. The third draws out four lessons for the present.

In reconstructing the theory, the authors identify four concerns. The first is organisation: a tightly disciplined vanguard, with Party members' quality prized over their numbers, against Menshevik proposals for a looser membership. The second is democracy: the Party congress as supreme authority, convened regularly, with elected rather than appointed committees whose members can be recalled. The third is members' agency: rights to be informed and to decide, and wider discretion for local organisations. The fourth is unity: free discussion and comradely criticism, minority rights, majority rule and a single programme and statute, together with opposition to the Economists, the Mensheviks and factionalism. The authors present these as developing the Marx–Engels model of congresses, elections and reporting systems.

For the present, the authors draw four lessons. They call for a better-developed institutional system, so that institutional strengths become governance capacity. They call for stricter discipline and Party spirit, with the Party's self-reform leading social revolution; they cite figures from anti-corruption investigations since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They also urge holding to a people-centred stance and upholding collective leadership together with the Two Upholds. Democratic centralism is described as the Party's greatest institutional advantage. Read the original if you want to see how Lenin's Party-building is turned into a Chinese Party-building agenda, and how Chinese scholarship links Lenin to current Party discipline and leadership.
quoteEn: Democratic centralism, as an institutional norm, has correctly handled and strictly regulated political life within our Party, protected relations between Party and masses and the interests of the people, and ensured that Party policies are correctly formulated and effectively implemented; it is our Party's greatest institutional advantage.
quoteZh: 民主集中制”作为一种制度准则，正确处理并严格规范了我们党内的政治生活，维护了党群关系和人民利益，确保了党的政策方略的正确制定和有效执行，是我们党最大的制度优势。

glossary.explanation: The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining internal democracy (elections, discussion) with centralised discipline and subordination of minority to majority. The Communist Party of China treats it as its basic organisational principle.
An official term for the Party's efforts to correct its own errors and purge corruption and misconduct, presented as the Party's way of staying vigorous and avoiding decay.
The official requirement to uphold the authority of General Secretary Xi Jinping as the core of the Central Committee and the Party's centralised, unified leadership.

t: The rebuilding of community: a historical-materialist examination of Chinese modernization
zh: 共同体的重建：中国式现代化的历史唯物主义审视
paras: Yan Song asks how Chinese modernization relates to the dissolution of community under capitalism, and answers that it rebuilds community in a way Western modernization cannot. In Yan's account, Western modernization dissolved traditional communities and put in their place a "false community" in the form of the capitalist state. Chinese modernization, drawing on Marx's ideas about modernity, is said to produce a different path, expressed in what the article calls Xi Jinping's thought on community.

The article is in three parts. The first traces the dissolution of community in Western modernization: civil society and the political state, atomised individuals, commodity and capital fetishism, and the harms caused within capitalist states and across the world system. The second sets out four kinds of community in Xi's discourse: a community with a shared future for mankind, together with its cyberspace variant; the Chinese nation community; the social governance community; and the human–nature community of life. The third assesses the theoretical, institutional and practical significance of this rebuilding. Yan notes that existing scholarship tends to treat each type separately.

Yan's central move is to read Marx's critique of civil society and the state as showing that capitalist modernity turns people into atomised wage-labourers. In this reading, the bourgeois state offers only formal belonging and welfare that secure the capitalist mode of production. Against this, Yan treats the four communities as one system embedded in the features of Chinese modernization: a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advance in step, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Yan also argues that China's development is "parallel" rather than the Western "serial" sequence, and so did not pass through bloody primitive accumulation. Because it rests on a socialist system aimed at communism, the article claims, it moves toward Marx's "real community".

Yan concludes that Chinese modernization theoretically criticises Western dissolution of community, institutionally supplies the security and belonging people have lost, and practically promotes harmony between people and nature, society, nations and states. It is also presented as a model for late-developing countries, and as no return to premodern community, since it combines the "common good" of traditional communities with modern features. Yan adds that the theory is still being developed in practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal links Marx's concepts of false community and fetishism to the Party's current vocabulary of community.
quoteEn: Xi Jinping's thought on community is embedded within the theoretical logic of Chinese modernization.
quoteZh: 习近平共同体思想内嵌于中国式现代化理论逻辑之中

glossary.explanation: The Party's official term for China's own path of modernization, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013, calling for joint global governance, peace and shared development.
A concept first put forward at the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). It describes governance in which Party, government, society and citizens all take part.
The idea that China's 56 ethnic groups form one national community with a shared identity. Official policy calls this "forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation".
An ecological-civilisation concept holding that humans and nature form an integrated whole, so harming nature harms humanity.

t: The genesis and contemporary value of Lenin's "theory of inculcation"
zh: 列宁“灌输论”的生成逻辑与时代价值
source: Journal of School Party Building and Ideological Education, 2022 no. 22
paras: Hong Yan and Wang Shengzhen take up the long-running dispute over Lenin's "theory of inculcation" (灌输论). They note that, after Dewey and others, "inculcation" shifted in Western educational debate from a near-synonym of education to its opposite, and became a target of criticism. The authors argue that, against such charges, Lenin's theory should be understood completely and accurately from a Marxist standpoint, restoring its original meaning and bringing out its value for the present.

The article has three sections. The first traces the theory's genesis, from Marx and Engels's ideas on communist education through Kautsky's first formulation to Lenin's mature version. The second sets out what the authors regard as the theory's genuine content. The third turns to its value in the "new era", drawing on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It was published in a 2022 issue of a journal on Party building and ideological education.

On genesis, Hong and Wang identify three needs in Russia: the Social Democratic Party had to separate itself from the "Economists", who revered the spontaneity of the workers' movement; the Russian movement needed a theory suited to Russian conditions rather than copied from abroad; and a backward country swamped by petty-bourgeois influence made the task of bringing Marxist theory to the proletariat urgent. On meaning, they argue that social-democratic consciousness cannot arise spontaneously, because it is a class consciousness (they cite Lukács) rather than the sum of individual workers' thoughts. It is also a consciously created theory that intellectuals must develop. They hold that the Marxist claim that social being determines consciousness does not mean consciousness emerges automatically. Inculcation is therefore, in their view, a unity of theoretical innovation (the writer) and theoretical education (the agitator).

The authors conclude that the theory remains relevant in three ways: as a basis for continued theoretical innovation, including the creation of Xi Jinping Thought; as support for ideological and political education in a period of sharp ideological struggle against hostile forces; and as a guide for the ideological side of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They claim that Chinese practice shows the theory has not become outdated but is a "key" to the Party's successes. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-journal scholarship defends Lenin's inculcation theory and links it to current ideological work.
quoteEn: The authentic meaning of what Lenin calls "inculcation" should be the organic unity of Marxist theoretical innovation and education.
quoteZh: 列宁所说的“灌输”，其本真内涵应是马克思主义理论创新与教育的有机统一

glossary.explanation: Lenin's argument, developed from Kautsky and set out in What Is to Be Done?, that socialist consciousness must be brought to the working class from outside its spontaneous economic struggle.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for strict discipline, anti-corruption work and organisational and ideological construction within the Party.
A tendency in the Russian Social Democratic movement around 1900 that stressed workers' economic struggle and spontaneity over political organisation; Lenin attacked it in What Is to Be Done?

t: The Communist Party of Denmark's exploration of socialism and the reasons for its decline
zh: 丹麦共产党对社会主义的探索及衰落原因
paras: Bai Hu and Chen Jinxiang ask why the Communist Party of Denmark, once an organisation of some influence in the Nordic countries, ended its 70-odd years of existence in decline and collapse. They argue that its theory and practice of socialism centred on parliamentary struggle and peaceful transition, and that its demise resulted from a combination of objective and subjective factors, with the external environment the main one.

The article first traces the party's history in three phases: founding and growth through revolutionary struggle (1919–1945), the search for a new path in the Cold War (1946–1989), and survival and extinction after 1990. It then surveys four areas of the party's exploration: the peaceful road to socialism, the labour movement and anti-capitalist struggle, bilateral and multilateral inter-party activity, and the struggle for peace. A final section sets out three reasons for failure.

In the authors' account, the party dropped the phrase "dictatorship of the proletariat" from its 1952 programme and later held that an anti-monopoly democratic struggle could reach socialism without civil war. It joined strikes, such as the 1973 national strike, May Day rallies, Nordic communist conferences, and campaigns for peace and a nuclear-free Nordic zone. The authors attribute its decline to three factors: nearly ten splits over ideological disputes, including those after the 1956 Soviet Party Congress and the expulsion of Axel Larsen, who then founded the Socialist People's Party; its long confinement in the shadow of the Social Democrats and that party; and an uncritical pro-Soviet, anti-Chinese stance that, they say, eroded its independent judgement. They report that its membership fell to about 2,000 by 1992. They also state that the party calling itself the Communist Party of Denmark today is a different body, re-formed in 1993.

The authors conclude that the party's fate resembles that of many Western communist parties and reflects a general problem. For all foreign communist parties, they say, adapting Marxism to local conditions and to the times remains a long and arduous task. Understanding the Danish case, they suggest, helps explain why socialism in Western countries has fallen into a trough. Read the original if you study Western European communist parties, Nordic left politics or how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars assess the decline of foreign communist parties.
quoteEn: The decline and eventual demise of the Danish party is a microcosm of the trajectory of most Western communist parties in the international communist movement, and the result of long accumulation and the combined action of many factors.
quoteZh: 丹共的衰落直至败亡，是国际共运中西方多数国家共产党演进轨迹的一个缩影，是长期积累与多种因素共同作用的结果

glossary.explanation: The strategy of reaching socialism through parliamentary and democratic means rather than armed revolution. Many Western communist parties adopted it after the Second World War.
A Marxist term for working-class political rule during the transition from capitalism to socialism. The Danish party dropped it from its programme in 1952.

t: Lenin's epistemological thought and its contemporary value
zh: 列宁的认识论思想及其当代价值
paras: Gao Bin takes up Lenin's theory of knowledge as it appears mainly in the Philosophical Notebooks, and asks what it inherited from Marx and Engels, what it criticised, and what it still offers today. The article's thesis is that Lenin developed a "practice-based epistemology" in which knowledge arises from practice, is tested by practice and aims at objective truth. Gao presents this as an important part of Marxist philosophy with continuing relevance.

The short article has three main parts: Lenin's inheritance and development of Marxist epistemology; his critique and transcendence of modern epistemological schools; and the contemporary value of his thought. It refers to Machism, Second International opportunism and Bogdanov's revisionism as the setting for Lenin's turn from historical questions to epistemology. It closes with a brief note on artificial intelligence and cognitive science.

Gao argues that Lenin defended the materialist position that the real world exists independently of consciousness, and described cognition as a dialectical movement from sensory to rational knowledge and back to practice. Lenin is said to have developed Marxist views of practice as the criterion of truth, of the objectivity of truth, and of subjective initiative. Gao then reports Lenin's criticism of idealism, metaphysics, empiricism, neo-Kantianism and logical empiricism, each charged with one-sidedness. Lenin is said to have gone beyond both rationalism and empiricism by joining sensory and rational knowledge, and by stressing contradiction between thought and being as the driver of cognitive progress. Gao adds that Lenin treated knowledge as historical and class-conditioned.

Gao concludes that Lenin's epistemology keeps its value in four ways. It puts practice first, stresses the historicity of knowledge, encourages theoretical innovation and promotes critical thinking amid globalisation and informatisation. Gao also claims that AI and neuroscience have moved epistemology from the relation between matter and consciousness to that between neural activity and consciousness. On this view, cognition is an active, dialectical process rather than simple stimulus and response, and Lenin's principles should guide the study of objective laws. Read the original if you want a brief, introductory Chinese overview of how Lenin's epistemology is presented for present-day teaching and research.
quoteEn: The core of Lenin's epistemological thought is the primacy of practice, that is, the aim of knowledge is to promote the development of practice.
quoteZh: 列宁的认识论思想的核心是实践第一，即认识的目的是促进实践的发展。

t: Review of frontier issues in contemporary foreign Marxism research
zh: 当代国外马克思主义研究的前沿问题述评
paras: Writing in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2023, no. 1), Kong Ming'an surveys the latest developments in foreign Marxism, the field that has existed as a discipline in China since the 1980s. The review opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the Politburo's 43rd collective study session (2017), which valued contemporary Marxist currents for their critical analysis of capitalism's structural contradictions, crises and new forms. Kong organises the field into ten thematic clusters.

The clusters are: ideology theory; digital capitalism and new imperialism; consumer society and the labour theory of value; political philosophy of fairness and justice; eco-Marxism; contemporary populism; the Frankfurt School's critical theory across four generations; biopolitics and life philosophy after COVID-19; postmodernism and post-Marxism; and spatial critique and urban Marxism. The thinkers discussed include Althusser, Žižek, Christian Fuchs, David Harvey, Hardt and Negri, Baudrillard, G. A. Cohen, Habermas, John Bellamy Foster, Laclau, Mouffe, Agamben and Lefebvre. A short conclusion notes further schools, including analytical, structuralist and feminist Marxism and recent Japanese Marxism.

Within each cluster Kong traces a line from Marx and the classical tradition to current theorists. Ideology moves from Marx's "false consciousness" through Gramsci to Althusser's interpellation and Žižek's ideological fantasy. Digital capitalism is presented as a new form of exploitation, through digital labour and "playbour", and as an extension of imperialism, discussed through Harvey's "spatio-temporal fix" and Hardt and Negri's immaterial labour. Kong also reports debates over justice (Habermas against Rawls, Cohen's critique of Nozick and Rawls), Foster's "metabolic rift", and Laclau and Mouffe's left populism against Žižek's criticism. Kong's own evaluations appear mainly in the populism section, which describes populism as destructive in practice and as present in China's online sphere.

Kong concludes that foreign Marxism is open and inclusive, and that its theorists try to combine Marxism with the features of the present age. In Kong's view this shows Marxism's vitality and explanatory power. Kong adds that Chinese scholars need not accept these thinkers' specific views, but should attend to their methods and the questions they raise. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-academy map of the main currents of foreign Marxism, with names and works, as a guide to how this field is presented to Chinese readers.
quoteEn: We may not endorse their specific views, but their research methods and the questions they explore are what we should pay attention to.
quoteZh: 我们可以不认可他们的具体观点，但他们的研究方法及其所探讨的问题则是我们应该关注的。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese academic discipline, established in the 1980s, that studies Marxist and left-wing currents outside China, including Western Marxism, analytical Marxism and others.
A term for capitalism in the information age, in which platforms and data are central to accumulation and exploitation.
David Harvey's concept that capitalism postpones crisis by expanding geographically and shifting capital across space and time.
A current, prominent since the 1960s, that links capitalism's basic contradictions to ecological crisis and draws on Marx's analysis of nature.
A postmodern-influenced current associated with Laclau and Mouffe that replaces class struggle and the working-class subject with discursive hegemony and plural identities.

t: Peripheral liberation in Samir Amin's perspective: substance, logic and possibilities
zh: 萨米尔·阿明视域中的边缘解放：实质、逻辑及其可能性
source: Dongwu Academic Journal (东吴学术), 2021 no. 5
paras: Can the periphery of the capitalist world system carry the hope of human liberation? Li Xiaole takes up this question through the Egyptian Marxist Samir Amin (1931–2018), especially his book The People's Spring (2017) on the Arab uprisings. Li argues that Amin's account of the Arab movement as a peripheral, national-liberation struggle has real insight but that peripheral liberation does not express a necessary law of human liberation.

The article has three parts. The first traces, on Amin's account, how the Arab world moved from centre to periphery. The second sets out the form and substance of the Arab movement as Amin reads it. The third is Li's own assessment, which weighs practical and theoretical weaknesses and ends by naming what Amin's work still offers Chinese scholarship.

In the first two parts, Li reports that Amin extends the world system back to the tributary systems of antiquity and treats Europe's rise and the decline of the Middle East as shifts in the centre–periphery structure. In Amin's view the Arab movement is anti-imperialist and potentially anti-capitalist, aimed at 'collective imperialism' (the United States, Europe and Japan). Its driving force is the popular masses, and its goals are social justice, national independence and thorough democracy. Li then criticises Amin on two grounds.
