Their supporters are younger, better educated and cross-class, unlike the working-class base of traditional left parties. Wu traces their rise to four drivers. Neoliberal inequality has deepened, and youth unemployment in Spain and Italy has been severe. Traditional party systems are fragmenting. Digital technology lowers the cost of organising. A series of European crises, including the financial, euro and refugee crises, has fuelled populism and Euroscepticism.

Wu concludes that the movements' mobilisation methods and organisational innovations offer lessons for the modernisation of traditional parties. Their growth is constrained, however, by a lack of governing experience, as shown by the Five Star Movement's decline after taking office. It is also constrained by competition from right-wing populists such as the National Rally and Alternative for Germany. Wu notes that the pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict deepen Europe's crises and give the left openings. Whether it can use them depends, in Wu's view, on improving its governing capacity and offering more credible alternatives. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic overview of the new European left's organisation, social base and prospects.
quoteEn: The new left parties that have grown out of social movements generally lack experience in governing; many of their political demands are too idealistic, radical and impractical, and their capacity to deconstruct European politics far exceeds their capacity to construct it.
quoteZh: 由社会运动转型而成的新兴左翼政党普遍缺乏治国理政经验，很多政治诉求过于理想、激进、不切实际，对于欧洲政治的解构能力远远超过建构能力。

t: Marching steadily on the road of human progress
st: New developments and trends among foreign communist parties in 2022
zh: 坚定行进在推动人类发展进步的道路上
zhSub: 2022年外国共产党的新发展与新动向
paras: This annual survey, published in early 2023, asks how communist parties outside China fared in 2022 and what trends marked their activity. Yu Haiqing argues that the parties held to their ideals and kept working for peace and social justice. The author also finds that they remained in a long-running phase of struggle against adversity, with electoral setbacks and deepening internal divisions.

The article is organised around five themes. It begins with commemorations: the 105th anniversary of the October Revolution, the centenary of the Soviet Union, and party anniversaries in Brazil, Japan and the Netherlands. It then reviews election results, mainly in Europe, Brazil, Japan, the Czech Republic, Russia and Nepal. Next it covers party congresses and plenums in ruling and non-ruling parties, and the parties' international meetings and disputes. It closes with their campaigns on peace, workers' interests, anti-communism and women's rights.

Yu's core assessment is that electoral and parliamentary politics were largely unfavourable. The author cites Portugal's worst-ever result, about 2% for the French candidate, and a divided Italian communist movement that won no seats. Nepal's communist reunification and return to government is the exception, which Yu describes as an expedient and fragile alliance. The more important point is the split inside the movement. Yu describes two clashes: one between the Communist Party of Greece and the Workers' Party of Hungary over ideology and unity, and one over the Russia–Ukraine conflict. In the latter, a joint statement backed by 23 parties blamed the United States and NATO, while a Greek-led resolution called the war imperialist and said only ending capitalism would end war. Yu reads these as a widening of internal contradictions.

Yu concludes that the parties are entering a new cycle, with more in-person contact and clearer goals, but that fundamental disagreements on major theoretical and practical questions obstruct unity and cooperation. The author calls on the parties to respect one another, seek common ground while setting aside differences, and look for a "greatest common divisor". Read the original if you want a detailed, country-by-country chronicle of communist party congresses, elections and international meetings in 2022, as seen by a scholar at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
quoteEn: Fundamental differences of position on major theoretical and practical questions in particular have become an endogenous obstacle to closer unity and cooperation among communist parties, and greatly restrict the advance of the world's communist and workers' parties.
quoteZh: 尤其是在重大理论和实践问题上立场观点的根本性分歧,成为各国共产党加强团结与合作的内生性阻碍,极大制约着世界共产党工人党发展前进的步伐。
keywords: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties

t: Badiou's philosophy of the event and the "Chinese question"
zh: 巴迪欧的事件哲学与中国问题
source: Marxism and Reality (Makesizhuyi yu xianshi), 2022 no. 6
paras: Alain Badiou's philosophy of the event is usually seen as a Western theory travelling east. Liu Xin argues that the influence ran both ways: Badiou's theory of the event was itself shaped by his encounter with Chinese thought. The article treats this interaction, and the "Chinese question of Western theory" it produces, as a way of seeing how event philosophy operates "in the world".

The article has four sections. It begins with Chinese and French readings of Hegel in the 1960s and 1970s, then turns to Badiou's "rediscovery" of the Hegel scholar Zhang Shiying. It next considers the place of literature and art in Badiou's event philosophy, citing Quentin Meillassoux and Slavoj Žižek as commentators. A short conclusion assesses the limits of Badiou's engagement with China.

Liu's central claim is that Badiou, dissatisfied with Althusserian and Kojèvian Hegel, found a revolutionary Hegel in Chinese Marxism. He set Zhang Shiying's reading of the "rational kernel" of Hegelian dialectics, which runs through Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong, against He Lin's conservative, state-centred and mystical reading. Badiou drew on Mao's principle of "one divides into two" and on Zhang's account of the leap from quantitative to qualitative change. In his reading, these ideas open space for a rupture that breaks an existing structure and gives rise to the event. Liu also notes that Badiou counts the Chinese Revolution and the poet Ai Qing among the events and subjects of the twentieth century. For Badiou, art can restore the sensuous force of an event in a way that retrospective political history cannot.

Liu concludes that Badiou's theory is the product of a two-way dialogue with Mao, He Lin, Zhang Shiying and Ai Qing. The author also criticises it as abstract. Badiou's event is portrayed as miraculous and unexplainable, and people can only wait passively for it. In Liu's view, Badiou had no direct experience of China, and his "revolutionary China" was a projection of the French cultural and political crisis after May 1968. Liu warns that bringing Badiou back into China as a hermeneutic tool should acknowledge the "misreading" involved and the theory's limits. Read the original if you are interested in Badiou's debts to Maoism and Chinese Hegel scholarship, or in how Chinese scholars critically assess Western radical theory's use of "China".
quoteEn: Between Badiou and Chinese theory there exists a dialogic relationship of "two-way travel".
quoteZh: 巴迪欧与中国理论之间存在一种“双向旅行”的对话关系

glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Mao Zedong's account of dialectics, stressing division and struggle of opposites rather than their merging into a unity (合二为一). Badiou took it up as a core principle.
Marx's phrase for the valuable core of Hegel's dialectic, which he held could be extracted from Hegel's idealist system. Zhang Shiying's essay on it is the main text Badiou discusses.

Badiou's philosophy holds that truths arise from rare, contingent events, and that subjects are constituted by fidelity to them. He identifies four domains of truth: poetry, mathematics, politics and love.
The wave of student and worker protests and strikes in France in May 1968. It strongly shaped Badiou's turn to Maoism and event philosophy.

t: The origins of Marx's concept of exploitation and its contemporary value
zh: 马克思剥削概念探源及其当代价值
orig: Actuel Marx, vol. 63, no. 1, 2018
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2022 no. 6 (abridged translation)
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by the French philosopher Emmanuel Renault, first published in Actuel Marx. Renault notes that Marx borrowed the concept of exploitation from the Saint-Simonians, and that it is now often dismissed as outdated. Some economists reject the labour theory of value it presupposes. Some philosophers and sociologists see economic reductionism in it, and some empirical researchers hold that today's profit-making no longer matches Marx's analysis. Renault takes the view that capitalist exploitation persists, and he defends the concept while updating its use.

The article has four parts. It traces the concept from the Saint-Simonians to the Communist Manifesto, then examines how exploitation is developed in Capital. It then answers three objections, and finally asks how far the concept explains neoliberalism. Renault says that a full test of the neoliberal case lies beyond a single article.

Renault argues that Capital turns exploitation into a theory with three strands: an economic theory of the source of profit, a sociology of structural inequality, and a socio-economic account of economic dependence and domination at work. He holds that the labour theory of value remains useful. It separates necessary from surplus labour, and it shows why labour must be commanded and disciplined in a way machines and raw materials need not be. Renault also argues that replacing it with a notion of injustice captures only one of three features of exploitation: the appropriation of surplus labour. It leaves out dependence and domination. Against the Foucauldian charge that Marx neglects micro-power, Renault notes that Foucault himself took Marx's analysis as a methodological model. On neoliberalism, Renault contends that its defining trait is a return to absolute surplus-value production. Evidence offered includes longer hours and working lives, greater work intensity, electronic monitoring, wage cuts, outsourcing, unpaid work and informal employment. Renault cites 'death from overwork' (karoshi) in Japan and South Korea. This return, Renault adds, is combined with the 'real subordination' of labour associated with relative surplus value.

Renault concludes that Marx's theory remains valid. It helps to distinguish forms of exploitation under neoliberalism. It also reveals a general logic of capitalist exploitation, which joins capital accumulation to mechanisms that constantly renew the extraction of surplus labour. Even without the value theory, Renault says, the distinction between absolute and relative surplus value still helps identify changes in the logic of accumulation. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist philosopher's defence of the exploitation concept against economic, Foucauldian and justice-based critiques, together with an analysis of neoliberal labour relations.
quoteEn: Marx's theory of capitalist exploitation remains valid in present-day society, not only because distinguishing different forms of exploitation helps us understand the specific features of labour exploitation under neoliberal capitalism.
quoteZh: 马克思的资本主义剥削理论在现实社会中仍然有效，这不仅是因为区分剥削的不同形式有助于理解劳动剥削在新自由主义资本主义条件下的具体特征

t: Developments in Western European left-wing social movements amid political upheaval
zh: 政治变局下西欧左翼社会运动的发展动向
paras: Since the turn of the century, left-wing social movements in major Western European countries have gained momentum and, after an initial social impact, quickly turned into new radical left parties. Wu Huiping argues that their political mobilisation and organisation are innovative, and that they are a good case for observing how left-wing currents spread and develop in Europe. The article traces their rise, their shared features, their drivers and their limits.

The article first surveys four national cases: La France Insoumise under Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Italy's Five Star Movement, Spain's Podemos, and the much weaker "Aufstehen" (Stand Up) movement in Germany. It then identifies three common traits: digital mobilisation, flat and loose organisation, and a young, cross-class support base. A third section gives four drivers, and a final section sets out the obstacles and likely direction.

Wu describes these movements as combining a pluralist programme centred on social justice with an openly left-populist stance that pits "the people" against elites. On the four drivers, Wu cites neoliberal inequality and youth unemployment, the weakening of traditional party systems, the digital revolution, and Europe's overlapping crises. In Wu's account, Italy and Spain succeeded most where those crises hit hardest. Wu argues that the internet allows leaders and even political outsiders to speak directly to the public and to replace hierarchical party machines with parallel, online structures. On this reading, the movements' ability to dismantle the existing order exceeds their ability to build a new one.

Wu concludes that the movements' innovations in mobilisation and organisation offer lessons for the modernisation of traditional parties. Wu names two main bottlenecks: a serious lack of governing capacity, illustrated by the Five Star Movement's decline after taking office, and fierce competition from right-wing populists such as the National Rally and the Alternative for Germany. Wu adds that the pandemic, the Russia–Ukraine conflict and the energy and price crisis may open space for further growth. Their future depends on raising governing capacity and offering a more convincing alternative programme. Read the original if you want a concise, China-based account of the new European left, with country data and a view of how Chinese scholars assess it.
quoteEn: Emerging left-wing parties that grew out of social movements generally lack governing experience, many of their demands are too idealistic, radical and impractical, and their capacity to deconstruct European politics far exceeds their capacity to build it.
quoteZh: 由社会运动转型而成的新兴左翼政党普遍缺乏治国理政经验，很多政治诉求过于理想、激进、不切实际，对于欧洲政治的解构能力远远超过建构能力。

t: New developments in North Korea's socialist theory and practice in the ten years of Kim Jong Un's rule
zh: 金正恩执政十年朝鲜社会主义理论与实践的新发展
source: Journal of Yanbian University (Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 1
paras: Qian Zhengyu asks what has changed in North Korea's socialist theory and practice since Kim Jong Un took over the Workers' Party of Korea and the army in December 2011. The article argues that the Party moved from songun (military-first) politics and the "parallel line" to a "frontal breakthrough" strategy centred on economic construction. In Qian's account, it made theoretical and practical gains even under heavy sanctions, natural disasters and the Covid-19 pandemic.

The article opens with the Seventh Party Congress (2016) and the Eighth Party Congress (January 2021), summarising how each assessed past work and set tasks. It then covers theory: the Party's guiding ideology, a sole leadership system, Party purposes, the basic political mode, the judgement of the international situation and of the present era, the nature of the socialist economy, and the place of science and technology. A third section reviews practice in five areas: Party and cadre building, economic work and living standards, ideological struggle, foreign relations, and the anti-epidemic campaign.

Qian presents the sequence as a consolidation of Party leadership. Kim-Il-sungism–Kim-Jong-Ilism became the sole guiding ideology (2012), and the 2021 congress replaced military-first politics with "the people-first principle" as the basic political mode. On the economy, Qian traces early experiments with enterprise autonomy and the "field responsibility system", which raised market activity. Citing Kim, Qian says these also disrupted planning and state control. The Eighth Congress therefore defined the economy as self-reliant, planned and people-serving, and re-emphasised the cabinet and unified state direction. Qian also describes a declared "our-state-first era", a hardening ideological front against Western and South Korean influence, summit diplomacy with South Korea, the United States and China, and strict border closure that kept the country free of Covid-19 infections.

Qian concludes that North Korea's exploration of a socialist path suited to its conditions, since the Soviet and East European upheavals, has enriched the theory and practice of the world socialist movement. The author adds that studying it helps China consolidate traditional Sino-Korean friendship, and that the peninsula's stability matters for Northeast Asia. Qian treats the article as a snapshot of the current stage. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school scholar's sympathetic, source-rich account of how North Korean official discourse and policy changed under Kim Jong Un.
quoteEn: The Eighth Congress's explicit definition of the nature of the North Korean-style socialist economy is a theoretical result of Kim Jong Un's ten years of exploring economic reform in practice, and it reflects the Workers' Party's current view of the basic theoretical question of what socialism is and how to build it.
quoteZh: 八大对朝鲜式社会主义经济性质的明确规定，是金正恩执政十年以来探索经济改革的实践中得出的理论成果，体现了现阶段朝鲜劳动党对于“什么是社会主义、如何建设社会主义”这个基本理论问题的看法。

glossary.explanation: The governing approach associated with Kim Jong Il, giving priority to the armed forces in state affairs and resource allocation. The article says it was later replaced as the basic political mode.

glossary.literal: line of advancing both at once
glossary.explanation: The strategy announced in 2013 of pursuing economic construction and nuclear weapons development together. It was declared complete in 2018.
A North Korean political principle that the Party's work should serve and rely on the people. The Eighth Congress wrote it into the Party rules as the basic political mode.
The Workers' Party of Korea's official guiding ideology, adopted in 2012. It builds on Juche (self-reliance) and military-first thought.
A principle that all state and social work is organised under the Party's sole leadership. It was codified in the revised Ten Principles of 2013.

t: China and Africa jointly building the Belt and Road with high quality: concept, foundations, difficulties and responses
zh: 中国与非洲高质量共建“一带一路”：理念、基础、困境及应对
paras: Writing in late 2022, Tong Fei asks how China and Africa can move their Belt and Road cooperation from rapid expansion to high-quality development. The article argues that the concept behind the cooperation, the material, institutional and popular foundations built over nearly a decade, and a set of targeted adjustments together make this shift feasible, even though serious obstacles remain.

The article has three parts. The first sets out five features of the China–Africa Belt and Road concept: a new view of international order, common development and win-win cooperation, keeping promises, step-by-step practical progress, and the goal of a China–Africa community with a shared future. The second describes the foundations of cooperation, and the third analyses four difficulties and proposes four responses. Tong draws on trade and investment figures, summit documents and opinion surveys such as Afrobarometer.

On foundations, Tong cites 2021 bilateral trade of 254.2 billion US dollars, 46 African countries with signed Belt and Road agreements by January 2021, the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation as a multilevel institutional platform, and survey data showing mainly positive African views of China. On difficulties, Tong identifies the unsustainability of China-financed contracting, a trade deficit of 43 billion dollars for Africa, coups and insecurity, uneven African perceptions (including 'debt trap' concerns), and growing competition from the United States, the EU's Global Gateway, India and Japan. Tong attributes part of the negative perception to Western narratives.

Tong proposes matching projects precisely to Africa's weak sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing and infrastructure, and improving institutions by linking the Belt and Road with African integration and the African Union. Tong also calls for fostering Africa's autonomous development through evaluation of Chinese-financed projects, diversified financing, greater transparency and the involvement of local firms. A fourth proposal is to tell the China–Africa story through localised communication. The article concludes that the cooperation should aim at 'high standards, sustainability and improved livelihoods'. Read the original if you want a Chinese policy-studies view of Belt and Road cooperation with Africa, with survey and trade data and a list of difficulties and recommendations.
quoteEn: China's keeping of its promises is an important reason it has won the sincere support of African countries for the Belt and Road.
quoteZh: 中国重诺守信是赢得非洲国家对“一带一路”真诚支持的重要原因。

glossary.explanation: A cooperation initiative proposed by Xi Jinping in 2013, comprising the Silk Road Economic Belt and the 21st-Century Maritime Silk Road, centred on infrastructure and trade links.

glossary.en: China–Africa community with a shared future
glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping first used on his 2013 visit to Africa to describe the overall direction of China–Africa relations; it is a regional application of the broader idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.
A multilateral platform founded in 2000 that holds summits and ministerial meetings between China and African states.
An official goal of prioritising quality, efficiency and sustainability over pure growth speed; here applied to Belt and Road cooperation.

t: The exploration of world socialism and the forward direction of human civilization
zh: 世界社会主义的探索历程与人类文明的前进方向
source: People's Tribune (Renmin Luntan), January 2023 (first half of the month)
paras: Writing just after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Chenguang asks what the history of world socialism reveals about its underlying logic and about where human civilization is heading. The article argues that world socialism is part of the transition from world capitalism to world socialism that Marx called "world history". In Liu's account, Chinese modernization and the new form of human civilization it has created will deeply shape that direction.

The article has three parts. The first reviews the exploration of world socialism, drawing on Xi Jinping's 2013 periodisation of five hundred years of socialism, and sets out four lessons. The second identifies three logics running through that history. The third projects three trends in human civilization. Liu draws on Marx's three social forms, Toynbee's plurality of civilizations, Kissinger, and the scholar Jiang Hui.

On the historical record, Liu stresses that socialism is a real movement rather than a finished doctrine. It has had to cross the "Caudine Forks" in backward countries, it aims at modernization, and it has no fixed model. The Soviet model is criticised as rigid and as having taken a "great-party chauvinist" stance. The core argument is that three logics overlap. The logic of doctrine is the historical necessity Marx identified, which unfolds unevenly. The logic of power covers class struggle, imperial rivalry and national liberation movements. The logic of civilization covers capitalism's claim to be the only civilization, set against the plural civilizational forms of socialism. Liu warns against a linear, idea-led view of history and describes world history as "polyphonic", with multiple modernities emerging against capitalist modernity.

Liu forecasts three trends: a reordering of the world as US unipolarity and Western dominance decline, a revival of socialism with China as its banner and mainstay, and the coexistence of diverse civilizations moving towards a community with a shared future for mankind. The rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is presented as a rejuvenation of Chinese civilization, fusing Marxism with that civilization. The article claims that the future of human civilization depends largely on how this new form develops. Read the original if you want to see how a Central Party School scholar links world-historical theory, civilizational discourse and official claims about China's role in world socialism.
quoteEn: The development of world history is a kind of \"polyphonic\" structure.
quoteZh: 世界历史的发展，乃是一种“复调”结构。

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A Party formulation, prominent since Xi Jinping's 2021 speech on the Party's centenary, for the civilizational outcome of Chinese modernization. The official account presents it as a new path distinct from Western modernization.
The official name for China's path to modernization, highlighted at the 20th Party Congress (2022). The Party presents it as an alternative to Western models for developing countries.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for China's vision of international relations, based on cooperation and shared interests. It is used in official diplomacy and theory.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, with 2049 as the target date for its full realisation.
A metaphor Marx used in his late writings on Russia. It asks whether a backward country could reach socialism without passing through the full suffering of capitalist development.

t: A study of the editions of Capital
zh: 《资本论》版本考究
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2022 no. 6
paras: Marking the 155th anniversary of the first volume of Capital, this article surveys the principal editions that have appeared as the work spread worldwide. Cui and Hu argue that collecting and studying the editions of Marxist classics is foundational work for theoretical research. They present the editions as a way to retell the history of Capital's circulation, from its German origins to the twenty-first century.

The article has four parts. It begins with the German editions, including Marx's three stages of preparation and writing, Engels's editing of Volumes 2 and 3, Kautsky's edition of Theories of Surplus Value, and later German collected works and the MEGA2 edition. It then covers the Russian, French, English and Japanese editions, followed by a shorter list of other languages. The third part treats publication in China, before 1949 and after, in minority languages and in Taiwan.

The authors stress the special status of the German text as the main reference for all translations. They describe the second German edition of 1872 as the last Volume 1 that Marx revised himself, and the fourth edition of 1890, edited by Engels, as the most widely used. They note that the French edition of 1872–75 was personally revised by Marx, who added new material and restructured it, so that it has independent scientific value. For China, they trace a path from fragmentary excerpts to the Guo Dali and Wang Yaonan complete translation of 1938, then to the translations of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau, including those in the second Chinese edition of the Collected Works (2001–03). They also list popularisations, from Kautsky's and Borchardt's abridgements to illustrated and comic versions, and cite figures: 22 editions in nine languages in Engels's lifetime and over 220 editions in 43 languages by 1967.

In the conclusion, the authors say the circulation of Capital expanded after the October Revolution and after the Second World War. It fell silent for a time after the Soviet collapse and has again become popular reading since the start of the twenty-first century. They end by calling for study of the basic principles of Marxist political economy under Xi Jinping's economic thought, to advance economic theory in serving socialist economic construction. Read the original if you need a detailed bibliographic guide to Capital's editions and translators in German, Russian, French, English, Japanese and Chinese, including the Chinese publishing history.
quoteEn: Collecting and studying the editions of Marxist theoretical works is foundational work for Marxist theoretical research.
quoteZh: 收集、研究马克思主义理论著作的版本是马克思主义理论研究的基础工作。

glossary.explanation: A body directly under the Party Central Committee, founded in 1953 to translate the works of Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin systematically. It produced the Chinese editions of the Collected Works and of Capital discussed in the article.

glossary.zh: 马克思恩格斯全集历史考证版
glossary.literal: Historical-critical edition of the Complete Works of Marx and Engels
glossary.explanation: The second Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe, a historical-critical edition begun in 1975. The article calls its Capital section, completed in 2012, the most authoritative and complete edition.

t: Root causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state (Part 1)
st: Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
zh: 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示（上）
zhSub: 写在苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟成立100周年之际
paras: Writing on the centenary of the USSR's founding and thirty-one years after its end, Li Shenming asks why the Soviet Party and state collapsed. Li's answer is that, among many causes, the decisive one was the ideological and political degeneration of the leading group from Khrushchev to Gorbachev. Li presents this as the first part of a two-part study and ties it to Mao Zedong's call to study the Soviet case and to Xi Jinping's warnings about it.

The article first argues that the top leadership, and the ideological and political line it follows, determine whether a ruling party keeps its character. It then sets out eight dimensions of degeneration: belief, theory, politics, economics, organisation, work style, foreign policy and outlook on life. Each is traced across the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods with Soviet and Russian testimony, memoirs and some American commentators. A closing section assesses twelve other explanations of the collapse.

Li contends that Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin, his theories of the 'party of the whole people' and 'state of the whole people', and his 'peaceful' foreign policy line began the break with Marxism-Leninism. Brezhnev's period brought theoretical neglect, patronage networks, privilege and corruption. Gorbachev then completed the turn through 'humane, democratic socialism', abolition of the Party's leading role, privatisation and concessions to the West. Li presents Gorbachev's circle as a product of the Khrushchev line, not an accident, and as conspirators who concealed their aims.

Li rejects rival explanations as one-sided or as reversing cause and effect. These include the 'original sin' of the October Revolution, the rigid Stalin model, nationality conflicts, the arms race, economic failure, Western pressure, one-party rule, and blaming Gorbachev alone. Li holds that the 'combined forces' view must identify the principal contradiction. Li warns that historical nihilism, which uses the denial of Soviet history to attack the Chinese Communist Party, must be resisted, and that a wrong conclusion could shake the foundations of the Party and the People's Republic. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading Chinese Party theorist explains the Soviet collapse and its lessons for the Chinese Party today.
quoteEn: The fundamental cause of the Soviet Party's demise and the Soviet Union's disintegration was, in the final analysis, the ideological and political degeneration of the leading group from Khrushchev to Gorbachev.
quoteZh: 苏共亡党、苏联解体的根本原因，说到底，就是从赫鲁晓夫到戈尔巴乔夫领导集团在思想上政治上的蜕变。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Party discourse for approaches that, in the Party's view, wholesale negate the history of the Party, the Soviet Union or socialism. Xi Jinping has repeatedly warned against it.
Khrushchev's formula at the 22nd Soviet Party Congress (1961), holding that the Party no longer represented one class. Li criticises it as abandoning the class nature of the Party.

glossary.zh: 人道的、民主的社会主义
glossary.explanation: The slogan Gorbachev adopted from 1988–1990 for the Soviet Party's aims. Li treats it as a social-democratic doctrine descended from Bernstein's revisionism.

t: The root causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state (Part 2)
st: Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
zh: 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示（中）
zhSub: 写在苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟成立100周年之际
paras: This is the second part of a serialised article by Li Shenming, written for the centenary of the USSR's founding, on why the Soviet Communist Party and state collapsed. Li argues that the most serious lesson is that the Party's own construction failed, above all within its leading group. He presents the collapse as a catastrophe for the Soviet peoples and a gain for the United States, and draws warnings for China.

This instalment sets out nine lessons. They cover Party-building and the fate of nations; the leader's convictions and the need for a strong leadership core; ideological and political clarity; constitutional entrenchment of Party leadership; communist ideals; two conceptions of reform; ideological work; absolute Party leadership of the army; and Western 'peaceful evolution' and the 'fifth column'. Li moves from Khrushchev through Brezhnev to Gorbachev, with citations from Russian officials, economists and former Soviet leaders.

Li holds that from Khrushchev onwards the Soviet leadership drifted from Marxism-Leninism: it promoted 'peaceful coexistence', an 'all-people's party' and abstract humanism, and a privileged bureaucratic stratum grew up that was cut off from the masses. Gorbachev's 'reform' is described as a rejection of socialism itself, marked by abolishing Article 6 of the constitution, introducing a multiparty system, depoliticising the army and spreading historical nihilism, such as slanders of war heroes like Matrosov. Li then contends that the West ran a long strategy of peaceful evolution. In his account this worked through scholarships, foundations, Nobel prizes, NGOs and the cultivation of a 'fifth column' that put figures such as Gorbachev, Yakovlev and Yeltsin in power. He supports this with claims about CIA files, Masonic membership and statements by Soviet and Western figures.

Li concludes that socialist states must never change their banner. They need a firm leadership core, Marxist guidance, control of ideological work, absolute Party command of the army and vigilance against infiltration. He ties these lessons to China, criticising 'constitutional democracy' as echoing Gorbachev's proposals and endorsing the post-2012 leadership's stress on ideology, struggle and the 2018 constitutional amendment on Party leadership. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist scholar draws political lessons for China from the Soviet collapse, including claims about Western subversion that readers will want to weigh against other sources.
quoteEn: If Marxism does not occupy the ideological front, non-Marxist and anti-Marxist currents of thought will inevitably occupy it.
quoteZh: 意识形态这块阵地，马克思主义不去占领，非马克思主义、反马克思主义思潮就必然会去占领。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese political discourse for an alleged Western strategy of undermining socialist states through ideological, cultural and economic influence rather than war.
A term for hidden internal agents who work for an outside power. Li uses it for Soviet officials he says served Western interests.
A Western-style liberal constitutional model that Party writers have criticised since around 2013 as incompatible with Party leadership.
A label used in Chinese official discourse for views seen as denying or distorting the history of the revolution, socialism and the Party.

t: Fundamental causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party and state (Part 2)
st: Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
zh: 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示（下）
zhSub: 写在苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟成立100周年之际
paras: This is the second part of Li Shenming's study of why the Soviet Communist Party lost power and the USSR dissolved, written for the 100th anniversary of the Soviet Union's founding. Part 2 turns from causes to implications for the Communist Party of China. Li's thesis is that the Soviet collapse is a warning to heed. He argues that China can avoid a similar fate only by upholding the Party's leadership core, its Marxist-Leninist orientation, public ownership and ideological struggle.

The text sets out ten "implications", each beginning with "must". They cover leadership and succession, the Party's self-reform, economic construction and public ownership, ideological work, the Party's purpose and style, Party control of the army, foreign policy against hegemonism, cadre selection and youth education, Marxist theoretical study, and the correct judgement of the historical era. Li draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Chen Yun and Xi Jinping, and contrasts the Soviet record from Khrushchev to Gorbachev with China's practice.

Li argues that the Party leader's being a firm Marxist can be decisive, so he calls for "unwaveringly" upholding the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds and for guarding against "two-faced" people and conspirators in the leadership. He holds that the Soviet collapse resulted from a degenerated leadership dismantling public ownership. He also holds that class struggle persists in socialist countries and that historical nihilism, Western ideological infiltration and calls to depoliticise the army must be countered. Li reports shortcomings in China's own reform record, among them widening income gaps and one-sided promotion of household contracting. Finally, he contends that the world is still in the era of imperialism described by Lenin, so that courage to struggle comes first. He predicts a revival of world socialism within two or three decades.

Li proposes concrete measures. These include education on the relations between leaders, Party, class and masses, five political criteria and public notice periods for senior cadre promotions, institutionalised Marxist study tied to appraisal and promotion, and the continued publication of Mao's Selected Works and of Xi Jinping's collected writings. He closes by expressing confidence in a bright future for world socialism and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading Chinese Party theorist, writing before the 20th Party Congress (2022), draws policy lessons from the Soviet collapse in ideology, personnel and foreign policy.
quoteEn: Without public ownership there is no socialism.
quoteZh: 没有公有制就没有社会主义。

glossary.explanation: A formula adopted in the Party's 2021 historical resolution. It affirms Xi Jinping's position as the Party's core and the guiding status of Xi Jinping Thought.
The requirement to uphold the authority of Xi Jinping as the core of the Central Committee and the Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership.

A term popularised under Xi Jinping for the Party's efforts to correct itself through anti-corruption work and Party discipline. It is presented as the answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall of regimes.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign policy concept of a cooperative international order based on shared interests.
In official Chinese usage, a label for views that criticise or negate the history of the Party, socialism or its leaders.

t: Lenin's critique of the "Economists" in What Is to Be Done? and its lessons for today
zh: 列宁《怎么办？》对“经济派”的批判及其当代鉴示
source: China Party and Government Cadres Forum (Zhongguo dangzheng ganbu luntan), 2022 no. 12
paras: Writing 120 years after Lenin's What Is to Be Done? (1901–02), Li Dongming asks what Lenin's polemic against the "Economists" was meant to achieve and what it offers the Chinese Communist Party now. The article argues that the critique served several purposes: defending the Party's leadership core and centralised, unified leadership, consolidating Marxism's guiding position as the Party's ideological basis, and strengthening its political leadership of the workers' movement. From these, Li draws practical lessons for Party building today.

The first part examines the Economists' positions and the Russian Social-Democratic Party's condition around 1900. Li describes a Party with little central leadership, strong circle mentality, police repression and exiled leaders, in which the group around Martynov flourished. The second part treats economism as a Russian variant of Bernstein's revisionism, citing the 1899 \"Credo\" and the Economists' slogan of \"freedom of criticism\". The final parts turn to the present, and the text closes with a section on unity and struggle after the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Li's central argument is that the Economists, by worshipping spontaneity, equating workers' economic associations with revolutionaries' organisations and denouncing a centralised organisation of professional revolutionaries as undemocratic, undermined the leadership core. Li adds that economism spread mainly because many members had little theoretical training. Lenin's response, in Li's reading, rested on the claim that there is no non-class \"third\" ideology, so that any disparagement of socialist ideology strengthens bourgeois ideology. Li reports that the struggle ended in 1902, when the Economists' main periodicals closed.

Li draws four lessons for the Party today. It must struggle against words and deeds that weaken the leadership core and the authority of the Central Committee. It must strengthen Marxist theoretical study across the Party. It must criticise erroneous currents, which Li names as historical nihilism, neoliberalism, constitutional democracy and \"universal values\", and win the masses with the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. And it must \"speak politically\" and raise its political leadership, in support of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style reading of Lenin's early polemic is used to justify present-day demands for discipline, ideological unity and leadership authority.
quoteEn: Political firmness comes from theoretical clarity, and unity of action stems from unity of thought.
quoteZh: 政治上的坚定来自理论上的清醒，行动上的一致源于思想上的统一。

glossary.explanation: A current in the Russian Social-Democratic movement around 1900 that stressed workers' economic struggle over political leadership by a party. Lenin attacked it in What Is to Be Done?

A term in Chinese Party discourse for the central leadership body or figure around which the Party is to be united. The article applies it both to Lenin's centralised organisation and to the present Central Committee.
In official Chinese usage, a label for views that are seen as denying or discrediting the Party's history and the revolutionary tradition.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the continuing project of fitting Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and contemporary circumstances. It is presented as the source of the Party's theoretical innovations.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of the Party, associated especially with Xi Jinping, of restoring China to national strength and prosperity.

t: Re-examining Plekhanov's thought in the course of the Russian Revolution
zh: 俄国革命进程中的普列汉诺夫思想再审视
source: Marxism and Reality (马克思主义与现实), 2022 no. 5
paras: Ma Jiahong argues that Georgi Plekhanov's life and ideas can be understood only within the internal logic of the Russian Revolution. Earlier studies, the author says, concentrate on his theory or on verdicts about his merits and faults, and neglect the particular features of Russian revolutionary history. The article re-examines his political activity to explain both his early achievements and his later failures, and to sharpen understanding of what made the Russian Revolution distinctive.

The article moves chronologically through four sections. It begins with Plekhanov's turn from Narodism to Marxism and the founding of the Emancipation of Labour group in 1883. It then covers his theoretical work of the 1880s and 1890s against the Narodniks. Next it looks at his clashes with Lenin over party organisation, the bourgeois-democratic revolution and the First World War. It ends with the deeper historical reasons for those clashes, drawing on Plekhanov's own writings on monism and the role of the individual in history.

Ma first rejects the common view that Plekhanov's conversion simply reflected Russian capitalist growth and a rising working class. In Ma's account the economy of the 1880s was stagnant and the workers politically immature. The turn instead came from Russian intellectual history meeting Western Marxism, so Russian Marxism carried a "leap-over" tendency from the start. Ma then defends Plekhanov's historical materialism against charges of fatalism or mechanism. Plekhanov's tragedy, Ma contends, was that he refused to recognise the peculiarity of Russia, where a mature party and theory had formed before the working class had. This led him to oppose Lenin's tactics, treated as Blanquism, to reject seizing power in 1917, and to take a defencist line in the war. Ma adds personal factors: long exile, a bookish life and ties to the Second International. The deeper cause lay in a changing world-historical situation that theory could not yet resolve.

Ma concludes that Plekhanov deserves credit for bringing Russian and Eastern socialism into the world movement, but that his theoretical outlook limited his political agency. He was remote from Russian conditions, strong in abstraction but weak in judging concrete situations and building a revolutionary organisation. He tended to ask whether revolution was feasible rather than what it made possible. For Ma, universal theory takes effect only through particular experience, and political possibility comes from uniting the two. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reassessment of Plekhanov that sets him against Lenin and the specific path of the Russian Revolution.
quoteEn: Compared with Lenin, Plekhanov tended to attend to the feasibility rather than the possibility of the Russian Revolution, and to the generality of socialist revolution rather than the particularity of Russian conditions.
quoteZh: 普列汉诺夫更倾向于关注俄国革命的可行性而非可能性，更偏重于关切社会主义革命的一般性而非俄国具体情况的特殊性。
keywords: role of the individual in history

t: An assessment of the predicaments of British neo-Marxist cultural studies
zh: 英国新马克思主义文化研究的困境评析
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2022 no. 5
paras: Li Xintong examines the path of British neo-Marxist cultural studies from culturalism to structuralism and then to cultural hegemony and articulation theory. The article argues that all three paradigms set out to overcome the "reflection theory" of culture, which treats culture as a mere reflection of the economic base. In Li's account, they ended in an original predicament and a contemporary one, both rooted in an unresolved view of the base–superstructure relation.

The article first reconstructs the three paradigms. Culturalism (Richard Hoggart, Raymond Williams, E. P. Thompson) stresses experience, human agency and culture as a whole way of life. Structuralism (Perry Anderson, Terry Eagleton, and Stuart Hall's turn to signification) treats culture and ideology as the precondition of experience. The third paradigm draws on Antonio Gramsci's hegemony and Ernesto Laclau's articulation, and is represented by the later Williams and by Hall. Li then discusses the "original" predicament and the "contemporary" predicament of cultural identity and openness.

Li contends that culturalism and structuralism stand in an either/or antinomy: humanism against anti-humanism, the logic of history against the logic of structure. Hall's articulation, in this reading, merely overlays two incompatible paradigms and discusses "unity in difference" only inside ideology. Li argues that it drifts into post-Marxism and away from Marxist political economy. Williams's revision of "base" as a process and Eagleton's historical account of culture are discussed as other responses. By the 1990s, Li says, the stress on autonomy had become an autonomy of the economy alone, and reflection on historical materialism was suspended. On the contemporary side, structuralism makes identity a closed belonging, while culturalism's openness empties identity. Li proposes reading identity as a dialectical tension, drawing on Hall, Zygmunt Bauman and Jacques Derrida, with structure understood as an open "field".

Li concludes that culture is meaningful only when studied within historical materialism, through social relations and practice. The author poses questions about Marx's broader conception of culture and practice, and about whether a new concept of culture could be derived from it. The article ends by claiming that socialism with Chinese characteristics, building on shared values and Chinese tradition, offers an open space for cultural dialogue. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese account of the Birmingham-school lineage and its theoretical dead ends, written from a historical-materialist standpoint.
quoteEn: Hall's so-called \"transcendence\" merely overlays the content of the two paradigms above, and discusses the \"identity in difference\" among elements only within ideology.
quoteZh: 霍尔的所谓“超越”不过是叠加了上述两种范式的内容，且仅在意识形态内部讨论要素之间“差异的同一”。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up. Here it is invoked as an open cultural space.
The view that culture and other superstructural phenomena merely reflect the economic base. The article treats it as the target that all British neo-Marxist cultural studies tried to overcome.
Gramsci's idea that a ruling class secures rule through consent, with its ideology becoming common sense. Hall and Williams used it to move beyond culturalism and structuralism.
Laclau's and Hall's idea that ideological elements have no fixed identity and take meaning from contingent connections that can be broken and remade.

t: The development path, internal difficulties and way forward of the Latin Americanisation of Marxism
zh: 马克思主义拉美化的发展理路、内在困境及其出路
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2022 no. 5
paras: Following Lenin's Russianisation of Marxism, the Peruvian Communist Party founder José Carlos Mariátegui began what Zheng Xiangfu and Ling Zhehong call the Latin Americanisation of Marxism. The article, published in 2022, asks why this localisation has produced real achievements yet also persistent difficulties. The authors argue that the answer lies in how Latin American Marxists understood the essence of Marxism and in the region's realities, and they trace the process historically to explain its necessity and mechanism.

The account is divided into three periods. From the late nineteenth century to 1917, Marxism was mechanically mixed with local currents, as in the work of Juan B. Justo, Manuel Ugarte and Luis Emilio Recabarren. From 1918 to 1959, it fought the thesis of 'Latin American exceptionalism' and dogmatism, through Mariátegui, Julio Antonio Mella, Victorio Codovilla and Vicente Lombardo Toledano. After 1960 it took diverse forms: Castroism and Guevarism, dependency theory and the philosophy of liberation, Cuba's 'updating' of socialism, and Hugo Chávez's 'socialism of the twenty-first century'. A final section sets out the difficulties and proposed remedies.

The authors present Mariátegui's call for a 'heroic creation', not a dogmatic copy of European models, as the turning point. They credit his Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality with finding Indigenous peoples to be the revolutionary subject and with applying historical materialism to local conditions. They then identify theoretical problems: the influence of Trotskyism, Stalinism and Browderism; a selective reading of Marxist conclusions that neglected its methodology; and the worship of Comintern directives or revolutionary leaders' slogans in place of concrete analysis. In practice, they say, the collapse of the Soviet Union weakened the communist parties, many of which became opposition or participating parties or turned to social democracy, leaving the socialist movement in a trough.

The authors propose four requirements. Marxism must be grasped as an organic whole of philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, and socialisms detached from historical materialism are rejected as unscientific. Indigenous peoples and their traditions must be the foundation. Party-building is the key to success. Communist parties must also study their own historical experience and explore a socialism with Latin American characteristics. The article is a historical survey rather than a case study. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Latin American Marxism from Justo to Chávez, and of how Chinese researchers assess its limits.
quoteEn: Concrete analysis of concrete problems is the living soul of Marxism.
quoteZh: 具体问题具体分析是马克思主义活的灵魂

glossary.explanation: The process of adapting Marxism to Latin American conditions, analogous to the Russianisation and Sinicisation of Marxism. The article dates it from Mariátegui's call for a Marxism rooted in the region.
The view, criticised by the authors, that Marxism is a European product unsuited to Latin America.

A body of theory, developed in Latin America from the mid-twentieth century, that explains underdevelopment through the dependence of 'peripheral' economies on 'central' ones. The article treats its Marxist strands as a Latin American contribution.
A Latin American philosophical current from the 1970s, associated with Leopoldo Zea and Enrique Dussel, that seeks a philosophy of the 'Third World' free from European dependence.
A strategy proclaimed by Hugo Chávez and taken up by other left governments in Latin America in the 2000s. It stresses national and Indigenous identity and rejects a fixed Soviet-style model.
In Chinese Marxist usage, the mechanical application of doctrines or foreign directives without analysing local conditions. The authors cite it as a main obstacle to localisation.

t: An investigation of the precious editions of Socialism: Utopian and Scientific
zh: 《社会主义从空想到科学的发展》珍贵版本探考
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2022 no. 5
paras: Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, which Marx called an introduction to scientific socialism, was excerpted and revised from Anti-Dühring. This article by Xu Meng and Guo Xiaoli asks how the work's many language editions published before 1949 differ in publication history, format and content. The authors argue that each edition is in effect an independent work shaped by its translator, editor and historical setting.

The article is a bibliographic survey based on editions the authors located, many of them held in China. It proceeds language by language: French, German, English, Japanese, Dutch and Chinese. For each it lists editions, publishers, prefaces, appendices, chapter divisions and annotations, and it also traces how the text circulated between languages.

The authors make three main moves. First, they follow Engels's own adaptations: the French text (1880) was shaped for French readers, the German edition (1883) roughly doubled the content and introduced the now standard three-chapter structure, and the 1892 English edition carried a long new introduction. Second, they show how editors and translators added their own material: Japanese editions by Sakai Toshihiko and others carried headings, notes and political commentary, and some bore the marks of state censorship. Third, they trace the Chinese editions, many translated via Japanese, German, French or Russian sources. These include a 1912 serialisation, Ke Bonian's 1925 full translation, Wu Liping's 1938 version and Bogu's 1943 Yan'an edition, which the authors say became the standard text of a cadres' required-reading series. They also raise unresolved dating and attribution questions, such as the Dutch translation and an undated publisher's note in a US edition.

The authors conclude that differences between editions reflect Engels's adaptation to different audiences and the translators' own understanding and circumstances. In their view each edition therefore has its own research value and historical limits. They argue that only by placing the editions in their historical and social contexts can the work's theoretical value and present significance be understood fully. They present the survey as a reference for tracing how Marxist classics spread worldwide and for understanding the sources of Marxism adapted to China. Read the original if you work on the textual history, translation or circulation of Engels's writings and need a detailed catalogue of early editions in several languages, especially the Chinese and Japanese ones.
quoteEn: This means that every language version and edition of Socialism: Utopian and Scientific is an independent work in its own right.
quoteZh: 这就决定了《社会主义从空想到科学的发展》的任何一个语种和版本都是一部独立的著作

t: Achievements of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化的成就
paras: This short commentary is a Chinese translation of a piece by the Brazilian economist Elias Jabbour, written just after the 20th Party Congress (2022). Jabbour argues that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is the key to understanding China's achievements in the new era and its future changes.

The text takes Xi Jinping's report to the Congress as its starting point. It touches on the economy, state-owned enterprises, national security, technological innovation, socialist democracy and the lessons of the Soviet collapse.

Jabbour contrasts the Chinese approach with capitalist states, whose ruling classes in his account turn state power into control over the people and serve only a rich minority. In China, he says, the large state-owned enterprise system, public finance and state asset management allowed innovative growth of the public sector, including in 5G, big data and artificial intelligence. He reads Marx as holding that technology can advance society but is monopolised by a few under capitalism, whereas under socialism it serves the people. He also points to risks from operating inside Western-dominated international rules and from an unstable world.

Jabbour concludes that a government system guided by Marxism is vital for socialist countries. He attributes the Soviet collapse largely to a failure to localise Marxism and to leaders abandoning it. He also presents the anti-corruption struggle and close ties between Party and people as strengthening China's capacity to meet challenges. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a foreign Marxist economist framed the 20th Party Congress for a Chinese readership.
quoteEn: Establishing a large-scale system of state-owned enterprises, a public finance system and a state asset management system is an important contribution of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times in the economic sphere.
quoteZh: 建立大规模国有企业体系、公共财政体系和国有资产管理体系，是马克思主义中国化时代化在经济领域的重要贡献。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: An official formula for applying Marxism to China's conditions and updating it for the contemporary era. It was given particular emphasis in Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress.

t: China's cause of common prosperity continues to develop with remarkable achievements
zh: 中国的共同富裕事业持续发展成就斐然
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a short commentary by Tang Mai (a British scholar, emeritus professor at the University of Sussex), published in Guangming Daily in October 2022. Tang argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Communist Party of China has given common prosperity growing priority, and that its policies have achieved notable results in material, ecological, cultural and governance terms.

The article surveys the policy areas it associates with common prosperity: innovation-driven high-quality development, regulation of illegal and excessive incomes, primary and secondary distribution, housing, education and health costs, targeted poverty alleviation, rural revitalisation, ecological civilisation and pandemic protection. It closes with China's international role.

In Tang's account, the Party encourages hard work and innovation while curbing corruption, financial and property risks, platform monopolies and entertainment-sector tax evasion. It expands the middle-income group, builds social insurance and basic public services, and uses the "double reduction" policy and affordable housing to stop key sectors being "hijacked by capital". The article cites targeted poverty alleviation as lifting nearly 100 million people out of extreme poverty. Tang also contends that the capitalist international division of labour widens global inequality, and that China's rise shows emerging economies can overcome this with good governance and help others, through the Belt and Road Initiative and the new development banks.

Tang concludes that common prosperity and high-quality development are the necessary path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that better distribution strengthens a domestic-demand-led model. The call for a community with a shared future for mankind is presented as the international expression of common prosperity. Read the original if you want to see how a foreign scholar presented China's common prosperity agenda to a Chinese Party-affiliated readership in 2022.
quoteEn: China's rise shows that, if well governed, emerging economies are able to overcome these obstacles step by step and, along the way, help other countries set out on the path to common prosperity.
quoteZh: 中国的崛起表明，如果治理得当，新兴经济体有能力逐步克服这些障碍，并在前进的过程中帮助其他国家走上共同富裕的道路。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal that the Party has stressed since the 2010s, meaning prosperity shared by all rather than a few; it covers distribution, public services and regional balance.
The official economic strategy since 2017, which stresses innovation, efficiency, greener growth and balance over speed of growth alone.
China's infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched in 2013, linking Asia, Europe, Africa and beyond.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formulation of China's vision for international relations, stressing common interests and cooperation.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal, usually framed as restoring China's strength and international standing by the mid-twenty-first century.

t: New features of contemporary capitalism
st: Neo-feudalism or communism
zh: 当代资本主义发展的新特征
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (国外理论动态), 2022 no. 4
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the American political theorist Jodi Dean. It responds to McKenzie Wark's provocation in Capital Is Dead: what if we are no longer in capitalism but in something worse? Dean answers by tracing trends rather than saying yes or no. Echoing Rosa Luxemburg's 'socialism or barbarism', Dean argues that the choice is between communism and neo-feudalism, and that digital capitalism is drifting towards the latter.

The article first defines capitalism, communism and the premise that capitalism has always lived off other modes of production. It then sets out four linked features of neo-feudalism: divided sovereignty, new hierarchies of lords and peasants, a split between privileged cities and desolate hinterlands, and amplified insecurity and apocalyptic feeling. It goes on to contest liberal talk of a 'democracy versus fascism' struggle, argue that neo-feudalism continues imperialism, and criticise parts of the contemporary left. It closes with a communist response to each feature.

Dean's central claim is that accumulation now works through rent, debt and coercive power more than through profit from production, so that the value-form is weakened as capital escapes the factory. Platforms such as Uber and Airbnb, land privatisation, private investor tribunals, fine-based municipal policing and data extraction are cited as examples. Drawing on Barabási's work on networks, Dean holds that power-law distributions make hierarchy inherent to digital networks, so that only political action can abolish it. The author also argues that the rightward turn comes from economic desperation and weak labour, not from fascism as such, and that localism, basic income and 'post-work' visions mirror neo-feudal tendencies.

Dean proposes reading divided sovereignty as the weakening of nation-states that a transnational communist order would need. The author also calls for siding with peasants and proletarians against the new lords, abolishing private ownership of the means of production, dissolving the town–country divide, and cultivating comradeship, courage and discipline. The author mentions Mao Zedong's strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside as one possible reference. The trend is not fixed, but without organised struggle the path leads to neo-feudalism. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist account of digital capitalism, rent and the hinterland, or a case study in how foreign Marxist work is presented to Chinese readers.
quoteEn: Our task is to reverse this trend and make capitalism pass over into communism.
quoteZh: 我们的任务是扭转这一趋势，使资本主义向共产主义过渡。

glossary.explanation: Dean's name for a possible successor to capitalism, in which accumulation runs through rent, debt and political power rather than profit from production. It is marked by fragmented sovereignty, steep hierarchy and territorial exclusion.
The article's term for the loss of the general ability to reproduce basic living conditions in areas left behind by cities. It shows up in rising suicide, addiction and falling life expectancy.

t: The essence of America's external "political infiltration"
zh: 美国对外“政治渗透”的本质
paras: Writing in 2022, Guo Yonghu asks what lies behind the United States' external "political infiltration", which the article defines as using political means, together with economic, military, cultural and diplomatic resources, to shape the ideology, perceptions and behaviour of other countries' leaders, elites and publics. Guo argues that, whatever President Biden says about not seeking a new Cold War, the historical record shows a consistent pattern. In the author's account its aims are to dominate world order, consolidate the capitalist world system and promote "peaceful evolution" in socialist states.

The article has three parts. The first traces the history of US infiltration from the 1820s Monroe Doctrine and Caribbean interventions, through hostility to the Russian Revolution and Cold War CIA covert action, to the post-Cold War period. The second sets out what Guo calls its essence. The third surveys how other states have resisted, then proposes responses for China. Examples include the 1964 Chilean election, Carter's human rights diplomacy, the National Endowment for Democracy under Reagan, the "Greater Middle East" plan and the Arab Spring.

Guo's central claim is that infiltration is first of all a tool for consolidating US hegemony, since national interest governs the behaviour of a hegemonic power. Its core content is "exporting democracy": installing pro-US regimes and then transplanting the American system. Its goal, the author argues, is the "absolute security" of American ideology. Guo reads current pressure on China in this light, saying that the Party's "new form of human civilization" is seen in Washington as a challenge to Western capitalist civilization.

Guo reviews counter-measures abroad. Russia has tightened laws on "foreign agent" organisations and passed a sovereign internet law. Kazakhstan and Belarus have controlled organisations and the opposition. Cuba has waged an "ideological battle" against neoliberalism, and left-wing Latin American states have formed regional alliances. For China, Guo calls for perfecting whole-process people's democracy, building a full ideological security system and forming an international united front against Western infiltration, promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic frames US democracy promotion as hegemonic strategy and what counter-measures the article recommends.
quoteEn: America's external "political infiltration" is a tool for consolidating its own hegemony.
quoteZh: 美国对外“政治渗透”是巩固自身霸权的工具。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019 to describe China's political system as democratic across all stages of political life, not only at elections. Official discourse presents it as an alternative to Western electoral democracy.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept advanced by Xi Jinping from 2012–13. It calls for a multipolar, cooperative international order.
A term in Chinese Communist discourse for the alleged Western strategy of undermining socialist states from within by non-military means such as ideology, culture and trade.

A formula used in the 2021 Party resolution on history, which says that the Chinese path to modernization has created a new form of human civilization. Official texts present it as going beyond Western capitalist civilization.

t: The German Greens' return to federal government and the likely direction of their China policy
zh: 德国绿党重返联邦政府及其对华政策走向
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2022 no. 3
paras: After the 2021 Bundestag election, the German Greens won 14.8 per cent of the vote, became the third-largest party and entered a "traffic light" coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Free Democrats (FDP), taking five cabinet posts including the foreign ministry. Xuan and Zhao ask what kind of party the Greens are, why they succeeded, how the coalition formed, and what stance they will take towards China. Their thesis is that the Greens have moved from the radical left to a pragmatic centre but remain strongly ideological, so their left-wing label gives no grounds for assuming better Sino-German relations.

Working within a framework of parliamentary politics, the article is organised in five parts. It divides the party's development since 1980 into three stages: grassroots opposition, "junior partner" in the 1998–2005 red–green government, and opposition from 2005 to 2021. It then examines the objective and subjective causes of the 2021 result, the reasons the SPD, Greens and FDP formed a government, and the Greens' positions on China.

On the causes of success, the authors point to Western fatigue with political polarisation, including Trump-era politics and signs of a return to moderation in France and the 2019 European Parliament "green wave". They also cite the hollowing-out of Germany's political centre: voters leaving the CDU/CSU, SPD and Die Linke for the Greens, and a campaign built on optimistic messaging and a reconciliation of "moral purity" with "electoral viability". On China, the authors argue that the Greens label it a "competitor, partner and systemic rival", pursue values-based diplomacy, tie trade to human rights, and may press on Xinjiang and Tibet. They also say that the party needs Chinese cooperation on climate and that Foreign Minister Baerbock's "dialogue and toughness" line reflects this tension.

The authors conclude that Greens' hard line is not pro-American, since the party also urges Europe to reduce dependence on the US and is harsher towards Russia, and that campaign rhetoric need not determine policy in office. In government, they argue, the Greens face a dilemma between value principles and the need to cooperate with China, Germany's largest trading partner for five years. The authors see room for improved relations in shared commitments to sustainability and peace, while warning China to stay sober about the Greens' influence. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of how the Greens' China policy was read in Shanghai in 2022, and of the party's electoral history.
quoteEn: One cannot simply judge, from the German Greens' left-wing colouring, that their coming to power is more favourable to the development of Sino-German and China–EU relations.
quoteZh: 不能因德国绿党的左翼色彩而简单地判断其上台更有利于中德关系、中欧关系的发展。

t: A decade of pursuing the Chinese Dream and building a shared future for humanity
zh: 追求中国梦与构建人类共同未来的十年
paras: This Chinese translation of a newspaper commentary by the Brazilian business figure and lawyer José Ricardo dos Santos looks back on China's last ten years ahead of the 20th Party Congress (October 2022). Dos Santos argues that since 2012 the Chinese Dream has moved from an idea some doubted to a concrete achievement under Communist Party leadership. He also holds that China's international role has become more important amid global crises.

The piece begins with the Chinese Dream and the two centenary goals. It then turns to domestic development: innovation-driven development, the five-sphere plan, environmental commitments and high-quality development. Its final sections cover global governance, BRICS and the Belt and Road Initiative.

Dos Santos treats the first centenary goal, the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, as already met. He credits people-centred policies and the slogan "leave no one behind", and expects the next goal to arrive on schedule or early. Abroad, he presents China as a pillar of BRICS and says the Belt and Road Initiative has added cultural exchange to trade and infrastructure. He describes both as expressions of a community with a shared future for mankind. He says the United States is trying to contain China, and that the Party has responded calmly while continuing to stress cooperation, respect for different social systems and common human values.

Dos Santos concludes that China works both for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and for a common future for humanity. He says the community with a shared future for mankind has moved from concept to practice and drawn wide international praise. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Latin American business commentator, published in a Chinese Party-affiliated newspaper, presents China's decade under Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: The Chinese Dream has become ever more vivid and concrete, letting the world further witness the speed and successful practice of Chinese modernization.
quoteZh: 中国梦越来越生动具体，让世界进一步见证中国式现代化的速度和成功实践。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping put forward in 2012, centred on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's official long-term goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely tied to the Chinese Dream.
A global infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative proposed by China in 2013.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations, stressing common interests, multilateralism and cooperation.
An official economic guideline that favours innovation, efficiency and sustainability over pure growth speed.

t: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is China's fundamental guide
zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想是中国的根本引领
paras: This short commentary is a Chinese translation of an article by Charles Onunaiju, director of a Nigerian centre for China studies. It argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the basic guide for China's deepening governance reform. Onunaiju presents it as the Communist Party's latest guide to governing, adopted as the Party's guiding ideology at the 19th Party Congress.

After a brief account of the Party's twentieth-century liberation and post-reform growth, the author takes the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a new starting point. Three areas of achievement are examined in turn: Party discipline, sustainable and inclusive development, and China's approach to global governance.

On the first, Onunaiju holds that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, carried out through the Party's self-reform, is the precondition for other reforms. The author contrasts this with African parties that lost power after their ideas and organisation decayed. On the second, high-quality development is said to link growth with livelihoods, ecology, fairness and regional balance, whereas some developing countries, including some African ones, grow without real development. On the third, the author describes the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development Initiative as cooperative, win-win alternatives to what is called Western zero-sum thinking.

Onunaiju concludes that these achievements strengthen the case for the Party's governance and bring benefits for world peace and development. The author also says that developing countries, Africa included, welcome China's contribution to South–South cooperation and North–South dialogue. Read the original if you want an example of how a Nigerian China specialist's view of the Party's new-era governance was presented to Chinese readers in the state press.
quoteEn: The Communist Party's deepening efforts to correct its internal conduct and enforce discipline are a necessary precondition for China's governance reform in the new era.
quoteZh: 中共深入推进党内正风肃纪，是新时代中国推进治理变革的必要前提。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Communist Party's official guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party constitution at the 19th Party Congress (2017).

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's campaign, since 2012, to tighten discipline and fight corruption and misconduct within its ranks.
An official phrase for the Party's claim to correct its own problems through internal discipline and renewal.
An official goal of shifting from high-speed growth to growth that stresses quality, balance, innovation and sustainability.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative announced by Xi Jinping in 2013.

t: China's elimination of absolute poverty is a bright sight for the world
zh: 中国消除绝对贫困是世界亮丽风景线
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a short commentary by Alessandra Ciattini, a professor at the University of Rome (the byline gives only her Chinese-rendered name). She argues that China's elimination of absolute poverty by the end of 2020 is one of the most notable achievements in the world today, and that it contrasts sharply with growing impoverishment in the West.
