quoteEn: The parties are weak in strength, but their courage in speaking out and holding their positions is a bright spot of the world socialist movement in the twenty-first century.
quoteZh: 各党力量弱小，但勇敢发声、坚持立场，是21世纪世界社会主义运动的亮点。

glossary.explanation: In Chinese Party discourse, a charge against interpretations that, in the Party's view, distort or deny the achievements of socialist history. Here it is applied to Western and local portrayals of 20th-century socialism.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013, calling for cooperation among states and civilisations on shared global problems.

t: Historical nihilism in the course of the Soviet Union's transformation
zh: 苏联演变进程中的历史虚无主义
paras: Thirty years after the Soviet collapse, Su Yang argues that historical nihilism, the wholesale negation of a country's and a party's past, was a factor that cannot be ignored in the Soviet Union's disintegration. Su opens with Xi Jinping's remark that the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) was due in large part to fierce ideological struggle and the negation of Soviet and Party history, of Lenin and of Stalin. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in December 2021, presents the Soviet case as a cautionary example.

The article has three parts. The first traces how historical nihilism spread under Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev. The second sets out its main harms: a mistaken view of history, distorted social values and the destruction of political belief. The third draws lessons for contemporary China.

On the Soviet record, Su points to Khrushchev's 1956 secret speech on the cult of personality and the literary 'thaw' as the start of the process. Su holds that it accelerated under Gorbachev, who declared that there should be no 'blank spots' in history. Su cites the destruction of school history textbooks in 1988, the abolition of courses such as the history of the CPSU and scientific communism, and the 1990 press law. According to the article, the Party controlled only 27 of 1,800 national periodicals (1.5%). Su also cites figures on Party resignations, including 4.2 million in the year before July 1991. In Su's account, 'glasnost', democratisation and 'pluralism' opened the way for anti-communist and anti-Marxist currents, and 'humane, democratic socialism' displaced Marxism as the dominant ideology.

For China, Su calls for upholding historical materialism and a correct view of Party history, strengthening education in Party history and Marxist theory, and holding the right to interpret Party history. Su also calls for firm cultural confidence, since historical nihilism leads to cultural nihilism. A third task is to strengthen governance of the internet, which Su describes as the main battlefield of ideological struggle, and to extend the reach of mainstream discourse online. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2021 used the Soviet collapse to justify ideological work against historical nihilism in China.
quoteEn: The key to resisting historical nihilism lies in firm cultural confidence.
quoteZh: 抵御历史虚无主义，关键在于坚定文化自信。

glossary.explanation: In official Chinese usage, a label for views that deny or belittle the Party's revolutionary and socialist history, or that are said to distort the historical record. It is widely used in Party discourse about the Soviet collapse.

A slogan stressing confidence in China's traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture. It was given prominence under Xi Jinping after 2012 and is counted as one of the 'confidences' alongside confidence in the path, theory and system.
Marx and Engels's theory that material conditions and social relations shape historical development. Chinese Party texts treat it as the basis for assessing history correctly.

glossary.en: the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU)
glossary.explanation: The ruling party of the USSR until 1991. In Chinese official discourse its fall is a standard cautionary reference.

t: French social inequality as refracted through immigration
zh: 移民折射下的法国社会不平等
paras: Writing in 2021, Peng Shuyi asks why social inequality has grown in France, a Western country once relatively attentive to fairness, and argues that immigrants, close to 10% of the population, show this inequality most clearly. The article holds that the Covid-19 epidemic exposed and deepened these divisions, and that the root cause is the rise of neoliberalism. Peng adds that the French left, above all the Socialist Party, objectively tolerated the worsening by shifting rightwards.

The article has five parts. It first describes immigrants' position in employment, schooling and health, using INSEE figures and the example of Seine-Saint-Denis. It then examines how the epidemic hit immigrants in health, income and children's education. The third and fourth parts turn to neoliberal policy and the changing Socialist Party, and a short conclusion follows. Peng draws on French bodies and commentators (the Observatoire des inégalités, Denis Lafay), on Thomas Piketty, and on André Gorz.

Peng's central claim is that immigrants act as a prism for structural inequality. Post-war labour migrants were concentrated in industries that deindustrialisation destroyed, were pushed into insecure service work, and were housed in suburban districts with weak schools and discrimination in hiring. In the epidemic, the article says, cramped housing, jobs that could not be done from home, poorer health and scarce hospitals produced higher infection and death rates. Peng traces the underlying causes to austerity in health and social spending and to state encouragement of informal, flexible employment, drawing on Gorz's argument that cheap personal services grow by impoverishing others. The Socialist Party, in Peng's account, lost its working-class base: workers and employees fell from 22% to 12% of members between 1985 and 2011, while the far-right National Rally absorbed abandoned voters and made immigrants scapegoats.

Peng concludes that as long as neoliberal policy orientation remains, the gap between rich and poor in France will not change and will only sharpen social conflict. As evidence of the pro-capital tilt, the article points to Macron's abolition of the wealth tax. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-leaning analysis of French inequality, immigration and the pandemic, with detailed statistics and a critique of the French left.
quoteEn: The root of France's growing social inequality lies first of all in the prevalence of neoliberalism.
quoteZh: 法国社会日益不平等的根源首要在于新自由主义的盛行。

t: The current state and prospects of the Latin American left
zh: 当前拉美左翼的发展现状与前景
paras: Writing in 2021, Yang Jianmin asks where the Latin American left stands after the "pink tide" that began with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999, and whether a new cycle of left government is opening. The article's answer is that the left has recovered since 2018 and may gain further ground, but is badly divided at home. Yang concludes that, whatever the outcome of a new cycle, the left will remain a lasting force in the region.

The article moves through four stages. It first traces the regional balance from the pink tide through the "left retreat, right advance" of 2015–2018 to the present situation of "left and right sharing power". It then examines how the Covid-19 pandemic, forthcoming elections and the 2020 US election affect the left, with country cases: Ecuador, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Mexico. A third section contrasts the left's growing international coordination with its domestic fragmentation. A final section sets out conditions for a new cycle and the structural bases of the left's persistence.

Yang argues that the pandemic has exposed the costs of right-wing neoliberal policy, citing rising public debt, higher poverty and scarce vaccines, and so favours the left; the author also treats Joe Biden's replacement of Donald Trump as easing external pressure. Internationally, the left has built coordination through the Puebla Group, and Yang reads Mexico's and Argentina's shifts and Peru's 2021 result as undermining the Lima Group's pressure on Venezuela. At home, however, Yang identifies three problems: new left forces competing with traditional ones (Chile, Ecuador), policy splits among governing leftists (Ecuador under Lenín Moreno), and political fragmentation and ideological polarisation.

Yang names three tests for a new left cycle: renewing social consensus and improving living conditions, demonstrating governing competence while keeping ties to social movements, and redefining the role of the state. In the author's assessment, the previous cycle failed to reform the armed forces, police and judiciary, and so did not replace neoliberalism. The left's staying power rests, Yang says, on political reform, party-system change, broader political inclusion and persistent inequality, with poverty still above 30 per cent. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of the Latin American left in 2021, with country-by-country electoral detail.
quoteEn: The existence and development of Latin America's left-wing political forces have political, economic, social and even demographic foundations, and the left and socialist currents that advocate social equality have broad space in which to exist.
quoteZh: 拉美国家左翼政治力量的存在和发展有其政治、经济、社会甚至人口方面的基础，主张社会平等的左翼和社会主义思潮拥有存在的广泛空间

glossary.explanation: A term for the wave of left and centre-left election victories in Latin America from the late 1990s onwards, beginning with Hugo Chávez in Venezuela.
The author's label for the period of about 2015–2018 when left governments lost power or elections across Latin America and right-wing forces gained.
A regional coordinating body of left-wing parties from 14 Latin American countries, which the article says has an election-observation arm intended to counter the Organization of American States.
A group of right-governed Latin American states and Canada, formed in 2017, which pressed the Venezuelan government of Nicolás Maduro.

t: A reader's guide to Latin American Marxism
zh: 拉美马克思主义阅读指南
source: Theoretical Trends Abroad (国外理论动态), 2021 no. 3
paras: This text is a Chinese translation of a bibliographic guide by the British-based scholar Jeffrey R. Webber. It sets out a periodised reading list for anyone approaching Latin American Marxism. Webber says that any periodisation simplifies and screens out counter-currents, but argues that a guide of this kind has no alternative. The list is admittedly incomplete and openly selective. It mixes recognised introductions with lesser-known works, and it leans towards history rather than theory.

Webber builds on the periodisation in Michael Löwy's anthology Marxism in Latin America from 1909 to the Present. He divides the story into six stages: emergence (1870–1910), revolution (1910–1932), stagnation (1932–1959), revolutionary experiment (1959–1980), abandonment of revolutionary strategy (1980–2000), and transformation and renewal (2000 to the present). Under each stage he recommends mostly English-language, but also Spanish and French, works. They cover Mexico, Peru, El Salvador, Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Guatemala, Cuba, Chile, Nicaragua and Venezuela.

Webber characterises each stage and then matches it with key books. The stage of revolution, for instance, centres on José Carlos Mariátegui, the Mexican Revolution and the 1932 Salvadoran uprising. In Webber's account, party documents show that the Salvadoran Communist Party took the decision to rise on its own, not on instruction from Moscow. The third stage is one of rigidity under Stalinism and its stagist doctrine, which confined revolutions to a national-democratic framework, and it ran alongside Peronism and Cold War terror. The fourth stage brings in Cuba, Allende's Chile, Sandinista Nicaragua and the dependency-theory debates on modes of production and the world system. Webber also notes that the history after 1959 is often reduced to guerrilla warfare, and he cites a study of the 1969 Córdoba uprising as a corrective.

For the neoliberal period, Webber points to retreat, defeat and self-criticism, with many intellectuals turning to post-Marxism or liberalism. He highlights counter-currents such as the Brazilian Landless Workers' Movement (MST) and the Zapatistas. He treats the current stage cautiously. Writing in 2021, he calls it too early to say the left cycle is over, and he sees both the originality of the fourth stage and signs of the dogmatism of the third. Read the original if you want an annotated, period-by-period bibliography of Latin American Marxism and its histories, with brief critical notes on each work.
quoteEn: The latest stage of Latin American Marxism shows both the originality and depth of the fourth stage and signs of rigidity and dogmatism like those of the third.
quoteZh: 拉美马克思主义的最新发展阶段，既有像第四阶段那样的原创性和深刻性，也有如第三阶段一样的僵化和教条迹象。

t: A critique of nature-centred ecological views and the construction of a new ecological philosophy
st: Slavoj Žižek's psychoanalytic reading of ecology
zh: 自然中心主义生态观的批判与新生态哲学的建构
source: Foreign Social Sciences (Guowai shehui kexue), 2021 no. 2
paras: Why has ecological crisis not eased despite decades of Western ecological thought? Shi examines this through the work of the Slovenian left thinker Slavoj Žižek. The article argues that nature-centrism (environmental ethics, wilderness philosophy, deep ecology) rests on a utopian ontological assumption of a perfectly balanced, original nature. Žižek, in Shi's account, rejects this assumption from a psychoanalytic standpoint and offers a new ecological philosophy built on the future perfect tense and collective action.

The article has three main parts. The first reconstructs nature-centrism: Schweitzer, Leopold and Rolston's ecological ethics, which extends ethical concern to non-human beings; wilderness philosophy; and Arne Naess's deep ecology with its principles of biocentric equality and self-realisation. The second sets out Žižek's claim that "nature does not exist". The third presents his new ecological philosophy, and a conclusion compares it with Marx and Engels.

Shi's core argument is that the "original nature" is a retroactive construction of thought. Humans need to imagine nature as an ordered whole in order to live, and the past cannot be verified. Žižek, Shi reports, calls humanity "nature's wound" (a psychoanalytic trauma). He argues that nature is inherently disastrous and unbalanced, citing a dialectical reading of Darwin and the claim that most human DNA is "junk". Since the emergence of humans, nature has also been a "second nature", and genetic engineering threatens to end it altogether. From this follows an ecology of the "future perfect": disaster is to be accepted as fate, so that action retroactively changes what was possible. Collective action is its counterpart, drawing on Badiou's four moments of egalitarian justice. It calls for strict equality in resource burdens, terror against violators, voluntarism and trust in the people, including the figure of the informer.

Shi concludes that nature-centrism has raised environmental awareness but drifts towards ecological utopia. Žižek's philosophy, though imperfect, shifts attention to practical solutions centred on human value. Shi sees links with Marx's view of nature as humanised and socio-historical, with Engels's warning that nature takes revenge for human victories, and with Marx's concept of practice. Shi presents it as a new path for global ecological problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Žižek's ecology and its comparison with Marx and Engels.
quoteEn: Žižek's new ecological philosophy, drawing on the psychoanalytic concept of "trauma", brings us a new way of thinking about ecological problems.
quoteZh: 齐泽克的新生态哲学正是从精神分析视野下的“创伤”概念为我们带来了有关生态问题的新思考

glossary.explanation: The label the article gives to Western ecological currents such as environmental ethics, wilderness philosophy and deep ecology. It treats nature as having intrinsic value and rights, in opposition to anthropocentrism.
The world of human creations, nature as transformed by human activity and society. The article links Žižek's use of it to Marx's view of nature as a product of industry and history.
A French tense for an action completed before another future action. Žižek uses it as a model of time in which a projected future retroactively determines present action.

t: Foreign left commemorations and reflections on the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth
zh: 国外左翼对恩格斯诞辰200周年的纪念与省思
source: Socialist Studies (社会主义研究), 2021 no. 3
paras: Writing in a 2021 issue of Socialist Studies, Yuan and Wang survey how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China marked the 200th anniversary of Friedrich Engels's birth in 2020. They note that disputes over Engels, especially his late thought, have persisted since Marx's death in 1883. The article argues that the foreign left's commemorations affirmed Engels's historical standing and the continuing guiding value of his ideas, at a time the authors describe as a turn from the low tide of world socialism towards revival.

The article opens with an inventory of events: seminars in Lisbon, Hanoi, Vientiane and Japan; joint declarations by Marxist-Leninist-Maoist parties; commemorative essays by figures such as Gennady Zyuganov, Brinda Karat and Marcello Musto; and the 'Engels Year' in Wuppertal, with film premieres, demonstrations and wreath-laying. It then turns to four themes: Engels's status as co-founder of Marxism, the world significance of his works, the contemporary value of his thought, and the strategies the foreign left proposed. A short conclusion links the event to the 2018 Marx bicentenary.

In the authors' account, commentators from the Communist Party of Vietnam, the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and others rejected claims of a 'Marx–Engels opposition' and of Engels's late abandonment of revolution, and defended him as the indispensable 'second violin'. They credit him with contributions to dialectical materialism, political economy (his 1844 Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy), scientific socialism, women's liberation and military science. Speakers cited the global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic, including the rise in billionaires' wealth, as confirming Engels's and Marx's analyses of capitalism.

The authors report that the foreign left drew practical conclusions: building revolutionary working-class parties, strengthening the study, publication and teaching of Marxist theory, and forming broad anti-war and united fronts under the slogan 'Workers of all countries, unite!' They conclude that Engels's doctrines on scientific socialism, party building and the state still guide the socialist movement, and that these left forces, working in the heartlands of imperialism, combine revolutionary optimism with sober judgement. Read the original if you want a detailed catalogue of the parties, scholars and publications involved in the 2020 Engels commemorations, as presented from a Chinese Marxist viewpoint.
quoteEn: This commemoration was also a vivid practice of Marxist-Leninist education.
quoteZh: 这次纪念活动更是一场马列主义教育的生动实践。

t: The Chinese path as seen by foreign left-wing scholars
zh: 国外左翼学者眼中的中国道路
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 31 December 2020
paras: Writing in China Social Sciences Today at the end of 2020, Liu Mingming and Liu Qi take up how foreign scholars assess the Chinese path. They note that criticism and praise coexist abroad. Their thesis is that a growing number of left-wing scholars outside China are shedding earlier ideological constraints, judging the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics more objectively, and placing hope in the contemporary value of the Chinese path.

The short commentary is organised in four parts. It first reports the reasons foreign scholars give for the path's success, then the debate over its nature, then its significance for the world, and finally the claim that it represents hope for socialism. It draws on Russian specialists, the German China expert Sebastian Heilmann, Samir Amin, the British scholar Martin Jacques, and the American economist David Schweickart (named in the text as Schweickart), among others.

On success, the authors report foreign views that Communist Party leadership is the key factor, together with a gradual reform path that avoided copying other countries, preserved state-owned enterprises and macroeconomic regulation, and was preferable to "shock therapy". They add a view that China's commitment to peaceful development lets it avoid the fate of rising powers that sought hegemony. On the question of nature, they cite Amin, who holds that state ownership of land shows China is not capitalist, and Schweickart, who argues that China fails the test of a market economy with dominant private ownership and wage labour because state firms still dominate core sectors.

On global significance, the authors present scholars who see the Chinese path as an alternative to Western models, a challenge to Fukuyama's "end of history" and a driver of global growth. They also cite views that public ownership of key sectors and state intervention guard against financial excess, and that Chinese success makes socialism the best practical hope of the twenty-first century, with Vietnam and Laos named as followers. They conclude that the Chinese path is a vivid contemporary expression of scientific socialism and points to a new direction for socialist development. Read the original if you want a brief, selective overview of favourable foreign left-wing opinion of China, as presented in Chinese official-academic media.
quoteEn: In sum, the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics is a vivid contemporary manifestation of the theory of scientific socialism and represents a new direction for socialist development.
quoteZh: 总之，中国特色社会主义道路是科学社会主义理论在当代的生动展现，代表着社会主义发展的新方向。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, associated with the reform era from Deng Xiaoping onwards. It combines Party leadership, a socialist market economy and public ownership as the main body.
A common shorthand in Chinese discourse for China's distinctive route of development under Party leadership. Foreign scholars' discussions of it are often cited in China as external validation.
The rapid, radical market liberalisation and privatisation adopted in Russia and Eastern Europe after 1989–91. Chinese commentary typically contrasts it with China's gradual reform.

t: Policy adjustment and practical exploration of the South African Communist Party across a century of political change
zh: 百年政治变迁下南非共产党的政策调适与实践探索
paras: Marking the centenary of the South African Communist Party (SACP, founded 1921), this article asks why the oldest and largest socialist party in Africa has survived apartheid repression, the democratic transition and the collapse of the Soviet bloc. Zhang argues that the fundamental reason is the party's consistent use of Marxism to analyse South Africa's concrete conditions, together with timely strategic and tactical adjustments to changing circumstances.

The article follows the party chronologically. Part one covers the apartheid era in three phases: 1921–1950, the underground period after the 1950 Suppression of Communism Act (with refounding in 1953), and 1960–1990, when it turned to armed struggle. Part two treats the 1990s transition and the post-Soviet crisis. Part three examines the party's search for socialism after the 1994 election, and a short conclusion assesses its present difficulties.

Zhang's central claim is that the SACP's durability rests on a theoretical line and an organisational form. The theory is "colonialism of a special type" and the "two-stage revolution": a national democratic revolution first, then socialism. The form is the Tripartite Alliance with the African National Congress (ANC) and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU). After 1990 the party reassessed socialism, following Joe Slovo's argument that the Soviet model, not socialism, had failed. It kept Marxism-Leninism while accepting multiparty politics, and it defined itself as a "mass vanguard party" focused on organised industrial workers. After 1994 it pursued socialism by three routes: taking part in government through ANC lists, reshaping the Alliance (notably the Alliance Political Council from 2008 and the 2019 reconfiguration document), and mass campaigns such as the Red October Campaign, which Zhang links to the National Health Insurance plan.

Zhang concludes that the SACP, now said to have over 300,000 members and to be the second-largest party, still depends on the Alliance. Its two pillars are weakened: the ANC by factionalism and corruption, and COSATU by fragmentation. The party therefore pushes for ANC renewal and Alliance reconfiguration while exploring contesting elections independently. Zhang notes that whether it eventually leaves the Alliance depends on the Alliance's development and the ANC's direction. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-perspective history of the SACP and its strategy within the ANC-led Alliance.
quoteEn: The most fundamental reason the SACP has endured for a century is that it has always applied Marxism to analyse South Africa's concrete situation and promptly adjusted its strategy and tactics as circumstances changed, so that its development suits South Africa's national conditions.
quoteZh: 南非共产党历经百年而不衰，最根本的原因在于该党始终坚持运用马克思主义分析南非的具体形势，并根据形势发展变化及时作出战略与战术上的调整，从而使自身发展能够适应南非的具体国情。

glossary.explanation: A theory developed by the SACP in the 1950s–60s. It holds that South Africa combines a white imperialist state and a colonised black population within one country, so class struggle and national liberation are fused.
The SACP strategy of first achieving a national democratic revolution and then moving on to a socialist society.
The alliance of the ANC, the SACP and COSATU, formalised in 1988 against apartheid and continued after 1994 as a governing alliance.
In SACP theory, the first stage of revolution: ending colonial and racial domination and building a non-racial democracy, seen as the basis for socialism.
The SACP's post-1990 self-definition: a party with a broad popular base that remains the political vanguard of the working class.

t: Historical nihilism in the Soviet Union under Gorbachev: its manifestations, essence and harm
zh: 戈尔巴乔夫时期苏联历史虚无主义的表现、实质及危害
paras: Writing in 2021, thirty years after the Soviet collapse, Wang Tingyou asks how historical nihilism, as it spread under Gorbachev, helped destroy the Soviet Communist Party and state. The article defines historical nihilism, in the sense used by socialist states, as a current of thought that disparages Communist leaders and heroes and distorts the party's history. In the author's account, its aim is to dissolve socialist ideology, shake the party's ruling position and restore capitalism. Wang's thesis is that it was an important, unavoidable factor in the collapse, driven by Soviet leaders and Western ideological penetration.

The article has five sections. It first examines Gorbachev's unrestricted "openness" (glasnost) and the press freedom it brought. It then surveys the nihilist tide in literature, journalism and historiography, including the "blank spots" campaign, the "Great Purge" death tolls, and attacks on Lenin, Marxism and the army. A third section deals with the role of Gorbachev and Yakovlev. A fourth covers Western broadcasting, exchanges, Nobel prizes and foundations, and a fifth draws lessons.

Wang argues that Lenin's idea of openness was limited and bounded by discipline and secrecy, whereas Gorbachev's became a one-way street for anti-communist views. The Nina Andreyeva affair is the author's example. Wang concedes that deep-seated Soviet problems gave nihilism its soil, but holds that Gorbachev and Yakovlev played the decisive part. They attacked Marxism-Leninism as an "ideological monopoly", used the language of humanism and "alienation" to call for abolishing the party's leading role, and replaced editors with sympathisers. The author adds that the West used media, student exchanges, prizes and foundations to cultivate pro-Western figures. The harms Wang lists are the loss of the party's ideology and legitimacy, the dismantling of socialist institutions and the stoking of ethnic separatism.

Wang draws four lessons, citing Xi Jinping's 2013 remarks on the Soviet collapse. History and leaders such as Stalin must be assessed scientifically, which the author says the Soviet party never did. Marxism's guiding position and communist ideals must be maintained. Ideological work and its leadership must be taken seriously. Defences against Western ideological penetration must be strengthened, along with core socialist values and national unity education. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic account of the Soviet collapse that is rich in Soviet-era citations and explains how historical nihilism is understood in China's current ideological debates.
quoteEn: If Marxism does not occupy the ideological front, non-Marxist and anti-Marxist currents of thought will occupy it.
quoteZh: 意识形态这块阵地，马克思主义不去占领，非马克思主义、反马克思主义思潮就会去占领

glossary.explanation: In official Chinese usage, a political and intellectual trend said to denigrate the Communist Party's history, leaders and heroes in order to undermine socialist ideology and the Party's rule. The term is contested outside China.
Gorbachev's policy of greater transparency and freedom of expression from the mid-1980s. The author contends that it was turned into unrestricted exposure of Soviet history's dark sides.
The Party's work of shaping thought, public opinion, education and culture in line with Marxism. Chinese authors treat its leadership as a central task of the Party.
General Secretary of the Communist Party of China since 2012. The article cites his 2013 remarks on the lessons of the Soviet collapse.

t: The historical evolution and present predicament of the German Social Democratic Party
zh: 德国社会民主党的历史变迁与现实困境
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2021 no. 5
paras: Wu Huiping asks why the German Social Democratic Party (SPD), the country's oldest party and once the political voice of the working class, has fallen into a lasting crisis in the twenty-first century. The article presents the SPD as a microcosm of the condition of Western left parties, especially centre-left parties in Europe. Wu argues that the crisis stems from a mix of structural change in Western democracy, shifts in the electorate and the party's own strategic choices, and that the party's reforms have so far had only partial success.

The article opens with the SPD's history from Lassalle's General German Workers' Association (1863) to the present, covering its periods in opposition, persecution and government. It then traces the eight party programmes from Eisenach (1869) to Hamburg (2007), and describes the party's social base and organisation. A section on current symptoms uses figures on vote share, polling, membership and age structure. The analysis of causes draws on Oskar Niedermayer's framework of party competition, and the article ends by reviewing the SPD's reform measures up to the 2021 federal election.

Wu's core explanation works on three levels. First, the framework conditions have changed. Parties have lost standing to social movements, and the Greens, German unification and the refugee crisis have intensified competition from both left and right. Second, the electorate has fragmented. Industrial workers fell from 42.9% to 24% of employment between 1950 and 2020, and loyal voters have given way to swing voters. Third, the party itself has weakened its profile. The 1959 Godesberg Programme moved it to a centre-left catch-all stance, and Schröder's market-oriented labour reforms alienated its working-class base. Wu also points to the dilemma of junior partnership in grand coalitions, factional struggles and unstable leadership.

Wu reviews the SPD's response: renewing the social justice agenda (minimum wage, a citizens' income), taking up digitalisation and climate protection alongside a critique of capitalism, and widening intra-party and public participation through primaries and member ballots. The article notes that the SPD narrowly came first in the September 2021 federal election, which Wu attributes largely to mistakes by rival candidates and the steadiness of Olaf Scholz. Wu holds that two structural problems remain: a split over whether to return to a social justice profile or keep the politics of consensus, and low participation in the new democratic procedures. Read the original if you want a data-rich account of the SPD's programmes, decline and reforms, written from a Chinese academic standpoint just before the 2021 election.
quoteEn: The SPD's strategy of moving towards the centre gave it strong advantages in forming alliances, but it also brought its positions ever closer to those of the centre-right parties and blurred its programmatic profile. It also left a representation vacuum on the political margins, giving small fringe parties room to grow.
quoteZh: 社民党向中间靠拢的策略尽管赋予其很强的政治结盟优势，但也导致其与中右翼政党的政治主张日益接近，纲领特色不再清晰，同时也在政治边缘地带留下代表性真空，为边缘小党的发展提供了空间。

t: Main challenges, lessons and implications for centenarian political parties abroad
zh: 国外百年政党面临的主要挑战、经验教训及启示
paras: Written for the centenary of the Communist Party of China (2021), this article looks at what the history of other long-lived parties can teach. The authors note that more than 70 well-known parties abroad are at least a century old and still active. They include the British Conservative and Labour parties, the US Democratic and Republican parties, the German and Swedish social democrats, the African National Congress and the Indian National Congress. Qian and Zhong argue that these parties face growing, largely unprecedented difficulties, but that their record also holds experience and warnings useful as a mirror for the CPC.

The article has three parts. The first sets out four shared challenges since the Cold War, especially since 2000. The second draws five historical lessons of success and five of failure from cases across Europe, Latin America, South Asia, Africa and Mongolia. The third offers five reflections on what drives the rise and fall of such parties. Much of the evidence is electoral and membership data, for example the fall in Labour's vote share and the Indian National Congress's 2014 defeat.

On the challenges, the authors point to globalization, informatization and new media weakening old parties' mobilising power. They also cite depoliticization, falling public trust and membership, the rise of new and populist parties, and the decline of some major parties, especially centre-left socialist parties. Among the successes they list a relatively clear guiding ideology that is adjusted flexibly, a broader social base, relatively democratic and tolerant inner-party life, historical contributions to nation-building or welfare states, and electoral systems favourable to the established parties. The failures they list are weak and frequently replaced leaders, factionalism and splits, corruption, sharp policy swings, and dynastic or family rule. From this the authors derive five points. Steadfast ideals sustain parties, including non-governing communist parties that survived hostile conditions. Leaders matter directly. Unity is a party's lifeline. Reform and self-renewal are essential but must be kept in proportion, as the German social democrats' case shows. Strong delivery on promises is needed to hold public trust.

Qian and Zhong conclude that the comparison helps clarify the laws of party development and supports the CPC's confidence as the world's largest Marxist governing party in pursuing its second centenary goal. They say some declining parties still retain a capacity for self-repair. The article is written from within the Party's own framework and uses Xi Jinping's July 2021 speech as its closing frame. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-affiliated scholars' overview of foreign centenarian parties, with the country-by-country data and cases behind the authors' lessons for the CPC.
quoteEn: Party unity is the lifeline that ensures a party's survival and development.
quoteZh: 团结是确保党生存发展的生命线

glossary.explanation: The goal of building China into a modern socialist country by 2049, the centenary of the People's Republic. It follows the first centenary goal of a moderately prosperous society, marked by the CPC's centenary in 2021.

t: An assessment of the Polish Communist Party's understanding of new trends in contemporary capitalism
zh: 波兰共产党对当代资本主义发展新态势的认识评析
paras: Yang Yousun examines how the Polish Communist Party, a small non-governing party founded in 2002, understands contemporary capitalism. The author treats the party as representative of communist parties in Central and Eastern Europe that are out of power. The article's thesis is that the party's views are both scientific and progressive in many respects and clearly dogmatic and limited in others.

The article first traces three successive parties called the Polish Communist Party, from the Luxemburg-led party of 1918 to the present one, which Yang describes as relatively moderate and stable. It then sets out the party's positions under six headings: the collapse of socialism and Poland's capitalist transition; domestic problems under capitalism; the stage of world capitalism; opposition to hegemonism and to NATO and the EU; labour rights; and plans to rebuild socialism. Yang then assesses these positions using Luke March's typologies of the far left, and ends with the party's prospects.

The party calls the transition after 1989 a restoration of capitalist relations of production, and describes the current stage as 'globalized imperialism'. It blames capitalism for corruption, bloated administration, a Catholic Church that has become capitalism's appendage, and worsening conditions for workers. It also demands nationalization, central planning, a shorter working week and Poland's exit from the EU and NATO. Yang classes the party as a conservative member of the radical left and a mainly reformist communist party that keeps some conservative traces. Yang praises its support for labour rights, secularism, gender equality and free education, and its pragmatic choice to take part in elections. Yang criticizes its blanket opposition to free-trade bodies, globalization, the Church and the market economy. Yang cites 2018 Eurobarometer data showing 71 per cent of Poles feel close to the EU, and notes that over 90 per cent of Poles are Catholic.

Yang concludes that membership remains small (300 registered members in 2017) and that revival will take time, but that the party has long-term vitality. Three reasons are given: capitalism's basic contradictions persist and have been sharpened by the 2008 crisis and the pandemic; the working-class base survives in the employer–worker cleavage; and communist parties are increasingly cooperating internationally. The right-wing Law and Justice government's repression is expected to bring only short-term pressure. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of a small European communist party, with detail on its programme, its typology and the evidence behind the author's verdict.
quoteEn: The party's anti-EU stance clearly does not accord with Poland's national interests, and runs even more sharply against the wishes of Poles, especially young people.
quoteZh: 波共的反欧盟立场，显然不符合波兰的国家利益，更与波兰人——尤其是年轻人的愿望背道而驰。

t: Reflections on the historical limitations of contemporary Western identity politics
zh: 当代西方身份政治历史局限性反思
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories
paras: Writing in 2021, against what they call a world undergoing changes unseen in a century, Fang Min and Zhu Yun ask why Western developed countries have struggled since the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. They note that thinkers such as Mark Lilla and Francis Fukuyama point to identity politics. The authors argue that contemporary Western identity politics is a historical product of capitalism at a certain stage. In their view it expresses economic and political inequality within capitalism in cultural form, and only the sublation of capitalism can fundamentally resolve it.

The article defines identity politics as the politics, arising from the new social movements of the 1960s, of recognising the difference of groups and protecting their rights. It has three parts. The first surveys four forms: the New Left, minority rights movements, the new feminism, and white conservative identity politics. The second examines economic, political and cultural causes. The third sets out three historical limitations.

On causes, the authors point to neoliberal globalisation, which they say widened inequality (citing US Census Bureau income shares and Piketty). They also point to a crisis of capitalist democracy, marked by "veto democracy", interest-group capture and declining trust in parties, and to the internal contradictions of multiculturalism. The core argument is that identity politics, as cultural contestation, does not touch private ownership of the means of production. They cite Marx's remark that a Black person becomes a slave only under certain relations. On this reading, the left abandoned class analysis, shifted from emancipatory to performative politics, and became an unwitting ally of neoliberalism. The authors link this to the 2016 Trump vote.

The authors further argue that identity politics makes populism a normal feature of Western politics, with left and right populisms each claiming to speak for "the people". They also hold that it threatens world peace through separatism, anti-globalisation and Huntington-style "clash of civilizations" thinking. As an example of the last, they cite a 2019 remark by a US State Department official about China. They conclude that the world's peoples should face the challenge together, and that only by sublating capitalism and building a community with a shared future for mankind can the problem be resolved. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western identity politics that draws on Lilla, Fukuyama and Huntington.
quoteEn: Contemporary Western identity politics is a politics of difference, whose essence is the expression, at the socio-cultural level, of economic and political inequality and conflict within the framework of capitalism.
quoteZh: 当代西方身份政治是一种差异政治，其本质是资本主义框架内经济、政治不平等和冲突在社会文化层面的表达。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for common development and joint management of global challenges.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's and Marx's Aufhebung. It means negating something while preserving and transcending its valuable elements.

glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping and Chinese officials since 2017–18 to describe a shift in the global balance of power and international order.
Western movements from the 1960s onward (civil rights, feminism, environmentalism, student protest) organised around identity and culture rather than the traditional labour–capital conflict.

t: A new look at Spivak's postcolonial feminist critique
st: From the perspective of the theory of imperialist crisis control
zh: 斯皮瓦克的后殖民女性主义批判新探
zhSub: 基于帝国主义危机控制理论的视角
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2021 no. 4
paras: Does Marxism still explain exploitation in an age of post-industrial prosperity and cultural critique? He and Dai take up this question through Gayatri C. Spivak, whom they present as the first feminist scholar in postcolonial criticism to explain imperialist "crisis control". Their thesis is that Spivak uses a deconstructive reading of Marx's labour theory of value to show how contemporary capitalism shifts its crises onto the Third World and, above all, onto poor women there. For Spivak, they report, cultural and ideological critique alone conceals the material suffering involved.

The article has three main sections. The first sets out the contemporary turn in crisis control: its spatial transfer from the imperialist core to the Third World, its transfer from class conflict to gender, and its mixing of pre-modern and modern features. The second gives the political-economy reading, covering use-value, global exploitation and what Spivak calls "epistemic violence". The third turns to her postcolonial feminist critique, which the authors group under three headings, and a short conclusion follows.

The authors' central move is Spivak's reading of Marx on use-value. In their account, commodity exchange abstracts away the human labour embedded in goods, as in her example of Nike shoes and Indonesian women workers. This residual labour is a "ghostly" presence, and Spivak treats use-value as a "lever of deconstruction" that could interrupt capitalist circulation. Building on this, she argues that the old worker–capitalist contradiction has become a North–South one. Gender ideology and patriarchal relations obscure the labour–capital contradiction, and women in the global South become a new super-exploited labour force.

Spivak's critique of Western feminism has three parts, according to the authors. She deconstructs its claim to universal "sisterhood", which she sees as complicit with imperialism. She traces how the voices of subaltern women are "foreclosed". She also insists on speaking for women within wider institutions and organisations of production, citing the SEWA and Women's World Bank case. The authors conclude that Spivak keeps labour as the sole source of value and sees North–South relations as a continuation of the nineteenth-century capitalist–worker relation. They also note Arif Dirlik's criticism of her. Read the original if you study postcolonial theory, Marxist feminism or the Chinese reception of Spivak as a Marxist thinker.
quoteEn: Spivak's attempt to deconstruct the capitalist system of value determination is both a vivid unfolding of the contemporary significance of the labour theory of value and a call to end the silence of Third World women in culture, politics and the economy.
quoteZh: 斯皮瓦克试图解构资本主义价值决定体系，这不仅是劳动价值理论的当代意义的生动展开，也是在呼吁改善第三世界女性在文化、政治和经济中的沉默状态。

t: Anti-corruption governance of the Communist Party of Vietnam in the Đổi Mới period: stages, results and basic lessons
zh: 革新时期越南共产党的腐败治理：阶段历程、主要成效与基本经验
paras: Since the launch of Đổi Mới (renovation) in 1986, Vietnam has grown quickly, but the authors note that corruption, which Vietnamese citizens call a 'national calamity', has been one of its 'four major crises'. This article asks how the Communist Party of Vietnam has governed corruption over the period and what China might learn. The authors argue that the Party's approach has moved through three stages, produced real results, and yielded experience that offers 'some reference' for China's own anti-corruption drive.

The article has three parts. The first periodises Vietnamese anti-corruption into a campaign stage (1986–2005), a rule-of-law stage (2006–2015) and a comprehensive stage (2016 to the present). The second sets out three results: better institutions and specialised bodies, a cleaner political ecology that strengthens the Party's hold on power, and a better climate for economic growth and foreign investment. The third distils four groups of lessons, supported by figures on Party purges, prosecutions, asset declarations and whistle-blower reports.

In the authors' account, the early Party rectification campaigns expelled large numbers of members but fell short: a 2000 survey cited in the article found that about 43 per cent of members were suspected of or involved in corruption. The shift began with the 2005 Law on Anti-Corruption, the creation of a central steering committee and an anti-corruption police bureau, and, after the 12th Party Congress (2016), a 'no forbidden zones' policy reaching the military, energy and finance. The authors present the lessons as multi-layered. They list strengthened Party leadership and an anti-'peaceful evolution' struggle, cadre rotation, salary reform and asset declaration, and intra-Party democracy with checks such as the 'four pillars' division of top posts. They add National Assembly questioning, repeatedly amended legislation and Party discipline rules, and combined supervision by the Party, public reporting with rewards, and media exposure.

The authors conclude that Vietnam's anti-corruption has curbed corrupt practices to a degree, eased relations between Party and people and consolidated the Party's governing base, though they acknowledge earlier phases did not fundamentally change the situation. They suggest these lessons can inform China's governance of corruption. Read the original if you want a Chinese-published, Party-friendly overview of Vietnamese anti-corruption institutions, with dates, laws and figures, and an indication of what Chinese scholars take from a fellow socialist state.
quoteEn: The history of Vietnam's Đổi Mới development is also the history of the Communist Party and government's continuous struggle against corruption.
quoteZh: 越南的革新发展史，也是越南共产党和政府不断地同腐败现象作斗争的历程

glossary.explanation: The comprehensive reform policy adopted by the Communist Party of Vietnam at its Sixth Congress in 1986, opening the economy while keeping one-party rule.
Mass campaigns to re-educate members and purge those deemed unqualified or corrupt, a method inherited from the Leninist and Chinese communist tradition.
A term used in socialist-state discourse for alleged Western efforts to undermine socialist systems by non-military means such as ideological and cultural influence.
The authors' label for Vietnam's division of the four top posts (Party general secretary, prime minister, state president, National Assembly chair) among different people.

t: New trends in the unification of the world's communist parties in recent years and how China should respond
zh: 近年来世界共产党联合化新趋势与我们的应对
paras: Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China, Yu Weihai asks what the state and trajectory of the international communist movement are amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century. Yu's thesis is that the world's many communist and workers' parties are showing a clear tendency to unite. In Yu's account this differs from the Internationals of the 19th and 20th centuries and amounts to a "new historical feature" that China must study and respond to.

The article has four parts. It first describes four manifestations of unification: standing organisational platforms, joint statements, coordinated international struggles and a shared spirit. It then identifies four new features: equal and diverse participants, networked and resonant spatial patterns, continuous and dense activity, and issue-based rather than organisation-based forms. The third part evaluates the trend, and the last sets out policy responses. Evidence includes a list of platforms founded since 1993, the 93-party statement for Lenin's 150th anniversary in 2020, and Yu's own 2019 fieldwork in the United States.

Yu argues that unification strengthens the forces opposing capitalism, enlarges the voice of world socialism and renews the content and forms of the movement, which no longer follows "one centre, one line, one model". Yu also stresses limits: some 400 parties, sectarian rivalry, exclusionary platforms, dogmatism and a tension between short-term issues and long-term goals still weaken unity. Many of these parties, Yu notes, criticise socialism with Chinese characteristics, and some call for a new Comintern-style body.

Yu proposes that China strengthen research on the international communist movement and on Xi Jinping's theory of a "new type of party relations". Yu rejects calls for the CPC to take up the banner of uniting world socialism and advises a policy of not leading, not carrying the banner, not participating and not opposing. China should instead "develop socialism with Chinese characteristics well", while using the parties' goodwill, as in their praise for China's pandemic response in 2020. This would operate through united-front work, International Department dialogue mechanisms and think tanks. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic and policy view of how the CPC regards the foreign communist parties, with data on their platforms and joint statements.
quoteEn: Developing the great cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics well is the greatest contribution to the international communist movement.
quoteZh: 认真发展好中国特色社会主义伟大事业，就是对国际共运的最大贡献。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up, used as the core formula of Party ideology.

A concept associated with Xi Jinping for the CPC's relations with other parties abroad, stressing independence, equality, mutual respect and non-interference. Yu presents it as a basis for CPC party diplomacy.
The worldwide movement of communist parties and organisations, from the Communist League and the Internationals to the present. In Chinese usage it is often abbreviated as 国际共运.
The CPC's practice of building alliances with and influencing non-Party groups. Here Yu applies it to foreign communist parties.

t: Marxist political science in Monthly Review in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪美国《每月评论》的马克思主义政治学研究
source: Foreign Social Sciences (Guowai shehui kexue), 2021 no. 2
paras: Fu Hao and Cheng Enfu examine how the American journal Monthly Review, founded by Leo Huberman and Paul Sweezy, has treated Marxist political science since 2000. They argue that the journal has become a representative new force in American left-wing political critique, marked by a radical style, serious scholarship, pluralism and innovative thinking. They also hold that its discussion of some political questions is limited and that its influence on world socialism remains underdeveloped.

The article has four parts. It first covers the journal's work on the Marxist theory of the state, then its theory of twenty-first-century imperialism, which the authors divide into three stages. It next turns to its proposals for socialist and eco-socialist revolution. A final section assesses the journal's innovations and limitations. The authors draw mainly on István Mészáros, Michael Lebowitz, Jean-Claude Paye, Noam Chomsky, Samir Amin, William Tabb and John Bellamy Foster.

In the authors' account, Mészáros calls for going beyond capital's "Leviathan" state and pursuing substantive equality and democracy. Paye and others criticise the fusion of war law and criminal law, the constitutionalisation of emergency powers, and the prison system. On imperialism, the journal is said to describe a "barbaric empire" (2000–2007), then a period of "cracks in the empire" after the 2008 financial crisis, and from 2016 a "late empire". Foster and Amin reject theories of a "new imperialism" and hold that the present is a stage of global monopoly-finance capital. The journal also characterises Trump's presidency as neo-fascist. For the future, Lebowitz's twenty-first-century socialism rests on a "basic triangle" of social property, social production and social needs, and on producing a "new socialist human being". Foster's eco-socialism relies on an "environmental proletariat" and a two-stage programme, with a minimum programme now and a maximum programme later.

The authors credit the journal with three innovations: new theory suited to its time, bold new propositions that go beyond classical Marxism, and an international, pluralist scholarly community. They name three limitations. The journal faces suppression by right-wing forces and financial constraints. It mixes Marxism with Western Marxism and is sometimes metaphysical rather than practical. Its understanding of existing socialist countries, above all socialism with Chinese characteristics, is in their view prejudiced and mistaken. They hope Western left scholars will come to understand it better. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of Monthly Review's political theory, including how Chinese authors judge its treatment of China.
quoteEn: Monthly Review has also shown some controversies and deviations in its Marxist political science research; it still has considerable room for development and improvement, and the political spring of the American left is far from arriving.
quoteZh: 《每月评论》在马克思主义政治学研究中也出现了一些争议与偏差，在未来仍具备较大的发展与提升空间，美国左翼的政治春天远未到来。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current path, theory and system, combining Party leadership, a socialist system and market-oriented reform. It has been used since the 1980s.

t: Knowledge monopoly as an important feature of contemporary capitalism
st: The case of US technological hegemony
zh: 知识垄断是当代资本主义的重要特征
zhSub: 以美国科技霸权为例
paras: Writing in 2021, Li Yan asks how knowledge and capital combine in contemporary capitalism and argues that international monopoly capital now practises a "knowledge monopoly" as a defining feature of the system. In the author's account, transnational firms and strategic alliances monopolise the conditions of knowledge production, namely intellectual property and specialised personnel. This gives them control over core technology and, through it, command over non-core production stages, from which they extract surplus value worldwide.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs how Marx and Harry Braverman analysed the union of science and capital. The second sets out five features of present-day knowledge monopoly. The third takes US technological hegemony as a case: domestic promotion of science, the containment of the Soviet Union, Japan and China, and the harms of monopoly.

Li draws on Marx's account of science becoming an independent power opposed to labour, and on Braverman's analysis of Taylorism and the separation of "head" from "hand". The author applies this logic to the world economy. Lead firms keep research and design and outsource manufacturing, which sets workers against one another across countries. Intellectual property regimes, patent pools, standards alliances and state power then entrench the monopoly, producing a "centre–periphery" division of labour between "brain" and "limbs". For the US, Li describes federal research funding, talent recruitment, the Bayh-Dole Act (1980) and the TRIPS Agreement (1994). Li contrasts these with export controls on the USSR, trade and technology war on Japan, and entity-list sanctions, visa limits and investigations targeting Huawei and Chinese researchers. In Li's reading, these measures aim to protect monopoly capital's dominance and to keep China "locked in" at the middle and low end of global value chains.

Li concludes that knowledge monopoly runs against the socialisation of production and the internationalisation of innovation. It obstructs international cooperation and widens uneven development between countries and between knowledge workers and ordinary workers. Drawing on Lenin on the parasitic character of monopoly capitalism, the author holds that private appropriation turns knowledge, which is shareable and non-rival, into a fetter on scientific progress. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy framing of US–China technology conflict, built on Marx, Braverman and Lenin, and a view of how Chinese scholars described it in 2021.
quoteEn: The implementation of knowledge monopoly by international monopoly capital in global economic activity is an important feature of contemporary capitalism.
quoteZh: 国际垄断资本在全球经济活动中实施知识垄断是当代资本主义的重要特征。

glossary.explanation: The article's term for monopoly capital's control of the conditions of knowledge production, such as intellectual property and specialised personnel, in order to command global production and profits.
Legal exclusive rights over knowledge products such as patents and trademarks. The author treats them as the legal form of private appropriation of knowledge and as a tool of monopoly.

A formulation from Marx and Braverman on the split between mental and manual labour under capitalism. The article extends it to a global division of labour between countries holding core knowledge and those doing manufacturing.
A model of the world economy, common in dependency and world-system theory, in which advanced core countries dominate less developed peripheral ones.

t: The current state and prospects of the Latin American left
zh: 当前拉美左翼的发展现状与前景
paras: Writing in 2021, Yang Jianmin asks where the Latin American left stands after the "pink tide" that began with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999, and whether a new cycle of left government is opening. The article argues that the region has moved from "the left retreats, the right advances" (2015–2018) to a phase of mixed gains and losses and power-sharing. The right retains an overall advantage, but Yang holds that the left is recovering, remains seriously divided, and will persist in the region over the long term.

The article has four parts. It first traces the shifting political map, from right-wing offensives during the pink tide (the 2002 Venezuelan coup, Honduras 2009, Paraguay 2012) through the rightward swing after 2015 to left victories in Mexico, Argentina, Bolivia and elsewhere. It then examines the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, elections in Ecuador, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Mexico, and the 2020 US election. A third part contrasts left coordination abroad with fragmentation at home, and a fourth assesses prospects.

Yang argues that the pandemic, with its rising poverty, public debt and vaccine scarcity, has led many Latin Americans to question neoliberal policies, which favours the left. Abroad, left parties have cooperated through bodies such as the Puebla Group, while the right-wing Lima Group has weakened after Argentina's withdrawal and Peru's change of stance. At home, Yang identifies three problems: new left forces competing with the traditional left (Chile, Ecuador), policy disagreements once in office (Ecuador under Lenín Moreno), and political fragmentation and ideological polarisation, including the rise of far-left figures.

Yang concludes that a new left cycle depends on restoring living conditions and building consensus, proving administrative competence while keeping ties to social movements, and redefining the role of the state. In Yang's view, the previous cycle failed to reform the armed forces, police and judiciary and so lost power. Persistent inequality, poverty of over 30 per cent, expanding political inclusion and party-system change give the left a lasting base. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's 2021 assessment of Latin American left politics, country by country, including the electoral data it cites.
quoteEn: The existence and development of the left-wing political forces in Latin American countries rest on political, economic, social and even demographic foundations.
quoteZh: 拉美国家左翼政治力量的存在和发展有其政治、经济、社会甚至人口方面的基础

t: Lenin's historical contribution to the ideological doctrine of the new-type Bolshevik party
zh: 列宁创建布尔什维克新型政党意识形态学说的历史贡献
paras: Chen Xingliang asks how Lenin's treatment of ideology equipped the Bolsheviks to become a new type of proletarian party able to carry the proletarian political revolution over into a socialist social revolution. The article argues that Lenin, working under Marxist guidance and attentive to the changing epoch, established a scientific socialist ideology and interpreted it creatively. In Chen's account this enriched Marxist ideology theory and tied it to Bolshevik practice.

The article has three main parts plus a short closing section. It first examines the preconditions: the Russian context at the turn of the twentieth century and Lenin's philosophical and political struggles, including his polemic against empirio-criticism and Bogdanov. It then sets out the distinctive features of Bolshevik party ideology, and finally considers their effect on the fate of the Soviet Union after the October Revolution, through moral education, the Proletkult controversy and the idea of a cultural revolution.

Chen's central claim is that, in Lenin's view, the spontaneous workers' movement produces only trade-unionism, which means intellectual subordination to the bourgeoisie. Since no third ideology exists, any weakening of socialist ideology strengthens bourgeois ideology, so socialist consciousness has to be brought to workers by the vanguard through what the article calls inculcation. The Bolsheviks therefore had to act as producers of a scientific, class-based ideology, uniting criticism with revolutionary purpose and treating Marxism as a method rather than a dogma. After 1917, Chen says, Lenin applied this to communist morality for the young and to culture. He rejected the Proletkult school's nihilism toward past culture and held that proletarian culture must absorb the valuable achievements of human thought, while warning against haste in cultural work.

Chen concludes that Lenin's ideological principles remained 'living principles' and that the Soviet Union's fate became closely bound up with the Russian Communist Party's reliance on ideology and the way its functions were exercised. In a brief closing section addressed to the present day, Chen calls for safeguarding socialist ideological positions, strengthening cultural confidence and cultural leadership, and for Chinese Communists to build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding force. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Lenin's theory of ideology, the Proletkult dispute and the link between party ideology and Soviet history.
quoteEn: It was precisely in advancing proletarian cultural construction that Lenin, holding to principle and a combative spirit, gave full play to proletarian ideology's role in educating and guiding the people and in leading the development of the state and society.
quoteZh: 正是列宁在推进无产阶级文化建设过程中，坚持原则又富有战斗性的精神，充分发挥了无产阶级意识形态对人民的教育与引导作用以及对国家、社会发展的引领作用。

glossary.explanation: A movement in early Soviet Russia that sought to create a distinct proletarian culture independent of the Party and of 'bourgeois' heritage. Lenin criticised it, and Chen treats it as an ultra-left current.

Here it refers to Lenin's late idea of raising the educational and cultural level of the population, especially peasants, as a condition for socialism. It is not the Chinese Cultural Revolution of 1966–76.
A concept stressed in Chinese Party discourse since the 2010s, referring to confidence in China's cultural traditions and socialist culture.
Chinese rendering of the idea of leadership or hegemony in the cultural and ideological sphere, used by the author to describe the Party's role in guiding culture.

t: Trends in the socialist movements of South Asia since the 21st century
zh: 21世纪以来南亚社会主义运动的态势分析
paras: Zhang Shulan asks how the socialist and communist movements of the eight South Asian states (India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Bangladesh and Afghanistan) have developed since 2000. Zhang notes that earlier Chinese studies covered only four of these countries and paid little attention to the 21st century. The article's thesis is that the movements share a fragmented structure but show common new trends in domestic alliances, regional geography and international networks. Overall, Zhang judges the movement still weak, with little prospect of near-term revival, yet its trajectory worthy of approval and expectation.

The article is organised in four parts. The first sorts the movements into three types: moderate left parties committed to parliamentary struggle, radical left parties within the system, and extreme left parties outside it that pursue armed struggle. Zhang surveys party histories and election results country by country. The remaining parts examine alliances and mergers inside each country, the shifting regional spatial pattern, and the growing international links of South Asian parties.

Zhang argues that moderate left parties have declined since the Cold War and are now at a low point, strongest in the mountain states and weakest in the island states. Radical left parties survived the first two decades after the Cold War, but diverge by country: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan are near their lowest point, while Pakistan shows signs of recovery and Nepal's communists have grown. Extreme left groups, mostly Maoist, have multiplied but face harsher armed struggle because of right-wing repression and because many groups lay down arms and enter parliament. Zhang says left parties increasingly merge or form electoral fronts that last longer than before, driven by a rightward shift in politics, the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, and wider cultural and media support. Fragmentation persists, Zhang argues, because of ideological diversity, personality cults and family dominance, and localised bases. Zhang also finds the movement's centre of gravity moving from coastal and island states inland to the mountain states, citing Nepal's 2015 constitution, and legal space expanding, with Afghanistan, Bhutan and the Maldives only recently permitting party politics.

On the international side, Zhang reports that moderate and radical parties have joined more international bodies, such as Socialist International and the International Conference of Communist and Workers' Parties. Extreme left groups have built a regional Maoist coordination body, revived a global Maoist platform and joined newer coordination bodies. Zhang concludes that Maoism is a bright spot of the world movement, but that the traditional left remains weak. Read the original if you want a country-by-country survey of South Asian left parties, their alliances and international affiliations, written from a Chinese academic perspective.
quoteEn: The socialist forces of South Asia as a whole are still not strong enough, and the hope of revival in the coming period is relatively small.
quoteZh: 南亚整体的社会主义力量仍然不够强大，在未来一段时期内复兴的希望比较小。

t: Marxism in the course of the African socialist movement
zh: 非洲社会主义运动历程中的马克思主义
paras: Zheng and Shu ask how Marxism has travelled with, and shaped, socialist movements in Africa, and whether it can return to the continent after their collapse. They argue that Marxism in Africa went through three phases: introduction and emergence, flourishing, and decline with reflection. In their view the Marxist-Leninist experiments failed mainly through dogmatism and dependence on the Soviet Union, but Marxism remains a potential alternative to neoliberalism, and its return will be long and tortuous.

The article follows African socialism from the 1920s to the present. It covers the founding of the South African and Algerian communist parties, the role of colonial-era intellectuals, Pan-Africanism, the first wave of 'village-community' and democratic socialism, and the second wave of 'African scientific socialism' in states such as Congo, Ethiopia, Angola and Mozambique. It then turns to the post-1990 retreat and closes with three proposals for Africa's future.

In the early phase, the authors say, Comintern guidance, Marxist-influenced colonial intellectuals and Pan-Africanism spread Marxism, which for a time served only as one element of Pan-Africanism. After independence, neocolonialism exposed Pan-Africanism's limits, and leaders such as Nkrumah turned towards scientific socialism. The authors list the features of the Marxist-Leninist regimes: vanguard parties, acceptance of class struggle, planned economies and nationalisation. They judge these experiments failures. The causes they identify are reliance on the Soviet model and its patrons, and a failure to resolve the tension between Marxism's universality and Africa's particularity, which left mechanical, dogmatic application in place of real adaptation.

The authors offer three conclusions. Neoliberalism's thirty-year record in Africa is a reason for Marxism's revival, and Marx's analysis of capital's expansion explains Africa's poverty. Africa should learn from socialism with Chinese characteristics, a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, and should combine Marxism with national conditions. It should also develop its productive forces first, using the market and accepting aid with care, citing Lenin on state monopoly capitalism as preparation for socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Marxism's history in Africa and of how Chinese scholars see China's role there.
quoteEn: In short, in the phase when the socialist movement arose, Pan-Africanism, as a nationalist current upholding the lofty aim of 'Black unity', had a major influence on Africa's independence and liberation movements.
quoteZh: 总之，在社会主义运动兴起阶段，泛非主义作为一种民族主义思潮，在秉承“黑人团结统一”的崇高旨趣下，对非洲的独立解放运动产生重大影响。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current system and theory of socialism, developed since reform and opening up. Chinese writers often present it as a model for other developing countries.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept associated with Xi Jinping. The article links it to China–Africa cooperation.
China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched in 2013.
The authors' label for the orthodox Marxist-Leninist regimes that emerged in Africa from the late 1960s, such as Congo, Ethiopia, Angola and Mozambique.

t: The ever-growing South African Communist Party
zh: 不断发展壮大的南非共产党
source: Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2020–2021), Social Sciences Academic Press, June 2021, pp. 314–330
paras: This chapter, from the Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2020–2021), asks how the South African Communist Party (SACP) has managed to grow in a hostile, unequal capitalist society, when most communist parties in capitalist countries declined after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Liu argues that the SACP has become a relatively mature Marxist party by combining Marxism-Leninism with South African conditions, preserving unity and adapting its tactics, while still facing serious financial and structural limits.

The article has three parts. It first maps South Africa's political landscape: economic inequality, the 2019 election, the African National Congress (ANC) and its alliance with the SACP, and the opposition parties (Democratic Alliance, Economic Freedom Fighters, Inkatha Freedom Party). It then reviews the SACP's hundred-year history from its founding in 1921 through the 1950 ban, underground work, armed struggle and the constitutional negotiations that led to the 1994 election. A third part assesses the party's recent achievements and difficulties, followed by a short conclusion.

Liu's core argument is that the SACP pursues a class-based national democratic revolution, as opposed to the race-based politics Liu attributes to the Economic Freedom Fighters. Its tactics have included petitions, non-violent non-cooperation, armed struggle through Umkhonto we Sizwe, negotiation and participation in government. Liu credits it with four achievements since 1994: participation in state administration through the alliance with the ANC and the trade union federation COSATU; leadership of mass movements such as strikes and the annual 'Red October' campaign; support for the poor during the Covid-19 pandemic; and the pursuit of a socialist future. Against these, Liu lists the party's poverty (no office building of its own, 66 per cent of members unemployed), its thin base among workers and professionals, and the difficulty of keeping independence within the alliance. Liu presents the party's decision not to contest elections alone as dictated by its weak social base and by anti-communist and narrow nationalist currents.

Liu concludes that the SACP shows that a communist party in a capitalist country is not 'an academic salon for a few advanced intellectuals' and can achieve things if it remains firm in conviction, united and grounded. The author expects it to keep strengthening the ANC-led alliance, enlarge its membership and build conditions for socialism while removing the legacy of apartheid. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the SACP's history, membership data and alliance strategy, and of how Chinese researchers present it as a model for non-ruling communist parties.
quoteEn: For the SACP to regard itself as a ruling party would be nothing short of suicide.
quoteZh: 南非共产党认为自己是执政党就无异于自杀。

glossary.explanation: The SACP's strategic concept for the current stage in South Africa: completing national liberation and democratic transformation, particularly ending racial domination, as a step towards socialism.

t: The "new material scarcity" crisis of Italian welfare capitalism
zh: 意大利福利资本主义的“新物质匮乏”危机
paras: Italy was among the first European countries to build a welfare state, yet Li Kaixuan argues that it now faces a worsening "new material scarcity" crisis. The article holds that this crisis, visible well before the 2020 pandemic and sharpened by it, stems from an unjust system of wealth distribution and from the "democratic deficit" of representative democracy.

The article has four parts. It first documents the crisis through figures on relative and absolute poverty, inequality, youth unemployment, child poverty, migrants and the North–South gap, drawing mainly on OECD, World Bank and Italian national statistics. It then analyses distribution (financialization, taxation, welfare design), then politics (party representation, EU influence, technocratic governments), and ends with a short conclusion.

On distribution, Li draws on Piketty and Anwar Shaikh to argue that financialization lets property-income earners accumulate faster than wage earners. In Italy, firms turned towards financial assets, labour costs fell as a share of turnover, and taxes on property income are lower than those on labour income. Li adds that public-debt interest crowds out social spending. The welfare system is described as doubly unbalanced: pensions dominate spending while unemployment, family and social assistance are thin, and local services differ sharply by region. Neoliberal "recalibration" cut pensions and health spending instead, and the 2019 basic income scheme is judged too restrictive to reduce poverty. On politics, Li contends that the mainstream centre-left Democratic Party has converged with the centre-right, while left parties such as Communist Refoundation have been excluded from parliament. EU rules and technocratic cabinets are said to move reforms beyond voters' scrutiny, and the populist Five Star Movement is judged not to have repaired this lack of representation.

Li concludes that the crisis has deep institutional roots: financialization, a regressive tax regime, a welfare system that mainly redistributes within the employed workforce, and a de-politicized reform process.
