They also note that divisions within the left, including over assessments of China, remain a long-standing problem, and call for openness, unity and a new strategy to help world socialism revive. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of how Western communist and left currents interpreted 1989 and its aftermath, as reported from a Chinese academic perspective.
quoteEn: For the world's left and socialist forces, only by recognising where they have come from can they find a way out, and so widen the space and dimensions of socialist action, extend socialism's influence and move world socialism from its low ebb towards revival.
quoteZh: 对世界左翼和社会主义力量来说,只有认清来路,才能找到出路,进而拓展社会主义的行动空间和维度,扩大社会主义的影响力,推动世界社会主义从低潮走向振兴。

t: The dissemination of Capital in Russia and the formation of Lenin's view of capitalism
zh: 《资本论》在俄国的传播与列宁资本主义观的形成
paras: Between the 1870s and 1890s, Russian intellectuals of different camps read Capital in conflicting ways and argued over the future of Russian capitalism. Zhang asks how Lenin, drawing on historical materialism and the economic theory of Capital, answered that question. The article argues that by criticising the liberal Narodniks and the "legal Marxists", Lenin arrived at a Marxist view of capitalism.

The article has four parts. It first reviews the 1877–79 Russian debate over Capital, then the 1880s–90s dispute on Russian capitalism, then Lenin's formation of his own view through three stages of writing, and finally Lenin's book The Development of Capitalism in Russia. Zhang draws on the debaters' articles and on letters from Marx, Engels, Danielson, Plekhanov and others.

Zhang reports that the debate began with Zhukovsky's attack on Capital and was answered by Mikhailovsky and Sieber. Marx's reply to Mikhailovsky objected to turning his sketch of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history. By the 1890s three views had emerged. The Narodniks, such as Danielson and Vorontsov, feared capitalism and wished Russia to avoid it. The legal Marxist Struve stressed its necessity but played down its destructive effects. Plekhanov held that Russia was already capitalist but, in Zhang's account, did not establish a Marxist view of capitalism. Lenin criticised Mikhailovsky's "subjective sociology" and the Narodnik market theory. He briefly allied with Struve, then criticised Struve's "objectivism" and misreading of Marx's theory of realisation.

Zhang concludes that The Development of Capitalism in Russia, which the article calls in a sense "Russia's Capital", marks the establishment of Lenin's view. In it, capitalism's progressive role is held to be consistent with recognising its dark sides and its historical transience. Lenin is presented as having both understood the method of Capital and applied it to Russian conditions. In Zhang's reading this advanced the Russianisation of Marxism and brought Russian Marxism into the stage of Leninism. Read the original if you want a source-based account of the Russian reception of Capital and the Narodnik and legal Marxist debates behind Lenin's early economic writings.
quoteEn: Lenin's criticism of the Russian liberal Narodniks and the legal Marxists was precisely an application of the methodology and economic theory of Capital, which not only answered the question of the fate of Russian capitalism but also resolved how Capital should be applied to Russia.
quoteZh: 列宁对俄国自由民粹派和俄国合法马克思主义的批判正是对《资本论》的方法论和经济理论的运用，不仅回答了俄国资本主义命运的问题，而且解决了《资本论》如何运用于俄国的问题。

glossary.explanation: A current of Russian populist thinkers, including Danielson and Vorontsov, who saw the peasant commune as a way to avoid capitalism. Lenin criticised them as representing the interests of small producers.
Russian intellectuals of the 1890s, such as Struve, who used Marxist ideas in legally published works and accepted capitalism's necessity. Lenin criticised them for glossing over its contradictions.
Marx's analysis, in volume 2 of Capital, of how the total social capital is reproduced and its products sold. Lenin used it against Narodnik and bourgeois market theories.
The Marxist theory of history that explains social development through material production and social relations. Zhang treats it as one of two foundations of Lenin's critique.

t: The general intellect and the utopia of emancipation
st: A renewed reflection on contemporary Western left theories of the subject, based on Marx and Engels on the "mental-labour proletariat" and its historical mission
zh: 一般智力与解放的乌托邦：当代西方左翼主体理论的再反思
zhSub: 基于马克思恩格斯对“脑力劳动无产阶级”及其历史使命的阐释
source: Journal of Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Social Sciences Edition), 2020 no. 3
paras: Sun Leqiang asks how Marx and Engels understood the relation between intellect and class, and what that means for Western left theories of the revolutionary subject that emerged with the "knowledge economy" of the 1990s. The article takes up the multitude (Hardt, Negri, Paolo Virno) and the "cognitariat" or cognitive worker (Yann Moulier-Boutang, Carlo Vercellone and others). Sun argues that these theories misread the Marxist logic of class, because for Marx and Engels the line between mental and manual labour does not define class, and that Engels's "mental-labour proletariat" is a category that should be fought alongside manual workers.

The article has four parts. It first reconstructs the autonomist and cognitive-capitalism accounts of the subject, then their diagnoses of new contradictions and their strategies of struggle. It next sets out Marx and Engels's own treatment of intellect, class and labour-power, and uses it to assess the Western theories. It ends with Engels's 1893 letter to the International Socialist Students' Congress and the historical mission of the mental-labour proletariat.

Sun argues that, for Marx, intellect is a shared human attribute, not a criterion of class: "rank is a property of intellect", not the reverse. Class is fixed by position in the relations of production. Sun reads Marx and Engels as distinguishing three kinds of non-material labour: ideologists of the bourgeoisie, autonomous intellectual producers, and intellectual workers subordinated to capital who produce surplus value. Only the last, together with those who put their intellect at the service of universal interests, form the mental-labour proletariat. On this basis Sun criticises Hardt and Negri for splitting proletariat and multitude along the material/non-material line, and Virno for making the general intellect the multitude's unifying principle. Sun also faults the cognitive-capitalism school for opposing "creative power" to labour-power, although labour-power already combines physical and mental capacities, and for blurring bourgeois ideologists with cognitive workers. Sun credits that school with keeping a class logic and credits Virno's point that labour-power is the bearer of life.

Sun concludes that proletarian revolution needs both manual and mental-labour proletarians, and that the Western left has forgotten Engels's advice to fight side by side. Without Party leadership, scientific theory and a class alliance, multitude autonomy or cognitive-worker networks are called a postmodern fantasy, a "storm in a teacup". Sun adds that socialism needs intellectuals who serve the people and universal interests, not "refined egoists". Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Negri, Virno and Moulier-Boutang that rests on Marx and Engels's texts on intellect, class and non-material labour.
quoteEn: Whether manual and mental labourers can become a proletariat in the Marx-Engels sense depends neither on their level of intellect nor on how much knowledge they possess, but on the position they occupy in the relations of production.
quoteZh: 体力劳动者和脑力劳动者能否成为马克思恩格斯意义上的无产阶级,并不具取决于他们的智力水平,也不取决于他们拥有多少知识,而是根源于他们在生产关系中所处的位置。

t: Contemporary interpretations of the idea of communism by the Western Left since the 21st century
zh: 论21世纪以来西方左翼对共产主义观念的时代阐释
paras: Liu Qingyun asks why Western left-wing scholars have returned to the idea of communism since the turn of the century, and how far their reinterpretations can be trusted. The article holds that the idea moved from affirmation, to rejection after the Soviet collapse, to revival, especially after the 2008 capitalist crisis. Liu argues that these thinkers offer useful and innovative insights but are limited by weak revolutionary content and by a diluted use of historical materialism.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the pressing conditions and favourable factors behind the revival, drawing on Alain Badiou, Slavoj Žižek, Bruno Bosteels, Jodi Dean, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. The second reconstructs their reasoning on two levels: theory (subject theory, immaterial production, egalitarianism) and practice (the revolutionary subject, forms of struggle, the party). The third assesses the strengths and weaknesses of this work, citing mainly English-language books and articles by these authors.

Liu reports that these thinkers see capitalism's antagonisms as unresolved. Žižek lists ecological crisis, conflicts over private property and shared knowledge, bioengineering and the divide between the included and the excluded. Dean describes a drift towards neo-feudalism. Hardt and Negri argue that immaterial production creates a shareable "common" that capital can only tax as rent. Practical proposals diverge: Badiou widens the revolutionary subject and rejects the party, Dean defends a communist party, and Hardt and Negri rely on the "multitude". Liu credits Badiou's three-phase periodisation of the communist hypothesis and the autonomist lineage of immaterial labour. Liu then faults these thinkers for treating communism as philosophy rather than revolutionary strategy, and for making Badiou's reliance on contingent "events" and an abstract equality axiom stand in for Marx's analysis. Liu also finds that Žižek's "proletarianised" excluded differ essentially from Marx's proletariat, and that the authors lack economic analysis of capitalism's workings.

Liu concludes that Western left thinkers broaden the global outlook on communism and help in understanding its contemporary value. These ideas, Liu says, should be assessed with Marx's historical materialism and materialist dialectics. Liu suggests that subject theory and party-building merit further comparative study for Chinese communist theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Badiou, Žižek, Dean, Hardt and Negri on communism, with notes pointing to their original English sources.
quoteEn: They all, to varying degrees, neglect the revolutionary character of communism, confining their content to theoretical discussion or philosophical interpretation.
quoteZh: 他们都不同程度地忽略了共产主义的革命性特征，将内容局限于理论探讨或哲学阐释上

t: The dialectic of contemporary capitalist crisis and the movement against inequality
st: Nancy Fraser's theoretical construction of a contemporary Western left emancipation project
zh: 当代资本主义危机与反抗不平等运动的辩证法
zhSub: 南希·弗雷泽对当代西方左翼解放规划的理论建构
source: Journal of Sichuan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2021 no. 1
paras: Why rebuild a theory of emancipation in the twenty-first century? Fu and Li present Nancy Fraser, a third-generation Frankfurt School thinker, as answering that question from two sides: developing Marxism, whose ultimate aim is human liberation, and criticising a capitalism whose economic, political, social and ecological crises are now intertwined. The article argues that Fraser reworks the legacy of twentieth-century Western emancipation movements into a broader project aimed at overthrowing capitalist domination. It judges this project theoretically and practically valuable, though still incomplete.

The article has three parts. The first reviews Fraser's reflection on twentieth-century movements: her multi-dimensional account of postwar capitalist crisis, her reading of postwar movements, her critique of feminism and her analysis of neoliberal hegemony. The second sets out her reconstruction of emancipation in five respects: its concept, goals and values, critical dimensions, women's emancipation and tasks. The third covers her later work after the 2008 financial crisis, namely Feminism for the 99 Percent (2019) and Capitalism: A Conversation in Critical Theory (2018). Fu and Li set this beside Jameson and Piketty.

Drawing on Karl Polanyi, Fraser finds that postwar movements were neither market forces nor protective counter-movements. They followed a "third logic" of emancipation, which Polanyi's double movement lacks. The authors report that she defines emancipation as opposing every form of domination and equality as its highest value. They add that she locates three targets for critique: misrecognition in culture, maldistribution in the economy and misrepresentation in politics. They then present her later criteria for telling emancipatory from non-emancipatory claims: non-domination, functional sustainability and democracy. They also present her "4D" model of capitalism's contradictions (division, dependence, disavowal, destabilization). In the authors' account she also calls for a broader working class that includes migrants, women and people of colour, and for stronger trade unions and organisation.

Fu and Li conclude that Fraser joins Marxist emancipation theory to critical-theory ideas of justice. They credit her with a new vantage point on capitalism's institutional crisis and with insight into where emancipation may be heading. They also acknowledge that she is still searching for a practical route beyond capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Fraser's emancipation theory, covering her move from justice to emancipation and her recent work on capitalism, unions and the working class.
quoteEn: Fraser's new emancipation project offers a comprehensive and profound critique of the institutional crisis of contemporary capitalism, and provides a new perspective for analysing and understanding capitalist crisis today.
quoteZh: 弗雷泽的解放新规划全面而深刻地批判了当代资本主义的制度性危机,为分析和认识当今的资本主义危机提供了一个新的视域。

t: An analysis of the limitations of research on Western Marxism in the narrow sense
zh: 狭义西方马克思主义研究的局限性剖析
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories (毛泽东邓小平理论研究), posted 2021
paras: Tai Lihua asks why nearly a century of research on Western Marxism has yielded results of limited quality and persuasive force. The article argues that the cause lies in the narrow definitions of the field inherited from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s and 1930s, and that these definitions disagree with one another. Tai holds that the concept needs to be integrated and widened, and proposes a broader conception of Western Marxism as the alternative.

The article identifies four ways in which Western Marxism in the narrow sense has been defined: by geographical space, by time, by research standpoint, method or viewpoint, and by field of study. Each gets its own section, which sets out the definition, names the scholars who use it and states its drawbacks. The thinkers discussed include Korsch, Perry Anderson, the Yugoslav scholar Gerkoćikov, Lukács, Roemer, Hodgson, Laclau and Mouffe, and the ecological Marxists James O'Connor and John Bellamy Foster.

Tai argues that each definition produces a specific harm. Definitions by geography, such as Western Europe or Germany, France and Italy, exclude Marxist research in Britain, the United States, Japan and elsewhere, and set Western Marxism against classical and Soviet-East European Marxism. Definitions by time, with labels such as post-Marxism, neo-Marxism and Marxology, are said to blur the concept and to feed claims that Marxism is outdated or defunct. Definitions by standpoint or method, in Tai's account, cover positions that are non-Marxist or anti-Marxist or that rest on idealist method, such as Marxology's opposition between the young and mature Marx, Lukács's retention of method alone, and Roemer's neoclassical modelling. Definitions by field, mainly philosophy, literature, aesthetics and culture, lead to what Tai calls a loss of economics. Tai sees this as sapping the theory's explanatory power and its wholeness, while noting that ecological Marxism's union of interpreting and changing the world deserves praise despite its reformist and utopian risks.

Tai concludes that the four definitions respectively entrench regional barriers, intensify nihilism about Marxism, weaken its scientific character and neglect its integrity. The article calls for integrating and widening the narrow concept in order to raise the quality of Western Marxism research and strengthen Marxism's persuasiveness and practical influence. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism criticises the standard ways of defining Western Marxism and argues for a broader definition.
quoteEn: In short, the "de-economization" of Western Marxism is an important reason for the exhaustion of its theoretical vitality and the shrinking of its power to explain reality.
quoteZh: 总之，西方马克思主义的“去经济学化”是其理论活力枯竭和现实解释力萎缩的重要原因。

glossary.explanation: In the strict sense, the tradition associated with Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School. Chinese scholars often debate whether to define it narrowly or broadly.

glossary.en: Western Marxism in the narrow sense
glossary.explanation: The restricted definitions of Western Marxism, by region, period, standpoint or field, which the author criticises. The author contrasts them with a broader definition.
A Western field, mainly from the 1960s, that studies Marx's life and writings. The author associates it with setting Marx against Engels, Lenin and Marxism.
A current, associated with Laclau and Mouffe among others, that revises or deconstructs classical Marxist theory. The author sees it as a sign of Marxism's weakening.
A strand of Western Marxism, from the 1970s, that combines Marxist analysis with ecological problems. Figures include O'Connor and Foster.

t: An analysis of contemporary Western neo-Marxist class studies
zh: 当代西方新马克思主义阶级研究探析
source: Journal of Hainan Normal University (Social Sciences Edition), 2020 no. 2
paras: How should one assess the class research produced by Western "new Marxists" since the 1970s? Chen and Liu begin from the challenge that the new technological revolution, the rise of a "new middle class" and the internal division of the working class posed to Marx's class theory. They argue that these scholars share Marx's humanist concern and critical spirit, yet depart from his class theory in nature, focus and specific claims, while still offering insights of some value.

The article first sketches the field, using the broad sense of "new Marxism": non-orthodox currents including the Frankfurt School and the post-1970s schools. It then surveys figures such as E.P. Thompson, Poulantzas, Foucault, Jameson, Gorz, John Roemer, Erik Olin Wright, Laclau and Mouffe, Habermas and Honneth, and French critical Marxists. Next it identifies four theoretical features, and finally compares these studies with Marx's theory.

The authors identify four features: diversity of approaches, strong engagement with real problems, a shift of critique towards culture, everyday life and micro-level power, and interdisciplinary methods combined with growing academicisation. On the relation to Marx, they accept a shared humanist orientation and a concern with alienation. They hold, however, that the neo-Marxist turn to a de-classed pluralist politics of identity, gender, ecology and race reduces the basic class contradiction to ordinary social conflict. In their account this abandons historical materialism.

They list three specific divergences. On the revolutionary subject, Marcuse and Gorz look to students, the unemployed and intellectuals rather than the proletariat. On strategy, the Frankfurt School proposes a "cultural" or "psychological" revolution rather than violent revolution. On criteria of class, they replace ownership of the means of production with occupation, politics and culture. Even so, Chen and Liu say these studies enrich Marxist class theory and offer lessons for China, such as recognising the plurality of interest groups, building channels for their demands and loosening rigid thinking about class. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical overview of how Western neo-Marxist schools handled class after the 1970s.
quoteEn: Contemporary Western neo-Marxism, grounded in the reality of contemporary capitalism, has extended and diverged from Marx's class theory.
quoteZh: 当代西方新马克思主义立足于当代资本主义的现实,对马克思阶级理论进行了延异和拓展。

glossary.explanation: A broad label for non-orthodox Marxist currents. The authors use it for the Frankfurt School and for post-1970s schools such as analytical, post-modern and post-Marxism.

t: The labour-relations theory of the French Regulation School and the "Yellow Vests" movement seen through it
zh: 法国调节学派劳动关系理论及其视角下的“黄马甲”运动透视
paras: The article asks what the French Regulation School, a strand of Marxism outside China, says about labour relations, and what that theory can explain about the "Yellow Vests" movement that began in France in November 2018. Zhang and Yu argue that the school's account of four historical forms of capitalist labour relations helps explain the movement's causes. They also argue that the school misses the essence of capitalist labour relations because it does not address exploitation or private ownership of the means of production.

After a short introduction and a review of Chinese scholarship, the article sets out the school's "mode of regulation" approach, which works at an intermediate level between micro and macro analysis. Its five components are the monetary and credit regime, the capital–labour relation, forms of competition, the state, and the international system. The authors then compare the school with Marx, apply the theory to the Yellow Vests, and close with an assessment. The school's main figures, Michel Aglietta and Alain Lipietz, are presented as openly drawing on Marxian economics.

The authors summarise the school's periodisation: competitive, Taylorist, Fordist and finance-dominated labour relations, each tied to an accumulation regime. Fordism is described as a bargain of mass production and mass consumption, with collective bargaining and long contracts, but also deskilled work. Finance-dominated relations bring flexible, short-term employment, weakened unions and a "Walmart" style of anti-union employment. On comparison with Marx, they find shared ground in treating labour relations as basic relations of production. They contend, however, that Marx saw the capital–labour conflict as irreconcilable, while the school treats it as an empirical political struggle over wages that regulation can ease.

Applying this lens, the authors attribute the Yellow Vests to an imbalance in labour relations. They cite neoliberal policy since the 1980s, the decline of manufacturing from 18% to 10% of GDP, labour-law reform, income inequality, and insecure work in peripheral regions dependent on cars. They argue the movement lacked organisation and clear demands, and that the state had no effective channel for mediating labour conflict. Their conclusion is that the school widened Marx's perspective but advises workers to compromise with the bourgeoisie. They also call for a labour-relations model suited to China's conditions that raises the standing of the working class and supports high-quality development. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical reading of Regulation School theory and its use on the Yellow Vests.
quoteEn: Compared with Marx, the Regulation School's understanding of the relationship between labour and capital fails to grasp the essence of the matter.
quoteZh: 与马克思相比，调节学派对劳资双方关系的认知没有抓住事物的本质。

glossary.explanation: An official slogan since around 2017 for growth that stresses efficiency, innovation and balance over sheer speed. The article invokes it as the goal that harmonious labour relations should support.

A heterodox school of political economy that emerged in France in the 1970s, associated with Michel Aglietta and Alain Lipietz. It analyses capitalism through accumulation regimes and modes of regulation.
The Chinese academic category for Marxist currents developed outside China, covering a wider field than Western Marxism in the narrow sense.

t: Marxism in the course of the African socialist movement
zh: 非洲社会主义运动历程中的马克思主义
paras: Zheng Xiangfu and Shu Wenhao ask how Marxism spread and developed in Africa, and why it fell back after the Cold War. Their thesis is that Marxism in Africa has been bound up with the continent's socialist movements and has passed through three stages: introduction and rise, flourishing, and decline. They argue that its return to Africa is possible but will be long and winding.

The article follows these three stages in turn. It first traces the rise of African socialism from the 1920s, then the two waves of socialist movement from the independence era to the mid-1980s, and finally the post-Soviet downturn and its aftermath. Cases include South Africa, Algeria, Senegal, Guinea, Sudan, Ghana, Tanzania, Congo, Ethiopia, Mozambique and Angola.

For the early period, the authors identify three channels of transmission: the Communist International and the communist parties, colonial and migrant intellectuals, and the Pan-African movement. They hold that Marxism was then only one element within Pan-Africanism. Later, they argue, leaders such as Nkrumah turned from Pan-Africanism and village-community socialism to Marxism in response to neo-colonialism. Regimes professing 'scientific socialism' set up vanguard parties, accepted class struggle and pursued planned economies and nationalisation. The authors judge these regimes failures. They blame over-reliance on the Soviet model and a dogmatic handling of the tension between Marxism's universality and Africa's particularity, and they say the regimes fell with the Soviet Union.

Looking ahead, the authors say the failure of three decades of neoliberalism has revived interest in Marxism. They call on African states to study socialism with Chinese characteristics and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, and to develop productive forces, partly by drawing on market mechanisms, as Lenin's view of state monopoly capitalism suggests. They also urge states to accept foreign aid critically. They present China's Belt and Road Initiative and its Africa policy as helpful examples. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly periodisation of Marxism in Africa and a view of how Chinese academics link Africa's prospects to the Chinese experience.")
quoteEn: African countries must raise their level of productive forces before the return of Marxism to Africa can become possible.
quoteZh: 非洲国家必须提高生产力水平，才能为马克思主义在非洲的复归提供可能。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for shared development and cooperation among states, and Chinese writers often apply it to relations with Africa.
A Chinese infrastructure and investment initiative launched in 2013 to link China with Asia, Africa and Europe.
The official name for the theory and path of socialism developed in China since reform and opening up.
Marx's and Engels's own term for their socialism. In the African context it denotes the Marxist-Leninist orientation that several regimes adopted from the late 1960s.
A form of 'African socialism' that drew on traditional communal village life, associated with leaders such as Nyerere.

t: Social inequality and an opportunity for the revival of the Western left
zh: 社会不平等与西方左翼复兴的契机
paras: Writing in 2020, after the debate sparked by Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) and the protests following George Floyd's death, Xing argues that inequality is an incurable chronic ailment of capitalism. Since the 2008 financial crisis, the author says, it has worsened in the West, producing economic, political and social turmoil and challenging the capitalist system. This, Xing contends, gives the Western left a chance to revive, provided it adapts its theory and strategy to the actual sources of inequality.

The article has three parts. The first documents growing inequality in the United States and Europe, using figures on wealth shares, racial wealth gaps, unemployment during the Covid-19 pandemic, and income divergence within Europe. The second sets out five ways inequality is said to strike at the capitalist order: recurrent economic crisis, political polarisation, populist revival, intensified social conflict and labour and social movements, and growing doubts about neoliberalism. The third turns to the left's opportunities and tasks.

Xing's central move is to reject explanations that locate the roots of inequality in globalisation, technology, weakened unions or interest-group politics. Citing Marx, Engels and Lenin, the author holds that these are all products of the capitalist system itself, so patching it up cannot overcome its predicament. Movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, together with rising interest in Marx and in socialism among young people, are read as signs of disillusion with capitalism. Xing also notes that such movements lack a clear definition of the 'other world' they want, and that the left has so far offered mainly tax-based remedies.

Xing concludes that the left must give a scientific account of the root causes of inequality rather than target individual policies. It must also take part in and lead workers' and social movements, spreading its theory and working with trade unions so that these movements turn into a socialist movement able to challenge capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western inequality data, populism and the prospects of the Western left after 2008 and during the pandemic.
quoteEn: To seize the opportunity that social inequality offers, the left must adjust in both theory and practice, arm itself with scientific theory so that more and more people recognise and accept it, and ultimately play a leading role in the workers' movement.
quoteZh: 要抓住社会不平等所提供的契机，左翼必须在理论和实践上都做出调整，用科学的理论武装自己，以使其被越来越多的民众所认可和接受，最终发挥在工人运动中的引领作用。

t: Western left-wing media's new discussions of the crisis of capitalism in the context of COVID-19
zh: 新冠疫情背景下西方左翼媒体对资本主义危机的新探讨
source: Journalism and Communication (新闻传播), 2020 no. 9
paras: Writing in 2020, Xing Caili asks how Western left-wing media and theorists have interpreted the COVID-19 pandemic in relation to the crisis of capitalism. The article argues that, since the collapse of the Soviet bloc, the Western left has revived as capitalism has again fallen into crisis, and that new media have given it wider channels to spread its ideas. Xing reports that left commentators divide over whether the pandemic deepens the crisis or leaves capitalism essentially unchanged, and that the article itself stresses the working class as the decisive force.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the state of Western left media, which Xing calls "marginal" beside the BBC, CNN or the New York Times, and sorts them into three types: websites of Marxist parties (for example People's World and Liberation News in the US), general left sites (Solidnet, Peoples Dispatch, Monthly Review Online, Jacobin), and personal sites and blogs of activists and theorists such as David Harvey. The second part reviews the debate over the pandemic's effect on capitalism. The third turns to workers' protest and the question of the agent of struggle.

In the second part Xing first presents the view that the pandemic aggravates the crisis. Slavoj Žižek says it has dealt capitalism a blow and revived an implicit communism, citing Trump's stimulus and use of the Defense Production Act as a "socialisation" of the economy; Judith Butler speaks of a revived socialist imagination. Harvey argues that consumerism, which has sustained capitalism since 2008, is collapsing alongside a crisis of neoliberalism. Against this, Xing sets Alain Badiou, who holds that an epidemic does not bring political revolution, and Byung-Chul Han, who predicts that capitalism will emerge stronger, with digital surveillance promoted as a success. Polanyi and Mike Davis are cited on how the pandemic exposes class and regional inequality, undermining the claim that the virus treats everyone equally.

Xing concludes that whether capitalism changes depends less on the epidemic than on struggles waged by the working class in production. Antonio Negri's call to enter the fight is contrasted with Badiou's advice to stay at home, and a March 2020 statement by communist and workers' parties, initiated by the Communist Party of Greece, is quoted as saying workers must not pay for the crisis. Xing also draws on Marx and Engels to present the working class as the subject of fundamental social change. Read the original if you want a short survey of the Western left websites and thinkers who commented on the pandemic and capitalism in spring 2020, as seen from a Chinese Marxist viewpoint.
quoteEn: Whether capitalism changes depends not only on the epidemic itself and the economic crisis it causes, but chiefly on the struggles and revolution that the working class launches in the sphere of capitalist production.
quoteZh: 资本主义是否将发生改变不单取决于疫情本身及疫情导致的经济危机，更主要的决定性因素是工人阶级在资本主义生产领域所发动的斗争与革命

t: The alienated substance and the substance as subject: Žižek's new inquiry into Marx's philosophy of capital
zh: 异化的实体与主体的实体——齐泽克对马克思资本哲学思想的新探讨
paras: Kong Ming'an and Tan Yong take up Slavoj Žižek's charge that Marx wavers in Capital between two views of capital: as an alienated substance within a historical process, and as a substance that is already subject. The authors note that the choice bears on the proletariat's historical role and on the path from capitalism to communism. They argue that Žižek misreads Marx: the two views are a dialectical double characterisation, and Marx fundamentally treats capital as an alienated substance.

The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Žižek's reasoning, drawn from Tarrying with the Negative, on Hegel's infinite and negative judgments, unequal exchange and "absolute freedom". It then turns to Lukács's History and Class Consciousness, read as a case of the alienation reading. The third part examines Marx's own texts in Capital, volumes 1 and 3, and a short conclusion follows.

In the authors' account, Žižek holds that Hegelian reconciliation does not mean the subject reappropriating the whole substance. He sees Marx's vision of proletarian revolution as such a "closed economy", in which every loss is repaid. If capital is already a self-mediating subject, humans become its instruments, and resistance becomes impossible. The authors answer with Lukács's analysis of reification and proletarian class consciousness, which they read as following Marx's treatment of capital as alienated substance. Turning to Marx, they show that he does call capital self-moving value, a vampire living on living labour, and a "subject" in the forms M–C–M′ and M–M′. They then give three reasons why the subject-substance view is conditional. It holds only under capitalism, which is a transitory stage. Capital's internal contradictions, including the falling rate of profit and the conflict between productive forces and relations of production, limit its self-valorisation. The proletariat, created by capitalism, will make a revolution and bring production under the conscious control of freely associated people.

The authors conclude that Marx's two views of capital are dialectical, like use-value and exchange-value or concrete and abstract labour. They hold that the alienation view is basic, since it ties in with capitalism's historical transience and the proletariat's revolutionary role in reappropriating alienated substance. Žižek's claim of ambiguity in Marx is therefore, in their view, a misreading. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Žižek's reading of Marx on capital, set against Lukács on reification.
quoteEn: Viewing capital both as an alienated substance and as a substance that is subject is in fact Marx's dialectical understanding of capital.
quoteZh: 既将资本作为异化的实体来看待,又将资本作为主体的实体来看待,实际上是马克思对资本所作的辩证认识

t: Foreign voices praise the achievements of China's ecological civilization construction in the new era
zh: 国外高度评价新时代中国生态文明建设成就
paras: This short commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, collects favourable assessments by foreign scholars, officials and organisations of China's ecological civilization construction since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu's thesis is that, under the guidance of Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization, China has found a path suited to its own conditions. In the article's account, this path has won broad international attention and approval and has contributed to improving the global environment.

The piece is built almost entirely from quotations and paraphrases of named foreign speakers. They include academics in Australia, Britain, the United States, Japan, Germany and Nepal, and figures from UN agencies, the World Bank and environmental NGOs. It is organised in four sections: praise for China's achievements, interest in the experience behind them, and recognition of China's contribution to global ecological civilization. The text gives no independent data beyond the policies and initiatives it lists.

Liu reports foreign commentators as saying that China's green development is among the world's leaders, that China has met its 2020 climate and nature-reserve targets early, and that its pollution control offers a model. The experience they identify includes clear and determined top-level direction, the "two mountains" concept (that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets), and a strong institutional capacity to implement policy. They also cite innovations such as the river chief system and green finance, wide public participation, and roots in the traditional idea of harmony between heaven and humanity. John B. Cobb Jr. is quoted as saying that the socialist system with Chinese characteristics does better than Western capitalism in reconciling environmental protection with economic growth.

The article concludes that China's ecological civilization offers "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese sample" for global environmental governance. It points to initiatives such as the national plan for the 2030 Agenda, ratification of the Paris Agreement, the Belt and Road green development coalition, and desertification-control experience that Morocco and other countries are drawing on. Read the original if you want a compact sample of how Chinese official media present foreign endorsements of the country's ecological policy, with the names and affiliations of the people quoted.
quoteEn: While affirming the achievements of China's ecological civilization construction, people from various foreign circles are paying more attention to summing up the experience behind those achievements.
quoteZh: 国外各界人士在肯定中国生态文明建设取得成就的同时，更加注重总结中国生态文明建设取得成就的经验。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese Party and state policy that makes harmony between humans and nature a goal of development. It was written into the Party's programme and the national strategy from the early 2010s.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization
glossary.explanation: The part of Xi Jinping's thought that deals with environmental protection and green development. Official sources present it as the guiding theory of China's ecological policy.

The slogan "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" (绿水青山就是金山银山), put forward by Xi Jinping in 2005. It holds that environmental protection and economic development can support each other.
A system in which local Party and government officials are made personally responsible for the management and protection of particular rivers. A parallel lake chief system also exists.
A traditional Chinese philosophical idea of unity between humans and the natural order. Official discourse cites it as a cultural root of ecological civilization.

t: Western political parties' positioning of "the people" and the paradox of their practice
zh: 西方政党的“人民”定位及其实践悖论
source: People's Tribune (Renmin Luntan), August 2020 issue (second half), posted 2021
paras: Yu Haiqing asks why Western party politics has fallen into difficulty in recent years and finds one main cause in the gap between ideas and practice. In the author's account, Western parties proclaim themselves representatives of "the people" while pursuing a "de-peopling" (qu renminhua) practice, and this conflict has pushed some of them into a crisis of representation. The article is a short commentary in a Chinese current-affairs journal.

The first part surveys how parties across the Western spectrum invoke "the people". Yu looks at mainstream conservative, liberal and Christian parties, with the US Democrats and Republicans as examples. The article then turns to social democratic parties, which moved from a working-class identity to that of "people's parties", and to green parties and populist parties. The second part sets out four ways in which practice contradicts this rhetoric, drawing mainly on examples from the Covid-19 pandemic and the Trump administration.

Yu's central claim is that every party is by nature the representative of a particular class, and that mainstream Western parties are bourgeois parties tied to big capital and interest groups. The four contradictions are these. First, when popular and capital interests conflict, parties favour capital; the author cites hesitation over lockdowns early in the pandemic. Second, parties put their own interests first, because they operate as vote-seeking machines in a political "market"; the author cites the mask dispute between the two US parties. Third, populist parties do not truly represent the people but "hijack" the popular will through identity politics, and the author cites the US–China trade war and the withdrawal from the World Health Organization as harming Americans themselves. Fourth, slow decision-making, winner-takes-all rules and parliamentary thresholds erode public trust in the party system.

Yu concludes that a lack of representativeness weakens the legitimacy of Western party systems and, in the long run, the foundations of liberal democracy. Efforts to make parties more flexible cannot succeed, in the author's view, because of their class nature. Drawing a lesson for China, Yu argues that the "people-centred" development philosophy must be carried into practice, answering "what to do" and "how to do it", in order to show the Communist Party's "people first" character. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship framed Western party politics and the pandemic in 2020.
quoteEn: The mutual contradiction between rhetorical positioning and real-world practice has become an intractable paradox in Western party politics.
quoteZh: 话语定位与现实实践的相互矛盾成为西方政党政治中一个难解的悖论。

glossary.literal: taking the people as the centre
glossary.explanation: A development philosophy stressed in Party discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012), which holds that development should serve the people's interests. Official English renderings vary, including "people-centered".
A slogan of Party discourse stating that the people's interests take the highest priority in the Communist Party's governance.
The author's phrase for Western parties' practice of sidelining popular interests while claiming to represent the people.

t: The COVID-19 pandemic and catastrophe capitalism
zh: 新冠肺炎疫情与灾难资本主义
orig: Monthly Review, 2020
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by John Bellamy Foster and Intan Suwandi, apparently first published in Monthly Review in 2020. It asks how the COVID-19 pandemic should be understood within global capitalism. The authors argue that it is neither an external shock nor an unpredictable "black swan", but a product of late imperialism and monopoly-finance capital, whose global commodity chains breed pathogens and then transmit them.

The article has four parts. It begins with circuits of capital and the ecological-epidemic crisis, introducing "Structural One Health". It then examines the disruption of commodity chains and a global "bullwhip effect". The third part takes up imperialism, class and the pandemic, including debates over social distancing in poor countries and the US–China trade war. The last part places the crisis in Marx's account of social production and the metabolism between humans and nature.

Foster and Suwandi's central move is to bring Marx's dual focus on use value and exchange value to commodity-chain analysis. Drawing on Robert Wallace and colleagues, they argue that agribusiness monocultures, deforestation and land grabs create conditions for new zoonotic diseases. They describe global labour arbitrage and land arbitrage as the basis of late imperialism, and cite just-in-time production and health-sector austerity as reasons why chain disruptions produced shortages and financial fragility. They also criticise a Yale-linked analysis, written for Foreign Policy, that suggested poor countries forgo distancing measures to keep supply chains running. In their reading this trades millions of lives in the Global South for the growth of the imperial centre.

The authors conclude that the pandemic belongs to a wider catastrophe of ecological rift, inequality, stagnation and war risk, and that the system responsible could be charged with "social murder", as Engels did. They call for a social reorganisation based on common ownership and a rational regulation of the social metabolism with nature, as the basis for human survival. Read the original if you want a Marxist ecological account of COVID-19 that links epidemiology, global value chains and imperialism, and that cites specific supply-chain data from 2020.
quoteEn: The COVID-19 crisis should not be seen as the result of external forces, nor as an unpredictable \"black swan\" event, but is largely predictable.
quoteZh: 新冠肺炎危机不应被视作外部力量作用的结果，亦并非不可预测的“黑天鹅”事件，而是大体上可以预测的。

glossary.explanation: Foster's term for the present phase of imperialism, marked by monopoly-finance capital and transnational commodity chains linking developing and developed countries.

The practice of moving production to low-wage regions so that firms in rich countries profit from wage differences larger than productivity differences. The authors treat it as a mechanism of international exploitation.
An approach that builds on the mainstream "One Health" model but grounds disease emergence in historical materialism and circuits of capital.
A supply-chain term for the way small changes in demand are amplified as information passes upstream from customers to suppliers.
A production model that keeps inventories to a minimum by producing parts only when needed.

t: Foreign left-wing scholars' dual reflection on capitalism and socialism in the context of COVID-19
zh: 新冠疫情背景下国外左翼学者对资本主义和社会主义的双重反思
source: Journal of Wuhan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2020 no. 5
paras: Han and Chen start from Bernie Sanders's withdrawal from the Democratic primary in April 2020, in the middle of the US outbreak, as a sign that capital came first even during a plague. They ask whether Western capitalist ideology will lead humanity into the abyss or towards salvation. Their thesis is that foreign left-wing intellectuals read COVID-19 as a crisis of neoliberalism and a reopening of socialist or communist imagination, and that China's response gives that imagination practical support.

The article surveys 2020 commentary by Western and other left-wing figures, including Slavoj Žižek, David Harvey, Thomas Piketty, Antonio Negri, Noam Chomsky, Andres Piqueras, Aleksandr Buzgalin and John Bellamy Foster. It also draws on statements by communist parties abroad. It has three parts: the crisis of neoliberalism and the possibility of transition; the reconstruction of order through socialist or communist imagination; and left-wing evaluations of China's anti-epidemic response.

In the first part, the authors present neoliberalism's "Chernobyl moment" as a collapse of consumerism, deepening inequality and political legitimacy, and ecological rupture, ending in a choice between communism and barbarism. They note a Marxist objection that Harvey's argument rests on an underconsumption theory and leaves private ownership and wage labour untouched. The second part argues that the epidemic exposes the illusion of equality, since risk spreads across classes. It also treats "green capitalism" as a false proposition, citing Foster, Xun Qingzhi and Sarah Sarkar, and the authors describe it as masking "ecological imperialism". In the third part they credit China's response to a political commitment to a community with a shared future for mankind, and to public ownership, which in Engels's terms organises production for common need. Foreign communist parties and left writers such as Carlos Martinez are cited as endorsing this.

The authors conclude that the crisis is a historic occasion to re-educate the world's workers through communist discourse. They hold that the Western left's attempt to revive it is not utopian, and that China's practice shows the superiority of the socialist system over neoliberal arrangements led by the United States. The text is openly partisan and relies largely on online commentary and open letters from 2020. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of how Western left voices responded to the pandemic, and how Chinese scholars use them to argue for socialism.
quoteEn: Left or right? This is at once a choice about survival and a choice between "communism" and "barbarism".
quoteZh: 向左还是向右？这既是一个生存的选择，同时也是一个“共产主义”与“野蛮主义”之间的选择。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s, calling for shared responsibility and cooperation among nations. Chinese official commentary invoked it in discussing the global response to COVID-19.
Ownership of the means of production by society or the state, which Chinese theory treats as the essential attribute of the socialist system. In China it coexists with a large non-public sector.

t: Studies of world left-wing thought and movements amid changes unseen in a century
st: An overview of foreign left-wing thought research in 2019
zh: 百年未有之大变局中的世界左翼思潮和运动研究
zhSub: 2019年国外左翼思想研究概览
paras: This is a literature review, published in Scientific Socialism in 2020, of foreign left-wing thought and movements in 2019. The authors start from the premise that the world is undergoing changes unseen in a century, in which the basic contradictions of capitalism are taking new forms. They report that foreign left-wing scholars sought to answer pressing questions in ways that display the contemporary value and vitality of Marxism.

The review has four parts. It first surveys the year's developments, including left forums and festivals in New York, Chicago and London and two Beijing conferences: the tenth World Socialism Forum and the sixth national forum on foreign Marxism research. It then covers major theoretical themes: imperialism, neoliberalism, contemporary capitalism including digital capitalism, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third part reports on the left in North America and Europe, Russia, the Middle East and Africa, and Latin America.

On theory, the authors report that John Smith and David Harvey debated the contemporary applicability of Lenin's theory of imperialism. Intan Suwandi, R. Jamil Jonna and John Bellamy Foster analysed global commodity chains, and Foster described a late imperialism marked by stagnation and declining US hegemony. Foster, Utsa and Prabhat Patnaik and Sitaram Yechury are cited as treating neoliberalism as the root of capitalist crisis and of the rightward turn in politics. Other work is summarised on digital capitalism and labour control. Egon Krenz, Russian scholars and Toma Ivan are cited as praising the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. On movements, the review reports declining centre-left parties in Europe, the rise of populist and radical left forces, the German Left Party's difficulties, the Yellow Vests, the Russian revival of socialist ideas, and a weakening Latin American left after the Bolivian coup.

The authors conclude that left thought will keep advancing so long as capitalism's contradictions persist. They also cite Zhang Liang's warning that foreign Marxism research looks prosperous but is weak in innovation. They call for Chinese scholars to move beyond textual study towards ideas and their adaptation in China, to absorb foreign critiques of financial monopoly capitalism, neoliberalism and imperialism, and to strengthen exchange with foreign left scholars. Read the original if you want a map of 2019 Chinese-language and Western left-wing sources, with references to Monthly Review and Chinese journals, and a sense of how Chinese academics frame foreign Marxism.
quoteEn: Foreign left-wing scholars' research on Marxism and capitalism, especially on new changes in today's financial monopoly capitalism, neoliberalism and imperialism, provides important intellectual resources for developing twenty-first-century Marxism and contemporary Chinese Marxism.
quoteZh: 国外左翼学者对马克思主义和资本主义的研究，特别是对当今金融垄断资本主义的新变化、新自由主义、帝国主义等问题的研究，为发展21世纪马克思主义、当代中国马克思主义提供了重要的思想资源。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership with a market economy.
An annual international conference held in Beijing and organised by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, gathering Chinese and foreign Marxist scholars.
The Chinese academic field studying Marxist and left-wing thought outside China, broader than the Western Marxist tradition.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèiyǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A phrase in official Chinese discourse describing a period of profound shifts in the global order.

t: Foreign leftist critiques of capitalism during the COVID-19 pandemic
zh: 新冠肺炎疫情下国外左翼对资本主义的批判
paras: Writing in 2020, Lei Xiaohuan surveys how left-wing thinkers and organisations outside China read the COVID-19 pandemic and the responses of the United States and some European states. The article argues that these critics see the pandemic as a blow to global capitalism and that their commentary shows both the nature of the capitalist system and the direction of world socialism. Lei treats this reaction as an indicator of the ideological climate in Western societies.

The article draws on statements by Noam Chomsky, Joseph Choonara, Andrea Catone, Prabhat Patnaik, Radhika Desai, Judith Butler, Jo Cottenier, Sam Gindin, Albert Bender and others, as well as a joint statement by communist and workers' parties initiated by the Communist Party of Greece. It has four parts: capitalism's role in spreading the pandemic; capitalism's inability to cope with it and the crises that followed; the claim that Western countries urgently need socialism; and the conditions under which socialism might be achieved.

Lei reports that these critics trace the outbreak's severity to the logic of capital, under which profit is put ahead of lives. In their account neoliberal privatisation and cuts to public health, such as Italy's regional health system and Britain's NHS bed numbers, left societies unprepared, while globalisation under capitalism speeded transmission. Lei says they contrast this with China, where the leadership of the Communist Party and the socialist system allowed a swift and effective response, which they credit with showing the superiority of socialism. The critics also read the economic downturn as a sign of long-term structural crisis, tied to climate and refugee crises. Some propose a 'socialism 2.0' based on collective ownership and planning.

Lei notes that many of these thinkers stress that revolutionary situations do not automatically produce revolution. They say it also needs a subjective condition, class consciousness and organised political forces, and that capitalism has survived earlier crises, so its imminent collapse looks unrealistic. Lei concludes that the pandemic has led foreign leftists to an unprecedented overall critique of capitalism and of the capitalist road to modernization, a return to Marx's critique of political economy that renews attention to class struggle. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic digest of Western leftist pandemic commentary, with its sources, and of how that commentary is used to praise China's response.
quoteEn: Foreign leftists have returned to Marx's original critique of the specific features of capitalism in political economy, and take the logic of capital as the entry point for revealing the essence of capitalism under the pandemic.
quoteZh: 国外左翼回归马克思对资本主义具体特性的原初政治经济学批判,以资本的逻辑为切入点揭示疫情之下资本主义的本质

glossary.explanation: A field of study and a term used in Chinese scholarship for socialist movements, states and theory worldwide, and for their development trends.

t: An analysis of the limitations of research on "Western Marxism" in the narrow sense
zh: 狭义西方马克思主义研究的局限性剖析
source: Mao Zedong Deng Xiaoping Theory Studies (Mao Zedong Deng Xiaoping lilun yanjiu), 2020 no. 8
paras: Tai Lihua asks why nearly a century of research on Western Marxism has produced so much disagreement and so little theoretical force. The article argues that the cause lies in the narrow definitions inherited from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s and 1930s. Each narrow definition, in Tai's account, has a specific limitation, and the concept needs to be integrated and broadened.

The article sorts narrow definitions into four types: by geographical space, by time, by research standpoint, method or viewpoint, and by field of study. For each type it discusses representative writers and schools. They include Korsch, Perry Anderson, Gerson Gorkicakov (as rendered in Chinese), Marxology, post-Marxism, Lukács, Roemer, Hodgson, cultural Marxism and ecological Marxism. Tai draws on Anderson, McLellan, Bowles and O'Connor, among others.

Tai holds that the geographical definition, which ties Western Marxism to Western Europe or to Germany, France and Italy, sets it against classical Marxism and Soviet-East European Marxism. It also leaves out research in Britain, the United States and especially Japan. The temporal definition blurs the boundaries between Western Marxism, post-Marxism and neo-Marxism. It also supplies material for claims that Marxism is outdated, mistaken or dying. The definitions by standpoint and method are criticised on several grounds. Marxology is said to set the young Marx against the mature Marx, Engels against Marx, and Lenin against Marx. Lukács's reduction of orthodoxy to method, Leibovitch's and Heilbroner's emphasis on human needs and desire, and the analytical Marxism of Roemer and Hodgson are all called idealist or vulgarising. Tai also argues that equating Western Marxism with philosophy, literature or culture breaks the wholeness of Marxism. In this account the field has dropped political economy, which Tai calls its "de-economisation", and so lost explanatory power. Tai acknowledges that ecological Marxism links explaining the world with changing it. Tai still regards it as reformist and in danger of ecological utopianism.

Tai concludes that the four definitions respectively entrench regional barriers, encourage the nihilistic dismissal of Marxism, weaken its scientific character and neglect its wholeness. The article calls for integrating and widening the category and advocates a broad-sense study of Western Marxism as the alternative, which it does not develop here. Read the original if you work on foreign Marxism and want a Chinese critique of how the label "Western Marxism" has been defined, with extensive references to Anderson, McLellan and other sources on the field.
quoteEn: The "de-economisation" of Western Marxism is an important reason for the exhaustion of its theoretical vitality and the shrinking of its explanatory power over reality.
quoteZh: 西方马克思主义的“去经济学化”[15]是其理论活力枯竭和现实解释力萎缩的重要原因。

glossary.explanation: Tai's proposed alternative to the narrow definitions: a wider and more integrated category covering Marxist research in the West, including political economy. The article names it but does not set it out in detail.
A Western field studying Marx's life, works and thought, which developed from the 1960s. Tai associates it with claims that Marx, Engels and Lenin were opposed to one another.
A current from the 1970s–80s, associated with Laclau and Mouffe among others, that deconstructs traditional Marxist theory. Tai treats it as a sign of the weakening of Marxism.
Tai's term for Western Marxism's turn away from political economy towards philosophy, culture and literature. She has written on it elsewhere (2013).

t: Three shifts in contemporary Western Marxist class theory
zh: 当今西方马克思主义阶级理论的三大转变
source: Journal of Hubei Administration Institute, 2020 no. 1
paras: Mi Haibo asks how Western Marxist scholars have responded to the claim that Marx's class theory no longer explains capitalist societies that have moved from industrial to post-industrial, information-based forms. The article argues that Western Marxism has shifted in three areas: class structure, the criteria for dividing classes, and class struggle. Mi describes and assesses each shift and concludes that Marx's class analysis remains valid, even though the forms of class have changed.

The article, published in 2020, has three sections. The first covers the move in class structure from simplicity to complexity, including the new middle class, the internal stratification of the bourgeoisie and the working class, and the weakening of class consciousness. The second covers the move from a single economic criterion to several criteria: exploitation (Erik Olin Wright, Philippe Van Parijs), power (Nicos Poulantzas, Ralf Dahrendorf) and knowledge or culture (John Kenneth Galbraith, Daniel Bell, Alvin Gouldner). The third covers the move in class struggle from political confrontation to democratic movements, drawing on Habermas, Laclau and Mouffe, Ralph Miliband and Vicente Navarro.

Mi's core argument is that each Western revision describes real changes but draws the wrong conclusion. Wage-earning managers, technicians and service workers, in Mi's view, still sell their labour-power and so are part of Marx's 'collective worker'. Theories that speak of the working class 'disappearing' (Marcuse, Poulantzas, Gorz) or of individualised identity (Ulrich Beck) are said to replace subjective perception with objective class position. Wright's 'contradictory class' is rejected because Marx divides classes by relations of production, not income. Dahrendorf's power criterion and the 'knowledge class' theories are criticised for ignoring that the economic base determines the political superstructure and that intellectuals without economic or state power cannot become a ruling class.

On class struggle, Mi accepts that new social movements (feminist, ecological, anti-racist and others) are plural and not aimed directly at the capitalist system. Mi argues that they still contain class elements, and that class conflict will not disappear while capitalism and wage labour persist. Globalisation, Mi adds, has made class issues global, citing Navarro's view that the main conflict is between alliances of ruling and ruled classes across North and South. The thesis that class struggle has died out is therefore called inaccurate. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese critical survey of Western Marxist debates on class structure, class criteria and social movements, with references to Wright, Dahrendorf, Gouldner and Laclau and Mouffe.
quoteEn: Therefore, the transformation of Western class structure from simplicity to complexity does not mean that class has vanished from social relations, or that class analysis has become irrelevant.
quoteZh: 因此，西方社会阶级结构由简单化向复杂化的转型，并不意味着阶级已从社会关系中消失了或者说阶级分析已经无关紧要了。

glossary.explanation: The tradition of Marxist thought in Western Europe and North America (Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and others). Chinese scholars often use the label broadly for non-orthodox Marxist and post-Marxist thinkers, as this article does.
Marx's term for the combined body of workers, including technical and managerial staff, who together produce the product. Mi uses it to place the new middle class within the working class.

t: Towards a new critique of political economy: from generalised surplus value to total subsumption
zh: 走向新政治经济学批判：从广义剩余价值到总体从属
source: Frontiers of Foreign Social Sciences (国外社会科学前沿), 2020 no. 11
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the French philosopher Étienne Balibar, translated by Wang Zhen. Balibar asks what a 'new critique of political economy' would involve, and how far it continues or departs from Marx. His answer is that Marx's central category, surplus value, must be broadened beyond its Smithian and Ricardian foundations. That broadening leads to what he calls 'total subsumption', which he uses to explain how finance capital governs everyday life in the age of neoliberal globalisation.

The article opens by asking what 'new' means: a critique of a political economy Marx never knew, or a continuation of Marxist critique in the face of ambiguities in Marx's own writing. It then treats capital as a social relation and identifies two tensions in Marx's definition of capital, as a process of exploitation and as a process of accumulation. Two examples follow, 'surplus health' and 'human capital'. A final section sets out total subsumption.

Balibar argues that Marx's notion of Verwertung (valorisation) carries two senses, the formation of value and its expansion as surplus value. These are circularly interdependent, and Marx's treatment of money and 'productive labour' leaves difficulties that surface in discussions of financialised capitalism. The 'surplus health' example, taken from Joseph Dumit, shows profit arising from consumption: chronic illness, lifelong multi-drug use and supply creating demand. Balibar reads this as a generalised form of surplus value. Gary Becker's human capital theory is presented as an inversion of the labour theory of value, treating labour as a capital that operates through credit, investment and profitability, and casting individuals as entrepreneurs of themselves.

Building on Marx's shift from formal to real subsumption, Balibar proposes 'total subsumption'. In it, commodification extends to life itself, the boundary between work and life, production and reproduction, disappears, and no 'natural' life remains outside value. He asks whether commodification has limits. Drawing on Lacan, he suggests that any totalisation contains an element of the 'Real', so that residues of resistance may appear in individual, mass or governmental forms. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist philosopher's attempt to extend Marx's concepts to health, human capital and financialisation, and to place it within debates over what is 'new' in the critique of political economy.
quoteEn: This is what I call total subsumption (which comes after 'formal' and 'real' subsumption), because it leaves nothing outside it (it leaves no space for 'natural' life).
quoteZh: 这就是我所说的总体从属（它出现在“形式上的”和“实际上的”从属之后），因为它没有留下任何外在的东西（没有给“自然的”生命留出任何的空间）。

t: Infinite form and the spark of truth: the materialist dialectic in Badiou's Immanence of Truths
zh: 无限形式与真理的星星之火——论巴迪欧《真理的内在性》中的唯物辩证法
paras: Lan Jiang reads Alain Badiou's 2018 book Immanence of Truths, the third volume of the Being and Event series and possibly his last major work, as an attempt to ask what happens to the finite world once a subject has touched a genuine infinity. The article's entry point is Mao Zedong's phrase "a single spark can start a prairie fire", which Badiou cites repeatedly. Lan argues that the book completes Badiou's "new materialist dialectic" by reversing the direction of his earlier inquiries.

The article has four main parts plus a conclusion. It opens with Badiou's re-translation of Mao's phrase and with Valéry's poem Le Cimetière marin. It then uses Plato's allegory of the cave to explain the book's "return" structure. It goes on to trace Badiou's turn from language to mathematics through his two manifestos of philosophy (1989 and 2009). It ends with the two enemies of the new dialectic, transcendence and "democratic materialism", and with Badiou's treatment of finitude.

Lan's central claim is that Badiou changes the logic of the spark. In the earlier works the spark causes the conflagration. In Immanence of Truths it is the concrete flash thrown up by an already-present infinity, so the finite appears only within the form opened by a truth procedure. Badiou, in Lan's account, fights on two fronts. Against transcendence, whether God, Substance or Nature, he asserts that "the One is not", relying on Cantor's "multiple without-one" and on Cohen's forcing. Against democratic materialism, whose axiom is that only bodies and languages exist, he claims that the finite is only the result of operations on infinite multiplicity. Lan illustrates this with the apple, which counts as an apple only within a counting-as-one framework, and with the invention of imaginary numbers. Hence only formal mathematics can break what Badiou calls the fetishistic "ideology of the finite". Lan notes that this explains Badiou's neglect of physics and chemistry, and his criticisms of Wittgenstein, Heidegger, Habermas and Deleuze.

Lan concludes that Badiou's envisaged future society is neither a return to the One nor a religious Eden. It would be a new form created after an event, through a generic truth procedure, in which subjects are incorporated and new objects take shape. The spark can spread across the world because it belongs to that new set, not because it embodies a transcendent One. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Badiou's mathematical ontology links to Maoist imagery and to the critique of finitude, written from within Chinese engagement with foreign Marxism.
quoteEn: Badiou has always believed in the revolutionary effect of the event: because the event is an absolute exception that the structure of the prior situation cannot count as one, a new structure has to be created to replace the old one completely.
quoteZh: 巴迪欧始终相信事件的革命性效果，因为事件是一个绝对的例外，原先的情势状态的结构无法对它进行计数为一的计算，势必意味着需要创造一个新的结构，来彻底取代原先的结构。

glossary.explanation: Badiou's term, from Logics of Worlds, for the contemporary outlook whose axiom is that "there are only bodies and languages". He treats it as confining thought to the finite.
Badiou's own revised version of the dialectic, whose axiom is that besides bodies and languages there are truths. It is distinct from the classical Marxist usage.
Badiou's concept from Being and Event, in which a structure turns inconsistent multiplicity into unified objects. In his ontology, unity is the result of this operation and is not given in being.

t: The theoretical landscape of Western consumer culture theory
zh: 西方消费文化理论图景
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 26 November 2020, p. 4
paras: Hou Dongmei sketches how Western Marxism has theorised consumer culture, treating it as an important part of Western Marxist social critique and a resource for developing Marxism today. The short article argues that mapping this tradition can advance Marxist consumer culture theory, support critique of present-day consumption practices and guide the building of a consumption civilisation in the new era.

Hou first traces the foundations: Marx and Engels on ideology, alienation and commodity fetishism; Lukács on reification; Gramsci on cultural hegemony; and the shift in capitalist society from production to consumption as the driver of accumulation. The article then surveys five approaches: culture-industry and technology critique (Horkheimer and Adorno), ideology critique (Marcuse), psychoanalysis (Fromm), cultural construction (John Fiske, rendered "Fiske" from the Chinese transliteration), and semiotics (Baudrillard).

In Hou's account, the thinkers share one move: they shift critique from production to everyday consumption. Horkheimer and Adorno see exchange value displacing use value; Marcuse sees false needs and the "one-dimensional" consumer; Fromm sees consumption as flight from loneliness. Fiske, by contrast, stresses that consumers can evade, resist or rework dominant ideology. Baudrillard treats consumption as a system of signs and, in Hou's reading, abandons Marx's political economy late in his career for semiotics and post-structuralism.

Hou concludes that later figures such as Bauman and Lefebvre also lack a historical materialist standpoint, so their solutions are elitist and weak. In this view, critique of consumption is at root critique of the logic of capital, and the way out must be a fundamental change in relations of production. Hou says that appeals to aesthetic utopias or individual awakening lose critical force. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how Western Marxist consumer culture theory is presented and assessed.
quoteEn: In essence, whether it is Marx's critique of the logic of material production or Western Marxists' critique of the logic of consumption, both are at bottom a critique of the logic of capital, and the way out must be a fundamental transformation of the relations of production.
quoteZh: 从本质上讲，无论是马克思对物质生产逻辑的批判还是西方马克思主义学者对消费逻辑的批判，其实质都是对资本逻辑的批判，其出路必然是生产关系的根本变革。

t: The "counterattack" of the Workers' Party of Belgium and its implications
zh: 比利时工人党的“逆袭”及其启示
source: Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2019–2020), Social Sciences Academic Press, June 2020, pp. 253–268
paras: The article asks how the Workers' Party of Belgium (PTB/PVDA) rose so quickly in 2019, when most European radical-left parties were declining, and what its experience means for communist parties elsewhere. It opens with the party's results that year: 8.7% in the European Parliament election, its first seat there, and a rise from 8 to 41 seats across Belgian legislatures since 2014. Yu argues that the decisive factor was a strategy combining "principledness" with "flexibility", adopted in 2008, and that this offers Western communist parties a "new road".

The text first traces five stages of party history: its origins in the late-1960s student movement (1966–79), formal founding and slow growth (1979–89), stagnation after the Soviet collapse (1989–99), crisis and strategic adjustment (1999–2008), and gradual rise since 2008. It then sets out the 2008 strategic turn, analyses five features of the party's practice, and ends with reflections for the wider communist movement. Membership figures, election results and campaigns are cited throughout.

On the strategy, Yu reports that the party's "principledness" rests on Marxism as worldview and method and on socialism as the goal, which the party calls "socialism 2.0". "Flexibility" means adapting tactics to circumstances, which the party compares to a body needing both a strong spine and supple limbs. In practice, Yu says, the party focuses on everyday concerns such as its free community health centres and a campaign for a minimum pension of 1,500 euros. It keeps a distinct Marxist-Leninist identity, redefines the working class broadly, and works on a "street–parliament–street" principle. It declines federal government participation for now, drawing lessons from Syriza in Greece. Leaders and MPs take an average worker's wage, and the party cooperates openly with trade unions and social movements.

Yu divides Western communist parties of the past thirty years into a "traditional" path, which tends towards dogmatism, and a "modernizing" path, which tends to over-compromise and lose its distinctiveness. Both, Yu says, are polarizing and have hit electoral ceilings or lost voters. The Belgian party is presented as avoiding both extremes through a dynamic balance, offering answers on combining parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, tactics versus long-term strategy, and identity versus broader alliances. Yu suggests it could be called a "third way" for Western communism. Read the original if you want a detailed, sympathetic Chinese account of the Belgian party's history and tactics, and of how Chinese scholars assess the lessons for communist parties abroad.
quoteEn: This "new" road also offers "answers" to a number of important theoretical problems that have long troubled the Western communist movement.
quoteZh: 这条“新”路也为长期困扰西方共产主义运动的一些重要理论问题提供了“答案”

glossary.zh: 原则性与灵活性相结合
glossary.explanation: The Workers' Party of Belgium's strategic formula from its 2008 congress: firm adherence to Marxism and socialism together with tactical adaptability. The article treats it as the party's defining strategy.
A principle drawn from the Paris Commune: party leaders and MPs receive only an average worker's pay, and the remainder goes to the party.
The collective term in Chinese scholarship for communist parties and related movements worldwide, here applied to Western parties.

t: Notable achievements in China's economic and social development during the 13th Five-Year Plan period
zh: “十三五”时期我国经济社会发展成就显著
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in autumn 2020, Wu reviews what the 13th Five-Year Plan period (2016–2020) achieved, taking as his starting point Xi Jinping's 22 October assessment to the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau. The article's thesis is that the plan was implemented smoothly, that its main targets will be met on schedule despite external pressure and the COVID-19 shock, and that this lays a solid base for completing a moderately prosperous society and starting a new journey of building a modern socialist country.

The piece is organised under five headings: stable overall economic performance, continued optimisation of the economic structure, faster cultivation of new growth drivers, expanded opening up, and faster progress in foreign-related rule of law. It draws on official statistics from the National Bureau of Statistics, the Ministry of Public Security, the Ministry of Commerce and the fourth national economic census.

Wu's core argument rests on figures. He cites average GDP growth of 6.7% for 2016–2019, GDP of 99.1 trillion yuan in 2019, per capita GDP above US$10,000, and China as the only major economy with positive growth in the first three quarters of 2020. He also reports a fall in rural poverty from 55.75 million to 5.51 million people between 2015 and 2019, capacity cuts in steel and coal, and a stabilised macro leverage ratio that kept financial risk below systemic levels. On structure, he points to a rise in the share of the 'three new' economy in GDP from 14.8% to 16.3%, growth in high-tech and equipment manufacturing, and falling tariffs and shorter negative lists for foreign investment. He presents the Foreign Investment Law and the unified market-access negative list as steps from opening in goods and factors towards opening in rules and standards.
