Wu attributes the results to the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He closes by describing the 14th Five-Year Plan period as the first stage of the new journey, calling for adherence to the new development philosophy, high-quality development and a people-centred approach, and for the new development pattern of 'dual circulation'. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned statistical summary of how Chinese scholars presented the 13th Five-Year Plan record in late 2020.
quoteEn: The achievements in China's economic and social development during the 13th Five-Year Plan period are the result of the strong leadership of the Party Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core, of the scientific guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and of the unity and enterprise of the broad masses of the people.
quoteZh: “十三五”时期我国经济社会发展成就的取得，是以习近平同志为核心的党中央坚强领导的结果，是习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想科学指引的结果，是广大人民群众团结奋进、开拓进取的结果。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
A framework announced in 2015 that stresses innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development.
An official goal, prominent since 2017, that shifts emphasis from speed of growth to efficiency, innovation and sustainability.
A long-standing official target, set for completion in 2020, covering income, poverty elimination and living standards.
The new development pattern announced in 2020, with the domestic cycle as the mainstay and domestic and international cycles reinforcing each other.

t: Marx studies in Italy: an intellectual-historical survey
zh: 意大利的马克思研究：一个思想史的考察
source: New Era Marxism Forum (Xin shidai Makesi zhuyi luncong), 2019 no. 1
paras: Chinese scholarship on Italian engagement with Marx has mostly approached it through Italian Marxism, focusing on Gramsci and the Della Volpe school, with more recent attention to Labriola and to Negri's operaismo. Lu Kejian instead adopts the viewpoint of Marx studies (Marxology) and asks how Marx's texts reached Italy, how Italian thinkers read them, and how those readings interacted and were handed down. The article argues that Italian Marx interpretation has been shaped above all by a long oscillation between positivism and Hegelianism.

The article has three main parts. The first is a detailed chronology of the publication, translation and editing of Marx's and Engels's writings in Italy, from Marx's 1848 letter in Italian through the 1865 translation of the Inaugural Address, the 1886 Capital volume 1, and post-war editions of the 1844 Manuscripts and the Grundrisse, to the stalled Editori Riuniti Collected Works and its later continuation by the Institute for the Study of Capitalism in Genoa. The second part periodises Italian interpretation, treating Labriola, Croce, Gentile, Gramsci and Colletti. The third looks at interactions with France, between currents of thought, and across generations of teachers and pupils.

Lu's central claim is that Labriola, drawing on the Italian Hegelian tradition, was the first to read historical materialism as a philosophy of praxis rather than a positive science, and so initiated Hegelian Marxism. Croce, by contrast, accepted Second International orthodoxy, read Capital as historical materialism, and divided Marx into a scientific and an ethical element. In Lu's account this anticipated later themes of Western Marxology, such as the supposed split between Marx and Engels, and fed Bernstein's revisionism. Lu adds that Croce's critique rested on a misreading, though his originality is to be acknowledged. Lu also stresses neglected lineages: Spaventa's role behind Labriola, Croce and Gramsci, and Negri's revival of Gramsci's workerism through the Grundrisse's 'Fragment on Machines'.

In an overall assessment, Lu holds that Italian Marx research led French research from the Second International onwards, with Hegelian Marxism and a Della Volpe 'scientistic' school appearing before their French counterparts, Lefebvre and Althusser. Yet Lu says Italy remained relatively peripheral in the European map of Marx studies, because its philosophical tradition was thinner and it lacked the existentialist and phenomenological readings found in Germany and France. Lu adds that readers always interpret Marx through the currents of their own time, so no single legitimate reading exists. Read the original if you want a bibliographic chronology of Italian Marx editions or an account of the Labriola–Croce–Gentile–Gramsci line from a Chinese Marx-studies perspective.
quoteEn: Oscillation between positivism and Hegelianism has been the keynote of Italian Marx research since the end of the nineteenth century.
quoteZh: 在实证主义和黑格尔主义之间摇摆，成为19世纪末以来意大利马克思研究的主基调。

glossary.explanation: A field concentrating on philological, textual and historical study of Marx's works and their reception, often linked to the MEGA edition. In China it is distinguished from Party-doctrinal Marxist theory.
An Italian current of Marxism, prominent from the 1960s, that centres on the working class's autonomous struggles. Antonio Negri is its best-known representative.
A term used by Labriola and Gramsci for historical materialism understood as a philosophy of human practice, rather than a positive science.

t: Technology in the general and the historical mode: a critical analysis of György Markus's account of Marx's theory of technology
zh: 一般模式与历史模式下的技术——乔治·马尔库什的马克思技术理论之批判性分析
paras: Yan examines how the Budapest School theorist György (Georg) Markus reads Marx's theory of technology, a question tied to whether technological progress should be praised or criticised in relation to human emancipation. Markus separates a "general model" from a "historical model" in Marx and sees a tension between them. Yan argues that Markus misreads Marx. In Yan's account, Marx has only a critical, historically specific theory of technology, and a general model does not exist as a rival to it.

The article, published in 2020, has three parts. It first reconstructs Markus's use of the content/form dichotomy (material content versus social form) and the six conclusions he draws from treating labour as a technical process. It then turns to the historical mode of interpretation, taking up Markus's examples one by one: labour productivity, tool-centrism, the elements of the labour process, living labour and simple cooperation, and machinery. It closes by assessing Markus's claim that Marx has two faces, "theorist of technology" and "historian", and two souls, historical romanticism and political realism. Yan draws throughout on Moishe Postone's critique of traditional Marxism.

Yan's central move is to say that Markus's dichotomy abstracts labour and technology from social relations. In Yan's view this lands Markus in a traditional or positivist framework that criticises only exploitation and distribution, not the capitalist form of labour itself. Yan also charges that Markus quotes selectively. One example is a remark of Hodgskin's that Markus attributes to Marx. Another is the phrase about the "isolated man", which in the full passage describes the standpoint of bourgeois economists. Yan holds that Marx's general remarks on technology serve his historical analysis and the critique of capital. Machinery, for example, is for Marx a form of capital and a means of its domination over labour, not simply a tool. Measuring progress by labour time is, on this reading, a specific law of capitalism.

Yan concedes that Marx's thought is complex. The tensions in it appear as rejection, refinement or interweaving. Historical romanticism and political realism, in Yan's view, are two dimensions of one dialectic, not two souls. Yan draws three lessons: the general and critical theories should not be set against each other; socialism's transcendence of capitalism means a qualitative change in the form of technology, not just quantitative accumulation; and the content/form dichotomy is useful only if it is not made absolute. Read the original if you study Marx's theory of technology, Markus and the Budapest School, or the use of Postone in Chinese debates, and want the textual evidence for Yan's charge of selective quotation.
quoteEn: Although Marx advocated distinguishing content from form, he did not split the two apart; his general analysis of technology serves his historical analysis of technology and his critical theory of capitalism.
quoteZh: 马克思虽然主张区分内容和形式，但并没有将二者割裂开来，他对技术所做的一般性分析是服务于对技术的历史性分析以及资本主义批判理论的。

t: Commemoration of and reflection on the Communist International by the foreign left
zh: 国外左翼对共产国际的纪念与反思
paras: Writing in 2020, Xuan Chuanshu and Yu Ming ask how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China used the centenary of the Communist International (Comintern, founded in March 1919) to look back and to think about the present. The authors argue that these actors are less recalling history than questioning reality and looking ahead, hoping to revive the world socialist movement through renewed international unity. They also argue that the foreign left is seriously divided on how to achieve this, and that China should keep a sober, well-defined position.

The article draws on 2019 international conferences, party statements and articles in left-wing outlets such as Jacobin, Socialist Worker, Socialist Appeal and Globalizations. These come from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Communist Party of Greece, the Communist Party of Turkey, the Communist Party USA, Trotskyist groups and the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation. It is organised around five questions: why the Comintern was founded, its historical impact, its legacy, today's world situation, and what form future unity should take. A conclusion then interprets the commemorations and sets out China's position.

On origins, the article separates a world-revolution reading, in which the Comintern answered the collapse of the Second International, from a reading in which it served Soviet Russia's own needs. On impact, it sets praise (helping found communist parties, supporting national liberation in Africa and Latin America, strengthening proletarian solidarity) against criticism (subordination to Soviet interests, unrealistic directives, the Norwegian and Finnish cases). Commentators see parallels between 1919 and today in the crises of capitalism and the rise of socialist China. They propose three routes: a new international organisation, delay because conditions are not ripe, or looser forms such as conferences and exchanges.

In the authors' account, the three groups that commemorate are existing or successor communist parties, Trotskyist organisations, and critical left scholars. Their divisions reflect differing memories of the Comintern and the small size of most left forces, which want support from larger parties but fear manipulation. The authors call for a historical, dialectical judgement, citing Zhou Enlai's formula "good at both ends, problematic in the middle, yet not worthless". They also warn against overestimating the movement's recovery and say China should not seek to head a new "international". Instead it should strengthen its own development and cooperate with left parties on the basis of independence and equality. Read the original if you want a survey of foreign left and communist-party views on the Comintern centenary, together with a Chinese academic assessment of them.
quoteEn: Today's centre does not mean rebuilding an "International", nor "China taking the lead" as some left parties and scholars keep calling for, still less extending democratic centralism, a principle of intra-party organisation, to relations between parties.
quoteZh: 现在的中心,不是要重建“国际”,不是要像世界上一些左翼政党或左翼学者所不断呼吁的那样“中国当头”,更不是要将适用于党内组织原则的民主集中制推广到党际交往。

glossary.explanation: The Third International, founded in Moscow in 1919 to unite communist parties worldwide, dissolved in 1943. It is often abbreviated Comintern.
The international association of socialist and labour parties founded in 1889. It broke down when its leading parties backed their governments in the First World War.
A Chinese field of study and political framing covering the global socialist movement, socialist states and left forces.

t: Development trends of foreign Marxist currents in the twenty-first century and an assessment of their effects
zh: 21世纪国外马克思主义思潮的发展趋势及其效应评估
paras: Zhang Liang and Sun Leqiang ask how Chinese scholars should approach the development of Marxism outside China since 2000. Their answer is that China is no longer a follower of foreign Marxism but its contemporary: Chinese scholars should neither reject it wholesale nor copy it, but analyse it critically from the standpoint of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They take what helps Chinese theoretical innovation and leave the rest.

The article, published in 2019, has four parts. The first examines how foreign Marxists treat the basic theory of Marxism, including textual scholarship and four research paths. The second looks at four theoretical growth points: ecology, space, identity politics and biopolitics. The third turns to analyses of contemporary capitalism (production, crisis, class structure, democracy). The fourth is a conclusion on what to learn from this body of work and where to stand.

The authors argue that the new MEGA2 editions and related translations lean towards deconstruction and revive the thesis that Marx and Engels were opposed. They sort Western work into four paths: rereading Marx, localised constructions, grafting Marxism onto the "post-" theories, and outright rejection of Marxism. In their judgement all four fall short, and the field is increasingly fragmented. The ecological, spatial, identity and biopolitical currents are said to be fading, utopian or unable to move beyond the capitalist framework. On crisis, the authors credit left scholars with returning to Capital but hold that the basic contradiction between the productive forces and capitalist relations of production remains. Drawing on Marx and Engels, they argue that mental and non-material workers who sell labour-power and produce surplus value belong to the working class. They therefore call the labels "middle stratum" and "cognitive class" eclectic. Western critiques of democracy are called incisive, but their proposed alternatives are called weak.

The authors conclude that foreign Marxism offers useful lessons in textual editing, in exploring ideas Marx and Engels left undeveloped, in localising Marxism and in exposing capitalism's structural contradictions. They also call for vigilance against its deconstructionism, Eurocentrism, neoliberal premises and non-Marxist politics. After 70 years of the People's Republic, they say, Chinese scholars should drop the mentality of apprentices and turn Chinese experience into theory to develop twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western left currents, and of how Chinese scholars position themselves towards them in 2019.
quoteEn: We are not its followers but its contemporaries.
quoteZh: 我们不是它的追随者,而是它的同时代人。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. It is used as the standpoint from which foreign theories are judged.
A broad Chinese academic field covering Marxist and left thought outside China, wider than the specific tradition of Western Marxism.

t: Trends in Western left-wing thought as seen from the 2019 Left Forum in New York
zh: 从2019年纽约左翼论坛看西方左翼思想发展动态
source: Marxist Studies (马克思主义研究), 2020 no. 3
paras: This is a report on the 2019 Left Forum, held on 28–30 June at Long Island University in Brooklyn, written by Tian Xi and published in Marxist Studies in 2020. Tian places the event eleven years after the 2008 financial crisis, against a rise in American left-wing currents and in movements by Black people, women, ethnic minorities and LGBTQ groups. The forum had more than 160 panels and two special forums. Tian summarises what participants said about Trumpism, America's present predicament and opposition to capitalism in the twenty-first century.

The report has three parts. The first covers reflections on Trumpism: the threats it poses, its causes, and how to resist it in theory and in practice. The second covers the American predicament, taking up the political economy of the "long depression", the return of fascism and the immigration question, and US–Russia and US–China relations. The third covers opposing capitalism, through the "end of history" thesis, the legacy of Marxism and the idea of going beyond utopianism. The main voices are Joseph Choonara, Andrew Kliman, Anne Jaclard, Jason Stanley, David Kotz, David Laibman, Michael Hudson, David Harvey, Kevin Anderson and Julio Huato.

Tian records disagreement on where Trumpism comes from. Anti-neoliberal leftists such as Kotz, Hudson and Perelman see neoliberal failure as the root cause. Kliman, using Piketty's revised income figures, argues that a white working-class revolt against stagnation cannot explain Trump's victory and that white nationalism is the better explanation. Kotz rebuts three official explanations of US hostility to Russia and attributes it to class interests and hegemonic rivalry. In his account, the same logic explains the growing US wariness of China. Kotz also sees neoliberalism in crisis and two possible restructurings, authoritarian right-wing nationalism or green social democracy, and he favours supporting the latter as a step towards socialism. Anne Jaclard criticises "left-firsters" who tolerate Trump, and Huato and Paddy Quick argue that socialism needs organised mass activity and durable democratic structures.

Tian concludes that the Left Forum survives in the margins of American political life yet keeps considerable influence in North America. In this account it is a pluralistic, mixed "discourse field" in which discussion rests on the historical fact of capitalism and some analyses continue Marx's critical tradition. Tian also notes weaknesses: a mixed membership, a lack of ideological unity and a thin scholarly character. The article calls for a dialectical assessment of the views voiced there. Read the original if you want a detailed, China-based account of the positions and speakers at this American left gathering, with names and arguments that are hard to find elsewhere in Chinese.
quoteEn: Overall, however, the New York Left Forum suffers from a mixed membership, a lack of ideological unity and a scholarly character that needs strengthening.
quoteZh: 但整体来看,纽约左翼论坛存在人员混杂、思想不统一、学术色彩有待加强等问题。

t: The theoretical predicaments of contemporary Western Left critical philosophy
zh: 当代西方左翼批判哲学的理论困境
paras: Chen Xiangqin asks why contemporary Western Left philosophy, which mobilises nearly every theoretical resource to criticise the domination and alienation of modernity, ends in impotence. The article argues that this philosophy's political action is in effect its academic discourse, and that it has become a game of critique, deconstruction and resistance that yields only abstract opposition and a sense of futility. Chen contends that it inherits the critical spirit of Marxism but has not reached the critical and revolutionary height of historical materialism.

The article has four sections: the predicament of critique, the predicament of justification, the turn from a faith in progress to a faith in redemption, and the theoretical limits of this philosophy. Chen draws on Adorno, Horkheimer, Benjamin, Agamben, Žižek, Badiou, Laclau and Mouffe, Derrida and Bloch, with reference to Kant, Berdyaev and Marx. The notes also place the argument beside Zhang Yibing's thesis of the 'end' of Western Marxism and the later Frankfurt School's attempts to rebuild normative foundations.

Chen's first move is that, unlike classical Left thought, the contemporary Left attacks not only capital, technology and power but also the Enlightenment ideas of reason, freedom, humanity and progress. By doing so it dissolves its own normative ground. It is left with two options: critique as the sole principle of justification, or an eschatological and messianic faith that, in Chen's reading, replaces belief in progress with a theodicy of history. Drawing on Kant's distinction between progress and evolution, Chen argues that history cannot be morally justified from within its empirical course. A turn to transcendent redemption therefore ends in a rhetoric of justification that loses its critical edge. The second move is diagnostic: the Left stops at the philosophical critique that Marx had already sublated, and so rests its criticism on ideas that are either dialectical and negative or otherworldly and speculative.

Chen concludes that Marx's mature critique was a historical critique, centred on political economy and extended to the history of human society. For Marx, Chen says, the revolutionary force is the dialectical, negating process of history itself, not an ideal against which reality is measured. Chen calls on Western critical theory to move from philosophical critique back to Marx's critique of political economy. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Adorno, Benjamin, Agamben and Žižek, and of why their critique is said to lack a ground in historical materialism.
quoteEn: Contemporary Western Left philosophy meets this theoretical predicament because its critique stops at the philosophical critique Marx had already sublated, and has not advanced to the critique of political economy he inaugurated, still less to the critique of the history of human society guided by it.
quoteZh: 当代西方左翼哲学之所以遭遇这种理论困境,乃是因为它们的批判止步于马克思曾经扬弃的哲学批判,而没有进展到他所开创的政治经济学批判,乃至以政治经济学批判为导引的人类社会史批判。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory of history, which explains social change through material production and the contradictions of social formations. In Chinese Marxist writing it is treated as the core of Marx's thought.

Marx's mature project, the subtitle of Capital, which analyses capitalism as a historically specific social formation. Chen treats it as the stage of Marx's critique that the Western Left has not reached.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's and Marx's Aufhebung: to supersede something while retaining part of it in a higher form.

glossary.literal: theory of the justice of God
glossary.explanation: Originally the theological defence of divine justice despite evil. Chen uses it for the ultimate justification of the whole course of history through an eschatological or messianic frame.

t: Foreign left commemorations and reflections on the Communist International
zh: 国外左翼对共产国际的纪念与反思
paras: On the centenary of the Communist International (Comintern) in 2019, left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China held conferences and published articles to mark it. Xuan and Yu survey this body of commemoration and ask what it says about the Comintern's past and about the future of world socialism. They argue that the foreign left is less looking back than interrogating the present, and that it is deeply divided over how to rebuild international unity.

The article draws on conferences by bodies such as the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties in Europe, the International Marxist Tendency and the Russian Communist Workers' Party, as well as texts from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Communist Party of Greece and the Communist Party of the USA. It also uses Jacobin, Socialist Appeal, Globalizations and the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation. It is organised around five questions: why the Comintern was founded, its historical impact, its legacy, today's world situation, and what kind of union socialist forces now need. A concluding section gives the authors' own assessment.

On founding, the article reports two readings: a response to the Second International's collapse and to social democracy, or a tool to protect Soviet Russia. On impact, it sets praise (nurturing communist parties, supporting national liberation, fostering proletarian solidarity) against criticism of Moscow's dominance and unrealistic directives, citing the Norwegian and Finnish cases. Most speakers see parallels between 1919 and today's capitalist crisis and cite the contrast between 'Western disorder' and 'Eastern order'. On reorganisation, they split into three camps: a new proletarian international, either federal or democratic-centralist; those who think conditions are not ripe; and those who prefer looser forms such as conferences and exchanges.

Xuan and Yu conclude that the commemorations are driven by communist parties, Trotskyist groups and critical left scholars, and that divisions reflect both historical memory and the small size of most left groups. Their own stance is that the Comintern should be judged historically and dialectically, endorsing Zhou Enlai's verdict of 'good at both ends, poor in the middle'. They caution that the shift in global power balance does not mean socialism is rising against capitalism. They also state that China should not seek to 'lead' or rebuild an international, but should develop itself and cooperate with left parties on the basis of independence, full equality, mutual respect and non-interference. Read the original if you want a detailed map of 2019 left debates on the Comintern and a Chinese Party-affiliated scholarly reading of them.
quoteEn: Rather than looking back on and commemorating history, they are interrogating the present and looking to the future.
quoteZh: 与其说他们是在回望历史、缅怀历史,不如说是在拷问现实和展望未来。

glossary.explanation: The Third International, founded in Moscow in 1919 as a world party of communist parties. It was dissolved in 1943.

glossary.en: good at both ends, poor in the middle
glossary.explanation: Zhou Enlai's summary evaluation of the Comintern, which the authors adopt: its early and late periods were good, its middle period poor but not without merit.

t: Studying world left-wing thought and movements amid changes unseen in a century
st: An overview of research on foreign left-wing thought in 2019
zh: 百年未有之大变局中的世界左翼思潮和运动研究
zhSub: 2019年国外左翼思想研究概览
paras: This is a literature review of research on the foreign left in 2019. The authors begin from the premise that the world is undergoing "changes unseen in a century" and that the basic contradictions of capitalism are taking new forms. They report that left-wing scholars abroad sought to answer pressing questions in ways that show the contemporary value and vitality of Marxism.

The review opens with the year's main left-wing gatherings: the New York left forum, the Socialism conference in Chicago, the Marxism festival in London, the Revolution festival, the tenth World Socialism Forum in Beijing, and a Chinese forum on foreign Marxism. It then surveys five theoretical clusters: imperialism, neoliberalism, contemporary capitalism, socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Chinese appraisals of foreign left thought. A third part describes the left regionally: North America and Europe; Russia, the Middle East and Africa; and Latin America.

On theory, the authors report that David Harvey and John Smith debated the contemporary relevance of Lenin's theory of imperialism. Intan Suwandi, R. Jamil Jonna and John Bellamy Foster, they say, analyse imperialism through global commodity chains and labour arbitrage, and Foster describes a "late imperialism" of stagnation and declining US hegemony. Foster, the Patnaiks and Sitaram Yechury are presented as arguing that neoliberalism has reached a dead end and fed the political right. Studies of digital capitalism are said to show intensified control of labour. Egon Krenz, Russian scholars and Toma Ivan are reported as praising socialism with Chinese characteristics. Regionally, the review notes the weakening of centre-left parties in Europe, the "back to the working class" turn of US democratic socialists, the German Left Party's difficulties, and a retreat of Latin America's left, including the coup in Bolivia.

The authors conclude that foreign left thought will keep developing as long as capitalism's contradictions and crises persist. They call for Chinese scholars to draw scientifically on this work, which they see as a resource for twenty-first-century Marxism and for building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. They also urge more exchange with foreign left scholars, and say text-based study should aim at ideas and their transformation in China rather than at the texts themselves. Read the original if you want a quick map of the 2019 Chinese-language and foreign sources on the international left, with full citations to Monthly Review articles and Chinese journal studies.
quoteEn: The goal of research is not the text but the ideas within it and their transformation in contemporary China.
quoteZh: 研究的目标不是文本，而是其中的思想及其当代中国转化。

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great change not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Chinese official discourse, notably by Xi Jinping since 2017, to describe a perceived deep shift in the global order and balance of power.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path since reform and opening up, combining a socialist political system with market-oriented economic methods.
An annual international conference hosted in Beijing by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, bringing together Chinese and foreign scholars and left-wing figures.
The Chinese academic field studying Marxist and left-wing thought outside China, broader than the specific tradition of Western Marxism.

t: China's anti-epidemic action in the eyes of foreign left-wing parties
zh: 国外左翼政党眼中的中国抗疫行动
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexueyuan bao), 30 April 2020, p. 5
paras: This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences newspaper in April 2020, asks how communist and workers' parties abroad have assessed China's response to Covid-19. Hu and Yu argue that the epidemic is a "touchstone" of national governance and political systems, and that many such parties have praised China, criticised their own governments' slow responses and urged them to learn from China's experience.

The article reports statements from parties in Greece, Argentina, Vietnam, Australia, Italy, the United States, Canada, Luxembourg, Belgium, Puerto Rico, Mexico, South Africa, Norway, Britain and Sri Lanka. It is organised in three parts: calls to draw on China's measures, the fight against disinformation and xenophobia, and the claimed advantages of the socialist system.

The authors report that a joint statement initiated by the Greek Communist Party and signed by at least 82 parties recognised China's results and internationalism. Several parties, including those of Australia, Canada and the United States, are said to have denounced "Sinophobia" and blamed anti-China rumours on imperialism, summed up in the slogan "our enemy is the virus, not China". Other parties are cited as arguing that capitalist commercialisation and privatisation of health care exposed its inefficiency and "anti-people" character, while centralised, planned mobilisation in China showed the strengths of socialism.

Hu and Yu conclude that more countries are recognising the social mobilisation capacity of the socialist system, and that China's data sharing, aid and donations show its commitment to building a community with a shared future for mankind. They hold that the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics show the significance of that project. Read the original if you want a compact sample of how Chinese academics present foreign communist parties' statements on China's epidemic response.
quoteEn: "Our enemy is the coronavirus, not China" has become the common view of communist and workers' parties in many countries.
quoteZh: “我们的敌人是新冠病毒，而不是中国”，成为多国共产党和工人党的普遍共识。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13, calling for shared responsibility and cooperation among states on global challenges.
The official name for China's current political and economic system, associated with reform and opening up since 1978.

t: The institutional value of the Chinese path amid shifts in the world economy: views of foreign left-wing scholars
zh: 世界经济变局下中国道路的制度价值——国外左翼学者的视角
source: China Social Science Evaluation (中国社会科学评价), 2020 no. 1
paras: This report-style article covers the international conference "Contemporary China and the Modernization of Developing Countries", held at Peking University's School of Marxism on 12–13 October 2019 and known as the third "mini World Congress on Marxism". Song and Li gather the views of foreign, mostly left-leaning, scholars on changes in the world economy and on China's development path, and add their own corrections. They argue that the visitors rightly praise China's achievements but often treat the path as a mere economic method, whereas its essential attribute is socialism.

Speakers included David Kotz, Terrence McDonough, Daniel Cirera, Emir Sader, Yuri Vasilievich Taranukha, Stavros Mavroudeas, Balwinder Singh Tiwana, Chandrasekharan Saratchand, Pertti Honkanen and a group of Korean scholars. The article is organised in four parts: the shifting world economy (Brexit, Trump, populism, the crisis of neoliberal globalization); the institutional character of the Chinese path; proposals for its further development; and its significance for the world economy.

Most foreign participants, in the authors' account, read the Western upheaval as a systemic crisis rooted in finance-led accumulation; Kotz prefers the label "authoritarian right-wing nationalism" to populism. On China, they organise their views around economic growth, the Soviet model and neoliberalism. Most see the periods before and after reform and opening up as continuous, while McDonough stresses their differences. Saratchand and Cirera credit the public sector and China's resistance to neoliberalism and dollar hegemony. Song and Li then warn against three errors: reducing the path to a special growth method, severing the two periods, and overlooking the socialist nature of the socialist market economy. They also object to Vasilievich's claim that the middle class is socialism's pillar, and say the scholars' notion of "particularity" and "universality" is too thin.

The authors conclude that combining the socialist system with a market economy is the institutional basis of a new road to modernization. In their view it has broken the accumulation regime dominated by international finance capital and offers developing countries an option beyond the Soviet and neoliberal models. They name as preconditions the people as principal body, Party leadership and the socialist character of the market economy, aiming at common prosperity and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Foreign advice, they say, should be heard carefully while China keeps its composure and autonomy. Read the original if you want a detailed catalogue of how left-wing scholars from Europe, India, Russia, Latin America and Korea assess China, together with a Chinese academic response.
quoteEn: It must be stressed that, important as the Chinese characteristics of the Chinese path are, socialism is the essential attribute of China's system and path.
quoteZh: 对此必须强调,中国道路的中国特色固然重要,但社会主义才是中国制度和中国道路的本质属性。

glossary.explanation: The policy course launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, introducing market mechanisms and opening the economy to foreign trade and investment.
A goal of shared affluence for all the people, presented in Party discourse as an essential requirement of socialism.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-term national goal in official discourse, associated with the Chinese Dream and the aim of making China a strong, modern country.
The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining public ownership as the main body with market allocation of resources.
The shorthand used for China's own route of development under Party leadership, which the article treats as the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

t: Value-form: the theoretical positioning of Marx's critique of commodity fetishism
zh: 价值形式:马克思商品拜物教批判的理论定位
source: Social Sciences in China (Zhongguo shehui kexue), 2020 no. 4
paras: Wu Meng asks how historical materialism can be made contemporary ("contemporization") while remaining historical materialism, and takes Marx's critique of commodity fetishism as the test case. Wu argues that Western left thinkers who build critiques of contemporary capitalism on this critique have failed to achieve such contemporization, because they treat commodity fetishism as a basic fact of capitalist society. In Wu's reading, Marx's critique is instead a further formal analysis of the result of the value-form analysis, aimed at grasping historical real movement.

The article has four parts. It first surveys Western left thought, from Lukács to Benjamin, Backhaus and Žižek, distinguishing those who "reinterpret" historical materialism from Habermas-style "reconstruction". It then turns to the original context of the critique in Capital, comparing the first and second German editions. A third section reconstructs three aspects of the critique, and a final section draws out two working principles for contemporizing historical materialism.

Wu contends that Lukács treats fetishism as an "ideational fact" and Benjamin and Žižek as a "social fact". These readings end in an abstract revolutionary subject, a purely negative "dialectic of action", or a critique of commodity society in general. Through the first edition's fourth value-form, a commodity world in which every commodity can be a general equivalent, Wu shows that fetishism's starting point is non-actual. Marx's analysis therefore moves through producer fetishism, the political-economy fetishism of classical economics, and a third aspect centred on historically universal exchange. In this third aspect, labour acquires its twofold social character only under the compulsory shaping force of bourgeois "society".

Wu concludes that Marx's formal analysis shows two principles: a materialist method that questions contemporary real movement itself rather than applying fixed concepts, and a transcending theoretical outlook that moves from circulation into production, where capitalism's self-negation can be seen. Local empirical experience, Wu argues, cannot be the basis of contemporization. Read the original if you work on Marx's value-form theory, the Capital editions, or the Western Marxist reception of commodity fetishism and want a detailed, text-based challenge to it.
quoteEn: Marx's grasp of real movement in the critique of commodity fetishism is achieved not by directly "criticising" commodity fetishism as a "reality", but by revealing a specific historical dimension through formal analysis.
quoteZh: 马克思在商品拜物教批判中对于现实运动的把握,不是通过对作为“现实”的商品拜物教进行直接“批判”而实现的,而是通过在形式分析中展现特定历史性维度而实现的。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term in Capital, Volume I, for the forms through which value appears in exchange, from the simple form to the general equivalent and money.
Wu's name for Marx's method of starting from an abstract idea, examining its formal determinations, and uncovering the formal and historical preconditions that make it appear.
Marx's analysis in Capital of how social relations between producers appear as relations between things.

t: Opportunities and challenges together: prospects for world socialism today
zh: 机遇与挑战并存：当今世界社会主义发展前景
source: Party and Government Studies (Dangzheng yanjiu), 2020 no. 3
paras: Writing in 2020, Chai Shangjin asks where world socialism stands and where it is heading, and argues that the answer has to be read against the changing contradictions of capitalism. His thesis is that Western capitalism has entered a period of crisis and decline, which opens a favourable window for socialism. In his account socialism with Chinese characteristics is increasingly the mainstay and leading banner of world socialism. Yet the overall balance, which he calls "capitalism strong, socialism weak", will not change fundamentally because of any single event.

The article has four parts. The first describes the institutional predicament of Western capitalism: unequal globalisation, "vetocracy" in party politics, the rise of populism and extremism, and the erosion of the US-dominated international order. The second assesses communist parties in developed countries, using France, Spain and the 2019 European Parliament elections as cases. The third discusses China's role, and the fourth explains why the balance of forces remains unfavourable to socialism.

Chai holds that developed-country communist parties are stable but face persistent difficulties. They contest elections but have limited appeal: none won a seat in the 2019 European Parliament elections, and the French party's EU-level platform, he says, was far from its traditional voters' concerns. They are working on party building, but ideological splits and organisational fragmentation remain obstacles. They seek left unity, which is hard to achieve. They also struggle to win lower-income voters, whose loyalties are fragmented and whose demands populists often appropriate. Against this, Chai credits China's economic and poverty-reduction record, its institutional strengths (he cites the response to Covid-19, contrasted with the United States) and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with raising confidence among communist parties abroad.

Chai concludes that socialism replacing capitalism will be a long process. He points to Western hostility towards socialist states, the weakness of some non-ruling communist parties that have dropped ideology and democratic centralism, and Western dominance of international economic institutions. China, he writes, neither imports nor exports models, and it advances a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated researcher assesses communist parties in developed countries and the place of China in the international communist movement around 2020.
quoteEn: Overall, the present world pattern of \"capitalism strong, socialism weak\" will not be fundamentally transformed by any single international event or crisis, and the replacement of capitalism by socialism will remain a long process.
quoteZh: 从总体上看，当今世界“资强社弱”格局不会因发生某一国际事件或危机而产生根本性转变，社会主义取代资本主义仍将是一个长期的过程。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism combining Party leadership with a market economy, in use since the 1980s.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 at the 19th Party Congress.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, which calls for shared interests and cooperation across states and political systems.
A Chinese shorthand for the view that capitalist states currently hold greater economic, technological and discursive power than socialist ones.
The Leninist organisational principle of free discussion followed by binding unity of action, applied in communist parties.

t: The political predicament of modernity critique in contemporary Western left-wing thought, and a way out
zh: 当代西方左翼思潮现代性批判的政治困境及其出路
source: Journal of Southwest University (Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 1
paras: Zhuo Chengfang and Hu Daping ask why contemporary Western left-wing thought, which has produced radical discourse on almost every subject from economy and ecology to gender and psychology, has so little political purchase. They argue that the proliferation of radical language masks a political retreat: there is no longer a unified left programme aimed at changing the world, and "left" itself has become a sign of disagreement. The authors call this the political predicament of the left's critique of modernity. They trace it to a shift from seeking an alternative to capitalism to critiquing modernity, and to an anti-essentialist stance that leaves no shared values or theoretical premises.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the difficulty of agreeing on how to define politics, from the aftermath of 1968 through Habermas, Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Žižek, Amin and Thrift, and Rancière. The second examines four political issues the authors say Chinese scholarship has neglected: Virilio on speed, Bauman on globalisation and community, place and indigeneity in Appadurai, Dirlik and Mamdani, and Burawoy on the politics of production. The third returns to the question of commitment and the agenda of emancipation.

The authors argue that a theory without secured premises yields demands without practical commitment, so that the left's work becomes endless critique detached from construction. They read Laclau, Mouffe and Žižek as making "impossibility" or fundamental antagonism the basis of radical politics. Many fashionable themes, in their account, are either absorbed by power as politically correct discourse or never enter real political processes. Among the four cases, they single out Bauman as most conscious of the need to rebuild politics through public space, the political agenda and a clear vision, and they note his criticism of cultural pluralism as a reconciliation with the existing order. Burawoy shows, they say, that class politics in production has not vanished but become more complex.

Zhuo and Hu conclude that critique which avoids the capitalist mode of production and lacks a commitment to emancipation becomes an empty intellectual satisfaction. They propose returning to Marxism, reviving the emancipation agenda through major contemporary political issues and thinking again about alternatives to capitalism. They endorse Terry Eagleton's defence of Marx as a model, calling Marx the horizon of modern critique that has not yet been surpassed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of post-1968 Western left theory and of the thinkers Virilio, Bauman, Dirlik, Mamdani and Burawoy.
quoteEn: If the historical condition of the capitalist mode of production is avoided, and if there is no commitment to an emancipation agenda, critique itself becomes a meaningless intellectual satisfaction and the radical stance a purely empty gesture.
quoteZh: 如果回避资本主义生产方式这个历史条件, 如果缺乏解放议程的承诺, 批判本身将成为无意义的知识满足, 激进立场则流为纯粹空洞的姿态。

t: Three shifts in contemporary Western Marxist class theory
zh: 当今西方马克思主义阶级理论的三大转变
source: Journal of Hubei Administration Institute, 2020 no. 1
paras: Mi Haibo asks how Western Marxist scholars have revised Marx's theory of class as Western capitalism moved from industrial to post-industrial, information-based society, and whether those revisions hold up. The article argues that contemporary Western Marxism has shifted in three areas: class structure, class division and class struggle. In Mi's assessment, these revisions capture real changes but often overstate them, and class analysis remains valid.

The article is organised in three parts, one for each shift. The first moves class structure from a simple two-class model to a complex one. The second moves the criteria of class division from a single economic standard to several. The third moves class struggle from political confrontation to democratic movements. Mi discusses thinkers including Poulantzas, Gorz, Erik Olin Wright, Dahrendorf, Galbraith, Daniel Bell, Alvin Gouldner, Habermas, Laclau and Mouffe, and Ralph Miliband.

On structure, Mi accepts that new middle strata of managers, technicians and service workers have grown, and that both bourgeoisie and working class have become internally differentiated. Mi nonetheless argues that these groups sell their labour-power and so form a new stratum of the working class, part of Marx's "collective worker". Theories of the working class's disappearance, merging or individualised identity are judged misreadings. On division, Mi criticises Wright's exploitation-based "contradictory class" and the use of power or knowledge as class criteria. In Mi's account, class is determined by relations of production, and intellectuals cannot rule without economic foundations and state power. On struggle, Mi reads new social movements (feminist, ecological, anti-racist and others) as democratic struggles that are not identical with class struggle but contain class elements.

Mi concludes that while capitalism and wage-labour relations persist, class relations and class contradictions do not disappear, so claims that class struggle has died out are inaccurate. Class struggle, in Mi's view, has become more varied in its subjects and has moved towards everyday life, and it is increasingly global, as Vincent Navarro's argument about alliances of ruling and ruled classes across North and South is taken to show. Only a socialist movement, Mi holds, can finally resolve capitalism's underlying problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's critical overview of Western Marxist debates on the middle class, class criteria and new social movements, and a defence of Marx's class analysis against them.
quoteEn: Therefore, the transformation of Western class structure from simplicity to complexity does not mean that class has vanished from social relations, or that class analysis has become irrelevant.
quoteZh: 因此，西方社会阶级结构由简单化向复杂化的转型，并不意味着阶级已从社会关系中消失了或者说阶级分析已经无关紧要了。

t: Attempt and bankruptcy: rethinking Heideggerian Marxism
zh: 尝试与破产：反思海德格尔式的马克思主义
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today, 28 May 2020, p. 4
paras: Within Western Marxism, thinkers have repeatedly tried to join Marxism with other currents of Western philosophy. Deng Ding takes up one such attempt that receives less attention than it deserves: Herbert Marcuse's early project of a "Heideggerian Marxism", as opposed to his better-known "Hegelian" and "Freudian" Marxisms. This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, asks why dialectics must be combined with historical materialism and how a phenomenological materialist dialectic is possible. Deng judges Marcuse's methodological clarification worth pondering but his overall attempt a failure.

The piece follows Marcuse's reasoning in three steps. It begins with the Greek origins of dialectics in Plato and Hegel's synthesis of dialectics as reality and as logic. It then turns to how Marcuse brings in phenomenology and answers Heidegger's claim that phenomenology and dialectics are as incompatible as fire and water. Finally it covers Marcuse's turn away from Heidegger after the publication of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 in 1932, and Deng's assessment of what remains of the project.

On Deng's account, Marcuse treats dialectics first as a feature of reality's own movement of becoming rather than a logical tool. Marx turned Hegel's idealist dialectic into a materialist one, which suits the movement of human existence, and only humans are historical beings. Deng explains that the incompatibility Heidegger stressed applies to idealist dialectics, which aim at the reality of things and work through logic. Human history is both a movement of becoming, requiring dialectics, and a repeated disclosure of the meaning of being, requiring phenomology. Marcuse therefore held that phenomenology and materialist dialectics are both necessary moments of historical materialism.

Deng reports that the 1932 Manuscripts convinced Marcuse that Marx already supplied an account of human history and alienation, and that Heidegger stayed at the level of existential analysis without a "concrete philosophy". After 1933 Marcuse returned to Marx. Deng grants that phenomenology might help show how concepts such as worker, commodity and capitalist carry historical meaning within particular relations of production. But the author argues that Marcuse's attempt to redefine materialism and dialectics on a phenomenological basis was his main limitation, since only historical materialism reaches social reality. Phenomenology and existentialism, in Deng's view, still only interpret the world, while the power to change it lies in countries and peoples that inherit and develop Marxism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic assessment of Marcuse's early Heideggerian phase and its limits.
quoteEn: However, Marcuse's attempt to redefine materialism and dialectics on a phenomenological basis shows his main methodological limitation.
quoteZh: 但是，马尔库塞尝试以现象学为基础重新界定唯物主义和辩证法，这表明了他在方法论上的主要局限。

t: The historical evolution of theories of imperialism from the perspective of neoliberalism and ordoliberalism
zh: 新自由主义与秩序自由主义视域下帝国主义理论的历史演进
source: Frontiers of Foreign Social Sciences (国外社会科学前沿), 2020 no. 1
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by Vassilis K. Fouskas, translated by Li Yingdong. It asks how the Marxist tradition of imperialism theory can explain the two main contemporary accumulation regimes: Anglo-American neoliberalism and German-Austrian ordoliberalism. Fouskas argues that both are domestic public policies that are also imperialist projects. Each seeks to remake the internal social order of other states, and both are authoritarian in core.

The article first surveys the theoretical lineage. It starts with Marx's accumulation theory and British imperial expansion, then covers Luxemburg, Hilferding, Bukharin and Lenin on the monopoly stage before 1914. Next come the post-1945 American school (Baran, Sweezy, Magdoff, Frank, Wallerstein) and Mandel and Poulantzas. It ends with Arrighi, Harvey, Gowan, Callinicos, Panitch and others on financialisation, globalisation and US imperialism. A final section applies the framework to the eurozone crisis.

Fouskas's central move is to treat the core–periphery divide as analytical, not just descriptive, and to combine it with Baran and Sweezy's concept of surplus. Following Gowan, he describes neoliberalism as emerging after the collapse of Bretton Woods in 1971. In this account it rests on a "Dollar–Wall Street regime" and a hub-and-spoke power structure, with NATO tying Europe to the United States. He then argues that ordoliberalism is a German imperialist project in Europe. Its instruments are the Maastricht criteria, central bank independence, depoliticised economic rules and a currency union that denies peripheral members devaluation. On this reading Germany extracts surplus from the periphery, and Fouskas cites the European Central Bank's reported €7.8 billion profit on Greek bonds as an illustration. He adds that the eurozone crisis originated in Anglo-American financialisation, and that austerity has not delivered sustainable growth.

Fouskas concludes that imperialism exports not only capital but also models of economic management and sociopolitical order, with open-door policies as its preferred tool. He holds that ordoliberalism lacks military capacity and a global reach, so European security remains under NATO and thus US control. Both projects are incompatible with democracy, and authoritarianism forms at home before spreading abroad. Read the original if you want a survey of Western Marxist imperialism theory that is directly applied to the eurozone, German hegemony and Greece.
quoteEn: Imperialism is not merely the export of capital, but also the export of capital management and of specific socio-economic and political models.
quoteZh: 帝国主义不仅仅是资本的输出，还是资本管理与具体社会经济和政治模式的输出。

t: Nancy Fraser's new theory of capitalist crisis
zh: 南希·弗雷泽的资本主义危机新论
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2019 no. 10
paras: Chen Liangbin examines Nancy Fraser's account of capitalist crisis in Capitalism: A Conversation in Critical Theory (2018), co-authored with Rahel Jaeggi. Writing against the background of the 2007 financial crisis, Brexit, the gilets jaunes and the populist revolt of 2016, Chen argues that Fraser rebuilds Marx's method into a "foreground–background" model. In this model the roots of crisis lie in structural splits between the economy and its non-economic conditions. Chen judges the result a stimulating but logically incomplete theory.

The article has three parts. The first sets out Fraser and Jaeggi's four defining features of capitalism and the foreground–background method drawn from Capital. The second follows the history of crisis through four regimes (mercantile, liberal-colonial, state-managed and financialised capitalism) along three background dimensions: social reproduction, nature and politics. The third places the theory within Fraser's own development, within critical theory and among theories of crisis, and ends with critical questions.

Chen reports that Fraser reads Capital as moving from exchange to exploitation and then to expropriation, the open confiscation of labour, land, resources and bodily capacities. She treats expropriation as the more basic condition of accumulation, and as a continuing process that also underlies racial and status divisions. Capitalism is thus a "institutionalized social order" whose separations (exploitation/expropriation, production/reproduction, human/nature, economy/politics) generate crises that economic accounts neglect. Chen links Fraser's shift from the earlier redistribution–recognition framework to this model to feminism's turn from identity politics towards structural critique, and to worries about populism. He or she finds Fraser closer to Harvey's accumulation by dispossession than to Marx's surplus-value theory of crisis.

Chen concludes that Fraser belongs to a "de-orthodoxising" neo-Marxist current that seeks crisis causes outside the economy, as Lefebvre, Harvey, O'Connor, Foster and Baudrillard do. Chen credits its integrative breadth and its revival of political economy within critical theory. Chen also questions why only reproduction, nature and politics are chosen, how they relate logically, and whether foreground and background form a descriptive or an analytical distinction. Jaeggi raised similar doubts in the dialogue. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Fraser's late work and its place among Western Marxist crisis theories.
quoteEn: Fraser's \"foreground–background\" thinking seems to place greater weight on the importance of the \"background\".
quoteZh: 但是弗雷泽的“前景—背景”思维似乎更为看重“背景”的重要性

t: Exchange abstraction and its Gestalt-transformation logic: on Sohn-Rethel's reconstruction of Western historical epistemology
zh: 交换抽象及其格式塔转换逻辑——论雷特尔对西方历史认识论的重构
paras: Commodity exchange, the authors say, is the core problem of Marx's Capital and still holds unfinished philosophical questions, such as the analysis of commodity fetishism. They examine the German philosopher Alfred Sohn-Rethel (1899–1990) and the concept of "exchange abstraction" in his late book Intellectual and Manual Labour: A Critique of Epistemology. The article argues that Sohn-Rethel traces exchange abstraction back to Kant's transcendental philosophy and the origins of Western epistemology, which makes commodity exchange a central philosophical issue.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the meaning and features of exchange abstraction, which the authors treat as formal and as real. The second shows how exchange abstraction underlies "thought abstraction", with Kant's synthetic a priori judgement as the main foil. The third analyses three dimensions of exchange abstraction and the Gestalt transformation by which it passes into thought. The authors draw on Habermas, Žižek, Adorno and the Chinese scholar Zhang Yibing.

The authors report that Sohn-Rethel treats Marx's "commodity abstraction" as exchange abstraction, not labour abstraction. Labour does not abstract itself. Exchange relations abstract labour, and reduce it to a purely quantitative magnitude of value. This abstraction is "real", arising in action and not in thought, and so differs in kind from the thought abstraction of natural science, though it resembles it in form. The three dimensions are the suspension of use, the stripping away of sensuous qualities, and the Gestalt transformation, a social synthesis that works unconsciously, behind the actors' backs. In this account Greek coinage gave rise to concepts such as Parmenides' "One". Capitalist money-as-capital then supplies the unity that Kant attributes to a transcendental subject. The authors compare the logic to Lacan's "object a" as read by Žižek.

The authors conclude that Sohn-Rethel founds Kant's idealist epistemology on the materialist basis of exchange abstraction. They argue that this enriches the epistemology of historical materialism and addresses Habermas's complaint that Marx never assembled a materialist epistemology, though they do not fully agree with that complaint. They describe his analysis of the commodity form as the deepest and most detailed to date, and say its theoretical and practical significance is self-evident. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Sohn-Rethel that links Marx's commodity analysis, Kant and Žižek's psychoanalytic reading, and shows how Sohn-Rethel is received in China.
quoteEn: Sohn-Rethel's analysis of exchange abstraction, especially from the angle of Western historical epistemology, has indeed enriched the epistemology of Marxist historical materialism.
quoteZh: 雷特尔对有关交换抽象的分析,特别是他从西方历史认识论角度的分析,的确丰富了马克思主义的历史唯物主义的认识论

t: György Márkus on the four forms of Marx's critical theory
zh: 乔治·马尔库什论马克思批判理论的四种形式
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2020 no. 1
paras: Yan Yan takes up the long dispute over whether Marx's thought is marked by a break or by continuity between the early and mature works. The article examines how the Budapest School theorist György Márkus (Georg Markus) answers it by distinguishing four forms of Marx's critical theory and dividing Marx's development into stages. Yan argues that Márkus's scheme helps explain both the unity and the heterogeneity of Marx's thinking, but that Márkus misreads Marx at several points.

The article opens with the two versions of the "break" thesis, the Soviet account of the 1930s and Althusser's "epistemological break", and with the "continuity" thesis that arose against them. It then follows Márkus's stages in turn. These are the philosophical critique of political economy in the 1844 Manuscripts, a philosophically oriented critical economics in 1846–47, and a critique of capitalist political economy with a historical grounding in the Grundrisse and Capital. Yan interleaves Márkus's reading with his own corrections, drawing on Lukács, Kolakowski, Heller, Moishe Postone and Chinese scholars such as Zhang Yibing and Sun Leqiang.

Yan accepts Márkus's point that the 1844 Manuscripts contain a tension between a realist philosophy of human finitude and a utopian practical orientation. Yan adds that two logics coexist there: a dominant humanist logic of alienated labour and an objective materialist logic from which historical materialism grew. Yan also endorses the claim that Marx's attitude to classical political economy moved from near-total rejection, through qualified acceptance, to critical inheritance. The central dispute is over the Grundrisse and Capital. Márkus holds that they belong to different critical forms, and that Capital stresses continuity between capitalism and socialism and slides into Hegelian teleology. Yan replies that both texts combine subject and object dimensions, differing only in emphasis. In Yan's reading the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete does not oppose the essence-to-appearance method. Capital is anti-metaphysical, and Marx's necessity is historical rather than absolute.

Yan concludes that Márkus's periodisation is a valuable reference for tracing the logic of Marx's development. Two merits are singled out: it treats early and late Marx as a whole through both philosophical and economic discourse, and it criticises both the break and the continuity theses. Yan warns that Márkus exaggerates the gap between the Grundrisse and Capital, and misreads Marx on form and content and on the realm of necessity. Read the original if you study Marx's intellectual development, the Budapest School or the philosophical interpretation of the Grundrisse and Capital, and want a Chinese scholar's critical assessment of Márkus.
quoteEn: Only by holding to the unity of continuity and discontinuity can one grasp the real course and theoretical logic of the development of Marx's thought.
quoteZh: 只有坚持连续性和非连续性的统一，才能把握马克思思想发展的真实进程和理论逻辑。

t: Foreign communist and workers' parties on capitalist culture: critique and response
zh: 国外共产党和工人党对资本主义文化的批判与应对
paras: Opening with Xi Jinping's 2016 call for cultural confidence, Yu and Gao ask how communist and workers' parties outside China understand and respond to contemporary capitalist culture. They argue that these parties see the basic contradictions of capitalism as unchanged and see the bourgeoisie as pursuing cultural hegemony through ever more concealed means. Studying their views, the authors contend, deepens understanding of the features and harms of capitalist culture and strengthens confidence in the culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article draws on party programmes and constitutions, statements at the International Meetings of Communist and Workers' Parties (Sao Paulo 2008, Beirut 2012, Istanbul 2015) and Chinese secondary studies. It has three parts: new features of capitalist culture as the parties describe them; the role of culture in capitalism's domestic rule and external expansion; and the parties' countermeasures. Cited parties include those of Australia, Italy (Rifondazione Comunista), Pakistan, Guyana, the United States, Germany, India (Marxist), Greece, Portugal and Brazil.

Yu and Gao report that the parties identify four features: monopoly over mass media, intellectuals who lose their critical function and serve the bourgeoisie, commodified culture and consumerism, and discrimination and xenophobia. The parties are said to hold that culture is used to manufacture legitimacy at home through a "single thought", anti-communist campaigns and distorted accounts of the 2008 financial crisis. Abroad, they say, it is used to back extremist forces, stir ethnic and racial division, and promote "human rights above sovereignty" as cover for intervention. The parties' responses fall into three groups: strengthening ideological and political work (Marxist propaganda, party media and new media, party schools), adopting cultural policies that protect cultural identity and heritage and encourage exchange, and building public cultural institutions and independent media to resist ideological erosion.

The authors conclude that, after the Soviet collapse and the long ebb of the socialist movement, capitalist states led by the United States have besieged socialism and communist parties ideologically. They hold that the foreign parties' Marxist critique forms an important part of the Marxist theory of contemporary capitalist culture. Recognising the features and harms of capitalist culture is presented as necessary for resisting the infiltration of Western "universal values" such as democracy, freedom and human rights. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how foreign communist parties frame cultural struggle, with many citations to their programmes and international statements.
quoteEn: Foreign communist and workers' parties have recognised that the bourgeoisie and its governments have never given up the practice of pursuing cultural hegemony.
quoteZh: 国外共产党和工人党认识到,资产阶级及其政府从来没有放弃过推行文化霸权的做法

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping stressed in 2016, describing confidence in China's traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture. It is presented as a more basic and enduring force than confidence in the path, theory and system.
The official name for China's current political and economic system and its guiding theory, associated with reform and opening up.

glossary.zh: 共产党和工人党国际会议
glossary.en: International Meetings of Communist and Workers' Parties
glossary.explanation: Annual gatherings of communist and workers' parties from many countries, held since 1998. Their final statements are among the article's main sources.

t: The threefold critique of the contemporary Russian critical school of Marxism for reviving socialism
zh: 当代俄罗斯马克思主义批判学派复兴社会主义的三重批判
source: Journal of Soochow University (Philosophy & Social Science Edition), 2019 no. 3
paras: Chen Hong introduces the contemporary Russian critical school of Marxism, a post-Soviet current that works without institutional or state support after 1991. The article asks how this school builds its case for reviving socialism and argues that the case rests on three critiques: of the sidelining of dialectics, of Soviet socialism, and of late capitalism. Each critique supplies, in turn, a methodological basis, a historical lesson and a realistic ground for a 'new socialism' distinct from that of the twentieth century.

The article names Aleksandr Buzgalin, founder of the school and editor of the left-wing journals Alternatives and Problems of Political Economy, as its central figure. It also names Andrei Kolganov, Lyudmila Bulavka and Georgy Lobastov as core representatives. It is organised in three sections, one per critique, and ends with an overall assessment of the school and its self-descriptions as 'critical', 'innovative' and 'post-industrial' Marxism. Sources include Buzgalin and Kolganov's Global Capital and Ten Myths about the USSR, together with interviews with Buzgalin and Bulavka.

In the first section, Buzgalin and Kolganov explain why dialectics is shelved: positivist research favours narrow empirical questions, 'expert' society serves global capital, and spiritual alienation encourages rejection of grand narratives. Against this they defend ascent from the abstract to the concrete and the unity of the logical and the historical as dialectics' first and second principles. In the second, the school's reappraisal of the October Revolution, the first five-year plan, collectivisation and Soviet culture treats the USSR as a first large-scale attempt to move beyond capitalism. In Buzgalin's formula it was a bureaucratically 'mutated' socialism. The lessons the school draws are to use market and capitalist elements only under broad supervision, not to make wealth the goal, and to keep officials accountable to the people. Chen faults the school for treating the market economy as exclusively capitalist, and contends that socialism with Chinese characteristics has already shown socialism can combine with markets. The third critique describes late capitalism as global capital hegemony. Its internal contradiction is that it must absorb communist elements yet fears them, and its external one is the centre–periphery divide.

Chen concludes that the three critiques converge on reviving socialism understood as a non-linear transition from the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom. In this account socialism must end all forms of alienation and not only exploitation and private ownership, and it must free human creativity. Chen presents the school as a creative, non-dogmatic Marxism that responds to a changed 'post-industrial' era, and cites Xi Jinping on the value of foreign Marxist critiques of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of Buzgalin's school and its view of the Soviet legacy, or if you want to see how such Russian work is assessed from within Chinese Marxist scholarship.
quoteEn: This school is not simply a Marxist school but a critical Marxist school.
quoteZh: 该学派不是简单的马克思主义的学派, 而是批判的马克思主义学派。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up. The article invokes it to argue that socialism can be combined with a market economy.

t: Ontology and ethics: basic problems in the political philosophy of the Western radical left
zh: 存在论与伦理学——西方激进左翼政治哲学理论的基础问题
paras: Yin Shuguang takes up the "ontological turn" in Western radical left political philosophy. The question is whether political practice and a future community can be grounded in ontology, and whether ethics can be built directly into it. Yin argues that the turn rightly renews critical theory, but that it leaves three problems unresolved. These are the limits of general ontology for practice, the impossibility of expelling metaphysics, and the difficulty of embedding ethical concepts in ontology. The article first appeared in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2019, no. 5).

The article opens with a survey of Badiou, Meillassoux, Deleuze, Agamben, Rancière, Negri, Mouffe, Italian hermeneutic Marxism, Žižek, Harvey, Soja, Nancy and Esposito. It then looks at the history of the relation between being and ethics, from Heraclitus, Plato and Aristotle through Christian theology, Kant, Hegel, Heidegger and Gadamer. A long section follows on Heidegger's later thought on Seyn and Ereignis, and on Derrida's différance. The final section turns to practical philosophy, covering Lukács's social ontology, Habermas and discourse theory, and Marx's concept of practice.

Yin's central claim is that rejecting metaphysics does not remove the underlying question of being, which is how things appear and take form. In Yin's reading, Rancière, Deleuze, Agamben, Badiou and Žižek all still address this question of manifestation, even when they reject substance ontology. Yin treats Derrida's différance as an effort to unsettle being as presence that nonetheless stays inside the metaphysical questioning. Yin also contends that general ontological categories supply only formal ethical concepts, without the dialectical historical content of good, evil and freedom. The article sets this against proceduralism and political liberalism (Habermas, Rawls), which it says avoid philosophy and so leave real disputes untouched.

Yin concludes that developing a practical materialist philosophy remains an important theoretical task. Yin reads Marx's concept of practice as extending Aristotle's, uniting labour, critique, revolutionary action and free creative activity, and uniting freedom with necessity. Against a scientistic reading of Marx, Yin argues that the will to resist capitalism, and the critique of fetishism and of abstract formal equality, require a philosophical anthropology. Communism, on this view, is a new ethical form of defining what humans are. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of post-structuralist and radical left ontology, with extended treatment of Heidegger, Derrida and Aristotle.
quoteEn: Therefore, the main problem of contemporary philosophy is the problem of "emergence, manifestation, being-there".
quoteZh: 因此, 当代哲学的主要问题是“出现、显现、有”的问题。

t: Critique and reconstruction of the structure of needs
st: Agnes Heller's reading of Marx's theory of needs
zh: 需要结构的批判与重建
zhSub: 赫勒对马克思需要理论的解读
paras: Yan Yan takes up Agnes Heller's early work The Theory of Need in Marx to ask what Marx's theory of needs can contribute to understanding the shift in China's principal contradiction. Writing in 2020, Yan notes that this contradiction is now framed as one between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. The article argues that Heller's reading helps move attention from the quantity of needs to their quality, and clarifies what "a better life" and equality should mean.

The article has two main parts and a short conclusion. The first reconstructs Heller's critique of the alienated structure of needs under capitalism, in four aspects: the inversion of means and ends, the inversion of quality and quantity, the impoverishment of needs, and the rise of private interest as the dominant social logic. The second sets out, following Heller, the structure of needs in the society of associated producers, drawing on Marx's Grundrisse, Capital, Critique of the Gotha Programme and Theories of Surplus Value. The conclusion draws three lessons for China.

In Yan's account of Heller, capitalism produces ever more needs but subordinates them to capital's self-expansion, so that quantity overwhelms quality and people become one-sided. On this reading, workers rebel not because they are materially poor but because their rich qualitative needs go unmet. Heller also finds two different conceptions of labour in Marx: in the Grundrisse, labour becomes a primary life need, while in Capital it stays within the realm of necessity and survives as a social duty. In the associated-producers society, material needs fall to a secondary place, free time and individual capacities come to the fore, and Marx's rejection of egalitarianism follows from his refusal to turn qualitatively different needs into equal quantities.

Yan concludes that China must combine the development of productive forces with attention to the diversity of people's needs, which include political, cultural, social and ecological needs. In Yan's view China stands at the start of the first stage of communism, so distribution according to labour and the law of value still apply. Equality should mean giving equal attention to each person's different needs, not equal amounts of wealth. Yan sees the Party's reformulation of the principal contradiction at the 19th Party Congress (2017) as reflecting this transformation in the structure of needs. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's use of Heller's Marxism to interpret Marx's theory of needs and to bear on current debates about the principal contradiction and equality.)
quoteEn: Heller holds that Marx not only criticised the structure of needs of capitalist society but also put forward an entirely new structure of needs founded on the society of associated producers.
quoteZh: 赫勒认为马克思不仅批判了资本主义社会的需要结构，还提出了一种建立在联合生产者社会基础上的全新的需要结构。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official formulation of the main tension in Chinese society. The 19th Party Congress (2017) redefined it as one between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development.
Marx's term for the higher stage of communist society, free of alienation and compulsory division of labour.
The principle of the first stage of communism in Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, and in official Chinese doctrine the distribution principle suited to the socialist stage.

t: A renewed reflection on Hardt and Negri's Empire twenty years on
st: A defence of Luxemburg's theory of imperialism
zh: 二十年后对哈特和奈格里的《帝国》再反思
zhSub: 为卢森堡的帝国主义理论作一次辩护
paras: Zhang Xiaolong asks how Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's Empire (2000) relates to Rosa Luxemburg's theory of imperialism. Zhang notes that Chinese scholarship has moved from translating Hardt and Negri to interpreting and criticising their system, but has mostly ignored their critique of Luxemburg. The article argues that Hardt and Negri misread Luxemburg, and that her theory remains valid for understanding contemporary capitalism.
