The article has three parts. The first sets out what Hardt and Negri mean by Empire: a mode of state rule, a supreme power over the globalised world, and a constructed political order that supposedly succeeds the age of imperialism. The second answers three charges Hardt and Negri bring against Luxemburg. The third draws out the present-day value of her theory, setting her against Karl Kautsky, Lenin and Eduard Bernstein.

Zhang argues that Hardt and Negri rely too heavily on politics and neglect capitalism's internal contradictions, the very thing Zhang takes to be fundamental to Marx. On the three charges, Zhang replies that Luxemburg developed Marxism rather than departing from it, since she answered the changed conditions of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Zhang also holds that her work was political economy and not only political critique, citing her writings on Poland's industrial development, her polemic with Bernstein and The Accumulation of Capital. Finally, Zhang denies that her critique was merely external: she began from the stagnation inside capitalist production and so derived imperialism from capitalism's own economic structure. In Zhang's account she differs from Kautsky, who treated imperialism as a contingent policy, and from Lenin, who in Zhang's reading saw it as a by-product and not an inner necessity.

Zhang concludes that Luxemburg's theory is still an important means of analysing capitalism's present form, though Zhang concedes she overlooked the revolutionary potential of the wider masses and was less penetrating than Marx. Zhang says criticism of Hardt and Negri in China has often only spread their ideas, and urges that Luxemburg's theoretical contribution be put forward in response. Zhang also calls for Marxist theory to be used against Western claims that Marxism is outdated and that Lenin's and Luxemburg's theories of imperialism have been superseded. Read the original if you study Luxemburg, Hardt and Negri, or the Chinese reception of Western Marxist debates on imperialism.
quoteEn: Luxemburg's critique of imperialism is an internal critique.
quoteZh: 卢森堡对帝国主义的批判是一种内在批判。

t: From the ontology of the event to the phenomenology of the event
st: Badiou's philosophy of the event between Being and Event and Logics of Worlds
zh: 从事件本体论到事件现象学
zhSub: 巴迪欧的《存在与事件》和《世界的逻辑》之间的事件哲学
paras: Alain Badiou published Being and Event in 1988 and Logics of Worlds in 2006, the latter subtitled "Being and Event 2". Lan asks why Badiou chose that subtitle and how the two books relate. The article argues that Badiou's philosophy moves from an ontology of the event, built on mathematics at the level of pure multiplicity, to a phenomenology of the event at the level of appearing, and that the later book also makes the definition of the event stricter.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the ontology of Being and Event, starting from Badiou's reading of Pascal's miracles and the distinction between presentation and representation. The second turns to Logics of Worlds and the concepts of transcendental, identity function and existence function, using Badiou's own illustrations. The third covers Badiou's classification of changes and his account of how events become lasting, drawing on Sartre's bus-queue example and the Spartacus uprising. Lan also supplies notes on terms such as mathème and "generic".

In the first book, Lan explains, Badiou holds that "the One" is the result of a counting-as-one operation, and he sorts multiples into normal, singular and excrescent terms. Events can occur only at an "evental site", a singular term that is presented but not represented. In the second book, a world's transcendental measures how strongly objects appear, and an "inexistent" is an object whose existence value is at its minimum, as with Inuit and Amerindians in Quebec elections of 1918–1950. Badiou now separates four kinds of change: modification, fact, weak singularity and strong singularity (the event). Only a strong singularity keeps maximal intensity in its consequences.

Lan concludes that what matters for Badiou is the operation after the event: naming it, and building a body, such as Spartacus's detachment, whose militants are faithful to it. This produces the triad of event, name and body, which Lan relates to Lacan's Real, Symbolic and Imaginary. It also underlies Badiou's reply to "democratic materialism", with the slogan that there are only bodies and languages, "except that there are truths". Badiou's truths are plural procedures, not a Hegelian totality. Read the original if you want a close guide to the shift between Badiou's two major works, including his formal vocabulary and his emphasis on organisation and the vanguard.
quoteEn: For Badiou, what matters is not the occurrence of some rupturing event, but the operations that follow the event.
quoteZh: 对于巴迪欧来说,重要的不是某个断裂性事件的发生,而是事件之后的操作。

t: Marx and Marxism in the eyes of Vietnamese theorists
zh: 越南理论家视阈中的马克思和马克思主义
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2019 no. 3
paras: This review surveys how Vietnamese theorists approached Marx and Marxism around the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth in 2018. It aims to inform Chinese readers about the current state of Marxist research in Vietnam. The authors present the Vietnamese material as an example of Marxism's enduring vitality and as a vantage point on it.

The sources are the papers from the international conference held in Hanoi on 4 May 2018 at the Ho Chi Minh National Academy of Politics, together with 2018 articles in the Vietnamese Communist Party's journal Communism and the Party school's Political Theory. Contributors include senior Party leaders, scholars of the Academy and the Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences, and retired officials. The review is organised by theme: Marx's theoretical value; upholding and innovating Marxism; the transition period; political economy; Party, state and democracy; class struggle; and culture and human emancipation.

Pan and Zhou report that the Vietnamese authors treat Marx as a scientific and revolutionary thinker whose predictions about capitalism, including its crises, were borne out, and whose surplus-value theory is not outdated. They also report that Vietnamese theorists insist on applying Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought creatively. They describe warnings against dogmatism and against hostile ideas, such as claims that Marxism is foreign to Vietnam or that democratic socialism should replace Party leadership. Marx's theory of the transition period is presented as the key to Vietnam's path, which bypasses capitalism but uses its favourable elements. Vietnamese scholars also use Marx on ownership, distribution, alienation, the rule-of-law socialist state, democracy and human rights to justify a socialist-oriented market economy, multiple forms of ownership and the Party's "self-renewal".

The review concludes that Vietnamese theorists see Marxism as a living guide to Vietnam's renewal, and stress adherence to it together with adaptation to national conditions. It also notes that some of them call for further study of questions such as the withering away of the state. Read the original if you want a detailed overview of how Vietnamese Party-aligned scholars framed Marx in 2018, and which themes and sources they drew on.
quoteEn: Upholding and innovating Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought are two sides of one question: one must both uphold and innovate, otherwise one will fall into dogmatism, mechanism or opportunism.
quoteZh: 坚持与创新马列主义、胡志明思想,是同一个问题的两个方面:既要坚持,又要创新,否则就会犯教条主义、机械主义或者机会主义的错误。

t: The decline of the urban middle class in the West against the background of polarisation
zh: 两极分化背景下西方城市中间阶级的衰落
paras: Song Lidan asks whether contemporary Western society is an 'olive-shaped' middle-class society in which class opposition has disappeared, or whether it instead confirms Marx's claim that capitalist society splits into two directly opposed classes. The article argues for the second reading: the urban middle class is declining, polarising and becoming dependent on big capital, while most people have become wage earners.

The article first separates the Marxist concept of the middle class, meaning petty-bourgeois owners who work largely by their own labour, from the much wider 'middle class' of Western sociology. It confines itself to the urban middle class and divides it into non-exploiting groups (the self-employed, independent professionals) and lightly exploiting ones (micro-business owners, lower and middle managers). Evidence is drawn from the United States, the European Union, Britain, West Germany, Japan and Greece, with theoretical support from Marx, Engels, Hilferding, Braverman, Reich and William Robinson.

Song makes three main moves. First, citing statistics such as the high exit rates and low incomes of the self-employed in Britain and the EU, the author holds that non-exploiting groups are becoming proletarianised and impoverished, squeezed by monopoly-led globalisation and by unemployed workers entering petty trade. Second, micro-enterprises are said to survive only as appendages of large firms, as franchisees, subcontractors and low-cost 'flexible' units, while managers and professionals are pushed towards precarious temporary work by technology and AI. Third, the post-war alliance between big capital and the middle class, built on anti-monopoly laws, small-business agencies and subsidies, is described as a 'interest-inducing' political structure that kept workers from allying with the middle class. Song argues that this structure rested on colonial and neo-colonial gains and a favourable post-war environment, and is now eroding under neoliberalism, with Japan as the main case.

Song concludes that the gap between middle class and proletariat is narrowing and that the West remains a society of a rich minority and a wage-earning majority. The author treats movements such as Occupy Wall Street, the Yellow Vests and 'populism' as signs of this polarisation. Technological progress and globalisation are presented as harmful only under capitalism, and the middle class's decline is read as a foretoken of the eventual disappearance of classes. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist statistical and theoretical case against the 'middle-class society' thesis, with Japanese and European examples.
quoteEn: In sum, the middle class is a class tied to private ownership, a class that will be eliminated as society develops, and the law of capital accumulation is creating the conditions for its elimination.
quoteZh: 总之, 中间阶级是与私有制相联系的阶级, 是随着社会的发展将被消灭的阶级, 资本积累的规律正在创造消灭这个阶级的条件。

glossary.explanation: In the article's Marxist usage, the petty bourgeoisie: owners with some means of production who work mainly by their own or family labour. It is distinguished from the broad 'middle class' (中产阶级) of Western sociology.
The process by which small owners lose their independent means of livelihood and become wage labourers.

A term the article takes from the Japanese scholar Watanabe Masao. It describes a system in which big capital wins the middle class's loyalty through laws, institutions and subsidies, so that workers cannot ally with it.

t: Production "acceleration": Marx and the theoretical links to the critique of left accelerationism
zh: 生产“加速”：马克思与左翼加速主义批判的理论关涉
paras: Ma Xi and Liu Qinmin ask how left accelerationism, associated with Nick Srnicek and Alex Williams, relates to Marx. They note that Chinese scholarship has traced its roots to Deleuze and Guattari, or to social-time theory, and has paid little attention to its link with Marx as founder of social critical theory. The authors argue that Marx laid the foundation for a critique of capitalist acceleration, and that left accelerationism loses its critical edge if it abandons that foundation.

The article has four parts. It first reads the 2013 Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics and Srnicek and Williams's Inventing the Future (2015) to establish what left accelerationism claims. It then traces Marx's treatment of speed through the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology, the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital. A third section asks in what sense Marx is the founder of this critique, and a short conclusion follows.

In the authors' reading, Srnicek and Williams hold that capital has shifted from extracting absolute surplus time to disciplining the pace of life itself under post-Fordism, so that work and life merge in a "social factory". Left accelerationism, they say, criticises neoliberalism from within and aims to use capitalism's technologies to go beyond its value form. The authors find in Marx a double critique: private ownership of the means of production reduces human "life speed" to the speed of material production, while machine rhythms dominate the worker's natural time. Marx, they argue, ties this to the critique of private ownership rather than to ethics alone, and he anticipated the intensification of labour that later capitalism would produce.

The authors conclude that left accelerationism's origin lies in Marx's critique of political economy, though they stress this is a return in the logic of intellectual history, not its actual source. They say accelerationists claim to have gone beyond Marx. Without Marxist guidance, the authors warn, the school would lose its theoretical roots, become a phenomenology that explains capitalism without challenging it, and risk complicity with it. They call for re-examining current foreign accelerationist claims in light of Marx, while granting that the school offers real insight into new features of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist attempt to trace accelerationism back to Marx's texts on machinery, speed and labour time.
quoteEn: If left accelerationism throws itself wholly into the arms of postmodern theory and gradually loses the guidance of Marxism, it will lose its theoretical roots and its critical edge, and become a phenomenology of capitalism that evades reality.
quoteZh: 如果左翼加速主义一味投入后现代理论的怀抱，而逐渐失去马克思主义的指导，就会失去理论根基，失去批判锋芒，沦为一种逃避现实的资本主义解释现象学。

t: Anthropocene imperialism as the extinction phase of twenty-first-century capitalism
st: A review of Foster's latest critique of imperialism
zh: 人类世帝国主义是21世纪资本主义的灭绝阶段
zhSub: 福斯特对帝国主义的最新批判述评
paras: This is a critical review, published in World Socialism Studies in 2019, of 'Imperialism in the Anthropocene' by John Bellamy Foster, Hannah Holleman and Brett Clark (Monthly Review, July–August 2019). Niu Tiansheng presents the original as a deepening of Foster's ecological critique of capitalism. In Niu's account, the essay borrows the geological notion of the Anthropocene to show that the planetary crisis is rooted in imperialism and global capitalism, not in humanity in general.

The review follows the original's four-part structure. It first sets out what the Anthropocene is, citing the 2019 vote of the Anthropocene Working Group and the 'Great Acceleration' after the mid-twentieth century. It then lists the practices of 'Anthropocene imperialism': imperialist rent, material footprints, ocean grabbing and appropriation of the atmospheric commons. Next it covers US strategy on fossil fuels and water, and finally the way out of the crisis. Niu closes with a short assessment of the essay's strengths and limits.

Niu reports three main moves. First, the authors extend Samir Amin's concept of imperialist rent: the transfer of use-values and natural resources from the periphery to the core is treated as ecological imperialism, which leaves poor countries with the ecological costs. Second, the authors argue that Washington, while acknowledging climate change, responds with an 'energy dominance' strategy. This strategy includes pipeline expansion, fossil-fuel exports and a 'militarisation of energy policy'. It also includes a 'hydro-diplomacy' aimed at controlling water and countering China. Third, the authors conclude that imperialism is an organised reactionary force against ecological revolution, so that twenty-first-century imperialism is 'the exterminist phase of capitalism'. Any serious response, they say, must therefore criticise capitalism and imperialism together.

On the way out, Niu reports that the authors propose a 'species consciousness' and an 'extinction rebellion' movement. The authors also call for an anti-imperialist revolution joined to an ecological one, summed up in the line that the poor will inherit the earth or there will be no earth to inherit. Niu praises the essay's clear logic and its continuity with classical Marxist class analysis and colonial critique. Niu also faults it for resting on contingent, scientifically unargued proposals, for lacking an analysis of the agents of social change or a feasible path to overthrowing imperialism's economic base and superstructure, and for amounting to a 'politics of hope'. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's summary and assessment of Foster's 2019 ecological theory of imperialism and its reception in Chinese Marxist circles.
quoteEn: Foster and his co-authors' critique of and reflection on Anthropocene imperialism carries on the consistent class analysis, critical spirit and colonial discourse of traditional Marxism.
quoteZh: 福斯特等人对人类世的帝国主义的批判与反思,秉承传统马克思主义一贯的阶级分析、批判精神和殖民论述

t: Development trends of foreign Marxist currents in the twenty-first century and an assessment of their effects
zh: 21世纪国外马克思主义思潮的发展趋势及其效应评估
paras: Writing in 2019, Zhang Liang and Sun Leqiang ask how Chinese scholars should approach the development of Marxism outside China since 2000. They argue that China's researchers are no longer followers of foreign Marxism but its contemporaries. On this view, they should no longer rely on ready-made Western scholarship, and should instead judge foreign currents independently, from the standpoint of socialism with Chinese characteristics, taking from them selectively.

The article surveys Western left thought since the Soviet and East European collapse in three parts. The first examines how foreign Marxism treats Marxist basic theory: new textual scholarship and four research routes. The second takes four theoretical growth points: ecological Marxism, spatial theory, identity politics and biopolitics. The third looks at four areas of research on current capitalism: production, crisis, class structure and democracy.

The authors' central claim is that foreign Marxism offers sharp diagnoses of capitalism but weak or evasive alternatives. They criticise the MEGA2-era editorial approach as deconstructive, saying it revives an opposition between Marx and Engels. They sort the four routes into rereading Marx, localisation, grafting onto 'post-' theories, and wholesale rejection of Marxism. They find that spatial theory, identity politics and biopolitics drift into romanticism or utopianism, or fail to touch capitalism's economic roots. On class, they reject the 'middle stratum', 'cognitive class' and 'multitude' concepts as eclectic. Citing Marx and Engels on mental labourers, they hold that anyone who sells labour-power and produces surplus value belongs to the working class. They credit left writers who return to Capital for crisis analysis, but say these writers leave the basic contradiction between productive forces and capitalist relations of production untouched.

In conclusion, the authors credit foreign Marxism with useful lessons for editing classic texts, studying the classics, localising Marxism and understanding capitalism's structural contradictions. They add that it must be treated critically, given its deconstructive tendencies and its Eurocentric and neoliberal assumptions. They call on Chinese Marxists to strengthen a Chinese standpoint and a sense of historical position, and to move from Chinese experience to Chinese theory in order to innovate twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western Marxist trends since 2000, and of the stance Chinese scholars are urged to take toward them.
quoteEn: We are not its followers but its contemporaries.
quoteZh: 我们不是它的追随者,而是它的同时代人。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path and system of socialism since reform and opening up. The article uses it as the standpoint from which foreign theories should be assessed.
The official name for China's path and system of socialism since reform and opening up. The article uses it as the standpoint from which foreign theories should be assessed.
The tradition begun by Lukács and others, which the article says fragmented after the 1970s.
The view, which the authors reject, that Engels distorted or diverged from Marx's thought, including in his editing of Capital.

t: Policy trends and future prospects of the Communist Party of Nepal government
zh: 尼泊尔共产党政府的政策趋向及未来前景
paras: Writing in 2019, Yuan Qun and Wang Enming ask what the government led by the unified Communist Party of Nepal (NCP) is trying to do, and whether it can last. The article takes up the left alliance that won the 2017 elections and took office in February 2018. In May 2018 its two parties, the CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the CPN (Maoist Centre), merged into the NCP. The authors argue that the NCP is now Nepal's strongest party and its government the most stable since multiparty politics was restored in 1990. They also hold that its policies are producing early results and that it has good prospects of serving a full term.

The article has three parts. The first assesses the significance of the merger: the new party's leadership structure and seat counts, the stability of the government, and the effect on the international communist movement. The second reviews policy in four areas: perfecting the political system, transforming the economic structure, investing in people's livelihood, and bilateral and multilateral diplomacy. The third looks ahead at party integration, economic growth and India's likely efforts to increase its influence. It draws mainly on Nepali government documents, Nepali and Indian press reports and UN data.

The authors' central argument is that parliamentary dominance has ended the frequent changes of government they identify as the main cause of Nepal's economic and social lag. They cite 441 central committee members, with 241 from the former UML and 200 from the Maoist Centre. They also cite 174 of 275 lower-house seats, and 190 once the Federal Socialist Forum joined, above two-thirds. On policy, they report anti-corruption cases, new roads, bridges and hydropower, health insurance in 36 districts and new technical schools. They report projected growth of 6.81% for 2018–19, below the 8% target, and a shift in the sectoral shares of GDP.

The authors conclude that the main threat to the government is not the opposition Nepali Congress but whether the NCP can fully integrate its two ideological and organisational traditions. They note that posts have been shared roughly 6:4 and that debate continues on merging the two parties' theories of democracy. They expect India to try to regain influence, and expect Nepal to balance it by deepening ties with China. They say the NCP has already broken the 'curse' of earlier communist governments lasting under a year, and that its ability to govern long-term deserves close attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the NCP's first year in government, with Nepali sources and figures.
quoteEn: The establishment of the NCP government has inspired the international communist movement, boosted the confidence and resolve of communist parties and progressive forces in capitalist countries, and has a positive influence on the movement's development.
quoteZh: 尼共政府的建立鼓舞了国际共产主义运动，提振了资本主义国家共产党与进步力量的信心和决心，[7]对国际共产主义运动的发展具有积极影响。

glossary.explanation: The worldwide movement of communist parties and organisations. Chinese scholarship uses the term for the historical and present-day network of such parties, including those that survived the Soviet collapse.

t: The current state and development trends of the American left-wing movement
zh: 美国左翼运动的现状与发展趋势
paras: Why has the left in the United States revived in recent years, and why do its gains so often prove short-lived? Writing in 2019, Zhang argues that popular discontent with working and everyday life has revived left-wing movements, but that union-based mobilisation cannot consolidate their results. In response, newer left forces, above all the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), are moving towards a strategy of "returning to the working class".

The article has four parts. It first traces the accumulated grievances behind the revival since the 2008 financial crisis, then assesses the movement's present condition: its renewed activity, its lack of staying power and the rise of new organisational forces. The third part examines the DSA's strategic shift, and the last considers the theoretical and practical significance of the trend. Zhang relies largely on commentary in New Left Review's 2019 "America's New Left" series and on Monthly Review authors.

Zhang locates the discontent in three spheres: fragmented, Taylorist divisions of labour and guild-like trade associations that block mobility; consumerism and credit that bind people to finance capital in debt and anxiety; and distrust of a government pursuing neoliberal austerity, which pushes people towards "new social movements". Union-led campaigns, such as the Sanders-backed Amazon wage rise that Amazon offset by cutting paid hours, win only sector-limited, temporary gains. The DSA, Zhang says, wants to move beyond a problem-driven committee structure dominated by young, middle-class activists. It aims to root itself in workplaces and communities, to build a socialist party rather than lean on candidates such as Sanders, to remake unions from below, and to target financial capital and oligarchic firms rather than only government policy.

Zhang concludes that the trend has theoretical value, since it energises Marxist research in the United States, and practical value, since it may produce a cross-sector party built from the base. The author stresses its limits, however. Its goal is a gradual change of social order within capitalism, not Marx's overall transformation of the social system. The DSA has never committed itself to Marxism as a guide, and whether the movement will become a revolutionary force is left open. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic's assessment of the DSA and the post-2008 American left, drawn from Anglophone left sources.
quoteEn: Whether the left-wing movement in American society can become a revolutionary political force within the current political configuration remains to be observed.
quoteZh: 美国社会中的左翼运动究竟能否在当前政治格局中形成一股革命性政治力量,尚有待进一步观察。

t: Western sociology's changing stance towards Marxist theory and its implications
zh: 西方社会学对马克思主义理论的立场演变及其反思
paras: Western scholars disagree on whether sociology is moving away from Marxism or towards it. Wen and Gao argue that neither description is enough, and that the relationship has to be traced over the long term. Their thesis is that Western sociology's stance has passed through five stages, driven by changing political, economic and intellectual conditions. Sociology's main stance has been to move away from Marxism, and it has drawn on Marxism mainly in moments of theoretical crisis.

The article surveys the period from the mid-nineteenth century to the present. It first contrasts classical sociology (Comte, Durkheim, Weber) with Marx on how society progresses, how knowledge is produced and how facts are known. It then covers the 'amphibious' theorists Lukács, Gramsci and Polanyi, and the Frankfurt School. Next come the postwar American mainstream of Parsons, Merton and Lazarsfeld, the radical sociology of the 1970s and 1980s, and the post-1990 period of professionalisation and Michael Burawoy's 'public sociology'. A final section draws lessons for Chinese sociology.

The authors name five stages: divergence (to 1918), reflexive absorption (to 1945), extreme rejection (to the late 1960s), renewed integration through radical sociology (1970s to late 1980s), and Marxism as an implicit presence (from the 1990s). In their account, early sociologists modelled themselves on natural science and value-neutrality, while Marxism aimed to change society. Postwar functionalist and quantitative sociology marginalised Marxism, and the crises of the 1960s pushed sociologists back towards it. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, fragmentation, professionalisation and the search for disciplinary balance, in the authors' view, wore down sociology's critical edge. They argue that public sociology partly resists this, but remains weaker than the professional mainstream.

Wen and Gao propose that Chinese sociology go beyond the 'away from' or 'towards' Marxism choice and place Marxist sociology at the centre of China's body of social-science knowledge. They offer five recommendations: handle theory and practice together, reread the classic texts, promote exchange between sociology and Marxist studies, develop a sense of crisis, and combine the roles of interpreter and legislator. They reject dogmatic distortions of Marxism, but not Marxism itself. Read the original if you want a periodised history of sociology's engagement with Marxism, with detailed Western sources, and a Chinese view of what it means for sociology in China.
quoteEn: Between a sociology that upholds objectivism and seeks to explain society, and a Marxist theory that holds to ideals and convictions and seeks to transform society, a great gulf has existed since the day each was born.
quoteZh: 秉持客观主义、力求解释社会的社会学与坚持理想信念、力求改造社会的马克思主义理论之间从诞生之日起便产生了巨大的鸿沟。

glossary.explanation: One of Burawoy's four types of sociology. It aims to widen public debate on moral and political issues and to link sociology with civil society.

t: Instigation, interference and manipulation: British and American leftist views on the truth of the Hong Kong issue
zh: 教唆、干涉与操纵：英美左翼关于香港问题真相的看法
paras: Writing in late 2019, after months of unrest in Hong Kong and the US congressional committee vote on the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, Xing Wenzeng asks what really caused the Hong Kong problem and who is instigating, interfering in and manipulating it. The article answers by surveying statements from British and American communist parties and left-wing scholars, which Xing presents as "another voice" from the Western world. Xing's thesis is that these writers see foreign hands, chiefly British and American, behind the protests.

The article is organised in four sections. It first reviews left-wing accounts of US and British involvement. It then covers their link of Hong Kong to the US–China trade war and to Brexit. A third section deals with their rejection of the idea that colonial rule or Western democracy could bring freedom. The last compares Hong Kong's economy with that of the mainland. Sources include Ella Rule of the Communist Party of Britain (Marxist-Leninist), the Communist Party of Britain, Sara Flounders of Workers World Party, Ian Goodrum and John Bachtell in People's World, John Ross and Martin Jacques.

Xing reports that these authors describe Washington's contacts with Hong Kong opposition figures, and Marco Rubio's drafting of the bill, as evidence of orchestration. They also cite funding from foundations such as the National Endowment for Democracy. Ross is cited as arguing that the US launched the trade war while Britain, shaped by Brexit-era politics, took a provocative line on Hong Kong. Flounders and Goodrum are cited as saying that colonial Hong Kong had no elected government or basic labour rights, and that Western media coverage of the protests was selective and hypocritical. Jacques is quoted attributing Hong Kong's prosperity to mainland reform and opening up, not British rule. Bachtell's figures on inequality and housing costs are set against praise for mainland growth and Shenzhen, from which Xing concludes that socialism works better than capitalism.

Xing concludes that the left-wing views expose Western right-wing forces' manipulation, and that their aim is to split Hong Kong from China and destabilise the People's Republic. Xing calls for winning more Western left-wing support, countering mainstream Western media narratives and strengthening a united front with Western left forces. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences researcher selects and uses Anglo-American left-wing commentary in the official account of the 2019 Hong Kong unrest.
quoteEn: The observations of British and American left-wing parties and scholars on Hong Kong reflect the various tricks by which Western right-wing forces strongly support and manipulate the protests, and their aim of splitting Hong Kong from the motherland and undermining the stability of the People's Republic is plain to see.
quoteZh: 英美左翼政党及学者对香港问题的观察和认识，反映出西方右翼势力大力支持并操纵香港抗议行动的种种伎俩，其试图将香港从祖国分裂出去并破坏中华人民共和国稳定的目的昭然若揭。

glossary.explanation: The policy launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, introducing market-oriented reforms and opening China to foreign trade and investment.
A Chinese Communist Party strategy of building alliances with non-Party groups and outside forces to widen support for its goals.

t: Overview of research on the foreign Left in 2018
zh: 2018年国外左翼思想研究概览
paras: This is a literature review of work on foreign left-wing thought in 2018, published in Scientific Socialism in 2019. Zhou and Lei report that the year, marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th of the Communist Manifesto, brought wider and deeper research and steady progress in building the field.

The review has four parts. It first sketches the year's developments: key articles in journals such as Monthly Review, New Left Review and International Socialism, Chinese publications and books, the death of Samir Amin in August, and conferences including the New York left forum, the World Social Forum, the ninth World Socialism Forum in Beijing and the second World Congress of Marxism. It then surveys theoretical debates, followed by studies of left movements by region, and finally the field's characteristics, problems and recommendations.

On theory, Zhou and Lei cite Wallerstein, Žižek, Amin and John Bellamy Foster defending Marx's contemporary relevance, and Foster's call to move from criticism of neoliberalism to criticism of capitalism itself, using monopoly-capital theory. They also cite analyses of 'reverse globalisation' (Martin Upchurch), the long depression (Joseph Choonara) and Brexit as a move towards organised capitalism (Andreas Nölke). Other studies cover neoliberalism (Daniel Rodgers, Simon Springer), three visions of twenty-first-century socialism, and a 'return of communism' among Western radical thinkers. On regions, the review reports Chinese scholars finding European left parties in difficulty after the decline of the 'Third Way'. It reports resilience in Latin America despite a 'left retreat, right advance', and covers Mexico's first left-wing president in 89 years, the Indian left, the 2017 Nepali left alliance victory and divisions in the Lebanese left.

In their closing section the authors stress the field's breadth and the diversity of its schools, for example Jameson, Derrida, and Laclau and Mouffe as left, centre and right post-Marxists. They propose that foreign left views be judged by Marxist standards, including whether they help to uphold and develop Marxism, aid the study of contemporary capitalism and benefit world socialism and peace. They call for stronger research to help develop twenty-first-century Marxism and build a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a bibliographic map of 2018 Chinese and foreign scholarship on the Western and global left, and a view of how Chinese academics frame and evaluate it.
quoteEn: The scope of research on the foreign Left is also fairly broad and is interdisciplinary in character.
quoteZh: 国外左翼研究的范围也较为广泛, 并具有跨学科特征

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and governance concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, calling for shared development and security among nations. It appears as a conference theme in the review.
An international conference hosted by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in Beijing, bringing together scholars from socialist and left-wing traditions. The ninth was held in November 2018.
A Chinese scholarly shorthand for the shift of Latin American politics away from left-wing governments towards right-wing ones in the mid-2010s.

t: A study of contemporary left-wing accelerationism abroad
zh: 当今国外左翼加速主义思想研究
paras: Liu and Ma take up left-wing accelerationism, which they present as the most distinctive strand of the left-wing theory revived by the 2008 financial crisis. They ask what this school says about capitalism, how it relates to Marx, and what it offers Chinese thinking about the speed of development. Their thesis is that the school has real methodological value and also real flaws, and that its main lesson for China is to put the aim of development ahead of speed.

The article first reconstructs the accelerationists' claim that Marxism already contains a rich critique of acceleration. It then sets out four understandings of "acceleration" and the school's core ideas. It ends with a four-stage history of the school and an assessment of its present relevance. The authors name Nick Srnicek, Alex Williams and Benjamin Noys as representative figures. They also draw on Hartmut Rosa, Paul Virilio, Deleuze and Guattari, and Meillassoux.

In the authors' account, accelerationists read Marx's passages on automation, the "automatic system of machinery" and capital's tendency to undermine itself as a dialectical and materialist analysis. They argue that real emancipation depends on the productive forces that capitalism develops, and that capital is its own barrier. The accelerationists reject any return to a slower, pre-industrial age. They want instead to appropriate automation and digital platforms. Noys's slogan "start from the bad new things" is presented as a way of radicalising capitalism's own dynamic. Michael Laurence's objection is also reported: accelerationist strategy detaches itself from critical force and leaves politics without power. The historical sketch runs from the mid-nineteenth-century roots, through the 1970s to the 1990s, when Virilio's dromology and Deleuze and Guattari's "accelerate the process" fed the school. The Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics (2013) and later books then made it a systematic school.

The authors credit the school with concern for human wellbeing, for example its proposal of a universal basic income after automation. They also credit its sharp reading of digital technology and of the downsides of scientism. They describe its methodology as post-Marxist. Turning to China, they cite Deng Xiaoping's warning against blind pursuit of output and speed. They also cite the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), which moves from "high-speed growth" to high-quality development. In their view this places purpose before speed and takes Marxist thinking about speed out of the accelerationist trap. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of how accelerationism is received in China and tied to official ideas about the speed of development, with a Chinese-language bibliography of the school's sources.
quoteEn: This places the aim of development ahead of speed and lets purpose lead speed; the Marxist view of speed in the new era has escaped the vicious circle of accelerationism.
quoteZh: 这就将发展的目的放在速度前面，以目的引领速度，新时代的马克思主义速度观跳脱出了加速主义的怪圈

glossary.explanation: An official slogan, prominent since the 19th Party Congress (2017), for a shift in China's economy from fast growth to a growth model stressing quality, efficiency and sustainability.
A current of thought holding that capitalism's own dynamics should be intensified or repurposed in order to overcome it. Its left-wing form is associated with Srnicek, Williams and Noys.

t: New trends in foreign Marxist theory in the post-financial-crisis period: a review
zh: 后金融危机时期国外马克思主义理论研究新趋向述评
source: Journal of Northeast Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), first published online on CNKI
paras: Chen Xueming surveys work by Marxists and left-wing thinkers outside China since the 2008 financial crisis, the period the article treats as a new stage of "return to Marx". The review argues that the crisis revived interest in Marx, renewed the critique of capitalism and put socialism and communism back on the agenda. Chen also holds that this body of thought mixes valuable insight with dross and that Chinese scholars should engage with it critically.

The review has three parts. The first summarises new views under three heads: fresh explorations of Marxism, new critiques of capitalism, and new thinking on socialism. The second sets out four features of foreign Marxism and the third offers four predictions. The survey draws on figures such as Eagleton, Hobsbawm, Žižek, Harvey, Foster, Wallerstein, Badiou, Negri and Roemer. It also covers Latin American socialism and market socialism.

In Chen's account, the crisis prompted a defence of Marx's analysis, reflection on the Occupy movement, renewed reading of Capital, and work on social justice and political philosophy. Critiques of capitalism then centred on neoliberalism, ecological crisis, consumer society, the capitalisation of space, liberal democracy and the "new imperialism". On socialism, Chen reports arguments that "another choice is possible", a revival of the communist idea, and ecological and utopian socialisms. Chen also notes the rise of "post-Marxism" and the postmodern turn, which in Chen's view depart from Marxism's core. Chen sees four features: convergence with the radical left, postmodern influence, interdisciplinary fusion, and pluralism combined with a search for an organic whole.

Chen predicts that the twenty-first century will be a period of concentrated critique of capitalism, and urges attention to foreign left parties and to a possible turn to the right. Chen argues that foreign Marxism is weak in linking theory to practice and that Chinese scholars should draw on its methods in building their own discipline and discourse. The article ends by holding that Chinese and foreign Marxism are parts of world Marxism and that China's rise means a revival of Marxism in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a broad, name-rich map of post-2008 foreign Marxism as seen by a leading Chinese specialist, and an indication of how it is assessed in China.
quoteEn: Although contemporary foreign Marxist currents have made certain contributions in many respects, their theoretical systems, ideas and discursive logic are a mixture of the essence and the dross.
quoteZh: 虽然当代国外马克思主义思潮在诸多方面做出了一定贡献，但具体到其理论体系、思想观点、话语逻辑上则呈现精华与糟粕交织的特点。

glossary.explanation: The broad Chinese label for Marxist and left-wing thought outside China. It covers Western Marxism, ecological Marxism, post-Marxism and Latin American currents.

A current linked to Laclau and Mouffe's Hegemony and Socialist Strategy. The article criticises it for departing from Marx's analysis of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production.

t: The origins, claims and assessment of "Millennial socialism"
zh: “千禧社会主义”的缘起、主张与评析
paras: Li Xiang and Zhao Wanying ask whether the "Millennial socialism" spreading among young people in Western countries is a genuinely new exploration of socialism or another way for capitalism to rescue itself. Writing in 2019, they argue that it is essentially a left-wing current with a democratic socialist colouring. In their reading it seeks capitalism's self-adjustment rather than its overthrow, and it is not the scientific socialism of Marx and Engels.

The article has three main parts. The first sets out the origins of the phenomenon, drawing on opinion surveys from the United States, Britain and Australia that the authors cite to show weakening youth support for capitalism. It explains the rise through the unresolved contradictions after the 2008 financial crisis, a generational shift in values, and the decline of neoliberalism. The second part presents the movement's claims on the economy, politics, social welfare and the environment, including the "Green New Deal". The third part offers the authors' assessment, and a short conclusion follows.

The authors identify the movement's demands as state intervention and "big government", economic democratization through worker participation in company governance, progressive taxation, "participatory planning" in place of representative democracy, free education and healthcare, and public-led climate action. Their assessment rests on three points. First, the "socialism" is nominal: drawing on Engels, they say real socialism rests on public ownership and class opposition to capitalism, whereas Millennial socialists treat it as a tool for fairness and welfare, with the Scandinavian model as their ideal. Second, they reject revolution, prefer institutional adjustment to replacement, and rely on party politics, which the authors judge of limited effectiveness. Third, it is a new development of Western left thought, with internet-based mobilisation and an expanded ecological agenda, but largely a repackaging of older left ideas without a complete party system or theory.

The authors conclude that Millennial socialists misunderstand socialism, waver in their stance, are divided internally and have so far had limited influence on the political and economic order. They nonetheless see in the movement an attempt to redefine socialism in a more inclusive, gentler form. They hold that its main significance is as a reflection of present conditions: it shows the claim of capitalism's "absolute victory" to be overoptimistic and calls for continued vigilance and criticism of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic assessment of young Western support for socialism in the Corbyn and Sanders era, with the survey data it cites.
quoteEn: Rather than a negation of capitalism, "Millennial socialism" is a criticism of capitalism; rather than a pursuit of socialism, it is a yearning for certain elements of socialism.
quoteZh: 与其说“千禧社会主义”是对资本主义的否定,不如说是对资本主义的批判;与其说“千禧社会主义”是对社会主义的追求,不如说是对社会主义某些因素的向往。

t: The influence of left-wing political globalisation on literary and aesthetic theory
st: Intellectual implications of Hardt and Negri's "Empire" trilogy
zh: 左翼政治的全球化构想对文艺美学的影响
zhSub: 哈特与奈格里“帝国”三部曲的思想启迪
source: Journal of Shanghai University (Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 6
paras: Mai Yongxiong asks what Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's trilogy Empire (2000), Multitude (2004) and Commonwealth (2009) offers to literary theory and aesthetics in an age of globalisation and digitisation. The article argues that the trilogy, which it presents as a landmark of a twenty-first-century "theory renaissance", widens critiques of capitalism, semiotics, postcolonial criticism, cyberspace studies and Marxist aesthetics. It also names weaknesses in the work.

After brief biographies of the two authors, the article follows the three books in turn: the decline of old empires and the rise of a decentred new sovereignty, the "multitude" as the subject of resistance, and the "common" as a utopian future. It then sets "Empire studies" beside semiotics (through Liu He's interview), postcolonial criticism, Deleuze's smooth, striated and holey spaces, and Bruno Latour's political ecology. A long section places the trilogy in the history of Marxist aesthetics, and a short conclusion follows.

Mai reports Hardt and Negri's claim that postcolonial and postmodern theory "mistook the enemy". In their view, power has moved from modern sovereignty to a networked imperial form that has no outside, so these theories address only one historical stage. Mai treats the multitude as the new subject: a network of heterogeneous exploited people, broader than the working class and not the same as "the people". Mai applies Deleuze's three spaces to cyberspace, where netizens roam freely while administrators, rules and hackers contest the same ground. Mai also notes the role of Chinese netizens in anti-corruption exposure and public supervision in the new era.

Mai concludes that the trilogy continues Marxist aesthetics, develops Marx's theory of social stages and the world outlook of the Communist Manifesto, and enters dialogue with Wallerstein and David Harvey. It also expands class theory and the aesthetic dimension of teleology. Mai's own criticisms are that the multitude is too vague, dismisses national sovereignty casually and oversimplifies postcolonial and fundamentalist questions. The common, in Mai's reading, carries utopian force but leans on humanistic imagination, in contrast to Harvey's empirical approach. Read the original if you want a Chinese literary-theory reading of Hardt and Negri that links their politics to semiotics, postcolonial theory, Deleuze, Latour and Marxist aesthetics.
quoteEn: In the process, they activated the theoretical methods of Marxist social science, continental philosophy and the new pragmatism.
quoteZh: 在此过程中，他们激活了马克思主义社会科学、大陆哲学和新实用论的理论方法

t: Visual politics: aesthetic questions in the contemporary French Left
zh: 视觉政治：当代法国左翼的美学问题
source: Journal of Hubei University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2019 no. 6
paras: Wang and Qi ask how French left-wing thinkers since the May 1968 events have turned aesthetics into a political question through the problem of vision. Published in 2019 in the Journal of Hubei University, the article argues that 'visual politics' is the logical entry point to the French Left's contemporary aesthetics. In the authors' account, it differs from British and American visual culture studies in three ways: its political angle, its focus on vision and visuality, and its double critique of modernity and postmodernity.

The authors work through four dimensions: the politics of looking, visual representation systems and image production, the expressive mechanisms of images, and film as the contemporary form of visual politics. They treat a constellation of thinkers: Sartre, Lacan, Merleau-Ponty, Foucault, Guy Debord, Baudrillard, Roland Barthes, Deleuze, Jacques Rancière and Alain Badiou. These figures are grouped into phenomenological, psychoanalytic and structuralist currents of Marxism.

In the first part, Merleau-Ponty's reversible 'seeing and being seen', Lacan's mirror stage and gaze, and Foucault's medical gaze and panopticon show vision as a field of desire and power. The second part argues that Debord's 'society of the spectacle' reworks Marx's commodity fetishism, and that Baudrillard's simulacra and hyperreality describe a code-dominated image society in which signifier and signified separate. The third and fourth parts move to Barthes's analysis of myth in images and to Rancière's 'image-sentence' and 'distribution of the sensible'. Badiou's film as philosophical situation, Foucault's memory governance and Deleuze's 'missing people' extend this to cinema, where Rancière's 'those without part' are said to speak and an aesthetic equality is pursued.

The authors conclude that the French Left's critique of 'ocularcentrism', together with its mix of critique and absorption of Marxist theory, gives this work its distinctive character. In their reading, politics is no longer the grand narrative of traditional Marxism. It is now located in the sensing body and perceptual structures, as politics becomes aestheticised and aesthetics politicised. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language survey linking Lacan, Foucault, Debord, Baudrillard, Rancière and Badiou under the heading of visual politics, with its Chinese-language bibliography.
quoteEn: "Politics" is no longer the expression of the grand-narrative logic of the traditional Marxist research paradigm; instead, the sensuous body and perceptual structures in micro-level fields have become new objects of attention in contemporary aesthetic research.
quoteZh: “政治”不再是传统马克思主义研究范式中宏大叙事逻辑的表征，相反，微观场域中的感性肉身与感知结构已经成为当代美学研究中新的关注对象。

glossary.explanation: The authors' umbrella term for French left-wing work on how looking, images and visibility are shaped by power and can be turned to emancipatory ends.
Guy Debord's concept of a society in which social relations are mediated by images. The article treats it as a development of Marx's commodity fetishism.
Rancière's term for the way a social order divides what can be seen, said and heard, and by whom. It is the core of his political aesthetics oriented towards equality.

t: A new interpretation of commodity fetishism in the German "New Marx Reading"
st: With a comment on two interpretive paths in Western Marxism
zh: 德国“新马克思阅读”运动的商品拜物教新释
zhSub: 兼评西方马克思主义的两种解读路径
source: Journal of Northeastern University (Social Science Edition), 2019 no. 6
paras: Liang Yanxiao asks how the "mystery" of commodity fetishism in Capital should be explained, and contrasts two interpretive paths in Western Marxism. One draws on external resources (alienation, religious metaphor, Weberian rationalisation, the unconscious, sign-worship) and is traced to the early Georg Lukács. The other is text-based and starts from the theory of the value-form in the opening chapter of Capital. Liang argues that the second path, represented by Hans-Georg Backhaus of the German "New Marx Reading" (Neue Marx-Lektüre), is the sounder one.

The article has four parts. It first criticises the "non-value-form" reading, taking Lukács's History and Class Consciousness as its case. It then sets out the philological basis, comparing the first German edition, the French edition and Engels's fourth German edition of Capital, Volume 1. Next it presents Backhaus's "Dialectics of the Value-Form". It closes by assessing the New Marx Reading and its lessons for Chinese scholarship. Isaak Rubin, Chris Arthur, Helmut Reichelt and Ingo Elbe appear as related figures.

Liang argues that Lukács grafted Weber's rationalisation thesis onto Marx's passages. He thereby shifted attention to reified consciousness and ignored the value-form analysis. Liang also says Lukács borrowed material on machinery and the division of labour that Marx treats only after the chapter on commodities, which Liang calls a "misplaced appropriation". Against this, Liang reports Backhaus's philological point: fetishism first appeared in the appendix on the value-form in the first German edition, under the fourth peculiarity of the equivalent form. Backhaus therefore holds that fetishism can be understood only as part of the value-form section. In his reading, the equivalent form makes a natural object stand for a social relation (abstract labour), which gives commodities a "illusory independence". The root lies in a commodity-producing society that splits private from social labour, so the fetishistic structure can be broken only by changing that mode of production.

Liang concludes that the New Marx Reading combines philological work on the MEGA2 manuscripts with social critique, and does so by "returning the critique of political economy to the critique of society". The author calls on Chinese scholars to bridge the split between "MEGA studies" and "Frankfurt School studies". They should avoid Western Marxism's emphasis on social psychology and culture, and revive the critique of political economy and the analysis of production contradictions. Liang hopes a "Chinese New Marx Reading" will emerge. Read the original if you work on Capital's value-form theory, the Lukács–Backhaus contrast, or how Chinese scholars receive German Marx studies.
quoteEn: In my view, the first German edition, the French edition and the fourth German edition are the three most representative versions, because they are respectively Marx's first edition in his lifetime, his last edition, and Engels's final edited edition.
quoteZh: 在笔者看来,德文一版、法文版和德文四版是其中最具代表性的三个版本,因为它们分别代表了马克思生前的第一个版本、最后一个版本以及恩格斯的最终编辑版本。

t: A philosophical examination of the "three paths" for transcending the logic of capital
zh: 超越资本逻辑的“三条路径”之哲学审视
source: Journal of Guangxi Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 5
paras: How can the "logic of capital" be transcended? Wang Weihua defines this logic as the self-reproduction and self-expansion of capital as a reified social relation, which pulls the whole material world into commodification, monetisation and abstract rule over individuals. Since Hegel, Wang argues, philosophers' attempts to overcome it fall into three paths. Western Marxism takes a utopian, aesthetic-redemptive path of external transcendence, and postmodernism takes a nihilist external path. Marx alone takes an internal, practical path, by dissecting the negativity inherent in capital.

The article, published in 2019, is built in three main parts plus a conclusion. The first treats Western Marxism through Lukács's critique of reification and the antinomies of bourgeois thought, and Horkheimer and Adorno's critique of the "culture industry" and of identity in Dialectic of Enlightenment. The second takes Jean-François Lyotard's rejection of grand narratives and metanarratives in The Postmodern Condition. The third turns to Marx, tracing his inheritance of Hegel's dialectic of negation and applying it to contemporary capitalist crisis.

Wang's central claim is that Lukács, Horkheimer, Adorno and Lyotard remain at the level of cultural, ideological or theoretical critique. Lukács relies on proletarian self-consciousness to overcome reification, the Frankfurt thinkers never push their critique to capital and the political power protecting it, and Lyotard only fleetingly touches capital while placing his hopes in postmodern intellectuals. Marx, by contrast, takes from Hegel's Logic and the master–slave dialectic the idea of negativity as the engine of movement, and finds it in capital itself. Citing the Grundrisse and Capital volume 3, Wang reports four limits of capital (necessary labour, surplus labour, money, and exchange value over use value), which capital strives to break and thereby generates the seeds of its own dissolution. Wang applies this to the post-2008 crisis, stressing the spatialisation of capital, securitisation and leverage, and the coexistence of virtual-asset bubbles with a stagnant real economy.

Wang concludes that theoretical critique is necessary but far from sufficient, and that both Western Marxism and postmodernism remain trapped in what Heidegger called the "immanence of consciousness". Marx's route is a practical critique, which reveals capital's inner negativity and, in Wang's reading, points humanity towards communism. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language comparison of Western Marxism, Lyotard and Marx on capital, and of how Hegel's dialectic of negation is used to defend Marx's approach.
quoteEn: The logic of capital is both the logic of the self-expansion of capital's social power and the logic of that power's self-negation, self-collapse and self-destruction.
quoteZh: 资本逻辑既是资本的社会权力自我扩张的逻辑,又是资本的社会权力自我否定、自我崩溃、自我灭亡的逻辑。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese Marxist philosophy for capital's drive to expand and valorise itself and to subordinate society, nature and individuals to that movement. The article treats it as the core principle of capitalist society.
Lukács's term for social relations between people taking on the appearance of relations between things in commodity society. The article uses it in this Lukácsian sense.
Horkheimer and Adorno's term for the standardised mass production of film, radio and magazines. They saw it as manipulating the public.
The tradition of Lukács, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School, which focuses on philosophy, culture and ideology. The author criticises it for staying at the level of theory.

t: The reality and spectrality of ideology
st: An analysis of ideology theory in Žižek's psychoanalytic perspective
zh: 意识形态的现实性与幽灵性
zhSub: 齐泽克精神分析视野中的意识形态理论探析
source: Journal of Nanjing University (Philosophy, Humanities and Social Sciences), 2019 no. 5
paras: Kong Ming'an and Tan Yong take up the concept of the "spectre of ideology" that Slavoj Žižek proposes in Mapping Ideology. They ask how the "spectrality" of ideology should be understood and how it relates to social reality and the unconscious. Their thesis is that ideology has a double identity, an external, materialised side and a pre-ideological core, and that the spectre mediates between the two. In the authors' reading, the spectre is the unsymbolised remainder of reality that ideology cannot capture.

The article is organised in four sections. The first three test ideology against the three traits conventionally attributed to a ghost: ubiquity, a half-real, half-illusory character, and eternal existence. The fourth section turns to how the spectre appears and how it relates to ideology and social reality. The authors draw on Žižek, Althusser, Lacan, Derrida and Marx, and illustrate the argument with Žižek's examples: reporting on the Iraq and Bosnian wars, the East German intellectuals of Neues Forum, and a tribal village plan.

The authors argue that ideology is ubiquitous because even attempts to leave it, such as a "third way", remain ideological. It is half-real and half-illusory because it both reflects and conceals social reality, as in the two groups of villagers who draw the village differently and so mask an underlying antagonism. It is eternal in Althusser's sense, as "ideology in general" without history, which Althusser compared to Freud's unconscious and restricted to class society. The central move is that reality is the symbolised, ideologically structured reality plus the spectre, like two sides of a coin. The spectre therefore marks an empty place, the Lacanian real, which is antagonistic and cannot be occupied by any positive reality. If it is so occupied, one falls back into ideology. This gives ideology critique a reference point that is not itself ideological.

The authors conclude that the core of ideology is the spectre filling the hole of the real, while ideology's externality is its materialised form. They credit Žižek with building Althusser's conception on Lacanian psychoanalysis. They add that Marx's account of ideology as unconscious ("they do not know it, but they are doing it") supplies a materialist basis that Žižek's account lacks, and that without it ideology theory has no root. Read the original if you want a close, Marx-oriented reading of Žižek's Mapping Ideology that links spectre, real and symbolic reality.
quoteEn: Ideology and the spectre stand in a complementary relation, and together they constitute true, complete reality.
quoteZh: 意识形态与幽灵之间是互补的关系，它们共同构成真正、完整的现实

t: The value of Western Marxism research as a resource, and reflections on it
zh: 西方马克思主义研究的资源性意义及其反思
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2019 no. 5
paras: Zou Shipeng asks how China's four decades of research on Western Marxism should be understood and redirected in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that Western Marxism should be treated as a reference resource that serves Chinese theoretical construction. In Zou's view, this means studying it critically, with a sense of practice, and giving it a proper place in the disciplinary system.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the resource value of Western Marxism, from Lukács onwards, including its post-1968 developments and the Chinese leadership's framing of theoretical resources. The second offers three reflections on current research. The third looks at where foreign Marxism research sits within the Marxist theory discipline and how it relates to other disciplines.

Zou argues that Western Marxism carried Marx's critique into the era of modern and contemporary capitalism, and that its concepts, such as alienation, reification and totality, are irreplaceable in modern social science. Zou distinguishes Western Marxism as a school, which in this account ran from Lukács to Althusser and is now past, from Western Marxism as a continuing tradition. Zou also criticises a 'false heat' in recent research that chases radical left theories and social movements, which Zou says drift away from Marx and carry theoretical dangers, and calls for studies that stay calm and rest on solid texts. Research should not treat these theories as principles, Zou says, but use them to build the ability to analyse Chinese practice and to engage with modernity without rejecting it.

On disciplines, Zou notes that the Marxist theory discipline built its foreign Marxism field late and has no clear strengths there, unlike philosophy, political economy and literary theory. Zou calls for a strengthened second-level discipline that talks with other fields, without absorbing them, and for doctoral programmes at institutions able to support them. Zou also accepts that a large research force is unnecessary, though a certain scale is needed so that it can feed back into Chinese Marxist theory. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese specialist justifies and delimits the study of Western Marxism within the Marxist theory discipline.
quoteEn: The key question is whether research on theoretical resources can be turned into the researcher's practical awareness and capacity for theoretical innovation and creation.
quoteZh: 关键的问题在于是否能够将理论资源的研究转化为研究者的实践意识及理论创新与创造的能力。

glossary.explanation: The tradition running from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci through the Frankfurt School. Zou uses the term both for a school ending around Althusser and for a continuing wider tradition.
The broader field of Marxism outside China. In Chinese academia it also names a second-level discipline within Marxist theory.
The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up. The article treats Western Marxism research as subordinate to it.

A first-level academic discipline in China's university system, set up in the 2000s. It includes sub-fields such as basic principles of Marxism, the adaptation of Marxism to China, ideological and political education, and foreign Marxism.

t: The rupture between theory and practice: reflections on the current state of the European socialist movement
zh: 理论与实践的断裂:欧洲社会主义运动发展现状思考
source: Problems of Contemporary World Socialism, 2019 no. 2
paras: Why has the European socialist movement, represented by the European left, failed to benefit from the crises that followed 2008? Lin argues that the core problem is a rupture between theory and practice, which afflicts both social democracy and the radical left. Overcoming it, the article contends, requires the movement to face several new theoretical questions directly.

The article has three parts. The first describes structural change on the European left since 2000: the decline of the social democratic parties, the partial recovery of a radical left descended largely from the communist parties, the fading of left identity, and growing fragmentation. The second analyses the rupture separately for social democracy and for the radical left. The third sets out three issues that socialist theory must address: post-materialism, globalisation and technological change.

Lin argues that social democracy's long theoretical evolution, which fused socialist ideas with social liberalism, was driven by the need to be electable. Its "Third Way" modernisers shed the party's socialist and class character, which in Lin's account produced an identity crisis and eroded its working-class base, while a return to traditional positions would cost it electoral viability. The radical left, by contrast, lacks a shared identity, is stronger at criticism than at constructive proposals, and has no systematic policy theory on the European Union, the welfare state or direct democracy, and part of it has turned to left populism. On the three new questions, Lin calls for explaining how material and post-material concerns relate in socialist politics and for a globalisation theory that is open and selective rather than purely defensive. That theory should also rebuild the role of the nation-state instead of simply abandoning or returning to it. Lin further asks for study of how digital technology actually changes production relations and political organisation, beyond speculation about "digital socialism".

Lin concludes that the European socialist movement stands at a crossroads. Its basis in the critique of capitalism and the demand for alternatives remains real, but it can grow only by closing the gap between theory and practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's detailed account of European social democracy and the radical left after 2008, and of the theoretical agenda the author sets for them.
quoteEn: The contradiction of a rupture between theory and practice is the deeper problem restricting the room for the European socialist movement to develop.
quoteZh: 理论与实践之间断裂的矛盾是制约欧洲社会主义运动发展空间的更深层次的问题。

glossary.explanation: A centre-left political programme of the 1990s associated with Tony Blair and the sociologist Anthony Giddens. It claimed to go beyond left and right by accepting market capitalism while pursuing social goals.

In Lin's usage, parties to the left of social democracy but distinct from the far left, mostly successors of former communist parties, together with newer left groups. Lin treats the term as vague and internally diverse.

t: An analysis of the reasons for the decline of the American left in the twenty-first century
zh: 试析21世纪美国左翼运动衰落的原因
paras: Why have the two best-known left-wing movements of twenty-first-century America, Occupy Wall Street (2011) and Bernie Sanders's 2016 presidential campaign, achieved so little? Chen and Gao argue that the American left is in decline both against the contemporary right and against its own history. Measured against the right, the two movements failed to put their preferred candidates into key positions. Measured against earlier left movements, they failed to reverse growing inequality. The authors identify three interacting causes: economic (the 2008 financial crisis), political (a tradition of distrust of government) and ideological (a dilemma of choices).

The article is organised around these three causes and compares the left throughout with the Tea Party movement and Donald Trump's campaign. It begins with the history of the left coalition built by the Democrats through the New Deal and civil-rights legislation. It then examines survey data on poverty, the shrinking middle class and Democratic support. Next it takes up Pew and Gallup figures on distrust of government, and finally the slogans and programmes of Occupy and Sanders. A short conclusion draws out why the right succeeded.

The authors' first move is that the left coalition holds together in times of growth but fractures in times of scarcity. After 2008, they argue, different groups, and even members of the same group, competed for jobs and limited welfare, and Occupy's demands contained internal contradictions over affirmative action, manufacturing return and the environment. The Tea Party's membership was narrower, mostly higher-income white men, so the crisis did not split it. Second, Chen and Gao contend that Sanders's programme relies on 'big government' just as popular distrust of government and elites was rising. Trump and the Tea Party promised smaller government and so matched that mood. Third, Occupy's '99% versus 1%' framing avoided value claims in order to keep a diverse coalition, while Sanders built a coherent framework of 'justice', 'oligarchy' and 'democracy' that appealed mainly to young people. The authors argue that neither approach worked under crisis and distrust. The right, by contrast, joined free-market and traditional-morality themes into a coherent conservatism of liberty and virtue.

In the authors' conclusion, the right's success mirrors the left's failure: a homogeneous base, a promise of small government and a clear ideology. The article cites Urban Institute data that the wealth of the top 10% rose from about six to twelve times that of middle-class households between 1963 and 2016. Citing Eli Zaretsky and Michael Kazin, Chen and Gao hold that America needs a left, so the decline is not permanent. When the left revives, they say, will depend on the economic and political environment and on ideological exploration. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of why Occupy and Sanders failed, set beside the Tea Party and Trump, with the survey data the authors rely on.
quoteEn: In other words, whether viewed horizontally or vertically, the American left-wing movements of the twenty-first century are in decline.
quoteZh: 换言之, 无论从横向还是纵向维度看, 21世纪美国左翼运动都处于衰势之中。

t: The "choice" of path in the globalisation of the logic of capital
st: Russian Marxist research in the twenty-first century
zh: 资本逻辑全球化视域中的道路“抉择”
zhSub: 21世纪俄罗斯马克思主义研究
paras: Hu Xiaokun surveys twenty-first-century Russian Marxist scholarship and asks how Russian left-wing thinkers frame the country's choice of historical path under the globalisation of the logic of capital. The article argues that Chaadaev's nineteenth-century question of whether Russia has a future has been reopened after the 2008 financial crisis. In Hu's account, Russian Marxists answer by returning to Marx's historical materialism and "revolutionary" dialectic, and by treating transition to socialism as a contradictory, processual task.

The article has four parts. It begins with Russia's modernization impasse, drawing on Petr Buldakov and Dmitry Granin and on world-systems theory. It then turns to the nature of post-industrial society and the Russian engagement with Western Marxism (Baudrillard's simulation and consumer society, Bell, Drucker). The third part examines the "post-Soviet critical Marxism" of Alexander Buzgalin and Andrei Kolganov, notably their two-volume Global Capital (2015). The last part reviews debates among Russian leftists, including a 2011 round table on whether left thought is in crisis and a 2013 Moscow conference on Marxism and the working class.

Hu reports that Russian scholars attribute the modernization impasse to a gap between Western-style institutions and Russian tradition, and to a state that pursues technical "Westernisation" only. Granin proposes escaping Eurocentrism by seeing Russia as semi-peripheral. On post-industrial society, Russian authors see rising creativity and autonomy for workers alongside deeper alienation, as capital extends into consumption and intellectual labour. Buzgalin and Kolganov treat Baudrillard's "simulation" as a reflection of changing capitalist relations, not as reality itself. They call for a new system of categories modelled on Capital, drawing on the Soviet philosopher Ilyenkov's method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete.

In the round-table debate, Inozemtsev doubts that the left retains a revolutionary subject. Buzgalin answers with six points on the left, redistribution, post-industrial contradictions, rentiers, education and non-linear history. Voeikov favours gradual reform, while Slavin holds that wage labour under capital keeps workers' class position unchanged. Hu concludes that Russian Marxists treat transition to socialism as the task of finding its real basis and historical conditions, and of fostering revolutionary subjects, through a dialectical grasp of global capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of post-Soviet Russian Marxist debates on modernization, post-industrial society and the left, with references to Russian-language sources.
quoteEn: The crisis of today's left-wing thought and movements is at root a crisis of political practice, not a crisis of socialist theory.
quoteZh: 当今左翼思想和运动的危机,在根本上是政治实践的危机,而不是社会主义理论的危机。

t: Subject, structure, science: three dimensions in the logical course of twentieth-century French Marxism
zh: 主体·结构·科学:20世纪法国马克思主义逻辑进程中的三重维度
paras: Bai Hu asks how twentieth-century French Marxism developed and what logic ran through it. The article argues that its course unfolded along three dimensions: the question of the subject, structuralism, and science. Bai holds that the third is the most neglected, acting as a "fellow traveller" to the other two.

The article first sketches three phases: humanist Marxism centred on the subject; the structuralist period; and the post-1968 decline, when many currents drew on Marxist critique. It then devotes one section to each dimension. The subject section covers Kojève's Hegel seminar, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty. The structuralism section covers Saussure, Lévi-Strauss and Althusser. The science section covers Bachelard, Canguilhem, Althusser and Foucault. Derrida, Deleuze and Badiou appear as later thinkers.

Bai traces the subject question to the Cartesian "cogito" tradition. Kojève's anthropological reading of Hegel pulled the "I" back into sensuous reality, and Sartre then turned to Marxism by moving beyond both Hegel and Kierkegaard. Structuralism, as Bai reads it, answers the same problem by bypassing the cogito. Lévi-Strauss criticised Sartre as a prisoner of the cogito, and Althusser held history to be "a process without a subject", proposed an epistemological break in Marx, and treated determination by the economic base as overdetermination. Bai then separates French philosophy into a philosophy of consciousness (Descartes to Sartre and Merleau-Ponty) and a philosophy of the concept (Cavaillès, Bachelard, Canguilhem, Foucault, Deleuze). The latter branches into scientific epistemology, which shaped Althusser's problematic and break, and a philosophy of life, which led from Canguilhem's work on the normal and the pathological to Foucault's biopolitics.

Bai concludes that these three themes cover most of French philosophy's twentieth-century agenda and explain why Marxism flourished in France. Writing in 2019, Bai expects the subject and its dissolution to remain central in Badiou and Foucault, and structuralism's role in the 1960s peak to stay significant. Bai also predicts that science and epistemology will gain weight as biopolitics and philosophy of life advance. Read the original if you want a compact survey of French Marxism from Sartre to Foucault that gives special attention to the scientific-epistemological lineage.
quoteEn: The scientific dimension has been seriously neglected in contemporary studies of French Marxism; although it never formed a distinct school, it is certainly present in the landscape of twentieth-century French philosophy and Marxist theory.
quoteZh: 科学维度在当代法国马克思主义的研究中被严重忽略了, 尽管它并未形成一种专门的研究思潮, 但是它的确存在于20世纪法国哲学和法国马克思主义理论的图景之中

t: Foreign Marxist theories of labour relations
zh: 国外马克思主义的劳动关系理论
paras: This review, published in Theoretical Horizon in 2018, surveys how Marxist economists outside China have analysed labour relations in modern capitalism. Zhang and Wang open by noting that the 19th Party Congress (2017) called for building harmonious labour relations, and they present the foreign literature as worth attention alongside Chinese research. They divide it into four strands: labour process theory, the political economy theory of trade unions, the French Regulation School, and theories of capitalist class structure.

The article takes each strand in turn through its leading figure.
