For labour process theory it covers Harry Braverman's revival of the theme, Michael Burawoy's turn to worker subjectivity, and later work by William Lazonick, David Harvey and Ash Amin. It then presents Richard Hyman's typology of unions, the Regulation School's account of Fordist and finance-led accumulation regimes, and Erik Olin Wright's model of class structure.

In the authors' account, Braverman shows how scientific management fragments and deskills work, separating conception from execution, so that capital controls the labour process. Burawoy, studying Hungarian factories, finds that workers come to consent to their own exploitation through piece-rate games, internal labour markets and an internal state, and he proposes employee ownership. Hyman treats labour relations as shifting between cooperation and conflict and distinguishes market-, society- and class-oriented unions, each with internal tensions, so that he recommends combining the three orientations. The Regulation School traces Fordism's collapse to distorted labour relations and proposes labour law and collective bargaining to reconcile flexible work with security. Wright adds a 'middle class' of contradictory class locations and, in the authors' words, advocates 'class compromise' as a route to socialism through deeper democracy. The authors judge that this last approach neglects capitalism's long-run direction.

Zhang and Wang conclude that all four strands follow Marx's basic principles and agree that inequality and conflict between workers and capitalists are the essence of capitalist labour relations. They say the strands extend Marxist economics and that the Regulation School and Hyman's pluralist view offer practical lessons for institutional and union work. After the 2008 financial crisis, they note, radical currents revived in the West, which they take as a reason to give this literature due attention. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language survey of Braverman, Burawoy, Hyman, the Regulation School and Wright, and of how Chinese scholars frame them.)
quoteEn: Although their research emphases differ, scholars of every school agree on the essence of labour relations in modern capitalist society: the inequality between workers and capitalists and the labour–capital contradiction and opposition that accompany it.
quoteZh: 尽管其研究侧重有所差异，但是对于现代资本主义社会劳动关系的本质即工人与资本家之间的不平等以及如影随行的劳资矛盾与对立，各派学者都持一致看法。

glossary.explanation: A policy goal in Chinese official discourse of stable, cooperative relations between employers and workers, restated at the 19th Party Congress in 2017.
A French school of political economy that analyses capitalism through changing institutional forms and accumulation regimes, with the wage relation at its centre.

t: French Staatswissenschaft (statistics of the state), social materialism and historical materialism
zh: 法国国势学、社会唯物主义与历史唯物主义
source: Journal of Guangxi University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 2
paras: Liu Bingjing asks what intellectual context lay behind the young Marx's turn to historical materialism in 1845, and argues that a neglected strand is French guoshixue, the nineteenth-century 'science of the state's condition', ancestor of modern statistics. Liu contends that its materialist study of social reality influenced List, Schulz and Marx alike, and formed a logical foundation for Marx's critique and overcoming of German classical philosophy.

The article has three parts. The first traces the emergence of French guoshixue after the defeat of Napoleon's empire in 1815, through figures such as Chaptal, Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès, up to its absorption into a state economics ministry in 1936. The second analyses the 'social materialism' that this discipline produced. The third examines its reception by Friedrich List, the German statistician Wilhelm Schulz and Marx, drawing on Marx's Paris, Manchester and London notebooks.

Liu argues that French statisticians, working to restore national strength after decline, treated social reality and above all material production as the basis of a nation's power. This differs from the natural materialism of the Enlightenment (Helvétius, Diderot, Holbach), since its object was the non-intuitive productive capacity built up through social activity: population, technology, education, labour organisation. Dupin even called it 'productive force'. Liu adds that the discipline had only a limited sense of history, because it stayed within the standpoint of bourgeois society. Marx's repeated excerpting of Chaptal, Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès, Liu argues, helped fill a gap in explaining how he moved from German classical philosophy to a discourse of production in The German Ideology, whose 'real positive science' echoes guoshixue's empiricism.

Liu stresses that historical materialism is not an imitation of this social materialism. Guoshixue defended bourgeois society and could not see alienation, class contradiction or the dialectical self-supersession of social forms. Marx's distinctive contribution, in Liu's view, is a historical understanding of social being as the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse. Recovering this context, Liu concludes, helps define the philosophical character and limits of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the intellectual prehistory of historical materialism, Marx's reading notebooks, or the history of statistics and political economy in France and Germany.
quoteEn: A profound understanding of the historicity of social being is the fundamental difference between Marx's historical materialism and the social materialism implicitly highlighted in guoshixue.
quoteZh: 对社会存在的历史性的深刻理解，是马克思历史唯物主义与国势学隐性凸显的社会唯物主义的根本区别。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese name for Statistik/Statistique in its early modern sense: a state-oriented empirical discipline surveying population, economy, military and social organisation, which preceded modern statistics.
The author's term for the materialist outlook implicit in French guoshixue, which treats socially constructed productive capacity, not natural objects, as the basis of national strength.
Marx and Engels's theory that social history develops from material production and the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse.

t: A critique of the historical subject in Western Marxism
zh: 西方马克思主义视域下的历史主体批判
source: Journal of Central South University (Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 4
paras: Who changes history? Li Gaorong takes up this question of the historical subject and asks how Western Marxism has answered it since the 1960s. Classical Marxism treats the working (proletarian) class as the revolutionary subject. The article argues that Western Marxist views moved from affirming this subject, to denying it, to dissolving it altogether. In the author's judgement, this left theory detached from practice.

The article sets out Marx's and Lenin's account of class as both an economic and a relational concept, and Marx's move from a class "in itself" to a class "for itself". It then surveys Western thinkers under two headings. Under "practical subject" it treats E. P. Thompson and Ellen Meiksins Wood, who defend the working class; André Gorz and Nicos Poulantzas, who rebuild or reclassify it; and Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe, who abolish it. Under "theoretical subject" it covers Lukács, Marcuse, French existentialism, Althusser and Alain Badiou. A closing section turns to Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt's "multitude" and the 2018 "yellow vests" movement. The author says the selection is deliberately broad and limited to a few typical figures.

Li argues that, as class structure changed and class politics gave way to identity and discourse politics, the subject was progressively emptied. Gorz's "new working class" and "non-class of non-workers" and Poulantzas's "new petty bourgeoisie" redefine class by technical or ideological criteria. Laclau and Mouffe then reject economic determination and replace class with a discursively built "popular alliance". On the theoretical side, Marcuse's "alienated man", Sartre's "Other" and Althusser's "process without a subject" shift attention from real classes to abstract human essence or to structures. In Li's reading this recalls the "German socialism" Marx criticised in the Communist Manifesto. Wood is presented as the main defender of an orthodox, relations-of-production view of class.

Li concludes that Western Marxism has been speculative from the start. Its "practice" is the practice of class consciousness, not material exchange between humans and nature, so it swings between determinism and voluntarism and offers no real path beyond capitalism. It ends up proposing reforms within capitalism, such as democratic socialism and red-green alliances. Negri and Hardt's multitude, which has neither class nor party organisation, is judged unpromising, and the yellow vests movement is described as cooling. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of how Western left thinkers from Lukács to Negri have treated the revolutionary subject.
quoteEn: This is the greatest defect of Western Marxist research: theory is seriously divorced from practice, and although it explains present-day capitalism well, it cannot change capitalism.
quoteZh: 这是西方马克思主义研究最大的缺陷：理论与实践严重脱节，理论尽管很好地解释了当今资本主义，却无法改变资本主义。

glossary.explanation: The agent understood to make or change history. In classical Marxism this is chiefly the working class; the article traces how Western Marxists have redefined or dissolved it.
The tradition of Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and French Marxism. The author uses the term broadly, to include later Anglo-American Marxists and left thinkers such as Gorz and Negri.
Negri and Hardt's term for a plural, non-unified revolutionary subject in the age of global "Empire". It differs from the traditional Marxist categories of working class, people and masses.

t: Dialectical phenomenology and the critical theory of Western Marxism: centred on Marcuse
zh: 辩证现象学与西方马克思主义批判理论——以马尔库塞为中心
source: Journal of Nanjing University (Philosophy, Humanities and Social Sciences), 2019 no. 4
paras: How can radical Marxist critical theory avoid becoming an abstract postulate? Xue starts from the turn after Althusser's late "materialism of the encounter". Althusser, Badiou and Žižek, the article says, stress contingent situations, events or an inner "Real" as triggers of radical action, but neglect how the proletariat is actually formed in history. Xue argues that Herbert Marcuse's "historical-materialist phenomenology" (or "dialectical phenomenology") offers a benchmark for a critical reassessment of these theories.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the shared problem and the respective flaws of Lukács and Heidegger, which Xue presents as Marcuse's starting point in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when he studied under Heidegger at Freiburg. The second reconstructs how Marcuse combines dialectics and phenomenology through Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit and Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The third uses the result to assess Heidegger, Sartre and Žižek and to draw a conclusion about critical theory.

Xue argues that Lukács's History and Class Consciousness cannot explain the passage from individual reified consciousness to totalising class consciousness. Xue also holds that it ignores nature's objective limits on practice, which gives it an idealist tendency. Heidegger's analysis of the historicity of Dasein, by contrast, stays abstract and quasi-transcendental. Marcuse, on Xue's account, joins the two. From Hegel he takes the process of objectification and mutual public criticism among selves, and from Marx's Manuscripts the material content and sensuous, receptive character of human life. The result is a historical ontology that unites individual self-understanding with awareness of material constraints. Judged by this standard, Xue says, Žižek's "dislocation" universality, pure-negativity class struggle and "parallax Real" cannot explain how a revolutionary subject is formed. Marcuse's route to liberating the instincts through "aesthetic form" is presented as more concrete.

Xue concludes that Marcuse's approach can supply a theoretical basis for piercing capitalist reification and reactivating Marxism's radical content. Xue adds that theories built around the subject, Marcuse's included, understand capitalist cultural psychology to a degree but neglect the structural content of historical materialism. Critique of ideology, the article contends, must therefore be pushed on to the critique of political economy. Read the original if you study Marcuse, the Lukács–Heidegger relation or Western Marxist debates on revolutionary subjectivity, and want a Chinese assessment of Žižek's theory of class struggle.
quoteEn: Only by pushing the critique of ideology forward to the level of the critique of political economy can a real critique of capitalist society be achieved.
quoteZh: 只有将意识形态批判推进到政治经济学批判的层面，才是真正实现对资本主义社会的现实批判。

t: A review of recent domestic research on Western Marxist critiques of capitalism
zh: 国内西方马克思主义资本主义批判研究动态述评
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theory, 2019 no. 6
paras: This review, published in 2019, surveys Chinese scholarship (mostly from 2018) on Western Marxist critiques of capitalism. Han and Sun start from the 2008 financial crisis and the growing role of finance capital combined with digital technology. They argue that domestic research has become more attentive to real-world problems and now needs to draw out the meaning of these critiques for China and to build Chinese discourse.

The review is organised in three parts. The first maps the research frontier in three areas: political-economy critiques of new capitalist economic forms, critiques of modernity, and political-philosophical critiques of ideology. The second identifies the methodological features of this work. The third sets out where the field can develop.

In the first part, the authors report that Chinese scholars treat digital, platform and financial capitalism, and the spatial-production theories of Lefebvre, David Harvey and Ellen Meiksins Wood, as new forms that do not change capital's exploitative logic. Under modernity they list meta-level studies of Western Marxist theory, cultural critiques of alienation and surveillance capitalism, and ecological Marxism (Foster, O'Connor, Gorz). Under ideology they cover neoliberalism, biopolitics, post-Marxist discourse politics and spatial politics. Han and Sun describe the field's features as combining historical review with sharper thematic focus, and as interdisciplinary 'surround the point to strike the relief force' and 'blossoming from the centre' approaches that return to Chinese realities. They judge Western Marxist critiques to be diverse and incisive but class-limited, incomplete and sometimes at odds with Marxism.

The authors conclude that research remains too general about China's relevance, too academic and speculative, and too weak in building its own theory. They call for work that moves beyond 'speaking after' and 'speaking along with' Western thinkers to 'speaking for oneself'. They also call for a Chinese discourse system, comparison of contemporary Chinese Marxism with foreign Marxism, and use of Western Marxist methods on problems China shares with capitalist modernity. Read the original if you want a map of 2018 Chinese-language literature on Western Marxism and capitalism, or insight into how Chinese scholars frame the purpose of foreign Marxism research.
quoteEn: Some current domestic research on Western Marxist critiques of capitalism leans towards academic, speculative interpretation and is somewhat weak in building its own system of thought.
quoteZh: 当今国内对西方马克思主义资本主义批判的研究部分表现出倾斜于学院化的理论逻辑思辨解读与阐释，而在思想体系的自我建构方面则略显力薄。

glossary.explanation: The tradition of Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and later thinkers, which stresses culture, philosophy and critique. In Chinese usage the review's scope also extends to many contemporary Western left thinkers.
A term in Chinese policy and academic debate for a country's own concepts and language in the humanities and social sciences. The aim is to gain 'discourse power' internationally.

t: Foreign left-wing scholars' new thinking on the market economy since the financial crisis, and its implications
zh: 金融危机以来国外左翼学者对市场经济的新思考及其启示
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2018 no. 7
paras: Liu Mingming asks how left-wing scholars outside China have reassessed the market economy since the global financial crisis of 2008, and what this means for China. The article argues that these scholars broadly see the crisis as the end of the laissez-faire market, reject the idea that state and market are opposed, and question the claimed link between free markets and democracy. Liu then draws four lessons for China's socialist market economy.

Liu defines the left by four positions: reading the crisis as a failure of neoliberal policy, opposing capitalism's profit logic, supporting economic democracy and equality, and favouring state intervention to protect the weak. The article surveys mainly Anglo-American and Canadian economists, sociologists and political thinkers, including Stiglitz, Barbera, Turner, Altman, Reich, Malleson, Engler, Schweickart, Lane, Ollman and Campbell. It has five sections: the end of the laissez-faire market, the state–market relationship, markets and democracy, markets and the nature of the social system, and implications for China.

Liu reports that these scholars treat markets as constructed by the state through money, property and contract law, so that regulation creates markets rather than merely restricting them. Drawing on Malleson, the article sets out how unequal spending power, monopoly, externalities, public goods, short horizons and collective choice make markets undemocratic. On the market and the social system, Liu finds a split. Engler and the market socialists Schweickart and Lane hold that markets can be separated from capitalism and combined with public ownership or economic democracy. Ollman and Campbell hold that markets reproduce alienation and are incompatible with socialism.

Liu draws four lessons for China. China should keep to market-oriented reform and not swing 'leftward' because of the crisis. It should not use the market's decisive role in allocating resources to deny the government's role in public goods and risk regulation. It should not make excessive concessions to win market-economy status from the United States, the EU or Japan, whom Liu accuses of double standards on economic freedom. It should handle the relations between the market, socialism and democracy carefully, since the market is a tool that can serve different systems. Liu also warns that interest groups could use investment, employment and price monopoly to interfere in politics. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's survey of Western left debates on markets, with references, and the policy lessons drawn from them for China.
quoteEn: Clearly, the relationship between state and market is not a zero-sum game.
quoteZh: 显然, 国家与市场之间的关系不是零和博弈。

glossary.explanation: China's official name for its economic system, adopted in the early 1990s. It combines market mechanisms with public ownership and state guidance.
A strand of Western socialist thought that holds that markets and competition can operate under social or public ownership. Schweickart and Lane are among its advocates in the article.

A trade-law designation affecting how anti-dumping cases are assessed. Under China's WTO accession protocol, China expected to receive it after 15 years, but the United States, the EU and Japan have not granted it.

t: The contemporary value of Marxism and its implications, seen through foreign left-wing scholars
zh: 国外左翼学者视域下马克思主义的当代价值及启示
source: Frontiers of Foreign Social Sciences (国外社会科学前沿), 2019 no. 8
paras: Writing in 2019, Zhuo Mingliang reviews how foreign left-wing scholars have assessed the contemporary value of Marxism. The article is a survey of recent writing, prompted by anniversaries (the October Revolution, Marx's bicentenary, the Communist Manifesto, the Comintern) and by the 2008 financial crisis. Zhuo's thesis is that these scholars show Marxism remains vital and refutes claims that it is obsolete, and that China should draw lessons from them, including closer dialogue with them.

The review draws on articles from several dozen left-wing journals and websites, among them Monthly Review, New Left Review, Historical Materialism, Socialism and Democracy and Review of African Political Economy. It is organised in four sections: Marxism's continuing theoretical appeal; its critique of capitalism and the political options it offers the oppressed; its capacity to guide the future world socialist movement; and the need to keep Marxism dialectically open and adapted to national conditions. A short conclusion draws out three implications.

Zhuo reports that Victor Wallis, Masao Suzuki, Immanuel Wallerstein and David McLellan treat Marx's analysis of exploitation, surplus value and class struggle as still applicable to neoliberal capitalism and the 2008 crisis. Suzuki, for example, cites Amazon's profits against its workers' pay. Party leaders such as Jose Maria Sison, Sitaram Yechury and Elizabeth Rowley are cited as urging study of Marx's works and their application in struggle, led by the working class. Other voices, notably Kemal Okuyan, are reported as warning that Marxism offers no ready-made blueprint and must not be treated as a closed dogma.

Zhuo concludes that the foreign scholars' views support the truth and vitality of Marxism and rebut the 'uselessness' and 'obsolescence' arguments. The author adds that Marxism's vitality is also shown in the Party's adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and calls for greater confidence in theory and for arming minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhuo also urges stronger academic dialogue with foreign left scholars and communist parties. Read the original if you want a map of the left-wing journals and figures a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on to argue for Marxism's present relevance.
quoteEn: Foreign left-wing scholars are firmly convinced of Marxism's contemporary value, yet they also rationally point out that Marxism should not be seen as a fixed, self-enclosed theoretical system, nor should its specific theories be understood one-sidedly.
quoteZh: 国外左翼学者对马克思主义的当代价值深信不疑，但也理性地指出，不应当把马克思主义看成是牢固不变的自我封闭的理论体系，不应当片面地理解马克思主义的具体理论。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China, written into the Party constitution in 2017 and the state constitution in 2018.

glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism to Chinese conditions and developing it through Chinese practice. The article pairs it with 时代化 (adapting to the times).
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership with a market economy.

t: The crisis of civilisation and its challenge to the Left
zh: 文明的危机及其对左翼的挑战
orig: Introduction to Beyond Development: Alternative Visions from Latin America (Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, Quito), edited by Miriam Lang and Dunia Mokrani
source: Theory and Criticism (理论与评论), 2018 no. 1
paras: This is a Chinese translation of Miriam Lang's introduction to the volume she co-organised, Beyond Development: Alternative Visions from Latin America, published with the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation's Andean office. Lang argues that the overlapping financial, food, energy and ecological crises amount to a 'crisis of civilisation', felt most acutely at the world's margins. In her account, the Left must now do more than criticise capitalism: it must build alternatives to the very idea of 'development'.

The introduction opens with global extractivism and the 'green economy', then turns to the Andean region, where Bolivia, Ecuador and Venezuela adopted new constitutions after pressure from peasant, women's, urban and indigenous movements. It next presents the Permanent Working Group on Alternatives to Development, founded in 2010, and previews the book's chapters by Eduardo Gudynas, Alberto Acosta, Edgardo Lander, Ulrich Brand, Maristella Svampa, Raúl Prada and Elisa Vega.

Lang contends that the Andean 'progressive' governments, despite breaking in part with neoliberalism, remain trapped in what the working group calls the 'Latin American paradox': to fund social programmes they expand mining, oil, gas and agrofuels, which brings them into conflict with their own constitutions and grassroots bases. Citing Foucault and Arturo Escobar, she treats 'development' as a Western, capitalist and colonial power device that labels Southern ways of life 'backward'. She adds that 'really existing socialism' and much of the Latin American Left accepted the concept, equating prosperity with consumption. Against this she sets buen vivir, the rights of nature and plurinational statehood, while Gudynas proposes a gradual path from predatory to 'sensible' to 'indispensable' extractivism.

Lang presents the book as only a first attempt at a theory of alternatives to development, with the creation of models of good living in cities as the next task. She notes that the Left, which is skilled at critique and tends to define itself negatively, must now look for partners' strengths and think what has seemed impossible. The Chinese editors' preface claims the book exposes neoliberalism and offers ideas useful for socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want an overview of Latin American post-development and anti-extractivist debates, and of how the Andean 'progressive' governments are assessed from within the Left.
quoteEn: Development almost inevitably ties us to a particular way of thinking: a Western, capitalist and colonialist one.
quoteZh: 发展几乎不可避免地将我们与某种特定的思维方式相联系——即西方的、资本主义的、殖民主义的思维方式。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, in use since the 1980s. It appears here only in the Chinese editors' preface to the translation.

t: Greed and fear: a new interpretation of financial crisis in contemporary capitalism
zh: 贪婪与恐惧：当代资本主义金融危机的新阐释
source: Trends in Foreign Theory (Guowai Lilun Dongtai), 2019 no. 6
paras: Writing in 2019, with US stock indices at record highs and quantitative easing being wound down, Kong Ming'an asks whether the 2008 subprime crisis has really passed and how the new features of US-led financial capitalism should be explained. The article presents Slavoj Žižek's answer, which combines Lacanian psychoanalysis with Marxist dialectics. On this reading, Marx's analysis of capitalism is not outdated, but twentieth-century capitalism runs on financial speculation rather than labour and production. Kong holds that Žižek's approach is original yet cannot replace Marxist crisis theory.

The article is a critical exposition of Žižek's analysis, drawing mainly on his In Defense of Lost Causes and Tarrying with the Negative. It has four parts: the desiring subject and the signifier logic of financial markets; the empty subject and the remedies for crisis; Keynesianism and the fate of capitalism; and a conclusion on charitable giving by the rich. Kong also sets out Lacan's concepts of desire as metonymy, the objet petit a (surplus enjoyment), the Other and the 'Name-of-the-Father'.

Kong first reports that, for Žižek, market actors look rational but are driven by unconscious desire, so that greed and fear coexist in one paradoxical subject. Speculation on stock and futures markets becomes a game of sliding along a chain of signifiers, and rumour alone can wipe out a firm's value. Second, a crisis opens a 'void' like the one the Lacanian subject fears, and states fill it with Keynesian money-printing and deficit spending. Žižek calls this a poisoned remedy: it borrows from the future, and electronic money is a 'ghost' that cannot erase the debt. Kong adds that Žižek treats this as confirming Marx's prediction that capitalism will perish, though the end is postponed.

Kong concludes that Marx's judgement on capitalism's inevitable demise remains valid, and that virtual capital, credit expansion and expansionary policy have delayed the crisis rather than abolished it. Žižek also gives partial approval to philanthropy by billionaires, which he says delays crisis because capitalism cannot reproduce itself unaided. Kong criticises psychoanalysis for hiding the institutional dimension, since crises arise from the capitalist system itself. Kong adds that donations by Gates, Soros and Buffett are a drop in the ocean compared with private appropriation and do not change the system's nature. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Žižek's Lacanian account of finance, Keynesianism and digital capitalism.
quoteEn: Žižek's analysis obscures the dimension of institutional analysis: it overlooks that capitalist crises are caused by the capitalist system itself and are its necessary product.
quoteZh: 齐泽克的分析遮盖了“制度”分析的维度, 即忽视了资本主义危机的爆发是由资本主义制度本身所造成的, 是资本主义制度本身的必然产物。

t: The problem of the subject in the logic of capital: from Marx to Badiou
zh: 资本逻辑中的主体问题:从马克思到巴迪欧
paras: Yuan Bei asks how a human subject can escape domination by the logic of capital, at a time when 'the death of the subject' is a widespread theme in Western Marxism and radical left thought. Taking Alain Badiou as the leading radical-left figure engaging with Marxism, the article argues that his theory of a subject faithful to a 'truth event' responds to this problem. Yuan also contends that the theory is limited by its neglect of the economic sphere and suggests that Badiou should restore the revolutionary potential of truth events to the economy.

The article is built in three parts plus a conclusion. It first sets out Marx's treatment of the subject, in general history and under capitalism. It then traces two lines in the Marxist tradition: a subject-centred one running from Lukács to Sartre, and an 'anti-subject' one running from the Second International to Althusser, with the Frankfurt School as a pessimistic middle case. The third part reconstructs Badiou's theory of the subject through his critique of 'democratic materialism' and his distinction between being and event, drawing on Žižek, Harvey and Lazzarato along the way.

Yuan's central reasoning begins from Marx's claim that under capital the human being is only the personification of economic categories. Capital, as self-expanding value, acquires an apparent 'subjectivity' while workers and capitalists become its bearers, and Althusser's structure without a subject is read as a theoretical echo of this. Badiou's answer, in Yuan's account, is that the formal, counting-as-one structure of the capitalist commodity world has a 'void' at its edge. A contingent event can erupt there, and a subject is not given in advance but is generated by fidelity to that event, so that scattered individuals are gathered into a single revolutionary subject.

Yuan concludes that Badiou's subject theory is distinctly political: it treats the economy as belonging to the order of being, with no evental sites, and so leaves Marx's critique of political economy aside. Yuan reports the criticism that the event appears like a miracle, leaving people merely waiting. Citing Žižek's call to return to Lenin and Marx's remarks on the realm of freedom resting on the realm of necessity, Yuan holds that emancipation also requires developed productive forces as a material basis. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Badiou that links his event philosophy to Lukács, Althusser and the Frankfurt School debates on the subject.
quoteEn: It should be recognised that the key to the emancipation of the subject has never been confined to the ideological sphere; it lies in whether the universal interaction and association required for collective struggle have a highly developed productivity as their material basis.
quoteZh: 应该看到, 主体解放的关键从来不是仅限于意识形态领域, 而是集体性斗争所需要的普遍交往和联合是否有高度发展的生产力为其提供物质基础。

glossary.explanation: A theme in French structuralism and postmodern thought that the autonomous, rational human subject is dissolved by structures, language or power. The article traces its Marxist forms from the Second International to Althusser.
Badiou's label for the dominant Western ideology, summed up as 'there are only bodies and languages', which in his view replaces the pursuit of universal truth with plural opinions.

t: The difficulties of the Latin American left have no single cause
zh: 拉美左翼困境非单一因素所致
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 27 December 2018
paras: Writing in December 2018, Jin Chengwei takes up the "left down, right up" shift in Latin American politics. Drawing on interviews with leaders and officials of communist, socialist and other left-wing parties in several countries, Jin argues that the left's difficulties come from a combination of factors, not one cause, and that the left still has room to grow.

The short commentary has three parts. It lists the causes of the left's decline, sets out the tasks the left faces, and recalls the region's long left-wing tradition. It closes with four questions that Jin suggests scholars should study.

On causes, Jin reports seven factors. They include economic stagnation, which the right exploited after the financial crisis, and weak party-building and organisation. Others are the lack of strategic thinking, governing inexperience, a left that is united only in words and fragmented in practice, and a failure to keep close ties with the public. The last is US efforts to restore its hegemony and undermine regional integration. The interviewees name three urgent tasks: left unity, winning over public opinion against right-controlled media, and building stronger parties.

Jin ends with research questions. Why did the 2008 crisis not spur left social movements, and how does it compare with earlier crises? How should the left be defined, given disputed typologies? Why does fragmentation persist, and how can new media help parties reach the public? Read the original if you want a brief account of how Latin American left-wing party figures explained their setbacks, and an agenda for further research.
quoteEn: The struggle in the ideological sphere is the greatest struggle; ways must be found to educate and influence the public's thinking so that they understand why to struggle and how.
quoteZh: 意识领域的斗争是最大的斗争，要想办法教育、影响民众的观念，使其明白为何斗争、如何斗争。

t: Seventy years of research on foreign Marxist philosophy in China: review and prospects
zh: 国外马克思主义哲学研究70年：回顾与展望
source: Journal of Wuhan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 4
paras: Writing in 2019, Zhang Liang asks how Chinese scholarship on foreign Marxist philosophy has developed since 1949 and where it should go next. The article rejects the common view that the field began only with reform and opening up in 1978. Zhang argues that the seventy years form a process in which Chinese scholars, grounded in socialism with Chinese characteristics, steadily narrowed the distance to foreign Marxist thought. The field is now said to be running "alongside" it and seeking to break through and "lead".

The article is a periodised history of the field in five parts. It covers a neglected 1949–1978 "prehistory", the rise of research on Western Marxism from 1978, a phase of deeper development from the early 1990s, and the boom since the early 2000s together with its drawbacks. It ends with proposals for the future. Zhang draws on journals, translation series, institutional centres, rough publication counts and the debate between Xu Chongwen and Du Zhangzhi, as well as personal experience of the Foreign Marxism Forum.

Zhang holds that the "prehistory" was not empty. Information journals, translated reference collections and Soviet-era commentaries, notably the Chinese edition of Leopold Labedz's Revisionism, trained the first researchers and supplied theoretical preparation. The later phases are traced to specific causes: the global prominence of Western Marxism, the political meaning of the topic, and a sense that Western Marxism described China's own market-economy experience. The boom is traced mainly to the 2004 Marxist theory research and construction project and the 2005 creation of foreign Marxism as a second-level discipline. Zhang lists its features: a large academic population, high output, thematic diversity, and almost no time lag behind Western intellectual production. He also voices three worries: loss of the original purpose of serving Chinese problems, loss of a sense of historical position, and decline in scholarly discernment.

For the future, Zhang calls for using historical materialism to rethink China's position, so that Chinese scholars treat foreign Marxist philosophy as equal interlocutors rather than as followers. He urges scholars to study foreign Marxism in order to address Chinese problems and build a Chinese Marxist philosophical system. He also calls for testing foreign theories in the Chinese context, challenging their biases on actually existing socialism and the Chinese path, and moving beyond textual study. Finally, he urges China to become a world centre of Marxist philosophical research. Read the original if you want a detailed insider account of how foreign Marxism studies in China were organised, debated and justified, and of the policy stance behind the field's expansion.
quoteEn: The seventy years of research on foreign Marxist philosophy have been seventy years in which Chinese academia, grounded in the reality of socialism with Chinese characteristics, breathing with the times, sharing the fate of the people and merging with practice, steadily narrowed its distance from foreign Marxist philosophical thought.
quoteZh: 国外马克思主义哲学研究的70年，就是中国学术界立足中国特色社会主义现实，与时代同呼吸、与人民共命运、与实践共交融，不断缩小与国外马克思主义哲学思想距离的70年。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese academic field covering Marxist thought outside China and outside the orthodoxy China recognises. It became a second-level discipline within Marxist theory in 2005.
The tradition of Lukács, the Frankfurt School, Sartre, Althusser and others, named by Perry Anderson in 1974. It was long the main focus of Chinese research on foreign Marxism.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义理论研究和建设工程
glossary.pinyin: Mǎkèsīzhǔyì lǐlùn yánjiū hé jiànshè gōngchéng
glossary.en: Marxist theory research and construction project
glossary.explanation: A Party-led programme launched in 2004 to promote Marxist theory research, textbooks and disciplinary building in universities and research institutes.
The official name for China's current path and system, introduced in the early 1980s under Deng Xiaoping.
Marx and Engels' theory that social life and material production shape consciousness. Zhang uses it to reassess China's position relative to foreign Marxist currents.

t: French Staatenkunde, social materialism and historical materialism
zh: 法国国势学、社会唯物主义与历史唯物主义
source: Journal of Guangxi University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 2
paras: Modern statistics grew out of an older empirical science of state governance, known in Chinese as guóshìxué (here rendered "Staatenkunde" or science of the state's condition). Liu Bingjing argues that research on Marx's historical materialism has overlooked the link between the young Marx and this French tradition. In Liu's account, French Staatenkunde produced a "social materialism" that influenced List, Schulz and Marx alike, and formed a logical foundation for Marx's move in 1845 beyond German classical philosophy.

The article has three parts. The first traces the formation of French Staatenkunde after the decline of Napoleonic France (1815–1848), from Chaptal's statistical office to Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès, who established it as an independent government science; it was absorbed into the economics ministry in 1936. The second analyses its materialist discourse. The third asks why the subject matters, by tracing its reception by Friedrich List, the German statistician Schulz and Marx, whose Paris, Manchester and London notebooks record readings of Chaptal, Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès.

Liu's central claim is that French Staatenkunde treated social reality, above all material production, as the basis of national strength. Liu distinguishes this from the natural materialism of Helvétius, Diderot and Holbach, because its object was the non-intuitable productive capacity built up through social activity, which Dupin named "productive force". It also sought laws behind economic phenomena, unlike the abstraction Moreau de Jonnès saw in classical political economy, and it had a limited sense of history. Liu proposes that contact with this empirical literature helped Marx to turn from German classical philosophy to the German Ideology's "real, positive science", which Liu sees as echoing the field's slogan that sophistry collapses before facts.

Liu stresses that historical materialism is not a copy of social materialism. Because Staatenkunde defended bourgeois society, Liu argues, it could not see alienation, class contradiction or the dialectical movement between productive forces and forms of intercourse. Its significance, for Liu, is that it fills a gap in the account of Marx's 1845 turn and helps define the philosophical character and limits of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the intellectual prehistory of historical materialism, Marx's notebooks, or the links between statistics, political economy and Marx's thought.
quoteEn: A profound understanding of the historicity of social being is the fundamental difference between Marx's historical materialism and the social materialism implicit in Staatenkunde.
quoteZh: 对社会存在的历史性的深刻理解，是马克思历史唯物主义与国势学隐性凸显的社会唯物主义的根本区别。

glossary.explanation: An 18th–19th century European empirical discipline studying a state's population, economy, military and institutions, regarded as a precursor of modern statistics. It was named by Gottfried Achenwall in 1749.
The author's term for the materialist discourse implicit in French Staatenkunde, which takes social reality and material production, not nature, as foundational.
Marx and Engels' theory of history, which the author sees as first set out in The German Ideology (1845).

t: Several hot topics in world socialism studies in 2018
zh: 2018年世界社会主义研究的几个热点问题
paras: This is a review of the main themes in world socialism studies in 2018, written by two doctoral students and published in World Socialism Studies in 2019. It does not advance a single thesis. It reports what Chinese and foreign scholars, Party figures and research institutions said and produced on four topics, treating historical materialism as the guiding framework for the field.

The review is organised in four sections: using historical materialism to guide research on world socialism; research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; summing up the experience and lessons of the world socialist movement; and the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth together with the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. It draws on forums, conferences, journal articles, books and foreign commentary.

In the first section, the authors cite Xi Jinping's 2017 judgement that, seen across 500 years of world socialism, we still live in the historical era Marxism identified. At the ninth World Socialism Forum (November 2018), Zhu Jiamu, Li Shenming and Zhang Quanjing are reported as reading the present as an era of transition from capitalism to socialism or communism. Zhang Quanjing locates the main contradiction in US–China relations. The second section lists Chinese studies of the Thought's theoretical content and its logical structure, and quotes favourable foreign assessments. The third section reports a Party-education film on historical nihilism and the Soviet collapse, and publications from the CASS World Socialism Research Centre, including the annual tracking report, a popular book series and the ten-volume History of the Development of Marxism.

On the anniversaries, the review cites Xie Fuzhan's statement that Marxism is a developing theory, and Gennady Zyuganov's tribute to Marx. It also cites Western commentators who hold that the failure of Soviet socialism does not refute Marx. Chinese studies of the Manifesto are summarised for their bearing on globalisation, a community with a shared future for mankind, and distributive justice. The review ends without a separate conclusion, and its overall impression is of steady, institutionally backed growth in the field. Read the original if you want a quick map of the 2018 Chinese literature, conferences and publications on world socialism, with references to the sources cited.
quoteEn: Research on Xi Jinping's socialism with Chinese characteristics for a new era mainly addresses its theoretical content, its logic and its essence, along with politics, the economy, society, culture, Party building, ecology and poverty governance, and has produced a series of valuable results.
quoteZh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义研究主要涉及理论内涵、思想逻辑、精神实质以及政治、经济、社会、文化、党建、生态、贫困治理等，形成了一系列有价值的研究成果。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name for Xi Jinping's body of ideas, written into the Party constitution in 2017. Chinese official sources present it as the current stage of adapting Marxism to China.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept associated with Xi Jinping, calling for shared international development and security. It is presented officially as a guiding idea for China's diplomacy.
In Chinese official usage, a label for views that negate the Party's or socialism's history. Here the term is linked to the Soviet collapse.
The Marxist theory that material production and social relations shape historical development. The article treats it as the guiding principle of world socialism studies.
An international forum hosted by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The ninth was held in Beijing in November 2018.

t: Christian Fuchs: the internet has not changed the essence of capitalism
st: Digital labour from a Marxist perspective
zh: 克里斯蒂安·福克斯:互联网没有改变资本主义的本质
zhSub: 马克思主义视野下的数字劳动
paras: This is an interview, framed by the authors' commentary, with Christian Fuchs, a British Marxist communication scholar at the University of Westminster and editor of the journal triple C. Chang Jiang puts the questions. The authors present Fuchs as the developer of the concept of 'digital labour', and the interview's central message, as the title states, is that the internet has not altered the essential nature of capitalism. It was first published in the journal Journalism Review (Xinwenjie), 2019, no. 4.

The authors open with a short profile of Fuchs, listing his major books, including Digital Labour and Karl Marx and Culture and Economy in the Age of Social Media. The interview then moves through four themes: the definition of digital labour; the political economy of the internet and social movements; alternatives to commercial platforms; and the place of Marxism in communication studies. The authors add short evaluative passages after each section and end by suggesting that Chinese researchers apply the digital-labour framework to China's internet industry.

Fuchs argues that corporate platforms depend on capital accumulation and so exploit users, whose unpaid posting, sharing and uploading generates the data commodity sold to advertisers. He builds on Dallas Smythe's audience commodity theory, but notes new features such as real-time surveillance, prosumption and algorithmic ad auctions. He rejects 'immaterial labour' as a dualist notion, and calls social media 'targeted advertising platforms' whose profits are unstable. He criticises both techno-optimism and the dismissal of digital media in protest, and calls for empirical, Marxist research on social movements.

On remedies, Fuchs rejects 'Wages for Facebook' as reformism that would only lower exploitation. He proposes taxing advertising and corporations to fund a 'participatory media fee' for non-commercial platforms, public-service alternatives to YouTube, and university-run search engines. In his view a fair internet requires overthrowing capitalism, and he cites the choice between socialism and barbarism. The authors read him as pessimistic about digital media but committed to revolutionary change. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement of Fuchs's digital-labour theory, his criticisms of mainstream communication research and 'New Reading of Marx', and how Chinese media scholars received him.
quoteEn: Within a capitalist context, only a capitalist internet will develop.
quoteZh: 在资本主义背景下, 将只会发展出资本主义的互联网。

t: Digits, technology, capital: the generative logic of digital capitalism
zh: 数字·技术·资本:数字资本主义的生成逻辑
source: Journal of Shenyang University (Social Science Edition), 2018 no. 6
paras: Wang Zhidong and Ye Shenghua ask how digital data become capital and how digital capitalism comes into being. Taking up the concept introduced by Dan Schiller in the late 1990s, they argue that the apparently free and democratic internet is in fact an alliance of the internet with capital. In their account, digital technology has become the most advanced productive force, data the capital that capitalists compete to seize, and digital labour a new object of exploitation for surplus value. The article, published in 2018, is filed under foreign Marxism.

The article is organised in four steps: digital platforms, digital labour, digital capital and a concluding section. It begins with the commercial history of the internet, from a military and academic network to a corporate one, and with the rise of platforms such as LinkedIn, MySpace, Facebook and Groupon. It then reviews definitions of digital labour by Tiziana Terranova and Christian Fuchs, and Lan Jiang's notion of 'general data'. Next it examines how data are turned into capital, and it closes with proposals.

The authors make three main moves. First, they treat the digital platform as the equivalent of the factory under industrial capitalism, the field where capital invests in and exploits users. They argue that platforms use free services to enclose a user market and then turn to profit-making. Second, they hold that digital labour is the root of digital capitalism. Users' searches, reading, play and social activity generate data; under privacy terms and user agreements, control of these data passes to platform owners, who pay no wages while capital appropriates all the value created. Third, they argue that data become digital capital through commodification, monopoly and enclosure of the formerly public internet. Digital capital then earns profit by selling market analysis to industrial and financial capital and by targeted advertising, and later through paid services and further platforms.

The authors conclude that digital capital turns non-working time into labour time, blurs work and life, and draws in users of every age. Exploitation therefore persists in a more hidden form, supported by an ideology of free participation, sharing and fun. They do not call for abandoning digital technology. They propose cultivating critical media literacy and building a non-commercial internet governed by the logic of the people rather than of capital, with shared data and a mechanism for sharing 'general data', citing Marx on the community as the condition of individual freedom. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist account of digital labour and data as capital, drawing on Schiller, Terranova, Fuchs and Lan Jiang.
quoteEn: Digital labour has become a new form of exploitation in digital capitalist society and is the root of the formation and accumulation of digital capital.
quoteZh: 数字劳动成为数字资本主义社会一种新的剥削形态, 是数字资本形成与积累的根源。

t: The digital shadow of existence: a philosophical critique of digital capitalism
zh: 生存的数字之影：数字资本主义的哲学批判
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2019 no. 3
paras: Lan Jiang asks what happens to human existence when global capitalism enters a digital stage, and argues that the change calls for philosophical analysis as well as economic description. Using the film Ying (Shadow) as a metaphor, the article claims that the digital identities we hold online have become a 'shadow' that increasingly dominates the embodied subject it was meant to represent. Digital capitalism, in Lan's reading, therefore produces a new form of alienation.

The article moves in three steps. It first contrasts the body-centred existentialism of Merleau-Ponty and Michel Henry with today's online life, introducing the concept of the 'virtual body' (xuti), a data package produced by algorithms. It then draws on Marx's Grundrisse and Jean Baudrillard's Critique of the Political Economy of the Sign to describe how things become 'coded'. Finally it turns to Marx's alienated labour, with reference to Gorz, Virno, Negri, Lazzarato and Christian Fuchs on immaterial and digital labour.

Lan sets out a four-stage logic running from the concrete thing to the commodity to the sign and finally to a sign system that governs things. The article maps this onto the body and the virtual body: from occasional contact, as with email, to virtual bodies that are always online, then to a network of data exchange separate from bodies, and finally to a network that acts back on bodies. The relation 'body–body′' (B–B′) thus becomes 'body→virtual body–virtual body′→body′' (B→V–V′→B′), which Lan calls a new digital dialectic. Drawing on Virno's reading of Marx's 'general intellect', the article treats time spent on phones and platforms as unrecognised digital labour. The virtual body is cast as a product of that labour that returns to control its makers, as Lan sees in the Cambridge Analytica case.

Lan concludes that despair is not the answer. Data, like technology, has no stance of its own: in the hands of digital capitalists it is a tool of enslavement, but in the hands of users it could become a weapon. The article proposes data sharing, or a 'communism of sharing', as the prospect of liberation, and argues that digitisation brings Marx's communism closer. Read the original if you want a philosophical account, drawing on phenomenology, Baudrillard and Italian autonomist thought, of how digital identity, data and labour can be read as a new form of alienation.
quoteEn: Data, like technology, has no stance of its own; in itself it is only a sharp tool.
quoteZh: 数据与技术一样, 它们并没有立场, 它们本身只是一把利器

glossary.explanation: Lan Jiang's term for a person's digital identity, conceived as an algorithmically generated data package that exists in cyberspace alongside the physical body. Lan developed it in earlier work on digital capitalism.
A term Marx used in the Grundrisse for socially accumulated knowledge as a productive force. Italian autonomist thinkers such as Paolo Virno later developed it.

t: Reification: a reflection on culture, or on the economic and social whole?
zh: 物化:文化之思还是经济社会整体之思?
paras: Liu Senlin asks how the meaning of "reification" (Verdinglichung and Versachlichung, used here in a broad sense that covers both) shifts between Marx's Capital and its manuscripts and Lukács's History and Class Consciousness. The article argues that Lukács turned reification into a mainly cultural and aesthetic category. Marx, in his mature work, treated it within an integrated economic, social and cultural whole. Liu contends that reification research should return to Marx's method.

The article is organised in six parts. It treats reification in turn as an economic-philosophical, a social-philosophical and a cultural-philosophical category. It then discusses the balance between philosophy and economics, and traces Lukács's position to the intellectual climate of Dilthey, Simmel and Weber. Liu draws on Robert Albritton, Axel Honneth, Kafka, Alain Touraine and Lockmore, and compares Marx's 1844 Manuscripts with the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital.

Liu argues first that reification is in its basic sense an economic fact, the structural logic of capital. In this logic, people become bearers of functions and abstract social relations are "real abstractions". Marx, in Liu's reading, judged this stage historically progressive. Weber's rationalisation then neutralised the critical charge of Versachlichung, and Lukács added the themes of fragmentation, loss of totality and subjectivity. Second, Liu holds that Lukács equated reification with alienation on the basis of modern subject-philosophy. This is the "romantic" nostalgia Marx rejected, and Liu says Honneth repeats it. Third, Liu argues that Lukács claimed an interdisciplinary totality while excluding economics and law, so philosophy and economics fell out of balance. Liu reads this as closer to the 1844 Manuscripts than to Capital. Liu explains Lukács's stance as a worry about relativism and nihilism, which Liu calls understandable but methodologically open to question.

Liu concludes that reification must be assessed from economic, social and cultural angles together. It is legitimate within reasonable limits, since it serves efficiency, shorter socially necessary labour time and basic fairness. It also carries the negative tendency of replacing human value and dignity with commodities and social-relation things, and it should not erode higher values. Liu calls for a return from Lukács to Marx's methodological stance, and for bridges between philosophy and economics and between the two cultures. Read the original if you study the Lukács–Marx relation, the reification–alienation distinction, or Chinese scholarly readings of Western Marxism.
quoteEn: We must return from Lukács to the Marx of the Capital period.
quoteZh: 必须从卢卡奇回到《资本论》时期的马克思。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of both Verdinglichung and Versachlichung. Marx used these terms for how human relations take the form of things, and Lukács developed them in History and Class Consciousness.
Entfremdung: the estrangement of workers from their product, activity and species-being, discussed in Marx's 1844 Manuscripts. Liu argues it is a different category from reification.
A notion Liu takes from Albritton: abstractions such as value and abstract labour are produced by capital's own operation, not just by thought.
The tradition associated with Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School. In China it falls within the broader field of foreign Marxism.

t: Rediscovering the critical logic of reification in Marxism
st: A conceptual-history study of Marx, Lukács and the Frankfurt School
zh: 马克思主义“物化”批判逻辑的再发现
zhSub: 基于对马克思、卢卡奇与法兰克福学派的概念史考察
source: Social Science Research (Shehui kexue yanjiu), 2019 no. 3
paras: Zhang Yixiu asks why discussions of "reification" in Chinese and English-language Marxist scholarship have left the overall line of Marxist reification critique unclear. The article's answer is that the literature has repeatedly merged two German concepts with different meanings, Verdinglichung and Versachlichung. Working from the German originals, Zhang proposes rendering the first as "reification" and the second as "thingification" (事物化), and reconstructs how the logic of critique develops across Marx, Lukács and the Frankfurt School.

The article has three main sections. The first clarifies terms, separating Vergegenständlichung (objectification) from the other two, and then reads Marx's use of the paired concepts in his critique of fetishism, tracing their background to Kant and Hegel. The second re-reads Lukács's History and Class Consciousness, comparing his usage with that of Weber, Simmel and Sombart. The third follows the Frankfurt School from Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment to Adorno's Negative Dialectics, and closes with Hironaka Wataru's reading and Axel Honneth's Reification: A Recognition-Theoretical Study.

In Zhang's reading, Marx uses Versachlichung for the essential level, where production relations appear as relations among things, and Verdinglichung for the phenomenal level, where those things appear as personified objects with their own properties. Lukács, Zhang argues, was the first to systematise reification as a theory. He also critiqued Versachlichung, which Weber saw as rationalisation, and thereby turned Weber's modernity theory against itself. His critique, however, is anchored in the un-reified human being and in proletarian class consciousness, not in production relations, which gives it a humanist cast. Horkheimer and Adorno, in this account, kept the two concepts apart and went further: they treated the objective mechanism of Versachlichung as more fundamental than reification and as unshakeable. Adorno ultimately declared Lukács's project of negating reification both impossible and mistaken.

Zhang concludes that this reconstruction restores the thread of Marxist reification critique, which moves from Marx's relational method, through Lukács's philosophy of the subject, to Adorno's rejection of it. The article notes that Hironaka's critique of Lukács is on target even though his reading of Marx is not fully accurate. It also suggests that Honneth's work shows the two concepts still matter to the Western left. Read the original if you work on Lukács, the Frankfurt School or Marx's theory of fetishism and want a German-language terminological analysis of the reification/thingification distinction.
quoteEn: In short, Marx used the two concepts of "thingification" and "reification" together to outline the logic of capitalist fetishism: capitalist relations of production first transform themselves into things, achieving "thingification", and then appear in inverted form as merely mysterious objects, achieving "reification".
quoteZh: 总之, 马克思用“事物化”与“物化”这两个概念, 共同勾勒出资本主义拜物教的逻辑:资本主义生产关系首先将自身转化为事物, 实现了“事物化”, 而后又颠倒地表现为单纯而又神秘的对象之物, 实现了“物化”。

t: Correctly understanding the contemporary value of Marxism since the financial crisis
st: From the perspective of foreign left-wing scholars
zh: 正确认识金融危机以来马克思主义的时代价值
zhSub: 基于国外左翼学者的视角
source: Studies on Ideological Education (Sixiang jiaoyu yanjiu), 2018 no. 6
paras: Liu asks whether Marxism can recover vitality in the twenty-first century. The article sets this against the collapse of the Soviet bloc, the most severe recession since the 1930s and the charge that Marxism is outdated. It draws on Western and other foreign left-wing scholars. Liu's answer is that the 2008 financial crisis renewed Marxism's relevance, and that the twenty-first century will be a century of Marxism.

The article has four parts. The first surveys the revival of "Marx talk" after the crisis, citing Terry Eagleton, Stavros Tombazos, Marcello Musto, Eric Hobsbawm and the non-Marxist Ronald Dworkin. The second compares explanations of the crisis by Charles Dumenil-style underconsumption theorists and others, namely Charles Dumain's counterpart Charles Derber, David Schweickart and Andrew Kliman. The third examines how these scholars read Marx's vision of a future society, through Brian Jones, Ronaldo Munck, Alex Callinicos and Cleaver-style planners such as Kieran Allen. A final section draws four lessons.

Liu argues that the crisis stayed within the reach of Marxist explanation. Derber and Schweickart stress overproduction relative to workers' purchasing power. Kliman stresses the falling rate of profit, and holds that regulation can only postpone crises, so that capitalism is becoming more crisis-prone. On the future society, the scholars reviewed defend Marx against the charge of utopianism. They also try to separate his ideas from the Soviet model, and some keep democratic planning, workers' self-management and state-run large firms at the core of alternatives. Liu notes that left scholars should stay wary of bourgeois praise that casts Marx as a saviour of capitalism.

Liu concludes with four points. Opponents currently hold the upper hand in the debate. Some of Marx's views are time-bound, but his analysis of capitalism's secrets and his methods of social analysis are held to be lasting truths. Marxism stays current through theoretical innovation, both by Western left scholars and by socialist countries such as China, whose practice in ecology, poverty reduction, livelihoods and global responsibility is called the best contemporary manifesto for Marxism. Liu is optimistic about the twenty-first century, citing Marxism's academic penetration, lessons from socialist practice, a milder ideological climate and sharpening capitalist contradictions. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how foreign left-wing authors defended Marx's relevance after 2008, and how a Chinese scholar draws conclusions from them.
quoteEn: The vitality of Marxism lies in keeping pace with the times and continually responding to the questions of the age.
quoteZh: 马克思主义的生命力在于与时代同步, 能够不断回应时代课题

t: "New imperialism" and the contest over the sovereignty of "Empire"
st: The ruling form of contemporary capitalism and a critical reflection
zh: “新帝国主义”与“帝国”的主权之争
zhSub: 当代资本主义的统治形态及其批判性反思
paras: What is the ruling form of contemporary capitalism? Li and Wang treat this as the epistemological precondition for any macro-level critique of capitalism. They compare two Western answers: "new imperialism", which they describe as a theory advanced by right-wing scholars to defend the imperialist rule of the United States and other developed states, and "Empire", the new order of global capitalist rule proposed by the radical left thinkers Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. The authors conclude that both misjudge how capital's governing principle relates to national-state sovereignty.

The article has three parts. The first traces imperialism from pre-capitalist empires such as Rome to "capital's imperialism" (late 1860s to late twentieth century), drawing on Lenin, Hobson, Ellen Meiksins Wood and David Harvey. The second reconstructs Hardt and Negri's Empire, including their account of immanent sovereignty, the US constitution, and the passage from disciplinary to control societies. The third compares the two forms and assesses them with the help of critics such as Samir Amin, John Bellamy Foster and Wood.

The authors argue that new imperialism "sublates" imperialism: it keeps national-state sovereignty but adds an economic hegemony of monopoly capital. Wood and Harvey disagree on whether extra-economic political power is necessary to capital accumulation. In Li and Wang's view, new imperialism ignores the contradiction between capital's unlimited global expansion and the territorial limits of the nation-state, so it cannot cover capital's global rule. Empire, by contrast, discards imperialism, since capital's rules replace national sovereignty. Li and Wang say this absolutises the opposition and eliminates the very force that guarantees stability and predictability for capital, and that it cannot explain persistent global inequality, a point they support with Amin, Foster and Wood.

Li and Wang propose that capital's governing principle and national-state sovereignty stand in an "absent" relation: indirect and concealed, neither fully opposed nor fully synchronised. Capital exploits through its own principle, while the nation-state supports it indirectly. They therefore describe contemporary capitalism's ruling form as a new globalised order of Empire-style rule maintained under the imperialist sovereignty of nation-states. Read the original if you study Western Marxist debates on imperialism (Wood, Harvey, Hardt and Negri, Amin) and want a Chinese critical assessment of them.
quoteEn: In this sense, the ruling form of contemporary capitalism can be described as a new globalised order of Empire-style rule carried out under the protection of the imperialist sovereignty of nation-states.
quoteZh: 在这个意义上, 当代资本主义的统治形态可以说成是在民族国家的帝国主义主权维护之下进行的帝国式统治的新的全球化秩序。

t: Accelerationism and digital platforms: Srnicek's critique of platform capitalism
zh: 加速主义与数字平台——斯尔尼塞克的平台资本主义批判
source: Journal of Shanghai University (Social Sciences Edition), 2018 no. 6
paras: Dong Jinping introduces Nick Srnicek, co-author with Alex Williams of the 2013 Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics and author of Platform Capitalism (2016), as the founder of contemporary left accelerationism. The article argues that Srnicek's analysis of digital platforms can only be understood through accelerationism's reading of Marx. Dong also says that, although Srnicek writes about platforms in general, his account speaks most directly to present-day China. The article therefore treats his theory as a prism for Chinese reality, not as a doctrine to be reproduced faithfully.

The article first sets out accelerationism's roots in Marx's 'fragment on machines' in the Grundrisse and in Italian autonomism. It contrasts this with Lukács and the Frankfurt School, whom Dong reads as critics of modernity itself. It then presents Srnicek's definition of a platform and his typology of five kinds: advertising, cloud, industrial, product (sharing) and lean platforms. Dong illustrates each with Western firms (Google, Amazon, Uber, Apple) and Chinese ones (Alibaba Cloud, Didi, Ant Short-term Rental, Tencent). The last section covers platform competition and the future of labour.

Dong's central claim is that accelerationism shifts Marxist critique from the productive forces to the relations of production. Machines are neutral, and resisting them is likened to a mantis blocking a cart, so the left should push capitalism's machinery faster until its contradictions break it. For Srnicek, data is the raw material that platforms extract from user activity at almost no cost, much as oil is extracted. This displaces the attention economy of Pettman, and the 'immaterial labour' emphasis of Virno, Negri and Lazzarato. Platforms compete on three factors: data, key nodes (operating systems, AI, natural-language interfaces, acquired by building or by rhizome-like mergers) and users, who are locked in through ecosystems and rating systems. Dong adds that this departs from Marx's cost-price and profit-rate account of industrial competition, even though Marx's view of competition's essence is not overturned.

Dong reports Srnicek's view that platform control will become more despotic. Platforms employ no workers and own no plant, so people become dependent users, a 'mobilization' of the proletariat into precarious, scattered, low-paid work that is hard to organise. Srnicek offers no clear answer on where this proletariat should go. He ends with a hope that public understanding of digital infrastructure can underpin a better future. Dong remarks that the 'new planned economy' claims of lean platforms deserve attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Srnicek's platform typology, with Chinese platform examples, set against Western Marxism and autonomism.
quoteEn: Only in the accelerationist sense can we understand why Srnicek pays such close attention to production under platform capitalism in the digital age.
quoteZh: 在加速主义的意义上, 我们才能理解为什么斯尔尼塞克会如此关注数字时代平台资本主义的生产。

t: Althusser's critique and transcendence of capitalist law
zh: 阿尔都塞对于资本主义法的批判和超越
paras: Xu Kefei takes up a gap in Louis Althusser's best-known essay on ideology and the state: law, which the 1970 essay leaves out although Althusser treats it as both part of the repressive state apparatus and an ideological function. Xu argues that Althusser's theories of law, ideology and the state form one whole, aimed at explaining and criticising the reproduction of capitalist relations of production. On this reading, the critique of capitalist law is meant to cut that chain of reproduction and free human beings from it.

The article has four parts. It first clarifies the French terms le droit and la loi and Althusser's legal monism, which draws on Montesquieu and Hans Kelsen and rejects the split between natural and positive law. It then examines capitalist law and relations of production, then law and the state, and finally Althusser's idea of proletarian law and human emancipation. Xu draws mainly on On the Reproduction of Capitalism, with reference to Foucault, Poulantzas, Derrida and Laurent De Sutter's Althusser and Law.

Xu reports three moves. First, capitalist law presents free and equal contracting parties modelled on commodity exchange, so exploitation never appears in the legal system. Law recognises property and the wage contract, treats the division of labour as merely technical, and spreads an "economism/humanism" that promises advancement to middle-ranking employees. Second, law and the state are one "legal-political" body. Law turns the surplus of ruling-class force into state power and constructs rights-bearing "subjects", and in doing so ensures the reproduction of exploitative relations. Third, Althusser, unlike Foucault, does not reject law. He opposes the theory that law will end after revolution and treats law as a structure that the proletariat can build by deliberate articulation.

Xu concludes that emancipation requires revolution that changes relations of production, and that the legal "subject" must first be dismantled. Law would then be remade from within the people, releasing human puissance (capacity) rather than power. Xu adds that Althusser, as an academic philosopher, only sketched proletarian law and never had the chance to build it in practice. Read the original if you study Althusser, Marxist legal theory or the philosophical roots of the "subject" and rights, and want a systematic account that draws on the French sources.
quoteEn: Althusser's critique of capitalist law is meant to cut the chain of reproduction of capitalist relations of production and to liberate human beings from it.
quoteZh: 阿尔都塞对于资本主义法的批判是为了斩断资本主义生产关系的再生产之链, 让人从中解放出来。

t: Interpreting "On Contradiction" in the history of foreign Marxism
zh: 国外马克思主义发展史视域下的《矛盾论》解读
source: Studies on Mao Zedong Thought, 2018 no. 4
paras: How have Marxists outside China read Mao Zedong's "On Contradiction", and what should Chinese scholars take from those readings? Wang argues that the text has been an important resource for foreign Marxists. They have used it in debates over the scientific status of Marxism and over alternatives to capitalism. Wang holds that these readings are mostly shaped by Western intellectual agendas, and that they need critical assessment from the standpoint of Marxism in China.

The article opens with four general features of foreign interpretations. It then traces four paradigms in chronological order: Louis Althusser's scientistic reading in the 1960s, Norman Levine's neo-Hegelian reading in the 1980s, Ian Hunt's "new dialectics" reading in the 1990s, and Slavoj Žižek's Lacanian reading in the 21st century. Wang closes with an evaluation of each paradigm and an account of why such readings overstep the text.

On the general features, Wang argues that the readings are embedded in Western currents such as structuralism, existentialism and psychoanalysis. They tend to serve academic polemics rather than revolutionary practice, and they appear at moments of crisis in Marxism. They also use Hegel's or Marx's dialectic as an intermediary. In the case studies, Althusser is said to draw on the text for overdetermination, symptomatic reading and the theory of ideology. Levine is said to use it to argue for re-Hegelianizing Marxism, and Hunt to compare Mao's model with Marx's and Masaccia's. Žižek is said to criticise Mao's rejection of the negation of the negation. Wang judges that Althusser's reading is profound but over-interpreted and separates the text from "On Practice". Levine's overstates Hegel's role. Hunt misreads the transformation of contradictions as a simple swap of positions. Žižek's "negative dialectics" is, in Wang's view, a fundamental misreading. Wang attributes such "theoretical transgression" to Orientalist presuppositions, the imposition of Western concepts, differing historical contexts, the polysemy of texts, and neglect of Engels's dialectics.

Wang concludes that the purpose of evaluating these readings is not only academic dialogue. The aim is to draw methodological and conceptual lessons from "over-interpretation" and misunderstanding. Wang calls for building a dialectics of Marxism with Chinese characteristics, in keeping with Mao's unfulfilled wish to rewrite "On Contradiction". Read the original if you want a critical Chinese survey of how Althusser, Levine, Hunt and Žižek used Mao's dialectics, with a full list of the Chinese translations of their works.
quoteEn: The purpose of the evaluation is not merely academic dialogue. More important is to draw out what "over-interpretation" or "misunderstanding" may leave us in the way of methods and perspectives for research.
quoteZh: 评价的目的不仅仅在于学术上的对话, 更重要的在于挖掘“过度诠释”或“误解”背后可能留给我们在研究方法、视角上的启发

glossary.explanation: A 1937 philosophical essay by Mao Zedong. It is usually paired with "On Practice" as the "two essays" and treats the universality and particularity of contradiction, and principal and secondary contradictions.

glossary.zh: 中国特色的马克思主义辩证法
glossary.en: dialectics of Marxism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The author's phrase for a Chinese-context development of Marxist dialectics, which the article says should draw on critical study of foreign interpretations.
A current in Western Marxism, represented in the article by Ian Hunt, that defends and reconstructs Marx's dialectic against its dismissal by analytical Marxism.
Althusser's concept that a social contradiction is determined by many interacting contradictions, not by the economy alone. The article says he drew on "On Contradiction" for it.

t: The Spanish Communist Party's adjustment of ideology and theoretical strategy, and its causes
zh: 西班牙共产党意识形态与理论战略的调整及其原因
source: Problems of Contemporary World Socialism, 2019 no. 1
paras: Yu Haiqing asks why the Spanish Communist Party (PCE), long a pioneer of Eurocommunism and of early adaptation in the 1980s, has recently made what the author calls a near-subversive rethinking of its ideology and strategy. The article argues that the 20th Congress (2016–2017) marks a rupture with decades of increasingly moderate practice. In Yu's account, internal decline and a changed Spanish political environment together explain the turn.

The article first traces the party's history since its founding in 1921 in three roughly thirty-year phases: Bolshevization under Comintern and Soviet influence, Eurocommunism from the 1950s to the early 1980s, and a post-Eurocommunist period that Yu sees as continuous with Eurocommunist ideas. It then examines the 20th Congress, held in two stages in April 2016 and December 2017, and finally analyses the causes. A short conclusion considers whether the turn can be put into practice and whether it can revive the party.

Yu identifies three changes at the congress.
