For Zhao, Marx treated alienation as an objective product of material production, which only the development of production can abolish; consciousness can play only a secondary role. Zhao adds that their stress on class consciousness and cultural leadership reverses Marx's route from social being to social consciousness. Their separation of the young Marx from the mature Marx, and of Marx from Engels and Lenin, is said to miss the unity of philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism.

Zhao notes that Chinese studies of the three have become specialised and fragmented, and that some researchers use their non-Marxist elements to explain contemporary China. Zhao calls for closer reading of Marxist and Leninist classics, so that compatible and incompatible elements can be told apart, and for absorbing whatever remains valuable in the light of the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Citing the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), the article stresses the primacy of the Marxist standpoint and the direction of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS researcher in 2018 set the official terms for evaluating early Western Marxism, and how the case against Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci was made.
quoteEn: In exploring which path the proletarian movement should take, the founders of Western Marxism had barely climbed out of the Second International's swamp of "economic determinism" before they fell into the trap of "revolutionary subjectivism" and "romanticism".
quoteZh: 西方马克思主义创始人在探索无产阶级运动路径的选择上, 刚刚跳出第二国际“经济决定论”的泥沼, 就陷入了“革命主观主义”“浪漫主义”的陷阱

glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying and developing Marxism in light of China's conditions and practice. The article presents it as the proper purpose of studying foreign Marxisms.
The official name for China's current path and system, in use since the early 1980s. The article says foreign Marxist thought should not be used to judge it.
The tradition begun by Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s, which stresses philosophy, consciousness and culture. Chinese scholarship often contrasts it with Leninism and Soviet-style Marxism.

The reading, attributed to Second International theorists such as Kautsky, that the economic base mechanically determines the superstructure and that socialism will arrive through natural development. Western Marxism's founders attacked it.
Gramsci's idea (usually rendered hegemony) that the working class must win intellectual and cultural leadership before taking political power.
Lukács's term for the process by which social relations and human beings come to appear as things under commodity production. The article says he wrongly equated it with alienation.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: Western neo-Marxist spatial theory and the spatial theory of Capital: a comparative analysis
zh: 西方新马克思主义空间理论与《资本论》空间理论的比较分析
paras: Lin Chengyuan asks how the spatial theory of Western neo-Marxism relates to the spatial theory found in Marx's Capital. The article identifies two errors in existing scholarship: treating Western neo-Marxist spatial theory as the 'second generation' or 'upgraded version' of Marxist spatial theory, and attributing to Marx concepts such as the 'production of space' or the 'politics of space' that originate with Western neo-Marxists. Lin's thesis is that the two theories differ and must not be equated.

The article sets out the neo-Marxist side through its two central figures, Henri Lefebvre (the founder) and David Harvey (the synthesiser). It then reconstructs Capital's spatial theory as three spaces: production space, circulation space and land space. Lefebvre is compared with Marx on three points: the definition of space, the place of the city, and who produces space. Harvey is treated through his view of time and space, the 'spatial fix' and the 'right to the city'.

Lin argues that Lefebvre carries Marx's theory of capitalist production over into a vague, all-encompassing notion of space, which is then in practice identified with the city, and that he names architects, broadly defined, as space's producers. In Lin's reading of Capital, the only real producer of space is capital, or the bourgeoisie, which decides where factories, logistics and sales centres are sited and how land is farmed. Lin sees Lefebvre's 'politics of space' as a way of avoiding this conclusion. Harvey's 'annihilation of space by time' is traced to Marx's account of transport in Volume II, and his 'spatial fix' is read as capital's overseas expansion, which in Lin's view only displaces capitalism's contradictions. Lin also faults Harvey's claim that revolution must be urban, citing the Chinese revolution's rural path, and finds Harvey hesitant where Marx is firm.

Lin concludes that Western neo-Marxist spatial theory draws on Marx and Engels but is not Marxist spatial theory's contemporary development. It should be both drawn upon and critically assessed, with its scope of application examined. Lin calls for Chinese practice to absorb the best Western results and build a spatial theory with Chinese characteristics, in line with Xi Jinping's call at the 19th Party Congress (2017) to build a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a critical, Marx-centred comparison of Lefebvre and Harvey with Capital, written from a Chinese Party-school perspective.
quoteEn: In capitalist society there is only one true producer of space: capital, or rather its spokesman, the bourgeoisie.
quoteZh: 在资本主义社会中,真正的空间生产者只有一个,那就是资本,或者说是资本的代言人———资产阶级。

glossary.explanation: The phrase 'with Chinese characteristics' marks theories or systems presented as adapted to China's conditions. Here it describes the spatial theory Lin proposes to build.

t: The intellectual-historical premises of Hiromatsu Wataru's philosophical situation
st: A reading of "The Outpost of the Worldview of Events"
zh: 广松涉哲学构境的思想史前提
zhSub: 《事的世界观的前哨》解读
paras: Zhang Yibing asks how the young Japanese philosopher Hiromatsu Wataru built the foundations of his "worldview of events" (shi de shijieguan) out of earlier Western thought. The article argues that Hiromatsu never became a mere follower of any one thinker. Instead, in Zhang's account, he linked the logics of Kant, Mach, Husserl and Heidegger with contemporary scientific methodology. He also set out the "four-limbed structure" of the intersubjective world as the creative direction of his life's work.

The article is a reading of the first part of Hiromatsu's book The Outpost of the Worldview of Events (1971; Chinese translation 2002). It is divided into three sections: Kant, Mach, and the passage from Husserl to Heidegger. Zhang follows how Hiromatsu treats each thinker as a lower logical hurdle to be passed on the way to his own position. Zhang also adds his own judgements and cites his other books, including those on Heidegger, Sohn-Rethel and Stiegler.

On Kant, Zhang explains that Hiromatsu saw the thing-in-itself being "liquefied" into an epistemological event, so that ontology, epistemology and logic form one unity. Hiromatsu then argued that Kant's transcendental frame is itself a historical product of intersubjective interaction. Zhang agrees, but holds that the real basis of intersubjective structures is objective practice, not cognition, and he cites Sohn-Rethel and Stiegler as going deeper. On Mach, Hiromatsu accepted the relational picture of sensory elements but objected that the real world is "more than" a complex of elements, which gives the first two limbs: the given and the meant. Zhang adds that Mach's lasting influence on Hiromatsu was a habit of building the world from micro-level images. Husserl and Heidegger supply the other two limbs, the self and the other-self, and Heidegger's equipment-based ontology is faulted for mistaking relations for things (wuxianghua), as in the case of money.

Zhang finds Hiromatsu's critique of Heidegger too sweeping. In Zhang's view, Hiromatsu overlooked Heidegger's rejection of epistemology and could not know the "Ereignis" (appropriation) thinking in Heidegger's unpublished manuscripts, which Zhang says began in the 1930s. Zhang says he does not simply endorse that thinking but regrets the gap in Hiromatsu's understanding. The article presents Hiromatsu as a thinker who dissolved all substances into relations, and it locates his "four-limbed" theory in the history of its sources. Read the original if you study Hiromatsu Wataru, Japanese Marxist philosophy or Zhang Yibing's own approach to foreign Marxism, and want to see how he positions himself against Hiromatsu on Kant, Mach and Heidegger.
quoteEn: Dissolving every substance was the direction of Hiromatsu's unremitting effort. This is also the entrance to the edifice of Hiromatsu's philosophy.
quoteZh: 消解一切实体，是广松涉不懈的努力方向。这也是进入广松哲学大厦的入口。

glossary.explanation: Hiromatsu Wataru's name for his relational philosophy, which he set against the "worldview of things" (substance-based) of modern philosophy. It treats events and relations as primary.
Hiromatsu's model of cognition, with four poles: the given, the meant, the knowing someone and the self/other-self. Zhang traces its origins in Mach, Husserl and others.

Hiromatsu's term for the mistaking of social relations for things, adapted from Marx's critique of fetishism. Zhang notes that it differs from Marx's account of reification and has an epistemological flavour.

t: Politics of emancipation, biopolitics, politics of inaction
st: Aims and logical shifts in the technological critique of modernity
zh: 解放政治学·生命政治学·无为政治学
zhSub: 现代性批判技术视角的旨趣和逻辑转换
paras: Hu Daping asks how critiques of modernity have understood technology from the mid-nineteenth century to the present. The article opens with the Unabomber Kaczynski's claim that industry has become a disaster for humanity, as a sign that technology, once the source of modern self-confidence, is now widely seen as the root of catastrophe. Hu argues that the critical gaze on technology has passed through three perspectives: a politics of emancipation, a biopolitics and a politics of inaction (wuwei). In these, technology appears respectively as productive force, as instrumental reason and as technological law.

The article traces a line from Marx through Nietzsche, Spengler, Heidegger and the Frankfurt School to Baudrillard, Virilio, neo-Luddism and Bruno Latour. Part one treats Marx's historical context and his place for technology within the relation of productive forces to relations of production. Part two covers the biopolitical turn of the early twentieth century, including Lukács, Adorno and Horkheimer, Marcuse, Husserl, Mumford and Ellul. Part three examines contemporary radical critiques, and a short conclusion draws these together.

Hu holds that Marx neither hated machines like the Luddites nor worshipped productive forces. He located the harm of technology in capitalist relations of production, and saw modern science and technology as products of capital accumulation that carry its aims. The Frankfurt School, in Hu's reading, turned this into a critique of instrumental reason, with Marcuse insisting that technical rationality is historically specific and could become a liberating technology. After the 1970s, Hu argues, Baudrillard's hyperreality and Virilio's dromology treat technology and speed as autonomous structures that sideline human subjects. Neo-Luddism offers only rejection, and Latour proposes a "Parliament of Things" and a slowing down rather than revolution. Hu reads this quietism as a sign that technology has run ahead of society, so that the Enlightenment project of emancipation has itself become a constraint.

Hu concludes that technology is not an isolated natural matter but a social and existential problem tied to economics, politics and culture. The article says it does not aim to answer where reconstruction should begin. Hu warns that humanity has reached a critical moment at which, unless it grasps the reins, technology, like a runaway horse, may throw it to the ground. Read the original if you want an intellectual-historical survey, by a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism, of how Marxist and post-Marxist technology critique moved from emancipation to quietism.
quoteEn: The problem of technology is not only a natural problem but also a social one; in short, it is an existential problem that we must take seriously today.
quoteZh: 技术问题，不只是自然问题，也是社会问题，简言之，是需要我们今天严肃对待的生存问题。

glossary.explanation: Hu's label for the Marxian perspective, in which technology is a productive force whose liberating potential is realised by transforming relations of production.

Hu's label for the perspective of Heidegger and the Frankfurt School, which defends life and existence against technology understood as instrumental reason. It echoes Foucault's term for the political management of life.

Hu's label for contemporary radical technology critique, which rejects industrial civilisation but offers no practical political programme. The term draws on Daoist wuwei and the Western notion of quietism.

t: Adorno and post-Marxism: the historical echoes of negative dialectics
zh: 阿多诺与后马克思主义:否定的辩证法之历史回响
source: Journal of Guangxi Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2017 no. 5
paras: Studies of Theodor Adorno, Li Xixiang observes, tend to read him on his own terms and neglect his influence on later thought. Li argues that Negative Dialectics marks a decisive turning point in the history of Western Marxism: it is an important source of postmodern thought and an intellectual resource for many post-Marxist thinkers.

The article, published in 2017, has three main parts and a short conclusion. It first reconstructs Adorno's negative dialectics and philosophy of non-identity, including his critique of Hegel and Heidegger. It then relates Adorno to postmodernism, using the psychoanalytic notion of the symptom. Finally it turns to Adorno's engagement with Freud, as read by Slavoj Žižek in The Metastases of Enjoyment, and to the later reception of psychoanalysis in post-Marxism.

Li reads negative dialectics as Adorno's whole philosophy: dialectics is consciousness of non-identity, and the object is never fully absorbed by the concept. Li argues that this gives Adorno's thought a materialist root in the priority of the object over the subject, and that it opposes systems, ontology and metaphysics, with Heidegger's ontology seen as still bound to identity. Postmodernity, Li proposes, relates to modernity as a Lacanian sinthome (the irreducible symptom), 'in you more than you': non-identity is an internal, constitutive exterior of identity, and Adorno's negation does not resolve into a new affirmation. Following Žižek, Li presents Adorno's 'repressive desublimation' as a critique of mass psychology under totalitarianism, but one that stops short of the superego dimension. Lacan, in this reading, is Adorno's hidden heir, while Habermas dissolves the tension.

Li concludes that Lacanian psychoanalysis is not remote from Marxism but secretly linked to it. It has shaped Derrida, Foucault, Baudrillard, Laclau, Mouffe, Žižek and Butler, and Li says it has become a main tool for 'rewriting' Marxism and restoring its vitality. Li presents the meeting of psychoanalysis and Marxism as a result of the internal logic of theory and of reflection on the setbacks of the world communist movement, and as a major open theoretical task. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of how Adorno, Lacan, Žižek and post-Marxism connect, especially the symptom analogy for postmodernity and modernity.
quoteEn: Adorno's idea of negative dialectics in fact harbours the seeds of postmodernism.
quoteZh: 阿多诺否定的辩证法的思想, 实际上埋伏着后现代的种子

t: Overseas scholarship reassesses Marx
zh: 国外学界重新认识马克思
paras: Writing in People's Daily ahead of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth (5 May 2018), Feng Yanli examines the "Marx fever" that has appeared in foreign academia since the 2008 international financial crisis. Feng argues that this renewed interest is no passing fashion and that studying it should deepen Marxist belief and strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence.

The commentary is organised in three parts: how the "Marx fever" arose, evidence of Marx's growing influence, and the relevance of Marxism to present-day problems. It draws on remarks by foreign scholars including Jonathan Sperber, Jacques Derrida, Anthony Giddens, Thomas Piketty and Wolfram Adolphi.

Feng contrasts the present "return to Marx" with the post-Cold War mood of "farewell to Marx" after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. In Feng's account, the crisis exposed capitalism's inherent contradictions, such as inequality and unlimited capital expansion, and prompted a change of attitude. As evidence, Feng cites the Communist Manifesto as required reading at Columbia and Oxford, work on the historical-critical edition of the Marx-Engels works, and rankings naming Marx the most influential thinker. Feng holds that Marxism keeps its vitality because it explains general laws of development and aims to change the world, and notes that more scholars are turning back to Marxist political economy to examine capitalism's flaws.

Feng concludes that China's practice in the new era demonstrates the truth of Marxism. Under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Feng expects China to advance further and offer more "Chinese wisdom" and "Chinese solutions" to global problems. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese official commentary in 2018 used foreign scholars' remarks to support the continuing relevance of Marx.
quoteEn: The rapid rise of the "Marx fever" is by no means accidental, nor is it a passing academic fashion; it has a profound social and historical background.
quoteZh: “马克思热”迅速兴起绝非偶然，也并非一阵风式的学术时髦，而是有着深刻的社会时代背景。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party discourse for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It was set out in its full four-part form under Xi Jinping.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution at the 19th Party Congress in 2017.

t: A beacon lighting the way forward for human history
st: Communist parties around the world mark the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto
zh: 照亮人类历史前进方向的灯塔
zhSub: 各国共产党隆重纪念马克思诞辰200周年和《共产党宣言》发表170周年
paras: Writing in 2018, the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th of the Communist Manifesto, Yu Haiqing surveys how communist parties abroad have commemorated both. The article is a report-style commentary rather than a theoretical study. Yu argues that these parties stress the Manifesto's historical and theoretical contribution, its value as a method for analysing present-day capitalism, and its guidance for reviving the world socialist movement from its low point.

The article is organised in three parts. The first lists commemorative events in early 2018: quizzes and film reviews by the US party, a forum in Paris attended by over 2,000 people, a Lisbon congress of the Portuguese party, an international seminar in Hanoi, and a roundtable in Cuba. It then summarises how the American, Ukrainian, British, Spanish, Brazilian, Portuguese and Cypriot parties assess the Manifesto. The second part examines its contemporary relevance, and the third its guidance for socialist construction and movement strategy.

On relevance, Yu reports that foreign parties see the Manifesto's claims as still valid. They cite bourgeois domination of the state, capital's constant expansion (the Russian party's account of post-Soviet de-industrialisation and dependence), extreme wealth concentration (the Belgian and Chilean parties), and periodic crises rooted in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. The Spanish party likens the Manifesto to an "X-ray" of capitalism. On strategy, Yu summarises four themes from these parties: upholding the communists' historical mission as the working class's vanguard; building alliances with intermediate strata; uniting the left while avoiding sectarianism; and rejecting dogmatism, since there is no single road to socialism.

Yu concludes that the Manifesto and Marxism remain a "key" to understanding capitalism's essence and trends, and that Vietnamese and Laotian leaders credit them with guiding socialist construction in their countries. Yu presents the foreign parties' view that Marxism must be developed critically in light of changing conditions, not treated as a sacred formula. Read the original if you want a compact overview, from a Chinese academic viewpoint, of how a range of communist parties marked the 2018 anniversaries and what positions they took.
quoteEn: The Manifesto and Marxism are precisely the "key" that helps us understand and grasp capitalism's essential attributes and development trends.
quoteZh: 《宣言》和马克思主义正是帮助我们认识和把握其本质属性和发展趋势的“钥匙”。

t: Why Western left-wing currents of thought have stalled
zh: 西方左翼思潮为何陷入停滞
paras: Writing in 2018, Chen Jiangsheng asks why Western left-wing thought, which revived after the 2008 financial crisis, now appears to be stagnating. The article argues that uncertainty and stalled development are now the dominant condition of the Western left. It attributes this to three causes: the unclear course of Western economies and societies, a rethinking of the left's rapid earlier rise, and the lack of an effective guiding ideology.

The piece first describes the post-2008 revival, then surveys new trends since 2016 in the United States, Britain, Germany and France. For the revival, Chen cites Chris Harman's Zombie Capitalism (2009), Andrew Kliman's book on the capitalist crisis (2012) and Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century. The article also links the left's growth to opposition to globalisation and to shifts in national politics, such as the return of the left to power in France.

Chen reads the country cases as signs of retreat or confusion. In the United States, the defeat of Sanders and the election of Trump show that society did not endorse the left's rise, though Chen adds that the problems the left exposes persist, so the ebb may be temporary. In Britain, the Brexit vote looked like 'left-wing people doing right-wing work'. In Germany, Merkel's failure to form a coalition over refugee policy showed an irreconcilable left–right split alongside a rising far right. In France, Macron's victory is only a limited gain for the left, and Chen doubts how far left he really is.

Chen explains the stall in materialist terms: social being determines social consciousness, and the West faces internal stagnation and external competition from new theories and paths in the East, for which it has no agreed response. The left's rapid rise rested on discontent with the crisis, so disappointment with its results prompted rethinking. Chen concludes that Western left-wing thought, though it partly inherits Marxist ideas, is not guided by Marxism, criticises capitalism incompletely and cannot solve fundamental problems within the old framework. In Chen's view it will therefore only rise and fall in waves with popular discontent. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school view of the post-2008 Western left and its country-by-country prospects as of 2018.
quoteEn: Western left-wing thought lacks an effective guiding ideology, which leaves its development unsustainable.
quoteZh: 西方左翼思潮缺乏管用的指导思想，带来了其发展缺乏可持续性。

t: Green capitalism runs into difficulties
zh: 绿色资本主义发展遭遇困境
paras: Writing in 2018, Zhuang Guiyang asks whether 'green capitalism', the attempt to make capitalism sustainable through a green transition, can deliver on its promise. The article argues that it cannot: a capitalist system without moral guidance has left what was once an attractive project stuck in difficulties, and the limits of green self-adjustment under capitalism are plain in the politics of climate action.

The piece opens with the idea of green capitalism as presented in Paul Hawken and colleagues' 2000 book and with the case its supporters make, citing renewable energy investment figures for 2015 and 2017. It then sets out critics' objections, including the work of the British author Richard Smith. A central section treats the United States' announced withdrawal from the Paris Agreement in June 2017 as the latest illustration. The final section turns to cities and sub-national actors, such as city alliances and American states, that have kept up climate action.

Zhuang reports that supporters see the green economy as a natural evolution of capitalism, whose reward for scarcity and efficiency suits green growth. Critics, in Zhuang's account, say these supporters overestimate green production and underestimate the scale of ecological crisis, and that carbon or energy taxes cannot remove market externalities. For Zhuang, the contradiction between capital's expansion and finite natural resources is hard to overcome. Capitalist politics, shaped by voters and interest groups, tolerates only limited green repair. Trump's 'America first' withdrawal, European disagreements and rich countries' reluctance to meet the 100 billion dollar climate finance pledge are offered as evidence. Zhuang then notes that city networks such as the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, the 'We Are Still In' delegation at Bonn and the US Climate Alliance partly bridge the gap left by states.

Zhuang concludes that technology cannot save the world under the current system, and that countries must urgently build a development paradigm that goes beyond industrial civilisation. City alliances, being bottom-up and voluntary, cannot replace states under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, so the future remains uncertain. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese social-science commentary of 2018 used the Paris withdrawal to argue against the viability of green capitalism.
quoteEn: The current capitalist system, lacking moral guidance, has already spun out of control, and no amount of green patching will help.
quoteZh: 当前缺乏道德指引的资本主义制度已经失去控制，再多的绿色修补也无济于事。

glossary.explanation: The idea that capitalism can be made ecologically sustainable through green technology, markets and business principles. The article takes the term from Western debates, notably Hawken's 2000 book, and criticises it.

The mode of development based on large-scale industrial production and consumption. Chinese writers on ecological civilisation often contrast it with a proposed post-industrial or ecological paradigm.

t: The evolution of British Marxist theories of the subject since the 1950s
zh: 20世纪50年代以来英国马克思主义的主体理论流变
paras: After the Second World War, the British working class, in the article's account, became weak in class consciousness and even felt a 'cultural classlessness'. Xue asks whether this class can still carry out its historical mission of overthrowing capitalism, and argues that British Marxists answered through three successive but coexisting theories of the revolutionary subject: the experiential subject, the constructed subject and the plural subject.

The article is a theoretical-historical survey of British Marxism from the 1950s onwards. It takes the culturalism of E. P. Thompson, Richard Hoggart and Raymond Williams first. It then covers the structuralism of Perry Anderson, Tom Nairn, Terry Eagleton and Stuart Hall, and finally the post-structuralist and post-Marxist plural-subject theory of the 1980s, drawing especially on Laclau and Mouffe's Hegemony and Socialist Strategy.

Xue's central move is to show how each school answers one question: can workers' spontaneous experience grow into socialist revolutionary consciousness? Culturalists say yes, if the 'raw material' of lived experience is given cultural processing and the people's voice is amplified. Structuralists say no: Anderson and Nairn describe working-class consciousness as a product of bourgeois hegemony, so the subject is a 'subject position' produced by structure, and it must be formed by Marxist theory led by intellectuals. After the 1980s, new social movements of women, students, youth and ethnic groups led Hall and others to hold that subjects are built by discourse and joined only temporarily through 'articulation'. In Xue's reading this shifts struggle from practice to discourse and from critique of political economy to critique of hegemony.

Xue concludes that the three turns show the limits of traditional subject theory and the persistence of British Marxists' search for a route to socialism, which deserves recognition. The article nonetheless judges that each school erred: culturalists neglected economic laws, structuralists undervalued working-class cultural traditions, and the plural-subject theory drifted from Marx's starting point in 'real human beings'. Post-Marxism, Xue argues, ends by dissolving the working class's revolutionary status and the guiding role of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of how British Marxism moved from Thompson to Laclau and Mouffe on the question of the revolutionary subject.
quoteEn: The plural-subject theory goes further by grounding the construction of the revolutionary subject in discursive practice, gradually moving away from Marx's theoretical standpoint of 'starting from real human beings'.
quoteZh: 多元主体论更是将革命主体的建构落脚于话语实践, 逐渐远离了马克思的“从现实的人出发”的理论立场

t: The anti-dialectics of spectator and actor: understanding materialism and its contemporary revival
zh: 旁观者与行动者的反辩证法:如何理解唯物主义及其当代复兴
paras: Xia Ying takes up the quiet revival of materialism in contemporary Western philosophy, which the author sets beside the better-known ontological and linguistic turns. The article, published in Jiangsu Social Sciences in 2017, asks what materialism actually is and what the current revival, centred as before in France, implies. Xia's thesis is that a genuine materialist is defined less by the primacy of matter over consciousness than by two commitments: immanence, meaning no appeal to anything beyond the world, and a principle of action, meaning that humans can change the world.

The article has three parts. The first traces the materialist tradition from eighteenth-century French materialism, Marx's Holy Family and his doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, to Friedrich Lange's threefold division into theoretical, practical and ethical materialism. The second asks what it means to be a materialist, drawing on Badiou's remark on materialism, ancient metaphysicians, Epicurean hedonism and Marx's critique of political economy. The third turns to Fichte, Hegel and Marx, and then to Althusser, Badiou and Žižek.

Xia argues that Epicurus's swerving atom, which carries free will and breaks the causal chain, is what attracted Marx and Lange. Marx's materialism, in this reading, is a double break with Feuerbach's contemplative materialism and with Hegelian idealism. It is oriented to the conditions under which action can overthrow capitalism, and Capital is read, in a Kantian sense, as a study of the limits of political economy. Because theology, idealism and spiritualism imply a pre-determined course of history, only a non-deterministic materialism leaves room for real action. Xia contends that Hegel folds the actor into the spectator's explanatory system, while Marx's eleventh thesis on Feuerbach separates interpreting from changing the world, which Xia calls their anti-dialectical relation. Contemporary radical thinkers share this move: Althusser's 'conjuncture' and aleatory materialism, Badiou's 'event' and 'grace', and Žižek's non-reductionism each locate a 'remainder' that no system of ideas can absorb.

Xia concludes that the revival aims to supply a theoretical precondition for action and stays within Marx's demand to change the world. The author identifies a difficulty, however. These thinkers reject the proletariat as a pre-appointed agent and look to contingent events to generate actors, but they cannot show how conjunctures or events produce an actual subject. In Xia's judgement their radicalism therefore risks remaining a theoretical posture. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese philosopher links Marx's materialism to Althusser, Badiou and Žižek and criticises the agency problem in contemporary radical thought.
quoteEn: This is the real reason why Marx valued Epicurus.
quoteZh: 这是马克思看重伊壁鸠鲁的真实原因所在。

t: A critical review of the main views in contemporary Russian Marxist scholarship
zh: 当今俄罗斯马克思主义学界主要观点评析
source: Studies in Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theory, 2017 no. 6
paras: This review surveys Russian Marxist scholarship after the collapse of the Soviet Union, mainly work published around 2011–2013. Hu starts from the claim that the choice between socialism and capitalism was never settled in Russia. In Hu's account, Marxism returned to Russian academia as an unofficial ideology after a phase of extreme denigration and then one of objective reflection. Two schools stand out: the "reflective Marxism" of Oizerman, and the "critical Marxism" of Buzgalin, Kolganov and others.

The review is organised around three themes, drawn largely from the journal Alternatives (Al'ternativy) and a few other Russian journals. The first is the Russian Revolution and Soviet practice, with studies by Lyskov, Rüdiger, Pantin and Epstein. The second is the deeper causes of the Soviet collapse, with Belik, Istyagin, Bensaïd, Voeikov and Kolganov. The third is new thinking on twenty-first-century socialism, with Buzgalin, Belenky, Slavin, Laibman and Kolganov.

Hu argues that scholars have moved away from the politicised Soviet paradigm and from the post-1991 dismissal of the revolution. They now use a long-run, genetic approach that places the revolution within Russia's difficult path to modernization. On the collapse, they reject single-cause explanations. Kolganov, for example, locates the failure in an over-centralised, bureaucratic management system and not in socialism as such. Hu also notes the tension between planning and the market, which runs through Soviet economic history. On twenty-first-century socialism, Buzgalin draws ten lessons from the Soviet experience. Slavin proposes a "new socialism" that uses capitalist forms of ownership and the market. Laibman reads the Critique of the Gotha Programme in terms of stages.

Hu concludes that these studies treat Soviet socialism as an unavoidable link in the world system. In Hu's view they offer intellectual resources and research paths for exploring socialism with Chinese characteristics independently. Russian scholars, Hu says, have given themselves the task of restoring popular belief in socialism and seeking national rejuvenation through Marxism. Hu describes post-Soviet Marxism as having a practical orientation, sitting between criticism of the Soviet model and response to social reality. Read the original if you want a map of post-Soviet Russian Marxist debates, with sources, for comparison with Chinese discussions of the Soviet collapse and of socialism.
quoteEn: In this sense, the Soviet failure was not the failure of the socialist economic system itself, but the failure of a top-down, highly centralised management system.
quoteZh: 在这个意义上, 苏联的失败不是社会主义经济体系本身的失败, 而是自上而下高度集中的管理体制的失败。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current path and system, combining Party leadership, a socialist market economy and national conditions. The review treats Russian studies as resources for its independent exploration.
A term used by the author for the Russian aim of recovering national strength through Marxism. In Chinese official discourse a similar term, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, is a central goal.

t: Three questions to Marxist philosophy
st: On the relations among Western Marxism, Marxist philosophy and modern Western philosophy
zh: 对马克思主义哲学的三个追问
zhSub: 兼论西方马克思主义、马克思主义哲学与现代西方哲学之关系
source: Journal of Northeast Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2018 no. 1
paras: Chen Xueming asks what Marxist philosophy is and where it stands in relation to Western philosophy. The article poses three questions: whether Marxism is a philosophy at all; whether it belongs to early modern or to modern and contemporary Western philosophy; and whether, in surpassing the former, it also surpasses the latter. Chen argues that Western Marxism gives the most coherent answers: Marxism is a philosophy, it belongs to modern and contemporary philosophy, and it goes beyond that philosophy as well.

The article is organised in three parts: answers to the questions, the drawing of boundaries, and a section on Western Marxism. It sets Western Marxism, represented mainly by Korsch, Luxemburg, Lukács, Gramsci, Habermas and the Frankfurt School, against three rival readings. These are the Second International, the Third International and postmodernism. Chen also draws on ecological Marxism, citing Gorz and David Pepper.

Chen holds that Marx's talk of "abolishing" philosophy targeted bourgeois, early modern philosophy, and that Marx realised philosophy in order to abolish it. Marxist philosophy shares with modern Western philosophy a rejection of metaphysics, system-building and the subject–object dualism. It differs, Chen says, by grounding itself in concrete practice and labour, by keeping ontology and a proper place for reason, and by uniting subject and object through revolutionary practice. On this account the Second International reduced Marxism to economics and sociology, and the Third International recast it as a fixed system of dialectical and historical materialism on early modern lines. Chen presents postmodernism as rejecting reason and modernity wholesale, leaving it with nothing but reformism or utopian retreat.

Chen concludes that Western Marxism holds Marxist ontology to be a practice-based, social-historical ontology, and treats modernity dialectically. Habermas, Gorz, Horkheimer, Marcuse and ecological Marxists criticise modernity's pathologies but seek to rescue it by tracing them to capital's logic and to social institutions. Chen adds that this reading of ontology has spread widely in Chinese scholarship, and that whether it matches Marx's original meaning remains an open question. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's defence of Western Marxism's claim to interpret Marx's philosophy, and its contrast with Soviet-style and postmodern readings.
quoteEn: Marxist philosophy has not only surpassed modern Western philosophy but has also surpassed postmodernist philosophy.
quoteZh: 马克思主义哲学不仅超越了西方现代哲学,更超越了后现代主义哲学。

t: What is new about the new imperialism?
st: With a critique of neoliberalism
zh: 新帝国主义“新”在何处？
zhSub: 兼对新自由主义的批判
source: Guowai Lilun Dongtai (Trends in Foreign Theory), 2017 no. 7
paras: In this text, published in Chinese translation (by Qin Shiya) in Guowai Lilun Dongtai, 2017 no. 7, David Harvey asks what is genuinely new in contemporary imperialism. He engages Ellen Meiksins Wood's The Empire of Capital, which holds that classical theories of imperialism no longer fit a world in which capitalist laws are generalised. Harvey agrees with Wood on some points but argues that the novelty lies in how capital absorbs its surplus, not in a typology of empires. He sums this up in a rule: follow the surplus capital.

The piece opens by distinguishing two readings of 'new' (changed material conditions, or new concepts) and by assessing Lenin, Luxemburg, Bukharin and Kautsky. It then turns to surplus absorption and the 'spatio-temporal fix', the role of the state and of global capital, and the present forms of imperialist practice. Harvey draws on his own The Limits to Capital, The New Imperialism and A Brief History of Neoliberalism, and on Giovanni Arrighi, Neil Smith and others.

Harvey credits Wood's historical typology of empires but says it hides the dynamics of transition between hegemonies. He criticises her refusal to call Venice, Genoa or the Dutch Republic 'capitalist', and contrasts Arrighi's account of a continuous capitalist historical geography. In Harvey's account, capitalism faces a perpetual problem of surplus capital. It is absorbed through temporal displacement (long-term investment, credit), spatial displacement (geographical expansion, capital export), or both. Where it cannot be absorbed, crisis and devaluation follow. Since the 1970s, he argues, neoliberalism has served this end by crushing organised labour, pursuing 'globalisation', privatising public assets, feeding financial speculation and shifting devaluation onto particular places, a process he calls 'accumulation by dispossession' (rendered in this translation as 'exploitative accumulation'). He also holds that Wood's account of the state and 'American capital' is unclear, and that a new theory of the capitalist state is needed. Wood's emphasis on permanent war, he says, mistakes the particularities of recent US actions for what is new.

Harvey concludes that the novelty of the new imperialism lies in the neoliberal counter-revolution after 1970, consolidated by the Washington Consensus. He says it mobilised military, political, cultural and economic power to remove barriers to absorbing surplus. He observes that surplus capital is now concentrated mainly in East and Southeast Asia, so that a range of imperialist practices, rather than a single form, now exists. He sees a possible new turn, and a nascent unity of anti-imperialism and anti-neoliberalism in global movements. Read the original if you want a Marxist geographer's critique of Wood and of classical imperialism theory, or a compact statement of Harvey's surplus-absorption argument.
quoteEn: If we are to identify what is 'new' about the new imperialism, we need to hold to one simple golden rule: follow the surplus capital, and look for the geographical and territorial practices tied to its absorption or devaluation!
quoteZh: 如果我们要辨认新帝国主义“新”在何处,就需要坚持一个简单的黄金法则:追随剩余资本,寻找与它们的吸收或贬值相联系的地理的和基于领土的实践!

t: Seven problems of contemporary world imperialism
zh: 当代世界帝国主义的七个问题
orig: Chinese version in Political Economy Review (政治经济学评论), 2017 no. 1
paras: Watanabe Masao, a Japanese Marxist economist, sets out to rehabilitate the theory of imperialism, which he says many wrongly regard as outdated. The article, published in 2017 and translated into Chinese by Gao Chenxi, traces how the concept faded from left discourse after the 1970s and was displaced by 'globalization'. After the September 11 attacks, talk of 'empire' became fashionable, but Watanabe notes that a theory of imperialism was still not revived.

The article works through seven reasons why people avoid the concept and answers each in turn. They are imperialism without colonies; geopolitical rivalry; the global structure of power; the main arena of imperialism; the global distribution of risk; domination versus hegemony; and the method of imperialism theory. Watanabe draws on Lenin, Gramsci, William Appleman Williams, Gallagher and Robinson, Panitch and Gindin, Harvey, Callinicos, Brzezinski and Buzan.

Watanabe argues that imperialism never required formal colonies, citing Lenin's Argentina and Portugal, Williams's 'Open Door Imperialism' and the 'imperialism of free trade'. Hegemony does not end great-power rivalry but rests on it, and geopolitics is, in his phrase, imperialism's 'self-consciousness'. Citing a World Bank report and Callinicos, he holds that capital flows mainly among developed countries, so the driving force of imperialism lies in rivalry among them. In this reading, developing countries bear the risks, such as environmental damage, while advanced countries monopolise the benefits. The same pattern appears inside developed countries, for example the Fukushima nuclear accident, which he calls 'domestic colonies'. He adopts the three-pole view of Harvey and Callinicos over the single-pole US view of Panitch and Gindin. He also holds that US hegemony, in Gramsci's sense of leadership by consent, depends on its ability to impose its own standards on other capitalist states.

Watanabe concludes that modern imperialism is an imperialism of capital, rooted in the dynamics of capitalist societies. He sees two routes to modernising the theory. One is completing Marx's unfinished plan for a critique of political economy. The other is the classical approach of Luxemburg, Hilferding, Lenin and Bukharin, which combines a critique of politics with a critique of economics. Because imperialism lies at the crossing of economic and geopolitical competition, he argues, it falls mainly under a critique of politics that Marx abandoned. He faults Japanese Marxist economists for staying on the economic plane. Read the original if you want a Japanese Marxist's case for keeping imperialism theory alive against the globalization and 'empire' paradigms, and a sketch of its methodological agenda.
quoteEn: It can be said that geopolitics is precisely imperialism's 'self-consciousness'.
quoteZh: 可以说，地缘政治学正是帝国主义的“自我意识”。

t: Marx's inheritance and transcendence of Hegel's theme of contingency
zh: 马克思对黑格尔偶然性论题的继承与超越
paras: Where, exactly, did Marx inherit and where did he go beyond Hegel on contingency (偶然性)? Yan Yan argues that Marx took over Hegel's critical stance towards contingency, and that this gave his critique of capitalist society its tension. Marx then moved beyond Hegel through a double critique of contingency and necessity, a concern with human emancipation, and a turn to practice. The article was published in Philosophical Research in 2017.

Yan begins by sorting Chinese scholarship into two camps: those who rank necessity above contingency (a substance-based reading and a subject-based reading) and those who want contingency restored to Marx's thought. The article frames its own approach as a philosophy of history, not epistemology, centred on individual fate under modernity. It then takes Hegel's treatment in the Logic, the Philosophy of History and the Philosophy of Right, and follows Marx from early writings through The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto and the Grundrisse and Capital. A final section sets out the comparison, with a note on differences between Marx and Engels.

For Yan, Hegel treats contingency as a defective, unfree form that must be sublated into necessity, with the state as the ethical universal above civil society and its "contingent" private individuals. Marx first rejected contingency in abstract humanist terms. In The German Ideology he recast the problem as that of the "contingent individual", the atomised, class-bound person produced by capitalist modernity and ruled by the power of things, money and exchange value. Yan then identifies four advances over Hegel: from epistemology to ontology; from conceptual speculation to real history; from necessitarianism to a theory of possibility, in which the revolutionary subject must act; and from contingency's pre-assumed legitimacy to its empirically grounded rationality.

Yan concludes that Marx combined subjective and objective dimensions, which bears on the continuing Chinese dispute over whether to read him through the subject or the object. In practical terms, Yan holds, Marx's critique helps people recognise the nature of present social life and resist an "anything goes" postmodern way of living. His wariness of necessity also warns against retreating into fatalism out of fear of contingency. Read the original if you work on Marx's relation to Hegel, on the philosophy of history, or on how Chinese scholars debate necessity, contingency and the subject–object question in Marx.
quoteEn: If Hegel used the dialectic of concepts, Marx used the dialectic of history: the one an abstract, theoretical philosophical approach, the other a revolutionary path of practical philosophy.
quoteZh: 如果说黑格尔运用的是概念辩证法，马克思则运用的是历史辩证法，一个是抽象的理论哲学进路，一个是革命的实践哲学路向。

t: Shaping the political subject in the age of the "end of history"
st: The programme of Europe's psychoanalytic "radical left"
zh: “历史终结”时代政治主体的形塑
zhSub: 精神分析视野下欧洲“激进左翼”的方案
source: Journal of Shanghai Jiao Tong University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2017 no. 6
paras: Francis Fukuyama's claim that liberal capitalism marks the "end of history" has been taken up again by a group of European philosophers, chiefly Slavoj Žižek, Alain Badiou and Jacques Rancière. Zhou Zhijian treats them as a psychoanalytic "radical left" that shares Lacan's theory and asks one question: after the "end of history", how can a political subject capable of social change be formed? The article argues that this current offers a negative, ontological critique rather than a positive blueprint.

The article opens with the claim that this current arose in dissatisfaction with the previous generation of post-structuralist left thinkers, whom Zhou sees as absorbed into global capitalism. It then moves through three parts. The first reconstructs Lacan's Real, Symbolic and Imaginary, the "barred Other" and the death drive. The second turns to Žižek's and Badiou's accounts of the "event". The third sets the whole current against the Socratic tradition of negative philosophy and examines the candidates each thinker offers for a future political subject.

Zhou's central claim is that, for Lacan, the Symbolic order never closes: a remainder of the Real always escapes the Other, so every particular order stays open at the ontological level. Žižek reads Kant's antinomies and Hegel through the "parallax view", so that the gap itself becomes the solution. Žižek and Badiou diverge over the event. Žižek fears that Badiou's "truth-event" simply produces a new symbolic order, another Other, and prefers to move alone toward the death drive. For the future subject, Žižek points to the "excluded", Badiou to an "unidentifiable set" that forms only after an event, and Rancière to the "part of no part". Zhou presents all three as rejecting the classical Marxist proletariat and the identity politics of Laclau and Mouffe.

Zhou concludes that these thinkers supply no directly justified political programme. They keep a critical distance from existing power structures and mainstream ideology and insist that capitalism is not the end of history. In Zhou's account they envisage a "communism" reactivated under new historical conditions, and although they cannot offer a concrete alternative path, they guard against a slide into absolutist political theology. Read the original if you want a Chinese doctoral-level reading of Žižek, Badiou and Rancière that traces their common debt to Lacan and their disagreement over the event.
quoteEn: For the psychoanalytic "radical left", what really matters is not that the world must become a particular way, but that the world must not remain as it is now.
quoteZh: 对精神分析的“激进左翼”而言, 真正重要的不是世界一定要变成某种样子, 而是世界必须不是现在这个样子。

t: Recent advances in foreign Marxist political economy's study of "capitalism"
zh: 国外马克思主义政治经济学对“资本主义”研究的最新进展
paras: This literature review, published in 2017, surveys how Marxist political economists outside China have studied capitalism since the 2008–2009 global financial crisis. Chen Jianhua argues that, because contemporary capitalism has moved beyond the conditions Marx analysed and has become diverse, these scholars have redefined the concept, mapped its varieties and diagnosed its present difficulties. The review treats this work as a development of Marxist political economy and a source of lessons for China.

The survey has three main parts, followed by a section of commentary. The first covers new definitions of "capitalism", drawing on Sumio Shigeta, Joyce Appleby, Robert Heilbroner, Dieter Klein and Michael Brie, and David Harvey. The second covers capitalist diversity, including typologies by Paul Dragos Aligica and Vlad Tarko, Tsuruta Masahiko, Eyüp Özveren and colleagues, and Michele Mastroeni. The third covers the crises and contradictions of modern capitalism.

On definition, Chen reports a shift from capitalism as a mode of production to capitalism as a comprehensive social formation spanning economy, politics, culture and ideology, now extended globally. On crisis, Chen traces class polarisation and social stratification to the over-development of finance capital and the property sector, citing Heilbroner, Stockman, Michael Hudson and Takata Takakichi, and the class-analysis school and the Social Structure of Accumulation school. Scholars then split into two camps. Wallerstein, Collins, Calhoun and Goldner see structural crisis and possible collapse. Harvey and the Regulation School (Aglietta, Lipietz, Boyer) hold that regulation can renew capitalism.

Chen concludes that this work has strengthened Marxist political economy and offers three lessons for the study of socialism with Chinese characteristics. First, Marxist standpoints and methods remain useful. Second, research should rest on practice and attend to new problems, notably financialisation, property-sector dominance and income gaps. Third, holistic, interdisciplinary methods are needed. Chen also warns of three weaknesses: the concept of capitalism has been stretched so far that it loses rigour, some scholars over-rely on quantitative tools, and the conciliatory view that capitalism can renew itself is gaining ground. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of Western and Japanese Marxist debates on the definition, varieties and crises of capitalism, together with the lessons Chen draws for Chinese political economy.
quoteEn: Capitalism is a comprehensive social formation, encompassing politics, economy, culture and ideology, and not merely a mode of production.
quoteZh: 资本主义是一种全面的社会形态, 包括政治、经济、文化与意识形态, 而不仅仅是一种生产方式。

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学
glossary.explanation: The official name for China's model of socialism since the 1980s. The article asks how foreign Marxist work can inform political economy under this label.
A radical US school of the 1980s (Gordon, Edwards, Reich, Kotz) that explains long economic cycles through institutional structures that support profitable accumulation, and their breakdown.
A French-rooted school (Aglietta, Lipietz, Boyer) that analyses capitalism through changing regimes of accumulation and institutions of regulation.
A Marxist term for a historically specific whole of economic base, political institutions and ideology. The article uses it for capitalism understood as more than an economic system.

t: New trends in contemporary Western scholars' research on Capital
zh: 当代西方学者《资本论》研究的新趋向
source: Journal of Hebei University of Economics and Business, 2018 no. 1
paras: Marking 150 years since the first volume of Capital appeared, Tai Lihua asks how Western scholarship on the work should be characterised. Tai argues that Chinese attempts to divide it into historical periods are somewhat subjective and tend towards simplification. Instead, the article identifies three main tendencies: 'overall negation', 'communication and integration' and 'transcending reconstruction'.

The article first reviews Chinese 'periodisation' accounts: the two-stage view of Pei Xiaoge, the three-stage views of Yan Zheng and Wei Xun, and the four-stage view of Chen Shaohua and Guo Guangdi. It then examines each tendency in turn, drawing on figures such as Böhm-Bawerk, Schumpeter, Samuelson, Keynes, Sraffa, Paul Baran, Paul Sweezy, Michael Lebowitz, David Harvey and John Roemer.

Tai describes overall negation as an attack on the labour theory of value, often by pointing to a contradiction between volumes I and III. It also includes setting a 'young' Marx against the mature Marx, Marx against Engels or Lenin, and declaring Capital obsolete. Tai notes that this did not mean abandoning Marxian economics wholesale, since volume II in particular was used. Communication and integration, which Tai places after the Great Depression, compares Marx with Keynes, Sraffa, Walras, Leontief and Harrod–Domar in method, themes and specific theories. Transcending reconstruction, described as the mainstream tendency since the 1960s, alters concepts (Baran and Sweezy's 'economic surplus', Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession'), conclusions (the law of rising surplus against the falling rate of profit) and methods (Lebowitz's priority of human needs, Roemer's neoclassical modelling). Tai characterises Lebowitz's move as replacing a materialist with an idealist methodology.

Tai concludes that the three tendencies have no clear temporal boundaries and are not mutually exclusive. They coexist and overlap, and all remain visible in the debates after the US subprime crisis and the eurozone crisis. Tai states that whether these tendencies develop, innovate on or depart from Marxism is left to a later article. Following Western research is said to broaden Chinese scholars' horizons and help integrate Chinese study of Capital into international scholarship. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language map of Western schools of Capital interpretation and of how Chinese scholars periodise them.
quoteEn: The author has no intention of proposing a new historical periodisation of Western scholars' research on Capital.
quoteZh: 笔者无意就西方学者的《资本论》研究提出新的历史分期

t: The dissemination and reception of Marx's Capital in Britain and the United States
zh: 马克思《资本论》在英美的传播与接受
orig: Contemporary Economic Research (Dangdai jingji yanjiu), 2017 no. 1
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by Babak Amini of York University, Canada. It asks how Marx's Capital has been translated, published, circulated and interpreted in Britain and the United States since the first volume appeared in 1867. The article is one part of a larger project on the global reception of Capital, edited with Marcello Musto and timed for the 150th anniversary in 2017. Amini presents the history as a political as well as a bibliographical story: it shows how Marx's insights were taken up, distorted or ignored.

The article has two parts: the transmission of Capital through full and abridged translations and editions, and its reception through influential secondary literature in English. Amini first compiles a publication record, noting which volumes each edition contained and which German or French text it used. He then divides 1867–2017 into three periods: 1867–1914, 1915–1989 and 1990–2017. The article also recounts the editing of the three volumes, from Marx's revisions through Engels's posthumous editing, and explains why abridgements mattered in times of political repression such as the Red Scare and McCarthyism.

In the early period, Amini argues, Marx's ideas spread slowly in Britain because of the reformist character of the socialist movement. The first English-language extracts and translations (Aveling and Moore, 1887; Kerr's editions of volumes two and three, 1907–09) are set against a different American context shaped by German émigré socialists. In the middle period he follows the successive translations: Eden and Cedar Paul in 1928 (criticised by Riazanov), the Moscow editions, the Fowkes and Fernbach Penguin/New Left Review translation, and the Marx-Engels Collected Works. He also covers Kevin Anderson's 1983 critique, which stresses differences between the French and German editions, and the main English-language studies, including Althusser and Balibar's Reading Capital and works by Sweezy, Baran, Braverman and others.

For the post-1989 period Amini notes a lull in Marxist publishing, followed by a revival through the Collected Works volumes, edited collections, David Harvey's companion volumes and online lectures. He also reports the 2014 withdrawal of free online access to the Collected Works for copyright reasons. He suggests that, with the MEGA2 manuscripts now available, a new English translation is likely and that it will challenge dogmatic and contested readings accumulated over 150 years. Read the original if you want a detailed bibliographic and editorial history of English editions of Capital and a guide to the main Anglophone commentaries on it.
quoteEn: This research also points out how and why Marx's sharpest insights into the capitalist mode of production were accepted and understood by his supporters, or distorted and even ignored by his opponents.
quoteZh: 本项目研究还指出,马克思对资本主义生产方式的最锐利的洞察,是如何以及为何被其支持者所接受、理解,或被其反对者所曲解甚至忽视的。

t: Karl Marx: critique as emancipatory practice
zh: 卡尔·马克思:作为解放实践的批判
source: Studies on Marxist Theory in Higher Education (Gaoxiao Makesizhuyi lilun yanjiu), 2017 no. 3
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Dutch philosopher Robin Celikates. It asks what Marx's many critiques (of philosophy, religion, politics and political economy) have in common, and whether they still matter for contemporary critical theory. Celikates argues that Marx's notion of critique has three features: it targets both forms of knowledge and the social practices that match them; it is practical and emancipatory, aiming to change society as well as understand it; and it is immanent, rooted in the contradictions of capitalist society and its false self-understanding. Understood as a practice rather than a science, Celikates holds, it remains exemplary.

The article proceeds in four steps. It first outlines Marx's methodological and theoretical premises: historical materialism, the base–superstructure relation, class struggle, and a historically conditioned view of human nature. It then sets out Marx's critique of liberalism as an example of lasting relevance, and examines his critique of religion as the model for ideology critique. A final section returns to the three features and answers Jürgen Habermas's charge that Marxism wrongly understood itself as a science.

Celikates lists six strands of Marx's critique of liberalism: politics is shaped by economic conditions and is class struggle; bourgeois freedom and equality are individualistic; liberal practice reproduces exploitation; alienation pervades capitalism; ideology naturalises historical relations and presents class interests as the common good; and redistribution leaves production relations untouched. The author also names limits: economism, teleological and deterministic tendencies that sit uneasily with the stress on struggle, and the tension between scientific ambition and normative critique. The critique of religion is read as immanent: religion is a reflection of, and protest against, real social suffering. Marx therefore sublates it, preserving its vision of a life without suffering while removing the conditions that produce it.

Celikates concludes that Marx's text offers a third option between pure science and pure philosophy, combining description, explanation and normativity. Since the proletarian standpoint and a so-called science of history can no longer ground critique, critique should be understood as the self-clarification of contemporary struggles and wishes, as in Marx's 1843 letter to Ruge. Contemporary critical theory should recognise its own historicity, join philosophy, history and sociology, and avoid both dogmatic abstract norms and paternalism toward ordinary subjects. Read the original if you study Marx's method, the Habermasian reading of Marxism, or the debate over immanent critique in Western critical theory.
quoteEn: Critique should be understood as the "self-clarification of the struggles and wishes of the age", a creed of the young Marx that applies today just as it did in 1843.
quoteZh: 批判应当被理解为“当代斗争和愿望……的自我阐明”,这一青年马克思的信条在今天和在1843年同样适用。

t: The crisis of contemporary capitalism and the resistance of the Western Left
st: New trends in Western left-wing thought as seen from the 2017 New York left forum
zh: 当代资本主义的危机与西方左翼的反抗
zhSub: 从2017年纽约左翼论坛看西方左翼思想发展新动态
paras: This is a report and commentary on the left forum held in New York in June 2017 under the theme 'Resistance: Strategy, Tactics, Struggle, Solidarity and Utopia'. Writing in 2017, Jin Meng places the forum against the wave of protests that followed Donald Trump's inauguration. The article argues that the forum's speakers looked past Trump himself and aimed their critique at the capitalist system that produced him.

The report is organised around three themes debated at the forum: Marxism and its contemporary value; the crisis of capitalism and the future of socialism in the Trump era; and the history, present state and future of left-wing resistance. It closes with a short assessment by the author. Speakers named include David Schweickart, Nancy Holmstrom, Peter Hudis, David M. Kotz, Michael Hudson, Michael Perelman, Cinzia Arruzza and L. A. Kauffman.

On the first theme, Jin reports that, in the 150th anniversary year of Capital, participants held that it still offers the most persuasive tools for analysing exploitation, overwork, unemployment and alienated labour. On the second, Kotz and others are reported as tracing Trump's election to the crisis of neoliberalism. In Kotz's account Trump's right-wing nationalism scapegoats foreigners and migrants but leaves neoliberalism intact. Speakers presented women's oppression, climate change, racism and migration as products of capitalism, and proposed a universal basic income, public banks, workers' cooperatives and a political alliance of oppressed groups. On resistance, speakers named three weaknesses: the target is misplaced (the Democratic Party's co-optation), no alternative is offered, and forces are fragmented. They proposed educating the public about capitalism, building a united front and drawing in young people.

In her own assessment, Jin credits the forum with clarifying the direction of struggle and drawing the Left together. She also notes that participants include democratic socialists, anarchists and reformists with differing views of Marxism, and that their practical proposals lack unity and workability. The author concludes that the foreign Left needs a strong command centre and a broader united front. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of how the US Left framed Trump, capitalism and resistance in 2017, or a list of the forum's speakers and themes.
quoteEn: Left-wing scholars aimed the spearhead of left-wing resistance directly at the capitalist system, clarifying the direction of struggle and gathering left-wing forces together.
quoteZh: 左翼学者们将左翼反抗的矛头直指资本主义制度, 明确了斗争方向, 凝聚了左翼力量。

glossary.explanation: Used loosely here for left-wing scholars and activists outside China, including Marxists, democratic socialists and anarchists. The article treats them as a mixed field to be analysed critically.
A term from Marxist-Leninist and Chinese Communist Party practice for an alliance of different groups against a common opponent. The article uses it for uniting varied left forces.
The market-oriented economic policy regime that, in the speakers' account, replaced Keynesianism in the US from the late 1970s. It is blamed for inequality and the 2008 crisis.

t: Western left-wing scholars' theories of capitalist crisis from the perspective of the "mode of production" and their recent developments
zh: “生产方式”视域下西方左翼学者的资本主义危机理论及其新进展
source: Journal of Northeastern University (Social Science Edition), 2017 no. 4
paras: Since the mid-twentieth century, Western left-wing scholars have produced many theories of capitalist crisis. Yan Fangjie divides them into two research perspectives: a "cultural" one, concerned with ideology, aesthetics and everyday life, and a "mode of production" one that follows Marx's critique of political economy. The article takes up the second and argues that, although it looks conservative and traditional, it stays closer to the substance of Marxism than much culture-centred work.

The article surveys these scholars in three groups. The first stresses internal crises of the mode of production, represented by Ernest Mandel and István Mészáros. The second stresses "obstructive" crises arising from external conditions of production, represented by James O'Connor and, for the ecological case, André Gorz. The third applies the approach to the twenty-first-century financial crisis and splits into pessimists (Immanuel Wallerstein, Randall Collins) and optimists (Michael Mann, Craig Calhoun, and others).

Yan reads Mandel and Mészáros as locating crisis in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and in the gap between production and consumption. In this reading, arms spending and wasteful or destructive production deepen the contradiction instead of resolving it. O'Connor adds a "second contradiction" between capital and its conditions of production, such as nature, labour-power and infrastructure. Rising costs of these conditions produce ecological and social crisis. For the recent crisis, Wallerstein sees rising personnel, material and tax costs together with geopolitical disorder. Collins foresees technological displacement of middle-class work, with structural unemployment of 50 per cent by about 2040. Mann and Calhoun doubt that economic crisis alone is fatal. They point to ecological limits and the end of cost externalisation, and Calhoun speaks of "decline" rather than collapse. Yan describes the pessimists as system-theoretic and the optimists as Weberian in method.

Yan concludes that these scholars' specifics are sometimes far apart and open to question. Even so, their use of categories such as productive forces, relations of production, effective demand, underconsumption and the falling rate of profit is called valuable. Some of them treat the financial crisis as an extension of traditional economic crisis, not a purely technical accident. Yan argues that this makes their work an analysis of capitalism's essence, not an external study. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language map of Western left and critical theories of capitalist crisis, from Mandel to Wallerstein and Calhoun, organised around the mode of production.
quoteEn: To some extent it can be said that what they undertake is not an external study of capitalism but an analysis of its essence.
quoteZh: 在某种程度上可以说, 他们从事的不是关于资本主义的外在性研究, 而是一种本质性分析。

t: "Neoliberalism" and the Western New Left
zh: “新自由主义”与西方新左派
paras: Zhou Jiaxin asks how critique of neoliberalism has shaped the development of the contemporary Western Left, using New Left Review as the main vantage point. The article counts roughly 60 neoliberalism-focused papers in the journal since the 1990s. Its thesis is that neoliberalism is the theoretical system of monopoly finance capitalism, and that its apparent collapse after the 2008 financial crisis offers the Western "new left" a historic opening for theoretical breakthrough.

The article has four parts. It first defines neoliberalism and separates it from classical liberalism and from "New Liberalism" (Keynes, Rawls and others). It then analyses neoliberalism's political economy under three headings: financialization, globalization and structural crisis. The third part traces how the Left's own theory evolved in confrontation with neoliberalism, and the fourth maps five directions for the Left after 2008.

Zhou argues that neoliberalism is not simply a revived laissez-faire. Where classical liberalism defended private property and industrial capital, neoliberalism, in this reading, serves the freedom of monopoly finance capital, its "disembedding" from social and political constraints. The Washington Consensus is presented as its classic expression, and David Harvey's label "new imperialism" as exposing its ideological nature. Zhou endorses the view that globalization, financialization, internet technology and asset bubbles were only temporary "fixes" for the basic contradiction of capital accumulation, and that income inequality, separatism and migration tensions show neoliberalism's bankruptcy. On the Left's trajectory, Zhou holds that Western Marxism, a "Weberian Marxism" tied to the welfare state and organised capitalism, reached its logical end around 1979. Post-Marxism then set aside the dialectic, and a return to it followed around the turn of the century in Žižek, Christopher Arthur's "new dialectic", Foster, Harvey and Jameson.

Zhou identifies five post-2008 tendencies in Western left theory: world-system and globalization critique, with space and urban analysis; identity, ethnicity and migration; biopolitics; information, network and media critique; and a "return to the critique of political economy" via Capital. Neoliberal critique is proposed as a yardstick for assessing foreign Marxism since the 1970s. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of how New Left Review-centred debates linked neoliberalism, the fate of Western Marxism and the revival of the dialectic.
quoteEn: The end of "neoliberalism" constitutes a historic opportunity for the new currents of the Western Left to achieve a theoretical breakthrough.
quoteZh: “新自由主义”的终结构成了西方新的左派思潮实现理论突围的历史性契机。

glossary.explanation: A set of ten market-oriented policy prescriptions formulated in 1989–90 in connection with Latin American economic adjustment, backed by Washington-based institutions such as the IMF and World Bank. Zhou treats it as the classic expression of neoliberalism.
British left-wing journal founded in 1960 and edited for many years by Perry Anderson. The article treats it as a key forum and barometer of Western left theory.
The tradition running from Lukács to Adorno, distinct from Soviet orthodoxy. Zhou follows Perry Anderson in seeing it as a theory detached from political practice and economic reality.
The growing weight of finance in capitalist production and politics. Zhou presents it as a central feature of the neoliberal stage of capitalism.

t: The historical fate of twenty-first-century capitalism
st: Western left-wing scholars' new examination of the crisis of capitalism
zh: 21世纪资本主义的历史命运
zhSub: 西方左翼人士对资本主义危机的新审视
paras: Almost a decade after the global crisis of 2008, this article, published in 2017, reviews how Western left-wing scholars have reassessed capitalism and its prospects. Tong argues that these thinkers have become more rational and objective in their criticism, and that their views offer useful reference points for Chinese readers, even though many do not seek to replace capitalism.

The review is organised in four parts: whether the crisis is systemic; who bears its costs; how the crisis turns from danger into opportunity; and what scholars predict for capitalism's future. It draws on Berch Berberoglu, William I. Robinson, Immanuel Wallerstein, Chase-Dunn and Roberts, Niall Ferguson, James Petras and Henry Veltmeyer, Michael Koyama, Régis Debray, Fred Magdoff and Michael Yates, Wolfgang Streeck and Rémy Herrera.

Tong reports that most of these scholars see a systemic, institutional crisis, which some think could end capitalism as a system, while Koyama and others want it rescued through radical reform. Drawing on Petras and Veltmeyer, the article presents the working class as the real bearer of the crisis: corporate profits recovered, the 'revolving door' between Wall Street and the Treasury protected capital, and austerity brought unemployment, especially among young people. Tong then argues that capitalism is losing its historical rationality and its capacity for self-adjustment, because bailouts deepen financialisation. The same crisis, in this reading, hardens the working class's class consciousness and so trains capitalism's 'gravediggers'.

On the future, Tong notes that Debray lists Western weaknesses but also strengths, such as cohesion, control of 'universal' values, elite financial schools, media influence and technological lead. Streeck and Herrera expect a long decline, with Herrera saying that more and more people hope socialism will replace capitalism. Tong concludes that the replacement of capitalism by socialism is inevitable but will be long and tortuous. Citing Xi Jinping, Tong warns against blindly talking down capitalism and calls for using the crisis actively to advance world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of Western left-wing literature on the post-2008 crisis and of how it is used to frame socialism's prospects.
quoteEn: As the degree of exploitation of workers keeps deepening, the space for capital accumulation continues to shrink.
quoteZh: 伴随着工人受剥削的程度在不断加深, 资本积累的空间也在持续压缩。

t: Deepening methodological self-awareness in Chinese studies of Capital
st: The political reading of Capital in international scholarship and its assessment
zh: 深化中国《资本论》研究的方法论自觉
zhSub: 国际学界对《资本论》的政治式阅读及其评价
paras: Marking the 150th anniversary of the first volume of Capital, Tang argues that commemoration should prompt reflection on how Capital is read today. Since the 1970s, international scholarship has produced philosophical, economic and political readings, each tied to its own context. Tang contends that Chinese scholars should build their own reading of Capital from China's practical experience, and that this requires methodological self-awareness towards foreign readings rather than uncritical adoption.

The article concentrates on the "political reading" of Capital and its manuscripts, which it calls the most fashionable approach on the foreign left. It examines Antonio Negri (Marx beyond Marx, on the Grundrisse), Harry Cleaver (Reading Capital Politically) and, more briefly, Jacques Bidet's meta-structural reading. A closing section extends the point to philosophical readings centred on fetishism and reification, and to similar tendencies in Chinese scholarship.

Tang summarises the political reading in three claims: Marx wrote to build the working class's revolutionary subjectivity; his object, the commodity form, embodies relations of power and exploitation; and value survives only within surplus value, which exists only through class struggle. Negri locates this in the money form, which hides inequality behind equivalence; Cleaver locates it in the commodity form imposed on workers. Tang credits the approach with textual grounding and sensitivity to new phenomena, and finds Cleaver the more rigorous of the two. He nonetheless faults both for neglecting the production process. In his view they treat the commodity at the level of bourgeois exchange, and so miss that capital's logic is the production of capital as capital, and that Marx's concepts rest on historical materialism. Tang argues that they criticise unequal distribution while accepting that productive forces keep growing, and so pursue piecemeal political movements rather than revolution against the whole system. Bidet's recasting of Marx's method, he adds, oversimplifies Marx.

Tang concludes that Capital's political dimension matters but cannot be its only one. Political and cultural perspectives should be placed within the overall history of social development and its inner contradictions. Chinese scholars, whose aims differ from those of Negri and Cleaver, should not accept foreign readings merely because they are popular. Tang also links methodological self-awareness to the study of the laws governing the building of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical critique of Negri, Cleaver and Bidet, and an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars position Capital studies against Western left readings.
quoteEn: In my view, we should of course attach importance to the political dimension of Marx's Capital; this is beyond question.
quoteZh: 笔者以为, 我们当然应该重视马克思《资本论》中的政治维度, 这是不容置疑的。
