glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's line of socialist development since reform and opening up. Chinese scholarship often ties the study of Marxist classics to exploring its laws.

t: Marx's "near-Adorno" interpretation
st: John Holloway's reconstruction of the path of critiquing capitalism
zh: 马克思的近阿多诺阐释
zhSub: 约翰·霍洛威对资本主义批判路径的重构
source: Journal of Shanghai Jiao Tong University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2017 no. 5
paras: Many readings recast Marx as "near-Kant" or "near-Hegel", and Sun Liang asks what follows from the "near-Adorno" reading developed by John Holloway, a representative of Open Marxism. Sun argues that Holloway uses Adorno's negative dialectics to rescue Marx from a Hegelian tradition in which capitalism is criticised from within a closed category. Holloway also reproaches Hardt and Negri, who reject Hegel, for misunderstanding dialectics and falling back into traditional Marxism's limits. Sun judges the approach a forceful corrective that is nonetheless too idealistic.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why Holloway, following Adorno, rejects Hegelian dialectics as a "straitjacket" and how this differs from the post-structuralist rejection by Althusser, Deleuze, Hardt and Negri. The second explains Adorno's notion of non-identity and Holloway's concept of the "crack". The third turns to Marx's Capital and Holloway's shift from the "productive forces of capital" to the "social productive force of labour". Sources are mainly Holloway's Negativity and Revolution, Crack Capitalism and In, Against, and Beyond Capitalism, together with Adorno's Negative Dialektik.

Sun reports that Holloway accepts the charge that Hegelian dialectics reduces varied struggles to a single contradiction between labour and capital that ends in "reconciliation". But Hardt and Negri, in his view, also discard the dialectic's negative movement, and so still hope for a harmonious "common world". Adorno's non-identity, which Holloway ties to the idea that "we" overflow every identity, including that of the working class, becomes the basis for a critical theory that starts from capitalism's cracks and not from its domination. Holloway reads exchange as the social model of identity-thinking, and he rejects vanguard politics and the idea of seizing power.

On Marx, Sun reports that Holloway reads the productive forces under capitalism as the fetishised power of capital. He locates human creative capacity in the "social productive force of labour", which grows in the slippage between obedience and rebellion, and he points to wiki-style and sharing production as examples. Sun concludes that this dissolves Marx's concept of revolution and shifts liberation from ownership relations to inner freedom, ignoring the ordinary person's need to adapt to capital. Sun still finds it meaningful because life itself is precious. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Holloway and of Open Marxism's debts to Adorno.
quoteEn: Holloway's "non-identification" approach, which tries to burst this iron wall, is undoubtedly a forceful corrective to the long-popular near-Hegelian readings.
quoteZh: 霍洛威尝试爆裂这一铁壁的“非同一化”思路,无疑是对长期流行的近黑格尔解读一种有力地纠偏

t: Three interpretive paths for Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 《资本论》及其手稿的三种诠释路径
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2017 no. 8
paras: Lu Shaochen asks how Capital and its manuscripts have been read since the early twentieth century. The author argues that the history of their reception, even if it can be called a history of misreading, is what has kept Marx's thought lively and made dogmatic readings untenable. The article reviews and assesses three paths of interpretation in Western and foreign Marxism.

The article is organised in four sections. The first treats the early Western Marxist 'continuity thesis' (Lukács, Korsch, Fromm, with Luxemburg). The second treats the 'rupture thesis' of Althusser and its political and power-oriented continuation in Negri, Hardt and Harry Cleaver's 'political reading'. The third turns to the 'New Dialectic' and value-form readings (Chris Arthur, Tony Smith, Fred Moseley, Moishe Postone, Riccardo Bellofiore and others), made possible by the MEGA edition. A final section considers the philological work on the texts and gives Lu's own view.

In Lu's account, the first path stresses totality, the historicity of capitalism, alienated labour and reification, and sees no qualitative break between the young and the mature Marx. Critics, including Postone and Perry Anderson, are cited as saying that it criticises 'alienation' rather than 'capital' and drifts away from political economy towards philosophy and aesthetics. The second path reads capital as a power relation and gives priority to working-class subjectivity. Alex Callinicos, as presented by Lu, replies that it reduces Marx to a Foucauldian theory of power and collapses the three dimensions of capitalism (exchange, exploitation and domination, and competition among capitals) into one. The third path reads Marx through Hegel's Logic, treating value, abstract labour and the value form as social forms and capital as a 'living contradiction'. It is criticised for neglecting exploitation and class struggle, and for drawing too close a parallel between Capital and Hegel. The same school's study of Engels's editing of Marx's text, such as the changed subtitle of volume one and the altered passage on the falling rate of profit, is also reported.

Lu concludes that MEGA allows Capital and its manuscripts to be reread on a firmer philological footing and outside the tradition shaped by Engels. The author holds that Hegel's logic is for Marx mainly a method of scientific research. What keeps driving fresh readings, Lu argues, is the development and present condition of modern society. Read the original if you want a critical map of the main Western interpretive schools of Capital, with attention to the MEGA-based debates, as seen by a Chinese philosopher.
quoteEn: In my view, the text of Marx's Capital and its manuscripts is vast and its thought complex; as new historical circumstances and social development accompany it, it necessarily appears more 'open' and thereby richer and more alive.
quoteZh: 在我看来, 马克思的《资本论》及其手稿的文本是广博的, 思想是复杂的, 其必然伴随着新的时代境遇和社会发展, 而显得更为“开放”并因此变得更加丰富和有生命力。

t: From the principle of justice to the principle of community
st: With a note on the lessons of G. A. Cohen's socialist project
zh: 从正义原则到共同体原则
zhSub: 兼论柯亨的社会主义方案的启示
paras: Lin Yuchuan reconstructs the political philosophy of the analytical Marxist G. A. Cohen as an argument for the desirability, and then the feasibility, of an ideal socialism. Lin's thesis is that Cohen moves from principles of justice to a principle of community, built on generosity and mutual aid, which is meant to go beyond justice and equality.

The article reads Cohen in three steps: his exposure of a conflict between liberal justice as fairness and community; the return of community in egalitarian distributive justice (justice as equality); and his ideal socialism as a community that surpasses justice. It engages John Rawls, Ronald Dworkin, Will Kymlicka, Richard Miller and Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, and draws on Cohen's Rescuing Justice and Equality and Why Not Socialism?. A final section draws lessons for China.

Lin argues that Rawls's difference principle fits community through compensation, reciprocity and fraternity, yet loses it once incentives are used to justify inequality. On Cohen's interpersonal test, talented people who demand high pay as an incentive are in effect threatening to withdraw their labour, which signals a lack of community. Cohen's own luck egalism, equality of access to advantage, restores community by compensating involuntary disadvantage. Lin notes that it remains hard to apply, for example to non-material goods such as self-respect. Cohen's camping-trip model then places equality and community together, with community ultimately governing equality. Lin reads Cohen as differing from Marx: he doubts that material abundance will arrive, and puts his hope in mechanisms that draw out human generosity.

Lin concludes that Cohen's project is not a blueprint to copy and that its value is reflective. Lin draws three lessons for China. First, Cohen's sequence of distributive models, from Nozick to Rawls and Cohen, shows the limits of distribution according to work. Second, his critique of the market warns against market worship. Lin does not call for abandoning the market, but for limiting it in fields such as education and health. Third, just institutions need a social ethos of equality and community, because individual greed can erode institutions. Read the original if you study Cohen, Rawls or analytical Marxism, or want to see how a Chinese philosopher draws on Cohen's work to discuss distribution and social justice in China.
quoteEn: The lessons of Cohen's socialist project are reflective in nature and have no direct borrowable significance.
quoteZh: 柯亨的社会主义方案带来的启示在本质上是反思性的, 不具有可以直接借鉴的意义

glossary.explanation: The principle of the first stage of communism in Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme. It is the principle of distribution in socialist China.
A strand of egalitarian theory holding that inequalities caused by luck or involuntary circumstances are unjust and should be compensated, while inequalities from choice may be acceptable.

t: Negri on Spinoza's biopolitics
zh: 奈格里论斯宾诺莎的生命政治
paras: Feng Bo asks how Spinoza's philosophy relates to biopolitics, a link the author says has long been neglected. The usual story runs from Nietzsche's turn to the body to Foucault's account of biopolitics. Feng argues that Antonio Negri, himself a Spinozist Marxist, shows Spinoza had already made the turn to the body, and that Negri reads biopolitics very differently from Foucault. The article uses Negri's texts to clarify both the Spinoza connection and Negri's distinctive concept.

The article has three parts. The first compares Negri's definition of biopolitics with Foucault's account of biopower. The second examines Negri's reading of Spinoza's critique of biopower, through the terms conatus or striving, impulse, potentia (power as productive force), potestas (power as authority) and immanence. The third turns to how Negri sees Spinoza constructing a democratic biopolitics, through the critique of social contract theory in Hobbes and Rousseau. Feng draws on Negri, Hardt, Macherey, Foucault and Spinoza's own texts.

Feng reports that Foucault confines biopower to the modern power to make live, whereas Negri widens it to include sovereignty's power over death and disciplinary power. For Negri biopower is therefore as old as the state, and biopolitics is not its politics but its opposite: a stateless, immanent politics of the polis, built from the bodily impulses of singularities. Feng explains that Negri takes from Spinoza the distinction between potentia, an immanent, productive and bodily force, and potestas, a transcendent power that is constructed and speculative. He takes 'multitude' from Spinoza too. Negri also holds that Spinoza gave up contract theory and thereby sovereignty. Rousseau's general will, in Negri's reading, yields only a 'democratic monarchy', while Spinoza's 'will of all' tolerates difference and grounds absolute democracy.

Feng concludes that Negri's creative reading lets Spinoza dissolve sovereignty as biopower and ground a biopolitics collectively built from bodily forces and plurality. Feng also notes a tension. Negri ignores Spinoza's pessimism about the masses' superstition and fear, and optimistically affirms the free multitude as the agent of resistance. Feng therefore calls Negri a Spinozist who goes beyond Spinoza. Read the original if you work on Negri, Spinoza or biopolitics and want a Chinese scholarly account of how Negri's concept differs from Foucault's and of its Spinozist sources.
quoteEn: Negri's borrowing and interpretation of Spinoza's philosophy nonetheless reveals the real connection between Spinoza and biopolitics.
quoteZh: 奈格里对斯宾诺莎哲学的借用和解释还是呈现了斯宾诺莎与生命政治之间的现实联系

t: Alain Badiou on subjectivization and the subjective process
zh: 阿兰·巴迪欧论主体化和主体进程
paras: Ai Shiwei examines how Alain Badiou, whom the article calls a leading representative of post-Marxism, builds his theory of the subject. Badiou rejects both the idealist model, which separates subject from body, and the materialist model, which reduces the subject to the body. He proposes a third model in which the subject sits between event and truth and stays faithful to the event. Ai argues that this subject is split into two aspects, subjectivization and the subjective process, and that understanding them is essential to Badiou's theory. Ai notes that, apart from Ed Pluth's study, existing literature treats the two terms only in passing.

The article is organised in three sections: subjectivization, the subjective process, and their combination. It draws mainly on Badiou's Theory of the Subject (1982), with Being and Event, Logics of Worlds and Conditions as supporting texts. It also uses Bruno Bosteels's translator's introduction and Pluth's commentary. Ai traces the terms back to Lacan and compares Badiou's 'superego' with Freud, Foucault and Lacan. Badiou's analysis of class struggle in France serves as a worked example, and the closing pages place Theory of the Subject within his later development.

Ai presents subjectivization as brief, destructive and interventionist, a rupture with an existing situation, such as an uprising, and it takes two forms: 'anxiety' (pure destruction) and 'courage' (destruction that aims at a new order). The subjective process is lasting and reorganising, and it also takes two forms: the 'superego', which Badiou calls a terroristic process that fixes the excess elements in rigid places, and 'justice', which relativises law and blurs fixed positions. Their pairings produce the Ψ mode (anxiety–superego) and the α mode (courage–justice). Ai reads Badiou's 'imaginary diagonals' through Lacan: courage–superego yields a dogmatic function, and justice–anxiety a sceptical function that ends in nothing. Ai maps the pairings onto class struggle: riot and the dictatorship of the proletariat for Ψ, insurrection and communism for α. The two aspects, Ai says, verify and raise each other in a spiral, as in materialist dialectics.

Ai concludes that Badiou rejects Descartes' separation of subject and body, Nietzsche's exaltation of the body and mechanical materialism's reduction of the subject to the body. The subject is the body's subjective form, and the body is the subjectivized body. Ai adds that Badiou later extended the subject beyond politics to science, art and love, and criticised his early assumption that subjectivization simply 'exists'. Ai reads this as a move beyond pure deconstruction toward the possible formation and reconstruction of the subject. Read the original if you study Badiou, Lacanian philosophy or post-Marxist theories of the subject and want a close reading of Theory of the Subject.
quoteEn: Whether the Ψ mode or the α mode, each is a subjective procedure combining subjectivization with the subjective process.
quoteZh: 不论是Ψ模式还是α模式, 都是主体化与主体进程相结合的主体程序。

t: The Absolute and the event: what kind of Hegelian is Žižek?
zh: 绝对与事件：齐泽克是一个怎样的黑格尔主义者
source: Journal of Soochow University (Philosophy and Social Science Edition), 2017 no. 4
paras: Hegel is the modern philosopher of totality, and twentieth-century thought often charged that his system leaves no room for the event, understood as a rupture with reason and teleology. Wu Guanjun asks how Slavoj Žižek can call himself a committed Hegelian and also make the event an ontological category. The article answers that Žižek reads Hegel's Absolute as a whole with a gap built into it, and that this reading lets negativity itself produce the new.

The article first sets out the standard picture of Hegel, in which the Absolute is both the truth of all events and their cause, so that events have meaning only as parts of the whole. Wu then compares Žižek with Alain Badiou, who started out as a student of Hegel but turned anti-Hegelian once he developed his theory of the event in Being and Event. Wu also brings in Nancy, Derrida, Deleuze and Kojève. The later sections cover Žižek's account of dialectics, the parallax view, the Fall as the ultimate event, and Žižek's hidden debt to Kojève.

Wu argues that Žižek treats the dialectic as a change of framework, not a change of content: the negation of the negation overturns the whole symbolic frame, so that the law itself becomes the crime. Totality exists only with a gap, or absolute difference, embedded in it. Absolute knowledge therefore means recognising that gap and one's own limits, not seeing as God sees, and history has no endpoint. Against Badiou's claim that negation is derivative and creates nothing, Žižek holds that negation is ontologically primary. In his view the new affirmation is the positivised power of the negative, and the ultimate event is the Fall itself. Wu traces this stress on negation and creativity to Kojève's formula that freedom equals negativity equals creativity, a debt Žižek never acknowledges.

Wu concludes that Žižek rejects the image of Hegel as an all-knowing absolute idealist. In Žižek's reading, absolute spirit confronts the ontological wound between reality and the Real, and it keeps tearing apart any attempt by the present order to totalise itself. Wu also corrects John Gray, who traced Žižek's Hegel to Badiou and tied it to capitalism. On Wu's account it comes from Kojève and describes the ontological structure of the world. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Žižek, Badiou and Kojève relate to one another on Hegel, negation and the event, or if you want to trace Žižek's Hegel reading through its sources.)
quoteEn: On Žižek's radical reading of Hegel, absolute spirit (the final state of spirit's self-development) is no longer the substance/subject in the unfolding of History with a capital H, but the eventful confrontation with the wound, the ontological rupture between "reality" and the Real.
quoteZh: 在齐泽克对黑格尔的激进解读下, 绝对精神 (精神自我发展的最终状态) 不再是“大写的历史”之演进过程中的实体/主体, 而是事件性地直面创口—直面“现实世界”与真实之间的那个本体论裂缝。

t: "Truth procedure" and "subtractive politics": an analysis of Badiou's radical left philosophy
zh: “真理程序”和“减法政治”：试析巴迪欧的左翼激进哲学
paras: Fan Chunyan examines how Alain Badiou tries to revive universal truth and the idea of communism under postmodern and post-revolutionary conditions. In Fan's reading, Badiou refuses a return to essentialist, 'capital-One' conceptions and instead builds on the 'irreducible multiplicity of being'. The article argues that his project rests on two core concepts, 'truth procedure' and 'subtractive politics', which answer respectively the question of truth and the question of how to practise communism anew.

The article has two main parts. The first reconstructs the truth procedure through three steps: Badiou's mathematical ontology and the set-theoretic 'generic multiple'; the event and the production of 'pure novelty'; and the triad of truth, event and subject, including his three types of subject. The second part turns to political truth procedures and Badiou's account of two sequences of emancipatory politics since 1792. It discusses the Maoist principle 'one divides into two', 'subtractive negation' and non-party forms of organisation.

Fan explains that for Badiou truth is not a given transcendent unity but the result of a generic operation on multiplicity. It is produced when a contingent event breaks the existing situation. Subjects become part of a truth's 'body' through fidelity to the event, mediated by the Idea. Badiou distinguishes faithful, reactionary and obscure subjects. In politics, Fan reports, Badiou holds that the second sequence, from the October Revolution through Lenin and Mao, has exhausted its possibilities. The Leninist 'party-state' won power but produced statism and undifferentiated individuals rather than singular revolutionary subjects.

For a third sequence, Fan presents Badiou as proposing politics that keeps its distance from the state: it refuses elections and state funding, creates autonomous spaces, and works through minimal difference rather than pure destruction. Destruction is retained only as a defensive force, to protect what subtraction has created. Organisation would be loose, flexible and held together by Ideas rather than by a vanguard party. Fan presents this as an exposition of Badiou's thought and offers no sustained critique of it. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language introduction to Badiou's concepts of truth, event, subject and subtractive politics, as a case of Chinese engagement with foreign Marxism.
quoteEn: Badiou stresses that radical politics cannot be reduced to a purely destructive negation.
quoteZh: 巴迪欧强调, 激进政治不能被还原为一种纯粹的破坏性否定。

glossary.explanation: A Maoist formulation of dialectics that stresses the division and struggle of opposites. It was set against 'two combine into one' (合二为一), which stresses synthesis. Badiou takes it as a starting point for new emancipatory politics.

t: The crisis of contemporary capitalism and the resistance of the Western left
st: New trends in Western left thought as seen from the 2017 New York left forum
zh: 当代资本主义的危机与西方左翼的反抗
zhSub: 从2017年纽约左翼论坛看西方左翼思想发展新动态
paras: This is a report and short assessment of the left forum held in New York in June 2017 under the theme 'Resistance: strategy, tactics, struggle, solidarity and utopia'. Jin Meng places the event against the protests that followed Donald Trump's inauguration in January 2017, and reports that the forum's speakers treated women's, ecological, racial and immigration questions as products of the capitalist system. In this account Trump is a continuer of that system, not its originator, so resistance has to target capitalism itself.

The report is organised around three clusters of discussion by Western left scholars: Marxism and its contemporary value, especially on the 150th anniversary of Capital, Volume 1; the crisis of capitalism in the Trump era and the future of socialism; and the history, present state and future of left resistance. A brief assessment closes the piece. Participants named include David Schweickart, Nancy Holmstrom, Peter Hudis, David M. Kotz, Michael Hudson, Michael Perelman, Cinzia Arruzza and L. A. Kauffman.

On the first theme, Jin reports that speakers saw Capital as still the most scientific tool for analysing exploitation, overwork, unemployment and alienated labour. Holmstrom and Hudis are cited on gender equality, ecological crisis and a post-capitalist form of labour. On the second theme, Kotz and others traced Trump's election to the crisis of neoliberalism and described his government as right-wing nationalism that strengthens neoliberalism rather than ending it. The scholars proposed alternatives such as a universal basic income, a job guarantee, public banks, workers' cooperatives and eco-socialism, and held that gender, race, climate and migration struggles should merge into a proletarian class struggle. On the third theme, they named three weaknesses of current resistance: a misdirected target, absorption by the Democratic Party, and no alternative programme and no organised centre. They urged teaching the public to see capitalism as the target, forming a united front, and relying on young people.

In the concluding assessment, Jin credits the forum with clarifying the target of struggle and gathering left forces. Jin also notes that the left is a mixed body of democratic socialists, anarchists, reformists and others who differ on Marxism and scientific socialism, so their views must be treated dialectically. Their practical proposals are described as lacking operability and unity, and Jin calls for a strong command centre and a united left. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of how the 2017 American left framed Trump, Capital and the strategy of resistance.
quoteEn: Left scholars pointed the spearhead of left resistance directly at the capitalist system, clarifying the direction of struggle and rallying left forces.
quoteZh: 左翼学者们将左翼反抗的矛头直指资本主义制度, 明确了斗争方向, 凝聚了左翼力量。

glossary.explanation: The term for the Marxist theory of socialism, which Chinese writers distinguish from utopian and other non-Marxist socialisms. Jin uses it as a benchmark against which the varied views of left participants are measured.

t: A preliminary study of Marxist class psychology in contemporary social development
zh: 当代社会发展中的马克思主义阶级心理研究刍议
paras: Li Houyi asks how Marx's account of class psychology should be understood and defended now that classes have become more varied and class relations more complex. The article argues that much contemporary Western left-wing research has drifted from Marx's foundations, and that a return to his premises would let empirical and micro-level methods be absorbed without losing the critical orientation of Marxism.

The article has three parts. The first reviews Marx's view of class psychology and the revisions made by Western Marxist and sociological scholars, notably Eric Olin Wright, with Weberian ideas, Peter Blau and Otis Duncan on social mobility, and the concept of 'social closure'. The second sets out five principles that Li draws from Marx. The third looks at current trends in Western left-wing work and proposes three directions for improvement.

Li's central claim is that Marx grounds class psychology in ownership of the means of production, in alienated labour and in the aim of human emancipation. Li says Western scholars have replaced class psychology with occupational psychology, reduced it to feelings of exploitation or bargaining power, and explained psychological conflict through changes of status. In Li's view this detaches the field from relations of production. Against this, Li draws five lessons from Marx: class psychology arises from socio-economic position and is shaped dialectically by language and practice; it must be grasped within the totality of historical development; it can be studied through underlying structures of consciousness; it rests on practice, not on transcendent psychological theory; and it can absorb other methods. Recent Western work on class diversity, conflict and system dynamics, Li argues, has become micro-level and laboratory-based, and neglects the economic roots of power and consensus.

Li concludes that three recent themes in Western left-wing research (relations, labelling and performance) can be useful, but only if they are tied to their economic preconditions, root causes and a firm belief in Marxism. If class psychology is reduced to small-group psychology and laboratory verification, Li warns, the application of Marxism is distorted. Where researchers hold to Marxist theory and critique capitalism, quantitative, empirical and micro methods can become organic parts of Marxist research. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western class-psychology scholarship and of how Marx's views might be used to evaluate it.
quoteEn: Fundamentally, class psychology is the collective emotion and intention determined by ownership of property (the means of production).
quoteZh: 阶级心理从根本上来说是由财产 (生产资料) 所有权所决定的集体情感和意向

t: China and the Communist Party of China as seen by the international community
zh: 国际社会眼中的中国及中国共产党
paras: Written after the 19th Party Congress (2017), this commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts collects foreign reactions to the Congress report and to the Communist Party of China (CPC). Zhang notes that more than 600 foreign leaders, parties and organisations sent congratulations and that over 1,000 journalists from more than 130 countries reported on the event. The author argues that knowing how the world sees China helps to strengthen confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article is a compilation of quotations from foreign politicians, scholars and media, grouped under four headings. These are: the CPC's leadership as the key to China's stability and prosperity; China as a driving force of the world economy; the contribution of the "China solution" in the "new era"; and China as a promoter of peace and civilisational progress. Sources include Russian, Singaporean, British, American, Japanese, Brazilian, Cuban and Latin American commentators, among them Putin, Hatoyama Yukio, Martin Jacques, Arif Dirlik, the Financial Times, the BBC and the Washington Post.

Zhang reports that the cited voices praise the Party's anti-corruption work, cadre training, rule of law and long-term planning, which they contrast with short-term electoral politics in the West. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as a theoretical innovation guiding the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Foreign commentators are also quoted as saying that the Belt and Road Initiative makes China a locomotive of the world economy, that its green policies set an example, and that its development offers developing countries an alternative model. Several sources, including the Financial Times and the BBC, are cited as seeing a self-confident China moving toward "the centre of the world stage" while the West declines. Others are cited as saying that a community with a shared future for mankind offers a new possibility for global governance, and that Xi's emphasis on domestic strength weakens the "China threat" thesis.

Zhang concludes, through these citations, that the international community broadly regards the CPC's leadership as decisive for China's rise and sees China as a positive force for world peace and development. The commentary draws no critical distinctions among the sources and does not discuss dissenting views beyond a Washington Post piece criticising Western misreadings of China. Read the original if you want a sample of how Chinese official media in late 2017 selected and presented favourable foreign commentary on the 19th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Understanding how the international community assesses the report of the 19th Party Congress and the CPC helps us grasp its view of present-day China and further strengthens confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteZh: 了解国际社会对党的十九大报告及中国共产党的评价，有助于我们洞悉国际社会对当今中国的认识，进一步坚定中国特色社会主义道路自信、理论自信、制度自信、文化自信。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology, written into the CPC constitution at the 19th Party Congress in 2017.
A Chinese foreign-economic initiative launched in 2013 to build transport, trade and investment links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping describing China's vision of international relations and global governance based on joint consultation, building and sharing.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-term national goal in Party discourse, linked to the Chinese Dream, of restoring China's strength and international standing.
A phrase in official discourse for China's development experience and proposals offered as a reference for other countries and for global problems.

t: On contemporary Western Marxism
zh: 论当代西方马克思主义
source: Journal of Southwest Forestry University, 2017 no. 1
paras: Chen Xueming surveys what he calls contemporary Western Marxism, meaning the broader field of Marxism outside China, and asks what it has contributed and how Chinese Marxists should use it. He argues that since the mid-1990s, and especially since the 2007 credit crisis, this current has revived and renewed Marxism. In his view it offers new explorations of Marxism, a new critique of capitalism and a new outlook on socialism, all of which Chinese Marxism can learn from critically.

The article has three parts. The first traces how the current formed, from the split after Engels's death into Second International, Third International and Western Marxist paths, through the post-1991 setback to the post-2007 revival. It then lists six new features: convergence with the radical left, postmodern dominance, a shift to "post-Marxism", fusion with the humanities and natural sciences, study of Marxism as an organic whole, and acceptance of pluralism. The second part assesses its influence. The third makes seven proposals for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

In the central assessment, Chen reports foreign thinkers' work in each area. On Marxism, he cites Eagleton, Hobsbawm, Badiou and Žižek on the Occupy movement, the revived reading of Capital, and debates on social justice and "postmodern Marxism". On capitalism, he cites critiques of neoliberalism, ecological crisis, consumer society, the commodification of space, liberal democracy and the "new imperialism". On socialism, he cites the claim that "another choice is possible", the revival of communism, ecosocialism, market socialism, utopian socialism and Latin American twenty-first-century socialism. Chen also says these thinkers mix valuable and worthless ideas, are internally divided, and often offer critique without practical experience behind it.

Chen concludes that foreign Marxism has raised the quality rather than the quantity of Marxism and that, with its caveats, it should be absorbed. His proposals include widening theoretical horizons, comparing Chinese and Western Marxism, using foreign Marxism's rational elements to evaluate the Chinese adaptation of Marxism, and drawing on it for theoretical resources. He also calls for taking Chinese results abroad, giving foreign Marxism a fuller place in the history of Marxism, abandoning an attitude of "only we are Marxist", and training scholars versed in both domestic and foreign Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's broad map of post-2007 foreign Marxism and of how it is meant to inform Chinese Marxist theory.
quoteEn: Contemporary foreign Marxist currents are not a simple revival of traditional Marxist theory but have achieved an innovation upon it.
quoteZh: 当代国外马克思主义思潮不是对传统的马克思主义理论的简单的复兴, 而是在实现了对传统的马克思主义理论的创新。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism to Chinese conditions and developing it in light of current realities. In this 2017 article the shorter form "Sinicisation of Marxism" is used.

Strictly, the tradition begun by Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in Western Europe, which stresses subjectivity, class consciousness and culture. Chen uses the label loosely for contemporary foreign Marxism.

A current associated with Laclau and Mouffe's Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985). Chen describes it as keeping Marxism's critique of capitalism while abandoning its starting point in the mode of production.
A theoretical orientation that treats market and plan as tools separate from social systems. It combines market regulation with public ownership.

t: Crisis and reconstruction: a study of contemporary Marxist currents outside China
zh: 危机与重建：当代国外马克思主义思潮研究
paras: Huang asks how the left has responded to the crisis that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in the early 1990s, and what chances and obstacles face a rebuilding and revival of Marxism. The article argues that the upheaval was the product of a crisis of left movements dating from the 1960s and 1970s, not an accident. In Huang's account, the left has responded with new organisational forms, a renewed defence of the commons and a broadened Marxism that takes in culture and identity.

The article has three parts. The first looks at social movements and the challenges facing the left, drawing on Luciano Magri, Giovanni Arrighi, Naomi Klein, Michael Hardt and Rossana Rossanda. The second turns to identity politics and cultural identity, drawing on Stuart Hall, Eric Hobsbawm and Judith Butler. The third takes the Italian new left as a case study of how to analyse contemporary capitalism and renew the Marxist tradition.

Huang reports the dispute over whether attention to culture abandons Marxist political economy. Butler, as Huang presents her, argues that the opposition between the material and the cultural is a selective construction. Marx saw the economic and the cultural as historical products of the division of labour, and new movements keep the left's universalism in particular struggles because neoliberal capitalism itself works through particularity. Huang adds that immaterial labour and biopolitics show the material–cultural divide dissolving, and that Marxist reconstruction should start from there. The Italian case, in Huang's reading, shows the Italian Communist Party falling behind the workers' movement. The Il manifesto group and operaismo (workerism) developed outside it, with operaismo reinterpreting Marx's 1857–58 manuscripts and moving toward post-workerism under Antonio Negri.

Huang concludes that Italian new left thought of the 1960s and 1970s, praised by Hall and Hobsbawm as the European frontier of Marxism, has been little studied in China. Chinese work has focused on Gramsci and on recent radical thinkers such as Agamben and Negri. Huang holds that studying it would clarify Marxism's present crisis and its reconstruction. It would also give the Communist Party of China lessons on developing its own theory and avoiding deviations under rapid economic growth. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of how Western left currents, from anti-globalisation movements to Italian workerism, are read in Chinese debates on Marxist renewal.
quoteEn: The reconstruction of Marxism should start from this vantage point, reconsidering the problems of the material and the cultural in contemporary capitalist society, offering new readings of phenomena such as immaterial labour and biopolitics, and carrying forward the critical tradition of Marxism.
quoteZh: 马克思主义的重建应当从这一高度出发, 重新认识当代资本主义社会中的物质与文化问题, 对非物质劳动、生命政治等现象做出新的解读, 继承和发扬马克思主义的批判传统。

t: The German–French dispute between historicism and structuralism in the 1960s and 1970s
st: An intellectual contest based on readings of Capital
zh: 20世纪六七十年代德法历史主义与结构主义之争
zhSub: 一场基于《资本论》阅读的思想争锋
paras: Li Qiankun examines the clash between two Western Marxist ways of reading Marx's Capital in the 1960s and 1970s: a historicist model centred on the second generation of the Frankfurt School, and a structuralist model led by Louis Althusser and his school. Both returned to Capital and the manuscripts but reached different methods and conclusions. Li argues that the dispute ultimately turns on the problem of subjectivity and objectivity in Marxist philosophy, and that each side grasped part of Marx's text.

The article is built around three episodes. It begins with the 1967 Frankfurt conference marking a century of Capital, where Nicos Poulantzas confronted Iring Fetscher, Alfred Schmidt and Ernest Mandel. It then turns to Althusser's critique of historicism in Reading Capital (1965), aimed especially at Gramsci, Lukács and Sartre. It next takes up Schmidt's reply in History and Structure (1971), a book Li says has received little attention in Chinese scholarship. A short conclusion places the dispute within wider debates.

In Li's account, Poulantzas and Althusser held that historicism and humanism rest on a central subject and a Hegelian expressive totality, and that the mature Marx broke with this in an anti-humanist, anti-historicist, "subjectless" science. Schmidt, Mandel and Fetscher replied that the structuralists removed the historical dimension from Marx's analysis, and that Marx openly used Hegel's dialectic from the Grundrisse to Capital. Schmidt argued that Capital combines logical and historical methods, moving from the abstract to the concrete, and that Althusser himself fell into a speculative idealism of a timeless structure. Li also notes Schmidt's defence of Gramsci and observes that Schmidt's generation reconnected with the Hegelian Marxism of Lukács and Korsch, against Adorno and Horkheimer.

Li concludes that the structuralist critique had some force, since the 1968 May events showed the weakness of a subject-centred totality. He judges, however, that the German scholars grasped Marx's texts more fully, while structuralism overstated transcendent structure and drifted into a metaphysical postulate. He adds that the "New Reading of Marx" which began in 1965 absorbed both: it avoided humanist readings, used the historicist method in studying the value form, and in places converged with or went beyond Althusser on ideological forms. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the 1967 Frankfurt debate and of Schmidt's little-studied reply to Althusser, as background to philosophical readings of Capital.
quoteEn: At root, the dispute between historicism and structuralism concerns the problem we can never get around: subjectivity and objectivity in the system of Marxist philosophy.
quoteZh: 历史主义和结构主义之争,在根子上还是涉及那个我们总也绕不过去的问题,即马克思主义哲学体系中的主体性和客体性问题。

t: Contemporary Western Marxist theories of class formation
zh: 当代西方马克思主义的阶级形成理论
paras: Hai Bo asks how classes come to exist in social life, rather than only why they arise from economic relations. The article argues that Marxist research has mostly analysed class statically, through positions in production relations, and has paid little systematic attention to class formation as a dynamic process that extends beyond the economy. Hai's thesis is that, in contemporary Western Marxist accounts, class formation rests on the interaction of class consciousness, class struggle and political culture.

The article is a history-of-ideas survey in three sections, one for each of these elements. It draws on Marx's distinction between a class in itself and a class for itself and on Georg Lukács's History and Class Consciousness. It also covers E. P. Thompson, Pierre Bourdieu, Erik Olin Wright, Adam Przeworski, Antonio Gramsci and G. A. Cohen. It adds the Korean scholar Koo Hagen on workers' experience, and the Chinese historian Gao Yi on the political culture of the French Revolution.

In Hai's reading, Lukács treats proletarian class consciousness as the goal and weapon of the class itself, because it unites theory and practice. Thompson sees class as an event that happens through shared experience and struggle, so consciousness is a cultural response and not a direct product of production relations. Bourdieu and Wright extend this view. For Bourdieu, class boundaries are objects of symbolic struggle and mobilisation by spokespeople. For Wright, class structure limits, selects and is in turn altered by class struggle. Hai then turns to political culture. Gramsci's cultural hegemony and Thompson's inherited traditions are read as sources of unity from below. Koo's Korean workers are shown to have formed their identity under combined pressure from bourgeois culture and political power.

Hai concludes that class formation is open-ended and that classes are always forming and dissolving. Economic, political and cultural factors interact, and the three core elements permeate and transform one another. Class structure is a static, theoretical construct, while class formation is a practical process. Hai calls for class research to ask both what forms classes and how they are formed, and so to advance the Marxist cause of proletarian and human liberation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how Lukács, Thompson, Wright and others handle the subjective side of class.
quoteEn: Class formation is the result of the interaction of multiple economic, political and cultural factors.
quoteZh: 阶级形成是经济、政治和文化多重因素交互作用的结果。

t: The basic landscape of world Marxism in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪世界马克思主义基本格局
source: Study and Exploration (Xuexi yu tansuo), 2017 no. 10
paras: Wang Fengcai takes up the question of how to map "twenty-first-century world Marxism", which the article defines as foreign Marxism together with Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. Wang observes that Marxism revived after a brief silence following the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and that a "Marx fever" has appeared worldwide. The thesis is that, although many studies exist on particular countries, schools and thinkers, no overall, systematic study of this field has yet appeared, and that the field can be organised into five interpretive paths.

The article is built in four parts. It first surveys the state of research by region (continental Europe, the English-speaking world, the former Soviet bloc, and Asia, Africa and Latin America), listing institutions, journals, forums and key books, and then Chinese scholarship. It then sets out the five paths, followed by research objects and ten "hot topics", from the MEGA edition and Capital to class theory, neoliberalism, new imperialism, actually existing socialism and the new communism. It ends with research orientations, key difficulties and the significance of the field.

The core move is the typology of five interpretive paths: foreign Marxology, orthodox Marxism, Western Marxism, East European neo-Marxism, and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. Wang defines Western Marxism narrowly, as a non-orthodox current born and developed in the West, which excludes Marxology, orthodoxy, East European neo-Marxism and Western communist parties' theory but includes post-Marxism. Using Western Marxism as the reference point, Wang contrasts each path along three axes: scholarly rigour, intellectual depth and practical relevance. Marxology leans towards scholarship, orthodoxy towards ideology, East European neo-Marxism towards practice, and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context is called the most vital and practically oriented path. Wang also sorts scholars into four orientations, labelled the "lonely" Marxologists, the "isolated" orthodox, the "active" innovators and the "carefree" reconstructors.

Wang concludes that the central task is to unify scholarship, ideology and real-world concern, and to move from a "singular, unreflective Marxism" to a "plural, innovative Marxism". The author lists difficulties, including the absence of a unified conception of Marxism, the breadth of the field and the language demands. Wang argues that such research would help Marxism develop in the Chinese context, maintain its guiding position in Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and build a Chinese academic discourse. Read the original if you want a detailed bibliographic map of Marxist research worldwide around 2017, seen from a Chinese academic viewpoint, together with a typology of schools.
quoteEn: How can Marxist research unify scholarly rigour, intellectual depth and practical relevance? This is the core question of twenty-first-century world Marxism studies.
quoteZh: 如何实现马克思主义研究之学术性、思想性、现实性的统一?这是21世纪世界马克思主义研究的核心问题。

glossary.en: Marxism adapted to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The phrase goes back to Mao Zedong's 1938 report to the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee. It refers to combining Marxism's basic principles with China's revolution, construction, reform, history and culture.

A research tradition devoted to Marx's life, texts, editions and intellectual development, and to the differences among Marxist schools. Wang describes it as interdisciplinary, non-ideological and purely scholarly.
In Wang's usage, the line from Engels and the Second International through Lenin and the Third International to the Soviet-bloc textbook system, plus present-day orthodox currents.

Here a non-orthodox Marxism that arose and developed in the West, from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci to the Frankfurt School and post-Marxism. Wang's definition excludes Western communist parties' theory.

A humanist, non-orthodox Marxism that arose in post-war Eastern Europe, represented by the Yugoslav Praxis group and the Budapest School. It built a critique of actually existing socialism on alienation theory.
A term for the Soviet-model socialism that existed in the USSR and Eastern Europe, as distinct from socialism as an ideal.

keywords: Marxism adapted to the Chinese context

t: Five assessments by foreign left-wing scholars of the crisis of contemporary capitalism
zh: 国外左翼学者关于当代资本主义危机的五种评判
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Tong Jin surveys how foreign left-wing scholars have analysed the capitalist crisis that began in the early twenty-first century. The article groups their work into five assessments: the crisis is one of the mode of production, of democracy, of values, of ecology and of the capitalist system as a whole. Tong stresses that these are different readings of one crisis and overlap with each other.

The review moves through the five headings in turn, drawing on a range of Western and other foreign thinkers. They include David Harvey, Paul Jorion and Mary Wrenn on production; Noam Chomsky and Joseph Stiglitz on democracy; Harvey and Stiglitz again on values; John Bellamy Foster, Andrew Jones and Richard Smith on ecology; and Immanuel Wallerstein, Wolfgang Streeck, Michael Koyama and Samir Amin on systemic crisis.

As Tong presents them, these scholars locate the roots of crisis in the contradiction between socialised production and private capitalist appropriation, which is sharpened by globalisation and by Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession'. They describe Western democracy as rule by a wealthy minority, with money outweighing votes, and the ideals of freedom and equality as a myth. Ecological destruction is said to follow from capital's profit-seeking, so that 'green capitalism' cannot work. In the final category, Tong reports that Wallerstein, Streeck and Amin see capitalism's remedies as exhausted and its structure heading towards breakdown.

Tong judges the left's critique thorough and deep, but also flawed. Some scholars, in Tong's view, treat the crisis as capitalism's turning point and so overlook its capacity for self-regulation. Others replace critique of the relations of production with critique of the damage done to nature, and put the contradiction between humans and nature in place of that between people. Tong calls for critical absorption, borrowing the insights while recognising the limits of the scholars' standpoint, method and understanding. Read the original if you want a compact map of the main foreign left critiques of post-2008 capitalism, together with a Chinese academic's assessment of their strengths and weaknesses.
quoteEn: Without criticising capitalist relations of production and attending to the contradictions between people, it is fundamentally impossible to find a way to resolve the crisis.
quoteZh: 脱离对资本主义生产关系的批判以及人与人的矛盾的关注，是根本不可能找到化解危机的途径的。

t: Growing positive assessments of the Communist Party of China among American scholars in recent years
zh: 近年来美国学者对中国共产党的肯定性评价越来越多
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Xue Nianwen and Sun Jian argue that American scholarship on the Communist Party of China (CPC) is the most advanced in the West and that, in recent years, US China specialists have paid it more attention and judged it more favourably. The authors present this as a general trend rather than a unanimous view.

The article is organised in three parts, each reviewing English-language work by US-based scholars: assessments of CPC leaders, assessments of Party building, and expectations for the Party's future. It draws on books and journal articles, including studies of Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping by Arif Dirlik, Ezra Vogel, Xiong Jie (Lawrence Xiong) and others, and on articles in The China Quarterly and similar journals.

In the first part, Xue and Sun report that American scholars praise the leaders' sense of responsibility to country and people: Roderick MacFarquhar on Mao's and Deng's paths, Vogel on Deng's pragmatism, and Zhao Suisheng on Xi's refusal to split the People's Republic's history into Mao and post-Mao eras. They also report approval of collective wisdom, the leaders' grassroots experience, and the Party's handling of Tibet and Xinjiang. In the second part, they cite Bruce Dickson on Party recruitment, Zeng Qinghe (Jeremy Zeng) on wider Party member participation in cadre selection, and John Naisbitt on bottom-up participation. The authors read these works as endorsing tighter entry standards, the anti-corruption campaign and intra-Party democracy. The third part covers mostly optimistic forecasts, such as Romi Jain's on environmental governance and Wang Huiyao's on attracting overseas talent. Xue and Sun say that hostile writing driven by arrogance and prejudice is now a minority.

The authors conclude that US scholars have studied the leaders, Party building and prospects in depth and have endorsed the Party's efforts at self-improvement, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and grassroots-rooted leadership under Xi Jinping. They say most American scholars are optimistic that the Party will lead China into a new stage. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic reading of how US China scholarship on the CPC is presented to a domestic audience, along with a bibliography of the English-language sources it cites.
quoteEn: American scholars' attention to the CPC's theory and practice of strengthening its own construction can be said to have grasped the core of China's reform and development.
quoteZh: 美国学者关注中国共产党加强自身建设的相关理论与实践，可以说是抓住了中国改革和发展的核心。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012) covering discipline, anti-corruption and Party-building measures under Xi Jinping.
The practice of broadening member participation in discussion, selection and decision-making within the Party, which official discourse treats as a basis for wider democracy.

t: How to view the past, present and future of socialism
st: An interview with Professor David Kotz of the University of Massachusetts Amherst
zh: 如何看待社会主义的过去、现在与未来
zhSub: 访美国麻省州立大学阿姆赫斯特分校经济学院大卫·科茨教授
paras: Published in Theoretical Horizon in 2017, this is an interview conducted by Tian Xi (School of Marxism, Peking University) with the US economist David Kotz, a specialist on the Soviet Union, in the centenary year of the October Revolution. Kotz, who began studying Soviet political economy in 1989 and co-authored two books on the end of the Soviet system with Fred Weir, is asked how socialism's past, present and future should be understood.

The interview has three parts. The first concerns the October Revolution: its conditions, whether it fitted Marx's expectations, socialism in one country, the Kaftin (Caudine) Forks question and the Stalin model. The second addresses the Soviet collapse, including five common explanations and the contrast with China. The third turns to the rise and decline of neoliberalism, the 2008 financial crisis, Trump and the prospects for socialism in the West.

Kotz argues that the Soviet Union did not collapse because of economic crisis, which he says was no worse than the US Great Depression. In his account, a large part of the top leadership turned against socialism between 1989 and 1991 because it wanted to expand its privileges, and ideology followed material interest. He rejects five other explanations: the sudden end of planning, a popular vote against socialism, Western subversion, the arms race and ethnic nationalism. He cites poll data showing that 80–85 per cent of citizens wanted to keep the USSR. He holds that China avoided the Soviet fate because Deng Xiaoping introduced markets and private ownership gradually, rather than following Milton Friedman's advice of immediate privatisation.

Kotz concludes that the Soviet system's fatal flaw was that ordinary workers held no real political power, and that lasting socialism requires its beneficiaries to hold such power. He says markets and private ownership can play a positive role for a time but eventually breed capitalists and inequality, so they must be turned into public ownership and planning. As an alternative to Soviet-style central planning he proposes a democratic, participatory planned economy. He also says neoliberalism has failed and that the world faces a choice among right-wing nationalism, social democratic capitalism and democratic socialism. Read the original if you want a US Marxist economist's view of the Soviet collapse, Chinese reform and the prospects for socialism after 2008.
quoteEn: In my view, if a long-term stable socialism is to be established, the beneficiaries of socialism must be given political power.
quoteZh: 在我看来, 如果要想建立起长期稳定的社会主义, 那么必须让社会主义的受益者获得政治权力。

t: The situation of Marxist philosophy in twenty-first-century Russia
zh: 21世纪俄罗斯马克思主义哲学的境遇
paras: How does Marxist philosophy fare in Russia after the Soviet collapse? Writing in 2017, Zheng describes a pluralised Russian philosophy in which Marxism is studied as one school among equals. The article argues that this is no true thaw: after the 'heat' of the late-1980s and early-1990s wave of criticism and the 'cold' of neglect in the mid-1990s, Marxist philosophy in the twenty-first century is in a 'chilly spring' that combines marginalisation, renewed attention and renewed reflection.

The article is organised in three parts that correspond to these three conditions. The first traces marginalisation from the early 1990s to the 2000s, including the post-Soviet 'denial', 'non-Marxist' and 'critical' camps. The second surveys renewed attention through conferences (2005–2011), publications, university teaching and research bodies. The third examines reflection on Marxism itself and on related questions: revisionism, the October Revolution, the Soviet collapse and socialist theory and practice.

On marginalisation, Zheng argues that the three dominant camps, which treat Marxism as a source of disaster, interpret Marx at a distance, or absorb him into Western humanism, keep it at the edge of both official and popular life. On renewed attention, the author cites growing numbers of conferences, reissued Second International and 1920s Russian Marxist works, surviving Soviet-trained teachers and Marxist centres, though these are staffed mainly by older scholars. On reflection, Zheng reports debates over what 'genuine Marxism' is, Teodor Oizerman's defence of revisionism and Bernstein, and rival readings of 1917 and of the Soviet collapse that draw on newly opened archives.

Zheng concludes that Russia's search for a path different from both the Western and Soviet models leaves no room for a fundamental change of attitude to Marxism, so marginalisation continues. Yet the reflection shows undiminished interest in Marxism, a calmer and more objective assessment of it, and a more practical need for it. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's survey of post-Soviet Russian debates on Marxism, with names of figures, conferences, journals and book titles to follow up.
quoteEn: The situation of Marxist philosophy in twenty-first-century Russia also includes a renewed reflection on Marxism and its philosophy, existing alongside 'marginalisation' and 'renewed attention'.
quoteZh: 21世纪的俄罗斯马克思主义哲学的境遇，还有与“边缘化”以及“重新关注”同时并存的对马克思主义及其哲学的重新反思。

t: Western communist parties' views and initiatives on the centenary of the October Revolution
zh: 西方国家共产党关于纪念十月革命100周年的观点与倡议
paras: Writing in 2017, Tong Jin asks how communist parties in Western countries have used the centenary of the October Revolution to state their positions. The article reports that these parties and other left-wing forces treated the anniversary as an occasion to restate the revolution's historical significance, rebut distortions of it and link its experience to present struggles against capitalism. Tong's overall finding is that the parties read the revolution as proof that socialism remains necessary now and in the future.

The article is a survey of speeches, reports and website articles from the parties of Portugal, Greece, Australia (Marxist-Leninist), Britain, Germany, Spain and France. It is organised in five parts: commitment to socialism; restoring the 'truth' about twentieth-century socialism; the working class as the force behind the revolution; applying the revolution's experience to national conditions; and plans for commemorative activities.

In Tong's account, the Portuguese, Greek and Australian parties hold that the Soviet collapse was temporary and that the twenty-first century will bring a decisive contest between capitalism and socialism. The Greek party rejects the claim that the revolution caused the collapse, arguing instead that the Soviet Union weakened the revolution's gains by adopting capitalist remedies. The Portuguese party argues that rulers keep rewriting history and present a distorted 'model' as inherent to Marxism-Leninism. Tong also reports that these parties see the revolution as showing the working class's capacity to fulfil its historical mission. The Greek party stresses assessing class forces objectively, and the Spanish party's general secretary calls for combining the revolution's lessons with present conditions. The article adds that the Greek, Australian and French parties apply this to current politics: daily struggles, independence from US policy towards China, and election campaigns focused on social questions.

Tong describes the planned commemorations. The Portuguese party scheduled events through 2017, including a seminar, exhibitions and a website. The British party tied the anniversary to the 150th anniversary of Capital, and the Morning Star helped set up the Russian Revolution Centenary Committee. Tong concludes that a correct view of the revolution is necessary for the past, present and future, and that its significance cannot be slandered or replaced. Read the original if you want a documented overview of how European and Australian communist parties framed the 1917 centenary, with many quotations from their statements.
quoteEn: It can be said with certainty that a correct view of the October Revolution is necessary for the past, the present and the future.
quoteZh: 可以肯定地说, 正确审视十月革命, 对过去、现在和将来都是必要的

t: Commemorating the 100th anniversary of the October Revolution: Austro-Marxism's political theory and Lenin's critique
st: Reformism, the "middle way" and "defensive violence" in Renner, Hilferding, Bauer and Max Adler
zh: 纪念十月革命胜利100周年
zhSub: 纪念十月革命胜利100周年
source: Journal of Anhui University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2017 no. 5
paras: Published in 2017 to mark the centenary of the October Revolution, this article asks how Austro-Marxist political theory responded to the Bolshevik seizure of power and to parliamentary democracy in Germany and Austria. Its thesis is that Austro-Marxism, from right to left, was eclectic and reformist. The authors conclude that its "middle way" cannot hold within the Marxist framework and that Austro-Marxism was therefore a non-Marxist theory and practice.

The article sorts the school into three camps after 1917. It treats Karl Renner as centre-right, with his view of the state as a supra-class servant of the workers. It treats Rudolf Hilferding as the centrist, with his ambivalent view of parliament and the general strike. It treats Otto Bauer and Max Adler as centre-left, with Bauer's theories of "social power factors" and "defensive violence". It then sets these positions against Lenin's State and Revolution and his criticism of Bauer at the Second Comintern Congress. It ends with the defeat of the Austrian Social Democrats in February 1934.

The authors argue that Renner's state theory ignored the class essence of the modern state and imagined that the bourgeoisie would allow a peaceful parliamentary route to power. Hilferding, they say, tried to balance Kautsky, Bernstein and revisionism and so treated the strike as a merely defensive weapon. Bauer held that democracy is a neutral form whose content depends on the balance of social forces, and that violence is justified only when the bourgeoisie destroys democracy. The article credits this with some Marxist value, and notes that Marx and Engels allowed for peaceful routes after the 1870s. It follows Lenin in holding that the real issue is the class character of democracy, not peaceful versus violent means. In its account, "defensive violence" leaves the proletariat passive, because it cannot choose the moment or secure the arms. The article presents the fascist crushing of the German and Austrian parties in the 1930s as proof of this.

The article concludes that the Linz Programme (1926) already treated dictatorship as a last resort, and that Renner, Bauer and Adler valued democracy above revolution and so lost sight of the essentials of communism. In its verdict, the "middle way" disarmed the workers ideologically, divided the revolutionary camp and in effect protected capitalism. Austro-Marxism neither transcended the old philosophy nor built a new socialist model. Read the original if you study Austro-Marxism or the Second International debates on democracy, dictatorship and violence, or want to see how Chinese scholars assessed them from a Leninist standpoint in 2017.
quoteEn: Austro-Marxism was, in the end, a non-Marxist theoretical system and political practice.
quoteZh: 奥地利马克思主义终究是非马克思主义的理论体系和政治实践

t: Marxism, political economy and sustainable human development
zh: 马克思主义、政治经济学和人类可持续发展
source: Journal of Nanjing Tech University (Social Science Edition), 2017 no. 3
paras: This text is a Chinese translation of an article by Paul Burkett, an economist at Indiana State University. It asks what Marxism can add to the idea of sustainable development as it is discussed within ecological economics. Burkett argues that ecological economics has three dimensions of sustainability that are poorly integrated with one another, and that Marx and Engels's picture of communism integrates them.

The first part sets out the three dimensions. They are nature as a common resource for present and future generations, the co-evolution of individuals, society and nature, and the need for common property in natural resources. Burkett reviews co-evolutionary theorists such as Mulder, Van den Bergh and Norgaard, and common-property researchers such as Hardin's critics, Ostrom, Swaney and Adger. The second part turns to Marx and Engels on post-capitalist society: non-alienation, common property, non-market allocation, land stewardship, free time and the transition to communism.

Burkett contends that the co-evolutionary school stresses changing human values and the 'good life' but neglects social relations of production, class and the market. The common-property school defends commons mainly as a limit on resource use and treats failures as caused by outside forces such as markets and colonialism. In Burkett's reading, those outside forces work through class relations, and the school underplays class inequality inside the commons. For Marx and Engels, communism overcomes the separation of producers from the conditions of production. In Burkett's account it treats land as the permanent common property of successive generations and gives everyone a share in consumption and social services. It also reduces working time, which Burkett says eases pressure on nature and allows scientific and aesthetic self-development.

Burkett concludes that Marx and Engels combine the three dimensions of sustainability, and that they left the future open rather than drawing up a blueprint. A fixed blueprint, he says, would contradict the principle that the emancipation of the working class must be the act of the working class itself. He treats the transition as a long, path-dependent struggle. He holds that the classical Marxist view of communism as the sublation of alienated production and the realisation of all-round human development still deserves attention. Read the original if you work on Marxist ecology or ecological economics and want a critique of co-evolutionary and common-property theories from a class-based Marxist position.
quoteEn: Like ecological economics, co-evolutionary theory cannot explain the shortcomings of market valuation, the anti-ecological character of capitalism, or the social differentiation of direct producers under the necessary conditions of production.
quoteZh: 协同进化理论和生态经济学一样, 无法解释市场评估的缺点、资本主义的反生态特征和必要生产条件下直接生产者的社会分化。

t: Critique and politics under parallax
st: An interpretation and critique of Karatani Kojin's alternative logic of resistance
zh: 视差之下的批判与政治
zhSub: 对柄谷行人另类反抗逻辑的解释与批评
paras: Kojin Karatani has become a focus of attention in Chinese academia, and Slavoj Žižek has compared his Transcritique to Roberto Unger's Politics trilogy. Wang asks what Karatani's reinterpretation of Kant and Marx offers as an alternative logic of resistance to global capitalism, and whether it holds up. The article's answer is that the theory is attractive to the radical left but flawed: it misreads the relations among Kant, Hegel and Marx, treats Capital in a formalised way, and romanticises resistance politics.

Writing in 2017, Wang applies Karatani's own method of parallax, offering a sympathetic reconstruction followed by criticism. Part one sets out Karatani's Kantian turn and his contrast between Kant and Hegel. Part two covers his exchange-based reading of Capital and his politics of consumer resistance. Part three gives Wang's critique, drawing on Lukács, Žižek, Antonio Negri, and Boltanski and Chiapello.

In Wang's account, Karatani treats Kant's parallax as the foundation of any transcendent critique. He casts Hegel as the thinker who dissolves parallax and treats the capital–nation–state as final, and he places Marx in a line from Kant. Karatani replaces the mode-of-production approach with a theory of four modes of exchange. He argues that surplus value arises chiefly from differences between value systems in circulation, and that the worker, as money-holder at the C–M′ stage, becomes a subject. From this he derives a strategy of buying and selling boycotts and global producer-consumer cooperatives, in place of labour struggle.

Wang objects on several grounds. Hegel too recognised modernity's divisions, so parallax does not separate him from Kant. Karatani confuses surplus-value realisation with its production. His claim that production is local and consumption global fails in an era of global supply chains. Consumer movements can be absorbed by capital, as Boltanski and Chiapello argue. Wang concludes that without changing the mode of production and power structure, non-capitalist enclaves would remain islands, even an aesthetic ornament of capitalism. Read the original if you follow Karatani's reception in China, or want a Marxist critique of consumer-based resistance and of the Kant–Hegel–Marx relationship.
quoteEn: Without changing the capitalist mode of production and its power structure, any attempt to build a non-capitalised space of production and circulation outside capital can at most create an island in the ocean of the capitalist economy.
quoteZh: 不改变资本主义的生产方式和权力结构本身, 试图在资本之外建立一个非资本化的生产和流通空间, 最多只是在资本主义经济的汪洋大海中建立一个孤岛

t: Where is postmodern politics heading?
st: An analysis of Ellen Meiksins Wood's critique of the postmodern left
zh: 后现代政治路在何方?
zhSub: 埃伦·伍德后现代左翼思潮批判论析
paras: Postmodern political thought was fashionable among the Western left in the last three decades of the twentieth century. Because its political programme bears directly on the goals and strategy of left movements, the Marxist scholar Ellen Meiksins Wood took it very seriously. Jiang Jiqing's article reconstructs and assesses her critique, arguing that Wood exposed the postmodern left's confusions, its underlying character and its harmful effects, while also showing some weaknesses of her own.

The article has three parts. The first sets out five features of the postmodern left's politics as Jiang presents them. The second reviews Wood's critique at three levels: the views, the essence and the harm of postmodern thought. The third analyses the strengths and shortcomings of that critique and draws lessons for Marxist theorists.

In Jiang's account, the postmodern left rejects anti-capitalist "grand narratives" and universal emancipation. It replaces material and class relations with language and culture, dismisses class politics because the working class is said to have been integrated into capitalism, turns to plural new social movements, and treats Marxism as either oppressive or obsolete. Wood answers that these positions are logically incoherent. For example, they reject universal values yet rely on them to defend pluralism, and they exaggerate real changes in capitalism into a fundamental break. She traces the outlook to the post-war "golden age", when defeated left intellectuals retreated into a mood of resignation. In her view, denying that capitalism is a totality amounts to submitting to it, and giving autonomy to discourse and culture places "revolution" in the hands of intellectuals. Wood concludes that postmodernism has become a disease rather than a diagnosis of one.

Jiang praises Wood's political alertness, her incisive treatment of the links between Enlightenment, modernity and capitalism, and a method that moves from views to essence to harm and still concedes some real changes. Jiang also names three flaws: weak analysis of why postmodernism arose, sometimes excessive sharpness that could hinder left unity, and generalisation across different thinkers. The lesson drawn is that Marxist theorists must stay alert to tendencies that depart from Marxism in its name, show courage when socialism meets setbacks, and connect classical Marxist positions to present realities. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Wood's critique of postmodernism and of how Chinese scholars assess her argument.
quoteEn: Wood's critique of the postmodern left also offers us many valuable lessons.
quoteZh: 伍德对后现代左翼思潮的批判也给我们诸多可贵启示。

t: Alain Badiou on subjectivization and the subjective process
zh: 阿兰·巴迪欧论主体化和主体进程
source: Journal of Hubei University (Philosophy and Social Science Edition), 2017 no. 4
paras: This article examines two paired concepts in Alain Badiou's Theory of the Subject (1982): subjectivization (主体化) and the subjective process (主体进程). Ai Shiwei notes that Badiou, described as a leading figure of post-Marxism, borrowed both terms from Lacan, and that apart from Ed Pluth's study little work has treated them in detail. Ai argues that Badiou's subject is a split one, built from a brief, destructive moment and a lasting, reorganising one, and that this structure underpins his later "third" model of the subject.

The article opens with Badiou's criticism of the idealist and materialist paradigms of the subject, which he links respectively to religious "sacrifice" and worldly "enjoyment". It then treats subjectivization, then the subjective process, then their combination in what Badiou calls the "torsade" (twisting together). It applies the scheme to the Cultural Revolution and to the French class struggle, and ends by tracing how Badiou's thinking on the subject shifted in Conditions and Being and Event.

Ai explains that subjectivization is brief, destructive and interventionist. It takes two forms: "anxiety", pure destruction that points toward death, and "courage", which breaks the existing order in the hope of building a new one. The subjective process is lasting and reorganising, and holds fidelity to the event. It too takes two forms: the "superego", a terrorising process that assigns every excess element a fixed place, and "justice", which relativises law and blurs fixed positions. Their pairings give two trajectories, a Ψ mode (anxiety to superego) and an α mode (courage to justice). Badiou reads Red Guards as α-type if they pursue the communist project, and as Ψ-type if they only defend absolute authority. Ai adds that the diagonal pairings, drawn from Lacan's "imaginary", yield a dogmatic function (courage–superego) and a sceptical function (justice–anxiety). Ai describes the first as reification that turns rebels into parts of a system, and the second as ending in nothingness.

Ai concludes that the subject is neither reducible to the body nor separable from it, but is joined to it as a "subjectivized body". Ai also notes that Badiou later widened the subject beyond politics to science, art and love, and that he criticised his earlier text for simply presupposing that subjectivization exists. Ai reads this as Badiou going beyond pure deconstruction to ask how a subject can form and be rebuilt. Read the original if you work on Badiou, Lacan or post-Marxist theories of the subject and want a systematic account of these two concepts.
quoteEn: Subjectivization and the subjective process are key concepts that Badiou put forward in Theory of the Subject, a work published in 1982 that belongs to his early period.
quoteZh: 主体化与主体进程是巴迪欧在《主体理论》中所提出的关键概念, 该书出版于1982年, 属于其早期作品。

t: The development of the Iraqi left and the Chinese experience as the Iraqi left sees it
zh: 伊拉克左翼的发展及其眼中的中国经验
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2017 no. 1
paras: The author, identified as a member of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the Iraqi Communist Party, gives an insider account of the Iraqi left and of how it views China. The name is given in Chinese as Basam Muxi, and the Latin spelling here is a reconstruction. The article, published in 2017 and translated into Chinese, argues that the left must unite around democracy, social justice and a collectively owned economy to meet Iraq's multiple crises. It also presents China's reform experience as a successful model of "socialist market economy".

The text has four parts. It first traces the left's emergence in the early twentieth century, the founding of the Iraqi Communist Party in 1934, its repression, and the post-2003 situation under US occupation. It then sets out the challenges and tasks facing the left, and discusses the left's alliance and its relation to socialism. The final section is a short assessment of the Chinese experience since reform and opening up.

On Iraq, Muhsin describes a country in structural crisis: corruption, sectarian politics, foreign interference, the advance of the Islamic State, and the mass protests of 2011 and 2015. He names three challenges: building a civil democratic state, countering political Islam and religious fundamentalism, and resisting capitalist globalisation. The left's answer is a national democratic programme and a broad, pluralist alliance of left and democratic forces, working with unions and civil society. Muhsin holds that socialism rests on political democracy, social justice and collective ownership of the means of production, and that class struggle cannot be set aside. He adds that the working class has changed and now allies with new social movements.

In the China section, Muhsin credits Deng Xiaoping's 1978 reforms and the "socialist market economy" under Communist Party leadership with producing stability and rapid growth. He claims that this system, resting on public ownership with several forms of ownership coexisting, has gone beyond the limits of capitalist development and serves social justice.
